## Albert Einstein
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/einstein/
Tags: Learning and growth, The industrial age, Imagination

Albert Einstein (Germany · 1879–1955) — Imagination. The physicist, and the father of relativity — but the legacy that travels furthest is not a formula, it is a way of working.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The physicist, and the father of relativity — but the legacy that travels furthest is not a formula, it is a way of working. What would I see if I rode alongside a beam of light? He first asked it at sixteen and carried it for ten years. He showed that an experiment impossible in any laboratory can be run in a head, and moved imagination out of the arts and into the centre of science.

### Q: What actually happened?
On 6 November 1919 the Royal Society heard the results of the eclipse expeditions: starlight had bent as general relativity predicted. The next morning he was famous everywhere, which is not a thing that had happened to a physicist before. He was dry about it. If the theory turns out to be right, he wrote, Germany will claim me as a German and France will call me a citizen of the world; if it turns out wrong, France will call me a German and Germany will call me a Jew. The theory had not changed between the two sentences. Only the audience had.

### The parts · The thought experiment
His central instrument was not mathematics but the Gedankenexperiment: build an idealised situation in your head and follow its logic until it breaks. Special relativity came from riding the beam of light; general relativity from a man in a falling lift, who cannot feel his own weight — an idea he later called the happiest of his life. e.g. Before building the thing, describe the impossible version of it and see which assumption has to give. That assumption is the actual project.

### The parts · Thirty years of being wrong, in public
He spent his last three decades trying to unify relativity with quantum mechanics and did not get there. He would not accept the probabilistic reading and said so — God does not play dice. Experiment has sided against him ever since. But the objection forced the field to say precisely what it meant, and a first-rate error did more than most careful agreement. e.g. The colleague who will not let a claim past without making it exact is doing work even when their own position is the one that loses.

### The parts · Curiosity is the whole engine
No special talent, only passionately curious — he said it too often for it to be modesty. He held the question about the beam of light for ten years because he wanted to know, not because anyone asked. Learning driven by curiosity and learning driven by obligation reach different depths, because only one of them keeps going past the requirement. e.g. You can tell which kind you are on by what happens the week after the deadline.

### The parts · Responsibility does not end at the discovery
A Jew and a pacifist, driven out after 1933, he signed the 1939 letter urging the United States to take fission seriously — and after Hiroshima spent the rest of his life on disarmament, calling that signature his one great mistake. Pushing the boundary and carrying what comes over it are the same job. e.g. Whoever builds the capability is not automatically the person who decides how it is used — but they are never simply a bystander to it either.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Next time something is declared impossible, run his order of operations: first ask whether physics forbids it; then build the idealised version in your head and follow it through. A great many impossible things turn out to be current tools cannot, which is a different sentence with a different expiry date.

### Lines to keep
Imagination is more important than knowledge. I have no special talent. I am only passionately curious. God does not play dice.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Richard Feynman — Both refuse to fool themselves; one starts from a picture in the head, the other from what the instrument says.

### Further
Elon Musk Bruce Lee Charlie Munger Socrates Peter Thiel Richard Feynman Karl Popper

## Alfred Adler
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/adler/
Tags: Family and relationships, The industrial age, Whose task is this

Alfred Adler (1870–1937 · Austria) — Whose task is this. The founder of individual psychology, an early colleague of Freud's who broke with him over a disagreement about direction.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The founder of individual psychology, an early colleague of Freud's who broke with him over a disagreement about direction. Freud said a person is settled by his past; Adler said a person is pulled by a purpose — the same childhood is a scar to one man, an excuse to a second and fuel to a third, and the difference is not in the events but in what he wants them for. He also left the sharpest line-drawing tool anyone has for relationships: work out who finally pays for the outcome and you know whose task it is.

### Q: What actually happened?
He is the best available evidence for his own theory. He had rickets and did not walk until he was four, nearly died of pneumonia at five, never reached five foot three, and grew up beside an older brother who was better at everything. On Freud's route that reads as a list of injuries. Adler's account runs the other way: those were the things that made him choose medicine and spend a career on how people get past their own limits. The term inferiority complex is his, and he meant something precise by it — not the feeling, which everyone has, but using the feeling as the reason not to act.

### The parts · Whose task is this
One test only: follow the consequence and see who finally pays it. The child who does not study carries the grade. A colleague's mood is his to carry. What other people think of you is their task, and you have no vote in it. e.g. Chasing homework until the house is at war means you have taken on his task. What is left to you is making the consequence clear and being available when he asks.

### The parts · Not because, in order to
He translates because of my past, therefore now into in order to reach some end, therefore now. A man says he cannot socialise because of his childhood; Adler asks what not socialising spares him. The answer is usually being turned down — and a purpose can be swapped where a cause cannot. e.g. I was too busy to write the proposal. Ask instead what not writing it spared you. Mostly it is being judged, which moves the block from your calendar to your fear.

### The parts · Inferiority is fuel, not illness
Adler took striving to be ordinary and the feeling of inferiority to be universal. What separates people is the use: healthy striving pushes you to change your position, a complex argues that the position cannot be changed. Same feeling, one accelerator, one brake. e.g. I did not train for this, if it sends you to fix the gap, is fuel. If it becomes the reason you never apply, it is the complex.

### The parts · Worth grows out of contribution
His definition of mental health is not self-realisation but social interest — the felt sense that you are of use to somebody. So his direction of treatment often points outward: not liking yourself more, but finding one concrete thing that helps a particular person. e.g. Affirmations repeated until they feel hollow do less than one small useful thing done for a named person. The second produces a sturdier sense of worth.

### Q: How do I use it today?
The next time a relationship is hurting, run the separation first: who finally pays for this? If it is not you, hand it back; if it is, someone else's opinion is not a reason. Then run the second question on yourself — what does staying exactly as I am spare me?

### Lines to keep
Whoever finally pays for the outcome owns the task. What other people think of you is their task, not yours. We are not determined by our experiences, but by the meanings we give them.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Thomas Gordon — Two ways of asking whose problem this is: Gordon's answer picks the method, Adler's decides whether it is yours to touch at all. Epictetus — The same cut two thousand years apart — what is up to me and what is not, against my task and your task. Brené Brown — Both are working on what other people think of me: Adler says it is their task and not yours, Brown says it is a mechanism that can be taken apart — one draws a boundary, the other dismantles a structure. Attachment Theory — Two routes into the same trouble: Adler asks what you are using it for, attachment asks how the template got built. Murray Bowen — Two knives for drawing a line: Adler asks whose task this is, Bowen asks whether their feeling has already got inside you.

### Further
Attachment Theory Carl Rogers Viktor Frankl Epictetus Nonviolent Communication Brené Brown Kristin Neff Murray Bowen

## Anders Ericsson
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/ericsson/
Tags: Learning and growth, Modern, Method over hours

Anders Ericsson (1993 · the violin study) — Method over hours. A psychologist who spent a career on how the best in any field actually got there. His best-known research reached the public as the ten-thousand-hour rule, which is the…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A psychologist who spent a career on how the best in any field actually got there. His best-known research reached the public as the ten-thousand-hour rule, which is the one thing he then spent the rest of his life denying. What decides the level is not the hours but what happens inside them: work at the edge of what you cannot yet do, with a specific goal and feedback fast enough to use. He called it deliberate practice. Repeating what you can already do is rest with better posture.

### Q: What actually happened?
Before the violinists there was a college student the papers call SF. Ericsson and William Chase sat him down several times a week and read him digits to repeat back. He started where everybody starts, at about seven. He was a distance runner, and began hearing strings of numbers as running times, so that 3492 became a near-record mile. Two years and a couple of hundred hours later he could hold eighty-two digits. His memory for letters stayed exactly average. Nothing general had improved. He had built one structure, and it fitted one thing.

### The parts · Practising what you can do is rest
Fluency is pleasant and it is the feeling of not improving. Progress happens in the region where you keep failing, which looks inefficient from outside and is the only part that changes what you are capable of. e.g. An hour of familiar pieces is an hour of enjoying yourself. What needed the hour was the passage you keep getting wrong.

### The parts · Feedback outranks hours
Repetition without correction does not teach. It makes the wrong version automatic. Thirty years of driving produces a driver of exactly the same standard, because nobody has ever told him which turn was bad. e.g. If nobody will say which paragraph they stopped reading, build the feedback yourself: put it away a week, then read it as a stranger.

### The parts · Experts hold models, not memories
What a specialist owns is a mental representation of the field, built by failing against real problems. A chess player sees a position rather than pieces. Watching and memorising do not construct one. e.g. Ten games played and gone back through afterwards teach more than a hundred watched.

### The parts · Ten thousand hours was never the finding
The number was an average for one group in one field, and half that group had not reached it. He objected to it for the rest of his life, because it converts a demanding result into permission to simply wait. e.g. Ten years in the job is not ten years of experience. It is often one year, repeated, under a longer title.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Split your last practice hour in two: the part you could already do, and the part you kept failing at. If the second part is small, that is your answer. Then find out what is going to tell you which attempts were wrong. If nothing is, build that before you add another hour.

### Lines to keep
Purposeful practice means working just past what you can do. Feedback ranks above hours. Without it, repetition teaches nothing. What an expert owns is a model of the field, not a memory.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Bruce Lee — Both refuse to count repetitions: Lee practises one kick ten thousand times, Ericsson says those ten thousand only count if something corrects them. Carol Dweck — She works on how a failure gets read, he works on whether the task was hard enough to produce one. Haruki Murakami — Both are about what to do daily over years: deliberate practice keeps you at the edge of what you cannot do, Murakami lowers the daily difficulty so you never break the chain. Cal Newport — Deliberate practice requires intense concentration, and Newport sets out why that concentration has become so hard to get hold of today. Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi — Both keep you at the edge of your ability: Ericsson on how to practise so the ability grows, Csikszentmihalyi on why that position is the one that absorbs you.

### Further
Bruce Lee Carol Dweck Lev Vygotsky Miyamoto Musashi Fukuzawa Yukichi Haruki Murakami Atomic Habits Cal Newport Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi

## Andy Grove
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/grove/
Tags: Starting and building, The industrial age, Strategic inflection point

Andy Grove (1936–2016 · Budapest to Intel) — Strategic inflection point. Intel's third employee and its fourth chief executive. He took over a memory company that Japanese competitors had driven into the wall, and left a chip company worth…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Intel's third employee and its fourth chief executive. He took over a memory company that Japanese competitors had driven into the wall, and left a chip company worth roughly thirty times more. His real contribution was not silicon: he wrote down how a company that has already won avoids dying. Only the Paranoid Survive is about strategic inflection points; High Output Management is the source of nearly every one-to-one and objectives system in use today.

### Q: What actually happened?
He was born in Budapest in 1936 to a Jewish family, survived the Holocaust as a small boy living under a false name, and at twenty escaped a Hungary under Soviet control, arriving in America with almost no English. He took a doctorate in chemical engineering, joined Intel as its third employee, and ended as the chief executive who cut the business the company had been built on. The alertness people later read as a management style was not learned in business. It is the residue of a childhood spent noticing early what the adults noticed late.

### The parts · The new chief executive test
In 1985 he asked Gordon Moore what a new chief executive brought in to replace them would do. Moore said, get us out of memories. Grove said, then why don't we walk out the door, come back and do it ourselves. What blocks the decision is never information. It is attachment. e.g. Neither Kodak nor Nokia lacked people who could see the trend. Kodak invented the digital camera. What was missing was somebody able to cut into who we are.

### The parts · Strategic inflection points
One of the forces around a business moves by a factor of ten, the old rules stop applying, and nobody sends a notice. The frightening part is that the beginning looks exactly like an ordinary bad quarter. By the time it is unambiguous in the numbers, the choice is no longer yours. e.g. To judge whether something is a tenfold change for an industry, ask whether it alters the cost structure or only the interface. The first rewrites the rules; the second is a new skin.

### The parts · Bad news has to travel faster than good
Somebody always feels the change first, and they sit near the customer, not near the board. The question is what happened to the last person who brought bad news. If they were quietly frozen out, everybody who saw it next learned to be quiet. e.g. Snow melts first at the periphery. In a review, ask who noticed first, whether they said so, and what happened to them next.

### The parts · A manager's output is the output of everyone he touches
It is the output of the organisation under him plus that of the organisations he influences. How much he did himself counts for nothing; only how much he multiplied counts. Which leaves three high-leverage activities — training, one-to-ones and decisions — and very little else. e.g. A ninety-minute one-to-one covers a fortnight of somebody's work. Run as a status report, it has only the value of a status report.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Once a quarter, run the new chief executive test on yourself. If somebody landed in your seat tomorrow with no attachment to anything you have built, what would they cut in the first week and what would they double? Write both lists, then answer honestly why you are not doing it. The answer is rarely the timing.

### Lines to keep
Only the paranoid survive. If we got kicked out, what would a new chief executive do? Let bad news travel faster than good news. Snow melts first at the periphery. A strategic inflection point looks at first like a bad quarter.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Steve Jobs — Jobs disrupted other people on instinct and taste; Grove disrupted himself on process and data. The same act performed by two temperaments. Jensen Huang — Both walked out of the business that was making the money. Grove left memory under fire; Huang left mobile chips while they were still growing. Peter Drucker — Grove solves execution, Drucker solves choice. One asks how a thing gets through the organisation, the other asks whether it is worth doing at all.

### Further
Jensen Huang Peter Drucker Steve Jobs Jeff Bezos Duan Yongping Xunzi The Innovator's Dilemma Konosuke Matsushita

## Arlie Hochschild
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/hochschild/
Tags: Family and relationships, Modern, Work nobody counts

Arlie Hochschild (1983 · UC Berkeley) — Work nobody counts. A sociologist who twice gave a name to work that had none. The Managed Heart (1983) named emotional labour: jobs that require not only that you do it right but that you…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A sociologist who twice gave a name to work that had none. The Managed Heart (1983) named emotional labour: jobs that require not only that you do it right but that you display a prescribed feeling — warmth for a flight attendant, hardness for a debt collector. The Second Shift (1989) named the unpaid shift that starts when the paid one ends, and put a number on it: about 15 hours a week, a year of which is an extra month of 24-hour days. Her whole contribution is making uncounted labour countable.

### Q: What actually happened?
Doing fieldwork with Delta flight attendants she kept meeting one phrase in the training material: a sincere smile. The airline was not satisfied with courtesy. It required the smile to be real — which means the employee has to manufacture the feeling internally, and that part of the job has no hours, no pay and no name. She put it beside physical labour: lifting boxes tires you, and so does producing cheerfulness, except the second bill arrives late and usually gets recorded as 'she's changed'.

### The parts · Work off the timesheet is paid for by whoever does it
Anything unmeasured gets treated as done in passing. It doesn't disappear for going unrecorded; it becomes one person's invisible load, and that person often has no language to complain in, because on paper nothing happened. e.g. Nobody schedules remembering the birthdays, noticing who has gone quiet, smoothing the meeting afterwards. It still takes hours, and the same person does it.

### The parts · Surface acting and deep acting bill differently
Putting the face on while knowing you are exhausts through tension. Persuading yourself you mean it exhausts because afterwards you can't find yourself. Both have a cost; they arrive at different times. e.g. Smiling through the call knowing you don't mean it leaves you tense. Talking yourself into meaning it leaves you unsure which part was you.

### The parts · Care time is rigid
You can write a document faster. You cannot feed a child faster or sit with a sick parent faster. So 'efficiency' barely applies — the work can only be taken over by someone else, or not done, and then someone else pays. e.g. You can review the document twice as fast this quarter. You cannot get a two-year-old to sleep twice as fast.

### Q: How do I use it today?
When the work at home lands on one person and saying so hasn't changed it, don't start with fairness. Log two weeks: every task, who did it, how long. Most negotiations fail because the two people are looking at different lists. At work, if you got little done and can't face speaking, ask how much of the day went on holding a required feeling — and whether any of that was counted.

### Lines to keep
That smile is not 'her' smile. The first shift is at work, the second at home. Only one pays. Labour nobody books gets billed to one person anyway.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Christina Maslach — Two kinds of uncounted work: the required feeling, and the six ways a job and a person fail to match. Arthur Kleinman — Both put a price on labour nobody counts: Hochschild on housework and emotional labour, Kleinman on long-term care, and both are assumed to fall on one person.

### Further
Thomas Gordon Christina Maslach Harvard Study of Adult Development Arthur Kleinman

## Arthur Kleinman
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/kleinman/
Tags: Body and daily life, Modern, Curing fails, care does not

Arthur Kleinman (1941– · Harvard) — Curing fails, care does not. A Harvard medical anthropologist and a practising psychiatrist, with years of fieldwork in China. His whole career splits one thing into two.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A Harvard medical anthropologist and a practising psychiatrist, with years of fieldwork in China. His whole career splits one thing into two. One half is what the clinician sees, the numbers on the chart and the lesion in the organ. The other is what the patient lives through: the pain, the fear, the person they have become at home. Modern medicine spends nearly all its effort on the first and people are undergoing the second. His wife Joan died in 2011 of early-onset Alzheimer's after ten years in his care, and the authority on caregiving says he was not remotely ready. That sentence is where the rest of his work starts.

### Q: What actually happened?
As a young medical student he was given one job on the burns ward: to hold the hand of a small girl, burned over most of her body, while her wounds were scrubbed each day. He tried what he had been taught, distraction and reassurance, and it did nothing against the screaming. One day he asked her instead what it was actually like to be burned like that and to go through this every morning. She stopped, and told him. After that she held his hand and got through the sessions, and he has said ever since that this was where his work began.

### The parts · Normal results is not the same sentence as you are fine
A chart can declare a lesion gone. It cannot declare gone what the months did to a life. Plenty of people feel worse once treatment ends, because medicine has completed its task and the other half has nobody assigned to it. It was never on the form. e.g. Every test comes back clean and you still cannot leave the house alone. That is not weakness.

### The parts · Eight questions, and the eighth is the one that matters
In 1978 he published a short list for clinicians: what do you call it, what caused it, why now, what does it do, how bad and how long, what treatment, what trouble has it caused, and what do you fear most about it. Seven ask for understanding. The eighth asks for the fear, which is usually what is in the way. e.g. The doctor keeps saying it is controllable. What he is afraid of is what the office will think.

### The parts · Cure and care are different goals with different owners
Cure asks whether this can be made to go away and the answer is sometimes no, and once it is no, anyone working to that goal has nothing left to do. Care asks whether today can be made a little easier, which has an answer every day, and the answer stays in your hands. e.g. After nothing more can be done there is still a whole day to get through, and how it goes is decidable.

### The parts · The carer is being used up, and that is a separate line
The least forgiving pages he wrote are about his own collapse: exhaustion, guilt, resentment surfacing where he did not want it. He insists this is structural rather than moral. The cost of long care has to be seen and shared, or two people go down instead of one. e.g. Two years of carrying it alone and the carer falls ill first. That is the norm, not the accident.

### Q: How do I use it today?
If you or someone at home has a diagnosis you will carry for years, write two columns: what the doctor described, and what is actually hard every day. They are rarely the same thing, and nobody has been assigned to the second. Before the next appointment, ask the person what frightens them most about it, and take that answer with you rather than a list of symptoms.

### Lines to keep
Illness is the lived experience of symptoms and suffering. What frightens him most tells you more than what he has. Treatment can be handed over. Being there cannot.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Viktor Frankl — Both answer what to do when a situation cannot be changed: Frankl points to the freedom of attitude in an extreme, Kleinman to the ordinary long grind where care is still available every day. Carl Rogers — Both start by understanding the other person's world: Rogers gets there by reflecting back until they nod, Kleinman by eight specific questions. Arlie Hochschild — Both put a price on labour nobody counts: Hochschild on housework and emotional labour, Kleinman on long-term care, and both are assumed to fall on one person. Shi Tiesheng — One is a doctor writing about patients, the other is the patient: Kleinman argues that what the clinician sees and what the patient lives are two things, and Shi Tiesheng is the one living the second.

### Further
Robert Sapolsky Viktor Frankl Arlie Hochschild Carl Rogers Shi Tiesheng

## Atomic Habits
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/atomic-habits/
Tags: Body and daily life, Modern, Change the system, not the goal

Atomic Habits (2018 · James Clear) — Change the system, not the goal. James Clear's book on how behaviour actually gets built. Its claim is that people overrate goals and underrate systems, because winners and losers usually hold the same…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
James Clear's book on how behaviour actually gets built. Its claim is that people overrate goals and underrate systems, because winners and losers usually hold the same goal and the difference lies in how the days run. It goes further into practice than most habit books, working on the four stages of a behaviour, cue and craving and response and reward, rather than asking anyone for more willpower.

### Q: What actually happened?
In his second year of high school a bat slipped out of a teammate's hands during practice and struck him full in the face, breaking his nose and fracturing his skull and both eye sockets. He had seizures, was flown to a larger hospital and put into a medically induced coma. A year on he was cut from the starting lineup of his school team. What he had at university was not a comeback plan but a set of very small habits held without interruption: sleep at a fixed hour, a tidy room, the gym. In his final year he was named his university's top male athlete.

### The parts · Goals are shared; systems are not
Every team in the race wants the title, so the goal separates nobody. The marginal return on setting a goal is low and on rebuilding the system is high, because that is where results are produced. It explains why this year I really will so rarely works: it changes the intention, not the process. e.g. Read twelve books this year, against move the charger to the living room and leave a book on the pillow.

### The parts · Start from identity, not from outcome
Clear's central swap is from I am trying to quit smoking to I am not a smoker. The first fights a craving and costs something every time; the second lets behaviour follow self-description. Every action is a vote for the type of person you wish to become, and enough votes remove the need for willpower. e.g. To start moving, take on I am someone who moves every day. Five minutes still counts as a vote.

### The parts · Make the good thing cheap and the bad thing expensive
Of the four stages, environment is the most workable. Kit by the bed the night before, phone in another room: changes that cost no willpower and directly alter the price of starting. Far more reliable than cultivating grit, because grit is the thing that runs out. e.g. To use the phone less, delete the app. Reinstalling takes two minutes, and two minutes stops the impulse.

### The parts · Never miss twice
His practical rule is that missing once is fine and you never miss twice in a row. Once is an accident; twice starts becoming the new normal. It plugs the most common collapse point, the moment you decide that since the streak is broken you may as well stop. e.g. No run today, so tomorrow is compulsory, even ten minutes. What you protect is that this is still live.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Take the habit you keep failing at and change two things this week. Name the identity it belongs to rather than the number you want, and make one change to your surroundings so that starting costs less than it did. Then hold one rule for a month: you may miss it once, and you never miss it twice in a row.

### Lines to keep
You do not rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of your systems. Every action is a vote for the type of person you become.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Benjamin Franklin — Two schemes of self-improvement: Franklin worked one virtue a week by attention, Clear takes the four stages of a behaviour apart and edits the surroundings instead. Zeng Guofan — Both accumulate by small daily acts: Zeng Guofan by a written daily examination of himself, Clear by design that removes the need for one. Augustine — One gives the method for redesigning the system, the other reports what is happening inside when no method will go in. BJ Fogg — Clear works on the system and the identity, Fogg on the trigger and the smallest possible action. One changes the frame, the other moves the starting line. Cal Newport — Both work by design rather than by will: Clear edits the environment to lower the cost of starting, Newport edits the diary to protect the block.

### Further
Benjamin Franklin Bruce Lee Anders Ericsson Zeng Guofan Augustine BJ Fogg Cal Newport Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi

## Attachment Theory
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/attachment-theory/
Tags: Family and relationships, Modern, The early template

Attachment Theory (1950s–1970s · Bowlby and Ainsworth) — The early template. Bowlby worked with children who had lost their families in the war and argued that the pull towards closeness is an instinct, not a dependency to be outgrown.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Bowlby worked with children who had lost their families in the war and argued that the pull towards closeness is an instinct, not a dependency to be outgrown. His collaborator Mary Ainsworth built the Strange Situation, separating one-year-olds from their caregiver and bringing them back, and read stable patterns out of the reunion rather than the parting. Those patterns become a person's default template for closeness ever afterwards — not a determinism, but the factory setting. Bowlby's own name for it is the internal working model.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1952 James Robertson, working with Bowlby, took a camera into a London hospital and filmed a two-year-old through eight days of a minor admission. Parents were then allowed in for an hour a week, or not at all, and the wards reported that children settled quickly. He filmed at fixed times each day, with a clock in shot, so that nobody could say he had waited around for tears. What the film shows is not settling. It is protest, then despair, then a terrible calm the staff had been reading as adjustment. The room it was first shown to was hostile. The visiting rules changed anyway.

### The parts · Watch the reunion, not the separation
The least intuitive part of the experiment: the child who does not cry is not the child who is not afraid. Avoidant infants showed arousal as high as the criers and had simply learned not to show it, because showing it had not worked. e.g. The person on the team who never raises a problem may not have none. Look at how his last request for help ended; it tells you more than asking him now.

### The parts · A secure base is what makes risk possible
Bowlby's core finding is that exploration runs on security: a child goes far out only while sure the mother is still there. Grown up, it is the same circuit. Support is not doing the thing for someone, it is their knowing that coming back is still possible. e.g. If you want someone to make the call, say plainly that a wrong one gets cleared up together. That sentence moves more than any incentive.

### The parts · A template, not a verdict
The patterns are stable and rewritable: a later steady relationship, therapy, one long friendship all change them. As an explanation the idea is worth a lot, as an excuse it does harm. It accounts for the starting position, not for where you finish. e.g. Noticing that you go silent in a conflict is progress. I am just avoidant, nothing to be done, is a tool turned into a shield.

### The parts · Two patterns lock together
The anxious partner pursues, the avoidant one withdraws, and each move produces the other: the closer she comes the further he goes, and the further he goes the more anxious she gets. Naming the loop converts you have a problem into we are stuck in a circuit, which is the version with a way out. e.g. One presses for an answer, the other goes quiet. That is not a question of who is right; it is two coping styles triggering each other.

### Q: How do I use it today?
To judge whether somebody in a relationship feels safe, do not watch how calm they look — watch whether they ask for help when something goes wrong, and how the last such request was answered. And if you want someone to take a risk, give them somewhere to come back to before you give them the encouragement.

### Lines to keep
The quiet child is not calm. He has learned not to show it. We are happiest when life is a series of excursions from a secure base. The early working model becomes the template for every later intimacy.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Alfred Adler — Two routes into the same trouble: Adler asks what you are using it for, attachment asks how the template got built. John Gottman — Attachment says where the pattern came from; Gottman measures how it is running in the room today.

### Further
Murray Bowen Carl Rogers John Gottman Harvard Study of Adult Development Alfred Adler Virginia Satir

## Augustine
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/augustine/
Tags: Mind and feeling, Qin, Han and the Six Dynasties, Grant me chastity, but not yet

Augustine (354–430 · Hippo, North Africa) — Grant me chastity, but not yet. A bishop in Roman North Africa, and the author of the Confessions, which he wrote in his forties about the first half of his own life.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A bishop in Roman North Africa, and the author of the Confessions, which he wrote in his forties about the first half of his own life. It is the first book in the West that reports from inside the experience of knowing exactly what to do and not doing it. He is here not as a theologian but as a witness: he wanted to change, he could not, and he took the failure apart while it was still happening to him. Sixteen centuries before habit science, he had already located the problem in the will rather than in the knowledge.

### Q: What actually happened?
Book Eleven of the Confessions stops the autobiography dead and asks what time is. The answer is one of the most quoted sentences in philosophy: if nobody asks me, I know; if I want to explain it to someone who asks, I do not know. Then, instead of retreating behind the paradox, he keeps going, and works out that past and future have no existence outside a present mind holding them. It is the same procedure he uses on his own failures. Take an experience everybody has, refuse the ready-made account of it, and keep looking until the mechanism shows.

### The parts · The wanting is real, and so is the not yet
Grant me chastity and continence, but not yet. He is clear that both halves were sincere: he wanted the outcome and he did not want today. So reinforcing the wanting does nothing, because that side was never short. Not yet is a permit that renews itself every morning, and it will not lapse on its own. e.g. How many times have you said after this busy stretch? Somebody has to tear that up; it does not expire.

### The parts · Some wrongs have no reason at all
At sixteen he and a gang stripped a neighbour's pear tree. There were better pears at home and they threw most of the stolen ones to the pigs. Decades later he hunts for a motive and concludes there was none, only an occasion: alone, he says, he would never have gone. e.g. If why did I do that has produced nothing after twenty attempts, cross the question out and look at who was standing there.

### The parts · Not a weak will, a divided one
In the garden he notices that the mind commands the body and is instantly obeyed, while the mind commands itself and is resisted. His conclusion is that there are two wills and both are his. That is why more resolve does not help: it adds to one side while the other stays exactly where it was. e.g. I do not want to is not laziness. Some part of you is guarding something. Ask what it is guarding before you decide again.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Take the thing you keep not starting and count how many times this month you have said not yet, then name the one comfort that starting tonight would cost you. That comfort, not a shortage of resolve, is what the other half of you is protecting.

### Lines to keep
He turned putting it off into a prayer, and meant both halves. The pears went to the pigs. He never wanted pears. The hand obeys the mind. The mind does not.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Wang Yangming — Both on knowing and not doing. Wang says knowing without acting was never real knowing; Augustine says the knowing is real and two wills are fighting. Atomic Habits — One gives the method for redesigning the system, the other reports what is happening inside when no method will go in.

### Further
Atomic Habits BJ Fogg Rat Park Wang Yangming

## BJ Fogg
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/bj-fogg/
Tags: Body and daily life, Modern, Too small to fail

BJ Fogg (2019 · Stanford Behavior Design Lab) — Too small to fail. Founder of the Behavior Design Lab at Stanford, working on how behaviour gets designed rather than willed.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Founder of the Behavior Design Lab at Stanford, working on how behaviour gets designed rather than willed. His formula is that a behaviour happens when motivation, ability and a prompt arrive at the same moment. Most people fail because they work only on motivation, which rises and falls on its own schedule, so anything resting on it will fall over. His proposal is the reverse: shrink the behaviour until it needs no motivation, then hang it off something you already do, and give yourself a signal the moment it is done.

### Q: What actually happened?
His standard illustration is flossing. Someone who resolves to floss properly every night does it for a week and stops, because the resolve was the only thing holding it up. Fogg's version is one tooth. After you brush, floss one tooth, and then celebrate on the spot. One tooth is small enough that no evening is too bad for it, so it never breaks, and almost nobody stops at one once the floss is in their hand. The habit gets built by the tooth that was never in doubt, not by the ones that got done.

### The parts · Motivation is unreliable, so do not lean on it
Motivation moves like tide and not on your schedule. Demanding of a low day what was planned on a high one guarantees the break. The correct move is to lower the difficulty until the lowest day can still clear it, and let the anchor do the rest. e.g. Buying the annual membership on the day you decide is borrowing against a high. What settles it is the empty day.

### The parts · Anchor it behind something you already do
The hardest part of a new habit is remembering it exists. Fogg hangs it off an action that happens every day without fail: after I brush my teeth, I will. The anchor supplies the prompt, so you are no longer relying on memory or an alarm. A vague window of time is not an anchor. e.g. After I pour the coffee I write three sentences beats write every morning, because it has a moment attached.

### The parts · Too small to fail
Two push-ups, one page, three sentences: small enough to finish on the worst day. The point is not the yield of that amount, it is keeping the state of this is still going and clearing the doorway. Once started most people carry on, because the resistance sits at zero to one. e.g. Change run three kilometres into put on the shoes and go out. Almost nobody puts them on and stays in.

### The parts · Celebrate at the moment you finish
This is where he parts from most habit theory: he holds that the brain fixes behaviour by emotion rather than by repetition count. So the instant you finish, give yourself a clear positive signal, a fist or saying it out loud. It sounds silly and it is doing the work. e.g. After the two push-ups, say I did it and mean it. Saving it for a big meal at the weekend helps almost nothing.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Take the habit that keeps breaking and shrink it until you could do it on your worst day, name the daily certainty it hangs off, and give yourself a signal the moment you finish. When it still fails, do not conclude that you need more discipline: work out which of the three broke, the prompt, the ability or the motivation, and repair that one.

### Lines to keep
Behavior happens when motivation, ability and a prompt come together. Shrink the behaviour until you could do it on your worst day. You change best by feeling good, not by feeling bad.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Atomic Habits — Clear works on the system and the identity, Fogg on the trigger and the smallest possible action. One changes the frame, the other moves the starting line. Benjamin Franklin — Franklin practised one virtue a week and ran on self-discipline. Fogg lowers the difficulty until no discipline is required. Haruki Murakami — Two ends of one idea: Fogg shrinks the behaviour until the worst day can do it, Murakami caps the daily output so the best day cannot overspend.

### Further
Atomic Habits Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi Cal Newport Benjamin Franklin Augustine Haruki Murakami

## Bai Gui
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/bai-gui/
Tags: Money and risk, Pre-Qin and classical, Against the crowd

Bai Gui (Warring States · 370–300 BC) — Against the crowd. The earliest contrarian in the written record, twenty-two centuries before Graham. He traded farm goods across seasons and across crops, and the Grand Historian records…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The earliest contrarian in the written record, twenty-two centuries before Graham. He traded farm goods across seasons and across crops, and the Grand Historian records the verdict of his own age: everyone in the empire who discussed making a living traced the craft back to him. He also set four conditions on who was allowed to learn it.

### Q: What actually happened?
He once told Mencius that his own management of the waters was an improvement on Yu the Great's. Mencius refused it. Yu, he said, led the water to the sea, which is what water wants; you lead it into the neighbouring state and make their country your drain. The exchange survives because Bai Gui was a man philosophers argued with as an equal, a merchant in a century that ranked merchants last, claiming his trade was a discipline with principles and then behaving as though it were.

### The parts · When the world sells, I buy
The oldest contrarian rule on record. Buy the thing nobody wants; sell into the scramble. The weight sits on the second half. He did not try to sell at the top, because the last stretch of a price is set by feeling, and feeling cannot be forecast. e.g. Eight characters that translate straight into modern practice: be greedy when others are fearful, and every pendulum argument written since.

### The parts · Four qualities, and no waivers
Wit to read the turn, courage to commit, humanity to give and take without chasing the last coin, strength to hold and to keep to the rules. The first two decide whether you make it; the second two decide whether you keep it, and most people fail on the second two. e.g. Seeing it and not acting earns nothing. Acting and never taking profit gives it back. Doing both and being shaken out in the chop ends the same way.

### The parts · He hedged cycles rather than hoarding
In a good harvest he bought grain and sold silk and lacquer; when the cocoons came in he bought silk floss and sold grain. Farm cycles do not line up, so one side is always cheap. He was not earning a scarcity premium. He was earning the gap between two clocks. e.g. Betting on one commodity and waiting is a gamble. Holding two whose cycles run opposite and taking the spread is a business, and a business repeats.

### The parts · He moved like a bird of prey
Sima Qian says that when the moment came he struck like a wild animal or a hawk. That is not in tension with the patience; it is the other half of it. Almost all the time is waiting, and the waiting exists so the strike can be immediate and full size. e.g. A year may hold two or three moments worth committing to. The discipline of the other three hundred and sixty days is what leaves you loaded on the day.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Score yourself on his four before your next large commitment: can I actually read this, will I commit at the size my reading implies, can I leave the last stretch to somebody else, and will my behaviour change when it goes sideways? The lowest score is where your losses are coming from.

### Lines to keep
When the world sells, I buy. When the world buys, I sell. Wit to adapt, courage to decide, humanity to give, strength to hold. He seized the moment like a wild beast or a bird of prey. All who speak of making a living take him as their founder.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Fan Li — Two ancient fortunes: Fan Li teaches how to get out intact, Bai Gui teaches a method you can repeat. Benjamin Graham — Twenty-two centuries apart, the same claim: price is set by mood, value by supply and demand.

### Further
Fan Li Benjamin Graham Warren Buffett Records of the Grand Historian Shang Yang

## Benjamin Franklin
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/franklin/
Tags: Mind and feeling, Early modern, Thirteen virtues, compounded

Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790 · Boston and Philadelphia) — Thirteen virtues, compounded. A rare full-stack life. A printer by trade, he arrived in Philadelphia at seventeen with nothing, was financially independent at forty-two, and then became a scientist…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A rare full-stack life. A printer by trade, he arrived in Philadelphia at seventeen with nothing, was financially independent at forty-two, and then became a scientist in electricity, an inventor of the lightning rod and bifocals, the author of Poor Richard's Almanack, the diplomat who brought France into the American war, and the only man to sign all four of the Declaration of Independence, the alliance with France, the Treaty of Paris and the Constitution. Charlie Munger has said Franklin is the man he spent his life imitating. The method underneath all of it is one idea: treat character as a system that can be practised deliberately and compounded.

### Q: What actually happened?
He had an opponent in the Pennsylvania Assembly, a man of standing whom he had no realistic way of winning over directly. Hearing that the man owned a scarce and curious book, Franklin wrote asking to borrow it for a few days. It came at once. He returned it a week later with a warm note. At their next meeting in the House the man spoke to him — which he had never done — and with great civility, and they were friends for the rest of his life. Franklin's own summary: he that has once done you a kindness will be more ready to do you another than he whom you yourself have obliged. Asking for a small favour is not taking on a debt. It hands the other person evidence that he likes you.

### The parts · The thirteen-virtue operating system
Temperance, silence, order, resolution, frugality, industry, sincerity, justice, moderation, cleanliness, tranquillity, chastity, humility. The list is not the point; the execution is. One virtue a week, a small book with a page each, a mark against every breach, thirteen weeks to a course and four courses a year. He kept at it for fifty years — the earliest habit tracker there is, turning character into an engineering problem with iterations. e.g. Zeng Guofan's daily disciplines are startlingly similar. Two of the most self-managed men in either hemisphere independently invented one method: record daily, work one point at a time, iterate for life.

### The parts · Appeal to interest, not to reason
He worked from interest rather than from argument. People are rarely moved by being shown the reasoning; they are moved by what a thing costs and pays them. Persuading the colonies to unite, persuading France into the war, he did not plead the higher cause. He totalled up the other side's account. e.g. Selling, raising money and getting another department to help are all the same operation: translate what I need you to do into what you get out of it.

### The parts · Compounding, applied to a life
Money is of a prolific generating nature. Money can beget money, and its offspring can beget more. He was the earliest to carry compounding out of finance and into everything else — knowledge, credit, relationships, habits all obey the same law. His will left a thousand pounds each to Boston and Philadelphia on condition that it sit for two hundred years. It came out in the millions. e.g. Naval Ravikant's case for compounding wealth and judgement together traces straight back to this.

### The parts · The Junto
At twenty-one he organised twelve men into the Leather Apron Club, meeting Friday evenings to discuss morals, politics and science, and introducing each other to business. That small group went on to produce America's first subscription library, its first volunteer fire company, and the academy that became the University of Pennsylvania. Do not grind away alone. Organise the capable people and you become the node. e.g. A standing group of a dozen people who meet on a fixed evening will out-produce any amount of individual networking, because the meeting happens whether or not anyone feels like it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Turn self-improvement from resolve into a system. Pick one behaviour for this week, mark every day, and change one thing at a time. Build relationships by asking for small favours rather than agonising over what gift to send. And when you state a view, swap it is certainly for I am inclined to think — it costs nothing and halves the resistance.

### Lines to keep
Never leave that till tomorrow which you can do today. It is hard for an empty bag to stand upright. Well done is better than well said. He that has once done you a kindness will be more ready to do you another.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Zeng Guofan — The matched pair of the two hemispheres: both of ordinary natural ability, both forging themselves with a daily ledger — between them the evidence that character is an engineering problem rather than a gift. Naval Ravikant — The same algorithm two hundred and fifty years apart: compounding, leverage, reputation, and the pursuit of knowledge once money stops being the question. La Rochefoucauld — Franklin believed virtue could be drilled in with a chart. La Rochefoucauld thought what gets drilled in is the appearance of virtue. Read the two together for a year. Atomic Habits — Two schemes of self-improvement: Franklin worked one virtue a week by attention, Clear takes the four stages of a behaviour apart and edits the surroundings instead. BJ Fogg — Franklin practised one virtue a week and ran on self-discipline. Fogg lowers the difficulty until no discipline is required.

### Further
Zeng Guofan Charlie Munger Warren Buffett Naval Ravikant Xunzi Atomic Habits BJ Fogg Cal Newport

## Benjamin Graham
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/graham/
Tags: Money and risk, The industrial age, Margin of safety

Benjamin Graham (United States · 1894–1976) — Margin of safety. The father of security analysis, author of Security Analysis and The Intelligent Investor.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The father of security analysis, author of Security Analysis and The Intelligent Investor. He taught at Columbia, and one of his students was Warren Buffett, who says most of what he does came from Graham. His achievement was to show, in a decade that treated shares as betting slips, that a share is a piece of a business and that price and value are two different quantities.

### Q: What actually happened?
Before the crash his accounts had made money every year and he was a Wall Street prodigy. Between 1929 and 1932 his fund lost seventy per cent and came close to the end; the household got through on his wife going back to work and help from his mother-in-law. The disaster is what produced the system. If a good judgement can still be wrong, the protection cannot be better judgement. It has to be built into the purchase price. Security Analysis appeared in 1934, and his fund did not have a losing year afterwards.

### The parts · Mr. Market
Imagine a partner who names a price every day and will buy from you or sell to you at it. He is elated one week and despairing the next. You may deal with him or ignore him entirely; he is not offended and he returns tomorrow. The market exists to serve you, not to instruct you. e.g. March 2020 and the long slide of 2022 were both his depressive episodes. Whoever read the screen as a quotation rather than a verdict was buying.

### The parts · Margin of safety
Three words for the whole of sound investment. Pay fifty cents for a dollar and a thirty per cent error still leaves you whole. The margin does not raise the return on a correct call; it makes an incorrect one survivable. Every blow-up is a zero-margin position. e.g. A bridge rated for thirty thousand tonnes is posted for ten. Graham took engineering redundancy and moved it into finance.

### The parts · Where investment stops and speculation starts
An investment operation, on thorough analysis, promises safety of principal and an adequate return; anything failing those tests is speculation. Note that the standard is adequate rather than maximal, and that the line is drawn in the operator rather than in the security. e.g. Two people can hold the same share on the same day, one investing and one speculating. The difference is the analysis standing behind it.

### The parts · The weighing machine
In the short run the market is a voting machine; in the long run it is a weighing machine. Votes are cast by mood, weight is set by earning power. The investor has two jobs: work out the weight, and wait for the weighing. Not reading the votes is survivable; not knowing the weight is not. e.g. Sell to the optimists, buy from the pessimists. The return comes from other people's mispriced feeling, not from a better forecast.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Before any commitment, a share or a job or a company, run his three questions: have I analysed this thoroughly, is the principal or the fallback safe in the worst case, and is the return I want adequate or greedy? Then add one rule: act when the market is in an extreme mood, and ignore the quotes the rest of the time.

### Lines to keep
One of your partners, named Mr. Market, is very obliging indeed. Distill the secret of sound investment into three words: margin of safety. In the short run a voting machine, in the long run a weighing machine. The investor's chief problem, and even his worst enemy, is likely to be himself.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Warren Buffett — The student past the teacher: Graham bought cheap ordinary companies, Buffett bought great ones at fair prices. George Soros — Graham assumes price returns to value; Soros trades the stretch where price drives value away from itself. Bai Gui — Twenty-two centuries apart, the same claim: price is set by mood, value by supply and demand. Peter Lynch — Both work from fundamentals, but Graham prices the liquidation and Lynch prices the room left to grow. Howard Marks — Graham answers what a thing is worth, Marks answers whether now is the moment to act — two separate skills, and most people have only trained the first. Scarcity — Both are about room to be wrong: the margin of safety leaves room in a valuation, slack leaves room in a life — one guards against misjudging, the other against accident.

### Further
Bai Gui Warren Buffett Charlie Munger Ray Dalio Nassim Taleb Peter Lynch Howard Marks Scarcity

## Brené Brown
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/brene-brown/
Tags: Mind and feeling, Modern, Shame and guilt

Brené Brown (2010 · University of Houston) — Shame and guilt. A social work researcher who spent twenty years on the thing most people will not touch: making shame into an object that can be studied, across thousands of interviews.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A social work researcher who spent twenty years on the thing most people will not touch: making shame into an object that can be studied, across thousands of interviews. Her most useful contribution is not encouragement, it is a distinction. Guilt is I did something bad; shame is I am bad. The first points at a behaviour, the second at the person, and the same mistake produces opposite consequences depending on which one you reach for. (Her conclusions linking shame to addiction, depression and aggression come from her own qualitative work and reviews, and the quantitative strength of them is disputed. This entry takes the distinction, not the coefficients.)

### Q: What actually happened?
The 2010 TEDxHouston talk on vulnerability was given to a local audience. She went home from it with what she later called a vulnerability hangover — certain she had said far too much about herself, hoping mainly that nobody she knew would ever see it. The video then went out to millions of people. A researcher who had spent two decades studying what happens to a person when the most private part of their life becomes available for public grading had, by accident, put herself inside her own experiment. When she next stood up to talk, the subject was not vulnerability. It was shame.

### The parts · Guilt points at the behaviour, shame points at the person
This is the root of the whole distinction. I made a mess of this leaves a road open: what to do next time. I am the kind of person who cannot get things done closes the road, because if the problem is who I am then there is no action available and only avoidance is left. One mistake, and the word you describe it with decides whether anything follows. e.g. The proposal went in late. I misjudged the time leads to a better estimate. I am unreliable leads to not accepting the next piece of work.

### The parts · Shame lives on three things: secrecy, silence, judgment
Her formulation is that shame needs those three to grow exponentially, which read backwards is the remedy: say it, and say it to somebody who will not grade you. This is not comfort, it is dismantling the conditions the mechanism runs on. All of shame's force comes from the line it is only me, and that line fails the moment it is heard. e.g. Take the hardest thing to say and say it once, to a person you are sure will not use it to define you. The wrong listener is worse than none, so choosing matters more than speaking.

### The parts · Vulnerability is exposure with the result unknown
Her definition contains no emotion at all, only a situation: uncertainty, risk, emotional exposure. On that definition, making the first friendly move, admitting you do not know something, and putting up a proposal that may be refused are all vulnerability. What separates it from weakness is whether you chose it. e.g. Saying in the meeting that you do not follow this part and asking somebody to explain is vulnerability. Asking quietly afterwards because of how it would look is avoidance.

### The parts · Shame does not work as a management tool
Driving people with shame works briefly and teaches concealment permanently. In her organisational work the same pattern turns up repeatedly: a team corrected by humiliation ends up not with fewer errors but with fewer errors reported. e.g. Ask who did this at the post-mortem and you will not hear about the next incident. Ask which step had too little information and people keep talking.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Next time the bad feeling starts, work out which sentence you are saying to yourself: I did something wrong, or I am no good. The first has an action after it and the second does not. If you find the second, rewrite it down to the specific thing and the specific act. Then say it once to somebody who will not use it to define you. Used wrongly: filing responsibility you actually owe under just a behaviour, or telling somebody else to stop feeling shame, which is not something that can be argued away.

### Lines to keep
Shame is I am bad. Guilt is I did something bad. Shame is really easily understood as the fear of disconnection. Vulnerability is uncertainty, risk, and emotional exposure. You can choose courage, or you can choose comfort, but you cannot choose both.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Alfred Adler — Both are working on what other people think of me: Adler says it is their task and not yours, Brown says it is a mechanism that can be taken apart — one draws a boundary, the other dismantles a structure. Carl Rogers — Rogers supplies the environmental condition, unconditional positive regard; Brown supplies the move the person in the chair can make for themselves. Zeng Guofan — Zeng turned self-reproach into a daily discipline; Brown would ask whether that sentence is pointing at the behaviour or at the man writing it. Tending the Roots of Wisdom — Both work on the fear of being found out. Her answer is to say it aloud so shame cannot survive being spoken; his is to stop putting so much on display. Montaigne — Both take shame and fear apart. She has the laboratory findings; he has one man running the experiment on himself four hundred years earlier. Sima Qian — Both on shame. She is the researcher and gives the mechanism; he is the subject and gives the sample of someone finishing the work while carrying it. Kristin Neff — Both are working on am I a bad person: Brown supplies the distinction, guilt against shame, and Neff supplies the replacement, self-compassion against self-esteem.

### Further
Alfred Adler Carl Rogers Viktor Frankl Nonviolent Communication Tending the Roots of Wisdom Montaigne Sima Qian Kristin Neff

## Bruce Lee
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/bruce-lee/
Tags: Learning and growth, The industrial age, Formless

Bruce Lee (Contemporary · 1940–1973) — Formless. The film star is the outermost label. He was a martial artist, a writer, a film-maker and a philosophy student, and in thirty-three years he left a worked-out position…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The film star is the outermost label. He was a martial artist, a writer, a film-maker and a philosophy student, and in thirty-three years he left a worked-out position on getting free of your own training. Jeet Kune Do is not a style; it is an argument against style itself — absorb what is useful, discard what is not, add what is uniquely your own.

### Q: What actually happened?
At the Long Beach International Karate Championships in 1964 he gave a demonstration: the one-inch punch, which sent a much larger man backwards off a chair, and press-ups on two fingers. It was a demonstration, not a fight, and it was watched by people who could open doors. One of them passed word to a Hollywood producer, which produced a screen test, which produced Kato. A twenty-three-year-old teaching in a small Oakland school got the rest of his life out of a few minutes spent showing what a very short distance can carry.

### The parts · Absorb, discard, add
His method compresses to three moves: take what is useful from every source, cut what does not work for you, and put in what is yours alone. It applies to any learning. The point is never to reproduce one master's system intact, but to draw from several and let practice settle the remainder into something of your own. e.g. Finishing the course is not the goal and not finishing is not a debt. The question is which parts survived contact with your actual work.

### The parts · A style that refuses to become a style
He built a martial art whose founding rule is not to be bound by any martial art, his own included. That is freedom one level up: not only thinking about the problem, but thinking about the way you go at problems. Most systems cannot do this, because a system that can refuse itself is hard to sell. e.g. Any framework you cannot imagine abandoning has stopped being a tool and become a membership.

### The parts · Knowing yourself comes before the technique
His notes keep returning to it: understand yourself before you learn anything external. What is your body actually built for, where does your attention fail, what do you do when frightened? Without that, absorb what is useful has no criterion, because useful is useful to somebody in particular. e.g. Two people copy the same routine. It works for one of them, and the difference was decided before either of them started.

### The parts · Thinking is a delay
He read philosophy seriously and was severe about substituting it for action. Knowledge exists to make the action better, not the conversation about the action better. Anything he could not test against a person trying to hit him he treated as unfinished. e.g. The strategy that has been in review for six weeks has already lost to a worse strategy that shipped in the second week.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Next time you take up a new field, run his three steps: read widely without hurrying to find the right answer; actively delete the parts that do nothing for you, without guilt about not finishing; then add your own judgement in practice until the method is yours. The system belongs to whoever built it. The method has to be yours.

### Lines to keep
Absorb what is useful, discard what is not, add what is uniquely your own. Knowing yourself is the most important knowledge of all. Do not think too much. Feel, and hit.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Anders Ericsson — One counts the repetitions, the other refuses the fixed form — and both are describing the same ten thousand. Miyamoto Musashi — Three hundred years apart and the same instruction: Musashi says rely on nothing, Lee says be like water. Fukuzawa Yukichi — Both say the inherited set of moves stops working, but Fukuzawa is the more literal of the two: change the content the day you see it, keep the method.

### Further
Wang Yangming Tao Te Ching Socrates Charlie Munger Miyamoto Musashi Fukuzawa Yukichi Haruki Murakami Atomic Habits Anders Ericsson Albert Einstein

## C.S. Lewis
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/cs-lewis/
Tags: Family and relationships, Modern, The notebooks after she died

C.S. Lewis (1898–1963 · Oxford) — The notebooks after she died. A writer and professor at Oxford and Cambridge, author of Narnia and of many books arguing people into belief.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A writer and professor at Oxford and Cambridge, author of Narnia and of many books arguing people into belief. He married at fifty-eight; his wife Joy died of cancer four years later. In the months that followed he recorded his own state in four exercise books and published them under a pseudonym. He is here because the situation — someone who mattered has died — needs someone who was actually in it, not someone reasoning about it from outside.

### Q: What actually happened?
He published it as N.W. Clerk, and it sold almost nothing. The pseudonym was not modesty: the most famous Christian apologist in the English-speaking world had written a book in which the arguments he had made for thirty years stop working on him, and he was not prepared to sign it. Friends began recommending it to him, not knowing he had written it. It went out under his own name only after his death.

### The parts · Name it correctly and you know how to treat it
He assumed grief was sadness and found it closer to fear — the churn in the stomach, the inability to sit still. Sadness is met by thinking it through, fear by letting the body settle. The wrong name gets you the wrong method.

### The parts · A belief never tested may not be a belief
Everything he had argued held in good weather and collapsed at the first real event. He didn't rush to rebuild; people who do generally build the same house out of the same cards. What is still standing afterwards is the actual foundation.

### The parts · Gripping the memory deforms it
The harder he tried to remember his wife, the more she warped into someone gentler and more agreeable. Worse than forgetting: replacing her with someone he had made. When he stopped trying, she came back as herself.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Just after losing someone, ask whether the feeling is more like sadness or more like fear, and treat it accordingly. Write three lines a day about how the day was — not conclusions. And if you're rehearsing the person daily out of fear of forgetting, check whether the one you're holding has become gentler than the real one.

### Lines to keep
Not like sadness. Like fear. You don't know how much you believe something until it's life or death. The harder he tried to remember her, the more she warped.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Marie Curie — Two records of the same year: he wrote to find out what grief was, she wrote to keep talking to him. Su Shi — Both wrote through the worst of it. Lewis to find out what he actually believed, Su Shi to find out what was still enjoyable.

### Further
Marie Curie John Gottman

## Cal Newport
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/cal-newport/
Tags: Body and daily life, Modern, Concentration is scarce

Cal Newport (2016 · Georgetown University) — Concentration is scarce. A computer science professor who also writes about how knowledge work actually gets done. He sets two things against each other.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A computer science professor who also writes about how knowledge work actually gets done. He sets two things against each other. Deep work is concentrated thinking without interruption, which creates new value and is hard to copy. Shallow work is the logistical business of the day, easy to copy and building no new capability. His claim is that as collaboration tools make everyone interruptible, deep work is becoming rare, and the rarity is exactly what makes it one of the few remaining ways to pull ahead.

### Q: What actually happened?
Newport is a working academic with a full publication record, several books and no social media account of any kind, and he closes the laptop most evenings by half past five. He does not present that as discipline; he presents it as design. The book opens with people who went further. Donald Knuth gave up email in 1990 and asks correspondents to write to a postal address so that an assistant can batch it, on the grounds that email is a wonderful thing for people whose job is to be on top of things, and his job is to be at the bottom of things.

### The parts · Attention residue: the cost is not the five minutes
After a switch, part of your attention is still hooked on the last task and needs time to move across. The real cost of one quick look at a message is the poor half hour that follows, and you cannot feel that part, because on returning to the work you feel focused. e.g. Answer a message midway through a proposal and the next twenty minutes usually need rewriting the following day.

### The parts · Fragments do not add up to a block
Four fifteens are not an hour, because each one pays the switching cost again and deep thinking needs a climb. It explains why a person whose diary is cut up by meetings produces nothing requiring continuity even when the total hours are there. e.g. The forty minutes between two meetings is hard to think in. Most people can only spend it on small chores.

### The parts · Book the block; do not manage the will
Self-control is consumable and a diary is not. Fix the deep hours the way a meeting is fixed, announce them, and enter them when the time comes. A gap never appears by itself, because shallow work expands like a gas to fill whatever space is available. e.g. Marking two hours each morning as unbookable beats asking yourself every morning when you will write.

### The parts · Cap the shallow work rather than abolishing it
Mail, coordination and meetings are necessary and they build no new capability. He does not propose removing them. He proposes a ceiling and a fixed slot, so the total is unchanged and what remains can join up into blocks. e.g. Handle mail at ten in the morning and four in the afternoon rather than whenever it lands.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Look back at yesterday and find whether there was a single stretch over ninety minutes with no interruption in it. If there was not, put one into tomorrow's diary the way you would put in a meeting, tell the people who would otherwise interrupt it, and push the mail into two fixed slots so the rest of the day can join up.

### Lines to keep
Deep work is becoming rare exactly as it becomes valuable. A gap never appears by itself. You have to schedule it. Four fifteen-minute pieces do not make an hour.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Atomic Habits — Both work by design rather than by will: Clear edits the environment to lower the cost of starting, Newport edits the diary to protect the block. Anders Ericsson — Deliberate practice requires intense concentration, and Newport sets out why that concentration has become so hard to get hold of today. Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi — One sets out the internal conditions for concentration, the other the external ones, the diary and the environment that protect it. Scarcity — Both keep an account of attention: Newport counts what switching costs, Scarcity counts what how far short am I occupies all day.

### Further
Atomic Habits Anders Ericsson John Ratey Benjamin Franklin Haruki Murakami BJ Fogg Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi Scarcity Ivan Illich

## Cao Cao
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/cao-cao/
Tags: Power and organisation, Qin, Han and the Six Dynasties, Ability only

Cao Cao (Late Han · 155–220) — Ability only. The novel made him the archetypal villain. The historical record shows the earliest systematic meritocrat in China: three orders seeking talent, each one saying that…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The novel made him the archetypal villain. The historical record shows the earliest systematic meritocrat in China: three orders seeking talent, each one saying that birth, reputation and conduct would not be examined and ability would. He was also the man who fed his own army by farming rather than seizure, and a poet good enough to be read for his verse alone.

### Q: What actually happened?
He had issued an order that no soldier was to trample the standing grain, on pain of death. Then his own horse startled and went through a wheat field. He called the officers together and moved to take his own life; when they stopped him he drew his sword, cut off his hair and said the hair would stand in for the head. The credibility of a rule is built at exactly that moment. It applies to everyone, including the man who wrote it.

### The parts · Ability only
Three orders, one core sentence: put forward ability alone, and I will use it. Not birth, not reputation, not an old grudge, not conduct. The result was a density of capable people that neither of his rivals matched. e.g. A job posting with eight requirements hires people who pass on all eight. The one capability actually wanted gets squeezed out by the other seven.

### The parts · The hair in place of the head
Under a rule, the leader punishing himself matters more than the leader not punishing at all. If the man at the top can break it without cost, nobody below him is ever really following it. He chose a penalty that was visible and survivable, and applied it publicly. e.g. The exception granted to the founder is the moment the policy stops being a policy and becomes a suggestion.

### The parts · Take the legitimacy resource first
In 196 he was first to receive the fugitive Han emperor at Xu, and governed thereafter in the emperor's name. The move costs little and puts every subsequent action inside an accepted frame, while forcing rivals to argue against the frame rather than against him. e.g. Whoever defines the category, the benchmark or the standard gets to have their own choices read as the default and everyone else's as the deviation.

### The parts · Burn the letters
After Guandu he found the secret correspondence his own officials had sent to Yuan Shao before the battle. He burned it unread, in public, saying that when Shao was strong he had not been sure of surviving either. Some accounts can be settled and must not be. e.g. Investigate one incident to the bottom and assign blame to everyone, and nobody reports the second one.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Take the role you are hiring for and cross out every requirement except one — the single capability the seat genuinely cannot do without. Then look at what you crossed out and ask which of those you were about to reject someone over. If you keep the loosened bar, write the behavioural boundaries down the same week.

### Lines to keep
Put forward ability alone, and I will use it. If only blameless men could serve, how did Duke Huan rule? The old warhorse in the stable still longs for a thousand li.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Liu Bang — Two ways of holding people: Liu Bang gave away money and trust, Cao Cao built rules and screened for ability. Han Feizi — The theory and its practitioner. Han Feizi wrote the system down; cutting his hair in place of his head is that system demonstrated on the man at the top.

### Further
Liu Bang Sun Tzu Han Feizi Sima Yi Guan Zhong Zhuge Liang Shang Yang Zhu Yuanzhang The Comprehensive Mirror Guo Jia Machiavelli
