## Carl Jung
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/jung/
Tags: Mind and feeling, The industrial age, The afternoon has its own programme

Carl Jung (1875–1961 · Zurich) — The afternoon has its own programme. The founder of analytical psychology, Freud's most valued student and his most famous defector.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The founder of analytical psychology, Freud's most valued student and his most famous defector. Parts of what he left are hard to test — the collective unconscious, archetypes, synchronicity — and three of his concepts have been in constant use for a century because they bear directly on how a person lives: a life has a morning and an afternoon with different tasks; what you push down comes back out of other people; and the mask you wear outside can grow in.

### Q: What actually happened?
The afternoon was not a theory he read about. After the break with Freud in 1913 he resigned his university post, lost his professional standing and spent roughly six years in what he called a confrontation with the unconscious — recording visions and dialogues in the notebooks that became the Red Book, which he kept private and which was not published until 2009. He was thirty-eight when it started. The stages of life essay comes from someone who had already lost the morning's programme and had to find another.

### The parts · Stalling at forty is the hour, not a fault
The morning's task points outward and its standards come from outside. People stall in midlife not because capacity declined but because they are still running the afternoon on the morning's programme. What was great in the morning will be little at evening.

### The parts · What you push down comes back out of other people
To become acceptable everyone suppresses something — ambition, laziness, temper, wanting to be seen. It reappears as an inability to tolerate the people who show it. Disproportionate dislike is the signal.

### The parts · The mask is necessary and it has to come off
Without it you can't deal with the world. The danger is taking it for yourself, and the test comes when it's removed from outside — retirement, redundancy, children leaving. How badly you panic measures how much grew only on the role.

### Q: How do I use it today?
If you're doing well and increasingly can't summon anything, ask whether the effort is still answering the morning's question. If that one is largely answered, adding more won't work. And if there is a type of person you can't think about without anger, write down the exact quality — then ask whether you have it and never let it out.

### Lines to keep
What was great in the morning will be little at evening. When the dislike is out of proportion, it isn't only about them. The mask is necessary. The trouble is taking it for yourself.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Excellent Sheep — Both describe a life built to someone else's standard. One catches it at twenty-two, the other at forty.

### Further
Excellent Sheep Zhuangzi

## Carl Rogers
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/carl-rogers/
Tags: Family and relationships, The industrial age, Held first

Carl Rogers (1902–1987 · United States) — Held first. The founder of humanistic psychology, and the first person to record whole courses of therapy and hand them over to be studied — before that, what happened in the room…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The founder of humanistic psychology, and the first person to record whole courses of therapy and hand them over to be studied — before that, what happened in the room existed only in the therapist's summary. His central claim ran against the practice of the day: the therapist should not be an interpreter or a director but should supply three conditions — congruence, unconditional positive regard, empathic understanding — inside which a person grows in a good direction on his own.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1956 he and B. F. Skinner set out their disagreement in public, and Science printed it. Skinner's position was that behaviour is shaped by its consequences whether or not anyone admits it, so the honest course is to design the shaping well. Rogers did not answer that control fails; he granted that it works. He answered that a person is not raw material, and that what should be engineered is the conditions in which people choose, not a better set of levers. Almost everything else he wrote is a working out of that one refusal.

### The parts · Unconditional is not without standards
It means acceptance is not withdrawn because of what you said, not that whatever you do is fine. The person is accepted; the behaviour still gets judged. Get that right and people will tell you the truth, because the truth no longer costs them the relationship. e.g. A child owns up. Take the telling first, then deal with the damage. In the other order he does not tell you next time.

### The parts · Empathy is restating until they nod
For Rogers empathy is not the sentence I understand how you feel; it is putting the other person's meaning back in your own words until he confirms it. And the effect is not only that he feels understood — often he is hearing what he means for the first time. e.g. When a friend is pouring it out, hold the advice and start with so what you mean is. After two corrections the thing is frequently clear to him.

### The parts · Genuineness outranks technique
Of the three conditions he rated congruence highest: the therapist cannot act. Performed acceptance gets detected, and it does more damage than plain non-acceptance, because it also says you are not worth the truth from me. Skill raises the ceiling; performed skill destroys the floor. e.g. Empathic phrasing over private impatience will be heard for what it is. I am in a bad state, let us talk later, is the more honest instrument.

### The parts · People do not need pushing, they need releasing
His premise is that people tend towards their own development, and that being stuck is usually not missing drive but conditions in the environment — you are worth something if you are like this. Take the conditions away and the direction appears by itself. e.g. With someone who has gone flat, ask what is in the way rather than what the goal is. Most often what is in the way is the fear of being wrong in public.

### Q: How do I use it today?
To get the truth out of someone, first make sure that telling it cannot cost them the relationship. To help them think, put their meaning back in your own words until they say yes, that is it. And when you cannot manage genuine acceptance, say you are in a bad state rather than act it.

### Lines to keep
When I accept myself just as I am, then I can change. If I can listen to what he tells me, I can help him. What I am is good enough if I would only be it openly.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Thomas Gordon — Teacher and student: Rogers set the condition, Gordon turned it into three sentences an ordinary parent could say. Socrates — Two ways of making somebody find their own answer: Socrates presses with questions, Rogers removes the conditions. Brené Brown — Rogers supplies the environmental condition, unconditional positive regard; Brown supplies the move the person in the chair can make for themselves. Arthur Kleinman — Both start by understanding the other person's world: Rogers gets there by reflecting back until they nod, Kleinman by eight specific questions.

### Further
Thomas Gordon Nonviolent Communication Alfred Adler Virginia Satir Brené Brown Arthur Kleinman Attachment Theory Crucial Conversations

## Carol Dweck
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/dweck/
Tags: Learning and growth, Modern, Ability can grow

Carol Dweck (2006 · Stanford) — Ability can grow. The Stanford psychologist behind the distinction between fixed and growth mindsets: whether you believe ability is a fixed quantity or something that grows with effort…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The Stanford psychologist behind the distinction between fixed and growth mindsets: whether you believe ability is a fixed quantity or something that grows with effort and method. The two beliefs produce different behaviour — if ability is fixed, a challenge you might fail is a threat, because failing proves the quantity; if it grows, failing is information. The idea had enormous reach, and was simplified and overused on the way, which has to be handled separately.

### Q: What actually happened?
The correction matters as much as the finding. Over the last decade several large replication studies have measured mindset interventions at a fraction of the effect the popular version implies, close to zero in some populations, with the clearer benefits concentrated among disadvantaged students. Dweck herself has spent years arguing against the version of her own idea that spread, in particular against 'false growth mindset' — schools putting the words on a wall, praising effort that produced nothing, and treating the belief as a substitute for teaching.

### The parts · Praise the move, not the label
'You're clever' is a label and labels need protecting. 'You went back through every wrong answer' is a move and can be repeated. The test: can they do this praise again next time?

### The parts · The moment of failure decides the direction
In good weather the two mindsets look identical. The watershed is the instant something fails: one reads 'I can't', the other reads 'that approach can't'. The difference is whether anyone goes looking for the cause.

### The parts · Mild and real, not a master switch
Knowing the boundary is what makes it usable. It is worth the cost of one sentence — change how you praise, add the word 'yet' — and it is not worth a training programme. Treat it as a master key and you'll ignore resources, teaching and sleep.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Giving feedback, check whether you're praising talent or a specific move, and whether they could do it again. And when someone explains a result as a problem of attitude, ask whether the heavier variables have been checked first. Attitude is the laziest available attribution and the least fair to anyone short of resources.

### Lines to keep
Praise for talent makes people avoid challenge. Praise for process doesn't. In a growth mindset failure is information. In a fixed one it's a verdict. Replications find the effect far smaller than the book conveyed.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Lev Vygotsky — Both about where learning happens. He locates it in the task's difficulty, she locates it in the reading of failure. Kristin Neff — Two ways of editing the same sentence about who I am: Dweck moves ability from fixed to growable, Neff moves the attention off am I good enough — one changes the conclusion, the other changes the question. Scarcity — Both get used to explain why people do not change: Dweck points at belief, Scarcity at circumstance — rule out the circumstance first. Anders Ericsson — She works on how a failure gets read, he works on whether the task was hard enough to produce one.

### Further
Lev Vygotsky Excellent Sheep Kristin Neff Anders Ericsson

## Charlie Munger
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/munger/
Tags: Learning and growth, The industrial age, Invert

Charlie Munger (Contemporary · 1924–2023) — Invert. Buffett's partner for more than half a century, and the reason Berkshire stopped buying cheap broken companies and started buying good ones at fair prices.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Buffett's partner for more than half a century, and the reason Berkshire stopped buying cheap broken companies and started buying good ones at fair prices. His own contribution is a method rather than a portfolio: work out how a thing fails, then don't do that.

### Q: What actually happened?
Invited to give a commencement address at Harvard Law, he told the graduating class he would explain how to guarantee a miserable life, and then listed the ways: unreliability, envy, resentment, learning only from your own experience, giving up after the first reverse. It is the method demonstrated on itself. If you knew where you were going to die, he liked to say, you would simply never go there.

### The parts · Invert, always invert
There are countless routes to a thing going well and only a handful of ways it reliably goes wrong. Listing the failure modes and avoiding them is a shorter, more tractable problem than working out how to win. e.g. Nobody could say what would make the launch succeed. Everyone could name the three things that would sink it, and two were already true.

### The parts · One hammer is not enough
To a man with only a hammer everything looks like a nail. He collected models from other fields — compounding from mathematics, critical mass from physics, selection from biology, the standard biases from psychology — because a problem rarely arrives in the shape of your one discipline. e.g. The retention problem was not a product problem. It was a queueing problem, and nobody in the room had ever been handed that model.

### The parts · Look at the incentive first
Show me the incentive and I will show you the outcome. To understand why a system produces what it produces, do not start with what people say they value; start with what they are paid, promoted and forgiven for. e.g. The review process rewarded shipping. Nobody was ever promoted for deleting a feature, so the surface grew every year and nobody had decided that.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Take the plan you are about to commit to and spend twenty minutes writing only the ways it fails. Then check how many are already true. That list is more useful than the plan.

### Lines to keep
It is remarkable how much long-term advantage we have got by trying to be consistently not stupid. Knowing what you don't know is more useful than being brilliant. Spend each day trying to be a little wiser than you were when you woke up.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Warren Buffett — Same desk for fifty years: Buffett holds the temperament, Munger supplies the checklist of ways to be wrong. Elon Musk — Reduce to physics, or carry many borrowed models at once — two opposite cures for the same blindness. Kazuo Inamori — Two versions of character as a business input. Munger treats reliability as a way of not being stupid; Inamori puts it in the formula as the one factor that can turn the answer negative.

### Further
Warren Buffett Han Feizi John Boyd Elon Musk Influence Benjamin Franklin Ray Dalio Benjamin Graham Peter Lynch Jim Simons George Soros Richard Feynman Socrates Thinking, Fast and Slow Thinking in Systems Bruce Lee Albert Einstein

## Chris Voss
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/chris-voss/
Tags: Reading people, Modern, Label it first

Chris Voss (2016 · Never Split the Difference) — Label it first. A former lead international kidnapping negotiator for the FBI, with a career spent on sieges, abductions and hostage-takings.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A former lead international kidnapping negotiator for the FBI, with a career spent on sieges, abductions and hostage-takings. His method runs almost opposite to the one taught in business schools: before any trade of interests, deal with the state the other person is in. The finding underneath it is that people do not take in terms while their own feelings are still unacknowledged. So the opening move is not a number, it is saying the other person's position back to them accurately enough that they feel known.

### Q: What actually happened?
A kidnapping in Haiti. The gang opened with a ransom the family could not come close to and set a deadline, the standard shape of the trade. Voss did not counter-offer and did not argue about the sum. His people kept returning one question in a calm, unhurried voice: how am I supposed to do that? Not a refusal, not a plea, just a problem handed back across the table. Each time, the kidnappers had to answer it themselves, and each time the number came down. The hostage came home for a fraction of the opening demand, and nobody had won an argument.

### The parts · Label the feeling, do not judge it
It seems like, it sounds like, it looks like. Voss calls the move labelling, and the sentence opening matters more than the content. It seems like is an observation and can be denied. I think you are is an assertion and provokes a defence. Get the label right and they add to it; get it wrong and they correct you. Both are progress. e.g. When a client goes quiet, it sounds like something in here is worrying you works far better than how do you feel about it, because it gives them a specific door.

### The parts · Aim for that's right, not for yes
Yes is the cheapest word available; people produce it to get out of a conversation. The valuable answer is that's right, which means the other side believes you have understood their position in full. Negotiation begins after those two words, not before. e.g. Fine, fine, no problem usually means they want the meeting to end. That's exactly it means you have reached the thing they care about.

### The parts · Calibrated questions hand the problem back
Replace closed questions that want a nod with open ones starting how and what. How am I supposed to do that moves the pressure across the table without any confrontation in it. Either they produce a way, or they hear for themselves that the demand does not work. e.g. When someone pushes the price below your cost, do not argue. Ask how you are supposed to hold the quality at that number. Most of the time they retreat unprompted.

### The parts · No deal beats a bad deal
The strongest position in any negotiation is being able to walk away at any moment. Hostage negotiators never have that option, which is why he knows exactly what it is worth. Someone genuinely willing to end without agreement cannot be pushed into damaging terms by a deadline or by what they have already spent. e.g. Write your alternative down before you walk in: what happens if this collapses. The more concrete it is, the calmer you are at the table.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Next time a conversation jams, stop adding arguments and label the other person instead: it seems like you are worried about something here. You are not trying to get a yes, you are trying to get a that's right. And when you are pushed into a corner, hand it back with how am I supposed to do that.

### Lines to keep
Negotiation is not an act of battle; it's a process of discovery. That's right is better than yes. No is the start of the negotiation, not the end of it.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Nonviolent Communication — Both start from the feeling and want different things: Rosenberg so that both sides' needs get onto the table, Voss so that you get a result out of an adversarial room. Thomas Schelling — The two halves of bargaining: Schelling works on structural commitments and threats, Voss on the language in the room. One alters the payoff matrix, the other alters the person. Crucial Conversations — Both handle the feeling before the content: Voss labels it across a table from an adversary, this rebuilds safety among people who still have to work together tomorrow.

### Further
Nonviolent Communication Influence Guiguzi Thomas Schelling Crucial Conversations

========================================================================
## Christina Maslach
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/maslach/
Tags: Body and daily life, Modern, Burnout is the job

Christina Maslach (1946– · UC Berkeley) — Burnout is the job. Burnout became measurable largely because of her work. Her 1981 inventory split it into three components — emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation, and a fall in…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Burnout became measurable largely because of her work. Her 1981 inventory split it into three components — emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation, and a fall in personal accomplishment — of which only the first overlaps with being tired. Her most persistent and least popular claim is that burnout is a problem of the work environment, not of individual resilience: nearly every remedy on the market teaches people to relax, which asks the person absorbing the damage to repair its cause.

### Q: What actually happened?
There is an earlier thing she is known for. In August 1971 she was a recent Stanford PhD, and her partner Philip Zimbardo was running a prison simulation in the psychology building. Visiting on the sixth night, she saw prisoners being marched to the lavatory with bags over their heads and objected — not as a methodological point but as a moral one. The experiment was shut down the next morning. Her career since has been one long version of the same argument: look at what the situation is doing to people before you look at the people.

### The parts · Only one of the three is tiredness
Rest fixes exhaustion. It does not fix detachment or a collapse in accomplishment, and those two usually arrive first. So somebody can look like they're working normally, and still be delivering, months into it. e.g. He came back from three weeks off rested and still couldn't care about the release. The sleep debt was gone; the other two weren't.

### The parts · Fix the job, not the person
Told the problem is their attitude, a person adds a layer of self-blame and stays in the same environment. Personal remedies aren't useless — they're second. Reverse the order and they stop being support and start being cover. e.g. The wellness app arrived the same quarter the team lost two people and kept the same roadmap. Everyone downloaded it. Nothing changed.

### The parts · Six ways to be mismatched
Workload, control, reward, community, fairness, values. Most people watch only the first. In her data, having no say and doing work that runs against what you believe are often more lethal than volume. e.g. The hours were fine. Being told what to ship and then blamed for shipping it is the one that emptied him out.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Before deciding you need a holiday, check which of the three you have: drained, nothing left for people, no satisfaction on finishing. Then score the six areas one at a time. 'Work is exhausting' implies no action; the six-line version usually names something specific — decision rights, fairness, or different work.

### Lines to keep
Sleep fixes tired. It does not fix detachment. Asking the person absorbing the damage to repair its cause is backwards. If a month off returns you to the same arrangement, it isn't your mindset.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Robert Sapolsky — Same conclusion from two directions: she measures the job, he measures the hormone, and both land on control. Arlie Hochschild — Two kinds of uncounted work: required feeling, and the shift that starts when the paid one ends.

### Further
Robert Sapolsky Arlie Hochschild

## Chu Shijian
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/chu-shijian/
Tags: Starting and building, Modern, Up the mountain at seventy-four

Chu Shijian (1928–2019 · Yunnan) — Up the mountain at seventy-four. A man from Yunnan who ran a cigarette factory from the age of fifty-one and made Hongtashan the best-selling brand in China, known for nailing down the standard at every…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A man from Yunnan who ran a cigarette factory from the age of fifty-one and made Hongtashan the best-selling brand in China, known for nailing down the standard at every step and tying every person's pay to quality. At seventy-four it was all gone: the position, the name, most of the savings, his health. He and his wife leased four hundred acres of bare hillside and planted sugar oranges, which take four or five years to bear. The fruit sold properly a decade later, when he was eighty-four.

### Q: What actually happened?
He was fifty-one when he was put in charge of a cigarette factory in Yuxi. What he did there was unglamorous and relentless: a written standard at every step of the process, and every person's pay tied to the quality of what came out rather than the quantity. Within a decade Hongtashan was the best-selling cigarette in the country. Two decades after that he was seventy-four, living in a work shed on a mountain with none of it left — no position, no name, no savings to speak of — except the way he ran things.

### The parts · Too late is a subtraction problem
He never argued that he was still young. He counted: an orange tree fruits in four or five years, he was seventy-four, so the first crop landed at seventy-nine, an age most people reach. The numbers cleared, so he went. Too late is nearly always a feeling, and feelings cannot count years. e.g. When something feels too late, write down the years it needs and the years you probably have, and look at the two numbers together.

### The parts · The years with nothing to show are the years for foundations
While the trees carried nothing he built the irrigation, had every plot's soil tested, brought in agricultural researchers for the fertiliser mix, and cut the planting density because crowded trees give sour fruit. None of that is possible in a year with a harvest to bring in. e.g. Spend the stretch before results arrive on the underlying work you will never get back to once you are busy.

### The parts · The method travelled; the industry knowledge was hired
Tobacco and oranges have nothing in common, and he first touched an orange in his seventies. The management did not change: each plot contracted to one household, paid on quality rather than weight, pruning and fertiliser and picking all written down as rules. He never pretended to know oranges. He hired the people who did. e.g. Changing field, sort what you know into two piles: what belongs to the industry and can be hired, and how you work, which travels with you.

### The parts · A title is lent. A skill is grown
The first reaction to losing a position is that you are now nothing. The hillside proved the reverse: the title came from the seat and the skill came from the man, and only one of them could be taken back. Good times never make that distinction visible. e.g. After the position goes, do not start with who am I. Start with what can I do. That list is longer than it feels.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Before deciding something is too late, put two numbers on paper: how many years the thing needs before it shows a result, and how many years you can reasonably expect to have. Only if the first fits inside the second does the question get interesting — and then ask what you are still holding as a route back.

### Lines to keep
Too late is usually a feeling, and feelings cannot count years. The years with no harvest are the years for building the irrigation. A title is lent by the seat. A skill is grown by the man.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Su Shi — Both began with one small concrete job after losing the position: Su Shi broke ground at Huangzhou, Chu Shijian built the irrigation first. Neither waited to be recognised again. Kazuo Inamori — Both are about running one thing properly to the end. Inamori works on the motive and the way of thinking; Chu Shijian works on the written standard and pay tied to quality.

### Further
Kazuo Inamori Li Ka-shing Taiichi Ohno Duan Yongping

## Crucial Conversations
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/crucial-conversations/
Tags: Family and relationships, Modern, Safety first

Crucial Conversations (2002 · Patterson, Grenny, McMillan and Switzler) — Safety first. Four authors studied more than twenty thousand people across a thousand organisations to answer one question: why can some people hold a conversation where the stakes…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Four authors studied more than twenty thousand people across a thousand organisations to answer one question: why can some people hold a conversation where the stakes are high, the opinions differ and the feeling is running hot, when most cannot. Their answer is that the instant a person feels unsafe he drops into one of two reflexes, silence or violence, and that once a conversation is in either of them, being right about the content buys nothing at all. So the work is not assembling the argument. It is building the safety first.

### Q: What actually happened?
They did not start from a theory. They asked large numbers of people to point at the colleague who was unusually good at exactly this — the one you would want in the room when the subject was money, or blame, or somebody's performance — and then went and watched those people work, for years. What came back was not vocabulary and not tone of voice. Those people were all doing something before the content: watching for the moment the other person left the conversation, and dealing with that first.

### The parts · Watch the state before the content
Two things need your attention at once: what is being said, and where the other person is. The moment he turns to silence or to attack, stop the content, because nothing said now will be taken in. Repair outranks finishing your point, always. e.g. Sure, whatever you think, is not agreement. Do not ask so are we agreed; ask whether something you said came out too hard.

### The parts · Start with heart: what do I really want
As feeling rises the goal changes without permission, from solving this to winning, or to not looking foolish. Their method is to ask on the spot what result you actually want and what you want this relationship to be. The question pulls the goal back. e.g. You notice halfway that what matters to you is not letting him think you were wrong. The goal has moved, and admitting it is how the conversation comes back.

### The parts · Contrasting: say what you are not saying
When your intent has been misread, deny the misreading first and restate the meaning second: I am not saying you cannot do the job, I am saying we both underestimated the schedule. Take the threat down and the content goes in. In the other order it is never heard. e.g. One line before the criticism, saying you are not raising it to pin it on anyone, stops most of the defending before it starts.

### The parts · The pool of shared meaning
Disagreement is often not two conclusions but two people holding different facts. Put the facts and the reasoning from both sides on the table before discussing conclusions, and a good share of the argument dissolves while you are laying them out. e.g. Two departments fighting over priority each say what data they saw and what they were promised, and often find they were arguing about two different things.

### Q: How do I use it today?
When a conversation goes rigid, do not turn up the argument. Work out whether the other person has gone to silence or to attack, stop the content and repair the safety. Before you open your mouth, ask once what result you actually want. And when you are misread, use I am not saying, I am saying.

### Lines to keep
A conversation fails the moment somebody stops feeling safe. When people feel unsafe they move to silence or to violence. At the heart of most chronic problems sits a conversation never held.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Chris Voss — Both handle the feeling before the content: Voss labels it across a table from an adversary, this rebuilds safety among people who still have to work together tomorrow. John Gottman — Gottman tells you which signals in a fight predict the end; this tells you what to do in the next three minutes.

### Further
John Gottman Carl Rogers Thomas Gordon Chris Voss

## Du Fu
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/du-fu/
Tags: Body and daily life, Medieval, Left office at forty-eight

Du Fu (Tang · 712–770) — Left office at forty-eight. A poet, ranked in China beside Li Bai and read for twelve centuries. He arrived in the capital at thirty-five to find a post and spent ten years at it, sitting the…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A poet, ranked in China beside Li Bai and read for twelve centuries. He arrived in the capital at thirty-five to find a post and spent ten years at it, sitting the examination and sending poems to anyone who might help, with nothing to show until a minor armoury job at forty-four, just as the rebellion broke out. In the winter of 755 he reached his family at Fengxian and found his youngest son dead of hunger. In 759 he gave up his post and took the family southwest, nearly starving on the road, and in 760 built a thatched hut at Chengdu with help from friends. Most of the best work belongs to the ten years after that.

### Q: What actually happened?
In the autumn of 761 a gale stripped the thatch off the hut at Chengdu and flung it across the river. Boys from the village carried some of it off in front of him; he shouted himself hoarse and came back to a roof that leaked all night, the bedding worn through and his children kicking it apart in their sleep. The poem he made of it does not end on his own misery. It ends on a wish for a great house of a thousand rooms that would shelter every cold and struggling scholar under heaven, and on the line that if that house stood he would be content to freeze to death in his own broken hut.

### The parts · A decade with no result still needs a record
Ten years of nothing is easiest to handle by never mentioning it. He wrote it down instead: at dawn knocking at the gates of the rich, at dusk following the dust of their horses, leftover wine and cold scraps. Not I was holding to an ideal. A record that flatters nothing is the kind that survives. e.g. Do not write that you are persevering. Write whose door you knocked on today and what it felt like.

### The parts · Put the worst of it first
The Fengxian poem runs five hundred words about the suffering of an empire, and it opens with his own house. Shamed to be a father, no food, and so the boy died young. War and poverty and an absent career were all true and he names none of them. Owning it cleanly is what lets a thing finish. e.g. I did not do it is enough. Everything that comes after because can be left off.

### The parts · Starting again means a roof, not a rank
The first thing he did in Chengdu was put up somewhere to live, not look for another post. People rebuilding in middle age reach first for the title and the old standing. The desk comes after the roof, and the verdict too late usually comes from an option still held in reserve. e.g. The first step in starting over is the smallest setup a life runs on, not the return of your old standing.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Take the years that are not working and write a page a month on them exactly as they were: what you tried, whom you asked, how it felt, with no language about perseverance in it. Then look beside the thing that has not worked for the thing that has been quietly growing the whole time. If the road you were on has closed, ask whether you are after a roof or after your old position.

### Lines to keep
Ten years came to nothing, and he kept the books year by year. He put the thing he least wanted to write at the front. The best of it was written in the hardest decade.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Su Shi — Both rebuilt after forty: Su Shi broke ground at Huangzhou, Du Fu put up a roof at Chengdu, and both took what a life runs on before any position. Su Shi went back; Du Fu never did. Tao Yuanming — One walked, one had no choice: Tao Yuanming knew where he was going the day he resigned, while Du Fu left office and searched the whole way southwest before stopping at Chengdu.

### Further
Su Shi Pu Songling Tao Yuanming Sima Qian

## Duan Yongping
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/duan-yongping/
Tags: Starting and building, Modern, The stop-doing list

Duan Yongping (Contemporary · 1961–) — The stop-doing list. Founder of BBK, and the source of the culture behind OPPO and vivo, two of the largest phone brands on earth, neither of which invented anything.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Founder of BBK, and the source of the culture behind OPPO and vivo, two of the largest phone brands on earth, neither of which invented anything. He is the Chinese investor who paid over six hundred thousand dollars for lunch with Warren Buffett. His two rules are subtractive: do the right thing before doing the thing right, and the moment you find something is wrong, stop, whatever it costs.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 2006 he won the auction for a charity lunch with Warren Buffett, bidding six hundred and twenty thousand dollars. What he says he took away was not a stock. It was a subtraction: an account of what a person will simply not do, held to long enough that it stops having to be argued each time. He has said as much about his own record — that it went well not because he knew what to do, but because he knew a great many things not to do.

### The parts · Do the right thing, then do the thing right
The order is the whole point. Doing a thing right is a question of skill and can be learned slowly. Doing the right thing is a question of choice, and once that choice is wrong, more effort makes the result worse. Direction is the sign; execution is only the magnitude. e.g. A team polishing the wrong product to a superb finish has built a motorway to the wrong destination. The better the road, the larger the loss.

### The parts · The moment you find it is wrong, stop
Whatever it costs to stop today is the smallest cost available, because today's cost is fixed and known while the cost of continuing compounds and is not. The severity of the rule is that it deletes the most comfortable option in business, which is to watch it another quarter. e.g. Every quarter a wrong direction survives pulls in another cohort, another budget and a few more public promises. The cut in three months is twice as thick.

### The parts · Dare to be last
When a category first appears nobody knows whether the demand is real or where the holes are, and the pioneers answer with their own money. Enter once the answers are visible and build it better. The condition is brutal: on entry day your version has to be visibly better, or late is only late. e.g. Music players, smartphones, electric cars — in each category the eventual winner was not the inventor.

### The parts · A stop-doing list is more reliable than a to-do list
What you should do is uncertain and keeps moving. What you should not do follows from your principles and holds for years. The list also saves judgement: when something on it arrives there is nothing to argue about and no meeting to hold. e.g. Write your three no matter how profitable, never rules. Half your future opportunity reviews will end in ten seconds.

### Q: How do I use it today?
This week find one thing you know is wrong and are still doing, and stop it. You do not need a replacement lined up first. Stopping the wrong thing is a separate action from finding the right one, and it is the one that gets postponed.

### Lines to keep
Do the right thing, and then do the thing right. However large the cost of stopping today, it is the smallest one. Dare to be last, then come first from behind. I know a great many things not to do.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Warren Buffett — Duan Yongping is Buffett's most serious Chinese student, but he moved the moat from investing to operating: Buffett buys the company that has one, Duan builds one by entering last and building better. Peter Thiel — Thiel says be first into a category nobody believes in; Duan says be last into one somebody else has already proved. Both are refusals to fight in a crowd, from opposite ends. Jensen Huang — Opposite entries into a new category. Huang goes in before it exists and pays for a decade; Duan waits until somebody else has proved it and then builds the better version.

### Further
Warren Buffett Kazuo Inamori Jensen Huang Chu Shijian Andy Grove Kevin Kelly Konosuke Matsushita Zhang Yiming Peter Lynch

## Elon Musk
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/musk/
Tags: Starting and building, Modern, First principles

Elon Musk (Contemporary · 1971–) — First principles. Co-founder of PayPal, Tesla, SpaceX and Neuralink. The method is a single move repeated: go back to what is physically true and re-derive everything from there.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Co-founder of PayPal, Tesla, SpaceX and Neuralink. The method is a single move repeated: go back to what is physically true and re-derive everything from there. When told a thing is impossible, his first question is whether physics forbids it. If not, impossible is a description of current engineering and current prices, and both of those are temporary.

### Q: What actually happened?
2008 was the year it nearly ended. The first three Falcon 1 launches failed, Tesla could not fund production of the Roadster, and the money was gone. The fourth Falcon flew in September and reached orbit; the Tesla financing closed on Christmas Eve. He has said that if the fourth launch had failed there was nothing left for a fifth. The interesting part is not the survival. It is that the same method produced three catastrophic failures and then the thing nobody else had done, and there was no way to tell those apart from inside.

### The parts · Physics is law; the rest is advice
The limit of any technology is set by physical law, not by what the current industry can do. Working back from the physical limit rather than forward from today's practice changes what counts as an acceptable answer, and forces engineering that the incremental route never reaches. e.g. Asking how much lighter this can be given the material produces a different programme from asking how much lighter than last year's.

### The parts · Most of the week should go into making the thing
He has said roughly eighty per cent of his time goes to engineering and design. That is a budget, not a boast: meetings without an output, reviews that only inform, and reporting that changes no decision are the default state of any organisation past a certain size, and they consume exactly the hours the product needed. e.g. Cancel the standing meeting for a month and see what actually breaks. Usually the answer is the feeling of being informed.

### The parts · The method does not tell you when you are wrong
Reasoning up from fundamentals is equally confident when the fundamentals are misjudged, and it removes the handrail that convention provides. That is the real cost of it: no external check, and a strong internal one. It belongs on the few questions worth that exposure. e.g. The schedule derived from physics is right about what is possible and famously wrong about when. Both come from the same calculation.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Next time something is described as impossible or as simply costing what it costs, ask what physical law or published price actually sets the floor. Everything between that floor and today's number is somebody's decision, and decisions can be remade.

### Lines to keep
Physics is the law. Everything else is a recommendation. We reason from first principles rather than by analogy. Try to be useful. Do things that are useful to other people.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Charlie Munger — Reduce to physics, or carry many borrowed models at once — two opposite cures for the same blindness. Taiichi Ohno — Both attack cost by refusing the answer they are given. Musk goes down to the physics of the materials; Ohno goes down the chain of causes on a stopped machine.

### Further
Peter Thiel Jeff Bezos Charlie Munger Jensen Huang Albert Einstein

## Epictetus
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/epictetus/
Tags: Mind and feeling, Qin, Han and the Six Dynasties, What is yours, what is not

Epictetus (c. AD 55–135 · Rome and Nicopolis) — What is yours, what is not. Born a slave; his owner was Epaphroditus, a secretary to Nero. One leg was lame and stayed lame.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Born a slave; his owner was Epaphroditus, a secretary to Nero. One leg was lame and stayed lame. Freed, he taught in Rome until Domitian expelled the philosophers from Italy in AD 93, then moved to Nicopolis in north-west Greece and taught there until he died. He wrote nothing: the Discourses and the Handbook are lecture notes taken by his student Arrian, which is why the tone is blunt and often scolding. The Handbook runs to fifty-three chapters and the first sentence of the first one is the dichotomy of control. Eighteen centuries later that sentence became the opening lesson of cognitive behavioural therapy.

### Q: What actually happened?
There was almost nothing in his room. The one thing worth stealing was an iron lamp, and one night it was stolen. Tomorrow, he told his students, you will find an earthenware one here — a man loses only what he has. Asked whether he was not angry, he said the thief had traded his own character for a lamp. For a lamp he became a thief; for a lamp he became a man nobody can trust. It was a bad deal, and it was the thief who made it. That is not good temper. It is the direct output of the philosophy: the lamp was outside his control, his view of the lamp was inside it, and the only thing that was ever truly his — how he responded — was never once taken.

### The parts · The dichotomy of control
The Handbook opens with a filing rule. Some things are in our power — opinion, impulse, desire, aversion, in a word our own acts. Some are not: body, property, reputation, office. His claim is extreme: almost all suffering comes from putting something in the second class into the first. The practice is not becoming stronger, it is re-filing every painful thing as it arrives. e.g. In trading you control the size, the discipline and the basis of the decision. You do not control the outcome of this one trade. Stake your feelings on outcomes and randomness will take you apart by instalments.

### The parts · It is not the thing, it is the view you took of it
What disturbs a man is not the thing itself but the view he takes of it. The event is neutral; the pain is made between the event and the verdict that this is bad for me. When somebody angers you, he says, what angers you is your own judgement — so watch the judgement before you answer. Albert Ellis lifted this straight into rational emotive therapy, and it is the floor modern CBT stands on. e.g. One piece of harsh feedback. Read as I have been rejected it flattens you; read as a free piece of outside information it improves the work. Identical facts, and the verdict in the middle decides everything after it.

### The parts · The actor and the script
Remember that you are an actor in a play, and the play is whatever the author wants. If he wants it short, it is short. If he casts you as a beggar, play a beggar; a cripple, an official, a private man, the same. Your business is to act well the part given you. Choosing the part is somebody else's business. It is the coldest available handling of an unfair start: neither denying it nor stopping at the protest. e.g. Where you were born, which way the industry is turning, the slot the company put you in — that is casting. What you do at that level is the performance.

### The parts · Rehearse the loss
When you kiss your child, he says, say to yourself that tomorrow she may die. It sounds cruel and the effect runs the other way: rehearsing a loss in advance blunts the shock when it lands and makes the thing valuable while you still have it. The Stoics called it the premeditation of evils. It is not pessimism, it is inoculating the feeling. e.g. Before a large bet, walk all the way through total failure and the capital gone, and accept it, and then act. People who can carry the worst outcome do not lose their shape mid-move.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Take a sheet of paper and write down the three things that hurt most this week. Split each into two columns: what I control, what I do not. Most people find that nearly everything eating their emotion sits in the right-hand column. Then do one thing only — put next week's attention entirely on the specific actions in the left. The value is not in having understood something. It is in seeing, in your own handwriting, what you have been paying for.

### Lines to keep
Men are disturbed, not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things. Some things are in our control and others not. Never say of anything, I have lost it; but, I have restored it. You may fetter my leg, but my will not even Zeus himself can overpower.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Marcus Aurelius — The slave and the emperor on one doctrine: one owned nothing, was lame and was exiled, the other ruled the known world, and they arrive at the same conclusion — and Marcus was reading these lecture notes when he wrote the Meditations. Viktor Frankl — The same finding eighteen centuries apart: Frankl said in the camps that the last human freedom is the choice of one's attitude, which is the dichotomy of control tested at the floor of human experience. The Bhagavad Gita — The same border drawn in two places. Epictetus draws it between what is up to you and what is not; the Gita draws it between the act and its fruit. Alfred Adler — The same cut two thousand years apart — what is up to me and what is not, against my task and your task.

### Further
Marcus Aurelius Seneca Viktor Frankl Zhuangzi Socrates Nassim Taleb The Bhagavad Gita Alfred Adler

## Esther Perel
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/perel/
Tags: Family and relationships, Modern, Flat isn't broken

Esther Perel (1958– · Belgium and New York) — Flat isn't broken. Thirty years of couples therapy, nine languages, and a caseload across many cultures. She doesn't work on how to argue — Gottman covered that in detail — but on…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Thirty years of couples therapy, nine languages, and a caseload across many cultures. She doesn't work on how to argue — Gottman covered that in detail — but on something harder to raise: everything is fine and we feel nothing. Her explanation blames neither party. Intimacy wants closeness, familiarity and predictability; desire wants distance, the unknown, the thing not yet fully held. Both are real needs and they point in opposite directions.

### Q: What actually happened?
Her framing came from noticing what was missing in the literature. Couples therapy had a great deal to say about conflict, communication and repair, and almost nothing about desire in a long relationship, which was treated either as a medical question or as a symptom of an unfixed conflict. So the people who arrived saying nothing is wrong and nothing is there had no category to be put in, and were routinely treated for a problem they did not have. Naming it was most of the contribution.

### The parts · Two needs crowding, not love fading
Read as love fading, the only moves are blaming yourself or blaming them. Read as crowding, the move is clear: not repairing the love, but making room again for the one that got squeezed out.

### The parts · A wound and an emptiness need opposite moves
Rupture has a wound — contempt, betrayal, sustained attack — and mending starts with stopping and apologising. Flatness has none and needs adding to. Get it backwards and it worsens: apologising when you should be adding, booking trips when you should be apologising.

### The parts · Count presence, not hours
Together is duration, present is attention. The first stacks up easily and the second can be zero for a week. Fifteen minutes a day facing each other with the phones down changes how it feels; a whole weekend in the same room may not.

### Q: How do I use it today?
If you don't fight and aren't close, check for a wound first: in the last three months, any contempt, old grievances, belittling in front of others? If none, this is emptiness, and repeatedly sitting down to discuss the relationship will talk away the last of the ease. Ask instead when you each last did something separately and came back with something to say.

### Lines to keep
Intimacy wants closeness. Desire wants distance. Both are real. A wound is mended, an emptiness is filled. Opposite directions. Same sofa, separate phones: zero minutes present.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
John Gottman — He can tell you whether it will last; she can tell you why it stopped feeling like anything while lasting. Virginia Satir — Both look past the argument on the surface — Perel at what the relationship is missing, Satir at which layer the argument is really on.

### Further
John Gottman Harvard Study of Adult Development

## Excellent Sheep
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/excellent-sheep/
Tags: Learning and growth, Modern, Can clear, can't choose

Excellent Sheep (2014 · William Deresiewicz) — Can clear, can't choose. A critique of elite education by someone who taught at Yale for ten years and sat on admissions.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A critique of elite education by someone who taught at Yale for ten years and sat on admissions. His observation: the system produces young people who are extraordinarily good at clearing a series of set hurdles — grades, competitions, internships, the CV — and who generally cannot say what they want. Very capable, entirely externally directed, lost the moment there is no next hurdle, and unusually afraid of failure because they have never been allowed to fail.

### Q: What actually happened?
He left academia after writing it. The book began as an essay that circulated very widely, and the argument it makes — that the institutions doing the selecting are the problem, not the students being selected — is not one that makes a person welcome inside those institutions. That is worth knowing before reading it as a lecture to young people. His target is the machinery: every step in it rational, and the sum a life with no direction.

### The parts · Two abilities that don't substitute
'Be best at this' is drilled constantly inside any evaluation system. 'Decide what's worth doing' can only be trained where there is no correct answer. So the smoother the run, the likelier the second is blank. e.g. Ten years of being the person who clears every bar, and the first question with no right answer — should we even build this — is the one he can't start.

### The parts · Never having failed makes failure unimaginable
The price of an unbroken record is no experience of failing, so failure gets imagined as catastrophic — and the result is avoiding anything you might not be good at, with a range that narrows year by year. e.g. She picked the third language she already half-knew over the one she wanted, because a visible beginner year was unthinkable.

### The parts · The prescription is time with no scoreboard
Not a different subject or a different job, but a stretch long enough to get past novelty, doing something nobody is grading. Where a metric exists, attention slides to it, so the question can only surface somewhere without one. e.g. Six months of pottery with nobody grading it did more than another certificate, precisely because there was no number to optimise.

### Q: How do I use it today?
If you can say exactly what counts as doing well and can't say what you want, do one thing that isn't scored, for long enough to get past the novelty. Facing any opportunity, separate two things: is it the content that draws me, or is it simply the next hurdle on the track I'm already on?

### Lines to keep
Superb at clearing hurdles, and unable to say where they were going. Never allowed to fail, you imagine failure as unsurvivable. Only when nobody is grading you do you find out what you want.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Pu Songling — Two ways of having no scoreboard: they were never given one, he had one and it never once said yes. Harvard Study of Adult Development — Eighty years of data on what actually matters, against a system that scores none of it. Carl Jung — Both describe a life built to someone else's standard. One catches it at twenty-two, the other at forty. Fukuzawa Yukichi — Excellent Sheep diagnoses what happens to someone who lived on scores and then has no scores; Fukuzawa hands a beginner an order of operations instead.

### Further
Pu Songling Carol Dweck Carl Jung Fukuzawa Yukichi

## Fan Li
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/fan-li/
Tags: Money and risk, Pre-Qin and classical, When to go

Fan Li (Spring and Autumn · 536–448 BC) — When to go. The most successful exit in Chinese history. He spent more than twenty years helping the king of Yue climb from hostage to hegemon, and walked away on the day it was…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The most successful exit in Chinese history. He spent more than twenty years helping the king of Yue climb from hostage to hegemon, and walked away on the day it was finished — changed his name, moved three times, and built a great fortune three times over, giving it away on each occasion. He is remembered both as a strategist and as the patron figure of Chinese commerce.

### Q: What actually happened?
The part usually skipped is the twenty years before the exit. Yue had been crushed; its king was a servant in the enemy capital. Fan Li went with him and stayed through the whole of it, and the plan he ran was measured in decades, not seasons — grow the population, stock the granaries, keep the enemy complacent, and do not move early. The man famous for leaving at the right moment had first spent twenty years not leaving. Knowing when to go is not restlessness. It is the same faculty that knows when to stay.

### The parts · Read the person, not the situation
His judgement about the king wasn't 'this is dangerous now' but 'here is what this man becomes when things go well' — true long before it mattered. Situations change; the construction of a person doesn't. e.g. He was generous when the round closed and vicious when it didn't. That wasn't the market changing him; it was one man under two conditions.

### The parts · Buy what nobody wants
In drought, stock boats; in flood, stock carts. The entire difficulty of the rule is that at the moment of buying, every visible piece of evidence says the thing is worthless. e.g. The hard part is not spotting the empty office block. It is signing the lease in the month every person you respect tells you the sector is finished.

### The parts · Letting go is harder than accumulating
Three fortunes made and three given away, a chancellorship returned. Many people can accumulate. Almost nobody puts down a position already in hand and starts again. e.g. Plenty of people can build the team to forty. Almost nobody hands it over while it is still going well and starts again at one.

### Q: How do I use it today?
At every stage of a career, ask periodically: is this relationship, or this job, still in the phase where I gain from it, or has it hit its ceiling and started accumulating risk? The second phase looks exactly like the first from inside.

### Lines to keep
The birds are gone, so the good bow is put away. You can share hardship with him. You cannot share ease. In drought, stock boats. In flood, stock carts.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Li Ka-shing — Two and a half millennia apart, the same two rules: buy when nobody wants it, and leave before the top. Zhang Liang — The two men who understood leaving. Fan Li left to trade, Zhang Liang left to study the way. Different exits, identical result. Zhuge Liang — Two answers to having succeeded: Fan Li walked away at the summit, Zhuge Liang never put it down at all. Li Bi — Two versions of leaving without going far: Fan Li disappeared completely, Li Bi kept walking through the centre of power in a robe that let him leave at will. Guo Jia — Two ways a gifted adviser ends. Guo Jia burned out at thirty-eight inside the work; Fan Li walked away on the day it was won and lived a long time afterwards. Wang Jian — Two ways of leaving at the top: Fan Li vanished and became a merchant, Wang Jian resigned and went home to his fields. Bai Gui — Two ancient fortunes: Fan Li teaches how to get out intact, Bai Gui teaches a method you can repeat. Hu Xueyan — Both worked between officials and trade. Fan Li left at the summit; Hu Xueyan tied the knots tighter every year. Jesse Livermore — Both understood exits. Fan Li left at every summit; Livermore never once got up from the table.

### Further
Li Ka-shing Su Shi Sun Tzu Warren Buffett Han Feizi Pu Songling Guan Zhong Zhang Liang Zhuge Liang Li Bi The I Ching Napoleon Sima Yi Strategies of the Warring States Wang Jian Xiang Yu The Art of Worldly Wisdom Bai Gui Ray Dalio Hu Xueyan Jesse Livermore Records of the Grand Historian Nassim Taleb The Sovereign Individual

## Feng Dao
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/feng-dao/
Tags: Power and organisation, Medieval, Serving ten emperors

Feng Dao (Five Dynasties · 882–954) — Serving ten emperors. The hardest man in Chinese history to grade. He held office through the Later Tang, Later Jin, Later Han and Later Zhou, served ten emperors including the Khitan…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The hardest man in Chinese history to grade. He held office through the Later Tang, Later Jin, Later Han and Later Zhou, served ten emperors including the Khitan conqueror who took the capital, was chief minister under nearly all of them, passed through every change of dynasty untouched and died at seventy-three. Ouyang Xiu called him shameless and Sima Guang the worst of traitors, while in his own lifetime, it was written, wise and foolish alike looked to him as the elder of the age. He is not here to be acquitted. Everyone else in this collection is an example to follow, and a collection with no uncomfortable mirror in it is missing something.

### Q: What actually happened?
Yelu Deguang, having taken the capital, put a question to him in front of the court: and what sort of old fellow are you? The tone was contempt, and any dignified answer would have been an argument with a conqueror. Feng Dao said: an old fellow with no talent and no virtue, foolish and stubborn. No defence, nothing to push against, and the insult found nothing to land on. That was roughly his posture for seventy years. Never meet violence head on, and work in the gaps where it has let go.

### The parts · He moved the object of loyalty
In his scheme the emperor is a replaceable political symbol and the people are the constant. The Five Dynasties gave that view a real basis: fifty-three years, five dynasties, fourteen emperors, and dying for any one of them would have been a joke. It is also the most convenient defence an opportunist could have. The tension does not resolve, and that is the value of the entry. e.g. The useful reading is not guilty or innocent. It is noticing which standard you are judging by, and who set that standard, and for what.

### The parts · Minimum exposed surface
No faction, no troops, no fortune, no enemies, nothing left lying around to be used against him. At each new accession he was the man with the least reason to be purged. His safety came from nobody profiting by his removal, which is the opposite of picking a side. e.g. Hu Xueyan is the inverse case: the patron held tighter and tighter, the exposure grew, and when the patron fell everything was settled at once.

### The parts · Do the work where work is possible
He did not prevent a single change of dynasty and could not have. In office he argued against campaigns, organised famine relief, protected scholars and had the Nine Classics cut and printed, which carried the texts through the disorder and begins large-scale official printing in China. e.g. The fair question about an official in a collapsing order may not be who he was loyal to. It may be how many people were alive because he held that seat.

### The parts · Do not fight for the right to define you
Insulted, he agreed with the insult and made it smaller. There was no target left, so the contempt did no work. Arguing would have made him one. The price of the technique is that you have to genuinely not care about the verdict. e.g. Accepting a diminishing label in your own words removes its force. It also only works if you are not quietly keeping score.

### The parts · The real cost of this road
Do not read him as universal smoothness. Giving up a position meant giving up the power to change anything. He preserved himself and many others, and the Five Dynasties were the Five Dynasties precisely because the whole official class chose his method. e.g. Individually optimal choices can add up to the worst available system. That is the problem he leaves behind, and the reason he is not simply survival advice.

### Q: How do I use it today?
This entry is a diagnostic rather than an instruction. When you are inside something you cannot steer, a company changing direction or a decision you do not agree with, separate two things: what you must take a position on, and what you can still get done without taking one. His method was to make the first as small as possible and the second as large as possible. Keep the cost in view. If everybody chooses this, nothing ever changes, and one day you may find that what you preserved was no longer worth preserving. When to be Feng Dao and when to stand up is the question he leaves with you, and nobody can answer it on your behalf.

### Lines to keep
Not deceiving the earth below, nor men between, nor heaven above. The Buddha could come again and not save them. Only the emperor can. An old fellow with no talent and no virtue, foolish and stubborn. Just do good things. Do not ask about the road ahead.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Guo Ziyi — Two first-rate survivors of disorder, but Guo Ziyi stayed loyal inside one dynasty while Feng Dao crossed four. Where the boundary of loyalty sits, they answer differently. Machiavelli — Machiavelli argued in a book that outcomes outrank motives; Feng Dao spent a life doing it. Theory and specimen, both abused for centuries. Zeng Guofan — Zeng Guofan held an army and cut back his own wings to keep his name; Feng Dao had neither troops nor money and sought only to keep people alive.

### Further
Sima Yi Guo Ziyi Zeng Guofan Machiavelli Su Shi Tending the Roots of Wisdom The Art of Worldly Wisdom

## Finite and Infinite Games
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/finite-and-infinite-games/
Tags: How the world works, Modern, Win, or keep playing

Finite and Infinite Games (1986 · James P. Carse) — Win, or keep playing. A slim book by a professor of religious history at New York University: 101 short sections, no argument, only statements.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A slim book by a professor of religious history at New York University: 101 short sections, no argument, only statements. The distinction it offers is very simple — a finite game is played to win, an infinite game to continue the play. Once it is in your head it rearranges almost everything you thought about ambition, competition, careers and companies, because you start noticing how many of the games you are in were never required to have a winner at all.

### Q: What actually happened?
The book landed with almost no response. It was not a business book and not quite an academic one — a historian of religion writing in aphorisms about games, theatre and death, which pleased neither side. It was properly read only in the internet era, when founders found that it described precisely something they could not name: why some companies win every battle and die, while others never declare victory and are still there. Its best-known reader in China is Wang Xing, and the Meituan value about being patient for the long term stands on this book.

### The parts · Two kinds of games
A finite game has a fixed start, end and winner, its rules cannot change, and players play inside the boundaries. An infinite game has no end, its rules must change so that the play can continue, and players play with the boundaries themselves. e.g. A funding round, a sale, a quarter are finite. A company, a relationship, a person's craft are infinite. Play an infinite game as a finite one and on the day you win you will not know what to do.

### The parts · The rules point in opposite directions
A finite game's rules cannot change or the game is over; an infinite game's rules must change or the game is over. This is the sharpest edge in the book: every 'we have always done it this way' is quietly demoting an infinite game to a finite one. e.g. The policy that made the company work at thirty people, left untouched at three hundred, is not tradition. It is a countdown.

### The parts · Power and strength
Finite players compete for power, which is respect attached to a title and is handed to you by other people. Infinite players play with strength, which needs nobody's recognition and cannot be taken away. e.g. Whatever is still there after the title is swapped out is the strength. Most career anxiety comes from the two having been treated as one thing for years.

### The parts · Serious against playful
Finite players are serious, because the outcome touches their title. Infinite players are playful, because they can change the rules at any moment. Playful does not mean careless; it means having kept the freedom to change something. e.g. The person who can laugh in the middle of a negotiation usually has another option. Seriousness is often just the absence of one.

### The parts · Titles need an audience
A finite game needs spectators to certify the win — a champion nobody saw does not hold. An infinite game has no audience, only players. Any achievement that has to be watched in order to exist is a finite game. e.g. If the reason to do it evaporates the moment nobody will know, that was a finite game wearing a long-term costume.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Next time a situation has you tense, ask one question before any other: is this finite or infinite? If it is finite, define what winning means, play it out, and leave it at the office. If it is infinite, stop chasing an endgame and put your attention on staying able to keep playing. It works especially well on careers — a promotion is a finite game, capability is an infinite one, and only one of them ends.

### Lines to keep
A finite game is played for the purpose of winning. An infinite game is played for the purpose of continuing the play. Finite players play within boundaries; infinite players play with boundaries. The rules of a finite game may not change; the rules of an infinite game must.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Sun Tzu — Sun Tzu solves competition entirely as a finite game and every technique serves the win; Carse asks why you assumed this round had to end at all. Peter Thiel — Thiel's monopoly is a finite game won completely, and Carse would point out that the moment you have won, that game is over. Zhuangzi — The use of the useless runs the same way as the infinite game: not winning inside the given rules, but keeping room to change them.

### Further
Wang Xing Zhuangzi Thinking in Systems Naval Ravikant Nietzsche Ivan Illich

## Friedrich Hayek
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/hayek/
Tags: How the world works, The industrial age, Dispersed knowledge

Friedrich Hayek (Austria–Britain · 1899–1992) — Dispersed knowledge. The man who turned why planning goes systematically wrong into economics. Not because planners are lazy, but because the knowledge a plan needs sits in thousands of…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The man who turned why planning goes systematically wrong into economics. Not because planners are lazy, but because the knowledge a plan needs sits in thousands of separate heads and will not travel. Prices are the transport protocol for that knowledge. He argued with Keynes for a lifetime, and what won in the end was not rhetoric but this one point about who can know what.

### Q: What actually happened?
By the 1950s he was, inside his own profession, close to forgotten. Keynes had won the argument, governments were managing demand, and Hayek had moved to Chicago into a committee on social thought rather than the economics department, which did not want him. He was seventy-five when the Nobel came in 1974, and he used the lecture to attack his own discipline: he called it The Pretence of Knowledge, and argued that economics had made itself unscientific by imitating physics, measuring what could be measured and ignoring the causes that could not.

### The parts · Knowledge is dispersed
The knowledge that matters is not in papers; it is the detail of here and now — who is short-staffed, who has stock left, which road is blocked. That list exists in no single head, and no reporting line can assemble it before it expires. e.g. Zhang Yiming's feed gathers scattered clicks into a signal: the price mechanism as a product. A head-office spreadsheet meant to replace the market is the counter-example.

### The parts · A price is a protocol
A price is not a verdict on value; it is a compressed message. You do not need to know why it moved, only that it moved, in order to change what you do next. e.g. When oil rises, drivers and chemical plants across the world change behaviour within days, and no minister had to call them together.

### The parts · Spontaneous order
An order nobody designed is still an order. Language, markets and legal custom are all of this kind. You can intervene in them, but the cost of the intervention usually turns up somewhere you were not watching. e.g. Taleb's antifragility says do not sand a system down until one person can control it. Hayek is the ancestor of that sentence.

### The parts · The pretence of knowing
The dangerous thing is not ignorance; it is mistaking your local knowledge for the complete list. The planner's standard disease is the assumption that what he can see is all there is to see. e.g. Annual plans in large companies tend to expire around April, not because the people are stupid, but because the ground keeps moving under the plan.

### The parts · Rules beat commands
A good order constrains behaviour with rules rather than specifying results with orders. Give people a boundary and let them fill it in with the knowledge they have and you do not. e.g. Shang Yang legislated instead of issuing daily orders to each magistrate; Dalio's principles are a boundary, not a trading manual.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Before you write the annual plan, ask what share of the knowledge it depends on is not in your head, and write those blanks down as a list. If the list runs past one page, stop writing the plan as a set of orders and rewrite it as boundaries and signals: what people may not do, and what tells them how much something matters this week.

### Lines to keep
The curious task of economics is to demonstrate how little men really know. The price system is a mechanism for communicating information. Nobody holds all the knowledge that making the plan would require.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
The Wealth of Nations — Smith explains how the division of labour makes brute effort rich; Hayek explains how the information gets back afterwards. Nassim Taleb — Taleb is about not being able to foresee the shock, Hayek about not being able to centralise the knowledge — one handles randomness, the other handles the pretence of knowing.

### Further
The Wealth of Nations Nassim Taleb Zhang Yiming Ray Dalio

## Fukuzawa Yukichi
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/fukuzawa/
Tags: Learning and growth, The industrial age, Relearning

Fukuzawa Yukichi (Japan · 1835–1901) — Relearning. Educator of the Meiji period and founder of Keio Gijuku. In his early twenties he learned Dutch in Osaka and learned it extremely well; in 1859 he walked into the newly…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Educator of the Meiji period and founder of Keio Gijuku. In his early twenties he learned Dutch in Osaka and learned it extremely well; in 1859 he walked into the newly opened port of Yokohama and could not read a single sign, because they were all in English. He did not go back to his Dutch. The next day he started hunting for English textbooks. He then wrote An Encouragement of Learning, which opens with the line that heaven creates no man above or below another, and sold over three million copies, mostly to young people who did not know what to study.

### Q: What actually happened?
In the summer of 1868 the Boshin War reached Tokyo. Fighting broke out at Ueno, close enough that the guns could be heard across the city, and most schools shut. Fukuzawa kept his open. He went on lecturing his students from an American textbook on economics while the battle ran its course a few miles away, and the school later took the date as a point of pride. The gesture was not bravado. It was the same claim his books make in flatter language: what a country and a person are short of is not spirit but usable knowledge, and the day you stop acquiring it is the day the trouble actually starts.

### The parts · Useless is information, not a verdict
Something being useless tells you about the direction, not about your capacity. Once the direction is clear, where the effort should go is obvious. Switch the same week, because every day of waiting adds another chip to the track you are leaving. The real waste is not learning something that expired; it is refusing to change. e.g. When what you trained for stops matching the work, ask what it tells you about direction before you mourn the years.

### The parts · Learn what you will use tomorrow first
His ordering rule has one term in it: frequency of use. Daily first, once a year later. Not because the later ones do not matter, but because a beginner has limited hours. Whether to keep studying is settled the same way, not by the level of the qualification but by whether the reading lands in your hands. e.g. When you cannot decide what to practise, write down the three things you will need at work tomorrow morning and practise those.

### The parts · Move the cause somewhere you can reach
The worst thing about I was born with less is not that it might be false. It is that it parks the cause where nothing can be done. He moves it to whether you studied. Someone looks steady because they practised something three years before you did; translate stronger into earlier and most of the anxiety goes. e.g. An explanation that leaves you with nothing to do is usually the comfortable one rather than the true one.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Write down the three things you will actually need at work tomorrow morning, and be honest about which of them you are still slow at. Practise those this week and nothing else. If you are carrying years of training that no longer fits, do not spend the week deciding whether those years were wasted; spend ten minutes a day on the new thing starting today, and separately list what you built while learning the old one, because the method transfers even when the content does not.

### Lines to keep
Heaven does not create one man above or below another man. Learn what you need tomorrow first. Once a year can wait. The gap was made after birth, so it can be closed.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Excellent Sheep — Excellent Sheep diagnoses what happens to someone who lived on scores and then has no scores; Fukuzawa hands a beginner an order of operations instead. Bruce Lee — Both say the inherited set of moves stops working, but Fukuzawa is the more literal of the two: change the content the day you see it, keep the method.

### Further
Anders Ericsson Excellent Sheep Kazuo Inamori Garry Kasparov Bruce Lee
