## Gandhi
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/gandhi/
Tags: Reading people, The industrial age, Nonviolence

Gandhi (India · 1869–1948) — Nonviolence. An Indian lawyer thrown off a train in South Africa who ended up leading an empire out of his country without a battle.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
An Indian lawyer thrown off a train in South Africa who ended up leading an empire out of his country without a battle. What he demonstrated is narrower and more interesting than the legend: under specific conditions, moral pressure plus sheer endurance beats military force. His instruments were salt, a spinning wheel, fasting and walking. The conditions matter, and he said so himself: the method works on an opponent who still needs to look legitimate.

### Q: What actually happened?
In South Africa he was jailed by Jan Smuts, the general who was his chief opponent there. In prison Gandhi made a pair of sandals by hand and, on his release, sent them to Smuts as a gift. Smuts kept them for a quarter of a century. In 1939, on Gandhi's seventieth birthday, he returned them, with a note saying he had worn them for many summers and had never felt worthy to stand in the shoes of so great a man. One pair of sandals accomplished what no speech of his ever did.

### The parts · The physics of nonviolence
Satyagraha, truth-force, is not passive non-resistance but an active moral offensive. Faced with unjust force you can answer in kind, which means entering the game the other side is expert at, or absorb it and transfer the moral cost to them. What a violent regime fears is not greater violence, it is a problem that violence cannot close. e.g. His demands on followers were severe: struck, do not strike back; insulted, do not answer; arrested, do not run. Every act of endurance accumulated capital, and every crackdown spent the other side's legitimacy.

### The parts · Do the thing you are asking for
Be the change you want to see has been worn into a greeting card, but he meant it literally. He asked Indians to spin their own cloth and boycott British goods, and he span for an hour a day until he died. He asked people to fast, and he fasted to the edge of his life more than once. Leadership was not go and do it, it was watch me first. e.g. Most reformers fail on exactly this line: they require of others what they have not done. He gave up a comfortable legal career, wore homespun, lived in an ashram and held no privileges.

### The parts · Keep the opponent human
He never defined the British as evil. He defined them as people acting inside a wrong system, and held that a conscience existed in each of them that the movement was there to wake rather than destroy. That framing is what made the campaign legible far outside India: not one nation against another, but conscience against an unjust arrangement. e.g. It also made surrender survivable. An enemy who has been declared evil cannot concede without disgrace, so he will fight past the point of sense.

### The parts · The means decide what you end up with
In Hind Swaraj he settled the question in 1909: the means are the seed and the end is the tree, and the connection between them is as fixed as the one between seed and tree. An India taken by force would be run by people who were good at force, which he called English rule without the Englishman. e.g. The test travels: whatever capability wins a fight becomes the capability the winners promote for, long after the fight is over.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Next time you face someone stronger, add a dimension nobody in the room is counting: what does pressure cost them in legitimacy? In some contests declining to hit back is the heaviest available blow, because it moves the entire moral cost onto the other side and leaves them no dignified move.

### Lines to keep
With this, I am shaking the foundations of the British Empire. The means may be likened to a seed, the end to a tree. Nonviolence is the weapon of the strong.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Nelson Mandela — The same idea one generation on: Mandela began with armed struggle and arrived at Gandhi's position after twenty-seven years in prison, which makes his version the tested one. Machiavelli — The two answers to whether the end justifies the means: Machiavelli says judge by the result, Gandhi says the result is already contained in the method.

### Further
Nelson Mandela Viktor Frankl Marcus Aurelius Socrates

## Garry Kasparov
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/kasparov/
Tags: Learning and growth, Modern, After losing to the machine

Garry Kasparov (1963– · Baku) — After losing to the machine. World chess champion for fifteen years, from 1985 to 2000. In 1996 he beat IBM's Deep Blue in Philadelphia; in the May 1997 rematch in New York he lost 2.5–3.5, the…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
World chess champion for fifteen years, from 1985 to 2000. In 1996 he beat IBM's Deep Blue in Philadelphia; in the May 1997 rematch in New York he lost 2.5–3.5, the first time a reigning world champion lost a match to a machine. Most people in this library are dealing with other people. He is dealing with something else: what is left of a craft you spent a life on after a machine passes you at the thing it is built on.

### Q: What actually happened?
The 1996 match is usually left out, and it matters. He won it 4–2, losing only the first game — the first time a machine had beaten a world champion under tournament conditions, which at the time was itself the headline. He then had a year to prepare, and IBM had a year to rebuild. What he faced in 1997 was not the machine he had beaten. That is the ordinary shape of it: you win the first round against a tool, conclude the threat was overstated, and meet a different thing the following year.

### The parts · Strike out what is already lost
The day machines won on depth of calculation, that track closed. Training on a closed track has no exit however hard you train. The first move isn't redoubling effort; it's removing the lost item from your own list of what you are worth. e.g. No amount of practice makes you faster than the model at drafting a first version. The real question is which part of the work that leaves you.

### The parts · Change the rules, not the effort
He didn't train harder and he didn't leave chess. A year later he staged a tournament where each side brought a computer to the board. When a tool matches an ability, the valuable position moves to how the tool is used — and someone has to define that position first. e.g. The translators who priced per word lost. The ones who charged for deciding what not to translate did not.

### The parts · The appeal and the next move cost the same hours
He spent years arguing the match hadn't been fair, and withdrew all of it in 2017. Proving the loss didn't count and working out what to train next come out of the same person in the same stretch of time. e.g. The months spent proving the review was unfair were the same months available for the work that would have made the review irrelevant.

### Q: How do I use it today?
When a core skill in your field gets matched by a tool, don't train harder first. Ask which item is now clearly lost, strike it out, and see what's left that the tool can't replace. And if you notice yourself repeating that it isn't actually any good, count how many times this month — then count what new thing you practised in the same month.

### Lines to keep
Calculation was already lost, so stop competing on calculation. The first step isn't more effort. It's striking out what's lost. Whatever replaced you does not need your agreement.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Norbert Wiener — One built the thing and warned the people it would displace; the other was displaced and redesigned the contest. Hannah Arendt — Both answer the tool did my thinking for me. Kasparov puts the human back where the machines disagree; Arendt says handing over judgement is a state in itself, whoever takes it. The Last Hot-Metal Edition — One is a single person overtaken by a machine and free to change the rules he plays by; this is a whole trade erased in a night, with no such room.

### Further
Norbert Wiener John Boyd Hannah Arendt Fukuzawa Yukichi The Last Hot-Metal Edition

## George Soros
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/soros/
Tags: Money and risk, The industrial age, Reflexivity

George Soros (1930– · Budapest and New York) — Reflexivity. Founder of the Quantum Fund, and the man who forced the Bank of England to give way, making a billion dollars in a day.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Founder of the Quantum Fund, and the man who forced the Bank of England to give way, making a billion dollars in a day. His larger contribution is not the money but reflexivity, which overturns the assumption that markets are rational. Participants' expectations move the market, and the market moves their expectations back, and the loop never settles into equilibrium. He is a student of Popper, and the whole method rests on one habit: taking seriously, in advance, that he may be wrong.

### Q: What actually happened?
16 September 1992, Black Wednesday. Sterling had been forced into the European exchange rate mechanism at a rate that flattered it, and the British economy was paying for the flattery. Soros judged that the position could not hold, that the government would eventually have to leave, and that sterling would fall hard when it did. He borrowed heavily and sold. The Bank of England bought pounds all day and spent billions failing to hold the line. That afternoon Britain announced its withdrawal, sterling collapsed, and his profit for the day passed a billion dollars. He said afterwards that he had not attacked the pound. He had corrected a false equilibrium.

### The parts · Reflexivity
Mainstream economics assumes markets tend towards equilibrium. Soros says that is simply wrong. Expectations shape behaviour, behaviour shapes the market, and the market reshapes expectations. It is a loop that never converges, and the market is not a machine seeking balance but a system being made by the beliefs it is also making. e.g. Houses rise, buyers expect more rises, more buyers arrive, prices rise again, speculators pile in, the bubble forms. It runs until something outside it breaks the circuit.

### The parts · Fallibility as a working method
I am more aware than anyone that I might be wrong, and he means it operationally: every position is built on the assumption that the assumption behind it could be false. When it turns out false he cuts immediately and does not argue for himself. e.g. Before shorting sterling he kept asking where his own case could break — what if the Bank defends the rate at any cost? He sized the bet only after judging those branches survivable.

### The parts · Boom and bust
Applied to the macro picture: every large boom contains a trend that participants have misread, the misreading drives the boom, the boom reinforces the misreading, and the gap between belief and reality eventually grows too wide to hold. Naming the current misconception is his core analytical move. e.g. 2008: the misconception was that house prices only go up. It drove the subprime boom, the boom confirmed the misconception, reality punctured it, and the system went down.

### The parts · Knowing when you're wrong
He credits his fortune to recognising his mistakes rather than to being right, and pairs it with the rule that what matters is not whether you are right but how much you make when you are and lose when you are not. The two together are one system. e.g. Wrong ten times at a small cost each and right once at ten times over is a winning year, and it is only reachable if your pride has been moved off being right.

### The parts · The open society
Fallibility is a political philosophy too. No institution or ideology is perfect, so a society has to stay open enough for error to be found and corrected. A closed society is one that claims it cannot be wrong; an open one accepts that it will be and builds the machinery to fix it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
On the next decision that matters, write down your core assumption first, then interrogate it one line at a time: under what circumstances would this be falsified? If it is falsified, what is the plan? Fix the falsifying condition and the exit before you commit, and give somebody else the job of holding you to it. The point is to build might be wrong into the decision process rather than admitting it afterwards, when the admission costs the most and convinces you least.

### Lines to keep
I'm only rich because I know when I'm wrong. Market prices always distort the underlying fundamentals. There is no shame in being wrong, only in failing to correct our mistakes. Markets can influence the events that they anticipate.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Warren Buffett — Two poles of investment philosophy: Buffett trusts that the market gets there in the end, Soros treats it as permanently wrong. Nassim Taleb — Two bets on uncertainty: Soros finds the market's error and pushes on it, Taleb builds a structure that pays when the error finally breaks. The Crowd — Reflexivity is the financial version of this book: the crowd's mistaken belief moves the price and the price confirms the belief. Le Bon describes the pathology, Soros priced it. Benjamin Graham — Graham assumes price returns to value; Soros trades the stretch where price drives value away from itself. Jim Simons — Soros uses reflexivity to understand the market, Simons gave up understanding entirely — and the money comes out of the same place.

### Further
Ray Dalio Warren Buffett Nassim Taleb Charlie Munger The Crowd Jesse Livermore Howard Marks Jim Simons Thinking, Fast and Slow

## Guan Zhong
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/guan-zhong/
Tags: Power and organisation, Pre-Qin and classical, Granaries first

Guan Zhong (Spring and Autumn · 723–645 BC) — Granaries first. The first statesman in China to think systematically about the relation between the economy and government.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The first statesman in China to think systematically about the relation between the economy and government. He took Qi from an ordinary state to the leading power of its age, and Confucius, who disliked much about him, still said that without Guan Zhong we would be wearing our hair loose and folding our coats to the left. His method is consistent: fix the material floor first, then design along what people already want.

### Q: What actually happened?
As young men he and Bao Shuya ran a business together, and Guan Zhong took the larger share of the profit. Bao Shuya did not call him greedy; he said the man's family was poor. Later, with Duke Huan newly on the throne and Guan Zhong on the losing side of the succession, Bao Shuya pressed his case: if you only want to govern Qi, I am enough; if you want to lead the realm, it has to be Guan Zhong. Near the end of his life Guan Zhong said his parents gave him life, and Bao Shuya was the one who knew him.

### The parts · Make the people rich, then the state is strong
The way to govern must begin with making the people prosperous. Full granaries, and the people know propriety; sufficient food and clothing, and they know honour and shame. Below a certain material floor, moral instruction is not wrong, it simply does not do anything. e.g. A team paid below market holds a values workshop and leaves faster. The identical workshop after the pay correction is a different event entirely.

### The parts · Put the tax inside the price
He placed the state monopoly on salt and iron, so revenue arrived through the price of goods people were buying anyway. The treasury filled without anyone experiencing a levy. The collection mechanism matters as much as the rate. e.g. A platform taking a percentage of each transaction feels different to sellers from an invoice for the same amount, even when the number is identical.

### The parts · Choose the frame the contest is fought in
He gave Duke Huan the slogan of honouring the king and repelling the tribes, which converted an ordinary struggle between states into a contest between order and disorder. Once the frame is accepted, every move inside it reads differently. e.g. Whoever names the category is choosing which comparisons the audience will make. That is a cheaper advantage than any product feature.

### The parts · Design along what people already want
Government flourishes by following the hearts of the people and fails by going against them. He starts every design from what people hate — toil, poverty, danger — and makes sure the measure does not touch it. He does not reform desire; he digs it a channel. e.g. A rule that cuts against a widespread preference is never opposed openly. It is quietly worked around, and the workarounds keep improving.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Before the next conversation about culture or mission, check the pay. If someone on the team is worrying about rent, a session on values is not just ineffective, it reads as a substitute for the money. Fix the floor first and hold the same session a month later.

### Lines to keep
Full granaries, and the people know propriety. The way to govern a state must begin with making people rich. One year, plant grain. Ten years, trees. A lifetime, people. My parents gave me life. Bao Shuya is the one who knew me.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Shang Yang — Two routes to a strong state: Guan Zhong enriches the people and the state follows, Shang Yang installs the law and the wealth follows. Zhuge Liang — Two first ministers serving an ambitious lord. Guan Zhong's man became hegemon; Zhuge Liang's cause never arrived. Lee Kuan Yew — Two operators building a small state from nothing, twenty-six centuries apart: Guan Zhong through trade and price control, Lee through institutions and balance. The Wealth of Nations — Two origins for the idea of national wealth: Guan Zhong steers prices and money from the centre, Smith lets price discover itself. The argument has not moved in twenty-five centuries.

### Further
The Wealth of Nations Fan Li Sun Tzu Han Feizi Cao Cao Lee Kuan Yew Shang Yang Zhang Juzheng

## Guiguzi
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/guiguzi/
Tags: Reading people, Pre-Qin and classical, Open, close, sound out

Guiguzi (Warring States · c. 400–320 BC) — Open, close, sound out. The founding text of the Warring States persuaders, attributed to a recluse of Ghost Valley about whom nothing verifiable survives.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The founding text of the Warring States persuaders, attributed to a recluse of Ghost Valley about whom nothing verifiable survives. It is the one Chinese classic that is a systematic handbook on moving a single specific person: not whether a thing ought to be said, only how speech should be opened, closed, tested and locked. Orthodox scholars called it a book for small men and had it suppressed repeatedly. It never disappeared, because anyone whose work depends on getting one other person to move ends up needing what is in it.

### Q: What actually happened?
Tradition sends both Su Qin and Zhang Yi to the same teacher in Ghost Valley. Su Qin then sold the vertical alliance, six states banded against Qin; Zhang Yi sold the horizontal one, six states each cutting its own deal with Qin. One school, two men on exactly opposite sides, each carrying a chancellor's seal, fighting each other for half a lifetime. It is usually told against him, as proof that the school had no position. That is the point of the book. Vertical and horizontal are two faces of one technique, and which face gets used is decided by the situation. The silk manuscripts found at Mawangdui place Su Qin a generation after Zhang Yi, so the shared classroom is probably a later reconstruction; the story lasted anyway, because it names the thing accurately.

### The parts · Opening and closing are a pair of tools
To open is to speak, to close is to keep silent, and the mouth is the door of the heart. Speech and silence are two weapons rather than one default state. Most people's problem is not that they cannot speak; it is that they cannot stop. e.g. The most expensive sentence in a negotiation is usually the one that breaks the silence after your own price.

### The parts · To hear him speak, be silent
Four reversals: to hear him, be silent; to have him open out, draw in; to stand high, stand low; to take, first give. Each of them is a sequence rather than a posture — nothing is exchanged until something has been put down first. e.g. Want their timeline? Give yours. Most people match it, and it is information you cannot get by asking for it directly.

### The parts · Weigh the hard facts, then sound out the wants
Two separate operations. Weighing is the countable side — what he holds, where he stands, what his fallback is. Sounding is the other one: what he actually wants and what he is actually afraid of, read at the moments when he has no attention left for editing. e.g. Diligence before terms and terms before diligence are two different transactions. The second argues price over an assumption nobody checked.

### The parts · Knowing begins with yourself
Know yourself and then you know others. Every judgement you make about a person passes through your own instrument, and an uncalibrated instrument adds the same error to everything it measures. This is the precondition the manipulation reading skips. e.g. If slow talkers always strike you as unreliable, that is a fixed offset, not a talent for reading people.

### The parts · Hold the initiative rather than be held
The whole book lands here: it is better to control others than to be controlled by them. Whoever defines the question, sets the tempo and decides when it ends is holding the exchange, whatever the stated agenda says. e.g. Look at last week. Did you write the calendar, or did their moves write it for you?

### Q: How do I use it today?
Before the next conversation that matters, write down two lines instead of a script: what am I putting down first, and what does not have to be given at this stage. Then ask your question and count to five before saying anything else. The silence will return more than the follow-up would have.

### Lines to keep
The mouth is the door of the heart. To hear him speak, be silent. To take, first give. Knowing begins with yourself; know yourself, then you know others. It is better to control others than to be controlled by them.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Influence — The same set of human switches, approached from opposite ends: Cialdini runs experiments and teaches you to spot them being pulled, Guiguzi writes the operating manual. The Analects — Confucius asks whether a thing should be said at all; Guiguzi asks only how to say it so that it works. The avowed and the suppressed halves of the same tradition. Nonviolent Communication — Two opposite arts of persuasion: Guiguzi works out what the other side is holding before moving on them, Rosenberg puts both sides' needs on the table in the open.

### Further
Strategies of the Warring States Han Feizi Influence The Art of Worldly Wisdom Zhang Liang Chris Voss Nonviolent Communication

## Guns, Germs, and Steel
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/guns-germs-steel/
Tags: How the world works, Modern, Environment, not race

Guns, Germs, and Steel (1997 · Jared Diamond) — Environment, not race. Diamond's 1997 book, which took the Pulitzer the following year. It answers a question almost everyone has had and few ask out loud: why did Europeans arrive in the…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Diamond's 1997 book, which took the Pulitzer the following year. It answers a question almost everyone has had and few ask out loud: why did Europeans arrive in the Americas and Oceania with guns, germs and steel rather than the other way round. His answer is environment rather than people — the gaps between continents in domesticable species and in geographical axis, run through food production as the intermediate variable, widened over thirteen thousand years into gaps in technology, writing, organisation and immunity.

### Q: What actually happened?
At Cajamarca in 1532, Pizarro took the Inca emperor with a hundred and sixty-eight men. The story is usually told as nerve, horses and steel. Diamond's version starts earlier: smallpox had already crossed the continent ahead of any Spaniard, killed the previous emperor and his heir, and left a civil war behind it. What those hundred and sixty-eight men walked into was a state that had just finished fighting itself. The germs did more of the conquering than the guns, and the germs came from thousands of years of living beside domesticated animals.

### The parts · Proximate and ultimate causes
Guns, germs and steel are only proximate causes; they are results. Trace back and the ultimate cause is food production: whoever got farming and herding first got density, surplus and specialisation, and after those came states, writing, metal and armies. e.g. Asking why the Spanish had steel swords leads nowhere. Ask why Eurasia could feed a class of blacksmiths who did not have to farm.

### The parts · Domesticable species are very unevenly spread
Of the world's wild mammals over forty-five kilograms, only fourteen were ever domesticated, and thirteen of those came from Eurasia. He calls it the Anna Karenina principle: domesticable animals are all alike, and each undomesticable one fails in its own way — temperament, diet, breeding, herd structure. e.g. A zebra looks like a horse and has never been domesticated: it bites and will not let go. Africa tried. That route was simply closed.

### The parts · The direction of the continental axis
Eurasia runs east to west, so one latitude gives similar climate and crops, livestock and techniques shift sideways for thousands of miles. The Americas and Africa run north to south, and spreading across climate zones is slow or impossible. A line on a map set the speed of diffusion. e.g. Wheat needed no re-domestication to reach Europe and India. Maize took thousands of years to get from Mexico to eastern North America, and had to be bred for it.

### The parts · Germs are a by-product of livestock
Smallpox, measles and influenza all came out of densely kept animals. Eurasians paid for them over millennia and carried the immunity as a result. When those germs reached the Americas with people, they killed far more than the guns did. e.g. In the century after contact, disease is reckoned to have removed the large majority of the population of the Americas, most of whom never saw a European.

### The parts · Optimal fragmentation
Europe's broken terrain produced a long-running system of competing states: one king turned Columbus down and there was another to ask. China's unity meant a single bad decision could lock the whole country — Zheng He's fleets were stopped by one court order and there was no second backer. e.g. Unity buys efficiency, fragmentation buys options. It holds for countries, and it holds for industries and for companies.

### Q: How do I use it today?
What it gives you is a discipline of attribution: when you see a large gap in outcomes, do not reach first for quality, will or culture. Step back two moves and look for structural starting conditions — initial resources, routes of transmission, density, time. It works on industries, companies, cities and even on a person's CV, and it will almost always make your judgement a little more accurate and a little less moral.

### Lines to keep
History followed different courses for different peoples because of differences among peoples' environments. Domesticable animals are all alike; every undomesticable animal is undomesticable in its own way. What conquered the Americas was not mainly the guns, but the germs that arrived with them. The largest patterns in history come from the differences between continental environments.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Why Nations Fail — The most direct argument in the library: Diamond makes geography the ultimate cause, Acemoglu makes institutions the root and geography only the backdrop. The two sides have answered each other in public. Sapiens — Both work at the ten-thousand-year scale; Diamond explains why the continents differ, Harari why this one species is peculiar. Thinking in Systems — Axes, diffusion, density, feedback — Diamond is writing a system-dynamics case study that runs for thirteen thousand years.

### Further
Sapiens Why Nations Fail The Wealth of Nations Thinking in Systems The Old Regime and the Revolution

## Guo Jia
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/guo-jia/
Tags: Strategy and competition, Qin, Han and the Six Dynasties, Count, don't cheer

Guo Jia (Three Kingdoms · 170–207) — Count, don't cheer. Cao Cao's most trusted adviser, and the one he called his extraordinary aide. He arrived at twenty-seven and for the next eleven years stood behind almost every decision…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Cao Cao's most trusted adviser, and the one he called his extraordinary aide. He arrived at twenty-seven and for the next eleven years stood behind almost every decision that mattered: the ten defeats and ten victories before Guandu, the argument for striking north at once, and the plan for Liaodong that he left behind when he died. What the three have in common is a refusal to work in impressions. Each replaces a feeling with something that can be checked, subtracted or waited out.

### Q: What actually happened?
He went to Yuan Shao first. After one meeting he told his friends that Shao was full of schemes and short on essentials, fond of planning and unable to decide, and would never come to anything, and he left, at a time when Shao was the strongest man in the north and Cao Cao was not. He was introduced to Cao Cao, and they talked. This, he said afterwards, is truly my lord. He was twenty-seven. Eleven years later he was dead at thirty-eight, and after the defeat at Red Cliff Cao Cao said that had Guo Jia lived, he would never have come to this.

### The parts · Ten defeats and ten victories
Facing a stronger opponent, his method was not encouragement but decomposition: turn who will win into ten specific sub-questions and answer each. The value is that a feeling becomes a judgement, and a judgement can be argued with item by item. e.g. We cannot beat the incumbent is a mood. Cost structure, delivery time, decision speed and channel depth, compared one by one, usually show you are not weak everywhere.

### The parts · The window that closes
After Yuan Shao died and his son fled to the Wuhuan, everyone advised securing the rear first. Guo Jia pressed for an immediate march north: speed is the essence of war, and a chance that exists briefly is gone once the other side is settled in. e.g. The first two years of a new technology are the cheap years, because nothing is fixed yet. Enter after the positions harden and the price doubles.

### The parts · The last plan, and the patience in it
Dying, he left word not to attack Gongsun Kang but to wait for him to send the heads himself. Press two wary parties and they combine against you; ease off and the old account between them reopens. Withdrawal here is a specific act, not a surrender. e.g. Two departments stop fighting each other the moment you intervene, and align their story against you instead. Step out and the real conflict comes back.

### The parts · The person hardest to replace
What Cao Cao lost was not an executor. It was the one man who could see the shape of a situation and say so to his face. A team without anyone willing to say this one is wrong loses decision quality steadily, and not because anybody got stupider. e.g. Count the people in your last three meetings who contradicted the most senior person present. If the count is zero, that is the finding.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Take the competitive judgement you are least sure of and stop arguing about it as a whole. Write five to ten named dimensions, score each one, and start with a page listing the three ways the other side genuinely beats you.

### Lines to keep
Shao has ten defeats and you have ten victories. Speed is the essence of war. Press him and they combine; ease off and they plot against each other. Shao is full of schemes and short on essentials.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Zhuge Liang — The two great advisers of the age divide on risk: Guo Jia looks for the move nobody expects and takes the narrow window, Zhuge Liang builds the position that cannot be knocked over. Fan Li — Two ways a gifted adviser ends. Guo Jia burned out at thirty-eight inside the work; Fan Li walked away on the day it was won and lived a long time afterwards.

### Further
Cao Cao Sun Tzu Han Feizi

## Guo Ziyi
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/guo-ziyi/
Tags: Power and organisation, Medieval, Great merit, no threat

Guo Ziyi (Tang · 697–781) — Great merit, no threat. The general who put down the An Lushan rebellion, retook the capital twice, held off the Tibetans and kept the Uighurs friendly.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The general who put down the An Lushan rebellion, retook the capital twice, held off the Tibetans and kept the Uighurs friendly. His real achievement is not on the battlefield. He served four emperors, and the official history says his merit covered the empire and his ruler did not suspect him, his rank was the highest and nobody resented it. He died in bed at eighty-five. Han Xin and almost everyone else in his position did not, and what he did differently was a deliberate, expensive, lifelong piece of engineering.

### Q: What actually happened?
The eunuch Yu Chaoen hated him, and while he was away with the army had his father's grave dug up. The court waited for the response: he had the troops, and everyone assumed he would use them. He came back, wept in front of the emperor, and said that he had commanded armies for years and had not been able to stop his own soldiers desecrating graves, so what had happened to his family was heaven's judgement, not any man's doing. There was nothing left to accuse him of. Later Yu Chaoen invited him to dinner; everyone said it was a trap; he went with a few servants, and Yu Chaoen wept and became his protector.

### The parts · Swallow the blow you cannot answer
He could have retaliated and would have won the exchange. He would also have proved that a general with an army settles his own scores, which was exactly the charge against him. Refusing the fight cost him a grave and bought him the emperor's certainty. e.g. Winning an argument with someone who can outlast you often costs more than the argument was worth.

### The parts · Bind your own family first
When his son quarrelled with the princess and said something that could have ended the clan, Guo Ziyi tied him up and delivered him to the emperor before anyone else could. The point is not the punishment. Handing over the evidence yourself leaves nobody anything to prosecute. e.g. Reporting your own team's failure before it is discovered changes what the conversation can be about.

### The parts · Give the command back the same day
He was stripped of his armies repeatedly. Every time the order arrived he set out for the capital that day, and every time he was recalled he went the same day. He treated command as borrowed. Plenty of people can pick power up; the rare thing is putting it down without argument. e.g. Han Xin, in the same position, bargained for a bigger title. Each move proved he was a risk, and eventually he was treated as one.

### The parts · Do not present as flawless
In old age he lived lavishly and made no attempt to hide it. That was not decay, it was design. A man with an obvious appetite is legible and therefore manageable. A man who wants nothing invites the question of what he really wants. e.g. Wang Jian, before invading Chu, kept pestering the king for estates. Same craft: display one harmless want, to cover the suspicion that matters.

### Q: How do I use it today?
After a win, the safer position is being easy to see through, not being indispensable. Publish more than you are asked to, report your own mistakes first, and hand back whatever authority you no longer need. The question to ask after doing something well is not what else can I get, but what should I put down.

### Lines to keep
His merit covered the empire and his ruler did not suspect him. I deal with people honestly, so what would I need defences for? Command is a borrowed thing: it comes when called and goes when waved away.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Han Xin — The same impossible position: Han Xin kept proving he was a threat and his clan was destroyed, Guo Ziyi kept proving he was harmless and died in bed. Zhang Liang — Two ways to survive success: Zhang Liang left the table, Guo Ziyi stayed at it with his cards face up, which is much the harder trick. Feng Dao — Two first-rate survivors of disorder, but Guo Ziyi stayed loyal inside one dynasty while Feng Dao crossed four. Where the boundary of loyalty sits, they answer differently.

### Further
Han Xin Zhang Liang Zeng Guofan Sima Yi Wang Jian Feng Dao Li Bi

## Han Feizi
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/han-feizi/
Tags: Power and organisation, Pre-Qin and classical, Law, method, position

Han Feizi (Warring States · 280–233 BC) — Law, method, position. The systematiser of Chinese Legalism, who combined law, administrative method and positional authority into one theory of power.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The systematiser of Chinese Legalism, who combined law, administrative method and positional authority into one theory of power. He is the most clear-eyed realist in the tradition — he never argues about how things ought to be, only about how they work — and his writing gave the first emperor the framework for unifying China.

### Q: What actually happened?
He had a stammer and could not argue in person, so he wrote. His essays reached the king of Qin, who read them and said that if he could meet this man he would die content, then invaded Han to get him. At the Qin court Han Fei was undone by a fellow student from his own teacher's school, Li Si, who was jealous of him and spoke against him; he was imprisoned and forced to take poison. The man who wrote the definitive analysis of persuasion and court intrigue was killed by a piece of court intrigue. Knowing and being able to do it are not the same faculty.

### The parts · Law, method and position together
Law is the written rule everyone is held to; method is how you assess and check the people below you; position is the authority the seat itself carries. Missing the first, the rules get bypassed. Missing the second, you get compliance in form only. Missing the third, nobody listens. e.g. The policy exists, nobody checks it, and the person enforcing it has no standing to say no. Any one of the three missing and the other two stop working.

### The parts · People follow interest, not exhortation
He doesn't believe in natural loyalty; he believes in incentives. Design the system well and people behave the way you wanted. It is Munger's 'show me the incentive and I'll show you the outcome', stated twenty-two centuries earlier. e.g. The all-hands asked everyone to prioritise quality. Bonuses stayed tied to shipped count. Everyone shipped.

### The parts · The difficulty of persuasion
The hard part of speaking, he wrote, is not what you know but working out what the listener actually cares about. He catalogued the fatal errors — exposing what they don't want exposed, speaking at the wrong moment, being too direct — and then died of one. e.g. Your deck answered whether it could be built. The one person who could approve it was worried about who gets blamed if it fails.

### Q: How do I use it today?
When designing incentives for a team, ask what this system will make people do, not what it ought to make them do. People act on interest. Aligning what you want with what pays is the whole of the job.

### Lines to keep
The ruler controls by two handles: punishment and favour. The difficulty of persuasion is knowing the listener's mind. A thousand-mile dyke collapses from an ant hole.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Zhuangzi — Same era, opposite answers: Han Feizi designs the machine, Zhuangzi declines to be a component. Thomas Gordon — Two theories of getting compliance: rules and consequences, or naming the effect on you. Both work, on different things. John Boyd — Two theories of an organisation that works: rules and consequences, or shared intent and delegated authority. Xunzi — The student pushed the teacher's training argument into a theory of control. Xunzi kept the rites; Han Feizi kept only the handles. Hannah Arendt — Han Feizi asks how to build a system that works without relying on goodness; Arendt asks where obedience inside such a system ends up. One writes from the designer's chair, one from the operator's. Cao Cao — The theory and its practitioner. Han Feizi wrote the system down; cutting his hair in place of his head is that system demonstrated on the man at the top. Mencius — Both are writing about how to govern. Han Feizi trusts reward and punishment; Mencius asks whether people are still willing to follow you at all. Shang Yang — Theory and practice of the same school: Han Feizi wrote the system down, Shang Yang ran it, and both were killed by the thing they had built. Machiavelli — The two closest political realists East and West, seventeen centuries apart: both studied how power actually works, and both were destroyed by the power they studied. Influence — Two systems for moving people: Han Feizi designed law, technique and position two thousand years earlier, Cialdini found six triggers. Both are asking how to make people act as you want.

### Further
Fan Li Sun Tzu Charlie Munger John Boyd Xunzi Hannah Arendt Cao Cao Guan Zhong Mencius Shang Yang Wu Zetian Zhang Juzheng Zhu Yuanzhang Guo Jia Thomas Schelling Strategies of the Warring States Guiguzi Machiavelli Influence

## Han Xin
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/han-xin/
Tags: Strategy and competition, Pre-Qin and classical, The middle state

Han Xin (Han · 231–196 BC) — The middle state. The most gifted commander in Chinese history, and the source of half the standard examples: the crawl between a bully's legs, the battle fought with a river at his back…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The most gifted commander in Chinese history, and the source of half the standard examples: the crawl between a bully's legs, the battle fought with a river at his back, the repaired plank road and the crossing at Chencang. His story has two halves that do not match. The rise is a military education in itself, and the fall is a single unforced error repeated for years: he would neither revolt nor hand over his power, and the middle position is the one that gets you killed.

### Q: What actually happened?
Liu Bang once asked him how many troops the emperor himself could command. No more than a hundred thousand, said Han Xin. And you? For me, the more the better. Liu Bang laughed and asked why, in that case, he was the captive. Because your majesty cannot command troops but is very good at commanding commanders, he said, and that is heaven's gift rather than anything a man learns. It is the most honest thing he ever said, and read back from the end, the least careful.

### The parts · Dead ground, and its two conditions
Throw them onto dead ground and they will live is the famous half. The half he added is that these were men levied off the market who would have run from open ground, and that two thousand horse were meanwhile changing every flag in the enemy camp. e.g. A hard deadline can weld a team that has just formed. The same move on people who could already fight destroys a better rhythm.

### The parts · Repair the plank road, cross at Chencang
He made a show of rebuilding the burned mountain walkways, which was slow, visible and exactly what the other side expected, and took his main force out through Chencang instead. Engage with the orthodox and win with the unexpected, executed once and cleanly. e.g. The announcement everyone can see is usually not the move. Ask what the same team is quietly doing in the same week.

### The parts · Neither revolt nor hand over
His error was not failing to rebel. It was holding an army that frightened his king while having no intention of using it, for years. Threat is assessed on capability, never on sincerity, and the middle carries both risks at once. e.g. The only person who can run the one critical system is a risk however loyal they are. The answer is a second person, not a protestation.

### The parts · He reviewed every battle
He went from an unknown drifter to the best general of the age in a very short time, and what he did after each engagement was go back over it. The gap between an expert and everyone else is not how few mistakes were made but how much came out of them. e.g. After the next project ends, write the three real reasons it went the way it did. Not the presentable reasons, the actual ones.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Find the one place where you hold something other people depend on and cannot replace. Then pick a side this month: either use that position for something, or deliberately make it replaceable. Do not stay in the middle for another quarter.

### Lines to keep
Throw them onto dead ground and they will live. He whose valour overawes his lord stands in danger. The hares dead, the hounds are cooked; the birds gone, the bow stored. For me, the more the better.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Zhang Liang — The same court, the same victory, opposite endings: Zhang Liang stepped all the way out and died old, Han Xin kept the power and the loyalty both and lost everything. Huo Qubing — Two kinds of military genius. Han Xin wins by arrangement and misjudges his own position; Huo Qubing wins by pure speed and never lives long enough for the position to matter. Guo Ziyi — The same impossible position: Han Xin kept proving he was a threat and his clan was destroyed, Guo Ziyi kept proving he was harmless and died in bed. Su Yu — Two commanders who made a habit of winning outnumbered: Han Xin by putting his own men where retreat was impossible, Su Yu by choosing what the enemy had to come and save. Wang Jian — Identical achievements, opposite endings: Wang Jian made himself look greedy and died in bed, Han Xin held on to his standing and did not.

### Further
Liu Bang Sun Tzu Xiang Yu Zhang Liang Guo Ziyi Mao Zedong Huo Qubing Su Yu Wang Jian Records of the Grand Historian

## Hannah Arendt
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/arendt/
Tags: Power and organisation, Modern, Not thinking

Hannah Arendt (1906–1975 · Germany to America) — Not thinking. Political thinker. In 1961 she went to Jerusalem to sit through a trial expecting a monster, and found a mediocre man: all stock phrases, unable to produce a sentence of…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Political thinker. In 1961 she went to Jerusalem to sit through a trial expecting a monster, and found a mediocre man: all stock phrases, unable to produce a sentence of his own, repeating that he had followed orders. She gave the thing a name, the banality of evil — done not out of wickedness but because he had never thought about it. Her own life is the other line: arrested in Berlin in 1933, in New York by 1941 at thirty-five with no English and no papers, and famous ten years later. What this page keeps to is the mechanism of not thinking, and her own restart.

### Q: What actually happened?
The book cost her friendships she had held for thirty years. In 1963 Gershom Scholem wrote to her that she lacked love for the Jewish people. Her reply was flat: she had never in her life loved any people or any collective — she loved her friends. The attacks ran for years, in print and at dinner tables, and she neither withdrew the argument nor softened the phrase. Whatever else that shows, it is the same claim turned on herself: the judgement was hers to make, and she was not going to hand it over to the room.

### The parts · Doing what the list says is itself a choice
Not asking why is not neutral. It hands judgement to whoever wrote the list, which is cheap because you then owe nothing to the outcome, and dangerous because you become the executing mechanism for any list at all. Every step compliant, and the sum a disaster. e.g. The more times you say I was told to do it this way, the faster your own judgement shrinks.

### The parts · Stock phrases are the symptom
She noticed the man had no language of his own. That is what a ready-made formula does: when there is a sentence available to say, nothing has to be thought. Someone speaking entirely in formulas has usually stopped thinking already. e.g. Listen to how you describe your own job. If every phrase is off the shelf, that part has been asleep a while.

### The parts · Everyone does it is not a reason
The excuse spreads responsibility across everybody so that each person is left holding a small share. But you did the thing, and your share does not get smaller because the crowd is large. e.g. Everyone in the industry does it explains the market. It cannot decide for you whether you are going to do it.

### The parts · What travels is method, not position
Arriving in New York her degrees, her circle and her standing were gone; what came with her was how she thought. Her first move was two months in a household learning English rather than looking for work, because language is the precondition for using anything else. e.g. Before starting over, sort your assets: what disappears the moment you leave the seat, and what walks out with you.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Take one thing you do purely because it is on the list, and write two sentences on why it is set that way. If you cannot write them, that is the finding. Do it once a day for a week; the point is not to change the rule but to keep the part of you that can question it from going to sleep.

### Lines to keep
Not done out of wickedness. Done without ever having thought. The crowd is large. Your share of it is not smaller. Papers can be taken away. What is in your head cannot.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Han Feizi — Han Feizi asks how to build a system that works without relying on goodness; Arendt asks where obedience inside such a system ends up. One writes from the designer's chair, one from the operator's. Garry Kasparov — Both answer the tool did my thinking for me. Kasparov puts the human back where the machines disagree; Arendt says handing over judgement is a state in itself, whoever takes it.

### Further
Han Feizi Machiavelli Garry Kasparov The Analects

## Haruki Murakami
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/murakami/
Tags: Learning and growth, Modern, Writing as physical work

Haruki Murakami (Japan · 1949–) — Writing as physical work. He ran a jazz bar into his early thirties, decided at a baseball game in 1978 that he could write a novel, and in 1981 closed the bar to write full time.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
He ran a jazz bar into his early thirties, decided at a baseball game in 1978 that he could write a novel, and in 1981 closed the bar to write full time. He began running at the same time for an unglamorous reason: sitting down all day was making him heavier and he smoked too much. Over the next thirty years he finished more than thirty marathons and one hundred-kilometre ultra, and ran his writing on the same method. His book about running is read by large numbers of people who do not run, because underneath it answers a different question: how do you keep at something for decades when nobody asked you to.

### Q: What actually happened?
He would like a gravestone, he writes, that carries his name, the dates, and then two lines: Writer, and in brackets, Runner. At Least He Never Walked. It is a joke, and it is also the whole standard he works to. Not the best, not the fastest, not acclaimed. Simply that on the days he was supposed to be moving, he did not stop and walk. Nobody sets that bar for you and nobody can check it. He has spent decades holding himself to a line that only he can see, which is exactly the problem most people run into with anything long.

### The parts · Stop while it is still flowing
Ten pages a day when he is writing a novel, filled on a bad day and stopped on a good one. The hard part is not writing but starting again, so he leaves the day at a point where he already knows the next sentence and tomorrow costs almost nothing to begin. e.g. Stop in the middle of a sentence. Tomorrow you sit down and simply keep typing.

### The parts · Set a ceiling, not only a floor
Most people give themselves a minimum and nothing else. The ceiling is there to stop the good day from borrowing against the next three. The real enemy of output is not laziness but swing, and swing is what an uncapped good day produces. e.g. Twenty thousand words over a weekend, then a fortnight of touching nothing. The books balance, or come out worse.

### The parts · Two things besides talent, and both can be trained
A novelist needs talent, focus and endurance. How much talent you were given is settled and worrying about it produces no action, while the other two grow under load the way muscle does. So the hours belong to the two that move. e.g. I have no talent may even be correct, and it still cannot tell you what to do today.

### The parts · Nobody asked, so the reason has to be yours
Work has reviews and school has exams, and both supply the reason from outside. Something you chose has none of that. Make the response your reason, the views and the verdicts, and it can be withdrawn at any time. His replacement is yesterday's version of himself, which is present daily and never runs out. e.g. Three posts, nobody reads them, and you stop. The reason for writing was in other people's hands from the start.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Pick the long thing you keep starting and stopping, and give it a daily amount low enough that your worst day still finishes it. Measure input, not output. Then add the part almost nobody adds: a ceiling, so the good days stop borrowing from the bad ones. Finish each session while you still want to continue, in the middle of a sentence if you can. And the next time you want to quit, say out loud whether it is because the work was bad or because nobody saw it, then decide.

### Lines to keep
The only opponent you have to beat is yourself. Set the daily amount where your worst day still finishes it. No readers is not a reason to stop; readers are not either.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Anders Ericsson — Both are about what to do daily over years: deliberate practice keeps you at the edge of what you cannot do, Murakami lowers the daily difficulty so you never break the chain. BJ Fogg — Two ends of one idea: Fogg shrinks the behaviour until the worst day can do it, Murakami caps the daily output so the best day cannot overspend. Kevin Kelly — Same question, nobody is looking, two answers: Kelly says you only need a thousand true fans, Murakami says the answer should not be sought outside at all.

### Further
Anders Ericsson BJ Fogg Cal Newport Kevin Kelly Bruce Lee

## Harvard Study of Adult Development
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/harvard-study/
Tags: Family and relationships, The industrial age, Relationships predict the end

Harvard Study of Adult Development (1938–present · Harvard Medical School) — Relationships predict the end. The longest study of adult life ever run. It began in 1938 with 268 Harvard sophomores, later merged with 456 boys from Boston's poorest neighbourhoods, asking how life…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The longest study of adult life ever run. It began in 1938 with 268 Harvard sophomores, later merged with 456 boys from Boston's poorest neighbourhoods, asking how life was going every two years and running medical exams every five — for most of them, for life, and now into their children. Robert Waldinger, its fourth director, compresses eighty years into one line: what makes people healthy and content late in life is neither wealth nor fame but the quality of their relationships.

### Q: What actually happened?
That is not what it set out to measure. In 1938 the question was what kind of young man grows into a healthy, successful adult, and the instruments were physical: build, blood pressure, family background. They measured skull dimensions. Decade by decade those predictors lost their explanatory power, and the one that survived was the thing nobody had planned to record. The sample contains men from excellent circumstances who ended isolated, and men from the tenements surrounded by people all their lives, and it is the second group whose health curves run higher.

### The parts · A predictor, not a consolation
It reads like a greeting card and lands on hard measures: satisfaction with close relationships at fifty predicted health at eighty better than cholesterol did. The body settles the bill. e.g. It sounds like a card in a gift shop until you see it beat cholesterol at fifty for predicting how eighty goes.

### The parts · Quality counts, headcount doesn't
And a long, high-conflict relationship does more damage than separating. What protects is what happens inside it, not whether it is still standing — 'staying for the children' does not balance on this ledger. e.g. Two hundred contacts and nobody to call at 2am is not a large network. It is a large list.

### The parts · The window stays open later than people assume
The clearest improvements came from people who started in their fifties and sixties: reconnecting with estranged family, turning acquaintances into regular company. Fifty is not too late for eighty. e.g. He rang the brother he hadn't spoken to in eleven years at fifty-eight. That call is inside the window, not past it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
If relationships feel like something to handle once this busy stretch is over, count one number: in the last month, how many times did you see someone for no practical reason? If you can't count one, it isn't a 'later' problem. The smallest useful move is one message a week to one person, about nothing in particular.

### Lines to keep
Your body at eighty is decided by your relationships at fifty. A marriage held together for the children bills both bodies. Nobody sets out to lose a friend. They get busy and it goes quiet.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
John Cacioppo — The same finding from opposite ends: he measures what the absence costs, the study measures what the presence buys. Excellent Sheep — Eighty years of data on what actually matters, against a system that scores none of it.

### Further
Mark Granovetter John Cacioppo Arlie Hochschild John Gottman Esther Perel Attachment Theory

## Howard Marks
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/marks/
Tags: Money and risk, Modern, Second-level thinking

Howard Marks (United States · 1946–) — Second-level thinking. Founder of Oaktree Capital, more than two hundred billion dollars under management, working in distressed debt and high yield — a trade that only has any business when…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Founder of Oaktree Capital, more than two hundred billion dollars under management, working in distressed debt and high yield — a trade that only has any business when other people are panicking. He has written investment memos since 1990, and Buffett has said they are the first thing he opens. What makes him unusual is that he publicly gave up forecasting. He does not guess the macro, the rates or next year. He does one thing: judge where in the cycle we are standing now.

### Q: What actually happened?
In September 2008 Lehman failed, the market went into free fall, and almost every institution was reducing. Oaktree had raised an eleven-billion-dollar distressed debt fund beforehand and had deliberately sat on it through the hot market of 2007. In the fifteen weeks after the collapse it invested roughly six hundred million dollars a week, about six billion in all. His reasoning was nearly crude: if the world really is ending, it does not matter what you own; if it is not, then not buying was the mistake. This gets told as a story about nerve at the bottom. The decisive half is the first one — raising eleven billion while everybody was making money, and then not spending it.

### The parts · Second-level thinking
First level: it is a good company, buy it. Second level: it is a good company, everyone knows it, the price already says so, sell it. You have to judge not the fact but whether the market has overpaid for the fact. Excess return needs a view that differs from the consensus and is more correct than it. Both, or neither. e.g. Different and wrong hurts far more than losing money with the crowd. The real cost of second-level thinking is looking like a fool for long stretches.

### The parts · Risk is permanent loss, not volatility
The academy treats volatility as risk because volatility can be measured. What actually puts people out of the game is capital that never comes back, and being forced to sell at the bottom. Volatility is harmless until it makes you sell. e.g. That is what leverage really costs. Without it only permanent loss can kill you; with it volatility can, and volatility is far more common.

### The parts · The pendulum
Markets swing between greed and fear, this time it's different and it will never recover, and they almost never rest in the middle. You cannot know when the swing reverses. You can always know which side of the arc it is on, and that is his entire standing ground.

### The parts · Measure the present instead of predicting the future
He keeps a concrete checklist: are investors discussing returns or risk, is a new fund easy or hard to raise, can poor assets get debt away, is diligence lengthening or being compressed. All observable, none of it requiring any forecasting ability at all. e.g. When everyone is asking how much there is to make and nobody is asking how much there is to lose, the thermometer has already given you its reading.

### The parts · You do not have to swing at everything
Nobody calls a strike on you for not swinging. The market quotes a price every day and you are under no obligation to answer. Most losses come not from a wrong judgement but from the pressure to be seen doing something.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Write a market temperature note once a quarter, answering only observable questions: is money easier or harder to raise than three months ago, are people discussing returns or risk, can weak projects still get funded, is diligence stretching or shrinking? Predict nothing; record the present. Six months later you will find you already knew. The harder discipline is the other half: in a good market, deliberately set aside money you do not invest. Its true cost is watching other people earn with it, and it only pays in the few weeks after a crash.

### Lines to keep
We may never know where we're going, but we'd better have a good idea where we are. Investment success doesn't come from buying good things, but from buying things well. You can't do the same things others do and expect to outperform. Being too far ahead of your time is indistinguishable from being wrong.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Benjamin Graham — Graham answers what a thing is worth, Marks answers whether now is the moment to act — two separate skills, and most people have only trained the first. Jesse Livermore — Both accept that the cycle is real: Livermore surfs the pendulum and is eventually swallowed by it, Marks moves only when it reaches an extreme. Nassim Taleb — Same premise, that the future is unknowable, and two routes out: Taleb builds a structure that survives it, Marks takes the temperature of the present.

### Further
Warren Buffett Benjamin Graham Ray Dalio Nassim Taleb George Soros Jim Simons

## Hu Xueyan
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/hu-xueyan/
Tags: Money and risk, The industrial age, The patron

Hu Xueyan (Qing · 1823–1885) — The patron. The most famous merchant of the late Qing, self-made, for a time the richest man in China, decorated with an official rank and the yellow riding jacket.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The most famous merchant of the late Qing, self-made, for a time the richest man in China, decorated with an official rank and the yellow riding jacket. He was also the first Chinese businessman to take on the foreign trading houses directly, and he lost completely: two years from the summit to the confiscation of his estate. Note that most quotable Hu Xueyan sayings in circulation come from a twentieth-century novel, not from the record.

### Q: What actually happened?
He was a clerk in a Hangzhou money shop when he met Wang Youling, a candidate official with a purchased rank and no money to take up a post. Hu advanced him funds out of the shop's own money and was dismissed for it. Years later Wang was a provincial official and steered government business his way, and everything that followed rests on that one bet on one man. The structure that made him is the structure that killed him.

### The parts · A patron is leverage and a single point of failure
His start was backing one broke official; his peak was tied to Zuo Zongtang, whom he supplied with grain, arms, foreign loans and campaign finance in exchange for rank and large official deposits. It is the most efficient structure available and it rests on one man keeping his power. e.g. Today it is customer concentration and one signature: sixty per cent of revenue from a single account, or an approval only one person can give.

### The parts · Obligation is the dearest asset and the frailest liability
He was superb at it, with free medicine, famine relief and something always left on the table for the other side. It made him nearly unstoppable while things went well. But a network of obligation runs on the expectation that you keep winning, and when the verdict flips it reverses at once. e.g. Bank runs, waves of resignations, suppliers all tightening terms in the same week. One mechanism wearing different clothes.

### The parts · The mismatch is what kills
The silk losses alone were survivable given time. What removed the time was funding a long silk position with deposits withdrawable on demand. Borrow short and invest long, and one push at the wrong moment finishes you while the balance sheet still looks solvent. e.g. Assets are fine, cash is just tight this month is the sentence every dead company said first. Insolvency does not kill; the cash running out does.

### The parts · Cornering a market whose supply you do not own
The hoard assumed raw silk supply was fixed and that buying it all would set the price. Italy also grew silk. Any attempt to buy price-setting power has to answer one question first: can the supply come from somewhere else? e.g. Unless the thing is genuinely scarce, a squeeze eventually meets new supply. It has replayed in commodities, in crypto and in hiring.

### The parts · The move that won will be the one that finishes you
He rose through official connections and was destroyed through official connections; he grew on his bank's liquidity and died in a run on it; he made his first fortune by daring a bet and lost everything on the largest one. He never changed the method, only the leverage on it. e.g. The thing you are best at tends to be how you go, because you reach for it without thinking, right up until conditions turn against it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Check your own structure for his three in combination: one patron, meaning a single client or channel or signature; a duration mismatch, meaning money that can leave supporting a position that needs time; and a network held together by other people believing you will win. Any one alone is survivable. All three at once and the timing of your ending belongs to somebody else.

### Lines to keep
No trade can afford the word cheat; medicine, which holds lives, least of all. Eight teapots and seven lids. Never wear arrogance; never be without a backbone.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Fan Li — Both worked between officials and trade. Fan Li left at the summit; Hu Xueyan tied the knots tighter every year. Li Ka-shing — Same game, opposite rules: never take the last coin and cash is oxygen, and Hu Xueyan broke both.

### Further
Li Ka-shing Zeng Guofan Fan Li Xiang Yu Nassim Taleb

## Huineng
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/huineng/
Tags: Mind and feeling, Medieval, Already complete

Huineng (Tang · 638–713) — Already complete. An illiterate woodcutter from the far south who became the sixth patriarch of Chan Buddhism.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
An illiterate woodcutter from the far south who became the sixth patriarch of Chan Buddhism. The record of his teaching is the only native Chinese text ever called a sutra. What he did was an extreme piece of subtraction: he took the practice out of the commentaries, the graded stages and the monastery, and reduced it to one sentence — the thing you are looking for is already in you, and the problem is that you keep looking outward.

### Q: What actually happened?
Years after receiving the transmission he was still living unrecognised among a band of hunters. Arriving at last at a monastery, he found two monks arguing about a banner moving in the wind — one saying the wind moved, the other saying the banner moved. Neither the wind nor the banner is moving, he said. Your minds are moving. The abbot, hearing it, understood who had just walked in. The remark is not a riddle. It is his whole method in one line: before adjusting the object, check the thing doing the looking.

### The parts · Sudden doesn't mean fast
Gradual practice assumes distance from the goal and so requires accumulation. Sudden awakening says the distance was never there — only a misrecognition. So 'sudden' isn't speed. It is the discovery that there is nowhere to travel. e.g. Nothing new arrived the day she stopped apologising for the price. She had the same evidence in January; what changed was that she stopped waiting to deserve it.

### The parts · No-thought is not blankness
It means a thought arises, you see it, and you neither follow it nor suppress it. This is the part of the text closest to something modern and operable — it describes keeping distance from a feeling rather than eliminating it. e.g. The urge to check the message is there either way. Watching it pass without opening the app is the practice; suppressing it is just a second urge.

### The parts · Everything outward rests on 'I am not enough'
Books, teachers, the next achievement: every outward search is built on a premise nobody examines. He puts the premise itself in question, which is why this is the only subtraction in a library otherwise made of addition. e.g. Another course, another certificate, one more year of preparation. Each purchase quietly restates the premise that you are not ready yet.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Almost all modern self-improvement is addition — one more book, one more course, one more streak — and the unstated premise is always that who you are now is insufficient. Next time something grips you, do one thing only: notice the thought, say 'there it is', and neither follow it nor scold yourself for having it. Most of the pain is in the long derivation that follows, not in the thought.

### Lines to keep
There was never a thing there, so where would dust settle? Not the wind moving, not the flag moving. Your mind is moving. The teaching is in the world. Awakening is not apart from it.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Wang Yangming — Huineng is upstream: 'the nature is already complete' and 'innate knowing' are one idea in two vocabularies.

### Further
Wang Yangming Zhuangzi Su Shi Tao Te Ching

## Huo Qubing
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/huo-qubing/
Tags: Strategy and competition, Qin, Han and the Six Dynasties, Undivided

Huo Qubing (Han · 140–117 BC) — Undivided. Nephew of Emperor Wu of Han. At seventeen he took eight hundred riders far behind the Xiongnu lines; at nineteen he ran two campaigns through the Hexi corridor; at…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Nephew of Emperor Wu of Han. At seventeen he took eight hundred riders far behind the Xiongnu lines; at nineteen he ran two campaigns through the Hexi corridor; at twenty-two he drove two thousand li north and made the sacrifice at Mount Langjuxu. He was dead at twenty-four. He is the clearest case in this collection of a talent that burns rather than accumulates: everything given to one thing, and then out.

### Q: What actually happened?
Emperor Wu had a grand residence built for him and told him to go and see whether it suited. Huo Qubing declined to look at it. The Xiongnu are not yet destroyed, he said; how can I make a home? The line became the most famous refusal of comfort in Chinese history, and it was not a performance. He genuinely did not care. Every day he was alive he was fighting or preparing to fight, and he was alive for twenty-four years.

### The parts · The strength of caring about one thing
No distraction. The emperor gave him a house and he did not look at it; gifts of food did not interest him; he stayed out of court politics entirely. That is not effort, it is singularity, and what a person can reach in the one thing he genuinely minds about is not available to anyone spreading themselves. e.g. Whatever you find yourself giving that kind of attention to is the thing to bet on. Do not dilute it with an argument about being well rounded.

### The parts · Never mind the old manuals
Offered instruction in the classics of war, he answered that what matters is how the plan for this campaign is drawn. The manuals encoded an army of infantry and chariots tied to a grain road; he had cavalry and no rear. The tools had changed, so the best answer had changed. e.g. The playbook that made the last decade of growth was written when attention was cheap. Copied faithfully now, it fails faithfully.

### The parts · War that feeds itself
No baggage train. He resupplied from the Xiongnu camps he broke on the way, which is what made raids of two thousand li possible. The hidden premise is that every encounter must be won fast and won with enough taken. The risk did not go away; it moved out of logistics and into fighting. e.g. Funding each new market from the cash the last one throws off works only while every one of them turns positive fast. It is not safer than raising money.

### The parts · What it cost, recorded in the same chapter
The historian who praised the marches also wrote that he was high-born and careless of his men, that he came back throwing away fine food while his own soldiers went hungry. Extreme tactical skill and neglect of the people carrying it sat inside one man, and both were written down. e.g. The manager with the best numbers on the floor can have the worst attrition. Read one fact without the other and you will staff the next team wrong.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Find the one thing you already treat the way he treated the steppe, and stop apologising for the balance you are not keeping. Then check the other half of the record: name one cost that concentration is imposing on people around you, and decide whether you are willing to pay it.

### Lines to keep
The Xiongnu are not yet destroyed. How can I make a home? What matters is the plan for this campaign, not the old texts. You do not have to carry the grain. Take it from them.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Sima Yi — The two extreme life strategies here: Huo Qubing burnt out at twenty-four, Sima Yi moved at seventy. Miyamoto Musashi — Both gave everything to one craft. Musashi got sixty years of it and wrote it down; Huo Qubing got seven. Han Xin — Two kinds of military genius. Han Xin wins by arrangement and misjudges his own position; Huo Qubing wins by pure speed and never lives long enough for the position to matter.

### Further
Han Xin Sima Yi Sun Tzu Steve Jobs Julius Caesar
