## Influence
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/influence/
Tags: Reading people, Modern, Triggers

Influence (1984 · Robert Cialdini) — Triggers. Cialdini spent three years undercover among salespeople, fundraisers and advertisers, studying how persuasion actually happens.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Cialdini spent three years undercover among salespeople, fundraisers and advertisers, studying how persuasion actually happens. What he found were six triggers: pull one and a person runs a preset routine rather than thinking it through. Reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity. Knowing them lets you see what is being done to you, and lets you ask for things in a way people can say yes to.

### Q: What actually happened?
A jewellery shop in Arizona could not shift a tray of turquoise. On her way out of town the owner scribbled a note to her assistant telling her to halve the price on everything in the case. She came back to find the whole lot sold. The assistant had misread the note and doubled the prices instead. Customers who knew nothing about turquoise had used the only rule available to them, expensive means good, and the trigger produced the purchase with no thinking in between. A great deal of human decision-making works like that.

### The parts · Reciprocity
A gift creates an obligation to repay. Take something from somebody, even something you did not want, and refusing their next request becomes difficult. The free sample, the opening concession in a negotiation, the unprompted kindness: all of them are switching on the same rule, and the initiative belongs to whoever moves first. e.g. The supermarket tasting stand is not there for the taste. The counter-question is whether you want this, or want it because they gave you something.

### The parts · Commitment and consistency
People stay in line with what they have already said and done, because contradicting it means contradicting themselves. Once a position has been stated in public, backing out costs more than going through with it. This is why a public commitment is one of the most reliable ways to change behaviour. e.g. A trainer who gets you to announce your goal to friends is using it. On the evening you do not want to go, consistency does the pushing.

### The parts · Social proof, authority, scarcity
If everybody is doing it, it is probably right, which is a sound shortcut most of the time and the engine of every panic and bubble. Authority is the same shortcut applied to expertise, and the appearance of authority is easy to fake while the competence is not. Scarcity says harder to get means more wanted. e.g. Research shows is the authority switch. Only three places left is the scarcity one. Ask whether the expert is speaking inside their field, and whether the thing is still worth having once the deadline passes.

### The parts · Liking
We are persuaded more easily by people we like, and attractiveness, similarity, familiarity and flattery all raise the odds. You buy what a friend recommends not because your friend has better judgement than a stranger, but because you like your friend. e.g. The first lesson in sales training is find something in common. The check is whether you are accepting the argument or the person making it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Before your next purchase, investment or significant decision, name the trigger that is pushing it. Reciprocity, because they gave you something? Social proof, because everyone is in? Scarcity, because it closes on Friday? Naming it is enough to pause it, and then you can put your own judgement back in its place.

### Lines to keep
We should try to repay, in kind, what another person has provided us. We determine what is correct by finding out what other people think is correct. The best defence is to slow down and ask why you are deciding this.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Han Feizi — Two systems for moving people: Han Feizi designed law, technique and position two thousand years earlier, Cialdini found six triggers. Both are asking how to make people act as you want. The Crowd — One reader at a time against a room at a time: Cialdini studies the switches inside one person, Le Bon what happens to all of them once they are gathered. Guiguzi — The same set of human switches, approached from opposite ends: Cialdini runs experiments and teaches you to spot them being pulled, Guiguzi writes the operating manual. The Art of Worldly Wisdom — One subject, three hundred years apart: Gracián found the handles by watching people, Cialdini turned the same material into six principles you can test. Maria Konnikova — Cialdini explains how the six devices work, Konnikova explains why the same devices work so well on certain people at certain moments. One studies the weapon, the other the target. Thinking, Fast and Slow — Two sides of one thing: Cialdini shows how the gaps get used on you, Kahneman shows why the gaps are there. Sapiens — Both explain why people are not rational: Harari from the species and its stories, Cialdini from the levers inside one head.

### Further
Han Feizi Charlie Munger The Crowd Maria Konnikova Guiguzi The Art of Worldly Wisdom Chris Voss La Rochefoucauld Thinking, Fast and Slow

## Ivan Illich
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/illich/
Tags: How the world works, The industrial age, A ceiling

Ivan Illich (Austria–Mexico · 1926–2002) — A ceiling. A priest who spent the 1970s taking apart four systems everybody treated as progress: schooling, transport, medicine, and the idea of a tool itself.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A priest who spent the 1970s taking apart four systems everybody treated as progress: schooling, transport, medicine, and the idea of a tool itself. One claim runs through all four — every tool crosses two watersheds, and past the second it starts producing what it was built to remove. Medicine makes patients, school makes a feeling of ignorance, transport makes distance. He is not against technology. He wants an upper bound on it.

### Q: What actually happened?
The man who wrote that medical treatment produces illness grew a tumour on his face in later life. The proposed treatment was surgery and radiation, with respectable odds, at the risk of his speech and his hearing — and speaking, and listening to people speak, was the entire form of his work. He declined. He lived nearly two decades with the growth, teaching, in pain, managing the worst days with opium he prepared himself, and died in Bremen in 2002. He never wrote it up as a manifesto; asked, he said it was his own arithmetic. He never denied the treatment worked. He questioned whether the word worked had counted everything it costs.

### The parts · The two watersheds
Before the first, a tool solves a real problem. Between the two it is steadily useful. Past the second it begins producing the opposite. So does it work is unanswerable — it does. The question is when what you pay to keep it overtook what it gives you. e.g. The group chat saved ten emails in week one. At two hundred people it takes an hour a day and anything real still arrives privately.

### The parts · The signal is the reverse, not the slowdown
Efficiency usually keeps climbing after the crossing, which is exactly why it is hard to notice. The reliable signal is production of the opposite: care that generates illness, communication tools that generate the fear of being unreachable. e.g. The reporting got beautiful and people started splitting tasks to make the board look right. What the tool wants is replacing the work.

### The parts · A convivial tool lets you leave
His test for whether a tool is yours is whether you can decline it. The higher the exit cost, the less it is your tool and the more you are its. That is a property of the arrangement, not of the features. e.g. A system you can export everything from and one you renegotiate with after lock-in can look identical on a comparison table.

### The parts · One ledger, not two
Tools advertise time saved and never report time spent — learning, maintaining, working to pay, and getting back into the work afterwards. Those land on different days, so nobody adds them. Added, the answer often flips. e.g. Convert the monthly fee into your own hours and add the weekly upkeep. A surprising number stop making sense.

### The parts · Professions monopolise the definition of the problem
His harder claim: past a point, a profession captures the right to say what counts as a problem. Doctors define illness, schools define having learned — and ordinary people lose the ability to name their own situation. e.g. Once a field only speaks in terms insiders share, an outsider's question is automatically unprofessional. Those are often the real questions.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Take the tool you lean on hardest and work out two numbers: the hours a week it costs to keep (learning, upkeep, recovering from its interruptions, and working to pay for it), and what it actually finished for you. Then ask the third question: what would leaving cost? Those three answers are worth more than any position on technology.

### Lines to keep
Past the second watershed a tool produces what it was meant to remove. Illness produced by the treatment itself I call iatrogenesis. A convivial tool is one you can master, repair, and do without.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Kevin Kelly — Both read where technology is heading: one asks what it will grow into, the other asks where it starts eating people. Peter Drucker — Both ask what comes after efficiency — do the right things, or put a ceiling on the tool.

### Further
Zhuangzi Peter Drucker Cal Newport Thinking in Systems Finite and Infinite Games

## Jeff Bezos
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/bezos/
Tags: Starting and building, Modern, The flywheel

Jeff Bezos (United States · 1964–) — The flywheel. Left a Wall Street job in 1994 to sell books out of a garage and built it into a two-trillion-dollar company across retail, cloud, logistics and hardware.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Left a Wall Street job in 1994 to sell books out of a garage and built it into a two-trillion-dollar company across retail, cloud, logistics and hardware. He is the most extreme practitioner of the long term on record: twenty years of thin profit and open ridicule while every dollar went back into the flywheel, and then twenty years of winning.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1994 he was a vice-president at a New York hedge fund and wanted to leave and sell books online. His boss told him it was a good idea, but a better one for somebody who did not already have a good job. So he invented a way to decide: project yourself to eighty and look back — which choice would you regret? He knew at eighty he would not remember a bonus he gave up in 1994, and would mind very much never having been part of the internet at all. He resigned within days. What makes the frame sharp is that it changes the timescale of the question by force, and once the timescale moves the answer surfaces on its own.

### The parts · Regret minimisation
For decisions large enough to define a stretch of life, shift the vantage point to eighty. Short-term losses — salary, standing, safety — shrink automatically from there, and the things that turn out to matter, whether you tried, whether you were there, enlarge automatically. It is built for the fork between safe and unremarkable and risky and alive. e.g. The offer you keep re-reading at midnight is not a spreadsheet problem. Run it from eighty and it usually stops being close.

### The parts · The flywheel is slow before it is fast
Lower prices bring customers, customers bring traffic, traffic brings sellers, scale lowers cost, and cost lowers prices again. No first step and no last one. The part people underestimate is the beginning, where it is heavy, exhausting and appears to do nothing — which is where almost everyone stops. e.g. Find the loop where each turn makes the next one easier, then accept that the first two years will look indistinguishable from failure.

### The parts · Your margin is my opportunity
Every comfortable high margin in an industry is a door held open for an attacker. He compressed his own margins deliberately to leave nothing worth attacking. Turn it around as a self-check: whatever you are earning comfortably from is precisely what somebody is currently aiming at. e.g. The product line nobody wants to touch because it funds everything else is the one a competitor is already modelling.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Sort your decisions by whether they can be undone: the reversible ones move fast and low, the irreversible ones get the meeting. Before starting anything new, write the press release you would publish on launch day — if you cannot make it exciting to a customer, do not start.

### Lines to keep
Your margin is my opportunity. If you think three years out you have many competitors. Think seven and you have few. Failure and invention are inseparable twins.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Steve Jobs — One cut the range to four; the other refused to stop adding — both were right about their own business. Mao Zedong — Opposite readings of what to hold steady. Bezos says bet on the need that will not change in ten years; this says the governing problem is different in every stage and yesterday's priority is how people die. The Innovator's Dilemma — Bezos ran Christensen's remedy deliberately — AWS was built outside the retail body, and that independence is what allowed it to be small.

### Further
Warren Buffett Elon Musk Steve Jobs Paul Graham Peter Drucker Andy Grove

## Jensen Huang
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/huang/
Tags: Starting and building, Modern, Zero-billion markets

Jensen Huang (Contemporary · 1963–) — Zero-billion markets. Founder and chief executive of Nvidia, still in the seat after more than thirty years. In 2006 he made a decision that looked like burning money: build CUDA, so a…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Founder and chief executive of Nvidia, still in the seat after more than thirty years. In 2006 he made a decision that looked like burning money: build CUDA, so a graphics chip could do general computation. There were no customers for it and no market. Seventeen years later the AI boom arrived and all of it was running on his foundations. He did not bet on an application. He bet on a capability, and then paid to keep it alive.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1995 Nvidia's first product shipped and failed. Microsoft's DirectX made the approach it was built on obsolete almost overnight, and the company was close to finished. He stood in front of the staff who were left and said, in effect, that he needed their help to get Nvidia out of this. Not I have a plan, follow me. I need you. It is a small thing to notice about a man now running one of the most valuable companies on earth, and it is why there was anybody left to run it.

### The parts · Zero-billion-dollar markets
Not billion-dollar markets: markets whose size today is zero, where there are no competitors because there are no customers. Enter one and the toolchain, the interfaces and the developers' habits are yours to define. What you buy is not a head start but the seat where the rules get written. e.g. Early in a category the valuable move is not selling units. It is making your interface the default that later arrivals have to build on.

### The parts · Two lines of blood supply
A zero market pays nothing for a decade. Gaming cards were the mature business feeding cash while CUDA burned it. Without the first the second is suicide; without the second the first is only a good business. Ambition shows up as a line you let look terrible for ten years. e.g. Most companies cannot hold a dark line open, not for lack of money but because they cannot survive the quarterly question about when it will earn.

### The parts · Always thirty days from going out of business
He says the company is thirty days from going out of business, and it is not modesty. Nvidia has been near the end at least three times. A permanent sense of the edge means that when the real emergency lands, nobody in the room is stunned by it. e.g. The teams that handle a crisis worst are the ones that had never once rehearsed the sentence this could end.

### The parts · Retreat is hardest for the ablest
Nvidia left mobile chips while they were still growing, on the structure rather than the quarter, and moved the engineers to robotics. He told the Taipei graduates that retreat does not come easily to brilliant people, and that deciding what to give up is central to success. e.g. The failing project hardest to kill is the one given to the best team, because nobody wants a loss on that record.

### Q: How do I use it today?
In your next plan, add a second question to how big is this market today. Ask which underlying capability, if it kept improving for five years, would unlock things that cannot be built now — and what it would cost to keep that line alive until then. Betting on a capability usually beats betting on an application.

### Lines to keep
We go after zero-billion-dollar markets. Our company is thirty days from going out of business. Retreat does not come easily to brilliant, successful people. Run, don't walk.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Peter Thiel — Thiel asks what important truth very few people agree with you on. Building CUDA in 2006, when the industry was certain a graphics chip was for drawing pictures, is a live specimen of the answer. Duan Yongping — Opposite entries into a new category. Huang goes in before it exists and pays for a decade; Duan waits until somebody else has proved it and then builds the better version. Andy Grove — Both walked out of the business that was making the money. Grove left memory under fire; Huang left mobile chips while they were still growing.

### Further
Andy Grove Peter Thiel Duan Yongping Elon Musk Kevin Kelly Ren Zhengfei Zhang Yiming

## Jesse Livermore
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/livermore/
Tags: Money and risk, The industrial age, Sitting tight

Jesse Livermore (United States · 1877–1940) — Sitting tight. The most famous speculator in American history and the model for Reminiscences of a Stock Operator.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The most famous speculator in American history and the model for Reminiscences of a Stock Operator. He started in bucket shops at fourteen, went broke four times and came back four times, made about a hundred million dollars short in the crash of 1929, and invented much of what trend following still uses. He went broke again in 1934 and took his own life in 1940, leaving a note that called his life a failure. He is the clearest case there is of a man who wrote the rules and died breaking them.

### Q: What actually happened?
In the summer of 1929 the market was euphoric and everyone was talking about a new era. He worked his own system: small probing shorts at his key points, several small losses, no increase in size, and waiting. In October the market broke, his positions came good, and he made roughly a hundred million dollars in a month. Papers called him the great bear of Wall Street and ruined strangers wrote to threaten him. Every rule that made that month work was one he personally broke five years later.

### The parts · Trade the pivotal point, do not predict it
Do not guess tops and bottoms. Wait until the price clears a key level and the trend confirms itself. He said he never bought at the low or sold at the high. Give up the first fifth of a move in exchange for the market telling you which way it is going. e.g. He did not call the top in the bull market. He waited until the index broke support and the rally failed, and only then went in size.

### The parts · Cut losses, let profits run
A losing position is evidence you are wrong: leave, and never average down. A winning one is evidence you are right: stay. The amateur instinct is exactly inverted, holding losers to avoid admitting error and taking gains quickly to bank being right. e.g. The workplace version: stop the wrong project early, and be willing to double the resources on the one that is working.

### The parts · Probe, then pyramid
Open small, add only after the market has confirmed the view, and make each addition smaller than the last. No single judgement should be able to reach the base of your capital. The opposite is the one big bet, which ties the judgement and the survival together. e.g. Put in a tenth first. Add on evidence rather than on conviction, and never in order to rescue an average price.

### The parts · Being flat is a position
Money is made by sitting, not by trading. When there is nothing there, doing nothing is optimal. Most of his profit came from a few large opportunities each year, and most of his losses from restlessness in between. e.g. Count the trades, or the decisions, you made last quarter out of boredom rather than because something had actually changed.

### The parts · Nothing new, because nobody is new
There is nothing new in Wall Street, because speculation is as old as the hills. Greed, fear, hope and regret run the same script in every bubble and every crash with a fresh cast. Whoever can read the cycle in people finds the same trade in any decade. e.g. Every mania has the same four acts. The asset changes; the sequence of feelings in the crowd does not.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Set a written stop on every serious commitment, money or career or project, and hand it to someone else to hold you to, because stops are kept by systems rather than by willpower. Then apply the multiplication rule: never take a bet that can take you to zero, however good the odds look.

### Lines to keep
There is nothing new in Wall Street. Speculation is as old as the hills. It never was my thinking that made the big money for me. Men who can both be right and sit tight are uncommon. Instead of hoping he must fear; instead of fearing he must hope.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Warren Buffett — Speculation against investment: Livermore took the price movement and rose and fell four times, Buffett took the business and compounded. Fan Li — Both understood exits. Fan Li left at every summit; Livermore never once got up from the table. Howard Marks — Both accept that the cycle is real: Livermore surfs the pendulum and is eventually swallowed by it, Marks moves only when it reaches an extreme.

### Further
George Soros Nassim Taleb Warren Buffett Fan Li

## Jim Simons
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/simons/
Tags: Money and risk, The industrial age, A small edge, repeated

Jim Simons (United States · 1938–2024) — A small edge, repeated. A mathematician first: a doctorate at twenty-three, teaching at MIT and Harvard, code-breaking for the defence establishment, and the Chern–Simons theory, which is his…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A mathematician first: a doctorate at twenty-three, teaching at MIT and Harvard, code-breaking for the defence establishment, and the Chern–Simons theory, which is his place in the history of mathematics and has nothing to do with money. He went into investing full time at forty-eight and founded Renaissance Technologies. Its Medallion fund has compounded at roughly sixty-six per cent a year before fees since 1988 and about thirty-nine after them, which is the best record anybody has. His method is the opposite of every traditional investor's: he does not study companies, meet management, or forecast the macro.

### Q: What actually happened?
Simons tried fundamental trading early on, made money and then lost badly, and the real turn came when he decided to give up judgement altogether. His hiring rule became famous for being strange: no people from Wall Street, only astronomers, cryptographers, linguists and statisticians — because the Wall Street ones arrive carrying a set of beliefs that have already been falsified. Inside Renaissance every researcher shares one model and one compensation formula; nobody keeps a private strategy or a private position. It is a firm that deleted the concept of the individual hero at the level of its constitution, and its results continued after Simons himself retired.

### The parts · A small edge, repeated enormously often
Win about half the time plus a fraction, and do it millions of times. This is the far pole from Buffett, who bets heavily on a handful of near-certainties. What they share matters more than the difference: both refuse to bet in the middle ground. Uncertain and heavy is the usual way to die. e.g. A casino's edge is one to five per cent and casinos never lose, because they repeat it endlessly and cap the size of any single bet.

### The parts · Data matters more than the model
Renaissance spent more time and money collecting, cleaning and aligning historical data than anyone else, and kept things others threw away: bad prints, cancelled orders, weather records, old newspapers. The reasoning is plain — models are public mathematics, data is a private asset. e.g. The modern parallel: nearly every AI company's architecture looks alike, and the gap that opens is the data pipeline.

### The parts · Don't predict, just recognise
He never asked whether a company was any good, only how often this price pattern had appeared before and what followed. That gives up causation and keeps correlation. The price is never knowing why you made money; the prize is never being fooled by a story you told yourself.

### The parts · Size is the enemy of return
Medallion closed to outside money in 1993, took only employees' capital, held itself near ten billion dollars and forced the profits out. Strategy capacity is finite: more money means your own trading moves the price and eats the edge. Refusing a fee that large is one of the hardest decisions in the industry. e.g. The firm's other, open funds are far larger and far more ordinary, which is the proof that the constraint was real.

### The parts · Take your hands off
Designing a system is easy; not rescuing it while it is losing money is very hard. During the 1998 collapse of Long-Term Capital, Medallion drew down and Simons considered intervening by hand, then decided not to touch it. That is the true entry barrier to every quantitative method, and it is not mathematical.

### Q: How do I use it today?
First work out which kind of fight you are in. If your edge is small but repeatable — sales, ad buying, A/B tests, distribution, interviewing — stop agonising over any single outcome, push the number of repetitions up, and hold a hard ceiling on what one attempt can cost. If your edge is large and the chances are rare — changing jobs, starting a company, marrying, a big investment — invert it: bet seldom, bet heavily, and be willing to hold cash for a long time. The worst outcome is confusing the two: heavy on a small edge is gambling, light on a large one is waste. One more counter-intuitive rule worth keeping: once a method starts earning reliably, the first thing to kill it is usually not a competitor but the scale you added yourself.

### Lines to keep
Be guided by beauty. Work with the smartest people you can find, ideally smarter than you. Don't give up easily, and hope for some good luck. We do not overrule the model. We improve the model.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Warren Buffett — The two poles of investing: Buffett bets heavily on a few near-certainties, Simons bets tiny amounts on millions of near coin-flips — and both refuse the middle ground. Nassim Taleb — Two mathematicians on opposite ends of one market: Taleb is paid at the moment models break, Simons is paid all the while they hold. George Soros — Soros uses reflexivity to understand the market, Simons gave up understanding entirely — and the money comes out of the same place. Peter Lynch — Same market, opposite routes: Lynch visited three hundred companies a year, Simons visited none.

### Further
Warren Buffett Nassim Taleb Charlie Munger Howard Marks George Soros Peter Lynch

## John Boyd
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/boyd/
Tags: Strategy and competition, The industrial age, Tempo

John Boyd (United States · 1927–1997) — Tempo. A US Air Force colonel known as Forty-Second Boyd, from a standing bet: any pilot, he starts from the disadvantaged position, and if he isn't on their tail within forty…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A US Air Force colonel known as Forty-Second Boyd, from a standing bet: any pilot, he starts from the disadvantaged position, and if he isn't on their tail within forty seconds he pays forty dollars. He is said never to have paid. He never made general and never published a book — his work exists as a briefing — and he reshaped American fighter design and the doctrine of manoeuvre warfare.

### Q: What actually happened?
The briefing was the medium. Patterns of Conflict ran to several hours and he refused to give the short version: if you would not sit through the whole thing he would not present it, because the argument was cumulative and a summary would be taken as a technique. So the ideas spread by people who had sat in a room with him for a day, which is why they arrived in doctrine before they arrived in print, and why the version that reached business books is mostly the one he refused to give.

### The parts · Fast means turning, not moving
Observe, orient, decide, act. The claim isn't that each step should be quick but that you operate inside the opponent's loop, so what he observes is the world your last move made and every reaction fights a version of you that no longer exists.

### The parts · The bottleneck is orient
Observe, decide and act can all be sped up with tools. Fitting new information into an existing frame cannot. The more successful the old frame, the less gets in — organisations do see the change and file it under the old map.

### The parts · To be somebody, or to do something
The talk he gave every young officer. One road: go along, get promoted, be somebody. The other: do what should be done. He took the second, stopped at colonel, and the aircraft and the doctrine are full of his work.

### Q: How do I use it today?
If you and a competitor are both accelerating and you're buying tools for every step, ask which step the loop is actually stuck on — usually the one where you saw it and didn't change the frame. Inside an organisation, the lever isn't speed, it's friction: every approval layer is delay, and every ounce of suspicion is paid for in confirmations.

### Lines to keep
Observe, orient, decide, act. One road: promotion and medals. The other: doing what should be done. Machines don't fight and terrain doesn't fight. People do.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Han Feizi — Two theories of an organisation that works: rules and consequences, or shared intent and delegated authority. Sun Tzu — Both put the decision before the clash. Sun Tzu settles it in preparation, Boyd in speed of turning.

### Further
Garry Kasparov Han Feizi Sun Tzu Charlie Munger Norbert Wiener On War Su Yu

## John Cacioppo
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/cacioppo/
Tags: Mind and feeling, Modern, Loneliness is a signal

John Cacioppo (1951–2018 · University of Chicago) — Loneliness is a signal. A founder of social neuroscience who spent a career on one question: what loneliness actually is in the body and the brain.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A founder of social neuroscience who spent a career on one question: what loneliness actually is in the body and the brain. His first move was to tighten the definition — loneliness is not being alone, it is the gap between the connection you want and the one you have, which is why a crowded room can be lonely. That change moves it out of the category of personality and into the category of hunger and thirst: a signal that something needed is missing.

### Q: What actually happened?
He started as a psychophysiologist — someone who attaches electrodes and measures what the body does. That is why the loneliness work landed. He did not arrive arguing that people should be kinder; he arrived with blood pressure, inflammatory markers, sleep architecture and cognitive decline, on a subject everyone else was treating as a mood. Once it had numbers attached it stopped being something you could be told to get over.

### The parts · A signal, not a character defect
Read as a flaw, the first instinct is to say nothing, which seals the only exit. As a signal it carries no shame: it doesn't say something is wrong with you, it says something needs doing. e.g. Read as 'something is wrong with me', the message stays unsent. Read as hunger, it gets sent.

### The parts · Vigilance grows it by itself
Lonely people read neutral faces as unfriendlier. The reading makes them withdraw, withdrawal thins the relationship, and the thin relationship confirms the reading. Nobody has to have rejected them for the loop to keep turning. e.g. He read the unanswered message as being dropped, so he stopped writing first, so the messages thinned, and the thinning proved him right.

### The parts · The effective intervention is the reading, not the opportunity
In the meta-analysis, more chances to socialise, more support and better skills all did little. What came first was correcting the automatic conclusions — which is why doing more events changes nothing.

### Q: How do I use it today?
If you feel lonely and embarrassed to say so, separate two things first: am I missing people being present, or people knowing me? Crowds help the first and do nothing for the second. If it's the second, don't add events — catch the automatic sentence ('they must find me tiresome'), write it down, ask what it rests on, and find one chance to test it.

### Lines to keep
Hungry, you go find food. This is the same kind of reminder. Loneliness will read an ordinary face as unfriendly. For loneliness, changing the reading beats changing the opportunity.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Mark Granovetter — Both are about the shape of a network. Granovetter asks what it brings you; Cacioppo asks what its absence does to you. Harvard Study of Adult Development — The same finding from opposite ends: he measures what the absence costs, the study measures what the presence buys. Rat Park — Both describe a gap that gets filled by whatever is nearest — one calls it dislocation, one calls it loneliness.

### Further
Harvard Study of Adult Development Robert Sapolsky Mark Granovetter

## John Gottman
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/gottman/
Tags: Family and relationships, Modern, Four fatal signals

John Gottman (1994 · University of Washington) — Four fatal signals. A psychologist who recorded thousands of couples in a laboratory, coding expression, tone and heart rate frame by frame, then tracked who divorced.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A psychologist who recorded thousands of couples in a laboratory, coding expression, tone and heart rate frame by frame, then tracked who divorced. His conclusion doesn't rest on theory: from fifteen minutes of one argument he classified couples with reported accuracy above ninety per cent. What predicts a breakup is not how fiercely people fight but whether four specific signals appear while they do.

### Q: What actually happened?
The ninety per cent needs a caveat, and it is the honest part of this entry. Those figures come largely from models fitted to the same data they were then measured on, which inflates accuracy; independent prospective tests have come out lower. What survives the criticism is the direction, not the number: contempt, criticism, defensiveness and stonewalling really do predict worse outcomes, and contempt really is the strongest of the four. Treat it as a set of things to watch for in yourself, not as an instrument.

### The parts · Criticism and complaint are different things
A complaint targets behaviour and can be solved. Criticism targets character and can only be defended. Many people think they're raising an issue while every sentence defines the other person — which is how one problem runs for ten years.

### The parts · Contempt is the strongest single signal
Eye-rolling, mockery, mimicking their tone. It differs from anger: anger is about the event, contempt says the person is unworthy. It destroys the foundation rather than one conversation.

### The parts · Repair succeeds on the ordinary days
Happy couples aren't the ones who don't fight; they're the ones who reach for the brake and have it taken. Whether it gets taken depends on the balance built up beforehand — roughly five positive interactions to one negative in stable relationships.

### Q: How do I use it today?
When the same thing gets fought about and every round escalates, check the last sentence you said: was it about the event or about the person? Any sarcasm? Were you explaining or returning the ball? And notice whether they offered a way out that you didn't take — taking it is harder than offering it, and it is where most of this stalls.

### Lines to keep
The strongest single predictor of divorce is contempt. Criticism targets the person. A complaint targets the act. Happy couples aren't the ones who don't fight. They repair.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Esther Perel — Two different illnesses: he treats the wound, she treats the emptiness, and the moves point opposite ways. Attachment Theory — Attachment says where the pattern came from; Gottman measures how it is running in the room today. Crucial Conversations — Gottman tells you which signals in a fight predict the end; this tells you what to do in the next three minutes.

### Further
Esther Perel Harvard Study of Adult Development C.S. Lewis Attachment Theory Murray Bowen Crucial Conversations

## John Ratey
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/john-ratey/
Tags: Body and daily life, Modern, Move, then think

John Ratey (2008 · Harvard Medical School) — Move, then think. A professor of psychiatry at Harvard Medical School who redefined what exercise is for. The primary return, he argues, is not the body but the brain: physical activity…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A professor of psychiatry at Harvard Medical School who redefined what exercise is for. The primary return, he argues, is not the body but the brain: physical activity prompts the release of proteins that support neuron growth and connection — fertiliser for the brain — with direct effects on learning, mood regulation and tolerance for stress. Filing exercise under the gym means leaving the cheapest cognitive and emotional medicine unused.

### Q: What actually happened?
The case he leads with is a school district outside Chicago. Naperville moved PE to first period and stopped grading on performance — no measuring who ran fastest, only whether each student held their own high heart-rate zone. That cohort went on to results far above their peers on international science and maths assessments. The design detail is the point: removing the comparison is what let unathletic children work hard, and working hard is the whole of the mechanism.

### The parts · Change the motive from your shape to today
Aimed at the body, the return arrives months later and runs entirely on willpower. Aimed at attention and mood, it arrives within hours. The second is real and easier to sustain, because the feedback is fast.

### The parts · Intensity beats duration
Good news for people with no time: you don't need long sessions, you need the heart rate to actually have gone up. Fifteen real minutes beats an hour of strolling, and the hard thing should be scheduled after.

### The parts · Anxiety is physical, so start there
The body is already on standby and talking yourself down barely reaches it. Exercise burns the standby hormones and signals that you already ran. Which is why a walk makes the thing less frightening while changing nothing about it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
When your head won't turn over, ask when you last raised your heart rate, and whether twenty minutes of moving is a better trade than another hour of grinding. When a thought has gone round twenty times, that's the signal to interrupt, not to continue — and moving is the most reliable interruption, because it occupies attention and burns the hormones at once.

### Lines to keep
Exercise doesn't only shape the body. It shapes the brain. Anxiety is heavily physical. Talking yourself down barely reaches it. The twentieth pass over a thought produces no new information.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Robert Sapolsky — Same system, two handles: Sapolsky on what keeps it switched on, Ratey on how to switch it off today.

### Further
Robert Sapolsky Rat Park Cal Newport

## Julius Caesar
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/caesar/
Tags: Strategy and competition, Qin, Han and the Six Dynasties, The crossing

Julius Caesar (Rome · 100–44 BC) — The crossing. Rome's most famous general and its dictator, and the source of the line about the die being cast.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Rome's most famous general and its dictator, and the source of the line about the die being cast. He went from an aristocrat buried in debt to the conquest of Gaul, victory in the civil war and dictator for life, in about twenty years. Two of his decisions are worth more than the biography: the pause at the Rubicon, which was arithmetic rather than nerve, and the policy of pardoning defeated enemies, which he explained in a letter and which eventually helped kill him.

### Q: What actually happened?
On the fifteenth of March, 44 BC he walked into the senate and was killed with twenty-three wounds. Among the men holding knives were Pompeians he had pardoned during the civil war and afterwards promoted, Brutus among them. He had waved away every warning that an attempt was coming, because he believed pardon bought loyalty. Suetonius reports that when he saw Brutus he spoke his last words in Greek: you too, my child? Everything he had built to defend himself faced outward, and nothing came from that direction.

### The parts · The pause is the decision
He halted at the Rubicon a long while and said out loud that they could still turn back, but that past the little bridge it would all be settled by arms. Reversible decisions deserve speed; a decision that deletes the way back deserves the night. e.g. Changing a tool is undone in a fortnight and needs no committee. An exclusive contract or a public side taken is worth a night at the bank.

### The parts · The sums were done before the sentence
Ten years in Gaul had made his legions the best in Rome, Pompey's forces were scattered in Spain, and the city had nothing to hold it with. He took Italy in sixty days and almost without blood. The famous line is theatre placed on top of a calculation. e.g. Before you commit in public, know your own core capability, the gap in theirs, and the position you can hold in the first month.

### The parts · Mercy as a policy, not a mood
At Corfinium he released every captured senator and returned their property, and wrote to his staff that mercy and generosity would be their new way of winning, in explicit contrast to Sulla's terror. It worked because it changed what the other side expected defeat to mean. e.g. When defeat means ruin, everyone fights to the end. When it means going home, resistance stops being worth paying for.

### The parts · The narrative was part of the campaign
He wrote the Gallic War while campaigning and told it in the third person, so that the account reads as record rather than boast while building the name Caesar at the same time. Winning a war and owning the story of the war are separate pieces of work. e.g. He did both. Most people who did the work do only the first, and then wonder why somebody else is credited with it.

### The parts · What outlived him was the design
His adopted son used the name to build an empire, and the name itself became the word for emperor in languages he never heard, Kaiser and Tsar among them. What lasts is rarely the memorial; it is whether the thing you set up runs without you. e.g. The test is unsentimental. Take yourself out for a quarter and see which of the things you built are still standing when you come back.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Sort your open decisions into two piles, the ones you can walk back and the ones you cannot. Move fast on the first pile immediately, and give one of the second pile a full evening with the numbers before you say anything out loud.

### Lines to keep
The die is cast. We can still turn back; beyond that bridge, arms decide everything. Let mercy and generosity be our new way of winning. I would rather be first in a village than second in Rome.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Xiang Yu — Both made the irreversible move famous, and only one of them had done the sums first: Caesar crossed after a long pause and a count, Xiang Yu sank the boats and trusted the nerve. Machiavelli — Machiavelli says an injured enemy must be either conciliated past all revenge or removed; Caesar pardoned and promoted his, which won the war and produced the men who killed him. Napoleon — The same arc a lifetime apart: both rose on a revolution's wreckage, both fell at the top, both left a legal order behind them.

### Further
Napoleon Liu Bang Huo Qubing

## Karl Popper
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/popper/
Tags: Learning and growth, The industrial age, It has to be refutable

Karl Popper (1902–1994 · Vienna and London) — It has to be refutable. A philosopher of science whose opening question was ordinary and whose answer changed the subject. Astrology explains events and so does physics, so what separates them?

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A philosopher of science whose opening question was ordinary and whose answer changed the subject. Astrology explains events and so does physics, so what separates them? Not explanatory power. A theory that no observation could contradict is not strong, it is empty. The test carries straight over into everyday judgement: a claim that fits every outcome has told you nothing about any of them.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1919, before any of the philosophy, he was volunteering in Vienna's child guidance clinics. He brought Alfred Adler a case that did not look to him like an Adlerian one, and Adler explained it in terms of inferiority feelings without difficulty, and without having seen the child. Popper, uneasy, asked how he could be so certain. Because of my thousandfold experience, Adler said. Popper could not stop himself: and with this new case, I suppose, your experience has become thousand-and-one-fold. What struck him was not that Adler was wrong. It was that nothing could have counted against him.

### The parts · Explaining everything explains nothing
If any result at all can be absorbed by a theory, the theory carries no information. The way to check is to ask what observation would make its holder abandon it. No answer means no test, and no test means no reason to lean on it. e.g. Sentiment drove the rise. And the fall? Sentiment again. It accounts for every outcome and therefore accounts for none.

### The parts · Write the refuting condition before the result
People are remarkably able to read any outcome as support. The only defence is to fix the criterion in advance. Standards set afterwards give you a position that cannot lose, and therefore cannot teach. e.g. Before shipping, write down the number that would mean the assumption was wrong, and the date on which you will go and look at it.

### The parts · Refuted is not the same as discarded
The usual misreading is that a theory shown wrong is finished. His demand was the opposite: that it be exposed to serious attempts to break it. Good ideas mostly get stronger by surviving those attempts. e.g. Once a quarter, go looking for the strongest evidence against your main position. Failing to find it is the only real endorsement.

### The parts · Collect counter-examples, not confirmations
The default is to gather cases that agree, and the hundredth one adds close to nothing. A single case that disagrees is decisive. So the productive hour goes on finding the exception, not extending the list. e.g. To find out whether people like the product, do not survey the people still using it. Talk to three who left.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Next time somebody hands you a confident claim, ask what would have to happen for it to be wrong. If nothing would, treat it as a story rather than a finding. And before your own next bet, write down the condition that would make you drop it, with a date attached.

### Lines to keep
We cannot prove a theory true. We can only fail to refute it. A claim that fits every outcome has told you nothing. One counter-example outweighs a hundred supporting cases.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Richard Feynman — The same rule from two sides: Popper gives the logical criterion, Feynman the psychological warning about who breaks it first. Thinking, Fast and Slow — Popper says what a careful mind should do; Kahneman measures how far an ordinary one departs from it.

### Further
Richard Feynman Albert Einstein Socrates Thinking, Fast and Slow

## Kazuo Inamori
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/inamori/
Tags: Starting and building, The industrial age, The multiplier

Kazuo Inamori (1932–2022 · Kyoto) — The multiplier. Founded Kyocera at twenty-seven and the telecoms company that became KDDI at fifty-two, both of which reached the Fortune 500.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Founded Kyocera at twenty-seven and the telecoms company that became KDDI at fifty-two, both of which reached the Fortune 500. At seventy-eight he was asked to take over Japan Airlines, then bankrupt, and did it for no salary; it was profitable within a year. His central idea is that acting for others is not a moral choice but the better long-term strategy, and he reduced it to arithmetic anybody can run.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 2010 Japan Airlines went bankrupt and the government asked a man of seventy-eight to run it. He took the job and no salary. The first thing he did was not to cut staff. He called the senior managers together and asked them what they were working for. Nobody answered. He told them: for your families, for the passengers on your aircraft, for the society you belong to. A year later the airline posted the largest profit in its history. The route-by-route accounting mattered too, but the silence in that room is where it started.

### The parts · The formula for a life
The result of life and work equals way of thinking times enthusiasm times ability. Ability and enthusiasm run from zero to a hundred. The way of thinking runs from minus a hundred to plus a hundred, and it is the only factor carrying a sign. Direction beats speed because multiplication carries the sign. e.g. A top performer who grabs credit and pushes blame down computes to a large negative. His ability is amplifying his direction.

### The parts · Six ways of improving
Work harder than anyone, stay humble, reflect daily, live in gratitude, do good and act for others, and do not brood on troubles. Six items, all pointing at one thing: taking the self out of the centre. e.g. Run the six as a checklist before sleep. Was I lazy today? Proud? Did I reflect, thank anyone, help anyone, or worry pointlessly?

### The parts · Amoeba management
The company is divided into the smallest units that can keep their own books, each with its own revenue, cost and profit, updated daily and visible to everyone in it. What it produces is not better reporting but ownership: at that size a person can see his own hand in the number. e.g. A team that cannot see its own revenue and cost line has no way to feel responsible for either, whatever the poster on the wall says.

### The parts · Acting for others is the better strategy
Is my motive pure, is there any self-interest in it: the question he put to himself nightly for six months before founding a telecoms company. Over a single round self-interest wins. Over a repeated game, the trust earned by letting the other side win first outruns it. e.g. The founder who takes no pay and gives shares away earns real trust. If the numbers are still wrong, that trust only makes everyone pull harder into the iceberg.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Before sleep, run the six briefly: did I work hard, stay humble, reflect, give thanks, do something for somebody, and refuse to brood? It takes a minute, and its value is not the score. It is that the questions are all about direction, and direction is the only factor in the formula that can go negative.

### Lines to keep
Respect the divine and love people. Result of life and work equals thinking times enthusiasm times ability. Is my motive pure? Is there any self-interest in it? Work is the best training.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Chu Shijian — Both are about running one thing properly to the end. Inamori starts from the motive and the way of thinking; Chu Shijian starts from the written standard and pay tied to quality. Charlie Munger — Two versions of character as a business input. Munger treats reliability as a way of not being stupid; Inamori puts it in the formula as the one factor that can turn the answer negative. Konosuke Matsushita — Inamori heard the dam lecture in person and never got over it; the difference is that Matsushita keeps his margin in the structure, Inamori keeps it in people and accounting. Ren Zhengfei — Two eastern versions of the company as a practice: Inamori binds people with an ethic of doing right by them, Ren drives them with self-criticism and a sense of crisis — one uses good, one uses fear. Zhang Yiming — Two kinds of extreme seriousness: Inamori is driven by an ethic he treats as almost religious, Zhang Yiming by a refusal to let anything stay vague.

### Further
Chu Shijian Taiichi Ohno Duan Yongping Warren Buffett Miyamoto Musashi Zeng Guofan Konosuke Matsushita Ren Zhengfei Nietzsche Viktor Frankl Fukuzawa Yukichi

## Kevin Kelly
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/kevin-kelly/
Tags: Starting and building, Modern, True fans

Kevin Kelly (2008 · founding editor of Wired) — True fans. Founding editor of Wired. In 2008 he turned the survival problem of the independent creator into arithmetic: a thousand true fans, a hundred dollars each a year, is a…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Founding editor of Wired. In 2008 he turned the survival problem of the independent creator into arithmetic: a thousand true fans, a hundred dollars each a year, is a hundred thousand dollars — enough for one person to live on. His definition of a true fan is strict: someone who will buy anything you produce and drive two hundred miles to see you play. The value of the sum is that it takes fame off the list of requirements. He attached a second condition most people forget: the money has to reach you directly.

### Q: What actually happened?
The fashionable idea in 2008 was the long tail — infinite shelf space, everything findable, an audience for every niche. Kelly's essay opens by granting the point and then turning it over. The long tail is famously good news for a handful of aggregators and for consumers; for the individual creator standing out in the tail it is a decidedly mixed blessing, because the tail is long and it is thin. So he asked a different question. Not how do I climb toward the head of the curve, but how many people, exactly, does one person need. Then he did the multiplication.

### The parts · A thousand can be counted; a million is a lottery
The solid part of the sum is that a thousand people can be reached three a day for a year, which is a schedule somebody can actually execute. A million is not assembled by effort. Swap the target and the working day changes shape immediately. e.g. Did one more person who will actually come back arrive today? You can ask that every evening. Did I go viral today? You cannot.

### The parts · A hundred dollars a year is a design brief
Read the number backwards and it stops being a revenue target and becomes a question about what you make: what must exist in a year that somebody who genuinely likes you will spend a hundred dollars on? That pushes you off producing more and onto producing one thing worth buying. e.g. A whole year of free updates is worth less than one thing they will pay for: a course, a printed book, an evening in a room.

### The parts · Whoever holds the list holds your living
There is one test, and it is unkind. If this platform throttled or banned you tomorrow, could you still reach those thousand people? If not, you never had a thousand fans — you were renting traffic and calling it an audience. e.g. A mailing list, a group chat, your own site: anything you could walk out with counts. A follower number does not.

### The parts · The cut takes the feedback, not only the money
With an intermediary in the middle you cannot see who bought, why they bought, or when they stopped. The percentage is the visible loss; the invisible one is the information that would have told you what to change next. e.g. One reply explaining why somebody unsubscribed is worth more than a retention curve on a dashboard.

### Q: How do I use it today?
If you make things and keep waiting for one to break out, count two numbers first: how many people would pay you today, and how many of them you can name. Then do the more urgent thing — before growing the audience further, solve how you would take them with you, by putting one direct route to yourself into every piece you publish. Do it in the other order and the day your follower count looks best is usually the day your leverage is lowest.

### Lines to keep
A creator needs to acquire only 1,000 True Fans to make a living. A True Fan is defined as a fan that will buy anything you produce. You must have a direct relationship with your fans; they must pay you directly.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Naval Ravikant — Both are about earning without an employer: Naval gives you specific knowledge times leverage, Kelly gives you a sum you can run backwards into a product. Paul Graham — Do things that do not scale and a thousand true fans are the two ends of one idea: the first says start by hand, the second says by hand can carry you all the way. Peter Thiel — Thiel wants a monopoly on a large market, Kelly wants depth with a thousand people — both routes avoid competition, one by scale, one by relationship. Haruki Murakami — Same question, nobody is looking, two answers: Kelly says you only need a thousand true fans, Murakami says the answer should not be sought outside at all. Ivan Illich — Both read where technology is heading: one asks what it will grow into, the other asks where it starts eating people.

### Further
Naval Ravikant Paul Graham Jensen Huang Duan Yongping Haruki Murakami

## Konosuke Matsushita
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/matsushita/
Tags: Starting and building, The industrial age, Tap water

Konosuke Matsushita (Japan · 1894–1989) — Tap water. He left school at nine to be an apprentice, started at twenty-three making a two-socket lamp fitting at home with two helpers, and ended with Matsushita Electric, now…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
He left school at nine to be an apprentice, started at twenty-three making a two-socket lamp fitting at home with two helpers, and ended with Matsushita Electric, now Panasonic. Japan called him the god of management. What makes him worth reading is not the size of the company but that he was the first to treat why does this company exist as a technical question with a technical answer: get the mission right and the organisation grows out of it; get it wrong and efficiency only makes you more dangerous.

### Q: What actually happened?
Late in life he lectured on what he called dam management: build a reservoir into your cash, your equipment, your inventory and your people, the way a dam holds water against a dry season. In the questions afterwards somebody asked, reasonably enough, how a company with no spare money is supposed to build a reservoir. Matsushita paused and said: first, you have to genuinely want one. The hall laughed. One man in the audience did not. Kazuo Inamori later said the sentence went through him like a current, and that it changed his life.

### The parts · Dam management
A dam on a river exists to hold water and regulate the flow, and a company needs one in capital, equipment, inventory and talent: a margin it does not currently use. In good years the reserve looks like waste. In bad years it is the only reason you still have choices. e.g. A firm with reserves can halve production and keep everybody. A firm without them can only cut people. The humane option is bought years in advance.

### The parts · Glass-box management
Financial and operating information is open internally, visible like glass. The point is not to move people emotionally, it is judgement: someone who knows the numbers can make a decision, and someone who does not can only carry out instructions. e.g. Show a team the unit economics of what they build and the arguments change register within a month.

### The parts · Make people before you make products
Matsushita Electric makes people, and also happens to make electrical goods. Countless companies have copied that sentence onto a wall, but he meant it literally, treating the manufacture of judgement as the main product and the appliances as the by-product. e.g. He asked staff who were questioned about their employer to answer with the people line first and the product line second.

### The parts · The divisional system
In 1933 he invented the divisional company, giving each product line its own accounts and its own profit and loss. The aim was not efficiency. It was to have as many people as possible practising decisions in front of a real statement. e.g. Modern business units, the amoeba system and internal startups all run down this line from 1933.

### The parts · Three blessings
He said he had three pieces of luck: a poor family, so he learned early where money comes from; a weak body, so he had to hand work to others; no schooling, so he had to ask everyone about everything. Three deficits, each converted into an organisational capability. e.g. Delegation was not a management theory he adopted. His health forced it, and the result was a company that learned not to depend on its founder.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Two things transfer directly. First, build a reservoir into cash, people and time: the reserve always looks excessive while things are good, and it decides whether a bad year leaves you with choices or only with layoffs. Second, write the mission until it can settle a concrete argument on its own — if it cannot help you judge whether this particular price should come down, it is still only a slogan.

### Lines to keep
Matsushita Electric makes people, and also makes electrical goods. Make goods as inexhaustible and as cheap as tap water. My three blessings: a poor family, a weak body, no schooling. The worse the times, the more the power of management counts.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Kazuo Inamori — Inamori heard the dam lecture in person and never got over it; the difference is that Matsushita keeps his margin in the structure, Inamori keeps it in people and accounting. Ren Zhengfei — Both put survival first and take opposite routes: Matsushita stores water in the good years, Ren manufactures a sense of crisis so nobody relaxes. Nassim Taleb — Dam management is antifragility in industrial form — redundancy is a cost in calm weather and the whole of your optionality when the shock lands.

### Further
Kazuo Inamori Ren Zhengfei Duan Yongping Andy Grove Nassim Taleb

## Kristin Neff
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/kristin-neff/
Tags: Mind and feeling, Modern, Self-compassion

Kristin Neff (2003 · University of Texas) — Self-compassion. The psychologist who in 2003 turned self-compassion from a devotional word into a measurable psychological variable; the scale she built has been used across a large…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The psychologist who in 2003 turned self-compassion from a devotional word into a measurable psychological variable; the scale she built has been used across a large body of research since. Her contribution is not advice to be nicer to yourself. It is an alternative algorithm to self-esteem. Self-esteem has better than others inside its definition, so it runs on comparison: strongest when things go well, first to leave when you fail. Self-compassion does not compare. It asks only what do I need now that this hurts. (Effect sizes in this field are disputed and the scales are self-report; this entry takes her structure, not the coefficients.)

### Q: What actually happened?
She has described where it started. After her son was diagnosed with autism, she found that everything which had taught her to be strong was useless, because all of it required her to prove first that she could take it. What let her keep going was permission to say that this was hard and that she was suffering, without adding the clause and therefore I am not up to it. That distinction — between admitting the difficulty and convicting yourself of inadequacy — is the whole of the research programme that followed, in one moment.

### The parts · Self-esteem runs on comparison, so it fails in the trough
While better than others sits inside the definition, the thing has to keep winning to keep supplying. One failure cuts the supply, and that is precisely the moment support was needed. Self-compassion is not indexed to rank, so it is present in the trough. This is not a quarrel about attitude, it is two different power sources. e.g. Overtaken by somebody from your own year, self-esteem says I am finished. Self-compassion says this hurts, that is normal, what is the next move.

### The parts · It does not lower the standard, it raises the will to correct
The standing objection is that kindness to yourself makes you lazy. The data run the other way: moving attention from am I a failure to what do I do about this makes people readier to own the error and quicker to start repairing it. Shame makes people hide; self-compassion makes them look again. e.g. An evening of self-abuse after a bad result means not opening the paper the next day. Change the sentence and the wrong answers get reviewed that night.

### The parts · Three parts, and all of them have to be present
Self-kindness, common humanity, mindfulness. The value of the model is diagnostic rather than motivational: when it hurts, check the three and usually exactly one is missing. Most people are missing common humanity, the sense that others have been here. A smaller number are missing mindfulness, and are either replaying it or insisting they are fine. e.g. Clear-eyed about the situation, aware other people go through it, and still refusing to be civil to yourself: the missing part is the first one.

### The parts · The best test is whether you would say it to a friend
Take the sentence you are saying to yourself and say it word for word to a friend in the identical position. If it will not come out of your mouth, then it is not the truth, it is an attack. The test needs no theory to run and is hard to cheat. e.g. You are too stupid to be attempting this. You would not say it to a friend, so it does not get said to you either.

### Q: How do I use it today?
After you make a mess of something, run one calibration first: try saying the sentence in your head, word for word, to a friend in the same position, and replace it if it will not come out. Then check the three parts. Am I willing to be civil to myself? Do I think this only happens to me? Have I weighed how serious it actually is, neither inflated nor denied? Usually only one is missing. Used wrongly: as a permit to stop reviewing what happened, or turning everyone goes through this into so stop complaining.

### Lines to keep
With self-compassion, we don't have to feel better than others to feel good about ourselves. Self-compassion is simply the process of turning compassion inward. Would you talk to a friend the way you talk to yourself?

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Brené Brown — Both are working on am I a bad person: Brown supplies the distinction, guilt against shame, and Neff supplies the replacement, self-compassion against self-esteem. Carol Dweck — Two ways of editing the same sentence about who I am: Dweck moves ability from fixed to growable, Neff moves the attention off am I good enough — one changes the conclusion, the other changes the question.

### Further
Brené Brown Viktor Frankl Alfred Adler Carol Dweck

## La Rochefoucauld
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/la-rochefoucauld/
Tags: Reading people, Early modern, Virtues in disguise

La Rochefoucauld (France · 1613–1680) — Virtues in disguise. A French duke and a loser of the Fronde. He spent half his life inside aristocratic conspiracies and came out of them with his political career finished and the sight of…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A French duke and a loser of the Fronde. He spent half his life inside aristocratic conspiracies and came out of them with his political career finished and the sight of one eye damaged. In retirement he wrote the Maxims, taking generosity, loyalty, modesty and pity apart one at a time and finding the same thing sitting underneath each of them: self-love. It is not misanthropy. It is a man who saw that world from the inside refusing to keep lying to himself about it.

### Q: What actually happened?
At the battle of the Faubourg Saint-Antoine in 1652 a musket shot hit him in the face and blinded him for a time. He had already backed the wrong side in several conspiracies; the family lands were cut, the political life over. When his sight came back he did not return to court, he went to the salons instead. The interesting part is what he dissected first. The earliest manuscript of the Maxims carries a long essay on self-love, which he says changes like a chameleon and lives in everything and in nothing. Every aristocratic pretence in the book is one he had spent twenty years performing himself, which is why it reads as a confession and not an indictment.

### The parts · Self-love is the floor under every motive
Self-love is the greatest of flatterers. It reports back to you continuously on what kind of person you are, and the report is always favourable. What you take to be your principles, your taste and your judgement are frequently just the version self-love picked out for you. e.g. In a review, change I did it for the team to I wanted to be seen as someone who did it for the team. A surprising number of decisions look different immediately.

### The parts · Virtues are vices in good clothes
Our virtues are most frequently but vices disguised. Generosity may be ambition spending money; modesty may be a longer route to praise; tolerance may be an unwillingness to be bothered. He is not saying virtue does not exist. He is saying do not infer motive from behaviour. e.g. A consistently generous person tells you only that generosity pays here. Change the conditions and the direction of what pays changes. Read the structure, not the character.

### The parts · Nobody complains about their judgement
Everyone complains of his memory, no one complains of his judgment. A weak memory is a hardware fault and costs nothing to admit. Weak judgement would mean every past decision rested on nothing, and nobody can hold that thought, so memory quietly rewrites the misjudgements instead. e.g. Write one page before a big decision saying what you expect and why. Read it half a year later. The first time is usually a shock.

### The parts · Hypocrisy tells you the exchange rate
Hypocrisy is the homage vice pays to virtue. Vice has to wear virtue's clothes to circulate, which proves virtue is the currency in that place, because nobody bothers disguising themselves as something worthless. So watch the direction of the pretending. e.g. To find out what an organisation truly rewards, ignore the values on the wall and watch what a new hire has learned to perform by month three.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Two uses. Inward: when one of your own justifications comes together a little too smoothly, stop and ask whether the reason happens to be extremely comfortable. Outward: judge a partner not by the motive they state but by whether the thing pays them, and by whether it would still pay them after the conditions change. Verify goodwill as a structure rather than believing it as a quality.

### Lines to keep
We all have strength enough to bear the misfortunes of others. Refusing praise is a wish to be praised twice. Old people give good advice to console themselves for no longer setting a bad example.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Two books of maxims with different jobs: Gracián teaches you how to get through this world, La Rochefoucauld only undertakes to stop you deceiving yourself. One supplies method, the other removes illusion. Benjamin Franklin — Franklin believed virtue could be drilled in with a chart. La Rochefoucauld thought what gets drilled in is the appearance of virtue. Read the two together for a year. The Analects — Confucius holds that self-cultivation leads to benevolence. La Rochefoucauld suspects self-cultivation is only the most sophisticated form self-love has found so far.

### Further
The Art of Worldly Wisdom Machiavelli Influence Nietzsche Thinking, Fast and Slow Tending the Roots of Wisdom

## Lee Kuan Yew
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/lee-kuan-yew/
Tags: Power and organisation, The industrial age, Survival first

Lee Kuan Yew (Singapore · 1923–2015) — Survival first. In 1965 Singapore was expelled from the Malaysian federation and forced into independence: an island with no hinterland, no fresh water, no resources, two million…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
In 1965 Singapore was expelled from the Malaysian federation and forced into independence: an island with no hinterland, no fresh water, no resources, two million people, riots between ethnic groups in living memory, and large neighbours. By the time he handed over, income per head had passed that of the country that once ruled it. Almost every ruler in this collection inherited a great state. He is the one who started from too weak to exist, which is where most people and most companies actually start.

### Q: What actually happened?
At the press conference on the day of separation he broke down and stopped for twenty minutes. He explained later that this was not weakness but arithmetic: roughly three quarters of Singapore's fresh water came through pipes from Malaysia, and a single decision at the other end could end the country. Among the first things he started was one that looked in no way urgent, and took decades: desalination and water recycling, until supply was close to self-sufficient. Asked why that came before the emergencies, he said that the place where somebody else can decide whether you live is your only real strategic problem.

### The parts · Deal with the hand around your throat first
A weak party does not sort its priorities by urgency but by who can end it with one decision. Water, defence and recognition got money when there was no money, rather than waiting until there was. e.g. Does your income come from one client, one platform, one boss? That is not efficiency. Somebody else is holding your water pipe.

### The parts · A small fish needs more than one big fish
Friendly with the United States without alliance, engaged with China without leaning, actively inviting several powers to be present in the region. The logic: while two or more great powers compete, a small state has room to manoeuvre. The worst outcome is a region with only one. e.g. Between two strong parties, staying useful to both beats picking early. Once you have one option, your price is whatever they say.

### The parts · Do not build systems that need people to be noble
Ministers were paid against top private salaries, and corruption was prosecuted without exception, including his own old friend the minister for national development. Two faces of one rule: make honesty the rational choice rather than the virtuous one. e.g. His own line: if you pay peanuts, you get monkeys.

### The parts · Cohesion is designed, not hoped for
In a city of Chinese, Malay and Indian residents that had just had race riots, he did not wait for integration to happen. Public housing was allocated by ethnic quota so blocks stayed mixed, English became the common working language because it favoured nobody, and mother tongues were kept in school. e.g. Unity in his hands was never a mood. It was a set of policies somebody had to enforce.

### Q: How do I use it today?
The first lesson for the weaker party is not how to get strong. It is to count the pipes somebody else is holding: one client, one platform, one income, one person who signs. Take the thickest of them and spend three years turning it into two, even though two costs more and runs slower. The second lesson is not to pledge loyalty early. The moment you have only one option, your bargaining power is zero.

### Lines to keep
If you pay peanuts, you get monkeys. Between being loved and being feared, I have always believed Machiavelli was right. The pipe somebody else can close is the only strategic problem you have.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Guan Zhong — Two operators building a small state from nothing, twenty-six centuries apart: Guan Zhong through trade and price control, Lee through institutions and balance. Why Nations Fail — The book argues inclusive political institutions are the condition for lasting prosperity, and Singapore is its most cited counter-example. Read them together. Otto von Bismarck — Two realists: Lee held a small state as a node, Bismarck held a large one as a pivot.

### Further
Guan Zhong Shang Yang Why Nations Fail Machiavelli Ren Zhengfei Mencius Otto von Bismarck
