## Lev Vygotsky
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/vygotsky/
Tags: Learning and growth, The industrial age, One notch higher

Lev Vygotsky (1934 · Soviet psychologist) — One notch higher. A Soviet psychologist who died at thirty-seven and left concepts that shaped the whole of education.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A Soviet psychologist who died at thirty-seven and left concepts that shaped the whole of education. The most important is the zone of proximal development: ability has two lines, what you can do alone and what you can do with help, and learning happens in the gap between them. Below it is repetition, above it is discouragement. He also argued that thinking is internalised from social interaction — first you do it with someone, then you can do it yourself.

### Q: What actually happened?
His work nearly disappeared. He died of tuberculosis in 1934, and within two years his writing was suppressed in the Soviet Union, where it stayed largely unavailable for two decades. Thought and Language was not published in English until 1962, twenty-eight years after his death. So a body of work contemporary with Piaget's arrived in the West a generation late, into a field that had already settled its questions without it — which is part of why it reads as fresh now.

### The parts · Look at the second line
Two children stopping at the same point alone can be far apart: give a hint, and one moves a long way and the other doesn't. Identical current level, completely different zone — and the zone decides what they can learn next. e.g. Two candidates fail the same task. One takes a single hint and finishes; the other needs the answer. Same score, different hire.

### The parts · Teaching runs ahead of development
Against the orthodoxy of his day, he held that you don't wait for readiness. Appropriate guidance pulls development forward. The pitch is: hard enough to need help, not so hard that help doesn't get it done. e.g. Handing him the migration with a review at every step taught more than three more months of tickets he could already do.

### The parts · Scaffolding goes up in order to come down
Help that stays becomes dependence and leaves the person at the level where they're held. Whether a piece of help worked isn't whether the task got done — it's whether less support is needed next time. e.g. If she still needs you on the call the fourth time, the help isn't working, however well each call goes.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Teaching someone, or teaching yourself, find the position where it can't be done alone and can be done with one hint. That gap is what to practise. And plan the withdrawal when you give the help: first time demonstrate a step, second time prompt the opening, third time nothing.

### Lines to keep
Between what you can do alone and with help lies the zone. Teaching should run ahead of development. Higher thinking happens between people before it happens inside one.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Maria Montessori — Both put the adult in the background, and disagree about when to step in: she waits, he leans in one notch. Carol Dweck — Both about where learning happens. He locates it in the task's difficulty, she locates it in the reading of failure.

### Further
Maria Montessori Carol Dweck Anders Ericsson

## Li Bi
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/li-bi/
Tags: Power and organisation, Medieval, Close in, never held

Li Bi (Tang · 722–789) — Close in, never held. The most skilled survivor in the whole tradition of Chinese advisers. He served four emperors, walked out of the court three times of his own accord, was called back…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The most skilled survivor in the whole tradition of Chinese advisers. He served four emperors, walked out of the court three times of his own accord, was called back every time, and ended as chief minister at an age most of his contemporaries did not reach. In an era of eunuch power and permanent purges this is close to impossible. It is harder than what Fan Li did: Fan Li vanished, while Li Bi kept moving through the middle of power without being swallowed by it.

### Q: What actually happened?
He was seven when Xuanzong had him brought to court. The emperor was at a game of go, and the minister Zhang Yue was told to test the boy: make something of square and round, movement and stillness. Zhang Yue did it as a description of the board itself — square like the board, round like the stones, moving when a stone lives, still when it dies. The child would not take the board. Square is acting justly, he said, round is using wit, moving is showing what you can do, still is having got what you wanted. Zhang Jiuling, later chief minister, took to calling him my young friend.

### The parts · The robe was a shield
Wearing a Taoist's robe to court was not piety, it was engineering. A man outside the world has a standing reason to leave, no faction, no post anyone is competing for, and no obligation to the usual forms. An identity can be a structural tool. e.g. The consultant and the employee say the same sentence. Only one of them is heard as saying it for a reason.

### The parts · Three exits, and each one timed early
Every withdrawal came before the danger arrived rather than after: jealousy from a chief minister, the end of a campaign he had won, the rise of the eunuchs. Leaving voluntarily each time is what preserved the standing to be called back. e.g. Leaving while people still want you to stay is what makes the door open again. Leaving after that is just leaving.

### The parts · Advise without contending
His plan to strike the rebels at their base was better than the one that was chosen. He did not insist, did not fight for it, and never said afterwards that he had been right, though he was. Proposing and demanding adoption are two different jobs. e.g. Being right and needing to be seen to be right cost most advisers their access. Not needing it is what kept his.

### The parts · Take no credit and hold no power
Declining honours was not modesty. Credit went to the throne, posts were refused where possible, and nothing was accumulated that anyone might want. With nothing to envy, there is nothing to attack. e.g. Guo Ziyi ran the same policy from the other end of the empire: results to the emperor, money to the sons, power handed back.

### Q: How do I use it today?
When you have something difficult to say, the problem is usually not the content but the attribution. Before you say it, work out what people will assume you are getting out of it, and see whether there is a footing — a role, a written record, a public declaration of your own interest — that removes the assumption. And notice which of your opinions you can only afford to hold because you have somewhere else to go.

### Lines to keep
I am a man outside the world; office is not on my mind. When the work is done, withdraw. That is the way of heaven. Riding out they shared reins; sleeping, facing couches; nothing was settled without him.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Fan Li — Two versions of leaving without going far: Fan Li disappeared completely, Li Bi kept walking through the centre of power in a robe that let him leave at will. Zhang Liang — One reign or four: Zhang Liang withdrew for good once the founding was over, Li Bi came back and left four times and finished holding the top office.

### Further
Fan Li Zhang Liang Sima Yi Tao Te Ching Guo Ziyi The Comprehensive Mirror

## Li Ka-shing
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/li-ka-shing/
Tags: Money and risk, The industrial age, Cycles

Li Ka-shing (Contemporary · 1928–) — Cycles. From a plastic flower workshop to a group spanning property, ports, telecoms, retail and energy.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
From a plastic flower workshop to a group spanning property, ports, telecoms, retail and energy. What is worth studying is not the scale but the survival: the 1967 riots, the 1997 Asian crisis and the 2008 crash all passed through Hong Kong without damaging him, on two rules he states plainly — buy counter-cyclically, and never run out of cash.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1967 Hong Kong was in the middle of riots. Bombs were being left in the streets, British firms were pulling out, and property prices collapsed. Everyone was selling. He was buying. Three years later the city had stabilised and his holdings were worth several times what he paid. The move looks like nerve and is mostly arithmetic: he had done the work of imagining how it could go wrong, and he had the cash to be wrong for a while.

### The parts · Counter-cyclical, in both directions
Buy in the trough, take money off the table at the peak. Land in the 1967 riots; a steady withdrawal from mainland property from the 2010s, roughly a decade before the consensus. Each time, acting before others noticed the turn. e.g. Hiring in the quarter everyone else froze feels like a mistake for eighteen months, which is exactly how long it has to feel wrong to still be cheap.

### The parts · Never take the last coin
He exits before his own estimate of the top, giving up the final ten or twenty per cent in exchange for certainty. Wanting the last coin means selling only once everyone agrees the top has passed. e.g. You sold at eight and it went to ten. The twenty per cent you left behind is what bought you never having to guess where the top was.

### The parts · Cash is oxygen
Large reserves at all times, accepting lower returns to keep liquidity. In 2008 several large groups ran out of funding. He didn't. Low gearing isn't caution — it buys more chances to be wrong. e.g. Six months of runway isn't caution. It is the number of times you get to be wrong before being wrong is fatal.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Once a year, run a cash stress test: if your main income stopped for six months, how long would your reserves last? If the answer is under six months, start building the reserve now rather than after the answer matters.

### Lines to keep
Never forget stability while growing; never forget growth while stable. Ninety per cent of my time, I spend considering failure. The first barrel must be solid before you add the second.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Fan Li — Both left before the top. Fan Li left the whole game; Li Ka-shing left one position and stayed in. Hu Xueyan — Same game, opposite rules: never take the last coin and cash is oxygen, and Hu Xueyan broke both.

### Further
Fan Li Warren Buffett Chu Shijian Hu Xueyan Scarcity The Wealth of Nations

## Li Shimin
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/li-shimin/
Tags: Power and organisation, Medieval, Taking counsel

Li Shimin (Tang · 598–649) — Taking counsel. The emperor most associated with actually listening, and the author of the Zhenguan period.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The emperor most associated with actually listening, and the author of the Zhenguan period. His paradox is unavoidable: he reached the throne by the least defensible route available, killing his brothers at the Xuanwu Gate and forcing his father's abdication, and then governed by the most defensible one — open channels, light taxes, reduced punishments. He is the proof that where power comes from and how it is used can be two entirely separate questions.

### Q: What actually happened?
Wei Zheng had served the rival crown prince and had argued for killing him. After the Xuanwu Gate, Li Shimin did not execute Wei Zheng; he gave him a senior post whose actual work was finding fault with the emperor. One day he was handling a fine sparrowhawk on his arm and saw Wei Zheng coming. He pushed the bird into his sleeve. Wei Zheng pretended to notice nothing and made his report slowly. By the time he left, the bird had suffocated. Taking counsel is not only listening. It is being changed by it.

### The parts · A man as a mirror
With bronze as a mirror you straighten your dress; with history as a mirror you see the rise and fall of states; with a man as a mirror you see your own gains and losses. When Wei Zheng died he said he had lost a mirror. Real counsel is not a performance of openness; it is treating the critic as an instrument. e.g. He was publicly contradicted many times, went back to his quarters furious, and never moved against the man. He knew what losing him would cost.

### The parts · Use the enemy's advisers
Wei Zheng and Yuchi Jingde had both been on the other side. His rule was that talent outranks a record of loyalty and ability outranks origin. The core of the Zhenguan administration was assembled out of people who had opposed him. e.g. The person who argued hardest against your plan usually understands its weak points better than anyone who agreed.

### The parts · The debt from the Xuanwu Gate
Sima Guang's verdict is that the deed succeeded and the killing of kin remained a stain on his virtue. He carried it for life, and it is part of why he had to keep paying in the quality of his government. A person carrying a moral debt often works harder than one who is clean. e.g. Something that cannot be undone can still be the reason the next twenty years are done properly.

### The parts · Reduce, and keep reducing
Lighter taxes, less forced labour, fewer punishments. He preferred an empty treasury to an exhausted population, and turned inherited quietism into something active: stop disturbing people, and build the institutions at the same time. e.g. Households in the empire went from roughly two million to three point eight million during the reign. That is the least arguable scorecard governance has.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Ask whether there is anyone near you whose job is to tell you you are wrong and who pays nothing for doing it. If there is not, you are missing the instrument, not the information. Name the role at the next significant decision and say out loud that arguing the other side will not count against them.

### Lines to keep
With bronze as a mirror you straighten your dress. Water carries the boat, and water can capsize it. Listening to all sides makes you clear; one source, dark.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Zhu Yuanzhang — Two theories of how an emperor handles talent: Li Shimin kept the critics and got a golden age, Zhu Yuanzhang removed the founders and got a secure throne. Zeng Guofan — Two ways to hold up a mirror. Li Shimin kept Wei Zheng in the room; Zeng Guofan used a journal nobody else read.

### Further
Zeng Guofan Zhuge Liang Liu Bang The Comprehensive Mirror Xunzi Mencius Shang Yang

## Liu Bang
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/liu-bang/
Tags: Power and organisation, Pre-Qin and classical, Using people

Liu Bang (Han · 256–195 BC) — Using people. The most famous rise from nothing in Chinese history. He began as a minor local officer in charge of a post station and finished as founding emperor of the Han.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The most famous rise from nothing in Chinese history. He began as a minor local officer in charge of a post station and finished as founding emperor of the Han. He was not the cleverest man in his own camp and not the best soldier in it, and said so out loud at his own victory banquet. His single skill was getting people stronger than himself to work for him, and then letting them decide.

### Q: What actually happened?
Two years into the dynasty, in 200 BC, he took three hundred and twenty thousand men north against the Xiongnu in person. He went in fast and got ahead of his own army, and Modu Chanyu closed around him at Baideng with four hundred thousand cavalry. Seven days and seven nights surrounded, with nothing coming in. He got out in the end by bribing Modu's wife. Nothing about it was unlucky. He had taken the methods that beat Xiang Yu and applied them unaltered to an opponent who was not Xiang Yu.

### The parts · Use a man and trust him
He handed Han Xin an army of a million knowing perfectly well that Han Xin was the better commander of the two. Trust has a price. Withholding it has a higher one, and the bill arrives later and larger. e.g. The specialist you hired either gets to make the call in his own area or he is an expensive way of confirming decisions you had already made.

### The parts · Scatter it and people gather
Money, authority, titles, credit: he gave them away and kept little. Xiang Yu, it was said, would hold a seal of office in his hand until the corners were worn round rather than pass it to anyone. e.g. A leader who cannot let go of the announcement, the customer relationship and the final signature will keep the people who need none of them.

### The parts · Take the advice in the room
In the captured capital his instinct was to enjoy the palace. Zhang Liang told him that a man who wants the empire does not loot it first. He stopped that day, withdrew his troops, and issued the covenant of three clauses instead. e.g. The measure of an open leader is not that advice is welcome. It is the interval between hearing it and changing the plan.

### The parts · Rules short enough to repeat
A killer dies; wounding and robbery answer for themselves. Three lines replaced the whole Qin code, and the population went over to him almost at once. He understood that confidence in the rules is worth more than goods. e.g. The policy nobody can recite is not in force, whatever the handbook says. Three lines on a wall outrank fifty pages in a drawer.

### Q: How do I use it today?
The next time you hire, write down two answers before the offer goes out: what is this person better at than me, and which decisions will I take from him rather than give to him? The sharper those two sentences are, the higher the ceiling of the team.

### Lines to keep
In the tent, settling a victory a thousand miles off, Zhang Liang beats me. These three are exceptional men, and I could use them. Scatter wealth and people gather. Hoard it and they scatter.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Xiang Yu — Both came out of the same collapse. Liu Bang gave things away and won the empire; Xiang Yu held on to everything and won the legend. Cao Cao — Two masters of using people, working from opposite ends: Liu Bang through generosity, Cao Cao through system. Zhu Yuanzhang — Two emperors from the bottom, opposite policies on the men who got them there: Liu Bang scattered wealth to hold them, Zhu Yuanzhang killed them to be safe.

### Further
Han Xin Zhang Liang Cao Cao Li Shimin Wu Zetian Zhu Yuanzhang Mao Zedong Julius Caesar Xiang Yu Machiavelli Records of the Grand Historian

## Machiavelli
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/machiavelli/
Tags: Reading people, Early modern, What is done

Machiavelli (Florence · 1469–1527) — What is done. A Florentine diplomat, secretary of the republic's second chancery, and the author of The Prince.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A Florentine diplomat, secretary of the republic's second chancery, and the author of The Prince. He was not teaching people to be wicked; he was the first to detach politics from moral instruction and study it on its own. The adjective made from his name now means unscrupulous, which flattens what he actually did: he wrote down how power behaves whether or not anyone approves, and he attached limits to it that the famous quotations leave out. His conclusions and Han Feizi's line up across seventeen hundred years, not because both men were sinister but because the mechanics repeat.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1512 the Medici returned to Florence, and the man who had run the republic's second chancery was arrested, put to the rope, and released into the countryside. He spent his days among farmers and card players. In the evening, he wrote to a friend, he took off the mud-caked working clothes, put on court dress, and entered the courts of the ancient men, where he was received kindly and was not ashamed to speak with them. That is where The Prince was written. He dedicated it to the new ruler hoping for a post and never received one. The man who understood power better than anyone then living could not obtain any of it for himself.

### The parts · Start from what is done, not what ought to be done
How one lives is so far distant from how one ought to live, he writes, that a man who neglects the first for the second learns his own ruin. That is a statement of subject matter rather than a licence: the book is about how politics runs, not how it should. e.g. An allowance everyone is trusted not to abuse gets used to the last unit. Assume that, then set the number.

### The parts · Feared rather than loved, and never hated
If one has to be given up, being feared is safer than being loved, because love runs on the other person's willingness. Then the clause that rarely travels with the quotation: avoid being hated, which means keeping off their property and their family. e.g. Cutting a bonus is inside the rules. Humiliating someone in front of the room, or withholding pay already agreed, is over the line and buys an enemy.

### The parts · Half is fortune, and the other half has a deadline
Fortune is the arbiter of about half our actions and leaves the rest to us. The river floods and carries everything away, but in quiet weather men can raise dykes and channels. The half you govern has to be finished before the water rises. e.g. Cash buffer, second supplier, a backup for the person who holds the system. All look like waste until the day they are the only things working.

### The parts · Injury is remembered longer than benefit
Men forget the death of a father sooner than the loss of a patrimony. Nine good turns and one injury leaves the injury standing. Read as design guidance rather than complaint, it says avoiding a memorable harm beats manufacturing a memorable delight. e.g. The first rule of interface design is not to let people make mistakes. One bad experience erases ten pleasant ones.

### The parts · New arrangements have weak friends and strong enemies
Nothing is harder to take in hand than the introduction of a new order, because those who would gain from it are lukewarm and those who lose by it are committed. That asymmetry, not stupidity, is why reforms stall. e.g. The people a change would help have no way to speak for it. The people it costs have every resource needed to push back, and they use them.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Take one rule or incentive you are responsible for and re-read it as though everyone using it were maximising their own position with no goodwill at all. Whatever breaks under that reading was built on ought. Rewrite that part before it is tested for you.

### Lines to keep
How one lives is so far distant from how one ought to live. It is far safer to be feared than loved, if you cannot be both. Men forget the death of a father sooner than the loss of a patrimony. Fortune is the arbiter of half our actions; she leaves us the rest.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Han Feizi — The two closest political realists East and West, seventeen centuries apart: both studied how power actually works, and both were destroyed by the power they studied. Socrates — Opposite poles of political philosophy: Socrates died for a principle, Machiavelli spent his life on the question of how to stay alive inside power. Feng Dao — Machiavelli argued in a book that outcomes outrank motives; Feng Dao spent a life doing it. Theory and specimen, both abused for centuries. Wu Zetian — Political realism written and political realism lived: he set down what a prince must actually do, she had already done it eight centuries earlier. Julius Caesar — Machiavelli says an injured enemy must be either conciliated past all revenge or removed; Caesar pardoned and promoted his, which won the war and produced the men who killed him. The Art of Worldly Wisdom — The same century's problem at two altitudes: Machiavelli instructs a prince on handling a state, Gracián instructs a man with no power on surviving among people who have it. Gandhi — The two answers to whether the end justifies the means: Machiavelli says judge by the result, Gandhi says the result is already contained in the method.

### Further
Han Feizi Liu Bang Cao Cao Sima Yi Sun Tzu Hannah Arendt Feng Dao Lee Kuan Yew Wu Zetian The Art of Worldly Wisdom The Crowd La Rochefoucauld

## Mao Zedong
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/mao/
Tags: Strategy and competition, The industrial age, Concentrate

Mao Zedong (Modern · 1893–1976) — Concentrate. Between 1936 and 1949 he wrote a set of essays that survive as method rather than as history: On Contradiction, On Practice, On Protracted War, and the strategy papers…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Between 1936 and 1949 he wrote a set of essays that survive as method rather than as history: On Contradiction, On Practice, On Protracted War, and the strategy papers of the Red Army years. One habit runs through all of them. In a confused situation, find the single contradiction that governs the others, and put everything on it. The military writing turns that habit into operating orders: fight with the weapons you actually have, concentrate a superior force, finish one opponent before starting the next. What is collected here is that method, not the later career.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1947 the Nationalist offensive was aimed at Yan'an, and he chose to give the town up rather than hold it. The columns that took Yan'an spent the following year garrisoning ground, strung out and tied down, while the field army stayed mobile and destroyed them piece by piece. Within a year the situation in the northwest had turned over completely. A place had been traded for the force that could still move, which is the same arithmetic as keeping the main body alive instead of reporting a win for every position held.

### The parts · One principal contradiction per stage
Many contradictions exist at any moment and one of them governs the rest. Solve that one and the others change shape by themselves. The work is not effort, it is identification, and then the harder half, which is putting the rest down for this stage. e.g. Weak product, few users, thin channel and a loud competitor were all shouting. Supply was the switch, and the money went there until it turned.

### The parts · Concentrate a superior force
Better to sever one finger than to wound ten. Do not fight several opponents at once; mass overwhelming strength at one point, break it, and only then move to the next. Spread evenly, it looks like fighting everywhere and punches through nowhere. e.g. Five features shipped in a quarter and not one of them gives anybody a reason to stay. One at full strength beats five at a fifth.

### The parts · No investigation, no right to speak
Conclusions belong at the end of looking into something, not at the beginning. A judgement that has not been struck back at by events is a sentence nobody has paid for, and the loop that makes knowledge is act, review, act again. e.g. Twenty books of method and no plan anyone can execute is normal. Those were twenty circuits other people walked.

### The parts · The weaker side plays for time
Against someone stronger, a quick decision is their game. The three stages are defensive, stalemate, counter-offensive, and the middle one looks most like no progress while it is doing the actual work of changing the rules of the fight. e.g. Nine months of cash left: cut three lines to keep one alive rather than starve four together, and stop reporting a win for every position.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Before the next quarter starts, get the team to answer one question out loud: what is the principal contradiction of this stage? Put the resources on that single thing, and name what is not being done because of it.

### Lines to keep
No investigation, no right to speak. Concentrate a superior force and destroy the enemy one by one. Better to sever one finger than to wound all ten. Keep the people and lose the ground, and you keep both.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Napoleon — Both mass everything at one point, and then split: Napoleon wants the whole thing decided in one quick battle, and On Protracted War is built on refusing that battle until the fist has formed. Jeff Bezos — Opposite readings of what to hold steady. Bezos says bet on the need that will not change in ten years; this says the governing problem is different in every stage and yesterday's priority is how people die.

### Further
Sun Tzu Liu Bang Han Xin

## Marcus Aurelius
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/marcus-aurelius/
Tags: Mind and feeling, Qin, Han and the Six Dynasties, Restraint

Marcus Aurelius (121–180 · Rome) — Restraint. Roman emperor from 161 to 180, and the most quoted of the Stoics, largely on the strength of a notebook he never intended anyone to read.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Roman emperor from 161 to 180, and the most quoted of the Stoics, largely on the strength of a notebook he never intended anyone to read. He ruled sixty million people through a plague, a long war on the northern frontier and a revolt by one of his own generals. What he wrote in private was not policy and not memoir: it was a set of instructions to himself, repeated because they kept being needed. A man holding absolute power spent his private hours on the only person he could actually govern.

### Q: What actually happened?
The book was never meant to exist. It has no title of its own; the heading that comes down to us means something close to to himself. He wrote it in Greek rather than in the Latin of his court, in camp on the northern frontier, and there is no sign he expected a single reader. It survived by accident, down a thin chain of copies that nearly broke more than once, and became the book most often carried by people who hold power. Nothing in it is addressed outward. Every entry is one man correcting himself, with no audience to perform for.

### The parts · Sort what is yours before you spend anything on it
Some things are up to you and some are not. Your judgement, your intention and your response are; events, other people and your own body are not. The discipline is not resignation, it is budgeting: attention is finite and most of it gets spent on the far side of the line. e.g. He could not stop the plague or the revolt. He could decide how the resources moved and how he treated the man who had failed.

### The parts · What stands in the way becomes the way
The impediment to action advances action. The mechanism is a fire: a small one is smothered by a large log, a big one turns the log into more flame. So the same setback lands differently on different people, and the difference sits in what was already burning, not in the setback. e.g. The server failed at the worst moment, and the rebuild it forced was sturdier than the thing it replaced.

### The parts · Rehearse the morning before it happens
Book Two opens with a script for waking: today I shall meet the busybody, the ungrateful, the arrogant, the deceitful. The reason he gives is that they cannot tell good from harm. Assuming ignorance rather than malice leaves you something to work on; assuming malice leaves only a fight. e.g. Before the meeting you dread, write the three hardest things they could say and what you intend to do at that moment.

### The parts · The notebook has no reader and no defence
Nobody was going to check it, which is why it can be trusted and also where its limit sits. Private discipline has no external audit. The record is a lifetime of self-correction, and it did not stop him from leaving the empire to his own son. e.g. Commodus was strangled twelve years later and Rome entered a century of disorder. On the one thing he fully controlled, he chose blood.

### Q: How do I use it today?
When something makes you angry or anxious, sort it in one pass: which part of this is mine, and which is not. Put everything into the first part and let the second go. Then, before the next difficult conversation, rehearse your own move rather than their behaviour.

### Lines to keep
The impediment to action advances action. A fire makes flame out of everything thrown into it. He governed sixty million people and audited only one.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Epictetus — A slave and an emperor reaching the same rule about what is up to you, from opposite ends of the same empire. Viktor Frankl — Two tests of the inner citadel: Marcus holds it voluntarily at the top of power, Frankl has it tested with everything else taken away. Zeng Guofan — The closest pair East and West: both wrote themselves down every day, and both used the writing to hold themselves in check at the top of their own power. Seneca — Two Stoics in opposite seats: the emperor writing a private notebook to himself, the courtier writing public letters to other people — one turns inward, the other stays practical.

### Further
Epictetus Seneca Zeng Guofan Viktor Frankl Montaigne Gandhi Nelson Mandela The Bhagavad Gita

## Maria Konnikova
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/konnikova/
Tags: Reading people, Modern, Why we fall for it

Maria Konnikova (2016 · The Confidence Game) — Why we fall for it. A writer with a psychology background who studies confidence tricks. Her conclusion turns the usual question round: whether you get taken in has little to do with…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A writer with a psychology background who studies confidence tricks. Her conclusion turns the usual question round: whether you get taken in has little to do with intelligence and a great deal to do with what you were short of at the time. The con artist does not manufacture trust, he locates a need you already have. What gets used is the wanting, not the judgement, which is why the educated and the well-travelled are on the victim lists too. Her second finding is more practical: the losses cluster in periods of transition, when the old way of reading a situation has just stopped working.

### Q: What actually happened?
The cases she worked through run from fake art dealers and fake doctors to Ponzi schemes and street hustles, and the victims include professors, lawyers and people who work in finance for a living. What repeats is not that these people were careless. It is that each of them needed something at that moment: to recover a loss, to be taken seriously, to have an explanation that finally made sense. Which is why she says raising your guard is the least useful defence available. Wanting is the thing that lowers the guard, so the guard is already down by the time you would need it.

### The parts · Ask which need it answered
When a proposal moves you, postpone the question of whether it is true and ask why it is landing now. The answer usually names the thing you are shortest of. This comes before checking, because checking gets bent by wanting and you go looking for what supports it. e.g. The people in a hurry to recover a loss are the ones who meet guaranteed high yield. That is selection, not coincidence.

### The parts · It is about circumstance, not intelligence
I was stupid is both inaccurate and expensive: it is the wrong diagnosis, and it makes the story too humiliating to repeat, so the same trick keeps working on the next person. What was I short of is a question with an actionable answer. e.g. The sentence victims say most often is that they are not normally like this. It is almost always true.

### The parts · Transitions are the high-risk window
A move, a new job, a divorce, a death, retirement, a windfall. What these have in common is not weakness, it is that no usable template exists for what you are now facing, so any story that hangs together sounds credible. This converts the problem from a character trait into a diary entry. e.g. Newly arrived in a city, you have no idea what a normal price is for anything. That is the window, and it is predictable in advance.

### The parts · Procedure, not vigilance
Rules are made while you are calm and take effect while you are not: above this figure, sleep on it; a second person has to see it; there has to be an independent source. This works precisely because it does not depend on your state at the time. e.g. Anything over this amount waits a day before I sign. That one rule has rescued more people than any talent for reading faces.

### Q: How do I use it today?
When somebody hands you an offer that is hard to refuse and something feels wrong, do not start checking. Start by asking which of the things you are short of it answers, and treat a clear answer as the warning. Then look at the calendar: have you just moved, changed jobs, lost someone, or come into money? If so, put a step in front of every large decision for three months and find one person outside the situation to look at it.

### Lines to keep
The con artist does not build trust. He uses the need you already have. What gets used is the wanting, not your judgement. It turns not being conned from a personality into a calendar.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Influence — Cialdini explains how the six devices work, Konnikova explains why the same devices work so well on certain people at certain moments. One studies the weapon, the other the target. Scarcity — Both replace how could they be so stupid with what were they short of: Scarcity is about bandwidth being taken, the con is about wanting being used.

### Further
Influence The Crowd Scarcity Zeng Guofan

## Maria Montessori
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/montessori/
Tags: Family and relationships, The industrial age, The room, not the discipline

Maria Montessori (1907 · Casa dei Bambini, Rome) — The room, not the discipline. One of Italy's first women doctors, who began with children with intellectual disabilities and then applied the same methods to ordinary ones, opening the Casa dei…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
One of Italy's first women doctors, who began with children with intellectual disabilities and then applied the same methods to ordinary ones, opening the Casa dei Bambini in a poor district of Rome. Her central finding is that children don't need to be shaped, they need a prepared environment — tools at their scale, the choice in their hands, and the adult stepping back from director to observer. Children thought incapable of concentrating began concentrating for long stretches on their own.

### Q: What actually happened?
The room came before the theory. She was given a set of apartment buildings full of unsupervised three- to six-year-olds whose parents worked, and a brief that amounted to keeping them from wrecking the stairwells. There was no curriculum to defend and no institution watching, so she could change the furniture and watch what happened. The method came out of a childcare problem in a slum, not out of a laboratory — which is why every part of it is about what the child can physically reach.

### The parts · Check whether the environment matches
A cup out of reach or a tool only an adult can work manufactures dependence and frustration. Change it so the child can finish alone and the behaviour problem often disappears. It holds for adults: plenty of self-discipline problems are environment problems.

### The parts · Concentration grows, it isn't demanded
Children concentrate for long stretches on self-chosen work and lose focus quickly on assigned tasks. So the route is attractive choices and no interruption — and the most common interruption is an adult's well-meant attention.

### The parts · Help me to do it myself
The boundary of help: the goal is that they can finish alone, not that the task finishes sooner. Taking over saves your time and spends their chance to learn. The right move is neither taking over nor leaving them — it's dropping the difficulty one notch.

### Q: How do I use it today?
When a child repeatedly can't do something and saying it again hasn't helped, ask whether it is physically possible at their height with their grip and these tools, and which single thing in the room could change. When you're about to take over, ask whether it's so they learn or so this ends sooner.

### Lines to keep
A child's work isn't taught in. It happens in a prepared room. Help me to do it myself. Every unnecessary help is an obstacle to development.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Rat Park — The same instruction in two fields: change the cage before you correct the creature in it. Lev Vygotsky — Both put the adult in the background, and disagree about when to step in: she waits, he leans in one notch. Thomas Gordon — Both ask the adult to hold back. She changes the room; he changes the sentence.

### Further
Thomas Gordon Lev Vygotsky Rat Park

## Marie Curie
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/curie/
Tags: Body and daily life, The industrial age, She took his course

Marie Curie (1867–1934 · Warsaw and Paris) — She took his course. Physicist and chemist, born in Warsaw, in Paris from 1891, and in 1903 a Nobel laureate in physics alongside her husband Pierre.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Physicist and chemist, born in Warsaw, in Paris from 1891, and in 1903 a Nobel laureate in physics alongside her husband Pierre. On 19 April 1906 Pierre was killed by a horse-drawn wagon in a Paris street; the Sorbonne gave her his chair, and on 5 November she gave her first lecture, with no eulogy, picking up where his last one had stopped. She is here because the situation — the person who mattered most is suddenly gone and the days continue — has too few people who have actually lived it.

### Q: What actually happened?
1911 was the year both things happened. She was refused admission to the Académie des sciences by a narrow vote, in a campaign that made much of her being a woman and a foreigner; and the press ran a scandal about her private life, with crowds outside her house. In the same year she was awarded a second Nobel Prize, this time in chemistry, and was advised not to come and collect it. She went. The composure that produced the November lecture was not a one-off temperament. It was the same thing, repeatedly.

### The parts · Catch hold of one thing with an hour and a place
An enormous blank can't be faced directly. What can be faced has a time, a place and a content. It doesn't solve the grief; it gives the day a shape you can put yourself inside. e.g. 'Sort out my life' is unfaceable. 'Thursday, nine to ten, the second drawer' is not, and the day now has a shape to stand in.

### The parts · What can't be said aloud gets written to them
For more than a year she wrote to Pierre in a notebook nobody saw in her lifetime. Said to the living it becomes a request for comfort; said to yourself it becomes analysis. Only addressed to them does the true thing come out. e.g. Written to a friend it becomes a request for comfort. Written to the person who died it stays what it actually is.

### The parts · Put the skill where it's most needed now
In the war she left the laboratory, raised money, fitted vehicles with X-ray equipment, learned to drive and repair them, and took them to the front. Those years are academically almost blank, and were not wasted. e.g. The year he stopped shipping features and rebuilt the on-call rota is missing from his promotion packet, and it is what the team remembers.

### Q: How do I use it today?
When the most important person has gone and life still has to continue, look for one thing in the next few days that has to be done at a set hour in a set place. If there are things you can't say to anyone, ask who they are actually addressed to, and write them to that person. Don't set yourself a date to be better by.

### Lines to keep
It doesn't solve the grief. It gives the day a shape. Who the letter is addressed to decides what you can write. Nobody at their worst owes anyone a performance of it.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
C.S. Lewis — Two records of the same year: he wrote to find out what grief was, she wrote to keep talking to him.

### Further
C.S. Lewis Winston Churchill

## Mark Granovetter
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/granovetter/
Tags: How the world works, Modern, Weak ties

Mark Granovetter (1973 · American Journal of Sociology) — Weak ties. A sociologist whose 1973 paper, The Strength of Weak Ties, has been cited tens of thousands of times.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A sociologist whose 1973 paper, The Strength of Weak Ties, has been cited tens of thousands of times. He surveyed 282 people about how they found work and found that among those who got there through a contact, 56% saw that person only occasionally and 28% rarely. The reason isn't willingness but information structure: your circle overlaps almost completely with a close friend's, so what they know you mostly know. From that he draws a harder line — no strong tie is a bridge.

### Q: What actually happened?
The finding has a consequence people meet without recognising it. Move to a new city or leave an industry and the close friends survive — those few hold. What disappears is the wide band of people you used to see occasionally, and that is precisely the layer that brings opportunities. So the drought after a move is not imagined and not a comment on you. It is structural, and rebuilding that layer takes time, which is why the first year somewhere new is so often silent.

### The parts · It isn't willingness, it's whether the news is new
Close friends want to help more and hold almost the same information you do. A weak tie isn't more generous. He is standing somewhere else, holding the part you can't reach from here. e.g. Your five closest friends have already told you every opening they know about. The person you met once at a conference knows the one you haven't heard.

### The parts · Closure is what strong ties produce
Close to A and close to B means A and B probably know each other. The circle closes, and once closed the three of you know largely the same things. Closure gives support and trust, and it stops new information arriving. e.g. Everyone in the group chat forwarded the same article. That is what a closed circle feels like from inside: agreement, and no new information.

### The parts · Maintain breadth, not depth
Rather than pouring everything into a few people, keep more weak ties in the 'still knows who you are' state. The cost is an occasional message with no request attached — and the line has to be kept while you don't need it. e.g. One message a year with nothing attached — congratulations on the new job — keeps a line open. Reappearing only when you need something closes it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
If you're looking for something — work, a partner, customers — and circling the same few people, count how many of the people you contacted in six months are ones you see a few times a year. If almost none, a whole source of opportunity is switched off. Just after a move or a career change, expect this and rebuild deliberately.

### Lines to keep
Of people who found work through a contact, 56% saw them only occasionally. No strong tie is a bridge. When you move, the layer that breaks first is the one that brought opportunities.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
John Cacioppo — Both about the shape of a network: Granovetter on what it brings you, Cacioppo on what its absence does to you.

### Further
Harvard Study of Adult Development John Cacioppo

## Mencius
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/mencius/
Tags: Power and organisation, Pre-Qin and classical, Winning the people

Mencius (Warring States · 372–289 BC) — Winning the people. The man who turned Confucius into an operating manual for government. Benevolence in his hands is not a slogan about virtue but the condition on which a regime keeps…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The man who turned Confucius into an operating manual for government. Benevolence in his hands is not a slogan about virtue but the condition on which a regime keeps existing: mishandle the taxes, the conscription and the power to punish, and authority goes hollow well before it falls. He travelled from court to court for decades and was never given office. The clarity cost him a career and produced the sentence every later ruler had to answer.

### Q: What actually happened?
King Xuan of Qi had once seen an ox being led past the hall to be killed for a ritual, saw it trembling, and ordered a sheep used instead. His people said he was being cheap. Mencius told him the instinct had been right: he had seen the ox and had not seen the sheep. Then the turn. You extended that feeling to an animal that happened to pass you, and not to the people of your own state, whom you never see. Not doing it, he said, is a different thing from not being able to.

### The parts · Win the people and the rest follows
He who has the way has many helpers; he who loses it has few. The way here is not scripture. It is whether people will still put themselves out for you. Tax past what is produced, demand past what can be given, punish past what is fair, and they do not revolt. They stop consenting. e.g. Mandatory overtime buys a quarter. The moment your best people start playing dead, the thing that made them useful has already gone.

### The parts · Force buys compliance, never judgement
Those subdued by force do not submit in their hearts, they submit because their strength is short. So force has to be reapplied continuously, and the standard is exactly as high as your attention. What you want is people holding the line where you cannot see them. e.g. Heavy monitoring lifts the weekly report and never lifts the work, which is why the numbers fall the week the manager is away.

### The parts · No settled livelihood, no settled heart
He is specific about sequence: first make sure people can keep their parents and feed their children, then lead them towards the good. Demanding standards from people whose footing is not secure is not strictness, it is a category error about what they have available. e.g. Asking for craftsmanship from a team that cannot see past next month's contract is asking a question their situation cannot answer.

### The parts · Born in adversity, dead in comfort
Not an argument for hardship as a virtue. It is a warning about attention: an organisation entering comfort starts losing its alertness first and its position later. Difficulty is a signal. Ease is an anaesthetic. e.g. Qin could remake itself while it was close to death and fell apart one generation after winning everything.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Before the next decision that costs somebody else something, ask three questions. Will the people carrying the cost still consent to the next thing? Will the standard hold while you are not there? Is what you are asking for actually available to someone in their situation? One no, and the decision is not ready.

### Lines to keep
The people come first, the altars of the state next, the ruler last. He who has the way has many helpers; he who loses it has few. Born in adversity, dead in comfort.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Han Feizi — Both are writing about how to govern. Han Feizi trusts reward and punishment; Mencius asks whether people are still willing to follow you at all. The Analects — The Analects tells a gentleman how to conduct himself; Mencius tells a ruler what will remove him. Xunzi — One holds that people can be taught, the other that people can be shaped. Mencius cultivates; Xunzi processes.

### Further
The Analects Han Feizi Shang Yang Li Shimin Lee Kuan Yew Xunzi

## Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/csikszentmihalyi/
Tags: Body and daily life, Modern, Flow

Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (1990 · University of Chicago) — Flow. The psychologist who named flow. He studied when people are most absorbed by experience sampling: several thousand people carrying pagers, recording what they were doing…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The psychologist who named flow. He studied when people are most absorbed by experience sampling: several thousand people carrying pagers, recording what they were doing and how it felt whenever one went off. The best experience turned out not to be relaxation but a state of concentration so complete that time disappears. The conditions are specific. The difficulty has to match your skill, the goal has to be clear, and the feedback has to be immediate. Lose one of the three and you are either anxious or bored.

### Q: What actually happened?
Before any of the pager studies he spent his time watching young painters at work in Chicago. They would stay at a canvas for hours, forgetting meals and sleep, in a state close to trance. Then the painting would be finished, and they lost interest in it almost at once and started another. Whatever they were working for, it was not the object at the end, because they barely looked at it once it existed. The reward had to be inside the doing, and finding out what it was became the rest of his career.

### The parts · Difficulty has to match skill
Too hard gives anxiety, too easy gives boredom, and only the narrow band just above your current ability produces flow. That is why the same activity is a different experience for different people, and why a skill that has grown makes an old challenge dull. Raise the load rather than switch subjects. e.g. Three years into a job and it feels pointless. Check whether the difficulty has stayed flat before changing industry.

### The parts · A clear goal and immediate feedback
Flow requires that you know at any moment how you are doing. Climbing, chess and playing an instrument supply that by nature, while writing a proposal or running a team gives feedback in weeks. The workable move is to cut out smaller pieces that carry their own feedback. e.g. Turn finish the report into get the argument in this section to hold. You know on the spot whether it holds.

### The parts · The best moments are at work, not in leisure
The most counter-intuitive line in his data. Leisure has a low threshold and flow has an entry cost, so people repeatedly choose a low-return activity in places where a high-return one was available. Knowing this has a direct effect on how you lay out a day. e.g. Two hours on the phone after work usually leaves you emptier. Two hours on something difficult tends to restore.

### The parts · Flow is not the same as pleasure
Inside flow there is no attention left over for judging whether you are enjoying yourself, and the satisfaction arrives afterwards. Which means choosing what to do by whether it feels nice right now will almost certainly choose wrong, and you will never begin. e.g. Writing a passage through to the end is not enjoyable. The solid feeling once it is done is the return.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Next time you cannot get into something, check the three conditions in order before you decide you have lost interest. Is the difficulty slightly above my current ability or far below it? Is my goal for this hour specific enough to be finished? Can I tell at any moment how I am doing? Repair whichever one is missing.

### Lines to keep
Enjoyment appears at the boundary between boredom and anxiety. The best moments come when body and mind are stretched to the limit. People assume leisure is happiest; the records put flow at work.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Anders Ericsson — Both keep you at the edge of your ability: Ericsson on how to practise so the ability grows, Csikszentmihalyi on why that position is the one that absorbs you. Cal Newport — One sets out the internal conditions for concentration, the other the external ones, the diary and the environment that protect it.

### Further
Anders Ericsson Cal Newport Atomic Habits Viktor Frankl BJ Fogg

## Miyamoto Musashi
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/musashi/
Tags: Strategy and competition, Early modern, Unattached

Miyamoto Musashi (Japan · 1584–1645) — Unattached. The most famous swordsman in Japanese history: more than sixty duels, none of them lost, the first at thirteen.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The most famous swordsman in Japanese history: more than sixty duels, none of them lost, the first at thirteen. At sixty he wrote the Book of Five Rings, which turned a lifetime of fighting into a general method. His claim is that the way of strategy is the way of everything, and the two rules he actually gives are both refusals: do not love a weapon, and do not look at the blade.

### Q: What actually happened?
At about sixty he withdrew to a cave outside Kumamoto and spent two years writing. He knew he had little time. Five scrolls came out of it, named for earth, water, fire, wind and the void, and the last is a few lines long. There is no boasting in them and no list of victories. What he sets down instead is a daily discipline: rise early, train, keep at it year after year, and understanding arrives by itself. He finished the book and died within weeks.

### The parts · No favourite weapon
Leaning too hard on one weapon is the same error as not knowing how to use it. A long blade has long-blade weaknesses; a short one has short-blade weaknesses. What he refuses is not the tool but the attachment, because attachment quietly lets a tool decide which fights you can take. e.g. The engineer who knows one framework and the team that only knows paid acquisition both started as specialists and ended as a shape of work.

### The parts · Perception strong, sight weak
He splits looking into two. Perception takes in the whole and the intention behind it and should be strong; sight tracks the particular movement and should be weak. See distant things as if close and close things as if distant. Watch the sword and the sword sets your tempo. e.g. Reacting to each of a rival's launches keeps you a beat late. Their hiring and where the money goes is the weight shifting before the launch.

### The parts · Two swords as a way of thinking
His school used the long and the short sword together, which is a tactic and also a habit of mind: hold two views at once, one attacking and one covering, one near and one far. He drilled the refusal of a single viewpoint until it lived in the body. e.g. Running an argument and its inversion at the same time is the same move. The discipline is holding both without collapsing early into one.

### The parts · The bout was decided before it began
At Ganryujima his opponent carried a famous long sword. Musashi came ashore with a wooden one cut from a boat oar, longer than the blade and belonging to no school anyone could read. Beating a man on the parameter he is proudest of turns years of his training into a liability. e.g. If their strength is response time, open where their response process does not reach. The stronger the strength, the slower the turn.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Name the tool you reach for first and write down the situation in which it must lose. Then check this week's calendar against that description. If you are in that situation now, the question is not how to use the tool better.

### Lines to keep
Do not have a favourite weapon. In all things whatsoever, rely on nothing. Perception is strong; sight is weak. See distant things as if close, and close things as if distant.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Bruce Lee — Three hundred years apart and the same instruction: Musashi says rely on nothing, Lee says be like water. Huo Qubing — Both refused the inherited manual. Musashi replaced it with a method he wrote down; Huo Qubing left none.

### Further
Bruce Lee Sun Tzu Tao Te Ching Zeng Guofan Kazuo Inamori Anders Ericsson

## Montaigne
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/montaigne/
Tags: Mind and feeling, Early modern, Weaknesses on the table first

Montaigne (1533–1592 · Bordeaux) — Weaknesses on the table first. French writer, and the inventor of the essay. At thirty-eight he resigned as a magistrate, went home to the family estate and turned the third floor of a tower into a…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
French writer, and the inventor of the essay. At thirty-eight he resigned as a magistrate, went home to the family estate and turned the third floor of a tower into a library, where he wrote for the next twenty years, serving two terms as mayor of Bordeaux in the middle of it. He had a medal struck for himself carrying the words What do I know? The whole book is about himself: his fear of pain, his terrible memory, his dithering, the riding accident that nearly killed him, the kidney stones that nearly finished the job.

### Q: What actually happened?
The book opens with a note to the reader that would be strange in any century. He says it has no purpose beyond a private and domestic one, that he has set out to be seen in his simple and ordinary fashion, and that the reader would be unreasonable to spend leisure on so frivolous a subject. Then the line that turned into a literary form: I am myself the matter of my book. He called the pieces essais, attempts, because none of them claims to arrive anywhere. Nobody had written like this before, and it is still the model.

### The parts · A card you play yourself cannot be played against you
People afraid of exposure are afraid that someone else will name the weakness first. He names it himself, more fully than anyone else would bother to, which takes it out of everyone's hand. Four hundred years on, nobody has found an attack on him that he had not already made. e.g. This part is not my area, said up front, costs far less than being caught out on it in a meeting.

### The parts · Mostly you fear the imagining, not the thing
Thrown from his horse in his thirties, unconscious long enough that those around him thought he was dead, he came back and found the experience had been light, like falling asleep. Decades of dread had been aimed at a version his own head had built. Only the unfamiliar is frightening; once familiar it is a fact. e.g. The fear that arrives at two in the morning is usually a film. Look at it in daylight and it flattens.

### The parts · Not withdrawal, a fenced-off piece
He did not become a hermit; he was mayor twice after moving into the tower. What he did was nail down one space and one stretch of time as his own and leave everything else running, with the decision carved into the wall so he walked past it every morning. e.g. One room and one hour a day nobody else can reach. Far easier to hold than a whole new life.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Pick the fault you would least like exposed and find a plain sentence for it that you can say first, before anyone asks. Then fence off one hour and one place as yours, write the decision down where you will see it, and leave the rest of the calendar alone.

### Lines to keep
He put his own cowardice in the book, and nobody has been able to use it since. He kept death as an acquaintance so it would stop being a stranger. Keep one piece for yourself. Let the rest run.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Brené Brown — Both take shame and fear apart. She has the laboratory findings; he has one man running the experiment on himself four hundred years earlier. Seneca — Both on learning to die. Seneca instructs from above; Montaigne writes outward from the afternoon he was thrown off a horse.

### Further
Seneca Marcus Aurelius Brené Brown Shi Tiesheng

## Murray Bowen
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/bowen/
Tags: Family and relationships, Modern, Differentiation

Murray Bowen (1978 · Family systems theory) — Differentiation. The psychiatrist who assembled family systems theory. His central concern is differentiation of self: whether a person can stay in contact with the people closest to him…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The psychiatrist who assembled family systems theory. His central concern is differentiation of self: whether a person can stay in contact with the people closest to him and still keep his own thinking and his own feeling. Poorly differentiated people are carried by the family's emotional field — somebody else is anxious, so they are anxious; a position gets given up to end a quarrel. His other major idea is the triangle: when two people carry more tension than they can hold, a third gets pulled in to spread it, and that fixes the tension in place.

### Q: What actually happened?
Between 1954 and 1959, on a research ward at the National Institute of Mental Health, he did something nobody else was doing: he moved whole families in to live. The identified patient was usually a young adult diagnosed with schizophrenia, and the point of having the mother, the father and the siblings on the ward was that you could then watch what everybody did, all day, for months at a time. What he saw was not one ill person among well ones. It was a system holding a shape, with the symptom sitting exactly where the system needed it to sit.

### The parts · Connection and separateness at the same time
Low differentiation has two forms that look opposite and share a root: being led by the family's feeling, and cutting the family off. He calls the first fusion and the second emotional cut-off. Differentiation is the third thing — in the room, and the position holds. e.g. Pressed about marriage over the new year: miserable all evening is fusion, never going back is cut-off. The third road is going as usual, without arguing and without changing your mind.

### The parts · The triangle fixes the tension
Two people under strain instinctively reach for a third: complaining about a partner to a friend, parents recruiting a child into their quarrel. It relieves the day, and the cost is that the pair no longer has to settle anything, because the pressure now has somewhere else to go. e.g. Rather than raise it with the colleague, you raise it with a third one. The problem does not go away; it becomes a permanent structure with three people in it.

### The parts · Anxiety runs through the system
In a family, anxiety behaves like water: it runs from wherever the pressure is towards whoever is most vulnerable, which is very often a child. So a parent handling their own share does more than any technique aimed at the child. It is his most usable conclusion. e.g. Your anxiety about his prospects reaches him whether or not a word is said. Deal with your part and his state often shifts on its own.

### The parts · It is practised, and it is inherited
Your level is largely set in the family you grew up in and gets passed down, and it can be raised on purpose. The practice happens in the relationship most able to sweep you off, and it sounds like this: I know you are unhappy, I understand, and my view has not changed. e.g. Meet a relative's feeling without going cold and without surrendering, and the capacity grows a notch. The next generation starts from that notch.

### Q: How do I use it today?
When your family's feeling is carrying you along, sort it first: am I fusing — going miserable, conceding fast — or cutting off? And when two people you know are stuck, notice whether you have become the third point. Handing the problem back is the only move that lets them solve it.

### Lines to keep
Differentiation is staying connected to people and still being yourself. Too much tension between two people automatically pulls in a third. Anxiety travels the family system and lands on the most vulnerable member.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Virginia Satir — Both read the family as a system: she reads the stance being taken today, he reads the level of differentiation across generations. Alfred Adler — Two knives for drawing a line: Adler asks whose task this is, Bowen asks whether their feeling has already got inside you.

### Further
Virginia Satir Alfred Adler Attachment Theory John Gottman

## Napoleon
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/napoleon/
Tags: Strategy and competition, Early modern, Concentration

Napoleon (France · 1769–1821) — Concentration. A poor Corsican who at twenty was not even a Frenchman by birth, emperor ten years later, and dead alone on Saint Helena ten years after that at fifty-one.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A poor Corsican who at twenty was not even a Frenchman by birth, emperor ten years later, and dead alone on Saint Helena ten years after that at fifty-one. His campaigns are the clearest demonstration anywhere of one idea: the side with fewer men in total can still be the larger side at the place where it is decided. The Civil Code he pushed through is still law in dozens of countries.

### Q: What actually happened?
Austerlitz, 1805. Seventy-five thousand French against ninety thousand Russians and Austrians. He deliberately left his right wing thin and visible, and the allies did what the sight of it invited: they moved weight onto it, which hollowed out their own centre. When they were fully committed he sent his best troops straight through the middle, cut the allied army in two and destroyed each half. French losses around nine thousand, allied losses around thirty-six thousand.

### The parts · More men where it is decided
The art of war, in his own maxim, is to have more force at the point attacked or defended even when the army as a whole is weaker. Comparisons of total strength are a summary table; outcomes happen at points of contact, and a smaller side can win each of them in turn. e.g. A small team cannot compete across a market and can outspend a large company inside one account. At that point you are the big company.

### The parts · Their dispersal is something you cause
The columns he beat piecemeal in Italy were not merely careless. His line of march threatened several objectives at once and forced them to cover each. Making the other side afraid to leave anything uncovered is the same act as making him too weak everywhere. e.g. Visible probes in three directions divide their defensive budget three ways. You mean to attack one; they have to hold all of it.

### The parts · The method runs on a time difference
Beating two forces in turn requires that turning from the first to the second is faster than the two can join. Lengthen the supply, add layers of approval, and the interior position inverts into encirclement. This is how it eventually failed in his own hands. e.g. Any strategy living off a timing gap loses a beat for every layer the organisation adds. Run the old lightning method through a long chain and it walks into a trap.

### The parts · A bet with no exit written into it
In 1812 he crossed into Russia with over six hundred thousand men and brought back fewer than a tenth. He lost no major battle and entered Moscow. What he had no plan for was winning while the other side declines to concede: an empty capital, a Tsar who would not negotiate, winter. e.g. Write the withdrawal date and the withdrawal number before you enter a new market. Write them while you are clear, because later one more push will feel obvious.

### Q: How do I use it today?
List the points where the contest you are in is actually settled. Pick one and put more into it than the larger side puts into that same point, and accept that you are giving up the others. Then, before you commit, write the date and the number at which you stop.

### Lines to keep
Have more force at the point attacked, even when weaker overall. In war, the moral is to the physical as three to one. From the sublime to the ridiculous there is only one step.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Julius Caesar — The same arc a lifetime apart: both rose on a revolution's wreckage, both fell at the top, both left a legal order behind them. On War — Clausewitz spent his life studying him: the first half of the book explains the victories, the second half the road out of Moscow. Otto von Bismarck — Napoleon rode momentum until his opponents collapsed; Bismarck fixed his winnings by halting. One won at fighting, the other at stopping. Mao Zedong — Both mass everything at one point, and then split: Napoleon wants the whole thing decided in one quick battle, and On Protracted War is built on refusing that battle until the fist has formed.

### Further
Sun Tzu On War Julius Caesar Fan Li Shang Yang Otto von Bismarck

## Nassim Taleb
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/taleb/
Tags: Money and risk, Modern, Antifragile

Nassim Taleb (1960– · Lebanon and New York) — Antifragile. Lebanese, an options trader before he was a theorist of risk. He watched the Lebanese civil war, the 1987 crash and the 2008 crisis at close range, and built a whole…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Lebanese, an options trader before he was a theorist of risk. He watched the Lebanese civil war, the 1987 crash and the 2008 crisis at close range, and built a whole philosophy of uncertainty out of real extreme events. His central claim: most of the systems we build are fragile, and break the moment something unexpected arrives. What we should be building is antifragile — systems that get stronger out of the unexpected.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 2008 Lehman failed and the global financial system shook. Taleb's fund made more than a hundred per cent that year. Not because he predicted the crisis, but because he had held, for years, a large book of tail-risk hedges — contracts that are very cheap and almost never pay out. In ordinary years they lose a little; in a Black Swan year they pay enormously. His barbell reaches its best outcome precisely in the worst state of the world, and it does that not because he is cleverer than anyone else, but because he refuses to assume that bad things will not happen.

### The parts · The three-way structure
Fragile is harmed by volatility and prefers calm; robust is unaffected by it; antifragile gains from it and prefers disorder. Most modern institutions are fragile — stable on the surface, collapsing under an extreme event. A muscle is antifragile: use strengthens it and disuse wastes it. e.g. Ask it of your own career, your organisation and your finances one at a time. Most people find all three sit in the first column.

### The parts · The barbell
Ninety per cent extremely safe, ten per cent extremely risky, and nothing in the middle. The logic is that the middle is the most fragile place to stand in a Black Swan: it holds neither enough safe assets to absorb the shock nor enough risky ones to profit from it. e.g. A stable main income plus a small, genuinely wild bet beats a portfolio of moderately risky things that all move together.

### The parts · Skin in the game
Advice from someone who bears no consequence is noise. Bankers gamble with client money and keep the bonus, analysts recommend what they do not own, politicians decide what will not touch them. Every one of those opinions should be discounted before you weigh the content. e.g. Ask instead what would you do, or what would you have done to your own mother — the heuristic Taleb credits to Gerd Gigerenzer.

### The parts · What a Black Swan actually is
The defining feature is not rarity but being outside your model's range — not that it seldom happens, but that you never conceived of it. A pandemic was a Black Swan to public health systems and not to epidemiologists. The label is relative to whoever is holding the model.

### The parts · The survivorship trap
We see the survivors and not the dead, so almost every lesson drawn from success is drawn from a sample that excludes failure, and the graveyard is silent. Studying where returning aircraft were hit tells you to armour the places with no holes. e.g. Startup literature studies companies that lived. The dead ones, which may have done exactly the same things, never got written up. Ask first how many of the failures did this too.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Audit the shape of your income the way you would a portfolio: ninety per cent from a stable main occupation, the cushion, and ten per cent aimed at high-risk, high-return exploration, the right end of the barbell. Both ends present is what lets you survive a surprise, and occasionally profit from one. Then run the same audit on advice: before weighing what somebody recommends, find out what they have staked on it.

### Lines to keep
The opposite of fragile is not robust. It is antifragile. Wind extinguishes a candle and energizes fire. Don't tell me what you think, tell me what you have in your portfolio. Those who don't take risks should never be involved in making decisions.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
George Soros — Two strategies for uncertainty: Soros hunts the market's error and acts on it, Taleb builds a structure that does not need to know what the error is. Ray Dalio — Two ways of handling what cannot be predicted: Dalio writes principles to hold the line against it, Taleb arranges to be paid by it. Thomas Schelling — Skin in the game and credible commitment are one coin: Taleb uses cost to decide whose word to trust, Schelling to make his own word land. Konosuke Matsushita — Dam management is antifragility in industrial form — redundancy is a cost in calm weather and the whole of your optionality when the shock lands. Friedrich Hayek — Taleb is about not being able to foresee the shock, Hayek about not being able to centralise the knowledge — one handles randomness, the other handles the pretence of knowing. Howard Marks — Same premise, that the future is unknowable, and two routes out: Taleb builds a structure that survives it, Marks takes the temperature of the present. Jim Simons — Two mathematicians on opposite ends of one market: Taleb is paid at the moment models break, Simons is paid all the while they hold.

### Further
Tao Te Ching Naval Ravikant Fan Li Sun Tzu Ray Dalio Thomas Schelling Konosuke Matsushita Epictetus Benjamin Graham Hu Xueyan Jesse Livermore Friedrich Hayek Howard Marks Scarcity Jim Simons George Soros Technological Revolutions Thinking, Fast and Slow Sapiens The Sovereign Individual
