## Naval Ravikant
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/naval/
Tags: Starting and building, Modern, Leverage

Naval Ravikant (Contemporary · 1974–) — Leverage. Co-founder of AngelList and an early investor in Twitter, Uber and Notion. In 2018 he posted a numbered thread called how to get rich without getting lucky, which has…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Co-founder of AngelList and an early investor in Twitter, Uber and Notion. In 2018 he posted a numbered thread called how to get rich without getting lucky, which has since been read millions of times. He is not a financial adviser. He is someone who worked out a route to personal sovereignty in a digital economy and then wrote the route down.

### Q: What actually happened?
The thread was later compiled into a book by a reader, Eric Jorgenson, and released free — the whole text, downloadable, with Naval taking nothing from it. For a man whose entire subject is leverage, that is the argument made in the form of a decision rather than a sentence: a book that costs nothing travels further than one that earns, and reach compounds where royalties merely add. He gave away the thing most authors protect, because giving it away was the higher-leverage move.

### The parts · Four kinds of leverage, and two need permission
Labour means managing other people and requires leadership. Capital means money making money and requires having some. Code runs once written, at zero marginal cost. Media is read once written, at zero marginal cost. The first two need somebody's consent; the last two need nobody's, and that is historically new. e.g. The essay published tonight and the fund raised next spring carry the same idea. Only one of them can start tonight.

### The parts · Wealth, money and status are three different games
Wealth is assets that work while you sleep and it is positive sum. Money is the instrument for moving wealth about. Status is your rank, and it is zero sum — for you to rise somebody falls. How much time goes into each decides which game you are actually in, whatever you say you are doing. e.g. A year spent on titles and a year spent on something that earns are indistinguishable while they are happening, and very distinguishable afterwards.

### The parts · Happiness by subtraction
He argues happiness comes from removing desires rather than satisfying them: every unmet want is a standing source of unhappiness, so peace is not owning everything but no longer being pulled by what you do not own. He read a great deal of eastern philosophy and is restating an old line in a modern setting. e.g. The list of things that would finally make it fine has been rewritten four times, and each version was believed completely at the time.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Ask which part of your work could be written once and used many times — code, writing, a process, a framework, a tool. Identify those and move your hours towards them, because everything else is priced by the hour and stops when you do.

### Lines to keep
Wealth is assets that earn while you sleep. If your income is measured in hours you will never truly be wealthy. Code and media are the permissionless leverage of this era.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Tao Te Ching — Both end at enough; one arrives through leverage, the other by never picking the load up. Kevin Kelly — Both are about earning without an employer: Naval gives you specific knowledge times leverage, Kelly gives you a sum you can run backwards into a product. Benjamin Franklin — The same algorithm two hundred and fifty years apart: compounding, leverage, reputation, and the pursuit of knowledge once money stops being the question.

### Further
Peter Thiel Tao Te Ching Warren Buffett Paul Graham Kevin Kelly Nietzsche Benjamin Franklin The Last Hot-Metal Edition Finite and Infinite Games Nassim Taleb The Sovereign Individual The Wealth of Nations

## Nelson Mandela
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/mandela/
Tags: Reading people, The industrial age, Reconciliation

Nelson Mandela (South Africa · 1918–2013) — Reconciliation. Twenty-seven years in prison, and no revenge on the way out. He chose reconciliation and built the rainbow nation instead, which is the strongest demonstration on record…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Twenty-seven years in prison, and no revenge on the way out. He chose reconciliation and built the rainbow nation instead, which is the strongest demonstration on record of putting hatred down. The part that matters is that he was not born saintly: as a young man he backed armed struggle and helped found the wing that carried it out. Prison turned an angry revolutionary into a patient builder. The adversity changed his method and left his objective exactly where it was.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1994, at his inauguration as the first democratically elected black president of South Africa, three of the white warders who had guarded him on Robben Island were seated among the guests of honour. He had invited them himself. Four years earlier, walking out of the prison gate after twenty-seven years with every camera in the world pointed at him, he had raised his fist and declined to say anything angry at all. He put it later in one sentence: as he walked towards the gate, he knew that if he did not leave the bitterness and hatred behind, he would still be in prison.

### The parts · Hatred is the second prison
Resentment is drinking poison and expecting the other person to die. He had unusual amounts of time to watch what it did to people: men whose bodies were released and whose minds stayed locked in the anger. What he chose was not forgiveness, which requires an apology from someone else, but letting go, which requires only your own decision. e.g. He read Stoic philosophy in prison, and Sun Tzu, and anything that kept him clear-headed. The cell became a school, which is the same move Frankl made in the camps.

### The parts · Twenty-seven years of conversion
He went in a militant who wanted the apartheid state overthrown by force. He came out the most patient man at the negotiating table. That is not softening, it is an upgrade: he had worked out that an overthrow manufactures more hatred, and that only reconciliation produces a country that lasts. e.g. The change is itself the argument. He had tried the other road first, which is why his conclusion is worth more than anyone's who only ever held one position.

### The parts · Inviting the warders was political design
Seating his own jailers in the guests of honour was not a display of magnanimity. It was an exactly aimed signal to white South Africa that there was a place for them in the new country. Reconciliation was the moral choice and also the optimal strategic one. e.g. Reconciliation that lasts always satisfies both the moral and the practical case, so both sides can accept it because it suits them, not only because it is right.

### The parts · Truth in exchange for amnesty
Forgiving needs the other side to admit what they did; letting go does not. Rather than demand universal apology he built the Truth and Reconciliation Commission: tell what happened and you can be pardoned. It gave perpetrators a way out and gave victims an answer, which is a form of justice that is not punishment. e.g. Societies coming out of conflict have studied the model ever since. Its insight is that sometimes the truth itself is the justice that was missing.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Next time you notice an old grievance still drawing on you, make his distinction: forgiving and letting go are separate acts. You do not have to forgive anybody. You can decide unilaterally to put it down, not for their sake but to get yourself out of the second prison.

### Lines to keep
It is an ideal for which I am prepared to die. Courage was not the absence of fear, but the triumph over it. Sport has the power to change the world.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Viktor Frankl — Extreme adversity at its highest setting: Frankl found meaning inside a camp, Mandela turned a prison term into a political education. Gandhi — Nonviolence inherited and revised: Mandela chose arms first and only arrived at Gandhi's position after twenty-seven years inside. Zhu Yuanzhang — Two minds shaped by an extreme start: it left Zhu Yuanzhang unable to trust anyone for the rest of his life, and left Mandela able to put the grievance down.

### Further
Gandhi Viktor Frankl Marcus Aurelius Su Shi Wang Yangming

## Nietzsche
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/nietzsche/
Tags: Mind and feeling, The industrial age, Overcoming

Nietzsche (1844–1900 · Germany) — Overcoming. The most misread philosopher there is. The Nazis used his overman to underwrite racism, while he himself loathed antisemitism and broke with his own sister over exactly…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The most misread philosopher there is. The Nazis used his overman to underwrite racism, while he himself loathed antisemitism and broke with his own sister over exactly that. What he actually argued is that a person can go past herd morality and become someone who creates their own values. He lost his father at ten, was physically wretched for most of his life, and collapsed mentally at forty-four — having written, before that, some of the most forceful prose in Western philosophy.

### Q: What actually happened?
In January 1889, in a street in Turin, Nietzsche saw a horse being whipped by its driver. He ran across, threw his arms round the animal's neck and wept, and then broke down. He never recovered his reason and spent the remaining eleven years in madness. A man who had spent his working life on the will to power finished his philosophy in front of an innocent horse, in tears. The thinking is full of strength and conquest and the life was full of weakness and pain. That contradiction is the most useful door into him.

### The parts · Eternal recurrence
If you had to repeat what you are doing now for ever, what would you choose? It is not a claim that the universe actually loops. It is a test at the limit: a thing worth repeating without end is a thing genuinely worth doing, and a thing you could not stand to repeat was never really what you wanted. There is no stricter instrument for checking what you value. e.g. Two hours on the phone tonight — would you take that for ever? Run the same question over the three things that took the most of today.

### The parts · The will to power
The essence of life is to expand, to overcome, to become more. His will to power is not political office, it is an internal drive to go past yourself. What he calls master morality is creating your own standard of value and beating yesterday's version of yourself, rather than using phrases like humility is a virtue to keep the strong in check. e.g. An athlete going past a limit, an artist breaking a style, a founder walking into unknown territory. None of it is taking something off somebody else.

### The parts · God is dead
God is dead, and we have killed him. Not an atheist announcement but a diagnosis of modernity: with the traditional moral system gone, the source of meaning goes with it and nihilism moves in. His remedy is that each person has to become a maker of values. The overman is not a superhero, he is someone able to create a meaning for his own existence. e.g. Inherited belief, family structure and national identity all coming apart at once, with no answer left to why am I alive. The modern crisis of meaning is what the sentence was pointing at.

### The parts · Perspectivism
There are no facts, only interpretations. What anybody sees is an interpretation issued from their own vantage, history and interest, and not the objective article. This is not relativism, it is epistemic humility: knowing your own angle is partial, and going out to collect the other angles on purpose. e.g. Ray Dalio's radical open-mindedness is perspectivism in practice — invite everybody to attack your judgement, because their vantage may hold what yours cannot.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Run the eternal recurrence test. Take the three things that took the most of your time today and ask, one by one, whether you would accept repeating them for ever. Cut the ones that come back no, and go deeper into the ones that come back yes. It is more direct than any system of time management.

### Lines to keep
What does not kill me makes me stronger. We should consider every day lost on which we have not danced at least once. Man is a rope, tied between beast and overman, a rope over an abyss. One must still have chaos in oneself to be able to give birth to a dancing star. He who has a why to live can bear almost any how.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Socrates — His fiercest target was Socrates: he held that the cult of reason had castrated the vitality of the Greeks and turned philosophy into a denial of life — the two of them side by side is the most important collision in Western thought. Viktor Frankl — He who has a why to live can bear almost any how is Nietzsche's line, and Frankl carried it into Auschwitz and tested it: one man worked it out in a study, the other verified it where verification cost everything.

### Further
Wang Yangming Kazuo Inamori Naval Ravikant Socrates Ray Dalio Viktor Frankl La Rochefoucauld Finite and Infinite Games

## Nonviolent Communication
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/nonviolent-communication/
Tags: Reading people, Modern, Observation first

Nonviolent Communication (1999 · Marshall Rosenberg) — Observation first. Rosenberg was a clinical psychologist who spent his working life mediating in race conflicts, divorces, prisons and war zones.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Rosenberg was a clinical psychologist who spent his working life mediating in race conflicts, divorces, prisons and war zones. What he found is that most arguments do not ignite on the disagreement itself but on an evaluation delivered as an observation. You never look after the children sounds like a statement of fact and arrives as a verdict. His structure has four steps: observation, feeling, need, request. It looks simple, and almost nobody manages the first one.

### Q: What actually happened?
He traced the whole project back to being ten years old in Detroit in 1943, during the race riots, when the family stayed indoors for days while people were killed in the streets outside. When school started again he was beaten for his name. Two questions came out of that summer and he spent fifty years on them: what happens to people that lets them turn violent, and what is it that some people have that keeps them compassionate even then. He trained under Carl Rogers, and the method he eventually wrote down is an answer to the second question rather than the first.

### The parts · Observation and evaluation have to be separated
You were late three times this week is an observation and there is nothing in it to dispute. You are always late is an evaluation and has to be disputed. Most conversations are lost on the opening sentence, because the speaker believes they are reporting a fact and the listener receives an accusation. e.g. Change you do not care about this project into you were not at three of this week's meetings. Same event, one provokes defence and one provokes explanation.

### The parts · A feeling is not a thought
I feel that you do not respect me is not a feeling, it is a judgement wrapped in one. The feeling is I am upset. The difference is the subject: a feeling is about me, a judgement is about you, and as soon as the subject slides across, the other person can only defend. e.g. Being ignored, in I feel ignored, is a claim about somebody else's behaviour. I am disappointed reports your own state, and nobody can contradict it.

### The parts · There is a need underneath the blame
His central claim is that all blame is an inept expression of a need that has not been met. Underneath how can you be so selfish there is usually I need to be seen. Take blame at face value and you argue on the surface forever. Bring the need up and the conflict often deflates on the spot. e.g. When a partner says all you care about is work, the surface is an accusation and the need is company. Answer the need instead of the accusation and the direction changes immediately.

### The parts · A request has to be something you could refuse
Could you show me a bit more respect is not a request, because nobody could tell you what would count as complying. Could you tell me before the meeting starts is. Vague requests fail, and after they fail both sides are more certain than before that saying anything is pointless. e.g. Change be more involved at home into can you do the Wednesday school run. The first is a complaint, the second is something that can be accepted or declined.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Before the argument starts, run what you are about to say through the four steps. What is the specific fact I saw, with no always or never in it? What am I feeling, with myself as the subject? What do I actually need? What exactly am I asking this person to do? Speak once all four have answers.

### Lines to keep
Observing without evaluating is the highest form of human intelligence. All criticism is a tragic expression of an unmet need. Everything we do is in service of our needs.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Guiguzi — Two opposite arts of persuasion: Guiguzi works out what the other side is holding before moving on them, Rosenberg puts both sides' needs on the table in the open. Socrates — Two ways of getting somebody to say the answer themselves: Socrates by questioning, Rosenberg by naming the need the other person has not said out loud. Chris Voss — Both start from the feeling and want different things: Rosenberg so that both sides' needs get onto the table, Voss so that you get a result out of an adversarial room.

### Further
Alfred Adler Guiguzi Socrates Chris Voss Carl Rogers Brené Brown Virginia Satir

## Norbert Wiener
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wiener/
Tags: How the world works, Modern, He warned them first

Norbert Wiener (1894–1964 · United States) — He warned them first. The founder of cybernetics: Cybernetics in 1948, The Human Use of Human Beings in 1950. His position here is unusual — he is both the person who put machine control into…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The founder of cybernetics: Cybernetics in 1948, The Human Use of Human Beings in 1950. His position here is unusual — he is both the person who put machine control into the world and the first to say publicly that it would displace factory workers on a large scale. In 1949 he wrote to Walter Reuther of the United Auto Workers saying he was unwilling for it to happen with no preparation. Automation had not yet been deployed and nobody had lost a job.

### Q: What actually happened?
Cybernetics came out of the war. He worked on the problem of aiming anti-aircraft guns at aircraft that were manoeuvring — which meant predicting where a human pilot would go, and correcting continuously from what the last shot did. The feedback loop was invented while trying to shoot at people. That origin is why the ethics arrive so early in his work: he had already spent years modelling a person as a component in a system, and had seen exactly what that framing permits.

### The parts · The people who see it coming aren't hit yet
The year he wrote to the union there was still time to arrange something. Once it lands you only get to react. The stretch while you still have work is the only window you get to plan in. e.g. The time to learn the next thing is while the current work still pays. Once it stops you are learning and job-hunting at the same time.

### The parts · 'It can' doesn't imply 'give it to it'
Whether a machine can do a task is technical. What is left of the person afterwards is a different question, and the answer isn't automatically good. Hand over the repetition, not the judgement. e.g. Let it draft the summary. Deciding which three of the twenty issues actually get raised is the part that was your job.

### The parts · Control is a loop, not an order
His definition: not issuing an instruction but correcting the next move from the actual result. Cut the report back and the movement goes off, however well it was aimed. It applies unchanged to managing people and to practising a skill. e.g. You set the goal in January and next heard about it in June. The instruction was fine; there was nothing correcting it in between.

### Q: How do I use it today?
When something is spreading through your field and hasn't reached your income yet, ask which of your tasks it can already do, and who in your field you have actually talked to about it. When shifting work onto a tool, check whether what's left needs any judgement — if it doesn't, you handed over the wrong half.

### Lines to keep
What a machine can do and what people are for are separate questions. He feared people being arranged like machines, not the reverse. Control isn't issuing an order. It's correcting from the result.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Garry Kasparov — Wiener warned before it arrived; Kasparov was the first person it arrived for.

### Further
Garry Kasparov John Boyd The Last Hot-Metal Edition Thinking in Systems

## On War
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/on-war/
Tags: Strategy and competition, The industrial age, Friction

On War (Prussia · 1832) — Friction. Clausewitz joined the army at twelve, lived through the catastrophe at Jena and the destruction of Napoleon's army in Russia, and spent a career studying defeats.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Clausewitz joined the army at twelve, lived through the catastrophe at Jena and the destruction of Napoleon's army in Russia, and spent a career studying defeats. He died of cholera at fifty-one with the book unfinished; his widow Marie edited and published it. Sun Tzu tells you how to win. This tells you why your plan will not survive contact, which is the half Sun Tzu leaves out.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1812 he was attached to the Russian army and watched the Grande Armee come apart. Nearly half a million men went in and under thirty thousand came out. What struck him was that the Russians had barely fought a proper battle. What destroyed the strongest army in Europe was mud, misdelivered orders, supply carts nobody could find, columns that lost each other, an early frost, and thousands of small things a day that should have gone smoothly and did not.

### The parts · Friction: the plan always deforms
Every step is feasible on paper and the whole is not, because each link carries a little resistance: fatigue, misunderstanding, weather, fear, a broken axle. Individually trivial, stacked they seize the plan. It cannot be removed, only budgeted for, and armies differ in whether they keep moving inside it. e.g. Every line of a schedule is reasonable and the sum of them is late. Not weak execution: nobody gave friction a budget.

### The parts · The fog: information is never complete
War is the realm of uncertainty, and three quarters of what action rests on lies in fog. He does not tell you to wait for the picture to clear, because it will not. He asks for a different capacity: judge well on partial and partly wrong information, and then hold to it. e.g. This collides with know your enemy and know yourself head on. Sun Tzu assumes the count can be completed; Clausewitz assumes it cannot.

### The parts · Centre of gravity
Every opponent has a hub that his strength and his freedom of action depend on: the main army, the capital, an alliance, public support. The core work of strategy is identifying it and concentrating against it. Ten successful attacks on secondary targets are worth less than one on the hub. e.g. Do not turn competitor analysis into a feature grid. Ask which single thing, if it went, would make the whole thing stop working.

### The parts · Defence is the stronger form
His most counter-intuitive result. The defender holds the ground, has shorter supply, wears the attacker down and has time on his side. Correspondingly the attacker has a culminating point, beyond which every further step weakens him. Napoleon went past his own in Moscow. e.g. Every new city, category and market lengthens the line. Most companies are not killed by a rival; they run past their own culminating point.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Add a friction audit to the next plan: list every handoff that crosses a person, a team or a time zone, because that is where the delay actually lives. For any expansion, name your culminating point and the signal that says you have reached it, in advance, because from inside you will not see it.

### Lines to keep
War is merely the continuation of policy by other means. Everything in war is very simple, but the simplest thing is difficult. Three quarters of the factors in war lie in a fog.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Sun Tzu — The two halves of the subject: Sun Tzu on how to win, Clausewitz on why the plan deforms. One assumes the count can be completed, the other that it never is. Napoleon — The book was written against his career: it explains both the concentration that won and the culminating point he ran past. Su Yu — He kept enlarging plans mid-operation, which is exactly the risk Clausewitz names: every step past your culminating point weakens you.

### Further
Sun Tzu Napoleon Su Yu Xiang Yu John Boyd

## Otto von Bismarck
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/bismarck/
Tags: Power and organisation, The industrial age, Alliance geometry

Otto von Bismarck (Prussia · 1815–1898) — Alliance geometry. The man who treated Europe as a geometry problem. He did not want friends, he wanted an arrangement in which three other parties could not do without him.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The man who treated Europe as a geometry problem. He did not want friends, he wanted an arrangement in which three other parties could not do without him. Having beaten Denmark, Austria and France in three short wars, he stopped, and spent the rest of his career holding the new Germany in place with treaties. Napoleon won by fighting. Bismarck won by stopping.

### Q: What actually happened?
The German Empire was proclaimed at Versailles in 1871 and he did not press further. He turned at once to arranging the rest of Europe around the new fact, negotiating separately with Russia, Austria and Italy, building the League of the Three Emperors, making each capital feel that leaving Berlin was more dangerous than staying. France stayed isolated for twenty years. Then he was dismissed, and the network tore within a few years, which tells you what it had been: not friendship, but one man's calculation, running only while he was there.

### The parts · The art of the possible
Politics is not the realisation of an ideal, it is extracting the most from the conditions available. The person who writes his objective as it must be this loses the position while defending the sentence. e.g. Unifying Germany, he left the south out at first and took the half Prussia could hold. Take the piece you can defend before the piece you can reach.

### The parts · Make three parties unable to do without you
The safest position is not the strongest one. It is the one where A needs you against B and B needs you against A. Neither can drop you, so you sit in the middle without being the biggest thing on the board. e.g. Being the component both giants have to design around beats being tied exclusively to whichever of them looks stronger this year.

### The parts · Stop when you have won
Three wars, and then he halted. One more would have turned the alliances. The move after a victory is not expansion, it is converting the victory into an arrangement the losers can live inside. e.g. Napoleon was still looking for the next campaign. Bismarck finished with France and immediately started negotiating the terms of the peace.

### The parts · Do not push on the other side's home ground
He kept away from British sea power and from Russian interests in the Balkans. A home ground is where the other party's survival is at stake, and pressure there buys you their entire strength rather than part of it. e.g. Zhang Juzheng reformed the Ming finances and the personnel system and never touched the throne itself. The same geometry.

### The parts · An alliance is a consumable
It runs on a person. When the person goes the paper remains and the structure disperses. Never let a calculation that lives in one head be treated as an institution. e.g. After he fell, Wilhelm II let the reinsurance arrangement lapse and Europe went back to two camps. Partnerships held together by a founder behave the same way.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Before agreeing to any partnership, draw three circles: why they cannot do without you, why you cannot do without them, and how a third party moves when the deal is signed. If the only real dependency runs from you to them, this is a favour you are giving, not a deal you are making.

### Lines to keep
Politics is the art of the possible, the attainable, the next best. We are a satiated state. An honest broker who really wants to put the business through.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Napoleon — Napoleon rode momentum until his opponents collapsed; Bismarck fixed his winnings by halting. One won at fighting, the other at stopping. Lee Kuan Yew — Two realists: Lee held a small state as a node, Bismarck held a large one as a pivot.

### Further
Zhang Juzheng Lee Kuan Yew Napoleon Thomas Schelling

## Paul Graham
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/paul-graham/
Tags: Starting and building, Modern, Do things that do not scale

Paul Graham (United States · 1964–) — Do things that do not scale. A Lisp hacker who built Viaweb in 1995 — the first commercial software that ran inside a browser — and sold it to Yahoo in 1998.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A Lisp hacker who built Viaweb in 1995 — the first commercial software that ran inside a browser — and sold it to Yahoo in 1998. In 2005 he started Y Combinator and rewrote what early-stage investment looked like. His real influence is in several hundred essays: most of what now passes for startup common sense has its earliest and clearest statement in one of them.

### Q: What actually happened?
Y Combinator began as a summer experiment with a deliberately strange shape: fund a whole batch at once, give each of them a small amount of money and three months, and have dinner with them every week. Every part of it was the opposite of how investment worked — small cheques, no track record required, founders as young as they came, decisions in a ten-minute interview. The batch was the point. Founders learn more from the company two tables over, at the same stage and similarly frightened, than from anybody with an office.

### The parts · Make something people want
It is the only thing on the wall at YC. His judgement after thousands of companies is that the fatal mistake is singular: building something nobody actually wanted. Everything else — the wrong hire, the wrong price, the bad quarter — is repairable. e.g. A team can survive being outbuilt. It cannot survive having been right about a need that was not there.

### The parts · Schlep blindness
The best openings often sit behind work that is tedious and unglamorous — bank integrations, compliance, refunds. The mind skips over those ideas so quickly that you never notice having skipped. Which is exactly why they are still available. e.g. Everybody saw the market. The reason nobody took it is that the first nine months are paperwork.

### The parts · A maker's day is not divisible
Managers work in hours, makers need whole blocks. A single meeting in the middle of an afternoon does not cost an hour; it costs the afternoon, because neither remaining piece is long enough to get into the work. e.g. Push every meeting to one end of the day. The output change is larger than any productivity system.

### The parts · Better a few who love it
A hundred users who love the thing are worth more than ten thousand who find it acceptable. The first group tells you why, brings other people, and forgives the rough edges. The second leaves quietly and teaches you nothing. e.g. Chasing a satisfaction score upward across everyone is usually how a product becomes something nobody would miss.

### Q: How do I use it today?
In the cold-start phase do not build channels, buy traffic or automate. Find the first hundred users by hand and serve each one until they are happy; when that work is crushing you, that is the signal to scale. Test an idea on three questions: do I want it, can I build it, and why has nobody done it — no answer to the third usually means it is not worth doing, or you have not yet seen the tedium hiding in it.

### Lines to keep
There is one fatal mistake: building something nobody wants. Do things that do not scale. It is the only route to scale. Better to have a few people love you than many find you acceptable.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Peter Thiel — Start from the users in front of you, or start from whether the market can ever hold a profit. Peter Drucker — Graham writes about the first hundred users and doing things that do not scale; Drucker writes about what happens after scale, when the activity outlives the reason for it. Kevin Kelly — Do things that do not scale and a thousand true fans are the two ends of one idea: the first says start by hand, the second says by hand can carry you all the way.

### Further
Peter Thiel Naval Ravikant Jeff Bezos Steve Jobs Peter Drucker Kevin Kelly

## Peter Drucker
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/drucker/
Tags: Starting and building, The industrial age, Results, not activity

Peter Drucker (1909–2005 · Vienna to America) — Results, not activity. The man who turned management from supervising people into being answerable for results. He did not write job descriptions.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The man who turned management from supervising people into being answerable for results. He did not write job descriptions. He wrote that you are employed not because you are busy but because something usable has to come out of you. General Motors, Japanese industry and the non-profit sector all worked through his list of questions. The core is one sentence: activity does not count, results do.

### Q: What actually happened?
During the war he was given the run of General Motors for two years. What struck him was not the strategy but the calendars: the executives were booked solid, and not one of them could say what he had actually produced that year. The advice he eventually gave is unglamorous — write down where your hours really went for one week, then look at the page. Almost nobody's best hours are on his most important work. It is not a time-management trick. It is the door into the argument that activity is not achievement.

### The parts · The purpose of a business is to create a customer
Not to create profit. Profit is the test of validity and the risk premium on the future, a result rather than a cause. Make it the purpose and everyone turns inward and decides from the statements, which is how a company comes to damage its customers in order to improve a reading. e.g. Four quarters of hitting profit by trimming costs, and in the fifth there is nothing left to trim and half the customers have gone.

### The parts · Efficiency is not effectiveness
There is nothing so useless as doing with great efficiency what should not be done at all. Ask whether the thing should be done before asking how to do it faster. With the direction wrong, efficiency is an amplifier. e.g. Plenty of companies break the wrong goal into beautifully specific quarterly targets, hit all four, and remain on the wrong track.

### The parts · What does the customer actually buy
The Cadillac customer buys not transportation but status. The first instinct always stops at the product. Push one layer down to what he solves with it, and the boundary of the business, its rivals and its openings are all redrawn. e.g. A cafe thinks it sells coffee until it notices the afternoon customer is buying a seat that is neither the office nor home.

### The parts · Time is the only material
You cannot manage time, only what you spend it on. Write down where a week really went and strategy occupies a thin slice of the page. He told executives to hand the unimportant work to somebody else, not out of laziness but because their hours cost more. e.g. The meeting that exists because it has always existed is the cheapest thing on the calendar to cancel and the least likely to be cancelled.

### Q: How do I use it today?
On Friday write three lines: what you produced this week, what should have been produced and was not, and one activity you will stop next week. A week in which you cannot write all three is a week your calendar ate.

### Lines to keep
There is only one valid definition of business purpose: to create a customer. Nothing is so useless as doing efficiently what should not be done. Efficiency is doing things right; effectiveness is doing the right things. If we were not in this already, would we go into it now?

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Andy Grove — Grove solves execution, Drucker solves choice. One asks how a thing gets through the organisation, the other asks whether it is worth doing at all. Paul Graham — Graham writes about the first hundred users and doing things that do not scale; Drucker writes about what happens after scale, when the activity outlives the reason for it. Taiichi Ohno — Drucker decides which thing to do; Ohno decides how a step is kept from going wrong. One sets the direction at a desk, the other sets the standard on the floor. Ivan Illich — Both ask what comes after efficiency — do the right things, or put a ceiling on the tool.

### Further
Andy Grove Jeff Bezos Taiichi Ohno Paul Graham Ivan Illich

## Peter Lynch
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/lynch/
Tags: Money and risk, The industrial age, Turning over rocks

Peter Lynch (United States · 1944–) — Turning over rocks. He ran Fidelity's Magellan fund for thirteen years, from 1977 to 1990, compounding at twenty-nine per cent a year and taking it from twenty million dollars to fourteen…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
He ran Fidelity's Magellan fund for thirteen years, from 1977 to 1990, compounding at twenty-nine per cent a year and taking it from twenty million dollars to fourteen billion. Magellan returned twenty-seven times over that stretch against 4.7 times for the index. He retired at forty-six, at the peak, because he did not want to miss his daughters growing up. There is no secret in the method, which is exactly why it is hard to copy.

### Q: What actually happened?
He used to gauge the market by what happened to him at parties. Stage one: people learn he runs a mutual fund and drift back to the dentist. Stage two: someone politely asks whether stocks are risky. Stage three: a ring forms and everyone wants to know what he is buying. Stage four: they start telling him which ones he ought to own, and that, he said, is when to leave. The indicator is not the price. It is how much authority strangers think they have.

### The parts · Invest in what you know, and finish the sentence
The amateur's advantage is not more information but earlier information, in one corner: your own industry, the product your children use, the shop you walk past. The full version has a second half. The observation is a start, and between a good company and a good share sits a set of accounts. e.g. Plenty of people shopped in Walmart every week for years while it went up many times over, and almost nobody connected the shop to the shares.

### The parts · Six categories, six different rulers
Slow growers held for the dividend; stalwarts bought on a thirty per cent fall; fast growers judged on whether the store or product repeats; cyclicals bought at high multiples and sold at low ones; turnarounds judged only on how long the cash lasts; asset plays valued on what the books miss. e.g. The common way to lose money is measuring a cyclical with a growth ruler. The first question is which kind of company this actually is.

### The parts · Tenbaggers live in dull places
He liked companies with unpleasant names and boring businesses that no analyst followed: waste disposal, bottle caps, funeral services, motels. Nobody watching means a higher chance of mispricing. He was equally firm about what to avoid, which is anything described as the next something. e.g. La Quinta was a budget motel chain growing profits over thirty per cent for five straight years. What it did right was cut the restaurant and the conference rooms.

### The parts · Do not forecast the market
Spend thirteen minutes a year on economic forecasting and ten of them are wasted. Over thirteen years he sat through nine declines of more than ten per cent, dodged none of them, and still compounded at twenty-nine per cent. Avoiding falls costs far more over time than absorbing them. e.g. The people in his own fund who traded around the dips ended with a fraction of what the fund returned, and many with less than they started.

### The parts · Turn over enough rocks
This is the floor under all of it and the part nobody copies: hundreds of company visits a year, walking the stores, driving the product, looking in other people's trolleys. The edge is not intelligence, it is labour, and labour is the one thing a book cannot transfer. e.g. The person who turns over the most rocks wins. It is a boring claim, which is exactly why it stays available.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Start a watch list from your own working life: things you use daily, that people around you have started discussing, that the press has not covered yet. Then force three answers before you buy. Which of the six kinds is it, which ruler prices it, and if it halved tomorrow would I add or panic? If the third has no answer, do not buy.

### Lines to keep
The key organ for investing is the stomach, not the brain. Investing without research is like playing stud poker and never looking at the cards. Never invest in any idea you can't illustrate with a crayon. The person that turns over the most rocks wins the game.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Jim Simons — Same market, opposite routes: Lynch visited three hundred companies a year, Simons visited none. Benjamin Graham — Both work from fundamentals, but Graham prices the liquidation and Lynch prices the room left to grow.

### Further
Warren Buffett Benjamin Graham Duan Yongping Charlie Munger Jim Simons

## Peter Thiel
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/thiel/
Tags: Starting and building, Modern, Zero to one

Peter Thiel (Contemporary · 1967–) — Zero to one. Co-founded PayPal, was the first outside investor in Facebook, and is the most consequential contrarian in the Valley.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Co-founded PayPal, was the first outside investor in Facebook, and is the most consequential contrarian in the Valley. His central claim: competition is an ideological trap, and what actually creates value is a monopoly rather than a fight.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 2004 Facebook was a few months old and looked to most people like a social directory for Harvard undergraduates. He put in half a million dollars for a bit over ten per cent. By the 2012 listing that half million was worth around a billion. What he had seen was not that students liked it. It was that once a network of that shape closes, leaving costs the user everything and nothing else can be substituted for it — which is his definition of the only kind of business worth owning.

### The parts · Zero to one, not one to n
Going from one to n is copying: more of something that exists, in a crowd, at thin margins. Going from zero to one is making a category that was not there. Almost all commerce is the first kind. The second is rare, and when it works the value is not competed away because there is nobody to compete with yet. e.g. A better version of an existing product is a fight over an existing pool. A thing people had no word for last year is not.

### The parts · The power law is not a slogan about focus
Venture returns are not normally distributed: a single investment can return more than everything else combined. The consequence is uncomfortable — spreading effort evenly for the sake of balance guarantees you miss the only outcome that mattered. Back the one you believe can be that, with everything. e.g. The portfolio designed so nothing can go badly wrong is also designed so nothing can go extraordinarily right.

### The parts · Definite optimism
He divides views of the future by two axes: optimistic or pessimistic, definite or indefinite. His complaint about the present is indefinite optimism — a belief things will improve with no plan for how. Definite optimism is having an actual picture of the thing you intend to build, which is what makes long projects possible at all. e.g. We are excited about the space is indefinite. We are building this specific thing and it will take six years is definite, and only the second can be worked on today.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Run the question on yourself: what important thing do you believe that most people disagree with? If you can give a real answer with evidence behind it, that is where your advantage probably is. If you cannot, your judgement is currently the room's average.

### Lines to keep
Competition is for losers. The best businesses are the ones that do not compete. What important truth do very few people agree with you on?

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Paul Graham — One starts from the structure of the market, the other from the hundred people in front of you. Duan Yongping — Thiel says be first into a category nobody believes in; Duan says be last into one somebody else has already proved. Both are refusals to fight in a crowd, from opposite ends. Jensen Huang — Thiel asks what important truth very few people agree with you on. Building CUDA in 2006, when the industry was certain a graphics chip was for drawing pictures, is a live specimen of the answer. The Innovator's Dilemma — Two sides of one event: the dilemma explains why a good company loses, Thiel tells you how to be the thing that makes it lose. Kevin Kelly — Thiel wants a monopoly on a large market, Kelly wants depth with a thousand people — both routes avoid competition, one by scale, one by relationship. Finite and Infinite Games — Thiel's monopoly is a finite game won completely, and Carse would point out that the moment you have won, that game is over.

### Further
Steve Jobs Sun Tzu Warren Buffett Elon Musk Paul Graham Naval Ravikant Thomas Schelling Jensen Huang The Innovator's Dilemma Wang Xing Technological Revolutions The Sovereign Individual Albert Einstein

## Pu Songling
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/pu-songling/
Tags: Learning and growth, Early modern, The side thing won

Pu Songling (1640–1715 · Shandong) — The side thing won. At nineteen he came first in three examinations and was locally famous. Then he sat the provincial examination for forty years and never passed, supporting his family as…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
At nineteen he came first in three examinations and was locally famous. Then he sat the provincial examination for forty years and never passed, supporting his family as a live-in tutor. Almost everyone else in this library eventually succeeded — even their defeats are defeats on the way somewhere. He is the exception. The work he considered his life's business never came off, and the thing he did on the side became one of the most-read books in the language.

### Q: What actually happened?
At seventy-one he was finally granted a minor honorary status — not passed, but awarded by seniority to a candidate who had simply been at it long enough. It was the only official recognition of his life and it arrived when it could change nothing. By then he had been writing his 'idle book' for four decades: nearly five hundred stories, revised repeatedly, circulated in manuscript among friends. He died before it was printed, and never knew.

### The parts · Failure with no turning point
There was no decisive year — not one big defeat and a restart, but once every three years, just short, until he was old. Most advice about failure assumes a turning point to point at. Here there isn't one, and none of it applies. e.g. Not one bad year: eleven rounds of interviews across four years, each ending at the final stage, with nothing to point at as the moment it went wrong.

### The parts · He never let it be the only thing
He didn't stop sitting the exam and he didn't stake his life on it. The tutoring continued, the family was kept, the stories accumulated. Running things in parallel means that when the thing that never works fails again, something else in your hands is working. e.g. Keeping the job while the thing you care about takes years means a bad year stays a bad year, instead of becoming the end of the story.

### The parts · The side thing got real investment
The stories weren't dashed off — forty years, nearly five hundred pieces, repeatedly revised. They were last in his ranking, not last in his investment. And he never quit the job: the tutoring fed him and gave him the forty uninterrupted years. e.g. Two hours every Sunday for six years is not a hobby. It was last in his ranking and first in his hours.

### Q: How do I use it today?
When something you've worked at for years hasn't happened and you can't say when it would, don't start with whether to persist. Ask what else moved forward this year. If you can't name one thing, fill that gap first. And if the side thing is growing, count what you've actually put into it over three years before you talk about swapping their status.

### Lines to keep
Almost everyone here eventually made it. He didn't. He called it an idle book until he died. It is why he is remembered. He didn't quit the job to write. He wrote on the job.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Excellent Sheep — Two ways of having no scoreboard: they were never given one, he had one and it never once said yes. Winston Churchill — Both spent decades unrecognised. His day came; Pu Songling's never did, and the advice has to work either way. Sima Qian — Two kinds of it never worked. Pu Songling came close for forty years with no turning point; Sima Qian has one catastrophe and a life visibly divided by it. Tao Yuanming — Both were poor for life: Pu Songling kept sitting the exam and never passed, Tao Yuanming stopped sitting it on purpose. One had no choice, the other chose.

### Further
Excellent Sheep Fan Li Winston Churchill Du Fu Tao Yuanming

## Rat Park
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/rat-park/
Tags: Body and daily life, Modern, Look at the cage

Rat Park (1978 · Simon Fraser University) — Look at the cage. A set of experiments from the late 1970s, plus a natural experiment nobody designed, which together unsettled a piece of common sense about addiction.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A set of experiments from the late 1970s, plus a natural experiment nobody designed, which together unsettled a piece of common sense about addiction. The standard method put a rat alone in an empty cage with morphine-laced water and watched it drink until it died — a conclusion that looks solid. Bruce Alexander asked a different question: what if the cage weren't empty? In a large enclosure with companions, wheels and tunnels, the same two bottles, the rats were far less interested. The point is not that the drug doesn't matter. It is that the situation has been badly underrated.

### Q: What actually happened?
The work was not welcomed. Alexander's papers were turned down by the major journals, funding stopped, and for something like thirty years the study sat outside the mainstream — too hard to replicate cleanly, and pointed at a conclusion the field was not organised around. Its rehabilitation came from somewhere else entirely: the follow-up data on American servicemen returning from Vietnam, where the overwhelming majority of men addicted to heroin abroad simply stopped once home. Same people, same drug, different place.

### The parts · The cage is a variable, not the background
The original design treated the cage as scenery and the drug as the only thing that varied. Make the cage vary too and the conclusion moves: same rat, same bottle, very different behaviour. e.g. Same person, same phone. Alone in a rented room at eleven at night, and in a house with people in it: the two evenings do not look alike.

### The parts · The empty space is manufacturing the demand
The park rats weren't restrained; they didn't much want it. Alexander's word was dislocation — pull someone out of the relationships and position they belong in and they will find something to fill the gap. e.g. The drinking started the year he moved cities and knew nobody, and thinned out once there was somewhere to be on Thursdays.

### The parts · It has a boundary, and it has to be said
Replications were not uniformly successful and the interpretation is still argued over. Situation is the underrated term, not the only one. Explaining everything with it delays people who need medical care. e.g. Telling someone in withdrawal that the cage is the whole problem leaves them holding an explanation and no treatment.

### Q: How do I use it today?
If you're trying to stop something and every attempt ran on holding out, don't fight the thing. Log the last ten times — hour, place, what else was in your hands, who was there — and look for the recurring empty slot. Withdraw the props one at a time and it gets harder by itself. Then fill the slot, because a vacated one refills the same way.

### Lines to keep
Same rat, same bottle. Different cage, different behaviour. Same people, same substance. Home again, and they stopped. The trigger is often not craving. It's one recurring empty slot.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Maria Montessori — The same instruction in two fields: change the room before you correct the person in it. John Cacioppo — Both describe a gap that gets filled by whatever is nearest — one calls it dislocation, one calls it loneliness.

### Further
Maria Montessori Robert Sapolsky John Ratey Augustine

## Ray Dalio
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/dalio/
Tags: Money and risk, Modern, Principles

Ray Dalio (Contemporary · 1949–) — Principles. Founder of Bridgewater Associates, for years the largest hedge fund in the world, and author of Principles.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Founder of Bridgewater Associates, for years the largest hedge fund in the world, and author of Principles. Forty years in markets produced one conviction: everything worth doing has principles behind it, principles can be written down, written principles can be systematised, and a system can be handed to other people. The book is that argument applied to himself.

### Q: What actually happened?
A colleague once emailed him after a meeting with a prospective client. Ray, you deserve a D-minus for your performance today; you did not prepare, and it was unacceptable. At most firms that message ends a career. Dalio forwarded it to the whole company. That is what radical transparency is for. Not a mood of openness, but a rule that the accurate account of what happened has to survive the seniority of the person it is about.

### The parts · Pain plus reflection equals progress
Pain marks a place where an assumption you relied on has failed. The common responses are avoidance or explanation. His is to go at it: name the belief, find where it came from, rewrite the rule. The failure is only free if the second term actually happens. e.g. The 1982 collapse nearly ended the firm. He took the forecast apart, found the faulty assumption, and made the post-mortem required reading inside the company.

### The parts · Radical truth and radical transparency
Meetings are recorded and anyone can pull them up, which turns criticism into something checkable rather than something whispered. The cost is the discomfort of being corrected in public. What it buys is the ability to know what actually happened. e.g. Most organisations choose comfort, and the price of comfort is a filtered picture of the business that nobody can correct because nobody can see it.

### The parts · Believability-weighted decisions
Not a head count and not a boss's ruling. Opinions are weighted by each person's record in that specific field, on the plain ground that a surgeon's view on surgery should outweigh a cook's, however good the cook is at everything else. e.g. Log predictions, reasoning and outcomes for six months. The list of who was accurate rarely matches the list of who spoke most.

### The parts · Debt cycles
The short cycle runs five to eight years: expansion, inflation, tightening, recession, easing, recovery. The long one runs decades, until debt can no longer be handled by cutting rates and has to be deleveraged. Knowing which part you stand in is the largest variable in allocation. e.g. 1929 and 2008 are both the end of a long cycle. Reading them as isolated disasters loses the pattern that made both of them arrive.

### Q: How do I use it today?
After your next serious failure, give yourself forty-eight hours and then run his review: which assumption turned out to be false, where did that assumption come from, and what rule should now produce a different decision next time?

### Lines to keep
Pain + Reflection = Progress. It gave me the humility I needed to balance my aggressiveness. An idea meritocracy is a system in which the best ideas win out. Failure is not the problem. Failing to learn from it is.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Zeng Guofan — The same instrument on two continents: thirty years of diaries and a decade of taped meetings, both aimed at self-deception. Nassim Taleb — Both organise around risk: Dalio systematises it with principles, Taleb structures a portfolio to profit from it. Technological Revolutions — Two clocks: Dalio times the debt cycle on the financial side, Perez the technology cycle on the production side. Overlay them to know the hour.

### Further
Zeng Guofan Wang Yangming Fan Li Charlie Munger Nassim Taleb Nietzsche Benjamin Graham Friedrich Hayek Howard Marks George Soros Technological Revolutions Socrates Thinking in Systems

## Records of the Grand Historian
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/records-of-the-grand-historian/
Tags: How the world works, Qin, Han and the Six Dynasties, A record with a verdict

Records of the Grand Historian (Western Han · 104–91 BC) — A record with a verdict. One hundred and thirty chapters, about half a million characters, covering some three thousand years from the Yellow Emperor to Emperor Wu.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
One hundred and thirty chapters, about half a million characters, covering some three thousand years from the Yellow Emperor to Emperor Wu. What makes it the founding work of Chinese history is not the span but the method: it is organised around people, it gives merchants, wandering swordsmen and assassins their own biographies, and every chapter closes with the historian's own signed judgement. In an age when history belonged to the emperor, it insisted that both the facts and the verdict belong in the record.

### Q: What actually happened?
The clearest sign of what kind of book it is sits in the table of contents. The Basic Annals are the section reserved for those who held the empire, and Sima Qian put Xiang Yu in it — a man who lost, who founded no dynasty, and who had been the enemy of the house then on the throne. Further down there is a chapter for merchants, in an age whose official line was that commerce should be suppressed; one for assassins; and one for men who kept their word outside the law. Nobody had ordered any of it.

### The parts · The Grand Historian says
Every chapter closes with a paragraph of first-person judgement. He sympathises with losers, criticises power obliquely, defends merchants, dignifies assassins. These are positions, not the neutral voice of an official history — and he took them while serving the emperor he was quietly criticising. e.g. History is written by the winners, except here. Xiang Yu, who lost everything, sits in the section reserved for rulers, because the weight of that life was judged to deserve the format.

### The parts · Failure carries more information
The best portraits in the book are of the defeated: Xiang Yu, Han Xin, Wu Zixu. Success has complicated causes and a great deal of survivorship inside it. The ways of failing are fewer, more general, and easier to put to use. e.g. Two thousand years before anyone wrote about survivorship bias, he had assembled a working catalogue of the ways a competent person comes apart.

### The parts · The chapter on the money-makers
He was the first Chinese historian to write merchants into the record, in an era whose official position was that farming should be encouraged and trade held down. He treats economic activity as the base the society runs on, and the pursuit of wealth as a legitimate human motive. e.g. He sets down how Fan Li and Zigong actually operated, treating the question of how money is made as a subject worth serious record.

### The parts · No empty praise, nothing concealed
Ban Gu's six-character verdict a century later became the standard for the form: straight writing, checked facts, no flattery, no covering up. The hard half is the second one — the flaws of the people he admired, and the failures of his own side. e.g. He gives Li Guang the line about the path that wears itself smooth beneath the tree, and also the eight hundred men who had surrendered and were put to death.

### The parts · A judgement of one's own
His stated aim was to examine all that concerns heaven and man, to penetrate the changes of past and present, and to complete the work of one family. Not to record but to understand, not to repeat but to judge, and openly the view of one house rather than a pretence of neutrality. e.g. A report that says plainly whose reading this is, and on what evidence, is more usable than one performing an objectivity it does not have.

### Q: How do I use it today?
When you want to understand a historical figure, go to the moment they failed first — the most valuable material in the Records is usually the Grand Historian's analysis of a loser. Success copies badly; how someone came apart is the part worth studying. And when you write up anything yourself, include the paragraph that says what you think, signed.

### Lines to keep
No empty praise, no concealment of evil: therefore, a true record. To examine all that concerns heaven and man, to penetrate the changes of past and present. Peach and plum trees do not speak, yet a path forms beneath them. I find myself in much perplexity. Is this so-called Way of Heaven right, or wrong?

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Sima Qian — The same story from two sides: his page is about why a man chose to stay alive in order to finish it, this one is about the method the book itself laid down. The Comprehensive Mirror — Two philosophies of Chinese historical writing: the Records write people, the Mirror writes the system — one shows how a person works, the other how power works. Sapiens — Two scales of historical narrative: Sima Qian lights up history through individual fates, Harari takes the species apart.

### Further
The Comprehensive Mirror Han Xin Liu Bang Fan Li Bai Gui Viktor Frankl Strategies of the Warring States Sima Qian

## Ren Zhengfei
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/ren-zhengfei/
Tags: Starting and building, The industrial age, Endurance

Ren Zhengfei (Contemporary · 1944–) — Endurance. In 1987, at forty-three, he put twenty thousand yuan into a Shenzhen company reselling other people's telephone switches.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
In 1987, at forty-three, he put twenty thousand yuan into a Shenzhen company reselling other people's telephone switches. Three decades later Huawei was the largest maker of telecommunications equipment in the world. Two ideas run through everything he writes to staff: self-criticism is the organisation's immune system, and the customer is its north star. He is unusual among founders in that most of his thinking survives as ordinary internal documents, published and readable.

### Q: What actually happened?
He started late. At forty-three, an age when most people have stopped starting things, he was reselling switches made by other companies out of an office in Shenzhen. Thirty years later the company was the largest equipment maker in its industry anywhere. Asked about that arc, his line was that Huawei has had no success, only growth. It is not modesty. In his vocabulary success is a place where you are allowed to stand still, and standing still is precisely what he has spent thirty years designing the company not to do.

### The parts · Survival is the goal
Staying alive is the plainest goal Huawei has, and also the highest one. A dead company's vision is worth nothing, so everything else is subordinate to the question of whether the firm is still here in ten years. The habit is what kept the organisation from freezing when trouble actually arrived. e.g. Ask of any strategy proposal: does this raise or lower our chance of existing in a decade? Many impressive plans do not survive the question.

### The parts · Self-criticism as an immune system
In the best year of Huawei's history he wrote an essay describing in detail how the company might die. Seeing risk while conditions are good is the whole trick: self-criticism is not self-doubt, it is the deliberate exposure of your own blind spots before someone else finds them. e.g. Put the near-miss, not the win, at the top of the weekly agenda and the organisation slowly grows a warning system instead of a congratulation system.

### The parts · Customer first, striver second
Customer-centred, striver-based is one sentence with two jobs. The first half sets direction, aiming every resource at customer value. The second half supplies the motive, by making sure the people actually doing the work are the people who get paid for it. e.g. A reward system that pays proximity to power rather than proximity to the customer will quietly reverse the first half of the sentence within a year.

### The parts · Sew the winter coat in summer
Winter passes and spring returns, but the coat has to exist before the cold does. Contingency, cash and a second capability are cheap to build in a strong year and impossible to build in a weak one, which is why the timing of his most famous essay is the argument. e.g. Run the stress test in the record quarter. The same exercise in a falling quarter reads as panic and lands on morale.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Once a year, write yourself the winter scenario: if the most important customer or the largest source of revenue disappeared next year, what exactly would you do? Write it while the numbers are good, because the same document written in a bad quarter is no longer planning, it is triage.

### Lines to keep
Staying alive is Huawei's plainest goal and its highest one. Huawei has had no success, only growth. For ten years I have thought about failure every day, not success. Let the people who hear the gunfire call in the artillery.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Kazuo Inamori — Two eastern versions of the company as a practice: Inamori binds people with an ethic of doing right by them, Ren drives them with self-criticism and a sense of crisis — one uses good, one uses fear. Zeng Guofan — The same method a hundred and thirty years apart: build the solid camp and fight the slow fight, no shortcuts, no clever moves, never be beatable before you try to win. Konosuke Matsushita — Both put survival first and take opposite routes: Matsushita stores water in the good years, Ren manufactures a sense of crisis so nobody relaxes.

### Further
Kazuo Inamori Zeng Guofan Steve Jobs Jensen Huang Lee Kuan Yew Konosuke Matsushita Wang Xing

## Richard Feynman
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/feynman/
Tags: Learning and growth, The industrial age, Do not fool yourself

Richard Feynman (1918–1988 · United States) — Do not fool yourself. Nobel physicist, Manhattan Project, and the member of the Challenger commission who insisted his own dissenting appendix be printed with the report.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Nobel physicist, Manhattan Project, and the member of the Challenger commission who insisted his own dissenting appendix be printed with the report. What he left people outside physics is larger than what he left inside it: a set of tests for whether you actually understand something. The standard is close to rude. If you cannot get a first-year student to follow it, you have not got it. He held science itself to the same line: the first principle is not to fool yourself, and you are the easiest person available to fool.

### Q: What actually happened?
He taught for a year in Rio and found students who could recite everything and use none of it. In a lecture he read out a definition of triboluminescence, the light emitted when crystals are crushed, and the room recognised it instantly. Then he asked why, when you crush a lump of sugar in the dark, you see a flash. Nobody connected the two. At the end of the year he told the assembled faculty and the education ministry that no science was being taught in Brazil at all.

### The parts · If you cannot teach it, you have not got it
A technical term compresses. Forbid it and you have to unpack the idea yourself, and the places you cannot unpack are the places you were storing a label. It is the cheapest accurate self-test there is. e.g. Describe your work to a relative. Each time you retreat into the trade word, mark it. That list is your real syllabus.

### The parts · The easiest person to fool is you
Fooling yourself takes no bad faith, only a stake in the answer. When you want a conclusion, evidence for it becomes strangely easy to find. So honesty here is a method requirement rather than a moral one. e.g. Before the review, write the case against your own proposal first. Written second, that column always comes out shorter.

### The parts · Reality before public relations
Challenger was not an engineering shortfall. It was an organisation that preferred a good-looking argument to a cold seal. Wherever people report upward, the same substitution is on offer every week. e.g. When the numbers disappoint, notice whether you are changing the judgement or the sentence. The sentence gets you through this meeting only.

### The parts · Derive it once instead of remembering it ten times
His way of learning was to throw the result away and rebuild it, going back whenever he got stuck. Slow, and what comes out transfers. A remembered answer serves only the question it came from. e.g. Rather than learn the conditions under which a formula holds, reconstruct once where it came from. The conditions then explain themselves.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Take one thing you believe you understand and explain it aloud to somebody outside your field, using no terms of art. Mark every place you stall; that list is what you have to go back to. And before any judgement where you gain if it goes your way, write the case against it first.

### Lines to keep
After you've not fooled yourself, it's easy not to fool other scientists. Nature cannot be fooled. Knowing the name of a thing is not knowing the thing.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Albert Einstein — Two physicists' habits: Einstein restated the problem until it turned simple, Feynman rebuilt the answer until it was his. Socrates — Both use questions to force ignorance into the open. Socrates aims them at other people, Feynman at himself. Karl Popper — The same rule from two sides: Popper gives the logical criterion, Feynman the psychological warning about who breaks it first.

### Further
Albert Einstein Socrates Charlie Munger Karl Popper The Last Hot-Metal Edition

## Robert Sapolsky
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sapolsky/
Tags: Body and daily life, Modern, Stress is a mismatch

Robert Sapolsky (1994 · Stanford) — Stress is a mismatch. A neuroendocrinologist who spent thirty years with a troop of wild baboons in East Africa while studying human stress physiology.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A neuroendocrinologist who spent thirty years with a troop of wild baboons in East Africa while studying human stress physiology. His book's title is the whole argument: zebras don't get ulcers, because their stress response runs full for the few minutes a lion is charging and shuts off the moment they've escaped. Ours is identical and gets used on mortgages, managers and unanswered email — a mechanism designed for seconds, left running for decades.

### Q: What actually happened?
The baboons made the second half of the argument. In a well-fed troop with few predators, most of the day goes on each other, so their stress hormones track social position rather than physical danger. Low-ranking animals ran chronically elevated cortisol and worse health across the board — and the exceptions were the ones with allies and with some ability to predict when they'd be harassed. That is where the real variable turned out to be: not how hard the pressure is, but whether it can be foreseen and whether you have anyone.

### The parts · Duration, not intensity
A week-long sprint damages nobody. Two years of being permanently on call does. The question isn't how tired you've been lately but when the system was last actually switched off.

### The parts · The bill is charged where you can't see it
What gets paused under stress is immunity, digestion and tissue repair, and those debts don't show the same day — which is why people misjudge how well they're coping until the symptoms arrive.

### The parts · Predictability and control beat reducing the load
At the same pressure, knowing when it's coming and having some say over order and pace cuts the damage sharply. Which moves the intervention from 'reduce stress' to 'add certainty' — usually far cheaper.

### Q: How do I use it today?
If you've been tense a long time with nothing specific wrong, ask when this system was last genuinely off. If you're managing people through something hard, give a firm date rather than a better outcome: people adapt to a certain bad and don't adapt to hanging. And swap 'these five, in this order' for 'these five, you choose the order' — same load, different physiology.

### Lines to keep
Zebras don't get ulcers because the response runs for minutes. What makes people ill is the response that won't switch off. People adapt to a certain bad. They don't adapt to hanging.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
John Ratey — Same system, two handles: Sapolsky on what keeps it switched on, Ratey on how to switch it off today. Christina Maslach — Same conclusion from two directions: she measures the job, he measures the hormone, and both land on control.

### Further
John Ratey Christina Maslach John Cacioppo Rat Park Arthur Kleinman
