## Sapiens
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sapiens/
Tags: How the world works, Modern, Fictions

Sapiens (2011 · Yuval Noah Harari) — Fictions. An Israeli historian's account of sixty thousand years, with an argument short enough to hold in one hand.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
An Israeli historian's account of sixty thousand years, with an argument short enough to hold in one hand. Sapiens run the planet not because we are the strongest or the cleverest animal, but because we are the only one that can believe in things that are not there. Money, nations, laws, gods, limited companies: all of them are shared fictions, and shared fictions are what let millions of strangers act as one. The same book then turns the agricultural revolution inside out and argues that the species won while almost everyone in it lost.

### Q: What actually happened?
He sets two documents side by side. The Code of Hammurabi, from about 1776 BC, states that people fall into superiors, commoners and slaves, and that the gods arranged it that way. The American Declaration of Independence, from 1776 AD, states that all men are created equal. Both claim to be describing reality. Both claim to hold everywhere and forever. Both are, in his terms, imagined orders held up by belief rather than by anything you could measure. That comparison is the whole book in one page, and it cuts in both directions.

### The parts · Fiction is the cooperation technology
Chimpanzees can coordinate a few dozen individuals, because coordination beyond that needs personal acquaintance. A shared story removes the acquaintance requirement. Two strangers who accept the same currency, the same law or the same brand can transact without ever meeting, and that is the only reason a million-person organisation is possible at all. e.g. A national border is a line nobody can see, enforced because enough people on both sides agree it is there.

### The parts · An imagined order is not a lie
Harari is careful about this. A lie is something the teller knows to be false. An imagined order is believed by everyone inside it, including the people it disadvantages, which is exactly why it holds. Calling it fiction says nothing about whether it is good, only about where it lives. e.g. Human rights cannot be found in a body or a rock. They still stop wars, because enough people act as though they were physical facts.

### The parts · The farmer worked more and ate worse
The standard story has farming as progress. Harari counts differently: longer hours, a narrower diet, new diseases, and a life more exposed to one bad harvest. What grew was the number of people, not the quality of any one life. He calls it history's biggest fraud. e.g. Wheat covers more of the earth than any forager could have imagined. Judged by copies of DNA it is the winner of the story.

### The parts · Capability rose; contentment did not follow
The last section of the book asks the awkward question. Modern people have more than any ancestor and are not reliably happier. If every measure of capability is up and subjective wellbeing is flat, then capability was never the thing being measured. e.g. Ask what the last decade of improvements actually changed in an ordinary day of yours. Some of them did nothing at all.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Take one rule at work you have never questioned and ask where it actually lives. If it exists only because enough people act as though it does, then it is maintained by belief, and the question stops being is it right and becomes what keeps it believed. That is a question you can act on.

### Lines to keep
Sapiens rule because we are the animal that can believe what is not there. An imagined order is not a lie. Everyone inside it believes it. The species won. Almost every individual in it lost.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
The Sovereign Individual — Two directions on the same story: Harari on how the system shapes the person, Davidson and Rees-Mogg on how the person gets out from under it. Influence — Both explain why people are not rational: Harari from the species and its stories, Cialdini from the levers inside one head. Guns, Germs, and Steel — Both work at the ten-thousand-year scale; Diamond explains why the continents differ, Harari why this one species is peculiar. Records of the Grand Historian — Two scales of historical narrative: Sima Qian lights up history through individual fates, Harari takes the species apart. Technological Revolutions — Harari explains why people come to believe shared fictions, Perez shows that belief turning into actual rail and fibre. Why Nations Fail — Both explain how humanity arrived here: Harari credits shared fictions and mass cooperation, this book credits the incentives institutions create.

### Further
The Sovereign Individual Tao Te Ching Sun Tzu The Comprehensive Mirror Nassim Taleb Guns, Germs, and Steel The Old Regime and the Revolution Why Nations Fail

## Scarcity
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/scarcity/
Tags: Money and risk, Modern, Bandwidth

Scarcity (2013 · Mullainathan and Shafir) — Bandwidth. A behavioural economist and a psychologist, writing not about how to make money but about what happens once there is not enough.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A behavioural economist and a psychologist, writing not about how to make money but about what happens once there is not enough. The claim is that scarcity itself occupies cognitive bandwidth: a person short of money is not being irrational, his mind is permanently part-occupied by how far short he is, and less judgement is left over. Their best-known evidence is the Indian sugarcane study, the same men tested when tight and again when paid. The model covers shortage of time as well as shortage of money, because both draw on the same bandwidth. (On sourcing: the specific size of the sugarcane effect has been contested — later replication work did not reproduce parts of the 2012 result, and the authors themselves ran higher-powered replications setting out which findings hold and which do not. This entry takes the direction and the mechanism, not the number.)

### Q: What actually happened?
A regional hospital in Missouri ran roughly thirty thousand operations a year and was permanently behind. Emergency cases arrived, scheduled operations were bumped, surgeons operated at two in the morning, and every room was booked solid. The advice they were given sounded absurd: keep one operating room permanently empty. An institution that had no capacity was told to give capacity away. It worked. With one room always free the emergencies had somewhere to go, the schedule stopped collapsing, and the hospital got through more operations than before. This is the book's argument in physical form: the room was not idle, it was slack, and without slack a single unexpected case takes the whole day down with it.

### The parts · One bandwidth, and both shortages draw on it
The most useful thing this model does is fold two apparently unrelated troubles into one. Doing the month's arithmetic and racing a deadline draw on the same attention, which is why the two together make people so much worse than either alone. e.g. Working out how far short this month is while finishing a proposal, and doing both badly. That is not laziness.

### The parts · The test is whether he does it when things are loose
Trading a character explanation for a situational one needs a checkable condition, and the sugarcane design supplies it: one group of men at two moments, rather than poor people measured against rich ones. Anything he does not do when comfortable does not belong on his personality. e.g. The mistake that stops after the harvest was never about the man.

### The parts · Tunnelling: the urgent pushes the important out of view
Scarcity narrows attention. Focus inside the tunnel does rescue the emergency, and the cost lands outside it — the check-up, the insurance, the call you owe somebody — and lands late. Run the tunnel as your normal mode and every month goes on paying for the last one. e.g. The productivity a deadline forces out of you usually costs a stretch with no check-ups, no replies and no long-term decisions.

### The parts · Slack is not waste, it is room to be wrong
A calendar and an account filled to the last unit look like maximum efficiency and are actually a tolerance for error set to zero. With room, one surprise stays one surprise. Without it the same surprise chains, and the same mistake costs the poorer side far more. e.g. An untouchable emergency fund is not there for the return. It is there so one accident does not become five.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Next time money or time is tight and you notice a run of decisions you cannot defend a week later, calibrate the attribution before you judge yourself: would I make these mistakes when things were loose? If not, do not start with your character, start by removing things that occupy the bandwidth. Move what matters into forms that need no memory — the payment that leaves automatically, the appointment already booked, the schedule somebody else watches — because reminders fail inside the tunnel. You did not forget; at that moment you could not see it.

### Lines to keep
Scarcity captures the mind. Being short-sighted can be the result of having no money, not the reason for it. Slack is not waste. It is room to be wrong. The comparison was not poor people against rich ones. It was one group of men at two moments.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Benjamin Graham — Both are about room to be wrong: the margin of safety leaves room in a valuation, slack leaves room in a life — one guards against misjudging, the other against accident. Cal Newport — Both keep an account of attention: Newport counts what switching costs, Scarcity counts what how far short am I occupies all day. Carol Dweck — Both get used to explain why people do not change: Dweck points at belief, Scarcity at circumstance — rule out the circumstance first. Maria Konnikova — Both replace how could they be so stupid with what were they short of: Scarcity is about bandwidth being taken, the con is about wanting being used.

### Further
Nassim Taleb Benjamin Graham Li Ka-shing Cal Newport Maria Konnikova

## Seneca
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/seneca/
Tags: Mind and feeling, Qin, Han and the Six Dynasties, Count the hours first

Seneca (4 BC–AD 65 · Rome) — Count the hours first. Nero's tutor, one of the richest men in Rome, and the Stoic who left the most letters behind.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Nero's tutor, one of the richest men in Rome, and the Stoic who left the most letters behind. What separates him from the rest of the school is his position: he was not discussing restraint from a quiet study, he wrote while manoeuvring at the centre of power, and in the end the pupil he had taught ordered him to die. On anger, on time, on death he writes with the concreteness of a man being tested weekly rather than the tone of moral instruction. The charge of hypocrisy has followed him for two thousand years, and it is worth keeping in view while you read him.

### Q: What actually happened?
In AD 65 he was named in the Pisonian conspiracy and Nero sent an officer with the order to die. Tacitus reports the scene. Forbidden to alter his will, he turned to the friends around him and said that since he was prevented from repaying what he owed them, he would leave them the one possession still his and the finest he had — the pattern of his life. Then he opened the veins of his arms. He was old and thin and the blood came too slowly, so he cut the veins behind the knees as well, took poison that failed to work, and was finally carried into a hot bath, where the steam suffocated him. He had written about dying for thirty years. This was the examination.

### The parts · Anger is a process you can take apart
On Anger says the thing is not one explosion but three movements. An impression arrives — he insulted me. Then you assent: yes, an insult. Only then the decision to retaliate. The second step is the only gate. The impression cannot be stopped and the retaliation is already motion, so the whole of the training sits in withholding the assent. e.g. Contradicted in front of people, do not certify he is picking a fight. Hold the second step for three seconds. A great many insults turn out to be clumsiness.

### The parts · Rehearse the worst and the fear shrinks
The Stoic premeditation of misfortune is not gloom, it is making the worst outcome specific: what bankruptcy would actually look like, what being sacked would actually look like. He argues that most of the intensity of fear comes from vagueness. Think it all the way down and you usually find you could carry it, and you no longer have to wait for the event to start preparing. e.g. Afraid of losing the job, write out how the three months after would go, in detail. The fear comes down, and you finish with a plan you did not have before.

### The parts · Time is the one cost that cannot be recovered
Money lost can be earned again; time cannot. People behave as if the reverse were true, comparing prices across three shops over a trivial sum and giving away an entire evening to something meaningless without a second thought. He wants time accounted for as the scarcest asset on the books: who is spending yours, and at what rate of return. e.g. Replace what will this cost with how many of my hours does this take, and what would those hours otherwise have been. Most invitations fail that test on the spot.

### The parts · You do not have to be ready to start living
His sharpest observation is that people keep postponing life — after the promotion, once the children are grown, in retirement — and the future is the least reliable thing they own. Such people, he says, are not living briefly. They have spent the whole of it getting ready. e.g. Once this project is done, I will. If that sentence is three years old, what it needs is not a better moment. It needs one small step today.

### Q: How do I use it today?
When anger rises, find the assent step and refuse to give it. Before a decision that matters, write the worst outcome out in full and read it back. And price everything in hours before you price it in money: how many of mine does this take, and where would those hours have gone.

### Lines to keep
It is not that we have a short time to live, but that we waste a lot of it. Life, if you know how to use it, is long. You live as if you were destined to live for ever. The greatest remedy for anger is delay.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Marcus Aurelius — Two Stoics in opposite seats: the emperor writing a private notebook to himself, the courtier writing public letters to other people — one turns inward, the other stays practical. Su Shi — Two ways of writing out of adversity: Seneca writes about restraint from inside the machinery of power, Su Shi writes about lightness on the road into exile, and both had been tested before either wrote a line. Montaigne — Both on learning to die. Seneca instructs from above; Montaigne writes outward from the afternoon he was thrown off a horse.

### Further
Marcus Aurelius Epictetus Su Shi Viktor Frankl Montaigne

## Shang Yang
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/shang-yang/
Tags: Power and organisation, Pre-Qin and classical, Credit before command

Shang Yang (Warring States · 390–338 BC) — Credit before command. The designer and enforcer of the reforms that turned Qin from a backward frontier state into the machine that conquered China.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The designer and enforcer of the reforms that turned Qin from a backward frontier state into the machine that conquered China. Two rounds of legislation rebuilt landholding, taxation, military rank and household registration. He was torn apart by chariots for his trouble. But the rules he wrote were still running a century after his death and they finished the job: the man died, the system lived, which is the best available ending for a reformer and not a happy one.

### Q: What actually happened?
After his patron Duke Xiao died, the old nobility charged him with treason and he ran. At nightfall he tried to take a room at an inn on the road, and the innkeeper turned him away: under Lord Shang's law, a guest without papers cannot be lodged, and the house would be punished. He is said to have understood at that moment what he had built. He fled to his own fief, raised troops, lost, and was executed and his family destroyed. The detail that everyone remembers is the inn, because it is the only case in which the law was tested on the man who wrote it.

### The parts · Certainty of reward, certainty of punishment
The core of the reform was not severity but reliability. One head taken in battle was one step of rank, whatever your birth. The Qin army did not outfight six states because its soldiers were braver; the arithmetic was simply clearer to them than to anyone else. e.g. People do what the system actually pays for. Announcing different priorities changes nothing until the payout changes.

### The parts · The man dies, the system lives
Compare Zhang Juzheng, whose reforms were being dismantled within two years of his death. Shang Yang's survived because they had created a large class — ordinary soldiers and farmers who could now rise — with a reason to defend them. e.g. Real reform is not I will push this through. It is I will manufacture a group of people who need this to continue.

### The parts · Break the land monopoly
Abolishing the well-field system ended aristocratic control of land and allowed it to be bought and sold. Farmers kept the surplus, so they had a reason to grow one. It is the oldest recorded case of a rule change releasing output that was already there. e.g. Whenever effort and reward are reconnected, production that looked impossible turns out to have been suppressed.

### The parts · The designer has to be inside the design
The inn is not an ironic footnote, it is the test result. A set of rules that binds everyone except its author is personal rule under another name. His death is the strongest evidence that what he built was real. e.g. Any leader who says the rules are for other people is dismantling their own system while announcing it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Before you push any new rule, do one small thing that proves you deliver: a visible case, settled immediately, at a cost large enough that people are surprised. Then, before you start, name the group who will be better off if the rule survives you — if you cannot name them, the rule dies the day you leave.

### Lines to keep
When the law is not carried out, it is those above who break it. A sage who can strengthen the state does not copy the past. Do not change the law for less than a hundredfold gain.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Zhang Juzheng — The same fate, opposite legacies: Shang Yang died and his system lived, Zhang Juzheng died and his was taken apart. The difference is who was left with a reason to defend it. Han Feizi — Theory and practice of the same school: Han Feizi wrote the system down, Shang Yang ran it, and both were killed by the thing they had built. Guan Zhong — Two routes to a strong state: Guan Zhong enriches the people and the state follows, Shang Yang installs the law and the wealth follows. Wu Zetian — Two people who broke a settled order: Shang Yang broke aristocratic privilege, she broke the bar on her sex, and both paid heavily for it. The Wealth of Nations — Both are designing a route to a strong state. Shang Yang binds people to the land and suppresses trade, Smith credits division and exchange. Both routes work, at wildly different prices.

### Further
Han Feizi Zhang Juzheng Guan Zhong Cao Cao Li Shimin The Wealth of Nations Mencius Lee Kuan Yew Napoleon Bai Gui The Old Regime and the Revolution Why Nations Fail

## Shi Tiesheng
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/shi-tiesheng/
Tags: Body and daily life, Modern, Illness is the job, writing the sideline

Shi Tiesheng (1951–2010 · Beijing) — Illness is the job, writing the sideline. A writer. His legs stopped working at twenty-one, and for fifteen years after that he wheeled himself almost daily to the old Temple of Earth park near his home and sat…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A writer. His legs stopped working at twenty-one, and for fifteen years after that he wheeled himself almost daily to the old Temple of Earth park near his home and sat there. The essay that came out of it is read in every Chinese school. From forty-seven he had kidney failure and went to dialysis three times a week until he died at fifty-nine, and the book of those years was written in the gaps between sessions. English readers will not know the name. He is the one person in this section who did not study any of this but had it.

### Q: What actually happened?
After the paralysis he went to the park every day and told his mother nothing about it. She was afraid to stop him and more afraid of what he might do, so she took to coming after him: walking the paths among the old trees looking for him, not calling out, and going home once she had seen him. He noticed this only years later. She died at forty-nine while he was still in his twenties, and what he wrote afterwards was that a son's misfortune is always doubled in his mother.

### The parts · Some questions are closed, not answered
Why me has no answer and needs none, because it is only a fact. It took him years to concede that this one is not solved but crossed off the list. Once it is crossed off, the strength goes to questions that have answers. e.g. Stop asking why me and ask what now, given that it is me.

### The parts · Put the illness first so the rest of the time can work
Dialysis three times a week, four hours each. Anyone who will not admit the illness is the main job spends the day competing with it for time, loses, and spends what is left in resentment. He reversed it: give the illness its hours first, and what remains is genuinely yours. e.g. Fix treatment and rest into the calendar first. What is left is my time. Do not do the arithmetic the other way round.

### The parts · One place you go back to every day
Fifteen years in the same park, and what he stresses is the daily part. A person who has come apart needs one coordinate that does not move. It solves nothing at all, and it is there every day, and that turns out to be enough. Rally too early and the feeling returns for a second collapse. e.g. Just after it happens, having one place you go to matters more than planning the next step.

### Q: How do I use it today?
If something has happened that cannot be undone, take why me off the list rather than trying to solve it, and find one place you can go back to every day. If you are carrying a long illness, stop competing with it for hours: give it what it needs first, then ask what the smallest thing is that the remaining hours can hold, and do that one thing properly.

### Lines to keep
He never made peace with fate. He only stopped arguing with why me. The park solved nothing, and it was there every day. Put death back in its place and the days have room again.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Arthur Kleinman — One is a doctor writing about patients, the other is the patient: Kleinman argues that what the clinician sees and what the patient lives are two things, and Shi Tiesheng is the one living the second. Viktor Frankl — Both answer what holds when a situation leaves no choice: Frankl says meaning, Shi Tiesheng answers much smaller, with one place he went every day and the gaps between dialysis sessions.

### Further
Arthur Kleinman Viktor Frankl Su Shi Montaigne

## Sima Qian
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sima-qian/
Tags: Mind and feeling, Qin, Han and the Six Dynasties, Disgraced, and finished the book

Sima Qian (Han · c. 145–86 BC) — Disgraced, and finished the book. Court historian to Emperor Wu of Han, and the author of the Records of the Grand Historian, the founding work of Chinese history writing.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Court historian to Emperor Wu of Han, and the author of the Records of the Grand Historian, the founding work of Chinese history writing. In 99 BC he spoke in defence of a general who had surrendered, was imprisoned for it and castrated the following year. The convention of his class was suicide; he declined, served on as palace secretary and finished the book. Years later he explained himself in a letter to a condemned friend, and that letter is one of the most direct accounts anyone has left of living with a disgrace that cannot be spoken about.

### Q: What actually happened?
The book he was finishing runs to a hundred and thirty chapters and covers roughly two thousand years, from the Yellow Emperor down to his own emperor. He invented its architecture: annals for the rulers, chronological tables, treatises on ritual and rivers and money, and then a long closing section of individual lives. The lives are not only the great ones. He wrote up assassins, merchants, physicians and court jesters. Two thousand years of Chinese historians copied the form, and almost everything later readers know about the period stands behind his account, including the parts that make his own emperor look bad.

### The parts · Swap the question about face for a question about work
Can I still show my face has no answer and sinks the longer you hold it. Is anything still unfinished has one, and the answer points at something to do. The letter is that substitution: the shame was not resolved, it was taken off the switch that decided whether he lived. e.g. After a public disgrace, do not ask whether you deserve to be here. Ask what you still owe and to whom.

### The parts · Find yourself a row of precedents
While a person believes nobody has ever had it this bad, no argument gets in. So he lists them: King Wen in captivity expanding the Book of Changes, Confucius in distress, Qu Yuan banished, Zuo Qiuming blind, Sun Bin without his feet. The list is the remedy, not the reasoning. e.g. If you think you are the only one this unlucky, go and find three who had it worse and finished something.

### The parts · Staying alive takes one thing only you can finish
The archives were in his hands, his father's notes were in his hands, and the framework was in his head. Nobody else could have produced that book, which is what makes if I go this ends true rather than vain. An obligation handed to you by someone else holds on the days you cannot hold yourself. e.g. Find the thing nobody picks up if you put it down. It carries more weight than any job you could be replaced in.

### Q: How do I use it today?
After something you cannot say out loud, stop asking whether you still deserve to be here and ask instead what is unfinished and only yours to finish. Tell the whole of it to exactly one person, start to end. Then work while the shame is still in the room, because it does not leave first.

### Lines to keep
The shame was real and so was the work. He let the work speak. The books that lasted were mostly written in the worst years. Sometimes staying alive needs a debt left outstanding.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Brené Brown — Both on shame. She is the researcher and gives the mechanism; he is the subject and gives the sample of someone finishing the work while carrying it. Pu Songling — Two kinds of it never worked. Pu Songling came close for forty years with no turning point; Sima Qian has one catastrophe and a life visibly divided by it. Records of the Grand Historian — The same story from two sides: his page is about why a man chose to stay alive in order to finish it, this one is about the method the book itself laid down.

### Further
Records of the Grand Historian Su Shi Viktor Frankl Brené Brown The Comprehensive Mirror Du Fu

## Sima Yi
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sima-yi/
Tags: Strategy and competition, Qin, Han and the Six Dynasties, Patience

Sima Yi (Three Kingdoms · 179–251) — Patience. He outlasted four rulers of Wei and at seventy took control of the state in a single morning.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
He outlasted four rulers of Wei and at seventy took control of the state in a single morning. The record has two operations in it that look opposite and are not: a march that arrived in eight days when a month was expected, and ten years of illness that were not illness. Both work off the same insight, which is that the other side's plan is built out of assumptions about what you will do.

### Q: What actually happened?
The standoff at the Wuzhang Plains. Zhuge Liang sent him a set of women's clothes, a public insult meant to shame him into giving battle. He did not lose his temper. He accepted the gift pleasantly, and asked the messenger how the chancellor had been sleeping. The messenger said his master rose early, stayed late and ate very little. Sima Yi turned away and said that Liang was not going to live long. Zhuge Liang died that year, at fifty-four. Sima Yi lived another seventeen.

### The parts · Their timetable is a list of your openings
Meng Da worked out precisely how long Sima Yi would need: the distance, plus a month for a memorial to the throne and a reply. Every figure was right. The one error was assuming the procedure would be followed. Sima Yi did not report, and was under the walls in eight days. e.g. They have always shipped at quarter end, so every defence is scheduled for quarter end. The real threat comes when they skip the process.

### The parts · Feign weakness until the watching stops
Half-hearted quietness leaves the eyes on you. When Cao Shuang sent a man to look him over, he could not hold the cup and let the porridge run down his chest, and mistook one province for another twice. The report came back that he was a breathing corpse. Then the surveillance went. e.g. To move a rival's attention off you, vague public positioning is not enough. There has to be nothing worth following up.

### The parts · The window is recognised, not made
He waited on one specific condition: the Cao brothers out of the capital on the same day, the centre of power and the centre of force both absent at once. He did not create that. The whole function of the patience was to still be there, intact, when it came. e.g. Turning points in an industry are usually triggered outside your control. What you control is being at the table that day with cards in hand.

### The parts · Defence as the cheaper form of attack
At the Wuzhang Plains he declined battle for months while the other side burned supply and, as it turned out, a life. His logic was plain: I do not need to win, I need not to lose, and the clock does the rest. He read life expectancy where others read order of battle. e.g. With fewer resources than a rival, stop trying to settle it in one engagement. Make each contact cost them more than it costs you.

### Q: How do I use it today?
If you are waiting, write down the exact condition you are waiting for, in a sentence someone else could verify. If you cannot write it, you are not waiting, you are stalling. Then ask the second question: on the day it appears, could you finish the whole thing at once?

### Lines to keep
Liang is not going to live long. Riding a tiger, you cannot get down. The patience exists to keep you alive until the window opens.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Zhuge Liang — The sharpest pairing on the site: one attacked to defend and spent his life doing it, the other defended to attack and outlived him. Huo Qubing — Two extreme strategies for a life: burn everything at twenty-four, or hold everything back until seventy.

### Further
Fan Li Li Bi Zhuge Liang Sun Tzu Cao Cao Feng Dao Guo Ziyi Huo Qubing Wang Jian Machiavelli

## Socrates
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/socrates/
Tags: Learning and growth, Pre-Qin and classical, Knowing you do not know

Socrates (Athens · 470–399 BC) — Knowing you do not know. He wrote nothing. Everything we have comes through other people's dialogues. He charged no fees, which made him the poorest professional philosopher in Athens, and spent…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
He wrote nothing. Everything we have comes through other people's dialogues. He charged no fees, which made him the poorest professional philosopher in Athens, and spent his days in the marketplace asking questions. The city executed him for corrupting the young and impiety, which in practice meant that his questions embarrassed people who could not afford to be embarrassed. His pupils arranged an escape and he refused it.

### Q: What actually happened?
Crito came to the prison before dawn with everything arranged: guards paid, a ship waiting, a household abroad ready to take him. Socrates would not argue about whether the verdict had been just. He asked instead whether a private citizen may set aside a judgement he dislikes, and what a city would be if everybody did. Crito had to agree that it could not stand. Then leaving, Socrates said, would teach exactly that, and would do Athens more harm than anything he stood accused of. He stayed, and drank the hemlock.

### The parts · Not knowing, and not pretending to know
The line on the posters says he knew nothing. What he actually claims is smaller and far more usable: about the things he does not know, he does not suppose that he knows them. That gap is the whole advantage. e.g. Say I have not checked that, and people bring you answers. Say I know, and people bring you agreement, which contains no information.

### The parts · Being good at one thing makes you sure about everything
He found the craftsmen genuinely skilled and, because of that skill, convinced they understood the largest questions too. A validated record in one domain is the hardest thing to leave at the door of another. e.g. The strongest technical judgement in the room decides the pricing as well, at the same volume, on none of the evidence.

### The parts · He questioned rather than answered
He compared himself to a midwife: unable to give birth to anything himself, only to help others deliver. A conclusion somebody reaches under questioning gets defended by them. One handed over gets dropped at the first objection. e.g. Show him the flaw and one line changes. Ask until he finds it and the same flaw gets fixed everywhere else in the document.

### The parts · The examined life had a price and he paid it
Offered silence or exile instead of death, he took death, on the ground that leaving would teach the city that inconvenient judgements may be ignored. Consistency between what he said and what he did cost him everything it could cost. e.g. Any rule you announce and then quietly exempt yourself from is not a rule. It is a preference with a press office.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Next time you are certain, run the three questions: what is this judgement resting on, under what conditions would it fail, and what have I not looked at? Run them especially when the conclusion suits you. Either the certainty gets firmer or a hole opens, and both are worth ten minutes.

### Lines to keep
The unexamined life is not worth living. Wisdom begins in not pretending to know what you do not. An answer handed over gets dropped. One delivered gets defended.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Wang Yangming — Two thousand years apart and the same move: Socrates delivers what is already in you, Wang Yangming says the knowing was there all along and only obscured. Machiavelli — The two ends of philosophy: one died for a principle, the other wrote the manual for staying alive inside power. The Analects — Near contemporaries who both taught by asking rather than telling, and both paid for holding a position against the people in power. Nonviolent Communication — Two ways of getting somebody to say the answer themselves: Socrates by questioning, Rosenberg by naming the need the other person has not said out loud. Nietzsche — His fiercest target was Socrates: he held that the cult of reason had castrated the vitality of the Greeks and turned philosophy into a denial of life — the two of them side by side is the most important collision in Western thought. Carl Rogers — Two ways of making somebody find their own answer: Socrates presses with questions, Rogers removes the conditions. Richard Feynman — Both use questions to force ignorance into the open. Socrates aims them at other people, Feynman at himself.

### Further
Wang Yangming Tao Te Ching Charlie Munger Ray Dalio The Analects Gandhi Nonviolent Communication Epictetus Nietzsche Viktor Frankl Richard Feynman Karl Popper Bruce Lee Albert Einstein

## Steve Jobs
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/jobs/
Tags: Starting and building, Modern, Subtract

Steve Jobs (Contemporary · 1955–2011) — Subtract. Co-founded Apple, was pushed out of it, spent twelve years at NeXT and Pixar, came back and turned a company weeks from insolvency into the most valuable one in the…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Co-founded Apple, was pushed out of it, spent twelve years at NeXT and Pixar, came back and turned a company weeks from insolvency into the most valuable one in the world. The centre of his thinking is that simple is harder than complex, that focus is a word for refusal, and that design is how a thing works rather than how it looks.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1985 he lost a board fight and left the company he had started. He has said the twelve years that followed were the most creative of his life, and the arithmetic supports him: NeXT built the operating system Apple eventually bought to save itself, and Pixar changed what an animated film was. Neither was a detour back to Apple. Both were the thing itself, done properly, by someone who no longer had a large company's permission to worry about.

### The parts · Simplicity is expensive
Making something simple is not removing features until it is thin. It is understanding the thing well enough that the shape becomes obvious. That takes longer than adding, which is why most products are complicated: complication is what you ship when you ran out of time to understand. e.g. The settings screen with forty switches is not generous. It is a record of forty arguments nobody was willing to settle.

### The parts · The product is every point of contact
He treated the box, the shop, the repair counter and the advertising as parts of the product, because the customer does not experience them separately. A company that is excellent in the object and careless at the counter has not made a good product; it has made a good component. e.g. Unboxing designed as a small ceremony does more for how the thing feels than another processor generation.

### The parts · Belief is a resource, and it is borrowed
The famous distortion field was not a trick. People delivered work they did not believe possible because somebody credible refused to accept it was not. Used well it raises what a group thinks it can attempt; used badly it is a way of demanding miracles and blaming people for the shortfall. e.g. The same sentence, this has to be twice as fast, is either the best week a team ever had or the reason three of them leave. The difference is whether the person saying it is also in the room at two in the morning.

### Q: How do I use it today?
List everything you are currently working on and ask which half you would keep if you could only keep half. Then stop the other half today, and write down who is accountable for having stopped it.

### Lines to keep
Simple can be harder than complex; you have to work to get your thinking clean. Focus means saying no to the hundred other good ideas that there are. Design is not just how it looks. Design is how it works.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Jeff Bezos — Cut to four products; the other man expanded into everything and won too. Andy Grove — Jobs disrupted other people on instinct and taste; Grove disrupted himself on process and data. The same act performed by two temperaments.

### Further
Peter Thiel Jeff Bezos Paul Graham Huo Qubing Andy Grove Ren Zhengfei

## Strategies of the Warring States
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/strategies-of-the-warring-states/
Tags: Strategy and competition, Pre-Qin and classical, Persuasion

Strategies of the Warring States (Warring States · 453–221 BC) — Persuasion. A collection of the persuasions that travelling strategists used on the rulers of the warring kingdoms, recorded close to the ground.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A collection of the persuasions that travelling strategists used on the rulers of the warring kingdoms, recorded close to the ground. Unlike a chronicle, it is not judging anybody: it preserves the argument that worked along with what the speaker wanted out of it. Su Qin assembling an alliance of six states, Zhang Yi taking it apart one at a time, Feng Xuan buying his lord a thing no ledger could hold.

### Q: What actually happened?
Pang Cong was about to leave as escort to a hostage prince and asked the king of Wei a question first. If one man tells you there is a tiger in the marketplace, do you believe it? No. If two do? I would begin to doubt. If three do? Then I would believe it. There is no tiger in the marketplace, said Pang Cong, and three men can produce one; I am going far away and more than three will talk about me. He went. The talk came. He never got an audience again.

### The parts · Three men make a tiger
Repetition does the work that evidence cannot. A claim heard from enough separate mouths stops being assessed and starts being assumed, and the person it is about is usually the last to hear it and the least able to answer. The mechanism needs nobody to be lying deliberately. e.g. A version of events that circulates while you are away on a long project is settled before you return. Answering it then costs ten times what noticing it early would have.

### The parts · Three people praise you, three motives
Zou Ji was told by his wife, his concubine and a guest that he was better looking than Xu Gong. When Xu Gong turned up he saw it was not true, and worked out that one favoured him, one feared him and one wanted something. The words were identical; only the relationships differed. e.g. Your report, your supplier and your investor all say the plan is good. Three different reliabilities, one identical sentence.

### The parts · Buying what the ledger cannot hold
Sent to collect debts at Xue, Feng Xuan checked the bonds against the people and then burned them, and told his lord he had bought righteousness, since the house lacked nothing else. A year later, out of office, that lord was met a hundred li from the town by the whole population. e.g. Over-compensating early users is pure loss in the accounts and the only asset that speaks for you when something goes publicly wrong.

### The parts · Persuasion is not argument
Almost every piece in the book has the same structure: find what this particular ruler is most afraid of or most wants, present your proposal as the only route to it, and leave him feeling he reasoned his way there. An argument makes the other person lose. A persuasion lets him win. e.g. Su Qin never said the alliance is good for everyone. To each king he said this is your only way out, and named the thing that king lay awake over.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Take the last decision that was praised by everyone around you and write, next to each name, what that person stands to gain or lose from you. Then go and find one reference point that owes you nothing: a rival's real numbers, a user talking when you are not in the room. Xu Gong has to walk in.

### Lines to keep
There is no tiger in the marketplace, and three men can make one. My wife favours me, my concubine fears me, my guest wants something. A cunning rabbit has three burrows, and only just escapes with its life.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Sun Tzu — One states principles that can be taught in public; the other records what was actually said to one man on one day to change his mind. The Analects — Two faces of the same broken age: one on what a person ought to become, the other on how people behaved. Read only one and you end up naive or cynical. Thomas Schelling — Two arts of negotiation: the persuaders change what the other side believes, Schelling changes what the other side can choose.

### Further
Sun Tzu Fan Li Records of the Grand Historian Han Feizi Guiguzi Thomas Schelling

## Su Shi
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/su-shi/
Tags: Mind and feeling, Medieval, Unbowed

Su Shi (Northern Song · 1037–1101) — Unbowed. One of the great Chinese poets, and also a calligrapher, a painter, a hydraulic engineer, a cook and a provincial governor.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
One of the great Chinese poets, and also a calligrapher, a painter, a hydraulic engineer, a cook and a provincial governor. He was banished three times, each further than the last, and got steadily more open-hearted as it happened — not enduring the worst circumstances of his life but finding the best of himself inside them. Almost everything he is remembered for was written after his career ended.

### Q: What actually happened?
It is worth knowing the range before the philosophy. The same man who wrote the most quoted lines in the language dredged the West Lake at Hangzhou and built a causeway across it that still carries his name; set up what may be China's first public clinic; campaigned to stop infant drowning in Huangzhou; lived on the city wall during a flood at Xuzhou saying that while he was there the water would not take the city; and left recipes. None of that is decoration on the poetry. It is the same disposition doing different work.

### The parts · The openness has a structure
It wasn't a temperament he was born with. His writing records the sequence: the blow lands, there is a long stretch of real pain, attention turns inward, the present moment turns out to be full, and only then the release. He didn't skip to serenity. He walked through the middle. e.g. Two people laid off the same week. One posts about the fresh start on day three and is still hollow in month six; the other is wretched for a month, then starts.

### The parts · The constraint produced the work
His three years in Huangzhou produced the two Red Cliff rhapsodies and his best-known lyrics. Having lost the ability to change anything outside himself, he was left with what he could still do — and that turned out to be the most concentrated output of his life. e.g. The book got written the year the funding fell through, because there was nothing left to run and the writing was the only thing still in his hands.

### The parts · He lost the politics and won everything else
He opposed the reformers' new laws, then opposed the conservatives when they abolished all of them. He held to the measure rather than the side, and both sides exiled him for it. In the political record he is a failure. A thousand years later he is the one people quote. e.g. The one who wouldn't sign either faction's memo got passed over twice, and is the person both sides quote when they explain what went wrong.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Next time you're overruled, shelved, or watching something fail, try treating the stretch that follows as an enforced turn inward. The best thinking and the best work often happen in the period when there is nothing to administer.

### Lines to keep
A bamboo stick and straw sandals beat a horse. Who's afraid? Looking back at that bleak road — no wind, no rain, no sun. Where the heart is at rest, that is my home.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Zhuangzi — Two ways of not being owned: Zhuangzi refuses the post, Su Shi takes it and refuses to be defined by losing it. C.S. Lewis — Both wrote through the worst of it. Lewis to find out what he actually believed, Su Shi to find out what was still enjoyable. Chu Shijian — Both began with one small concrete job after losing the position: Su Shi broke ground at Huangzhou, Chu Shijian built the irrigation first. Neither waited to be recognised again. Seneca — Two ways of writing out of adversity: Seneca writes about restraint from inside the machinery of power, Su Shi writes about lightness on the road into exile, and both had been tested before either wrote a line. Viktor Frankl — Creation under punishment: Su Shi wrote his best work in exile, Frankl finished logotherapy in the camps — both took the worst stretch of a life and made it the productive one. Du Fu — Both rebuilt after forty: Su Shi broke ground at Huangzhou, Du Fu put up a roof at Chengdu, and both took what a life runs on before any position. Su Shi went back; Du Fu never did. Tao Yuanming — Two ways out of office: Su Shi was exiled and moved by other people, Tao Yuanming walked out himself on the day. One is about living well inside an arrangement, the other about making the decision.

### Further
Wang Yangming Fan Li Zhuangzi Tao Te Ching Huineng Winston Churchill Feng Dao Nelson Mandela Sima Qian Seneca Du Fu Shi Tiesheng Tao Yuanming

## Su Yu
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/su-yu/
Tags: Strategy and competition, The industrial age, Outnumbered

Su Yu (China · 1907–1984) — Outnumbered. A field commander who was almost always the smaller force and who is worth reading for exactly that reason.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A field commander who was almost always the smaller force and who is worth reading for exactly that reason. He had no staff college behind him and built his method out of after-action review. The method is consistent: do not take ground, destroy force; attack what they cannot afford to leave alone; and treat an order from above as something you may argue with, once your own preparation is complete.

### Q: What actually happened?
Eastern Henan, the summer of 1948. Rather than look for the enemy's main force, he took Kaifeng, a provincial capital they could not afford to leave in his hands. The relief columns had to come, and they had to come along roads he had already chosen. He let go of the city and turned on the column, and the operation ended with over ninety thousand enemy casualties. Nothing about it was a stronger army beating a weaker one. It was a choice of target that removed the other side's options.

### The parts · Besiege what they must relieve
Attack the point the other side cannot afford to lose, and then fight the relief force on ground you picked. It puts them in a position where coming costs them and not coming costs them, and it converts a defensive advantage into an engagement on your terms. e.g. Do not attack a larger rival's flagship head on. Press something they are obliged to defend and fight where they have to come to you.

### The parts · Destroy force, do not take ground
Territory taken has to be held, and holding disperses you. The unit of account he used was enemy strength removed, not places occupied. It is an unglamorous scoreboard and it compounds, because every unit gone is one that does not come back next month. e.g. Chasing a market share number can leave a rival's core team and core customers intact. Those are what actually decide the following year.

### The parts · Fight when you can win, leave when you cannot
The line usually quoted as if it were about running away is about refusing an unfavourable field. Withdrawing intact from a fight you would lose preserves the force that wins a later one. The decision is made on the terms of the engagement, not on pride. e.g. Declining to compete in a segment where your economics cannot work is not retreat. It is keeping the budget for the segment where they can.

### The parts · Dissent with the execution already finished
Twice in 1948 he argued against a plan settled above him, while the preparations for that plan carried on at full speed. The second telegram did not repeat the first; it brought a finer set of numbers. When the recommendation was taken, he accepted a stated result in his own name. e.g. Oppose a settled direction only after its preparation is genuinely done, come back with better arithmetic rather than more conviction, and sign for the new route.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Facing something much larger, stop looking at its strongest product. Find the thing it is obliged to defend, apply steady pressure there, and concentrate somewhere else while its attention is committed. Count what you have removed from the other side, not what you have occupied.

### Lines to keep
Fight when you can win; withdraw when you cannot. Attack what they must relieve; destroy them as they withdraw. When the situation is clear, the decision can be bold.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Han Xin — Two commanders who made a habit of winning outnumbered: Han Xin by putting his own men where retreat was impossible, Su Yu by choosing what the enemy had to come and save. On War — He kept enlarging plans mid-operation, which is exactly the risk Clausewitz names: every step past your culminating point weakens you.

### Further
Sun Tzu Han Xin On War John Boyd

## Sun Tzu
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sun-tzu/
Tags: Strategy and competition, Pre-Qin and classical, Win first, then fight

Sun Tzu (Spring and Autumn · c. 500 BC) — Win first, then fight. Thirteen short chapters, and the most quoted strategy book in the world. The argument underneath it is not about cunning: the winner has already secured the win before…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Thirteen short chapters, and the most quoted strategy book in the world. The argument underneath it is not about cunning: the winner has already secured the win before the fighting starts, and the loser starts fighting and then looks for a way to win. Almost every famous line is a consequence of that one.

### Q: What actually happened?
The king of Wu wanted a demonstration, so he handed Sun Tzu the palace women to drill. Sun Tzu made the king's two favourite concubines the company commanders, explained the drill, and beat the drum. They laughed and did not move. If the orders are not clear, he said, that is the commander's fault — and explained again. They laughed again. If the orders are clear and still not followed, he said, that is the officers' fault, and he had both women executed. The king was appalled. The army that came out of it did not lose.

### The parts · Win first, then fight
The famous line is that the victorious army wins first and seeks battle afterwards; the defeated army fights first and looks for the win afterwards. It is a claim about where the work happens — in the conditions, not in the courage. e.g. The launch that went well had the pricing, the support load and the two biggest customers settled before anyone wrote a line of the announcement.

### The parts · The best fight is the one nobody has
Attacking the enemy's plan comes first, his alliances second, his army third, and his walled cities last. Every step down that list costs more and returns less. Winning the fight is not the top of the ladder; not needing it is. e.g. The competitor didn't enter the category, not because they lost a price war, but because the integration work would have taken them two years to match.

### The parts · Know both, and know what you don't
Know the other side and yourself and you are never in danger; know only yourself and you win half; know neither and you lose every time. Most people read this as reconnaissance. Half of it is about you. e.g. He had the competitor's roadmap and no honest number for how long his own team actually takes. That is the half that loses.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Before the next thing you are about to launch, argue, or confront, write down what would have to be true for it to be already won. If none of it is true yet, you are not ready to start — you are ready to prepare.

### Lines to keep
The victorious army wins first and seeks battle afterwards. Winning a hundred battles is not the height of skill. Subduing the enemy without fighting is. Know the other side and know yourself, and you will not be in danger in a hundred battles.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
John Boyd — Both put the decision before the clash. Sun Tzu settles it in preparation, Boyd in speed of turning. On War — The two halves of the subject: Sun Tzu on how to win, Clausewitz on why the plan deforms. One assumes the count can be completed, the other that it never is. Strategies of the Warring States — One states principles that can be taught in public; the other records what was actually said to one man on one day to change his mind. Finite and Infinite Games — Sun Tzu solves competition entirely as a finite game and every technique serves the win; Carse asks why you assumed this round had to end at all. Thinking, Fast and Slow — Reckoning in the temple is a forced start-up of the slow system: settle the count before deciding whether to fight at all.

### Further
Han Feizi John Boyd Fan Li Peter Thiel Cao Cao Guan Zhong Zhuge Liang Mao Zedong Guo Jia The I Ching Han Xin Huo Qubing Miyamoto Musashi Napoleon On War Thomas Schelling Sima Yi Strategies of the Warring States Su Yu Xiang Yu Machiavelli Nassim Taleb Sapiens

## Taiichi Ohno
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/ohno/
Tags: Starting and building, Modern, Ask why five times

Taiichi Ohno (1912–1990 · Toyota, Japan) — Ask why five times. The principal architect of the Toyota Production System. Three things he worked out on the shop floor became common sense across manufacturing: ask why five times, let…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The principal architect of the Toyota Production System. Three things he worked out on the shop floor became common sense across manufacturing: ask why five times, let any worker stop the whole line, and hold inventory down so problems have nowhere to hide. Read as techniques they are a toolkit. Read properly they are one idea — every instrument he built exists to make a problem visible at the second and the place it occurs.

### Q: What actually happened?
The book came out in 1978 and the world copied the visible half. Factories everywhere put up the boards, printed the cards, hung the cords, learned the vocabulary, and left their buffer stocks exactly where they were. The cord was there and nobody pulled it. What had been copied was the equipment; what had not was the point of it, which is that the whole system is an instrument for making problems impossible to cover up. Remove the willingness to be embarrassed in public, at the moment it happens, and none of the hardware does anything.

### The parts · The first cause is almost never the cause
A machine stops. The fuse blew — but why the overload? The bearing was not lubricated. Why not? The pump was not pumping. Why not? The shaft was worn. Why? No strainer was fitted and metal scrap got in. The fifth answer is the repair, and it is the cheapest thing in the chain. e.g. He was careless this time is a fuse. Keep going: why was he careless, and what made being careful impossible there?

### The parts · The power to stop belongs at the bottom
Whoever sees a problem first is on the line, not in the office. If only a manager may stop, the fault has to travel upward and wait for permission, and by then it has flowed past. An error caught at the first station costs a minute; found at the last it costs the whole unit. e.g. Letting the person doing the work say wait, this is not right is worth ten times any inspection afterwards.

### The parts · Inventory is water and problems are rocks
With the water high the boat runs smoothly, because every rock is submerged: the unreliable machine, the supplier who misses dates, the handover nobody sorted out. Lower the water and they surface one at a time. Every margin is underwriting some problem, and an underwritten problem never gets repaired. e.g. Whichever stage always keeps a margin has, underneath that margin, a problem nobody has fixed.

### The parts · Stopping is what produces
Management's instinct is to keep the line moving, because output matters. What keeps moving, though, is defective output, and more of it is worse. He inverted the order: you stop in order to produce, and refusing to stop is what actually cuts production. e.g. Get it out now and fix it later mostly produces rework, and rework costs far more than the pause would have.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Take one problem that has come back three times. Write the incident at the top of a page, then ask why underneath it five times, each answer becoming the next question. Stop when you cannot answer. If the change implied at the bottom is small and cheap, you have reached it. If it is large, you have not.

### Lines to keep
Repeat why five times and the real cause shows itself. The man who replaces the fuse will be back next week. When the water is high, all the rocks are underneath it.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Peter Drucker — Drucker decides which thing to do; Ohno decides how a step is kept from going wrong. One sets the direction at a desk, the other sets the standard on the floor. Elon Musk — Both attack cost by refusing the answer they are given. Musk goes down to the physics of the materials; Ohno goes down the chain of causes on a stopped machine.

### Further
Peter Drucker Kazuo Inamori Chu Shijian

## Tao Te Ching
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/tao-te-ching/
Tags: How the world works, Pre-Qin and classical, Subtract

Tao Te Ching (Spring and Autumn · c. 500 BC) — Subtract. Five thousand characters, and after the Bible the most translated book there is. Where most instruction is addition — learn more, do more, add another method — this one…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Five thousand characters, and after the Bible the most translated book there is. Where most instruction is addition — learn more, do more, add another method — this one runs the other way. In learning you gain daily; in the way you lose daily, until there is nothing left to force, and then nothing is left undone.

### Q: What actually happened?
Laozi rode west out of the pass on an ox, leaving a country he had given up on. The keeper of the pass stopped him and asked him to write something down before he went. He wrote five thousand characters and disappeared from the record. That is the whole biography, and the book is consistent with it: everything in it argues that the position of least insistence is the strong one.

### The parts · Reversal is how the way moves
Whatever reaches its extreme turns into its opposite. It is not consolation for bad times; it is a reading instrument. At the top, look for what is already turning. At the bottom, the same rule is working for you. e.g. The quarter everything was going right is the quarter nobody asked what would happen if the one channel bringing all the customers stopped.

### The parts · Water beats stone by not arguing
The softest thing in the world runs through the hardest. Not passivity — water keeps going and takes the shape of whatever it meets. Persistence in a form that nothing can push back on outlasts a harder push that has to be sustained. e.g. Two years of quietly fixing the thing nobody owned moved more than the reorg that was announced twice and cancelled twice.

### The parts · The empty part is the useful part
The wheel is useful because of the hole at the centre, the pot because of the space inside, the room because of the gaps where the doors and windows are. What you build gets the credit; what you left out is doing the work. e.g. The calendar with two empty afternoons is where the thinking happened. The full one produced attendance.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Take the thing you are trying to fix by adding — another tool, another rule, another meeting — and ask what you would remove instead. Try the subtraction first; it is cheaper and it is reversible.

### Lines to keep
In learning you gain daily. In the way you lose daily. The softest thing in the world runs through the hardest. Knowing others is intelligence. Knowing yourself is clarity.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Zhuangzi — Same tradition, different address: Laozi writes for whoever has to govern, Zhuangzi for whoever wants out. Naval Ravikant — Both end at enough; one arrives through leverage, the other by never picking the load up. The I Ching — Same observation, different resolution. Reversal is the movement of the Way states the law in one sentence; the I Ching cuts the same law into six positions and tells you what to do in each of them. The Analects — The two main lines of Chinese thought: Confucius adds — cultivate, practise, take part — where Laozi subtracts. Neither is complete without the other. The Sovereign Individual — Two thousand years apart and the same instinct: retire when the work is done, and know what is enough. The oldest sovereign individual is Laozi.

### Further
Zhuangzi Huineng Su Shi Naval Ravikant Zhang Liang Li Bi Miyamoto Musashi The Analects Tending the Roots of Wisdom Nassim Taleb Socrates Sapiens The Sovereign Individual Bruce Lee

## Tao Yuanming
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/tao-yuanming/
Tags: Body and daily life, Qin, Han and the Six Dynasties, Eighty days, then poor for life

Tao Yuanming (365–427 · Xunyang) — Eighty days, then poor for life. A poet, and the founder of the Chinese poetry of retreat. At forty-one he took the magistracy of Pengze and held it a little over eighty days.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A poet, and the founder of the Chinese poetry of retreat. At forty-one he took the magistracy of Pengze and held it a little over eighty days. An inspector came down from the commandery and his staff told him to dress properly and go out to receive the man; he said he could not bend his back for five pecks of rice to a petty official of the district, and unfastened the seal that same day. He never held office again. The poverty was real: at forty-four a fire took the house, and one year the grain ran out and he went out to beg and wrote a poem about it. He refused every summons the court afterwards sent.

### Q: What actually happened?
He wrote a short self-portrait in the third person and gave the man in it no name, only five willows by the house. Nobody knows where he came from. He does not chase reputation. He likes reading and does not labour over fine points, and when something in a book strikes him he forgets to eat. He likes wine and is too poor to buy it, so friends have him over, and when he drinks he means to get drunk and then leaves without ceremony. The walls are bare, the clothes patched, the food basket often empty, and he is at ease. He writes to please himself.

### The parts · Turning is cheap only while you have not gone far
What the resignation poem presses is not resolve but distance: the road was wrong and he has not gone far enough to be unable to return. The price of turning rises with time, and eighty days back is not the price of eight years back. What breaks it is usually something small. e.g. Turning the moment you notice is cheapest. Turning after a full term means you already owe the term.

### The parts · Take the price of the road you chose, without blame or polish
He writes himself as neither victim nor saint. He keeps accounts: hungry, went out to beg, could not get the words out at the door. Twenty-odd years poor and he never went back, both true at once, which is what shows the turn was priced rather than impulsive. e.g. The test of a wrong turn is whether you want to go back, not whether it hurts.

### The parts · The no is answerable when the yes is not
By mistake I fell into the dusty net, and thirty years went by. Note the wording: not I always wanted to farm, but I was never suited to that. Most people are stopped by what do you want, which demands a positive answer. Cross off what you definitely will not have and the field narrows by itself. e.g. If you cannot list what you want, list three things you absolutely will not have.

### Q: How do I use it today?
If you know this is not it and keep waiting for a better moment, work out how far from far you are, and what the small daily irritation is actually showing you. If you cannot say what you want, write down the three things you will definitely not have, and then set a next step small enough that you will certainly hit it.

### Lines to keep
He left at forty-one and never went back in twenty-odd years. Own the price of the road and there is nothing to resent. Cross off the no first and the road narrows by itself.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Su Shi — Two ways out of office: Su Shi was exiled and moved by other people, Tao Yuanming walked out himself on the day. One is about living well inside an arrangement, the other about making the decision. Pu Songling — Both were poor for life: Pu Songling kept sitting the exam and never passed, Tao Yuanming stopped sitting it on purpose. One had no choice, the other chose. Du Fu — One walked, one had no choice: Tao Yuanming knew where he was going the day he resigned, while Du Fu left office and searched the whole way southwest before stopping at Chengdu.

### Further
Su Shi Pu Songling Du Fu Viktor Frankl

## Technological Revolutions
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/technological-revolutions/
Tags: Money and risk, Modern, The bubble pays for the build

Technological Revolutions (2002 · Carlota Perez) — The bubble pays for the build. Carlota Perez uses two hundred years and five technological revolutions to argue something counter-intuitive: the financial bubble is not an accident of a technological…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Carlota Perez uses two hundred years and five technological revolutions to argue something counter-intuitive: the financial bubble is not an accident of a technological revolution, it is its financing mechanism. From the industrial revolution of 1771 to the information revolution that began in 1971, every one runs the same road — technological eruption, financial frenzy, crash, institutional rebuilding, and only then the golden age. The book is quoted constantly as a positioning tool among investors and answers a question almost nothing else on this site answers: what time is it now?

### Q: What actually happened?
Britain went mad for railways in the 1840s. Hundreds of railway companies listed, newspapers ran pages of prospectuses, and clergymen and housewives bought railway shares. The bubble burst in 1847, most investors were wiped out and most companies were wound up. But the track was laid — the shareholders went under and Britain's transport skeleton for the next century remained. A hundred and fifty years later the script ran again: telecom companies burned hundreds of billions laying fibre in the late 1990s, the crash came in 2001, Global Crossing and WorldCom went to zero, and by most estimates only a low single-digit percentage of that fibre was ever lit. The fibre did not disappear. It became the physical base of twenty years of internet, cloud and streaming, and the people who inherited it paid almost nothing. Hence her cold conclusion: money spent in a bubble is wasted financially and necessary at the level of a civilisation — a collective tuition fee for building new infrastructure very fast, paid by the first group and enjoyed by the second.

### The parts · Five waves, one rhythm
1771 the industrial revolution, 1829 steam and railways, 1875 steel and heavy engineering, 1908 oil, cars and mass production, 1971 information and telecommunications. Fifty to sixty years each, and each split into installation, led by financial capital chasing asset prices, and deployment, led by production capital chasing real output, with a crash in between. e.g. Which half you are standing in decides which playbook works. Installation rewards betting and expansion, deployment rewards efficiency and consolidation. Wrong half, and effort is a headwind.

### The parts · The bubble is how infrastructure gets financed
Rational capital will not lay track, pull fibre or build data centres before the demand exists. Only irrational enthusiasm raises that money. Afterwards the assets change hands cheaply to people who will actually use them, and the first investors carry the cost. So is this a bubble is a low-value question. e.g. What did the burnt money settle into is the high-value one. Fibre and data centres leave reusable assets; pure customer-acquisition subsidy leaves nothing to inherit.

### The parts · The turning point
Between the crash and the golden age lies a stretch in which institutions and regulation have to be rewritten, because the technology has outrun the rules. It is the most painful phase and the most decisive one. Technology does not deliver good times automatically; there is an institutional fight in the way.

### The parts · Financial and production capital, split and rejoined
During installation money circulates away from the real economy and valuation detaches from output. The crash drags the two back together. In deployment, capital serves production again. Asking who is currently in charge is more useful than asking whether valuations are high: the level is the effect, the leadership is the cause.

### The parts · The techno-economic paradigm
What a revolution really delivers is not a few inventions but a new common sense about what is now so cheap you can use it freely and what is now the obvious way to do things. Cheap oil produced not just cars but suburbs, supermarkets, disposable packaging and global supply chains. e.g. The cheap-computation paradigm has barely begun. The real change will appear where nobody has ever done it that way because it used to be too expensive.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Stop asking whether this is a bubble and ask three more useful questions. First, which half are we in — is money chasing assets or chasing output? Second, what reusable thing is this round of burnt money settling into: computation, model capability, density of talent, or nothing but customer-acquisition subsidy? Third, if it all crashed tomorrow, whose assets would I want to pick up? Remember that the winners of installation and the winners of deployment are rarely the same people. The first group proves the thing is possible and mostly dies; the second buys the estate at a tenth of the price.

### Lines to keep
Every technological revolution has an installation period and a deployment period. The frenzy builds infrastructure that rational capital would never have funded. Golden ages begin after the crash, on infrastructure the frenzy paid for. The crisis is not the end. It is the turning point.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
The Innovator's Dilemma — Christensen watches one firm get disrupted, Perez watches a whole society absorb the disruption — the same event under a microscope and a wide lens. Ray Dalio — Two clocks: Dalio times the debt cycle on the financial side, Perez the technology cycle on the production side. Overlay them to know the hour. Sapiens — Harari explains why people come to believe shared fictions, Perez shows that belief turning into actual rail and fibre.

### Further
Ray Dalio Nassim Taleb The Innovator's Dilemma Thinking in Systems Peter Thiel Why Nations Fail

## Tending the Roots of Wisdom
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/caigentan/
Tags: Reading people, Early modern, A method of ease

Tending the Roots of Wisdom (Ming · c. 1590s) — A method of ease. Three hundred-odd short entries by Hong Yingming, written in the Wanli years of the Ming, on how to live among other people.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Three hundred-odd short entries by Hong Yingming, written in the Wanli years of the Ming, on how to live among other people. It reads at first like an aphorism collection about being gracious, and it is not: each entry names a self-interested reason. Leaving a step for someone on a narrow path is filed under a method of ease, not under virtue. Keeping your skill out of sight is called a place to hide in, not modesty. And the sourness you feel when someone near you does well is traced not to their gift but to your own empty square.

### Q: What actually happened?
Almost nothing survives about Hong Yingming beyond a studio name and the decades he wrote in. What survives is the title, borrowed from a line by the Song scholar Wang Xinmin: a man who can chew through vegetable roots can do anything. Vegetable roots are what is left when there is nothing else — bitter, stringy, what the poor ate. The book never once promises that things will go your way. It assumes they will not, and then works on what is still yours: how much you show, how much you give up, and what you do with the ache when somebody else succeeds.

### The parts · Give way for your own sake, not theirs
Where the path is narrow, leave a step for others to pass. Two people wedged against each other on a narrow path means nobody passes. Whoever has to be first at everything wins each occasion and loses the next, because the man opposite braces on sight from then on. e.g. Enduring for somebody else's sake keeps a ledger and presents the bill later. Giving way so you need not stay braced is over when it is over.

### The parts · Three parts off, not the whole dish
The instruction is measured: a step, three parts. Whoever hands everything over ends up living on the other person's conscience, which is no steadier a position than having to win every time. Seven parts stay with you, and that is what makes it repeatable. e.g. Put a figure on the concession before you make it: how much this time, and what is still mine afterwards.

### The parts · The fear of exposure is an arithmetic problem
Being afraid of being found out means more has been put on display than is actually held. What wants treating is the gap, not the fear: fill in what you have, or take back part of what you showed. Both beat holding up a front that must never be tested. e.g. Do not exhibit your single best performance as the normal one. Expectations settle at whatever height you showed.

### The parts · Envy starts in your gap, not in their gift
Do not use your own strength to throw another's weakness into relief; do not let your own clumsiness turn into resentment of another's skill. Two clauses, one thing: hurrying to look strong and being unable to bear good news run off the same root. e.g. You can make someone smaller without a single hard word, simply by steering every conversation back onto the ground you are best on.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Take the next concession you are about to make and put a number on it before you make it: is this three parts or all of it, and am I doing it for him or so that I can stop holding myself tight? The measured version is the one you will still be able to do in a year.

### Lines to keep
Where the path is narrow, leave a step for others to pass. He calls it a method of ease, not a virtue. Hide skill in clumsiness; be bright by seeming dim. Not that he is too good, but that this square of yours is empty.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
The Art of Worldly Wisdom — Two collections of maxims on showing and hiding, written a generation apart at opposite ends of the world: Gracián teaches how to be seen well, this one how not to need to be seen. Brené Brown — Both work on the fear of being found out. Her answer is to say it aloud so shame cannot survive being spoken; his is to stop putting so much on display.

### Further
Brené Brown The Art of Worldly Wisdom Feng Dao La Rochefoucauld Tao Te Ching
