## The Analects
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/analects/
Tags: Reading people, Pre-Qin and classical, The answer fits the asker

The Analects (Spring and Autumn · 551–479 BC) — The answer fits the asker. A record of a teacher answering particular students, compiled after his death. In English it usually arrives as loose maxims, which loses the thing that makes it usable…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A record of a teacher answering particular students, compiled after his death. In English it usually arrives as loose maxims, which loses the thing that makes it usable: almost every line was said to one named person in one situation, and the same question gets different answers depending on who is asking. Later dynasties packaged it as a philosophy of obedience, which is close to the opposite of what he did — he resigned, he travelled for years looking for a ruler worth serving, and he criticised the ones he met. He was an unsuccessful politician and the most successful teacher in Chinese history.

### Q: What actually happened?
At fifty-five he set out with his students to find a ruler who would use him, and for fourteen years none would. Between Chen and Cai the party was cut off and the provisions ran out; seven days with nothing to eat, and some of the students began to give way. Zilu came to him angry: does a gentleman also come to the end of his rope? He does, Confucius said. The gentleman holds when he is cornered; the small man, cornered, will do anything at all. He went home to Lu in the end and spent what was left of his life putting the old texts in order.

### The parts · Every answer has a name attached
He was asked what ren is more than a hundred times and answered differently nearly every time, because the answer was cut to the person asking. Read the answers with the askers deleted and you get a bag of contradictions. Read them with the askers restored and you get a method. e.g. The impulsive student is told to restrain himself and return to form. The plodding one is told, simply, to love people. Same question, different prescriptions.

### The parts · Say what you do not know
Knowing what you know and knowing what you do not know is what he calls knowledge. He held to it himself: asked something by a countryman, he said his mind went blank and all he could do was work in from both extremes of the question. e.g. Guessing at a number in a meeting costs nothing that morning and costs three teams two weeks once they have planned against it.

### The parts · Three layers for reading a person
See what he does, mark his motives, examine where he rests. Behaviour can be staged for as long as somebody is watching, the route he took to get here is expensive to stage, and what he is comfortable with when nothing is at stake can hardly be staged at all. e.g. Two people hit the same number. One spent next year's budget to do it. The route, not the number, predicts the next quarter.

### The parts · Harmony is not sameness
The gentleman harmonises without conforming; the small man conforms without harmony. A room in complete agreement about something complicated has usually not agreed. The disagreement has moved outside the meeting, where nothing can be done with it. e.g. No questions at the review, and then the problems arrive one by one after launch — each of them seen by somebody beforehand.

### The parts · One rule for a lifetime, and it is a prohibition
Asked for a single word to act on all one's life, he gave reciprocity: what you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others. The negative form is the point. It needs no knowledge of the other person, only honesty about yourself. e.g. Read the hard email once as if it had landed in your own inbox before you send it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Pick the last decision you made that landed on somebody who had no vote in it, and run the one test: would you have accepted it if it had been done to you, in that manner, on that notice? Where the answer is no, the part that has to change is usually not the decision but how it was delivered.

### Lines to keep
Knowing what you know and what you do not: that is knowledge. See what he does. Mark his motives. Examine where he rests. What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others. The gentleman harmonises without conforming; the small man conforms without harmony.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Tao Te Ching — The two main lines of Chinese thought: Confucius adds — cultivate, practise, take part — where Laozi subtracts. Neither is complete without the other. Socrates — Near contemporaries who both taught by asking rather than telling, and both paid for holding a position against the people in power. Mencius — The Analects tells a gentleman how to conduct himself; Mencius tells a ruler what will remove him. Strategies of the Warring States — Two faces of the same broken age: one on what a person ought to become, the other on how people behaved. Read only one and you end up naive or cynical. Guiguzi — Confucius asks whether a thing should be said at all; Guiguzi asks only how to say it so that it works. The avowed and the suppressed halves of the same tradition. La Rochefoucauld — Confucius holds that self-cultivation leads to benevolence. La Rochefoucauld suspects self-cultivation is only the most sophisticated form self-love has found so far.

### Further
Wang Yangming Zeng Guofan Tao Te Ching Socrates Mencius Hannah Arendt

## The Art of Worldly Wisdom
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/art-of-worldly-wisdom/
Tags: Reading people, Early modern, Concealment

The Art of Worldly Wisdom (1647 · Baltasar Gracián) — Concealment. Three hundred maxims by a Spanish Jesuit, published in 1647 and in print ever since. Schopenhauer translated it into German himself and called it a companion for life…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Three hundred maxims by a Spanish Jesuit, published in 1647 and in print ever since. Schopenhauer translated it into German himself and called it a companion for life; Nietzsche thought Europe had never produced anything finer on the subject of mental nobility. Where Machiavelli tells a prince how to handle a state, Gracián answers a smaller and more common question: how does a clever man with no power of his own survive in a place that is full of it, and do more than survive.

### Q: What actually happened?
His own life is the book's footnote. He was a Jesuit priest, and the order forbade its members to publish secular work without permission. He used his brother's name and got the books out one at a time. Warned repeatedly, he did not stop. In 1651 he published the first part of El Criticon anonymously; the order was furious, and in 1658 it stripped him of his post, sent him to a remote town, and forbade him pen and paper. He died that year, aged 58. A man who wrote three hundred maxims about keeping something back was finished by the one thing he could not keep back.

### The parts · Keep something in reserve
Do not play out all your cards. A capacity everyone has seen is discounted; a capacity nobody has measured still carries weight. Always hold a margin, so that nobody can work out where your limit is. This is not deceit. It is declining to become a quantity that can be fully calculated. e.g. Deliver at a hundred and twenty per cent once and you are measured at a hundred and twenty from that day on, and nobody remembers it was ever extra.

### The parts · Hide the effort, not the result
The height of skill is to conceal the skill. Visible strain subtracts from the thing achieved. His word for the quality he wants is despejo, an unforced ease. The modern form of the rule: the person who keeps mentioning how hard they worked is assumed to be short of ability. e.g. Two people ship the same feature. The one who explains the weekend they spent on it is quietly marked down for it.

### The parts · Leave while you are winning
Gamblers and reputations are both ruined on the last hand. What people remember is not your best moment but your final one. He reaches the same conclusion as Fan Li and Zhang Liang, from a completely separate tradition and with no contact between them. e.g. The founder who sells at the peak is called shrewd. The same founder eighteen months later is called unlucky, for the same business.

### The parts · Everyone has a handle
He says every person has an asa, a handle, and that gripping the right one moves them: vanity for some, fear for others, the wish to be recognised, the wish to avoid trouble. It is the nearest thing in the book to Cialdini, three centuries earlier and considerably colder. e.g. Before asking anyone for anything, work out what the request costs them and which of those four it touches. Most refusals are aimed at the wrong handle.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Take the maxim that annoys you most and use that one first: do not spend your whole capacity on a single delivery. The point is not to work less, it is to separate finishing a task from spending your reserve. Keep the top fifth for the occasion that actually decides where you stand.

### Lines to keep
Leave your luck while winning. All the best players do so. Things do not pass for what they are but for what they seem. What is not seen is as if it did not exist.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Machiavelli — The same century's problem at two altitudes: Machiavelli instructs a prince on handling a state, Gracián instructs a man with no power on surviving among people who have it. La Rochefoucauld — Two books of maxims with opposite jobs: Gracián hands you a method for getting through the world, La Rochefoucauld only takes away the illusions you were using instead. Influence — One subject, three hundred years apart: Gracián found the handles by watching people, Cialdini turned the same material into six principles you can test. The I Ching — One says leave while your luck is still good, which is a conclusion. The I Ching says there is one more position above the good luck and it is called repentance, which is a scale. Tending the Roots of Wisdom — Two collections of maxims on showing and hiding, written a generation apart at opposite ends of the world: Gracián teaches how to be seen well, this one how not to need to be seen.

### Further
Machiavelli Zeng Guofan Influence Fan Li Feng Dao Tending the Roots of Wisdom Guiguzi La Rochefoucauld

## The Bhagavad Gita
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/bhagavad-gita/
Tags: Mind and feeling, Qin, Han and the Six Dynasties, A right to the act, not the fruit

The Bhagavad Gita (India · c. 200 BC–200 AD) — A right to the act, not the fruit. Seven hundred verses in eighteen chapters, embedded in the Indian epic the Mahabharata, and dated by most scholars somewhere between the second century BC and the second…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Seven hundred verses in eighteen chapters, embedded in the Indian epic the Mahabharata, and dated by most scholars somewhere between the second century BC and the second century AD. The whole of it is one conversation on the eve of a battle, between the archer Arjuna and his charioteer Krishna. Arjuna looks across at the opposing army, sees his own relatives and teachers in the ranks, and refuses to fight. Chapter two, verse forty-seven is the line the world quotes: your right is to action alone, never to its fruits. Gandhi called the book his spiritual dictionary.

### Q: What actually happened?
Most English readers have already met this book once, at second hand. Watching the first atomic test in 1945, Robert Oppenheimer said a line from its eleventh chapter came into his mind: now I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds. He had learned Sanskrit in order to read it. What that famous moment hides is the situation the book is actually about, which is much smaller and much more common. One man, before anything has happened, who can see exactly what his own action will cost and cannot make himself begin.

### The parts · The line falls between the act and the yield
Whether you do it, how, and how much today are on your side. Whether the market takes it, the committee approves it, the other person replies, are not. Not asking for the harvest is not the same as refusing to look at it: results are information for adjusting the next action, not a vote on whether to continue. e.g. Two columns, mine and not mine. Work the left one, and read the right one only to see what changes tomorrow.

### The parts · Being stuck is usually seeing the whole cost at once
Arjuna is the best archer alive; his ability is not the problem. He has loaded every consequence of the whole war into a single view, and under that load no individual step is bearable. Telling a man in that state that he can do it is useless, because confidence is not what jammed. e.g. Price today's step on its own. Stop costing out the entire road every time you sit down.

### The parts · The test is what happens if the reward is removed
Suppose the return is definitely gone. Do you still do it? If not, the payoff was the work all along and this was only the road to it. Opening the hand does not mean caring less; it means today's quantity is set by you rather than by the day's news. e.g. Decide the amount in advance and hold it whether or not anything good arrives in the inbox.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Name the parts of your stalled project that are genuinely yours, set today's amount in advance, and then check the result for one purpose only: which part of tomorrow's action changes. If you cannot move at all, stop costing the whole road and price only the next step.

### Lines to keep
The line falls on the side of the act, not the harvest. Eighteen chapters of argument, and he still has to walk over there himself. Take the reward away. Whether you still do it is the fact.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Epictetus — The same border drawn in two places. Epictetus draws it between what is up to you and what is not; the Gita draws it between the act and its fruit. Wang Yangming — Both on understanding without moving. Wang puts the weight on the knowing; the Gita puts it on arguing the consequences all the way down before anyone moves.

### Further
Epictetus Viktor Frankl Zhuangzi Marcus Aurelius

## The Comprehensive Mirror
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/zizhi-tongjian/
Tags: Power and organisation, Medieval, Why regimes fall

The Comprehensive Mirror (Northern Song · 1065–1084) — Why regimes fall. Sima Guang directed the compilation for nineteen years: two hundred and ninety-four volumes covering the thirteen hundred and sixty-two years from 403 BC to AD 959.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Sima Guang directed the compilation for nineteen years: two hundred and ninety-four volumes covering the thirteen hundred and sixty-two years from 403 BC to AD 959. The emperor Shenzong named it — a mirror of what has been, useful to the art of governing. It is a history textbook written for a ruler, and it asks one question throughout: why do regimes rise and why do they fall. The Records of the Grand Historian is about people. This is about power as a system.

### Q: What actually happened?
The book was finished by a man who had lost the argument. Sima Guang opposed Wang Anshi's New Policies, lost, and left the capital for Luoyang, where he spent fifteen years out of office with nothing to do but this. The discarded drafts kept there are said to have filled two rooms, and a later reader who went through them reported that not one character had been written carelessly. He returned to power in 1085, the year after the book was presented, and was dead within about a year. The work that outlasted everything was the one he did while sidelined.

### The parts · The consort clans and the eunuchs, again
One cycle recurs from the Later Han to the Tang: a child emperor, a dowager who brings in her own family, the family taking over, the emperor growing up and using the eunuchs against them, the eunuchs taking over, a new child emperor. Understand the loop and two dynasties become legible. e.g. The modern version has different names. A vacuum in authority is filled by whoever is standing closest, every time.

### The parts · What the hundred and eighty-six comments judge by
Sima Guang's own verdicts run on three things: the ritual order that fixes rank, government by character, and putting capable people in office. Reduced to one line, whoever holds the people holds the empire — offered as a finding from thirteen centuries, not as a sermon. e.g. He is arguing that legitimacy is a resource with a balance that can be spent down, long before anyone put it that way.

### The parts · The dangerous moment is the strong one
The pattern repeats: a capable ruler, hard work, prosperity, a peak — then the succession problem, the bad ministers, the consort clans, and collapse. He observed that nothing was ever destroyed from outside before it had rotted inside first. e.g. The An Lushan rebellion arrived at the height of the Tang. The fall of the Northern Song came at its richest. Neither was struck down while weak.

### The parts · Read it against the Records
The Records of the Grand Historian asks why a person succeeded or failed, and reads like a novel. This asks why a regime rose or fell, keeps to a timeline, and reads like a case file. One shows you how people work, the other how systems work. e.g. On the same event, the Records gives you the last words at the river. This gives you how the strategic position had shifted over three years.

### Q: How do I use it today?
To judge whether an organisation is healthy, use its questions rather than its finances. Is there anybody who can check the person deciding? Does bad news travel upwards? Would anyone say out loud that the emperor has no clothes? The answers move before the numbers do.

### Lines to keep
Good faith is the ruler's greatest treasure. No duty of a ruler is greater than keeping the order of rank. No dynasty fell to an outside enemy before it had rotted inside.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Records of the Grand Historian — The two histories that complete each other: the Records puts people at the centre, the Mirror puts power at the centre, and you need both. The Innovator's Dilemma — Structural failure, ancient and modern: the Mirror on why regimes rot, the Dilemma on why good companies lose. The underlying pattern is the same.

### Further
Records of the Grand Historian Sima Qian Cao Cao Zhuge Liang Li Bi Li Shimin Wu Zetian The Old Regime and the Revolution Sapiens

## The Crowd
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/crowd/
Tags: Reading people, The industrial age, How a crowd runs

The Crowd (1895 · Gustave Le Bon) — How a crowd runs. The founding book of crowd psychology, written a century after the French Revolution and just before the age of mass politics it predicted.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The founding book of crowd psychology, written a century after the French Revolution and just before the age of mass politics it predicted. Politicians, revolutionaries, advertisers and market operators have studied it ever since. The central claim is cold and precise: an individual entering a crowd is levelled downward, infected by the feelings around him, and released from responsibility by anonymity. Reading it is not about despising the public. It is about not being carried by a crowd, and about understanding every business that addresses one.

### Q: What actually happened?
Le Bon returns again and again to the September massacres of 1792, when improvised tribunals of Paris citizens put more than a thousand prisoners to death. The men doing it were not thugs. Most were shopkeepers, craftsmen and clerks, mild enough on any ordinary day. When they had finished they emptied the dead men's pockets and handed the valuables in to the committee, considered themselves to have performed a patriotic duty, and afterwards applied to the authorities for recognition. That, he says, is the real horror of crowds. Not bad people gathering to do harm, but ordinary people doing what none of them would have done alone, and believing throughout that they were doing good.

### The parts · Three laws of the crowd mind
First, intelligence levels downward: a crowd does not perform at the average of its members but near the floor, because only the simplest feelings and slogans travel in it. Second, feeling is contagious, and panic and enthusiasm move far faster than reasoning. Third, anonymity loosens restraint, because a contribution nobody can pick out costs nobody anything. e.g. Buying frenzies, bank runs, pile-ons online. To tell whether a room has gone crowd-shaped, watch whether a reasonable sentence still finds any buyer.

### The parts · Affirm, repeat, infect
His three moves for handling a crowd. Affirmation: state it flatly, explain nothing, prove nothing. Repetition: say the same sentence until it settles in as though it were a fact. Contagion: once enough people hold it, it spreads on its own and needs no further push. Every successful slogan runs down this line. e.g. Take any advertising line you can still recite. It carried no argument, and you heard it several hundred times.

### The parts · A crowd takes images, not logic
What acts on a crowd is not the fact but the way it is presented. Crowds are not reached by reasoning, they are reached by pictures, stories and symbols. Statistics delivered to a crowd do nothing; one specific person with a name does the work of ten thousand rows. e.g. An appeal built around one named child raises more than one built on three million out of school. Absurd arithmetically, inevitable psychologically.

### The parts · Turn it round and use it as a defence
Knowing how a crowd is worked tells you when you are being worked. Three signals: when your anger or enthusiasm arrives at the same moment as everyone else's; when an idea is so simple you want to pass it on without thinking; and when you catch yourself saying that this many people cannot all be wrong. e.g. Any of the three should send you out of the crowd to recompute the thing on your own, slowly.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Use it in two directions. When you are communicating, translate the argument into a story and a picture, and accept that repetition does the work that proof will not. When you are deciding, treat everyone thinks so as the exact moment to run your own numbers. Ask periodically whether the view you are holding was calculated or caught.

### Lines to keep
In crowds it is stupidity and not mother wit that is accumulated. Isolated, he may be a cultivated individual; in a crowd, he is a barbarian. In a crowd every sentiment and act is contagious.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Influence — Micro and macro of the same subject: Cialdini works on the switches that persuade one person, Le Bon on what happens to judgement when many are in a room together. George Soros — Reflexivity is the financial version of this book: the crowd's mistaken belief moves the price and the price confirms the belief. Le Bon describes the pathology, Soros priced it. The Old Regime and the Revolution — Le Bon explains why a crowd loses control once the revolution is under way; Tocqueville explains why it starts at the moment it least should — one is mechanism, the other timing.

### Further
Influence George Soros Machiavelli Thinking, Fast and Slow Maria Konnikova The Old Regime and the Revolution

## The I Ching
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/i-ching/
Tags: Strategy and competition, Pre-Qin and classical, When to move, when to wait

The I Ching (Zhou to Warring States · China) — When to move, when to wait. Sixty-four hexagrams, six lines each, and underneath the divination they are all asking one question: given where you are standing, what should you do?

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Sixty-four hexagrams, six lines each, and underneath the divination they are all asking one question: given where you are standing, what should you do? The bottom line of the first hexagram says the hidden dragon does not act, and the top line of the same hexagram says the overreaching dragon repents. The eleventh hexagram is free passage and the twelfth is blockage, sitting next to each other in the order. The Great Commentary condenses the whole thing: at the limit it changes, changed it passes through, and passing through it lasts.

### Q: What actually happened?
Sixty-four hexagrams at six lines each comes to three hundred and eighty-four short texts, and almost none of them says do this. They say, from where you are standing, do this. The same hexagram issues six different instructions depending on which line you occupy, and the two most famous lines of the first hexagram point in opposite directions. Read straight through, the book is one long argument that the right move is a function of position, and that no position lasts.

### The parts · Being able and being due are two different times
The bottom line and the fifth are both the dragon; what differs is position, not power. Rushing to prove yourself in a new place spends your own force and carries all of the risk, and the same act two lines later is ordinary. e.g. New to a team, change nothing in the first month. Not because it should not be changed, but because that is when it costs the most to change.

### The parts · There is one line above the summit
Most people take the flying dragon for the end of the hexagram. It is not. The trouble at a peak is not the height but the adding that continues after you have reached it, and what a long good run never trains is retreat, loss and letting go. e.g. Someone who has only ever added is clumsy the first time subtraction is the correct move.

### The parts · The hexagram after Peace is Standstill
The wall falls back into the moat is written into the top line of Peace, not into Standstill. The turn begins at the last position of the good stretch. Read the other direction, being fully jammed is the condition under which change finally becomes possible. e.g. The best year is the year to work out how this ends. Equally, stop forcing a change while it still half works and push when it genuinely seizes.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Take the thing you are in the middle of and answer one question before any other: which line am I on. If it is the bottom one, spend the month gathering rather than proving. If it is near the top, name what you have never practised.

### Lines to keep
The hidden dragon does not act. The overreaching dragon repents. At the limit it changes; changed it passes through, and so lasts. Now is not the normal state. It is one line of one hexagram.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Tao Te Ching — Same observation, different resolution. Reversal is the movement of the Way states the law in one sentence; the I Ching cuts the same law into six positions and tells you what to do in each of them. The Art of Worldly Wisdom — One says leave while your luck is still good, which is a conclusion. The I Ching says there is one more position above the good luck and it is called repentance, which is a scale.

### Further
Sun Tzu Fan Li Zhuangzi

## The Innovator's Dilemma
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/innovators-dilemma/
Tags: Starting and building, Modern, Disruption

The Innovator's Dilemma (1997 · Clayton Christensen) — Disruption. Clayton Christensen asked one of the most useful questions in business history: why do excellent companies fail?

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Clayton Christensen asked one of the most useful questions in business history: why do excellent companies fail? Not through laziness or stupidity, but because they did everything right — listened to their best customers, invested in their most profitable products, concentrated on their largest markets. Those correct decisions are exactly what leaves them blind to a disruptive technology. The book describes a mechanism, not a character flaw.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1975 a Kodak engineer named Steve Sasson built the first digital camera. He took it to management, and the response was: that is cute, but do not tell anyone about it. The reason was simple. A digital camera would eat the film business, and film carried extraordinary margins. Twenty years later digital had wiped out the film market and Kodak filed for bankruptcy. This was not a blunder. In 1975, judged purely as profit maximisation, suppressing the camera was the correct call. They took the short-term optimum and gave up long-term survival.

### The parts · Disruptive innovation
Disruptive innovation is not better technology. It usually starts out worse than what exists, but cheaper, simpler, and aimed at customers you do not serve. It begins in markets that are not good enough to matter, improves steadily, and by the time it serves the mainstream well enough the leader has run out of time to react. e.g. Early personal computers were far weaker than mainframes, but cheap and made for ordinary people. Mainframe firms judged them not a competitor, because their customers, enterprises, would never buy one. By the time a PC was good enough for the enterprise, the mainframe market had shrunk badly.

### The parts · The value network trap
Every company is embedded in a value network: particular customers, suppliers, partners and processes. That network decides what counts as valuable and what counts as pointless. A disruptive technology looks worthless inside the existing network and central inside the new one, and switching networks means rebuilding almost the whole company. e.g. Nokia was perfect inside the feature-phone network: carrier channels, low-cost global manufacturing, a formidable supply chain. Smartphones needed a different network entirely — software ecosystem, third-party developers, internet services. The advantage and the shackle were the same asset.

### The parts · The resource-allocation paradox
The daily work of a good manager is to send resources toward the highest margin and the largest market. That guarantees a disruptive technology never gets funded, because its market is small and its margin is thin. The failure is not a strategic mistake; it is the allocation machinery working correctly. e.g. Kodak knew digital was coming. Film contributed sixty per cent of profit, and any resource moving from film to digital damaged the current statement. Reasonable short-term decisions, accumulated, are the dilemma.

### The parts · The remedy is a separate organisation
Christensen's answer is to give the disruptive technology to an organisation that is genuinely independent, so it is not bound by the parent's value network and is small enough to be excited by orders the parent would round to zero. e.g. Amazon built AWS well outside the retail body, at a time when everyone considered cloud a fringe business. The independence is what let it build a value network of its own.

### The parts · The managers did nothing wrong
The most important line in the book is the least comfortable one: the managers of the disrupted companies usually made no mistakes. They served their customers, allocated capital well and chased higher returns. Every decision was right and the outcome was wrong, which puts the fault in the incentive system rather than in the people.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Look hard at your main business. Is there a slightly worse substitute growing in a market you look down on, at a margin you consider too thin to bother with? If there is, it may be your disrupter — not because it is better today, but because it runs on a logic your own process cannot switch to.

### Lines to keep
Good management was the most powerful reason they failed to stay atop their industries. Disruptive technologies are not born among your best customers. Listening to your customers can be the largest mistake you make. Small markets don't solve the growth needs of large companies.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Peter Thiel — Two sides of one event: the dilemma explains why a good company loses, Thiel tells you how to be the thing that makes it lose. Jeff Bezos — Bezos ran Christensen's remedy deliberately — AWS was built outside the retail body, and that independence is what allowed it to be small. The Comprehensive Mirror — Structural failure, ancient and modern: the Mirror on why regimes rot, the Dilemma on why good companies lose. The underlying pattern is the same. The Last Hot-Metal Edition — Same upheaval from two sides: the Dilemma stands with the company and explains why its decisions were reasonable, this stands with the workers the morning after. Technological Revolutions — Christensen watches one firm get disrupted, Perez watches a whole society absorb the disruption — the same event under a microscope and a wide lens. Thinking in Systems — Two accounts of good people producing bad outcomes: Christensen gives one mechanism in detail, Meadows gives the whole catalogue. A case study against a pathology.

### Further
Peter Thiel Wang Xing Zhang Yiming Andy Grove Technological Revolutions Thinking in Systems

## The Last Hot-Metal Edition
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/hot-metal/
Tags: Learning and growth, Modern, A trade erased

The Last Hot-Metal Edition (New York · 1978) — A trade erased. On 1 July 1978 the New York Times set its last edition in hot metal, and photocomposition took over the same day.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
On 1 July 1978 the New York Times set its last edition in hot metal, and photocomposition took over the same day. The trade took years to learn and the Linotype keyboard has nothing in common with a typewriter, so what came out of those years was a body of skill that worked in exactly one place. The next morning there was no position for it in the building. It is here not as nostalgia but as evidence: the one case in this library where a whole craft was erased on a fixed date, with a film of the night it happened.

### Q: What actually happened?
Read down the first two vertical columns of a Linotype keyboard and you get etaoin shrdlu, the letters arranged by how often English uses them. When an operator fluffed a line, the quickest repair was to run a finger down those two columns, fill the line with nonsense, and throw the slug away. Now and then one escaped into the printed paper. Every compositor knew the string on sight and nobody outside the trade had ever heard of it, which is why the film of that last night is called Farewell, Etaoin Shrdlu. A private vocabulary is the surest sign of a real craft, and it goes out with the craft.

### The parts · Replacement is a switch, not a decline
Once the equipment is installed and the workflow cuts over, the old roles stop as a block rather than thinning year by year. People counting on a few years of cushion in which to adjust usually do not get one. e.g. It is not that orders shrink each year. It is that from one month on, the whole line is run a different way.

### The parts · The most skilled took the hardest hit
Lines set per minute was the trade's public scoreboard, and the machine voided the whole board at once. The people near the top lost most, because every chip was on a position that could be lifted away whole. And every year until then, another hour on the main skill had been the best available move. e.g. Fastest, most accurate, most practised. Those are precisely the measures a tool catches up with first.

### The parts · Being able to say why is what travels
How it is done belongs to the tool; why it is done that way belongs to judgement. The first expires with the equipment, the second travels with the person. What tools match is the half of a craft that can be stated, which is why the unstated half needs stating most urgently of all. e.g. That looks wrong has to break down into three specific reasons before anyone can carry it anywhere.

### Q: How do I use it today?
List the five things you are best at in your work, and mark each one with the tool it is attached to. Anything welded to one specific system is on a clock you do not control. Then take the part of the job you do by feel, the part where you can see something is wrong but cannot say why, and force three specific reasons out of it this month. That is the half a tool cannot match yet, and it is also the half you cannot hand to anyone until it is in words.

### Lines to keep
Inside an industry, replacement is rarely gradual. A skill welded to one machine retires when the machine does. Touch the new tool while the old work still pays.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Garry Kasparov — One is a single person overtaken by a machine and free to change the rules he plays by; this is a whole trade erased in a night, with no such room. The Innovator's Dilemma — Same upheaval from two sides: the Dilemma stands with the company and explains why its decisions were reasonable, this stands with the workers the morning after.

### Further
Garry Kasparov Norbert Wiener Richard Feynman Naval Ravikant

## The Old Regime and the Revolution
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/old-regime/
Tags: How the world works, The industrial age, Improvement breeds discontent

The Old Regime and the Revolution (1856 · Alexis de Tocqueville) — Improvement breeds discontent. Tocqueville (1805–1859) came from the old French nobility and had family who went to the guillotine.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Tocqueville (1805–1859) came from the old French nobility and had family who went to the guillotine. He spent his life on one question: why did the Revolution happen in France of all places? The answer overturned everyone's common sense — it was not squeezed out by oppression, it was drawn out by improvement. The book appeared in 1856 and is still the sharpest account there is of why reform detonates a crisis.

### Q: What actually happened?
He wrote it after politics had thrown him out. Tocqueville had been foreign minister for five months in 1849; then Louis Napoleon seized power in 1851, and Tocqueville, who would not take the oath, was briefly arrested and finished with public life. He went to the archives at Tours instead — intendants' correspondence, tax rolls, parish complaints. His own parents had gone into prison under the Terror and come out only after Robespierre fell. The book is a man reading the file on the machine that nearly killed his family, and finding it still in service.

### The parts · The Tocqueville paradox
People never judge their situation by its absolute level, but by the gap between how fast things improve and how fast expectation rises. Once improvement starts, expectation always climbs faster than reality, so the gap widens rather than closes. Nothing about human nature has degraded; the frame of reference was replaced. e.g. Results recover, pay rises start, and attrition goes up — because the raise replaced 'this place is finished' with 'this place can give more', and the second always outruns the actual figure.

### The parts · The abolished privilege is the one that stings
What people hate is never oppression as such; it is oppression that can no longer state its reason. While feudal obligation was a complete system it was simply how the world worked. Cut down to a few scattered items, the survivors lose their covering and become naked humiliation. e.g. A company removes most management perks and keeps the executive parking spaces. The one that stays draws more resentment than the whole set used to.

### The parts · Centralisation is the old regime's legacy, not the Revolution's invention
The most easily missed and most important chapter. From the archives Tocqueville shows that the Revolution, which advertised the destruction of the old regime, in fact inherited its core: a highly centralised administrative machine. It changed the operators, kept the machine, and made it stronger. e.g. A team revolts against being micromanaged and gets rid of the old boss. Six months later the new one manages in more detail, because the reporting lines and the review system were never touched.

### The parts · Writers in place of politicians
The old regime had detached the nobility from actual governing, leaving them privilege without responsibility, and handed public discussion to men of letters with no experience of office. France produced a politics in which the most thrilling abstractions came from the people least answerable for results. e.g. In any organisation, once the people who propose and the people who bear the consequences are fully separated, proposals get more beautiful and less executable every round.

### The parts · Where liberty and equality part
The anxiety of his life: the desire for equality is far stronger than the desire for liberty. For equality people will accept a stronger central power that levels everyone, themselves included. The end of that road is not tyranny returning but a mild supervision people walk into willingly. e.g. The demand that everyone be the same very often ends in surrendering the right to decide for yourself, and flattening reorganisations are no exception.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Whenever you are about to start an improvement — a pay rise, devolved authority, a cleaner process, a redesigned product — do one thing first: work out which surviving unfairness it is about to push into the spotlight, and deal with that in the same move. Reform detonates a crisis almost never because too little was changed, but because A was changed and B was left where it was, so B became visible for the first time.

### Lines to keep
The most dangerous moment for a bad government is when it begins to reform. The regime a revolution destroys is almost always better than the one before it. A grievance becomes intolerable once the possibility of removing it crosses men's minds.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Zhang Juzheng — Two ways for a reformer to die: Zhang Juzheng touched interests and was settled with after his death; Tocqueville describes the quieter one, where the reform itself manufactures the force that overturns it. The Crowd — Le Bon explains why a crowd loses control once the revolution is under way; Tocqueville explains why it starts at the moment it least should — one is mechanism, the other timing. Why Nations Fail — Tocqueville recorded one extractive order collapsing in detail; this book supplies the model of why it had to.

### Further
The Comprehensive Mirror Zhang Juzheng Shang Yang The Crowd Sapiens Guns, Germs, and Steel Why Nations Fail

## The Sovereign Individual
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sovereign-individual/
Tags: How the world works, Modern, Exit

The Sovereign Individual (1997 · Davidson and Rees-Mogg) — Exit. Published in 1997, eleven years before the Bitcoin paper. Two British authors explain the whole of human history with one variable: the cost of using force and the cost…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Published in 1997, eleven years before the Bitcoin paper. Two British authors explain the whole of human history with one variable: the cost of using force and the cost of defending against it. Change that cost and every institution built on top of it has to be rebuilt. Running the model forward, they predicted encrypted money, work detached from place, and governments having to compete for the people they tax. Some of it landed early and exactly; the timetable did not.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1997 they described the money of the coming age: it would consist of encrypted sequences of multi-hundred-digit prime numbers; unique, anonymous and verifiable; divisible into the tiniest fraction of value; tradable at a keystroke in a global market beyond exchange controls. There was no such thing. There was barely a web. Eleven years later a nine-page paper produced almost exactly that object, and the description written before it existed still reads as a specification for it.

### The parts · Megapolitics: force has a price and history follows it
Their term for the underlying layer is megapolitics. Armour and castles made defence cheap relative to attack, and power fragmented into feudalism. Gunpowder reversed that, and power consolidated into nation-states large enough to fund artillery. Ideology arrives afterwards to explain whatever the cost structure already decided. e.g. Feudal loyalty and national patriotism are each the story told about the cheapest available protection of their day.

### The parts · Position assets versus portable assets
The most valuable industrial-age assets were positional: land, plant, licences. All of them sit still and can be taxed or taken. The most valuable information-age assets are portable: specific knowledge, reputation, a network. They live in a head and travel with it, which changes who has to negotiate with whom. e.g. Ask of anything you own: if somebody seized it, how much of its value would survive the seizure?

### The parts · Exit beats voice
The book's practical core is not rebellion, it is departure. When leaving is cheap you no longer have to win an argument for conditions to improve, because the option itself applies the pressure. That is why the authors spend so much of the book on portability rather than on politics. e.g. The colleague with a public body of work never has to raise his voice in a salary review. His alternatives speak for him.

### The parts · What they got wrong is instructive
The nation-state did not dissolve on schedule. Identity, welfare, safety and belonging are needs that will not fit in a suitcase, and they anchor most people regardless of what the tax arithmetic says. The model was not wrong about direction; it was wrong about how much of life runs on cost. e.g. Remote work arrived on time. The predicted stampede out of high-tax countries mostly did not.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Run one honest audit of your own portfolio of assets. Sort what you have into things that stay where they are put and things that travel with you, and write down the rough share of your income that depends on each. If nearly all of it sits in the first pile, you have no exit option, and every negotiation you enter for the next ten years will be conducted from that position.

### Lines to keep
The state keeps its taxpayers in a field to be milked. Money made of encrypted primes, tradable at a keystroke. Written in 1997. The sharpest divide of the information age is mobile against immobile.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Tao Te Ching — Two thousand years apart and the same instinct: retire when the work is done, and know what is enough. The oldest sovereign individual is Laozi. Sapiens — Harari asks how the system got its grip; this book asks what it would take to slip it.

### Further
Naval Ravikant Peter Thiel Nassim Taleb Tao Te Ching Fan Li Sapiens

## The Wealth of Nations
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wealth-of-nations/
Tags: How the world works, Early modern, The invisible hand

The Wealth of Nations (1776 · Adam Smith) — The invisible hand. Adam Smith was professor of moral philosophy at Glasgow, not an economist, because the subject did not yet exist.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Adam Smith was professor of moral philosophy at Glasgow, not an economist, because the subject did not yet exist. The book appeared in March 1776, the same year as the Declaration of Independence, under the title An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations. He wrote two books in his life: The Theory of Moral Sentiments in 1759, about fellow-feeling, and this one seventeen years later, about self-interest. Reading only the second produces a Smith who never existed.

### Q: What actually happened?
English readers know one phrase from this book, and it appears in it exactly once, deep in Book IV, in an argument about where merchants choose to put their capital. Smith observes that a trader prefers to invest at home rather than abroad because he can keep an eye on it, and so, intending only his own security and his own gain, is led by an invisible hand to promote an end which was no part of his intention. It is a narrow claim about home bias, written by a man who used the surrounding chapters to attack monopolists.

### The parts · Where the phrase actually sits
Three times in his whole output: once in the moral philosophy, once here, once in an essay on astronomy. It was never his headline. Later readers promoted a passing image into a doctrine and then argued about the doctrine rather than the book. e.g. Anyone quoting it as proof that markets are self-correcting is citing a sentence about why merchants prefer domestic investment.

### The parts · Division of labour is the real thesis
The argument that opens the book is that wealth comes from how work is arranged rather than from how hard anybody works. He separates the gain into dexterity, time saved not switching tasks, and machinery invented by specialists who repeat one motion. The pin factory is his proof. e.g. One person doing product, sales and support looks like two salaries saved. In practice all three stay amateur and the switching eats the day.

### The parts · He distrusted businessmen
The book is not a defence of merchants. Smith warns that people of the same trade seldom meet, even for merriment, without the conversation ending in a conspiracy against the public or a contrivance to raise prices. Modern antitrust starts in that sentence. e.g. He also held that consumption is the sole end of production, and that producer interests deserve attention only where they serve consumers.

### The parts · Natural price and market price
Smith separates the natural price, which just covers rent, wages and profit, from the market price set by supply and demand today. Market price oscillates around natural price: excess profit draws capital in until it is competed away. It is mean reversion, two centuries before the textbooks. e.g. Any business earning unusual profit is broadcasting an invitation. A moat is simply whatever stops the market price coming back down.

### The parts · Moral Sentiments is the foundation, not a contradiction
He wrote about sympathy first and self-interest second. The earlier book argues that the wish to be thought well of hardens into conscience, and conscience is what the market later stands on. Read apart, the two books look inconsistent; read together, they are one argument in order. e.g. Law and morals come first, markets second. Smith never claimed the second works without the first.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Measure a week of your own against the pin factory. How many things are you making end to end by yourself? Take the most important one, cut it into its actual operations, and see which of them can be handed off, automated, or dropped. Then check the other direction: is the market you can reach large enough to keep your one deep skill fed? When a skill pays badly it is often the market that is too small, not the skill.

### Lines to keep
It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker. The invisible hand appears once in the book, and it is about home bias. The division of labour is limited by the extent of the market.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Guan Zhong — Two origins for the idea of national wealth: Guan Zhong steers prices and money from the centre, Smith lets price discover itself. The argument has not moved in twenty-five centuries. Shang Yang — Both are designing a route to a strong state. Shang Yang binds people to the land and suppresses trade, Smith credits division and exchange. Both routes work, at wildly different prices. Friedrich Hayek — Smith explains how the division of labour makes brute effort rich; Hayek explains how the information gets back afterwards. Why Nations Fail — Smith says the market runs itself; this book says somebody has to build the institutions that hold the market up. The missing half, supplied two centuries later.

### Further
Guan Zhong Shang Yang Thinking in Systems Li Ka-shing Naval Ravikant Guns, Germs, and Steel Friedrich Hayek Why Nations Fail

========================================================================
## Thinking in Systems
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/thinking-in-systems/
Tags: How the world works, Modern, Leverage

Thinking in Systems (2008 · Donella Meadows) — Leverage. A book about why good people with good intentions produce bad results. Meadows was a lead author of The Limits to Growth and one of the clearest writers systems thinking…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A book about why good people with good intentions produce bad results. Meadows was a lead author of The Limits to Growth and one of the clearest writers systems thinking has had. She drafted this in 1993, died in 2001, and colleagues published it in 2008. Her central claim is that a system's behaviour comes from its structure rather than from anyone's intent: replace every person, leave the structure alone, and the bad result returns on schedule. That is why so much accountability produces so little change.

### Q: What actually happened?
She used to open a talk by holding a Slinky. One hand cups it from below, the other holds the top; take the lower hand away and the spring drops, bounces and oscillates. Then she asks what made it bounce. Not the hand: the hand only let go. The behaviour was latent in the spring the whole time, and the hand merely released it. Every diagnosis in the book runs on that distinction, and most organisational post-mortems get it exactly backwards by investigating the hand.

### The parts · Stocks, flows and delay
A stock is whatever accumulates: cash, users, trust, inventory. Flows are the rates in and out. Intuition watches the stock while behaviour is set by the flows and by how long the system takes to respond. Delay is what makes you add more, overshoot, then correct too hard. e.g. Headcount is a stock; hiring rate is a flow; the three to six months before a new person is productive is the delay. Ignore it and you will overhire.

### The parts · Two kinds of loop, and only two
Reinforcing loops widen any deviation: compound interest, word of mouth, arms races. Balancing loops pull the system back to a target: body temperature, restocking, competition. Sustained growth always has a reinforcing loop behind it, and growth that stops always has a balancing loop that has begun to bite. e.g. When a growth curve flattens, look for the balancing loop that just engaged rather than for the effort that supposedly stopped.

### The parts · The system traps have names
Meadows catalogues the failure structures that keep recurring: policy resistance, the tragedy of the commons, drift to low performance, escalation, shifting the burden to the intervenor, rule beating, seeking the wrong goal. None of them requires a villain. Each is generated by the arrangement itself. e.g. Drift to low performance is the quiet one: this quarter missed, so next quarter's target comes down a little. Every single step is reasonable.

### The parts · Bounded rationality
Everyone in a system optimises inside the information they can actually see, and the sum of those local optima is often the worst global outcome. So exhortation fails and replacement fails. What works is changing what people can see when they decide. e.g. Putting server cost per team into a weekly email beats ten meetings about reducing server cost.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Pick one problem you have solved repeatedly and that keeps coming back. Instead of asking whose fault it is, ask three things: what is accumulating here and how long is the delay, which loop is currently in charge, and what feedback is missing that would let the person deciding see the consequence immediately. Most chronic problems do not need more discipline. They need a meter moved into the hallway.

### Lines to keep
A system's behaviour cannot be read off its parts. People find the leverage point, then push it the wrong way. We cannot control a system. We can learn to dance with it.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
The Innovator's Dilemma — Two accounts of good people producing bad outcomes: Christensen gives one mechanism in detail, Meadows gives the whole catalogue. A case study against a pathology. Thinking, Fast and Slow — Kahneman repairs the individual head, Meadows repairs the surrounding structure. The same bad decision, charged to two different accounts. Guns, Germs, and Steel — Axes, diffusion, density, feedback — Diamond is writing a system-dynamics case study that runs for thirteen thousand years.

### Further
The Innovator's Dilemma Thinking, Fast and Slow Charlie Munger Norbert Wiener Ray Dalio Finite and Infinite Games Guns, Germs, and Steel Technological Revolutions The Wealth of Nations Ivan Illich

## Thinking, Fast and Slow
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/thinking-fast-and-slow/
Tags: Learning and growth, Modern, Fast mind, slow mind

Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011 · Daniel Kahneman) — Fast mind, slow mind. Daniel Kahneman's summary of forty years of work with Amos Tversky, and the founding text of behavioural economics.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Daniel Kahneman's summary of forty years of work with Amos Tversky, and the founding text of behavioural economics. He is the only psychologist to have won the Nobel in economics, in 2002. The frame everybody took from it: a fast, automatic, associative mind and a slow, effortful, reluctant one. The frame he warned about in the same book: they are fictitious characters, not parts of the brain, and naming which one is speaking does not stop it speaking.

### Q: What actually happened?
Teaching flight instructors in the Israeli Air Force, he said that praise works better than punishment. A senior instructor objected from experience: praise a cadet for a clean manoeuvre and the next one is worse, shout at a bad one and the next is better. Kahneman saw that the man had been watching regression to the mean and reading it as cause. An unusually good or bad flight is partly luck, and luck does not repeat. He called it the most important insight of his life: the mind will not leave a fluctuation alone without attaching a reason to it.

### The parts · Two systems, and one of them is lazy
The fast system answers almost everything and rarely reports difficulty. The slow one is expensive and avoids being started. The failure is not that the fast one errs. It is that the slow one signs off instead of checking. e.g. A bat and ball cost a dollar ten, and the bat costs a dollar more than the ball. Almost everybody says ten cents. It is five.

### The parts · Losses weigh about twice as much
Losing a hundred hurts roughly as much as winning two hundred pleases. It explains holding losers and selling winners, why you will lose this beats you could gain that, and why any reform meets more anger than gratitude. e.g. The people who lose from a change turn up to say so. The people who gain are busy, and mostly do not know yet that they gained.

### The parts · Anchoring, and where the first number came from
A number that arrives first shapes everything after it, even when it is plainly irrelevant. Opening offers, list prices before a discount, the tone set at the start of a review: one mechanism, used on purpose. e.g. Ask what you would have estimated if you had never heard their figure. The distance between the two answers is the anchor.

### The parts · The premortem
Plans get built from the inside, where this project is special, and ignore the base rate of comparable ones. The fix is to gather everybody before starting, assume it has already failed a year from now, and have each person write down why. e.g. His own textbook team estimated two years. Comparable projects ran seven to ten, with heavy attrition. It took eight.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Put three gates in front of any decision that matters. Sleep on it, so the fast answer loses its heat. Run a premortem: it is a year later and this failed, so write down why. And look up how comparable attempts actually went before you explain why yours is different.

### Lines to keep
We can be blind to the obvious, and we are also blind to our blindness. Nothing in life is as important as you think it is, while you are thinking about it. The mind will not leave a fluctuation without a cause attached.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Influence — Two sides of one thing: Cialdini shows how the gaps get used on you, Kahneman shows why the gaps are there. Sun Tzu — Reckoning in the temple is a forced start-up of the slow system: settle the count before deciding whether to fight at all. Karl Popper — Popper says what a careful mind should do; Kahneman measures how far an ordinary one departs from it. Thinking in Systems — Kahneman repairs the individual head, Meadows repairs the surrounding structure. The same bad decision, charged to two different accounts.

### Further
Influence Charlie Munger Nassim Taleb George Soros The Crowd La Rochefoucauld Karl Popper Thinking in Systems

## Thomas Gordon
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/thomas-gordon/
Tags: Family and relationships, Modern, The I-message

Thomas Gordon (1962 · Parent Effectiveness Training) — The I-message. A student of Carl Rogers who turned humanistic psychology into a course ordinary parents could take.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A student of Carl Rogers who turned humanistic psychology into a course ordinary parents could take. His two central tools predate and are more concrete than most of what came after: the I-message, which states what happened and what it did to you instead of what kind of person you are; and problem ownership, which asks whose trouble this actually is, because the answer changes the method completely.

### Q: What actually happened?
He observed that most parents know two moves — win (I decide) or lose (fine, have it your way) — and that both carry a long bill: the first produces compliance or opposition, the second produces someone who doesn't consider anyone else. His third method turns the conflict into a shared problem: name what each side actually needs and find something that meets both. Not a vote and not a compromise, because splitting the difference leaves everyone short. In the child-rearing thinking of 1962 this was close to heresy.

### The parts · Say the effect, not the character
Three parts: the specific behaviour, its actual effect on me, how I feel. Nothing in it judges the other person, so there is nothing to defend against. The part most often dropped is the middle one, and it is where the persuasion lives. e.g. 'You're careless' starts a defence. 'When the numbers arrive after five I redo the deck at night, and I'm worn out' does not.

### The parts · Work out whose problem it is first
A child upset about a bad grade owns it, and the move is listening. A child wrecking the room you work in — that's yours, and the move is an I-message. Getting it backwards is the common error, and it lays your anxiety on top of theirs. e.g. The teenager miserable about a grade needs listening to. The music through the wall while you work is yours to raise.

### The parts · No effect you can name may mean no problem
If you can't say what it actually does to you, this may be a preference rather than a problem. The step doubles as a filter: when you can't fill it in, ask why you're insisting. e.g. He couldn't say what the messy desk actually cost him. That was the answer: a preference wearing the clothes of a rule.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Before raising something, split it into behaviour, effect on me, and how I feel, with no line about what kind of person they are. And before you open your mouth, ask whose problem this is. If it's theirs, listen and say back what you heard; advice at that moment moves them from solving their problem to handling your opinion.

### Lines to keep
Say what this does to me, not what kind of person you are. Work out whose problem this is before choosing a method. Conflict doesn't have to end with somebody winning.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Maria Montessori — Both ask the adult to hold back. She changes the room; he changes the sentence. Han Feizi — Two theories of getting compliance: rules and consequences, or naming the effect on you. Both work, on different things. Alfred Adler — Two ways of asking whose problem this is: Gordon's answer picks the method, Adler's decides whether it is yours to touch at all. Carl Rogers — Teacher and student: Rogers set the condition, Gordon turned it into three sentences an ordinary parent could say.

### Further
Maria Montessori Arlie Hochschild Carl Rogers Crucial Conversations

## Thomas Schelling
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/schelling/
Tags: Strategy and competition, The industrial age, Commitment

Thomas Schelling (United States · 1921–2016) — Commitment. In the most dangerous years of the Cold War the most influential strategist was not a general but an economist.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
In the most dangerous years of the Cold War the most influential strategist was not a general but an economist. Schelling rebuilt the theory of deterrence out of bargaining, and shared the 2005 Nobel in economics for it. His most counter-intuitive result is that cutting away your own options, in public, is the most effective way to strengthen your position. Burning the way back is a tactic, not a gesture.

### Q: What actually happened?
The American garrison in West Berlin could not have held the city for a day against a Soviet attack, and everyone involved knew it. Schelling's point was that holding was never its function. Its function was to make American involvement automatic: any attack would kill American soldiers on the first morning, and no president would then be free to decide whether to respond. It was not a line of defence. It was a trip-wire, and its weakness was the whole design.

### The parts · Credible commitment: weaken yourself to gain leverage
Bargaining power comes less from what you can do than from what you can no longer do. While you keep the ability to concede, they keep pushing. Lock yourself in a way they can verify and the pressure reverses. Verifiable is the operative word; a private resolution is worth nothing. e.g. Announcing that a product will never carry advertising ties your hands now and builds trust a rival cannot copy without burning the same exit.

### The parts · Deterrence and compellence are not the same
Deterrence says do not do that or else, succeeds invisibly, and has no deadline. Compellence says you must do this or else, requires them to act, to be seen backing down, and to do it by a date. The second is far harder and costs far more. e.g. If you are late again there are consequences usually works. Apologise in front of everyone provokes a fight, because the price includes their dignity.

### The parts · Focal points: coordinating without talking
Asked to meet a stranger in New York with no way to arrange it, most people say Grand Central at noon. Nothing makes it optimal; it is simply the point everyone expects everyone to expect. Round numbers, precedent, the middle and the old boundary all work the same way. e.g. Prices ending in ninety-nine, splitting it down the middle, a ceasefire on the old border. When you design a rule, find the focal point before you argue the optimum.

### The parts · A commitment is only credible if it cost something
The thread through all his work: a signal carries information only when the sender paid a real and unrecoverable price for it. Free promises are not promises. Deposits, penalty clauses, public declarations and a founder's own money all convert words into sunk cost. e.g. Investors check whether a founder is full time and whether their own money is in. They are measuring the price of the promise, not the wording.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Next time you are stuck, do not raise the threat. Ask why they believe you will move, and the answer is almost always because you still can. Close that route where they can see it. Run the same test in reverse when it is used on you: what would it actually cost them to take that commitment back?

### Lines to keep
The power to constrain an adversary may depend on the power to bind oneself. In bargaining, weakness is often strength. A promise that costs nothing carries no information.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Strategies of the Warring States — Two arts of negotiation: the persuaders change what the other side believes, Schelling changes what the other side can choose. Nassim Taleb — Skin in the game and credible commitment are one coin: Taleb uses cost to decide whose word to trust, Schelling to make his own word land. Chris Voss — The two halves of bargaining: Schelling works on structural commitments and threats, Voss on the language in the room. One alters the payoff matrix, the other alters the person.

### Further
Strategies of the Warring States Han Feizi Peter Thiel Nassim Taleb Sun Tzu Otto von Bismarck Chris Voss

## Viktor Frankl
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/frankl/
Tags: Mind and feeling, The industrial age, Meaning

Viktor Frankl (1905–1997 · Vienna) — Meaning. Psychiatrist, camp survivor, and the founder of logotherapy. In Auschwitz he watched something he could not explain with physiology: under identical extreme conditions…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Psychiatrist, camp survivor, and the founder of logotherapy. In Auschwitz he watched something he could not explain with physiology: under identical extreme conditions some people broke and some did not, and the difference was not physical strength but whether a person had a reason to stay alive. His central proposition is that the last of the human freedoms, the one that cannot be confiscated, is the choice of your own attitude in any given set of circumstances.

### Q: What actually happened?
Entering the camp, his manuscript was taken from him — years of psychological work, gone in the first hour. Standing naked in the inspection line, he realised they could take everything and still not take how he chose to answer it. That realisation is what he lived on. He began observing systematically which prisoners came through and which gave up, and found that men with something unfinished waiting in the future — a book, a family, a task — outlasted men with nothing pulling at them. After the war he dictated the book in nine days.

### The parts · Meaning is the last freedom
In any circumstances a person can choose their own attitude. This is not positive thinking; it is a regularity he observed in a camp. External conditions can strip away food, health, liberty and family. The interpretation of that stripping — this is destroying me, or this is tempering me — stays in your hands the whole way down. e.g. Marcus Aurelius on the inner citadel and Frankl on the last freedom are the same proposition: a Roman emperor and a twentieth-century survivor, different vocabulary, one claim.

### The parts · The meaning of suffering
What he found most dangerous in extreme suffering was not the pain but the verdict that the pain is pointless. Once a person concludes their suffering means nothing, the collapse follows. Conversely the smallest sense of purpose — I will live to tell the world what happened here — will carry someone through an amount of suffering that should not be survivable. e.g. If there is a meaning in life at all, he wrote, then there must be a meaning in suffering. That sentence is not consolation, it is the load-bearing wall of the whole therapy.

### The parts · Pull from the future
Prisoners with a strong future object — a reunion waiting after the war, unfinished work, a specific mission — survived at higher rates than those with nothing ahead of them. Why you are living matters more than how you are living, because the direction sets how much you are prepared to spend. e.g. He kept picturing himself lecturing after the war on the psychology of the camps, which turned what he was enduring into material for work not yet done.

### The parts · The existential vacuum
Modern people have unprecedented material conditions and an increasing sense of hollowness. He called it the existential vacuum, and said it shows up as boredom, as imitation — doing what others treat as important — and as conformity, doing what others ask. The prescription is not less pain. It is a meaning that is actually yours. e.g. Don't aim at success, he wrote: the more you aim at it and make it a target, the more you are going to miss it. It arrives only as the side effect of dedication to a cause greater than oneself.

### Q: How do I use it today?
When the emptiness arrives, his question is not how do I become happy. It is what is life asking of me at this moment. Move the attention off what I want and onto what I can do for something outside myself, and the sense of meaning tends to arrive behind it rather than in front.

### Lines to keep
Everything can be taken from a man but one thing: the last of the human freedoms. If there is a meaning in life at all, then there must be a meaning in suffering. Don't aim at success. The more you aim at it and make it a target, the more you are going to miss it. He who has a why to live for can bear with almost any how.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Nelson Mandela — Two answers to extreme adversity: Frankl found meaning inside the camp, Mandela turned twenty-seven years in prison into a political transformation — one worked on the inner position, the other on the outer one. Su Shi — Creation under punishment: Su Shi wrote his best work in exile, Frankl finished logotherapy in the camps — both took the worst stretch of a life and made it the productive one. Marcus Aurelius — Two tests of the inner citadel: Marcus holds it voluntarily at the top of power, Frankl has it tested with everything else taken away. Epictetus — The same finding eighteen centuries apart: Frankl said in the camps that the last human freedom is the choice of one's attitude, which is the dichotomy of control tested at the floor of human experience. Nietzsche — He who has a why to live can bear almost any how is Nietzsche's line, and Frankl carried it into Auschwitz and tested it: one man worked it out in a study, the other verified it where verification cost everything. Arthur Kleinman — Both answer what to do when a situation cannot be changed: Frankl points to the freedom of attitude in an extreme, Kleinman to the ordinary long grind where care is still available every day. Shi Tiesheng — Both answer what holds when a situation leaves no choice: Frankl says meaning, Shi Tiesheng answers much smaller, with one place he went every day and the gaps between dialysis sessions.

### Further
Marcus Aurelius Epictetus Nietzsche Socrates Kazuo Inamori Wang Yangming Gandhi Nelson Mandela The Bhagavad Gita Sima Qian Seneca Brené Brown Kristin Neff Records of the Grand Historian Arthur Kleinman Shi Tiesheng Tao Yuanming Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi Alfred Adler

## Virginia Satir
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/satir/
Tags: Family and relationships, Modern, Under the iceberg

Virginia Satir (1964 · A founder of family therapy) — Under the iceberg. One of the people who invented family therapy. Her turning claim is that when one member of a family develops a problem, the system is often keeping its balance by…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
One of the people who invented family therapy. Her turning claim is that when one member of a family develops a problem, the system is often keeping its balance by putting the symptom on the most vulnerable person in it — so the person in the chair is not the whole case. She also left a way of recognising what is happening in a room: under pressure people fall back into four fixed stances, placating, blaming, super-reasonable and distracting, and a fifth, congruence, is the healthy one and has to be learned.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1951 she was seeing a young woman who was getting better, and the young woman's mother telephoned in a fury and threatened to sue her. Satir invited the mother in. With the mother in the room the daughter's progress went backwards, and a relationship Satir had never seen came into view. So she asked the father in, and the picture rearranged again; then the brother, and it rearranged once more. She had been treating one person and discovered she had been looking at a quarter of the case.

### The parts · The iceberg: layers under the behaviour
Above the waterline is behaviour; below it are feelings, perceptions, expectations, yearnings and the self. Conflict happens on the surface and gets settled underneath: anger is behaviour, under it disappointment, under that I want to be treated as though I matter. e.g. A partner complaining that you are home late is not really raising the calendar. Underneath is usually the question of where they rank in this house.

### The parts · Four stances under pressure
Placating gives up the self, blaming gives up the other, super-reasonable gives up both and keeps the logic, distracting gives up the subject. All four are automatic and all four dodge what is real. The fifth, congruence, holds self, other and situation at once, and is trained rather than inherited. e.g. You lay out the logic point by point and he gets louder: super-reasonable meeting blame, and neither of you is in the room.

### The parts · The problem is not the problem
Families are often stuck with difficulties that cannot be solved: money, illness, temperament. What decides how the days go is the coping. The sentence moves attention from who caused this to how we handle it, and only the second one is a live question. e.g. A child's grades falling cannot be reversed this week. Whether the household blames each other or works on it decides what the fall turns into.

### The parts · The symptom can belong to the system
One member's trouble is frequently doing a job for the whole: a child in difficulty gives two parents on the edge of separating something to unite around. Treat that person and leave the system alone and the symptom moves to somebody else. e.g. The parents start fighting the moment the child improves. That usually means the trouble had been standing in front of the marriage.

### Q: How do I use it today?
When the same conflict keeps coming back, hold off on who is wrong. Work out which stance each of you fell into, then look for the expectation under the words. And if one person's trouble clears up and something breaks elsewhere, the system is moving, not the person.

### Lines to keep
The problem is not the problem; coping is the problem. Under pressure people placate, blame, go super-reasonable, or distract. The symptom often belongs to the system, not the person showing it.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Murray Bowen — Two readings of one family: Bowen tracks differentiation down the generations, Satir works the stance being taken in the room right now. Esther Perel — Both look past the argument on the surface — Perel at what the relationship is missing, Satir at which layer the argument is really on.

### Further
Murray Bowen Carl Rogers Attachment Theory Nonviolent Communication
