## Wang Jian
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wang-jian/
Tags: Strategy and competition, Pre-Qin and classical, Self-preservation

Wang Jian (Qin · c. 280–220 BC) — Self-preservation. The leading general of Qin, who took Zhao, took Yan, took Chu and had a hand in the fall of five states: the man who actually executed the unification.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The leading general of Qin, who took Zhao, took Yan, took Chu and had a hand in the fall of five states: the man who actually executed the unification. He is here less for the campaigns than for a harder problem he solved. He is the person in this collection who handled being too useful to a suspicious ruler best. Bai Qi, his equal in talent, was ordered to kill himself.

### Q: What actually happened?
In Chu with six hundred thousand men, he refused to fight. He fortified the camp and kept it shut, had the men wash, rest and eat well, and ate with them. After a long while he asked what the troops were doing with themselves. Throwing stones and jumping for distance, he was told. Then they can be used, he said. The Chu army had by then given up on provoking him and turned east, and he moved the moment they did, and broke them.

### The parts · Give the real number
Asked what it would take to conquer Chu, Li Xin said two hundred thousand and Wang Jian said six hundred thousand. The king thought him timid and sent Li Xin, who was broken. His figure was not confidence; it was a count of ground, army and population, and he preferred to be called cautious. e.g. Optimistic estimates are almost always wrong. Count everything, add buffer, give the number you believe, and then do not move under pressure.

### The parts · Do not revise after the refusal
Turned down, he did not compromise at four hundred thousand. He pleaded illness and went home. Had he revised, he would have proved the first figure was padding. When the king came in person to apologise, the number he named was the same number. e.g. Estimate two people, get cut to one, then say you will try to make it work, and every estimate you give afterwards is discounted automatically.

### The parts · Show a weakness you choose
Setting out with almost the whole army of Qin, he asked for fields, houses and ponds, and asked five more times on the march. Not because he was greedy. Holding that much and wanting nothing reads to a suspicious ruler as a larger design; a small visible appetite reads as safe. e.g. Deliberately exposing a controllable weakness in a negotiation, such as a limited budget or a small team, often gets you more equal terms than projecting strength.

### The parts · Stay inside the job
He kept out of court politics, built no faction and offered no opinions outside his command, and after Chu he retired rather than wait to be suspected. Crossing out of your remit is what actually threatens the people above you; competence inside it rarely does. e.g. Influence acquired outside your defined responsibility is what gets read as ambition. The work itself almost never is.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Next time you name a number, name the one you believe, and then hold it through the meeting where holding it is expensive. Separately, if you have become unusually important to someone, make sure they know what you want and that it is something they can comfortably give.

### Lines to keep
It cannot be done with fewer than six hundred thousand men. The king is suspicious and trusts nobody. Revise the number after a refusal and you have proved it was padding.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Han Xin — Identical achievements, opposite endings: Wang Jian made himself look greedy and died in bed, Han Xin held on to his standing and did not. Fan Li — Two ways of leaving at the top: Fan Li vanished and became a merchant, Wang Jian resigned and went home to his fields.

### Further
Zhang Liang Han Xin Sima Yi Fan Li Guo Ziyi

## Wang Xing
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wang-xing/
Tags: Starting and building, Modern, Nine losses, one win

Wang Xing (Contemporary · 1979–) — Nine losses, one win. Founder of Meituan. Before it he had failed eight times: a Chinese Facebook, sold; a Chinese Twitter, shut down.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Founder of Meituan. Before it he had failed eight times: a Chinese Facebook, sold; a Chinese Twitter, shut down. On the tenth attempt he bet on group buying, survived the most violent competition in Chinese internet history, and turned Meituan into a platform for eating, staying and getting around. What he is worth reading for is the pair of tests he runs: what actually counts as our business, and what is all this activity replacing.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 2010 the group-buying model reached China and five thousand sites appeared almost overnight, in what became known as the war of a thousand groupons. Wang Xing did not burn money to buy share the way everyone else did. He required Meituan to expand only into cities whose numbers were healthy and refused orders that lost money. Everyone expected him to lose, because share needs speed, not thrift. Two years later ninety-nine per cent of those sites were gone and Meituan held the remaining one per cent. His account of it: we did not win by burning harder, we won by lasting longer.

### The parts · Nine losses, one win
Eight consecutive failed companies, each one fully reviewed afterwards and written up as why this failed and what must not repeat. That is a method rather than an inspirational story: failure is data, not a verdict. You make the available mistakes first and spend the accumulated understanding on the fight that matters. e.g. Having sold one company far too cheaply, he refused unequal terms when raising money for Meituan, taking less cash to keep control. The lesson from the eighth attempt decided the tenth.

### The parts · Slow is fast
He refused growth for the sake of growth, and required each city to have working unit economics before the next one opened. Short term that is slower than the competition. Long term the cities without working economics turn into holes that burn cash, and the competition falls in first. e.g. During the group-buying war several rivals were larger than Meituan and expanded on gross volume with no view of profit. Two years later Meituan was the only healthy company left standing.

### The parts · Jumping the S-curve
Every business has an S-curve, from emergence through rapid growth to maturity, and you have to find the next curve's beginning before the current one matures. Meituan entered delivery before group buying peaked, and started hotels while delivery was still accelerating. The jumps were designed, not lucky. e.g. Kodak sat at the top of the film curve twenty-two years after the digital camera had been invented and did not jump. The alternative is to go looking for the next curve before anything forces you to.

### The parts · User value is the north star
The first question on any new business is why would somebody use this — not how large the market is and not what the competition is doing, but the real motive of the person. He built the habit early by watching students use his product in their own rooms rather than reading reports about it. e.g. Against a subsidy war in food delivery he made courier speed and on-time rate the core metrics, because what the customer wants is food that is still hot, not food that is cheapest.

### The parts · A ten-year operating system
He reads heavily, science fiction included, on the grounds that it is a way of testing long-range logic with the imagination. Decisions get taken on a ten-year view: will this still matter in a decade, and if so it should be started now whatever this quarter's statement looks like. e.g. Ask of a proposal only that it clear three bars: will it matter in ten years, what does the user actually want, and do the unit economics close.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Next time you weigh a new business or a new direction, ask the three questions in order: will this still matter in ten years, what does the user actually want, and can the unit economics close. Only something that survives all three is worth the resources.

### Lines to keep
Most people will do anything rather than face real thinking. Choose the right thing to do, not the easy thing. We did not win by burning harder. We won by lasting longer. Too many people watch the boundary instead of the core.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Zhang Yiming — Two philosophies from the same generation: Wang Xing's nine losses and one win runs on endurance, Zhang Yiming's delayed gratification runs on arithmetic — two different kinds of slow. Warren Buffett — Two shapes of the long view: Buffett will not own something for ten minutes he would not own for ten years, Wang Xing asks whether the thing will still matter in ten years.

### Further
Zhang Yiming Peter Thiel Warren Buffett Ren Zhengfei The Innovator's Dilemma Finite and Infinite Games

## Wang Yangming
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wang-yangming/
Tags: Mind and feeling, Early modern, Knowing is doing

Wang Yangming (Ming · 1472–1529) — Knowing is doing. A philosopher who was also the most effective general of his generation — an almost unheard-of combination.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
A philosopher who was also the most effective general of his generation — an almost unheard-of combination. His central claim is that the principle you are looking for is not out in the things of the world but in the mind that meets them, and that anyone who says they know something and doesn't act on it has not yet understood it. He is the origin of most of what later East Asia means by practical philosophy.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1506 he offended a powerful eunuch, was beaten in open court and exiled to Longchang in Guizhou — a malarial posting on the edge of the empire where he had to build his own shelter and grow his own food. The officials sent there mostly died. He had a stone coffin made and slept beside it, on the reasoning that the only thing he had not yet let go of was the fear of dying. One night he woke shouting. The way of the sage is complete within my own nature — he had spent twenty years looking outside for something that was not out there.

### The parts · The mind is the principle
The meaning and value of a thing arrive with the mind that meets it. Practically, this moves the standard: your judgement doesn't come from an external authority that has to be consulted before you may act. e.g. You already know the deck is dishonest. Waiting for someone senior to say it first is not caution; it is looking for a person to hold the judgement for you.

### The parts · Knowing and doing are one
'I know I should get up early' from someone who never does is not knowledge, it's an idea about knowledge. Real knowing shows up in the body. This is the sentence he is most quoted for and the one most often quoted without being applied. e.g. 'I know I should exercise' from someone who hasn't in a year is not knowledge. The knowing showed up in the ones who went twice this week.

### The parts · The hardest campaign is interior
He never lost a battle, and wrote from the field that breaking the bandits in the hills is easy and breaking the ones in the heart is hard. What actually stops people is fear, laziness, vanity and self-deception — none of which appears on any plan. e.g. The plan was never the problem. Sending the email that admits the number was wrong is the whole difficulty, and no amount of planning touches it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
When a team knows what to do and doesn't do it, the problem is usually not execution. Either they don't actually believe it matters, or the incentives point elsewhere. Fix what they believe before you talk about delivery.

### Lines to keep
Breaking the bandits in the hills is easy. The ones inside aren't. When this mind does not move, you can move with the moment. Without a settled aim, nothing in the world gets finished.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Huineng — The same insight in two traditions: Huineng says what you seek is already complete in you, Wang Yangming says so and then goes and governs a province with it. Zeng Guofan — Doctrine and practice: Wang built the school of mind, Zeng spent a lifetime executing it. Reaching the insight against grinding it out daily. Augustine — Both on knowing and not doing. Wang says knowing without acting was never real knowing; Augustine says the knowing is real and two wills are fighting. The Bhagavad Gita — Both on understanding without moving. Wang puts the weight on the knowing; the Gita puts it on arguing the consequences all the way down before anyone moves. Socrates — Two thousand years apart and the same move: Socrates delivers what is already in you, Wang Yangming says the knowing was there all along and only obscured.

### Further
Huineng Su Shi Zhuangzi Xunzi Zhang Juzheng The Analects Zeng Guofan Nelson Mandela Augustine Nietzsche Viktor Frankl Ray Dalio Socrates Bruce Lee

## Warren Buffett
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/buffett/
Tags: Money and risk, The industrial age, The moat

Warren Buffett (Contemporary · 1930–) — The moat. Sixty years of compounding, and a method simple enough to say in a sentence: buy a business with a durable advantage at a sensible price and then do nothing for a very…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Sixty years of compounding, and a method simple enough to say in a sentence: buy a business with a durable advantage at a sensible price and then do nothing for a very long time. His real edge is not stock-picking. It is that he can sit still while other people cannot.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1973–74 the American market fell by half. The Washington Post went from thirty-eight dollars to sixteen. Everyone was getting out; he was buying. He wrote to the management that he had bought, for ten million dollars, a piece of a company they themselves valued at four or five hundred million. The position eventually returned more than a hundred times. Nothing about the company had changed in those months. What had changed was what other people could stand to hold.

### The parts · Four kinds of moat
A brand people ask for by name, a network that gets more valuable as it grows, a cost position nobody can match, and a switching cost that makes leaving expensive. The wider the moat, the less the future depends on being clever. e.g. Nobody switches accounting software to save nine dollars a month. That is a moat, and it was built by the tedium of migration, not by the features.

### The parts · The edge of the circle matters more than its size
You do not need to understand every business, only the ones you understand. He stayed out of technology for decades and said so plainly. Knowing where your competence stops is the part that protects you; the size of the circle is vanity. e.g. He passed on the deal because he could not explain how the company made money in one sentence. That is not timidity; that is the boundary doing its job.

### The parts · The moat that matters is emotional
Be fearful when others are greedy and greedy when others are fearful. In 1987, in 2000, in 2008 he was the one buying into the collapse. The analysis was available to everyone. The stomach was not. e.g. Everyone knew the rule about buying the dip. Almost nobody transferred the money on the Monday the number was red on every screen.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Before the next purchase, write in one sentence why this thing will still be earning in ten years. If you cannot write the sentence, you are not buying a business; you are buying a price movement.

### Lines to keep
Be fearful when others are greedy and greedy when others are fearful. Rule one: never lose money. Rule two: never forget rule one. You do not have to understand every company. Only the ones you own.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Charlie Munger — The partner who moved him from cheap and broken to good and fairly priced. Duan Yongping — Duan Yongping is Buffett's most serious Chinese student, but he moved the moat from investing to operating: Buffett buys the company that has one, Duan builds one by entering last and building better. Wang Xing — Two shapes of the long view: Buffett will not own something for ten minutes he would not own for ten years, Wang Xing asks whether the thing will still matter in ten years. Benjamin Graham — The student past the teacher: Graham bought cheap ordinary companies, Buffett bought great ones at fair prices. Jesse Livermore — Speculation against investment: Livermore took the price movement and rose and fell four times, Buffett took the business and compounded. Jim Simons — The two poles of investing: Buffett bets heavily on a few near-certainties, Simons bets tiny amounts on millions of near coin-flips — and both refuse the middle ground. George Soros — Two poles of investment philosophy: Buffett trusts that the market gets there in the end, Soros treats it as permanently wrong.

### Further
Charlie Munger Li Ka-shing Fan Li Jeff Bezos Peter Thiel Naval Ravikant Duan Yongping Kazuo Inamori Wang Xing Benjamin Franklin Bai Gui Benjamin Graham Jesse Livermore Peter Lynch Howard Marks Jim Simons George Soros

## Why Nations Fail
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/why-nations-fail/
Tags: How the world works, Modern, Institutions

Why Nations Fail (2012 · Acemoglu and Robinson) — Institutions. Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson, published in 2012. The argument is blunt: whether a country is rich or poor turns on neither geography nor climate nor culture nor the…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson, published in 2012. The argument is blunt: whether a country is rich or poor turns on neither geography nor climate nor culture nor the intelligence of its leaders, but on whether its institutions are inclusive or extractive. In 2024 the two authors shared the Nobel prize in economics with Simon Johnson for this line of research. The lasting value is less the conclusion than the blade, which cuts downwards without losing its edge: country, industry, company, team.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1589 William Lee brought a machine to London. He had built a stocking frame that knitted far faster than hands, and he wanted a patent from Elizabeth I. She refused. His invention, she told him, would ruin her poor subjects by taking away their employment and turning them into beggars. Lee took the machine to France, was refused again, and died in Paris with nothing. The queen understood the device perfectly. That was the problem.

### The parts · Inclusive against extractive
Inclusive institutions need three things: property that is secure, law that applies to everyone alike, and public provision that lets most people compete. Extractive ones let a few use power to take what many produced. The test underneath is single: can the person who created the value keep it? e.g. The company version is three questions. Do options really pay out, does promotion track results, and is the important information held by a handful of people?

### The parts · Creative destruction is the dividing line
Extractive arrangements resist innovation by construction, because innovation reshuffles position and the current holders lose. Rulers who blocked railways and knitting machines were not confused about the benefits. They were reading the political consequences correctly. e.g. Progress is rarely blocked by people who do not understand it. It is blocked by the people who understand it soonest.

### The parts · Extraction can grow fast, then hits a wall
Moving resources out of low-productivity agriculture into industry can raise output for decades without any inclusive institution at all. What that model cannot do is make the next transition, because the next one runs on innovation and innovation needs exactly what extraction will not permit. The ceiling is calculable in advance. e.g. Growth from a management dividend or a distribution dividend behaves the same way. It lasts a long time and ends needing an entirely different capability.

### The parts · Critical junctures and institutional drift
This is not determinism. Small institutional differences accumulate quietly, and then a shock arrives that amplifies them into completely different paths. Plague, Atlantic trade, industrial technology: each one widened gaps that had been almost invisible beforehand. e.g. It is their answer to why England and not Spain. Small difference plus large shock equals permanent divergence.

### The parts · Politics comes before economics
Good economic policy is not hard to design. The hard part is getting people with power to adopt policies that reduce their power. So the real subject of the book is how political power is distributed, and any reform plan that skips that layer is discussing technique. e.g. Poverty usually persists not because nobody knows what would work, but because doing it would cost somebody their position.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Point the framework at whatever organisation you are in and ask three questions. Does the person who creates value get to keep a share of it? Do the rules apply to everyone, or can some people be excused? When a new way of doing things appears, is it encouraged or quietly suppressed by whoever benefits from the old way? Two noes make it extractive. It may still be growing fast, but that growth is a reallocation dividend and its ceiling can be worked out before you join.

### Lines to keep
Nations fail because extractive institutions kill the incentive to invest and innovate. Creative destruction redistributes political power, which is why it is resisted. The poor stay poor because the powerful will not, not because nobody knows how.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
The Wealth of Nations — Smith says the market runs itself; this book says somebody has to build the institutions that hold the market up. The missing half, supplied two centuries later. The Old Regime and the Revolution — Tocqueville recorded one extractive order collapsing in detail; this book supplies the model of why it had to. Sapiens — Both explain how humanity arrived here: Harari credits shared fictions and mass cooperation, this book credits the incentives institutions create. Lee Kuan Yew — The book argues inclusive political institutions are the condition for lasting prosperity, and Singapore is its most cited counter-example. Read them together. Guns, Germs, and Steel — The most direct argument in the library: Diamond makes geography the ultimate cause, Acemoglu makes institutions the root and geography only the backdrop. The two sides have answered each other in public.

### Further
The Wealth of Nations The Old Regime and the Revolution Shang Yang Sapiens Technological Revolutions Lee Kuan Yew Guns, Germs, and Steel

## Winston Churchill
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/churchill/
Tags: Mind and feeling, The industrial age, Ten years out, back at 65

Winston Churchill (1874–1965 · Britain) — Ten years out, back at 65. Politician and writer. He went out with the government in 1929, lost the Exchequer, and held no office for ten years — the wilderness years.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Politician and writer. He went out with the government in 1929, lost the Exchequer, and held no office for ten years — the wilderness years. He wrote for a living through them, laid brick at home, and painted. Through the thirties he repeated in Parliament that Germany was rearming and British air strength was not keeping pace, was treated as bellicose and out of date, and read aircraft production figures into the record anyway.

### Q: What actually happened?
He was a working bricklayer with a union card. In 1928 he joined the Amalgamated Union of Building Trade Workers — an ex-Chancellor applying for membership as a bricklayer, which caused enough of a row that the union later revoked it. He built walls and a cottage at Chartwell with his own hands and wrote to a friend that he was spending his days laying bricks and writing a book. Two hundred bricks and two thousand words a day. It is the most exact description anyone has given of how to survive being shut out.

### The parts · When nobody calls, make things that leave your hands
The hard part of being sidelined isn't the idleness, it's not knowing whether you still count. His answer was daily delivery: a chapter, a stretch of wall, a painting. Output means you don't need an invitation to feel present.

### The parts · Put it in a form that can be checked
An emotional judgement can't be verified, so it can't be confirmed either; saying it ten times equals saying it once. Numbers and dates can be ignored today and reconciled later. A checkable sentence has a lifespan.

### The parts · Being prepared means having it ready
He became prime minister at sixty-five, an age then considered retirement. Nobody had time to develop anyone; he was called because on that subject he alone had a ready judgement, a ready record, and a line he had not altered in ten years.

### Q: How do I use it today?
If you've been pushed out of the centre and don't know how long it lasts, fix on one thing you can finish daily, and arrange one task that is physically hard — being sidelined traps people in an argument with absent colleagues, and sweat competes with it. Write your important judgements down with dates. That is your only evidence later.

### Lines to keep
Someone with output needn't wait for an invitation to feel present. A checkable sentence has a lifespan. A lament doesn't. Age is only the problem when your hands are empty.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Pu Songling — Both spent decades unrecognised. His day came; Pu Songling's never did, and the advice has to work either way.

### Further
Su Shi Pu Songling Marie Curie

## Wu Zetian
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wu-zetian/
Tags: Power and organisation, Medieval, Breaking the frame

Wu Zetian (Tang · 624–705) — Breaking the frame. The only woman to rule China as emperor in her own name. She entered the palace at fourteen as a junior concubine and abdicated at eighty, and in between she broke every…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The only woman to rule China as emperor in her own name. She entered the palace at fourteen as a junior concubine and abdicated at eighty, and in between she broke every rule that was supposed to stop her. Her method is worth more than her biography: she treated each rule not as a wall but as a thing certain people were choosing to enforce, and went to work on those people. Her reign expanded the examination system and the empire did not shrink.

### Q: What actually happened?
When Taizong died, a concubine who had borne no child was sent to a temple to become a nun, and she went. What she waited for at Ganye Temple was the day the new emperor, Taizong's son, came to burn incense for his father — a man who had already noticed her. She left the temple, re-entered the palace, and worked her way past the standing empress. The histories say she strangled her own newborn daughter and let the blame fall on the empress. Nobody could prove it. Everybody believed she was capable of it, and being thought capable of it was itself a kind of power.

### The parts · Take the rule apart into people
Every step of hers began at a wall: women do not govern, a childless concubine does not return, an empress cannot be deposed, a woman cannot take the throne. Her habit was to resolve each rule into who is enforcing this and what do they need, and to work on that instead. e.g. This market already has a giant, so there is no room. Break it down: who holds the position, what does it pay them, and under what conditions do they stop defending it?

### The parts · Alliances counted precisely
On the way up she kept an exact account of where each person stood: natural allies whose interests already matched hers, people who could be neutralised by being paid off, and those who had to go. She fought nothing for its own sake and moved when her side of the ledger was strongest. e.g. Most political energy in an organisation is spent on fights that were never going to change anything.

### The parts · Recruit past birth
She promoted men of no family, widened the examinations and added the palace examination, breaking the aristocratic clans' grip on office. This was not only progress, it was arithmetic: men with no clan behind them depended on the throne alone. e.g. Give opportunity to people who have no other route and you get loyalty that no incentive scheme can buy.

### The parts · The clear-eyed end
In old age she named her son, of the Tang house, as heir rather than her own nephew, which meant accepting that her dynasty would end with her. She understood that her power had been borrowed against the Tang rather than replacing it, and chose to give it back. e.g. Knowing what your position actually rests on is rarer than getting the position.

### Q: How do I use it today?
The next time something is described as impossible, do not argue with the word. Ask who is enforcing this, what does enforcing it pay them, and what would have to change for them to stop. An abstract impossibility has no handles. A named person with an interest has several.

### Lines to keep
Even an absurd man, if what he said fitted, was promoted out of turn. How did the chancellor come to lose this man? A wide gate is only safe if the exit is cheap.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Machiavelli — Political realism written and political realism lived: he set down what a prince must actually do, she had already done it eight centuries earlier. Shang Yang — Two people who broke a settled order: Shang Yang broke aristocratic privilege, she broke the bar on her sex, and both paid heavily for it.

### Further
Liu Bang Han Feizi Machiavelli The Comprehensive Mirror

## Xiang Yu
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/xiang-yu/
Tags: Strategy and competition, Pre-Qin and classical, Unbending

Xiang Yu (Chu · 232–202 BC) — Unbending. The most complete loser in Chinese history, which is why he is worth the time. He brought down the Qin almost single-handedly, something his rival could not have done…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The most complete loser in Chinese history, which is why he is worth the time. He brought down the Qin almost single-handedly, something his rival could not have done, and then lost everything to an unremarkable minor official. The failure was not in ability. It was in what he thought the contest was: he believed war was the strong crushing the weak, and Liu Bang was playing a game about people.

### Q: What actually happened?
Surrounded at Gaixia, hearing the songs of Chu coming from every side of the ring, he broke out with eight hundred riders. By the time he reached the Wu River twenty-eight were left. A boatman offered to take him across, and said the lands east of the river were small but enough to be king in, enough to begin again. He refused. Eight thousand sons of the east crossed westward with me and not one is going back; what face could I meet their fathers with? Then he turned and fought until he cut his own throat.

### The parts · Force without design
His generalship is not in question: sinking the boats at Julu, thirty thousand cavalry breaking a force many times the size at Pengcheng. But he only ever used force. He destroyed the enemy in front of him while Liu Bang was destroying the threat that had not arrived yet. e.g. At the Hongmen banquet Fan Zeng signalled to kill Liu Bang and he would not. Not mercy: in his logic enemies are beaten on a battlefield, not stabbed at dinner.

### The parts · The win too large to revise
Julu proved to him that overwhelming frontal attack answers everything, and a belief confirmed by an enormous success is close to unfalsifiable. Every later deadlock got the same treatment, right through to Gaixia. The most successful experience is the hardest one to overturn. e.g. A company built on one spectacularly successful method keeps running it after the conditions change. Not blind to the change: the success was too big to doubt.

### The parts · He could not use people
He had one first-rate adviser in Fan Zeng and repeatedly ignored him, and Han Xin left him to go and serve the other side. Placing your own judgement above everyone else's has a predictable result: the capable go, and the ones who stay cannot act. e.g. The seal is worn smooth in his hand because he cannot bear to hand it over. Reward withheld is read by everyone watching, not just by the person who did not get it.

### The parts · Deciding in order to be seen
Urged to keep Guanzhong, defensible and rich, he went home to Pengcheng instead, because to be rich and not go home is to wear brocade at night. The strategic gap was obvious. Recognition simply outranked it, and the man who said so out loud was boiled. e.g. Choosing the visible path over the one that compounds, with reasons ready, and the actual reason being who will see it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Look at your own team for the Fan Zeng: the person who has been right and whom you have been discounting. Then take the decision you are closest to making and ask whether you would still make it if the result were invisible to everyone you know.

### Lines to keep
To be rich and not go home is to wear brocade at night. Heaven is destroying me. It is no fault of my arms. Not one of the eight thousand is going back. What face could I meet them with?

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Liu Bang — The perfect loser against the imperfect winner: the ceiling of one man's talent against the ceiling of what many people will do for you. Julius Caesar — Two tragic ends in two traditions: Caesar killed by the people he trusted, Xiang Yu by refusing to get into a boat.

### Further
Liu Bang Han Xin Sun Tzu Fan Li On War Hu Xueyan

## Xunzi
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/xunzi/
Tags: Power and organisation, Pre-Qin and classical, Shaped, not born

Xunzi (Warring States · 313–238 BC) — Shaped, not born. Mencius said people are naturally good. Xunzi said people are naturally workable. The word usually rendered as artifice means made on purpose: rites, law, teachers and…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Mencius said people are naturally good. Xunzi said people are naturally workable. The word usually rendered as artifice means made on purpose: rites, law, teachers and repeated correction, taking a material that comes out disorderly and putting it into a usable shape. Han Feizi studied under him and the Qin system took its force from here. He is the first thinker in China to treat organisational design as the first question rather than the last.

### Q: What actually happened?
At Lanling he was asked about war. Lord Chunshen wanted the clever manoeuvres; Xunzi talked instead about two dull things — keep the weapons new, and make reward and punishment reliable. War in his account is not a contest of spirit but a test of whether ordinary people can be trained into usable instruments. He later served as magistrate of Lanling and applied the same argument to running a county. His student Han Feizi pushed the claim that people are workable to its limit and arrived at law, method and position. Xunzi never went there himself. He believed in training, not in fear alone.

### The parts · Nature transformed by deliberate effort
Human nature is bad; what is good in people is deliberate effort. What you are born with is a set of preferences, not a set of virtues. Virtue is manufactured — by rules, by ritual, by being pulled back into line often enough. Expecting employees to be self-motivated is declining to do that job. e.g. Benjamin Franklin scoring himself against a table of virtues once a day is the modern version. So is Andy Grove drilling managers with weekly one-to-ones and an output review.

### The parts · Bluer than the indigo it came from
The material does not set the ceiling; the process does. A student surpasses the teacher not because he was born with more but because he applies the teacher's method more thoroughly than the teacher did. e.g. Han Feizi took the workable-person claim and built a colder system out of it. A process has no moral brake fitted as standard.

### The parts · Compass and square
There is no straight line without an instrument. Xunzi says even a sage needs compass and square, which puts an ordinary manager some way further down the list. Having a feel for the standard usually means the standard has not been written down. e.g. Shang Yang moving the pole to prove the reward was real turned a promise into something observable. Most stated values never get that far, which is why they stay on the wall.

### The parts · Small steps accumulate into the visible
Without piling up small steps you never reach a thousand li. Large change is small change stacked. An organisation waiting for a breakthrough tends to come apart during the wait. e.g. Zeng Guofan changing one habit a day in his journal, and Kazuo Inamori breaking craft into actions repeatable every shift, are both this sentence in practice.

### Q: How do I use it today?
After you hire someone, do not open with self-direction. Write down three things first: what counts as done correctly, who checks it, and what happens when the check fails. A team with all three blank does not have a culture problem. It is still standing in the theory that people are naturally good.

### Lines to keep
Human nature is bad; what is good in people is deliberate effort. Blue is taken from the indigo and is bluer than the indigo. Without piling up small steps, you never reach a thousand li. Mugwort growing in a hemp field stands straight untied.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Mencius — One holds that people can be taught, the other that people can be shaped. Mencius cultivates; Xunzi processes. Han Feizi — The student pushed the teacher's training argument into a theory of control. Xunzi kept the rites; Han Feizi kept only the handles.

### Further
Mencius Han Feizi Wang Yangming Andy Grove Benjamin Franklin Li Shimin

## Zeng Guofan
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/zeng-guofan/
Tags: Reading people, The industrial age, Dull and unbreakable

Zeng Guofan (Qing · 1811–1872) — Dull and unbreakable. The most famous case in Chinese history of an ordinary man getting there by grinding. He was not gifted — he sat the examination seven times before passing — and he put…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The most famous case in Chinese history of an ordinary man getting there by grinding. He was not gifted — he sat the examination seven times before passing — and he put down the Taiping Rebellion, the largest of the century, with a method he admitted was stupid: build a solid camp and fight a dull battle. He kept a diary auditing his own conduct for thirty years and circulated it to friends. He hired by handing people real work rather than by interviewing them. Nothing about his method requires talent, which is exactly why it is worth reading.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1854, at Jinggang, the river force of the militia he had been ordered to raise met the rebels and was broken. His boats were scattered and his men ran. He went over the side into the river and was pulled out by his own staff. He was a civil official with no military training, humiliated in front of the province, and what he did afterwards is the whole of him: he stopped looking for a battle he could win. From then on the army dug before it fought, and the war became a matter of trenches, supply and time.

### The parts · Solid camp, dull fight
On arriving anywhere the army camped before anything else — trench, wall, stockade — and cities were encircled and squeezed rather than stormed. It converted taking a city from an event full of accidents into a question of time and supply. e.g. Anqing was held under siege for over a year and Tianjing for more than two. No single mistake could collapse either operation.

### The parts · A method that does not need talent
The other side of a dull method is that it copies. Any commander with any unit could follow it and reach a passing grade, whereas a brilliant stroke depends on that person on that day. An army raised from nothing could be carried by it for that reason. e.g. A process worth eighty that anyone can run beats one star worth a hundred. The first goes to thirty cities; the second leaves when he does.

### The parts · Watchfulness when alone
Anybody keeps the rules while being watched. His answer to the unwatched stretch was not willpower but record: write the day down, wrong thoughts included, and the moment acquires a witness. Then he handed the record to friends, which is cheaper than resolve and works better. e.g. Expenses nobody audits, code nobody reviews, a report nobody reads. Those three places describe a person more accurately than any appraisal.

### The parts · Daily disciplines have to be checkable
I will become more disciplined cannot be executed. His twelve were actions you can tick tonight: rise early, sit in stillness, read one book at a time, keep the diary, note what was said over tea. Small enough to answer did it or did not. e.g. Read more this year cannot be settled in December. Ten pages a day, three lines written after, settles itself every night.

### The parts · Take in widely, employ carefully
A low bar at the door and a high one at the far end. He kept a large staff and then judged people on a real piece of work under real pressure — how they reported, and what they did with the part they could not do. e.g. Li Hongzhang came up that way, from the staff to independent command. Ask where this is not finished; the clean answer is the one to promote.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Turn the goal you keep losing in week three into something you can tick tonight, then post this week's version where somebody else will read it. The grain size and the audience are doing the work; resolve was never the variable.

### Lines to keep
Watchfulness when alone brings peace of mind. Fight without haste: first make it stable, then look for change. Principle without officialdom, order in the head and few big words. Steady work that never breaks off beats a burst of courage.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Marcus Aurelius — The closest pair East and West: both wrote themselves down every day, and both used the writing to hold themselves in check at the top of their own power. Wang Yangming — Doctrine and practice: Wang built the school of mind, Zeng spent a lifetime executing it. Reaching the insight against grinding it out daily. Li Shimin — Two ways to hold up a mirror. Li Shimin kept Wei Zheng in the room; Zeng Guofan used a journal nobody else read. Feng Dao — Zeng Guofan held an army and cut back his own wings to keep his name; Feng Dao had neither troops nor money and sought only to keep people alive. Ren Zhengfei — The same method a hundred and thirty years apart: build the solid camp and fight the slow fight, no shortcuts, no clever moves, never be beatable before you try to win. Benjamin Franklin — The matched pair of the two hemispheres: both of ordinary natural ability, both forging themselves with a daily ledger — between them the evidence that character is an engineering problem rather than a gift. Brené Brown — Zeng turned self-reproach into a daily discipline; Brown would ask whether that sentence is pointing at the behaviour or at the man writing it. Ray Dalio — The same instrument on two continents: thirty years of diaries and a decade of taped meetings, both aimed at self-deception. Atomic Habits — Both accumulate by small daily acts: Zeng Guofan by a written daily examination of himself, Clear by design that removes the need for one.

### Further
Wang Yangming Kazuo Inamori Ray Dalio Zhuge Liang The Analects Li Shimin Feng Dao Guo Ziyi Zhang Juzheng Miyamoto Musashi The Art of Worldly Wisdom Maria Konnikova Ren Zhengfei Marcus Aurelius Benjamin Franklin Hu Xueyan Atomic Habits

## Zhang Juzheng
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/zhang-juzheng/
Tags: Power and organisation, Early modern, Reform and the reckoning

Zhang Juzheng (Ming · 1525–1582) — Reform and the reckoning. In two hundred and seventy years of Ming rule he is the one chief minister who actually changed the state.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
In two hundred and seventy years of Ming rule he is the one chief minister who actually changed the state. The single whip reform merged the tax system, the evaluation ledgers put every order on a name and a date, and land was resurveyed; the treasury went from empty to four million taels of silver in reserve. He was the most powerful man alive while he lived, and within a year of his death his house was raided and his family destroyed. This is the fullest version of the reformer's fate in the collection.

### Q: What actually happened?
His power rested on a triangle: a boy emperor who was the formal authority, the empress dowager who was the real one, and the chief eunuch who controlled the palace. He secured the last two, and only then could he govern. With the boy he was severe — diligence, frugality, lessons, a childhood entirely managed, from the age of ten. He died at the height of his power. The emperor, now grown, took his revenge within the year: the estate seized, the eldest son driven to suicide, the reforms picked apart. It was politics, and it was also ten years of a boy waiting.

### The parts · The triangle was not an institution
His authority came from three personal relationships, not from any power the office of chief minister actually held. When the dowager lost influence and the eunuch was purged, the base vanished at once. Personal power is fragile; only institutional power lasts. e.g. Ask what happens to your position if the two people who back you leave. If the answer is nothing survives, you have influence, not a role.

### The parts · A reform needs beneficiaries who can speak
The single whip helped ordinary taxpayers, who had no political voice at all. The officials and local gentry it hurt had plenty. So the moment the protection was gone, one side could act and the other could not. e.g. Design the beneficiaries deliberately, and check that they are people with the standing to defend what they got.

### The parts · Do not suppress the person who will outlive you
Ten years of strict tutoring produced an emperor who was competent and who hated him. In power relationships the benefactor and the oppressor are often the same person, and which one you turn out to have been is decided by the other party, later. e.g. The strong mentor makes the junior. The first thing the junior does once made is get out from under the mentor.

### The parts · Assessment is the dangerous reform
The evaluation ledgers made government work. They also created, one by one, every official who later had a reason to want him gone. The cost of a reform is not the resistance in front of you; it is the enemies waiting behind it. e.g. Everyone supports fairness before performance review arrives. Afterwards, the people it marked down start looking for a way back.

### Q: How do I use it today?
If you are pushing a change through an organisation, spend as much time designing who benefits as designing the change. Make the gains land on people with enough standing to defend them, and make sure they know the gains came from the new arrangement. A reform with no constituency is undone the week its sponsor leaves.

### Lines to keep
The hard part is not making the law; it is making sure the law is carried out. I am not a chief minister. I am a regent. A decision with no name and no date on it is a wish.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Shang Yang — The reformer's fate in two versions: Shang Yang died and his system stood, Zhang Juzheng died and his was dismantled. The difference is who was left to defend it. Zhuge Liang — Two tragedies of being irreplaceable: after Zhuge Liang there was nobody to take over, after Zhang Juzheng the whole programme collapsed at once. The Old Regime and the Revolution — Two ways for a reformer to die: Zhang Juzheng touched interests and was settled with after his death; Tocqueville describes the quieter one, where the reform itself manufactures the force that overturns it.

### Further
Guan Zhong Han Feizi Zeng Guofan Wang Yangming Shang Yang Otto von Bismarck Zhu Yuanzhang The Old Regime and the Revolution

## Zhang Liang
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/zhang-liang/
Tags: Power and organisation, Pre-Qin and classical, Asking for less

Zhang Liang (Han · c. 250–186 BC) — Asking for less. The cleverest of the three men credited with founding the Han, and the only one of them who died in his bed.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The cleverest of the three men credited with founding the Han, and the only one of them who died in his bed. The life runs in three acts: learning to endure, on a bridge at Xiapi; using the plan, at the Feast at Hong Gate; and leaving, when he asked for one small county instead of thirty thousand households. His comparisons are Han Xin, who did not withdraw and was killed, and Xiao He, who half withdrew and survived.

### Q: What actually happened?
Liu Bang had taken the capital first, and Xiang Yu was arriving with a far larger army and every intention of destroying him. Xiang Bo, an uncle of Xiang Yu, rode over in the night to warn Zhang Liang privately and get him out, because Zhang Liang had once saved his life. Zhang Liang refused to leave. He told Liu Bang, brought Xiang Bo in and had him introduced, and set up the meeting at Hong Gate the next morning where Liu Bang apologised in person and left the banquet alive. The favour he would not spend on himself is what saved everybody.

### The parts · The Liu county rule
Take what is enough, not what is most. Thirty thousand households is a symbol of achievement; one small county is a home. Asking for less was not modesty, it was a calculation: the smaller the request, the smaller the threat, the safer the man who made it. e.g. The largest available title comes with the largest available surface area for somebody else to aim at.

### The parts · Three men, three answers to the same danger
Facing the same problem of having served too well, Zhang Liang disappeared, Xiao He made himself look small and slightly disreputable, and Han Xin did neither. Two of them died in their beds. The strategy decided the outcome, not the loyalty. e.g. When a founder starts feeling crowded, the people who narrow their own footprint early are not being timid. They are reading the same signal.

### The parts · The timing question is when, not whether
When the birds are gone the good bow is put away. The difficult judgement is what counts as done. His answer was: before the other side has begun to wonder about you. After that, the same move means something else entirely. e.g. Han Xin knew the danger, and neither left nor handed back command. He spent the longest time of the three in the middle ground, which is the one place with no exit.

### The parts · The Tao Te Ching line, lived
Withdraw when the work is done: that is the way of heaven. He is the person who actually did it. Not passivity, but the best available survival play: step out of the contest while everyone else is still in it, and you no longer have opponents. e.g. Handing the thing over while it is going well converts a rival into a beneficiary. The same handover after the decline converts nothing.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Next time a promotion or a larger position is put in front of you, run the Liu county rule before you answer. Ask for the level that is sufficient and safe rather than the largest one on offer. The extra mostly buys exposure.

### Lines to keep
Enfeoff me at Liu and it is enough. I wish to drop the affairs of men and follow Master Red Pine. Withdraw when the work is done: that is the way of heaven.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Han Xin — Same founding, opposite endings: Zhang Liang withdrew completely and died old, Han Xin kept both his army and his ambitions and was killed. Fan Li — The two men who understood leaving. Fan Li left to trade, Zhang Liang left to study the way. Different exits, identical result. Guo Ziyi — Two ways to survive success: Zhang Liang left the table, Guo Ziyi stayed at it with his cards face up, which is much the harder trick. Li Bi — One reign or four: Zhang Liang withdrew for good once the founding was over, Li Bi came back and left four times and finished holding the top office.

### Further
Fan Li Li Bi Han Xin Tao Te Ching Liu Bang Guo Ziyi Wang Jian Guiguzi

## Zhang Yiming
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/zhang-yiming/
Tags: Starting and building, Modern, Delayed gratification

Zhang Yiming (Contemporary · 1983–) — Delayed gratification. Founder of ByteDance, the company behind Toutiao and TikTok. Relentlessly rational, hostile to vague language, willing to let a recommendation engine decide what a…

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
Founder of ByteDance, the company behind Toutiao and TikTok. Relentlessly rational, hostile to vague language, willing to let a recommendation engine decide what a person sees. He treats cognitive bias as the largest single source of wasted effort, which is why delayed gratification and a ban on hedging words became the operating system for himself and for his teams.

### Q: What actually happened?
One passage of his gets quoted constantly: I have met a great many clever people, but very few willing to delay gratification, and people at different orders of that willingness cannot usefully discuss a problem at all. He spent five years grinding on product with almost nothing said in public — no speaking slots, no profiles, just the work. The sentence is not advice about patience. It is a claim that this one trait sorts people into groups that cannot hold a conversation with each other.

### The parts · Delayed gratification
Giving up a present pleasure for a longer-run value is a scarce capability and, in his account, the sharpest way to tell people apart. When he picks a partner or an employee the first measure is not raw ability but how far out that person is willing to place the payout. e.g. Look at a record of past moves: always the highest immediate pay, or sometimes the steepest slope. The answer is already written down.

### The parts · Against vagueness
He asks people to speak without maybe, roughly, I feel and it seems, forcing precision. If you cannot say it clearly you have not thought it through, and something not thought through is most likely wrong before anyone starts building it. e.g. Rewrite a hedged claim as: I think X, because Y, confidence Z per cent. Half the sentences do not survive the rewrite.

### The parts · The company is the product
Develop the company as though it were a product: you are not only building the thing users touch but also the organisation, the incentives and the information flow behind it. Optimising one part in isolation is the usual way of manufacturing a problem somewhere else. e.g. A team rewarded on its own metric will improve that metric and quietly damage two others nobody is watching.

### The parts · User value has a time dimension
Will this product still be worth something in three years is the question he puts against short-term numbers, and he refuses trades that lift this quarter by taking from the experience that produces every later quarter. e.g. An extra advertising slot lifts revenue this month and is deducted from retention later. Put both curves on one chart before deciding.

### Q: How do I use it today?
At the next team meeting, ban maybe, roughly and I feel from everyone's speech, and require every judgement in the form: I think X, because Y, confidence Z per cent. The point is not precision for its own sake. It is that a claim in that shape can be proved wrong, and the ones that cannot be stated in it were never judgements at all.

### Lines to keep
People at different orders of delayed gratification cannot discuss problems usefully. Delayed gratification is one of the qualities I value most. A startup's biggest advantage is execution, not the idea. Keep an ordinary mind while doing extraordinary things.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Wang Xing — Two philosophies from the same generation: Zhang Yiming runs on algorithms and arithmetic, Wang Xing on intuition and endurance. Kazuo Inamori — Two kinds of extreme seriousness: Inamori is driven by an ethic he treats as almost religious, Zhang Yiming by a refusal to let anything stay vague.

### Further
Duan Yongping Jensen Huang Wang Xing The Innovator's Dilemma Friedrich Hayek

## Zhu Yuanzhang
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/zhu-yuanzhang/
Tags: Power and organisation, Medieval, Nothing to lose

Zhu Yuanzhang (Ming · 1328–1398) — Nothing to lose. The most complete rise from the bottom in Chinese history. Starting point: a sixteen-year-old orphan whose family had died in a famine, begging, then a monk.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The most complete rise from the bottom in Chinese history. Starting point: a sixteen-year-old orphan whose family had died in a famine, begging, then a monk. Finish: founding emperor of the Ming and ruler of a unified empire. His logic has nothing in common with the well-resourced founder — no capital, no network, one objective, which was to stay alive. The dark half is just as large: the men who founded the dynasty with him were killed almost to the last, and the four great cases took more than a hundred thousand lives.

### Q: What actually happened?
At seventeen he lost his father, mother and eldest brother to famine within weeks. He went to the Huangjue monastery to be a monk, and within months the monastery ran out of food too, so he was sent out to beg. For three years he walked the Huai river country. He saw how the poorest people lived and how the Yuan officials treated them, and by the time he joined the Red Turban army at twenty-five he was one of the few men of that generation who genuinely knew what the bottom of society was thinking. That knowledge later became the ability to turn desperate men into soldiers.

### The parts · Having nothing to lose is an advantage
Being able to lose everything is the most underrated competitive position there is. He had no way back, so he could commit fully. Chen Youliang and Zhang Shicheng had holdings to protect, and so they sometimes chose to be careful. e.g. It is why a founder with nothing occasionally beats a well-funded rival. One of them can afford to be wrong about everything except this.

### The parts · The begging years set his mind permanently
Coming from the bottom and having watched the officials at work left him with a permanent distrust of educated elites. That distrust drove the secret police, the extreme control of officials, and the destruction of his own founding generals. e.g. The men who could have been most use to his heirs were the ones he could least bring himself to leave alive.

### The parts · Clearing the ground for the next holder
The purges have a cold logic. He knew his grandson was mild and could not control the founding generals, so he removed them while he was still alive. Short-term infamy exchanged for long-term stability, decided by a founder about his own succession. e.g. It failed on its own terms. When the throne was challenged there was no commander left who could fight, because he had killed them all.

### The parts · Standardisation as a memory
He wrote the most detailed administrative code in Chinese history, specifying what an official must do in each situation and the penalty for not doing it. It came directly from what he had seen as a beggar: without a standard, there is only whatever the man in front of you feels like. e.g. Taking the knowledge out of individuals and putting it into the system is what lets the system run without exceptional people in it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Early on, when resources are thin, no way back can be converted into an asset: say plainly that there is one attempt and no reserve, and the focus that produces is not available to people with a fallback. The warning attached is his own: the mind that gets you through the scarce years is the one that will not let you trust anybody later.

### Lines to keep
I was a commoner of Huaixi. What does the empire add to me? I rose from Chuyang, a commoner with a three-foot sword. Having no way back is a real advantage and a permanent injury.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Liu Bang — Two emperors from the bottom, opposite policies on the men who got them there: Liu Bang scattered wealth to hold them, Zhu Yuanzhang killed them to be safe. Nelson Mandela — Two minds shaped by an extreme start: it left Zhu Yuanzhang unable to trust anyone for the rest of his life, and left Mandela able to put the grievance down. Li Shimin — Two theories of how an emperor handles talent: Li Shimin kept the critics and got a golden age, Zhu Yuanzhang removed the founders and got a secure throne.

### Further
Liu Bang Han Feizi Cao Cao Zhang Juzheng

## Zhuangzi
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/zhuangzi/
Tags: Mind and feeling, Pre-Qin and classical, Free and equal

Zhuangzi (Warring States · c. 369–286 BC) — Free and equal. The second peak of Daoism, and a very different writer from Laozi. Where Laozi addresses the person who has to govern, Zhuangzi addresses the individual who wants out.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The second peak of Daoism, and a very different writer from Laozi. Where Laozi addresses the person who has to govern, Zhuangzi addresses the individual who wants out. He held one minor post and never took another, was poor enough to borrow rice, and turned down the premiership of a large state. His thirty-three chapters use parables to make one point: how to get your interior life back when reputation, argument and gain have tied it up.

### Q: What actually happened?
He was fishing on the Pu river when two officials arrived from the king of Chu to offer him the government of the state. He didn't put the rod down. I hear, he said, that Chu keeps a sacred tortoise, dead three thousand years, wrapped in cloth and housed in the ancestral temple. Would that tortoise rather be dead and venerated, or alive and dragging its tail in the mud? Alive in the mud, they said. Then go away, said Zhuangzi. I intend to drag my tail in the mud. He refused the trade itself, not the job. Most of the strategists competing for those posts died in the resulting purges. He lived past eighty.

### The parts · The use of the useless
The tree too crooked to be timber is the one that reaches a thousand years. Things with no immediate use — a hobby that earns nothing, reading with no purpose, experience that won't fit a CV — are often what still holds when everything scheduled has been spent. e.g. The reading that earned nothing for six years is what made you the only person in the room who saw the second-order effect.

### The parts · Cut along the grain
His cook's blade lasts nineteen years because it never meets bone, only the gaps between joints. Effort that meets resistance everywhere is usually not short of force. It is in the wrong place. e.g. The rewrite that ate three weekends went in on a Tuesday evening, once he stopped fighting the framework and used the hook it already had.

### The parts · Whose standard is this
There is a right and wrong on that side and one on this side. What looks like stupidity from where you stand is generally coherent from where they stand. Holding several positions at once isn't fence-sitting; it's the thing that shrinks your blind spot. e.g. The team that moves too slowly is optimising for the outage you have never had. From where they sit, your speed is the reckless part.

### Q: How do I use it today?
In an environment where everyone is competing, the scarcest capacity is the ability not to enter. Before joining the race everyone else is running, ask whose right and wrong you are using. Keep a third of your time for things with no use — over a long enough horizon that is usually the best-performing position you hold.

### Lines to keep
Everyone knows the use of the useful. Nobody knows the use of the useless. A frog in a well can't discuss the sea. It is bound by its hole. The friendship of the wise is bland as water.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Han Feizi — The same century, opposite conclusions: Han Feizi builds the machine of state, Zhuangzi declines to be a part in it. Tao Te Ching — Same tradition, different address: Laozi writes for whoever has to govern, Zhuangzi for whoever wants out. Su Shi — Two ways of not being owned: Zhuangzi refuses the post, Su Shi takes it and refuses to be defined by losing it. Finite and Infinite Games — The use of the useless runs the same way as the infinite game: not winning inside the given rules, but keeping room to change them.

### Further
Su Shi Huineng Wang Yangming Tao Te Ching Carl Jung The I Ching The Bhagavad Gita Epictetus Finite and Infinite Games Ivan Illich

## Zhuge Liang
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/zhuge-liang/
Tags: Power and organisation, Qin, Han and the Six Dynasties, The Longzhong plan

Zhuge Liang (Three Kingdoms · 181–234) — The Longzhong plan. The most admired administrator in Chinese history, and the standard image of both strategic foresight and working yourself to death.

### Q: What did this one leave behind?
The most admired administrator in Chinese history, and the standard image of both strategic foresight and working yourself to death. He described the three-way division of the empire before he had left his farm, built the state of Shu with Liu Bei, governed it for twenty years with a legal system nobody accused of favouritism, and went north six times against a much larger enemy because waiting was the worse option.

### Q: What actually happened?
On the last campaign, held on the Wuzhang Plains, Sima Yi refused battle and questioned the Shu envoy about his opposite number's daily habits instead. The envoy said the chancellor rose early and went to bed late, personally reviewed every punishment above twenty strokes, and ate very little. Sima Yi turned to his staff: eating little and handling much, how can he last? He was right, and within months he was proved right. The campaign was settled by which man would live longer, not by which had more ability.

### The parts · A framework before there was anything to frame
Still on the farm, he sorted the board: Cao Cao not to be contended with, Sun Quan to be allied and not attacked, Jing province to be taken, Yi province to be the base. Then three moves in order, and a condition that had to appear before the last one. e.g. A plan that names what it will not touch, and what has to become true before the big move, survives contact. A list of ambitions does not.

### The parts · Attack because waiting is worse
If we do not attack, the royal cause dies anyway; better than sitting and waiting to die. Shu was the weaker state and time was working for Wei, so passivity was not the safe option, it was the slow version of the same defeat. e.g. When the gap with a larger competitor widens every quarter you do nothing, holding position is a decision with a cost, not the absence of one.

### The parts · The law that reached his favourite
Ma Su lost Jieting and was executed, though he was the man Zhuge Liang had promoted over everyone's advice and was personally close to. Then the second half: a memorial asking for his own demotion by three ranks. A system is credible at the point where it touches the favourite. e.g. Everyone learns what the rules are from the first case involving someone the boss likes. Nothing written down changes that lesson.

### The parts · The cost of doing all of it yourself
Every punishment above twenty strokes reviewed personally. He set a standard nobody else met, so he could not delegate, so nothing survived him. Being irreplaceable is a personal distinction and an organisational disaster. e.g. If you cannot name the person who could run this without you, the thing you have built has an expiry date and it is your own.

### Q: How do I use it today?
If you find that everything is passing through you, ask which of the two it is: nobody has reached the standard, or nobody was ever actually taught it. Then take one thing this week and teach the standard instead of applying it. Producing your own replacement is the job.

### Lines to keep
I shall bend to the task until my strength is spent, and only then stop. Without detachment no clarity of purpose; without stillness no reaching far. If we do not attack, the cause dies anyway. Better than sitting and waiting.

### Q: What should I read alongside?
Sima Yi — Talent against longevity: Zhuge Liang burned out at fifty-four, Sima Yi waited until seventy-three and collected everything. Fan Li — Two answers to having succeeded: Fan Li walked away at the summit, Zhuge Liang never put it down at all. Guan Zhong — Two first ministers serving an ambitious lord. Guan Zhong's man became hegemon; Zhuge Liang's cause never arrived. Zhang Juzheng — Two tragedies of being irreplaceable: after Zhuge Liang there was nobody to take over, after Zhang Juzheng the whole programme collapsed at once. Guo Jia — The two great advisers of the age divide on risk: Guo Jia looks for the move nobody expects and takes the narrow window, Zhuge Liang builds the position that cannot be knocked over.

### Further
Cao Cao Sun Tzu Zeng Guofan Fan Li Sima Yi Li Shimin The Comprehensive Mirror

## Alfred Adler · Whose task is this
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/adler/separation-of-tasks/
Source: Adler's individual psychology; the phrase separation of tasks comes from Kishimi and Koga, The Courage to Be Disliked (2013)
Tags: Deep read, Alfred Adler, Draw the line where the bill lands

Most of the pain in a relationship comes from crossing a line nobody drew. This is where the line actually runs.

### Q: What actually happened?
Adler's test for whose business something is has one item: follow the consequence and see who finally pays it. The child who does not study carries the grade; the parent who lies awake carries the insomnia. He pushes it further — what other people think of you is their task, and you cannot reach it. The line everybody quotes, that all problems are interpersonal relationship problems, is not his sentence but Kishimi and Koga's summary of him in 2013. The concept is Adler's. The slogan was written for him seventy-six years after he died.

### The parts · The test is who pays, not who cares
How much you love someone does not move the line. Only one question does: when this goes wrong, who lives with it? Writing the essay for him, redoing the deck for her — both settle your own anxiety tonight and take away the capacity the other person was about to build.
e.g. Chasing homework until the house is at war means you have taken on his task. What is left to you is making the consequence clear and being available when he asks.

### The parts · Separating is not going cold; it makes help invited
What Adler objects to is intervention nobody asked for, not care. The difference is who starts it. Support given when someone asks is collaboration; a decision taken on their behalf is a crossing. So the posture is I am here, say the word — not let me handle it.
e.g. A friend keeps choosing the same kind of partner. You can say what you see, once, and then stop, unless he asks you what to do.

### The parts · Their opinion of you is their task
This is the hardest one to run, because minding what people think is instinct. But the verdict forms inside somebody else's head, where you cannot go and have no vote. Once that lands, afraid of what they will say drops from a veto on action to noise you can walk past.
e.g. Going to every dinner in case a colleague decides you are unfriendly: the judgement lives in his head and the whole cost lives in your week.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a relationship keeps hurting and you keep trying to change the other person.
Ask first: who finally pays for this? If it is not me, why can I not put it down — whose unease am I really trying to settle?
Where it goes wrong: using it as a phrase for dodging responsibility, so your own share gets drawn on the far side of the line too; or running it on the people closest to you until it becomes indifference.

### Lines to keep
Whoever finally pays for the outcome owns the task.
What other people think of you happens where you cannot go.
Separating is not coldness. The difference is who spoke first.

## Alfred Adler · Not because — in order to
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/adler/teleology/
Source: Adler's individual psychology; the core of the break with Freud
Tags: Deep read, Alfred Adler, Swap the cause for the purpose

Freud asks what happened to you. Adler asks what you are using it for. Why changing the question unfreezes things.

### Q: What actually happened?
The two men split in 1911, and the split was about direction. Freud looked backward for a cause; Adler looked forward for a purpose. Somebody says he cannot speak up because he was put down as a child, and Adler changes the question: what does not speaking up spare you? The answer is almost always being put down again. On this reading the past is not a cage, it is a reason that got hired. We are not determined by our experiences, but by the meanings we give them.

### The parts · A cause cannot be edited; a purpose can be swapped
Because A, I cannot do B is a closed sentence, since A has already happened. Rewrite it as I avoid B in order to dodge C and C comes into view — fear of failing, of looking foolish, of being turned down. The problem moves from unchangeable to workable.
e.g. I never trained for this, so I do not apply. Ask what not applying spares you. Rejection, which you can survive; your background, which you cannot edit.

### The parts · A symptom is often doing a job
Adler kept noticing that trouble quietly works for people. Putting things off protects the line I never really tried; anger buys the floor; being ill buys attention. Nobody wants to suffer, but the suffering is paying something out. See the payment and you can go and collect it another way.
e.g. The headache that arrives on presentation day may be buying an hour off being judged. Name the job and you can look for a way to do it without the headache.

### The parts · Turned on other people it goes cruel
Asked of yourself this is liberating; aimed at someone else it becomes an accusation. You are depressed to get attention is both vicious and usually wrong. Adler's listener was the person who had come for help, and the question rested on real fellow feeling. Check your standing before you use it.
e.g. Telling somebody in real trouble that they chose this is not teleology, it is damage. It is a question to ask yourself, not a verdict to hand down.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you keep explaining what you cannot do now with something that happened then.
Ask first: what does staying the same spare me? If I walked into that thing, what is the worst that actually happens?
Where it goes wrong: using it to sit in judgement on somebody else's pain; or ignoring real constraints and turning every limit into you did not want it enough.

### Lines to keep
We are not determined by our experiences, but by the meanings we give them.
What matters is not what happened but what you make it mean.
Ask what staying exactly as you are is sparing you.

## The Analects · Knowing what you know
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/analects/know-what-you-know/
Source: Analects 2.17 and 9.8
Tags: Deep read, The Analects, The half that has to be said out loud

Read as modesty it is a platitude. Read as an instruction it is an operation that very few people can actually perform.

### Q: What actually happened?
He said it to Zilu, the hot-headed student who liked to look capable, and it is built as a pair: when you know a thing, hold that you know it; when you do not know a thing, allow that you do not know it. He held himself to the same rule. Asked something by a countryman, he said his own mind went perfectly blank, and that all he could do was take the question by its two extremes and knock them together until it was used up. He never supplied an answer he did not have.

### The parts · Draw the line before you use the judgement
Bad calls rarely come from missing knowledge. They come from using an uncertain thing as if it were settled. Marking the line tells you which items can carry weight and which are guesses wearing the same clothes.
e.g. Users will probably like this, and we asked thirty people and twenty said they would use it, are not the same sentence.

### The parts · Saying you don't know is the cheap option
The bill for bluffing arrives later, once other people have acted on it, and by then it has multiplied. The bill for saying you don't know is one moment of looking less impressive. The arithmetic runs the same direction every time.
e.g. He guessed at a number in a meeting. Three teams built schedules on it. Two weeks later the real figure arrived and all three rebuilt.

### The parts · Empty, then knock the two ends together
Admitting ignorance has to be followed by something, or it is only a way of handing the problem back. His method was to squeeze in from both extremes, worst case and best case, and let the truth sit in the gap. You can start without an answer.
e.g. You don't know the size of this market. Work out the ceiling and the floor and operate in between. It beats picking a number.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: someone has asked you, to your face, about something you have no real footing on.
Ask first: is there one thing that actually happened standing behind the answer I am about to give?
Where it goes wrong: producing a confident judgement in order to look professional; or stopping at I don't know and offering no next step, which is not honesty, only a handoff.

### Lines to keep
Knowing what you know and what you do not: that is knowledge.
I take hold of its two extremes and knock them together.
To have a fault and not mend it is the fault.
