## The Analects · Three layers of looking at a person
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/analects/see-how/
Source: Analects 2.10
Tags: Deep read, The Analects, Each layer is harder to fake than the last

Everyone misreads people. The useful part of his method is the order: the three layers get progressively harder to perform.

### Q: What actually happened?
See what he does. Mark his motives. Examine where he rests. The three clauses climb. The first is behaviour, which anyone can stage. The second is the road he took to arrive — what he spent, what he went around, who paid — and staging a road costs real effort. The third is what he is comfortable with when nothing is at stake, and almost nobody can hold a pose down there. Then the line that closes it, said twice over: how can a man conceal himself, how can he conceal himself?

### The parts · The first layer: what he did
Behaviour is the easiest thing to observe and the easiest thing to perform. A person can produce any behaviour you like for the three months somebody is watching. Read only this layer and what you are grading is the performance.
e.g. Excellent through probation, unrecognisable after. He did not change. The observation ended.

### The parts · The second layer: how he got here
The road shows what he was willing to spend, what he went around, and who carried the cost. Two people reach the same number by completely different routes, and the route is the stable part. People repeat their routes.
e.g. Both hit the quarter. One pulled next year's budget forward out of existing accounts; one opened three channels. The next quarter separates them without help.

### The parts · The third layer: where he rests
This asks what he can be at ease with. Some people cannot settle after shipping something they know is bent, and some can. It runs with nobody supervising, which is why it is almost impossible to fake and why it predicts what he does unwatched.
e.g. Handed in with a flaw he knows about, one person goes back to fix it and the other waits to see whether anybody notices.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: deciding whether someone can be handed something heavier than he has carried.
Ask first: how did his last real piece of work actually get done, and was he easy with himself afterwards?
Where it goes wrong: grading results and manner and calling it judgement; or substituting a longer watching period for a real question about the road, when time surfaces neither of the deeper layers on its own.

### Lines to keep
See what he does. Mark his motives. Examine where he rests.
How can a man conceal himself? How can he conceal himself?
The worry is not being unknown. It is not knowing others.

## The Analects · Do not do it to them
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/analects/reciprocity/
Source: Analects 15.24 and 12.2
Tags: Deep read, The Analects, The one word he said would last a lifetime

Zigong asked for a single word to live by. The part worth noticing is that what came back was a prohibition.

### Q: What actually happened?
Zigong asked whether there was one word a person could act on all his life. The answer was shu, reciprocity: what you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others. The shape of it matters. A positive rule makes you guess what the other person wants, and the guess is usually your own preference in a costume. A prohibition asks only whether you would accept being on the receiving end. That question costs nothing to run, needs no information, and is very hard to get wrong.

### The parts · A prohibition is cheaper to run
Do unto others as you would have them do unto you sounds warmer, but it assumes your taste is also theirs, and a great deal of damage is done inside that assumption. The negative form needs no knowledge of the other person, only honesty about yourself.
e.g. Pushing your own hours, your own way of talking and your own idea of a career onto the people below you is the positive rule at work.

### The parts · It checks you, not them
The rule runs entirely on your side, so it survives every information gap. You may know nothing about the person in front of you. You always know what you would refuse. That is why it holds in any relationship at all.
e.g. Before sending the hard email, read it once as though it had landed in your own inbox. The step takes thirty seconds.

### The parts · Reciprocity is a floor, not kindness
Shu is not forgiveness. It binds what you may do and asks nothing about how good you are. Treat it as a hard lower limit: you are allowed to fall short of generous, and you are not allowed to cross this.
e.g. Redundancies are never pleasant. How much notice, how it is said, whether you will vouch for them afterwards — calibrate each on whether you would accept it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: about to make a decision about someone who does not get a vote in it.
Ask first: if I were the one it was being done to, could I accept it?
Where it goes wrong: deciding for someone else what is good for them out of your own preferences; or treating for your own good as a licence to cross the line.

### Lines to keep
What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.
Is there one word to act on all your life?
Require much of yourself and little of others; resentment stays away.

========================================================================
## The Analects · Harmony is not sameness
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/analects/harmony-not-sameness/
Source: Analects 13.23
Tags: Deep read, The Analects, Agreement and consent are different things

Nobody objected in the meeting. That is usually not agreement, and the distinction he draws says what it is instead.

### Q: What actually happened?
The gentleman harmonises without conforming; the small man conforms without harmony. Harmony is different things holding together; conformity is flattening the difference until only one thing is left. He offers this as a way of telling two kinds of person apart rather than two kinds of atmosphere, and the reason is practical: whether difference survives in a room depends on whether people feel safe producing it, and that is settled by whoever holds the power in the room.

### The parts · A unanimous room is a bad signal
When a group agrees completely about something complicated, there are two possibilities. Either it does not matter, or somebody is not talking. It is usually the second. The disagreement has not gone anywhere; it has moved outside the meeting.
e.g. No questions at the review. After launch the problems arrive one by one, and every one of them had been seen by somebody beforehand.

### The parts · Someone has to pay for the first no
The first person to object carries the whole risk, and everyone who agrees afterwards carries none. So silence is not the absence of views, it is the price of going first. For harmony to happen, whoever holds the power has to buy that first no themselves.
e.g. Name the worst weakness in your own proposal, or ask the most senior person in the room to argue against it. Both beat telling people to speak freely.

### The parts · Difference does not have to be resolved
Harmony means the disagreement can stay where it is while the work goes forward. Plenty of arguments cannot be settled until something has been built and looked at. Forcing agreement before anyone moves pushes the disagreement underground.
e.g. Two camps, two directions. Rather than argue until one surrenders, agree on a number and a date that would settle it. The data answers faster than the room.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: an important decision, and not one person in the room raised an objection.
Ask first: if someone did disagree, what would it cost him to say so here?
Where it goes wrong: reading no objection as consent; or demanding that everyone be convinced before anything moves, which buries the disagreement rather than settling it.

### Lines to keep
The gentleman harmonises without conforming; the small man conforms without harmony.
The gentleman is inclusive and not partisan; the small man the reverse.
When three walk together, one of them is my teacher.

========================================================================
## Hannah Arendt · The banality of evil
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/arendt/banality-of-evil/
Source: Hannah Arendt, Eichmann in Jerusalem, 1963
Tags: Deep read, Hannah Arendt, Not wicked, just not thinking

What kind of state is I only follow the list and never ask why. What she saw in the courtroom changed her mind.

### Q: What actually happened?
She went to Jerusalem in 1961 expecting a monster and found a mediocre man. He spoke almost entirely in officialese and stock phrases, could not produce a sentence of his own, and returned again and again to duty, orders, and the promotions he had missed. She gave the thing a name: the banality of evil — done not out of wickedness but because he had never thought about it. His most striking feature, she wrote, was not stupidity. It was thoughtlessness: the whole faculty of judgement handed over, with only execution kept back.

### The parts · Doing what the list says is a choice, and the cheapest one
Not asking why is not neutral; it hands judgement to whoever wrote the list. It is cheap because you owe nothing to the outcome. It is dangerous because you become the executing mechanism for any list at all.
e.g. The more times you say I was told to do it this way, the faster your own judgement shrinks.

### The parts · Stock phrases are the symptom
She noticed the man had no language of his own, only ready-made formulas. That is what a formula is for: when there is a sentence available to say, nothing has to be thought. Someone who speaks only in stock phrases has mostly stopped thinking.
e.g. Listen to the words you use when explaining your own job. If every one of them is off the shelf, that part has been asleep a while.

### The parts · Not thinking is a trained habit
She insists the man was not born that way; he arrived there one step at a time. Every unasked question, every order simply carried out, reinforced it. The reverse is equally a habit: stopping once to ask why this is set this way builds the other one.
e.g. Once a day, take one thing you do by the list and ask why it is set that way. Not to change it — to keep that part awake.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: your work is mostly done by the list, and you can say less and less about why any of it is set that way.
Ask first: which steps here can I actually explain? When I describe my job, am I using my own words or off-the-shelf ones?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as everyone who carries out orders is guilty, or using it to judge the colleague who follows procedure — she is describing a state, not assigning blame; and it is not a call to question everything, only to keep the ability to stop and think.

### Lines to keep
Not done out of wickedness. Done without ever having thought.
The more you say I was told to, the less judgement remains.
A stock phrase saves you the trouble of thinking one up.

========================================================================
## Hannah Arendt · Stopping to think is your own job
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/arendt/thinking-as-a-duty/
Source: Hannah Arendt, Thinking and Moral Considerations, 1971
Tags: Deep read, Hannah Arendt, It cannot be outsourced

When the rules are someone else's and everyone around you complies, what is left. Why she calls thinking a duty rather than a talent.

### Q: What actually happened?
After the trial she kept chasing one question: what actually stops a person from doing wrong? Not good rules, and not a good education — both can be replaced overnight. Her answer is the act of stopping to think: going over it with yourself before you act. That kind of thinking produces no knowledge. What it produces is the line that says I could not do that. Rules can change and everyone around you can change; that line is one a person generates alone, and it cannot be outsourced.

### The parts · Everyone does it is not a reason
Almost every justification she heard came down to other people were doing the same. What makes it dangerous is that it spreads responsibility across everybody, leaving each person holding a small share. But you did the thing, and your share does not shrink because the crowd is large.
e.g. Everyone in the industry does it explains the market. It cannot decide for you whether you are going to do it.

### The parts · Thinking is not for reaching a conclusion
What she means by thinking is not research; it is a person in conversation with himself before he acts — what am I doing, and can I live alongside the man who does it. The dialogue needs no answer. It needs to occur. Once it occurs you stop sliding past.
e.g. Before you start, spend a minute on this: when this is done, am I willing to be around the person who did it?

### The parts · Someone with no say still owns one thing
She is addressing people without power: the rules are not yours to set and the orders are not yours to give, but whether you stop and think is yours alone. It is the last part of the situation nobody has taken from you, and the only one.
e.g. You genuinely have no say in this one. Whether you think it through has never once stopped being yours.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: someone else wrote the rules, you work inside them, and it feels like nothing here is yours.
Ask first: is there one rule here I would know I could not carry out, if I stopped and thought? When did I last go over something with myself before starting?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as refuse every rule — she is protecting the capacity to think, not calling for disobedience; and having thought about it does not discharge the responsibility, it only stops you sliding past.

### Lines to keep
Rules change, people change; that line you generate alone.
The crowd is large. Your share of it is not smaller.
No say in this one. Still your call whether you think.

## Hannah Arendt · New York at thirty-five
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/arendt/new-york-at-35/
Source: Arendt's life: arrested in Berlin 1933, the Gurs camp 1940, New York 1941; The Origins of Totalitarianism, 1951
Tags: Deep read, Hannah Arendt, No English, no papers, start again

New country, new language, no standing. What she had with her when she landed, what she did not, and what she did first.

### Q: What actually happened?
Arrested in Berlin in 1933, released, exile in Paris. When France fell she was interned at Gurs in the south and got out in the confusion. She reached New York in 1941: thirty-five years old, almost no English, no papers, no job. Her first move was two months living with an American family to learn the language — not job hunting. Then a column for a German-language paper for refugees, living off the fees. Ten years later The Origins of Totalitarianism appeared. The one thing she carried through that decade was a way of thinking, which requires no papers.

### The parts · Language first, everything else after
Her first act in New York was two months in a household to learn English, not a job search. In a new country language is the precondition for all the rest — unable to speak, you cannot deploy any skill you have. Fix the precondition before proving yourself.
e.g. Somewhere new, make being able to communicate solid first. Everything else queues behind it.

### The parts · What travels is method, not position
Her German degrees, her circle and her standing were all gone; what came with her was how she thought. That takes no luggage, needs no papers, and works on arrival anywhere. Before starting again it is worth sorting: which of my assets are position and which are method.
e.g. List them before you move: what disappears the moment you leave the seat, and what comes with you. Only the second kind is capital.

### The parts · Ten years is the normal length
From landing in New York to the first major book: ten years, filled with columns, editing and scattered teaching. She did not decide in year three that she had failed. Starting from zero is a ten-year account, and people who book it as three quit in year three.
e.g. Starting over somewhere else, give yourself ten years and treat the first three as not counting.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you moved city or country, you know nobody, and none of your old standing or accumulation transfers.
Ask first: which of my assets came from the position and which from the method? Have I actually cleared the language? Is my timetable three years or ten?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as a good way of thinking is enough to start again — she still did ten years of small, hard work; and ten years is not permission to go slowly, she wrote through every one of them.

### Lines to keep
The one thing she carried needed no papers: how she thought.
What disappears when you leave the seat was never yours.
Start from zero on a ten-year account, not a three-year one.

## The Art of Worldly Wisdom · Leave while you are winning
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/art-of-worldly-wisdom/quit-while-winning/
Source: The Art of Worldly Wisdom, maxim 38
Tags: Deep read, The Art of Worldly Wisdom, A long run of luck is the warning

Everyone reads it as timidity. Read as written it is a gambler's arithmetic: a long winning run is the thing to distrust.

### Q: What actually happened?
Gracián was a Jesuit in seventeenth-century Spain who spent his life watching men manoeuvre at court and inside his own order, and compressed what he saw into three hundred maxims. Number thirty-eight is about the card table. The reasoning is a gambler's: a run of luck that goes on too long is itself the warning, a long-continued spell of good luck is always suspicious, and the best players rise while they are still ahead. Fortune, he adds, soon tires of carrying anyone long on her back.

### The parts · A winning run raises your exposure, not your odds
Each success quietly adds to two piles: the stake on the table and your confidence in your own reading. The longer the run, the higher both stand, and the more a single reversal takes away. A streak is not evidence of a pattern. It is a measure of what is now at risk.
e.g. After four quarters of beating the forecast, the useful move is to cut a position or lower a target, precisely because nothing has gone wrong yet.

### The parts · Retreat well while retreating is still your choice
He rates a fine retreat as highly as a gallant attack, and the rating is entirely about timing. Leaving while the table is hot is orderly and your chips come with you. Leaving after the mood turns is not a retreat, it is being cleared out.
e.g. A business sold at its peak has buyers queueing and sets its own terms. The same business sold after the turn goes at a third of the price.

### The parts · You are cashing in this hand, not quitting the game
Stopping while ahead is not caution. It closes the hand, banks the winnings, and opens the next one on a fresh judgement. What it cuts is the automatic renewal that lets the last hand's luck stake the next one.
e.g. A hit product whose team and budget roll straight into the sequel is letting the previous round's luck pick the next round's bet.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: everything is going your way and you are thinking about adding to it.
Ask first: how large is the exposure now, and how much of it would a reversal tomorrow take back?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as never bet at all, or holding out for the exact top and therefore never leaving.

### Lines to keep
Leave your luck while winning. All the best players do so.
A long-continued spell of good luck is always suspicious.
A fine retreat is as good as a gallant attack.

========================================================================
## The Art of Worldly Wisdom · Do, and be seen doing
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/art-of-worldly-wisdom/do-and-be-seen/
Source: The Art of Worldly Wisdom, maxim 130
Tags: Deep read, The Art of Worldly Wisdom, Half the work is being known to have done it

The maxim is uncomfortable coming from a priest. What it argues is not vanity but arithmetic about whose ledger your work sits on.

### Q: What actually happened?
Maxim one hundred and thirty is its own title: do, and be seen doing. Gracián is blunt about the reason. Things do not pass for what they are but for what they seem; to be of use and to know how to show it is to be twice as useful; what is not seen is as if it did not exist. From a Jesuit this grates, but he had watched able men outranked by visible ones. Elsewhere he is just as firm that reputation without substance does not survive. He is describing a ratio, not a substitute.

### The parts · On someone else's ledger, unseen work was never done
Your own ledger records what happened. Everyone else's records only what they saw. Promotions, partnerships and trust are drawn against those other ledgers. Quiet work is not unrewarded through unfairness. It is held in an account nobody else can query.
e.g. The engineer who took uptime from ninety per cent to four nines lost the review to the one who handled a single visible outage.

### The parts · Showing is a craft, and it is not shouting
Being seen is not self-praise. The craft is in the carrier: a write-up colleagues pass on, a tool whose users say your name, an accurate crediting of your team when you report upward. The strongest version has somebody else doing the saying.
e.g. A note on what went wrong that circulates all year beats a line in a status report claiming a hard problem was solved.

### The parts · Two ways the ratio kills you
All substance and no visibility buries the work and eventually sours the person doing it. All visibility and no substance clears to zero the first time anyone checks, and someone always checks. The healthy ratio keeps the claim half a step behind the fact.
e.g. A firm that describes itself as slightly less capable than it is beats expectations on every delivery. The reverse pays down debt on every one.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have done real work and find promoting it distasteful.
Ask first: whose ledger does this exist on right now? Apart from you, who could look it up?
Where it goes wrong: letting showing become boasting, which spends credit you have not earned; or building the reputation first and waiting to be checked.

### Lines to keep
Do, and be seen doing.
Things do not pass for what they are but for what they seem.
What is not seen is as if it did not exist.

========================================================================
## Atomic Habits · Fall to the Level of Your Systems
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/atomic-habits/systems-over-goals/
Source: Atomic Habits, chapter one
Tags: Deep read, Atomic Habits, Goals do not separate winners from losers

Every team in the race wants to win it. What Clear says the difference actually is.

### Q: What actually happened?
British cycling had not won the Tour de France in a hundred years. Dave Brailsford took the parts apart and improved each by one percent: seat adjustments, riders bringing their own pillows, surgeon-standard hand-washing to cut colds. Individually trivial. Within five years the team had the Tour and a pile of Olympic gold. Clear uses it to show that compounding applies to behaviour too, and delivers the sharpest line in the book: you do not rise to the level of your goals, you fall to the level of your systems. Winners and losers have the same goals. The difference is in how the days run.

### The parts · Goals are shared; systems are not
The marginal return on setting a goal is low, since every competitor has roughly the same one. The marginal return on rebuilding the system is high, because that is where results are actually produced. It also explains why this year I really will so rarely works: it changes the intention, not the process.
e.g. Read twelve books this year, against move the charger to the living room and leave a book on the pillow. Only one changed the outcome.

### The parts · One percent compounds, but not visibly at first
One percent a day is thirty-seven times over a year, and for the first three months you can barely see a difference. This is where most changes die, in the stretch before the return shows. Understanding the shape of the curve is itself a reason to keep going.
e.g. Quitting the gym after two flat months means quitting just before the bend. Knowing the front is flat stops you reading flat as useless.

### The parts · Never miss twice
His practical rule: missing once is fine, never miss twice in a row. Once is an accident; twice starts becoming the new normal. It plugs the most common collapse point, which is the moment you decide that since the streak is broken you may as well stop.
e.g. No run today, so tomorrow is compulsory, even ten minutes. What you protect is not the mileage, it is that this is still live.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you set the goal and you keep not doing it.
Ask first: am I changing the goal or the system? What is the actual sequence of steps that makes this happen?
Where it goes wrong: using systems matter more as a reason to have no goal at all. A system still needs a direction to point in.

### Lines to keep
You do not rise to the level of your goals.
You fall to the level of your systems.
Winners and losers have the same goals.
Never miss twice.

## Atomic Habits · Start from Identity
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/atomic-habits/identity-first/
Source: Atomic Habits, chapter two
Tags: Deep read, Atomic Habits, Do not wrestle the craving

Anything given up by willpower usually comes back. Whether there is a route that does not need the fight.

### Q: What actually happened?
Clear's central swap is from I am trying to quit smoking to I am not a smoker. The first is a head-on fight with a craving that costs something every time. The second lets behaviour follow self-description and needs no fight at all. His formulation: every action is a vote for the type of person you wish to become. Collect enough votes and the behaviour no longer needs willpower to hold it up. The other half is environment design: drop the starting cost of what you want, raise it for what you do not. Both point the same way. Use as little willpower as possible, because it runs out.

### The parts · Identity leads, behaviour follows
An outcome goal, lose ten pounds, loses its engine the moment it is met. An identity goal, I am someone who moves every day, has no finish line. And the identity can start very small: five minutes is still a vote. What matters is who the vote went to.
e.g. To start writing, do not set a hundred thousand words a year. Set I am someone who writes a few lines daily. The count grows itself.

### The parts · Make the good thing cheap and the bad thing expensive
Of the four stages, environment is the most workable. Kit by the bed the night before, phone in another room: changes that cost no willpower and directly alter the price of starting. Far more reliable than cultivating grit.
e.g. To use the phone less, delete the app rather than control yourself. Reinstalling takes two minutes, and two minutes stops the impulse.

### The parts · Two minutes to start
Shrink the new habit to a version that finishes in two minutes: read becomes read one page. The point is not the yield of those two minutes, it is clearing the doorway. Once started, most people carry on. The doorway is where the resistance sits.
e.g. Change go to the gym into put on trainers and step outside. Very few people put the trainers on and then stay home.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a habit you hold up with willpower, failing again and again.
Ask first: can I turn this into an identity instead of a number? Where in my surroundings could it be made cheaper?
Where it goes wrong: talking about identity and changing nothing around you. I am a disciplined person alters no starting cost by itself.

### Lines to keep
Every action is a vote for the type of person you become.
True behavior change is identity change.
Make it obvious, make it attractive, make it easy, make it satisfying.

## Attachment Theory · The information is in the reunion
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/attachment-theory/strange-situation/
Source: Ainsworth's Strange Situation, Baltimore, 1970s
Tags: Deep read, Attachment Theory, Not crying is not the same as not frightened

The baby who screams when the mother leaves may not be the most frightened one in the room. Which moment to watch.

### Q: What actually happened?
Ainsworth's procedure separates a one-year-old from the caregiver for a few minutes and then brings them back together, and the information is not in the parting. Secure infants cry, are settled quickly on the return, and go back to playing. Avoidant infants look supremely unbothered and do not go to meet her — but heart-rate monitoring put their arousal as high as the criers'; they had only learned not to show it. Ambivalent infants demand to be held and push away at once, and stay unsettled a long time. The patterns are not temperament. They are what repetition taught.

### The parts · Not asking is not the same as not needing
The avoidant pattern is built in a specific order: asked, was not met, closed the channel. So he never says he is struggling is itself a reading, not a reassurance. What you want to know is not how calm he looks now but how his last request was answered.
e.g. The person on the team who never raises a problem is often the one who raised one and watched it die. Go back to that time; it tells you more than asking how he is.

### The parts · The pattern follows how predictable the answer was
What sorts the types is not how much the caregiver loved the child but whether the response could be predicted. Warm one day and absent the next produces more ambivalence than steady coolness does, because uncertainty forces the child to keep watching the relationship instead of the world.
e.g. A manager whose mood swings gets a team that spends its best hours working out whether today is a day you can raise something.

### The parts · A template, not a sentence
Attachment patterns are stable and they are not fixed. A later steady relationship, therapy, one long friendship can all rewrite them. Used as explanation the idea is worth a great deal; used as an excuse it does harm. It tells you the starting position, not the finish.
e.g. Noticing that you go silent in a conflict is progress. Saying I am just avoidant, nothing to be done, turns a tool into a shield.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you cannot tell whether somebody is genuinely fine or simply not saying.
Ask first: how did their last request for help end? Is my own response to them predictable from one week to the next?
Where it goes wrong: handing out the four types as labels, or using one of them to explain everything that has ever gone wrong in a relationship.

### Lines to keep
The quiet child is not calm. He has learned not to show it.
The reunion tells you more than the separation does.
What shapes the pattern is predictability, not how much love there was.

## Attachment Theory · A secure base
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/attachment-theory/secure-base/
Source: Bowlby, Attachment and Loss; A Secure Base
Tags: Deep read, Attachment Theory, You go far only if you can come back

Why some people will take a risk and others will not. The condition that has to be in place before nerve is available.

### Q: What actually happened?
Bowlby worked with children who had lost their families in the war, and argued that the pull towards closeness is an instinct rather than a dependency to be outgrown. His most productive idea is the secure base: a child explores only while sure the mother is still where she was, and the moment that is in doubt exploration stops and all attention comes back to the relationship. He insisted this is not a nursery phenomenon. Adults run the same circuit, with a partner, a friend or a steady institution standing in the base's place.

### The parts · Support is not doing it for them; it is that the base is still there
A secure base does not supply help, it supplies certainty. Which is why the sentence that works is not I will do it for you but if this goes wrong we clear it up together. It removes the surcharge on failure, and the surcharge is usually what people are actually afraid of.
e.g. If you want somebody to decide, say plainly that a wrong call will not land on them personally. It moves more than any incentive does.

### The parts · Uncertainty costs more than bad news
In Bowlby's observations the children in unstable relationships explored least — not because they had been hurt but because they had to keep monitoring. A clear bad outcome can at least be adapted to. An unresolved one keeps taking bandwidth for as long as it hangs there.
e.g. Announcing a reorganisation late usually costs more output than the reorganisation itself does.

### The parts · The base has to be reliable, not perfect
Caregivers of secure children get it wrong, lose patience, misread things. What separates them is that they are predictable overall and they repair afterwards. For anyone raising a child or running a team that is the load off: not right every time, but steady, and mended when it breaks.
e.g. You shouted, and afterwards said plainly that you should not have. The repair is worth more than the loss of temper cost.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you want somebody to carry more than they currently will.
Ask first: what does failure cost them here, and am I supplying help or supplying certainty?
Where it goes wrong: turning the base into cover for everything, so that nobody ever meets a consequence — that is not a base, it is a subsidy.

### Lines to keep
We are happiest when life is a series of excursions from a secure base.
The need for closeness is instinct, not a dependency to be outgrown.
An uncertain relationship costs more than a clearly distant one.

## Augustine · Grant me chastity, but not yet
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/augustine/not-yet/
Source: Confessions, Book VIII
Tags: Deep read, Augustine, The oldest sentence about putting it off

Everyone quotes the prayer as a joke. Read it in place and it is an exact account of how postponement works.

### Q: What actually happened?
Writing in his forties, he remembers the prayer he made as a young man: Grant me chastity and continence, but not yet. He is precise about why he added the last two words. He wanted the life he was asking for, and he was afraid of being answered too soon, because he preferred the appetite satisfied rather than extinguished. Both halves of the sentence were sincere: he wanted the outcome, and he did not want today. Postponement is not a weak want. It is a want with the date left blank.

### The parts · The wanting is real. So is the not yet
People who put things off get told they do not want it enough. He says the opposite: the wanting was never the weak part. Reinforcing it adds weight to the side that was already heavy, and the sentence still holds.
e.g. Stop asking whether you want it enough. Ask whether you said not yet again this week.

### The parts · Not yet never expires on its own
The clause works every single day, because tomorrow is also today when it arrives. It is not one decision, it is a permit that renews itself indefinitely. Seeing that is the difference between waiting for it to lapse and tearing it up.
e.g. How many times have you said after this busy stretch? It will not run out by itself.

### The parts · He feared being answered, not failing
He admits he was afraid the prayer would be granted quickly. What stalls most people is rarely the fear of not managing it. It is the loss that success would cost them today, and that loss is usually something they are quietly protecting.
e.g. Before you push yourself to start, name the one comfort that starting would take away tonight.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you know what to do, you want it done, and you keep starting tomorrow.
Ask first: how many times this month have you said not yet? What comfort would starting cost you tonight?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as start immediately — he did not turn around that afternoon either; the point is that the permit does not expire unless somebody tears it up.

### Lines to keep
Grant me chastity and continence, but not yet.
He wanted the outcome. He did not want today.
Not yet is not a decision. It is a permit that renews.

## Augustine · The pears
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/augustine/the-pear-tree/
Source: Confessions, Book II
Tags: Deep read, Augustine, Not for the fruit, for the theft

A man in his forties spends pages on a boyhood theft of fruit he did not even eat. The question is why.

### Q: What actually happened?
He was sixteen. A gang of them went out late and stripped a neighbour's pear tree. There were better pears at home; they tasted the fruit and threw most of it to the pigs. Decades later he circles the episode for pages looking for a motive and finds none: no hunger, no need, nothing but the pleasure of the theft itself. Then the detail that settles it. Alone, he says, he would never have done it. The condition was not his character. It was the company.

### The parts · Some wrongs have no reason at all
He tries every explanation and abandons all of them. Much of what people cannot get past stays open because they are still looking for the account that would make it make sense. Admitting there is no motive is the way out, not a failure to find one.
e.g. If why did I do that has produced nothing after twenty attempts, the question may have no answer.

### The parts · Who was standing there tells you more than what you are
Alone he would not have gone. The variable that produced the night was the group, not his nature. After doing something bad, people interrogate their character, which cannot be changed on a Tuesday. The company can.
e.g. Who were you with the day it happened? Change that before you decide what kind of person you are.

### The parts · Writing it out gives it edges
He is in his forties writing about pears, in detail. That is not a man who has failed to let go. Setting the whole thing down converts it from something permanently present into an episode with a beginning and an end, which stops it seeping everywhere.
e.g. Write the thing you cannot get past once, in full: what happened, and who was there.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you did something you cannot explain to yourself, and it keeps coming back.
Ask first: are you still hunting for a reason? Who was with you that day? Have you written it out once, in full?
Where it goes wrong: turning it into they led me astray — he keeps the responsibility and only relocates the condition; and writing it down gives it edges, it does not erase it.

### Lines to keep
It was foul, and I loved it.
Alone I would never have done it.
No motive, only company. That is the whole finding.

## Augustine · The mind commands itself and is resisted
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/augustine/the-mind-commands/
Source: Confessions, Book VIII, chapter 9
Tags: Deep read, Augustine, Not a weak will, two of them

He notices something strange in the garden: the body obeys instantly and the will does not. His explanation is a mechanism, not a scolding.

### Q: What actually happened?
Book Eight is an afternoon in a garden. He wants to change, cannot, and tears at his hair and beats his forehead. Then he sets the oddity down exactly: the mind commands the body and is instantly obeyed; the mind commands itself and is resisted. Why does the hand listen when he does not? The answer he reaches is that there are two wills, one old and one new, and both of them are his. Neither command ever gets more than half of him.

### The parts · Not too little will, but a divided one
People who understand everything and still do not move are told to want it harder. He says the resolve is already there, and so is a resolve pointing the other way. Adding to one side leaves the other side exactly where it was.
e.g. One more decision usually does nothing, because the part that refuses is pulling on the same rope.

### The parts · The half that refuses is also you
He does not call the reluctant will an enemy or a defect. He says both are himself. Treating the refusing half as an intruder to be crushed only tightens the deadlock. Granting that it is yours lets you ask what it is guarding.
e.g. I do not want to is not laziness. Some part of you is protecting something. Ask what.

### The parts · It broke by resolving, not by force
He did not finally shove his way across on willpower. Something happened in that garden that brought the two halves into one. The event cannot be copied, but the direction can: look for the condition that ends the tug of war rather than for more strength.
e.g. When you are stuck, stop escalating. Go looking for what would let both halves want the same thing.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you understand the argument completely, you have decided many times, and nothing moves.
Ask first: what is the half of you that refuses actually protecting? If that thing were met some other way, would the deadlock hold?
Where it goes wrong: concluding that will is useless and drifting — he did change, only not by force; and two wills is not an excuse, both of them are you.

### Lines to keep
The mind commands the body and is instantly obeyed.
The mind commands itself and is resisted.
Two wills, one old and one new. Both are yours.

========================================================================
## Bai Gui · Take what the others drop
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/bai-gui/take-what-others-drop/
Source: Records of the Grand Historian, Biographies of the Money-makers
Tags: Deep read, Bai Gui, Buy in the good year, sell in the lean one

Everyone knows buy low, sell high. What is missing is the part that makes it something a person can actually execute.

### Q: What actually happened?
His rule was eight characters long: when the world sells, I buy; when the world buys, I sell. In practice it was a calendar. In a good harvest he bought grain and sold silk and lacquer; when the cocoons came to market he bought silk floss and sold grain. Two crops whose cycles never line up, so one side is always cheap. Sima Qian writes that when the moment came he moved like a wild beast or a bird of prey. The rest of the year he ate plain food and lived alongside his own workmen.

### The parts · The hard part is being alone in it
When everyone is selling you are the only buyer, which means no colleague's judgement to check against and nobody to share the loss with. The price is low precisely because the consensus is on the other side, and consensus works by making you doubt yourself.
e.g. Entering a category everyone is leaving is not a money problem. It is six months with no outside signal agreeing with you.

### The parts · His signal was the harvest, not his nerve
He was not contrarian by temperament. He had observable inputs: which crop was in, what the year had been, how the cycles ran. Buying the bottom does not take courage; it takes a source of information that is independent of what the market is feeling.
e.g. Whether to spend more on a channel or pull out of it is answered by your own cost per customer and retention curve, not by who else is buying there.

### The parts · The crowd opens the window and the crowd closes it
The line about the bird of prey is usually skipped. All that patience exists to reach a moment that the consensus itself created, and the moment ends when the consensus turns. So there is no time to be slow, and no room for a small trial first.
e.g. The acquisition you waited two years for finally agrees to talk, and your own approval chain takes three months. The waiting was supposed to include preparing that.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something is priced low and every sensible person is leaving.
Ask first: is my reason for calling it cheap independent of what the market is feeling today?
Where it goes wrong: treating contrarianism as a stance with no signal behind it, and then wanting to test the moment with a small position when it finally arrives.

### Lines to keep
When the world sells, I buy. When the world buys, I sell.
He seized the moment like a wild beast or a bird of prey.
Cheap is what consensus looks like from the other side.

## Bai Gui · Four things, and no waivers
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/bai-gui/four-qualifications/
Source: Records of the Grand Historian, Biographies of the Money-makers
Tags: Deep read, Bai Gui, Missing one and the other three stop paying

He put trade on a level with statecraft and war, and then set an entrance requirement that most applicants would fail.

### Q: What actually happened?
He described his trade in company nobody expected: I trade as Yi Yin planned, as Sun Tzu fought, as Shang Yang legislated. Having claimed that much, he set a bar to match. A man short of the wit to adapt, the courage to decide, the humanity to give, or the strength to hold, he would not teach at all. Four conditions, and no partial admission. Sima Qian closes by noting that everyone in the empire who talked about making a living traced it back to him.

### The parts · Each one guards a different stage
Wit reads the situation, courage commits while the information is still short, humanity decides what to give away and to whom, strength holds the position through the stretch when nothing confirms it. They sit on one chain. Break a link and the other three stop paying.
e.g. Seeing it clearly and not acting is the same as not seeing it. Acting and being shaken out halfway is the same as never starting.

### The parts · The third one is about splitting, not about being nice
The humanity he means is the ability to give and to take: when to leave margin on the table, for whom, and how much. It is the condition people underrate most. Plenty of operators can read a market perfectly and still lose every partner they have.
e.g. Keeping the whole margin in your own link makes this year's accounts look best. Next year your suppliers and channels are all working for someone else.

### The parts · He was willing to say a person should not do this
The refusal is the striking part. He did not offer to build the missing quality on the job. Some methods have prerequisites, and a prerequisite is not a development area; handing the method to someone without it is not kindness.
e.g. Give a strategy that requires betting on thin information to someone who needs proof before deciding. That is not low effort. It is the wrong fit.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: deciding whether you, or someone you are backing, is suited to something highly uncertain.
Ask first: of reading it, committing, sharing it out and holding on, which one is the short leg?
Where it goes wrong: scoring only the first, and assuming the missing one can be picked up along the way.

### Lines to keep
Wit to adapt, courage to decide, humanity to give, strength to hold.
If any of the four is missing, I will not teach him.
All who speak of making a living take him as their founder.

## Jeff Bezos · Always Day 1
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/bezos/day-one/
Source: Amazon shareholder letters, 2016 and 2015
Tags: Deep read, Jeff Bezos, What Day 2 looks like

Someone asked what Day 2 would look like. The answer, and the four parts he installed to keep it away.

### Q: What actually happened?
He named the headquarters Day 1. In 2016 somebody asked what Day 2 looks like, and he answered in the shareholder letter: Day 2 is stasis. Followed by irrelevance. Followed by excruciating, painful decline. Followed by death. And that is why it is always Day 1. What follows is not a slogan but a recipe: customer obsession, resisting proxies, embracing external trends, high-velocity decisions. The last is the most quoted — most decisions are two-way doors you can walk back through, so they belong to small teams moving fast, at seventy per cent of the information you wish you had.

### The parts · Day 2 starts when process takes over from outcome
The first thing he names is the proxy: as an organisation grows, people start checking whether the process was followed rather than whether the customer was served. The process is not the thing, and it is a young manager's easiest confusion. When we followed the process becomes a defence, Day 2 has already begun.
e.g. When we went through every required review is treated as the conclusion of a post-mortem rather than the start of one, the process is now signing off on outcomes.

### The parts · Sort the door before you set the speed
One-way doors — irreversible — should be slow and heavy; two-way doors fast and light. Most organisations apply one-way approval to everything and drag reversible decisions out for months. Sorting is step one; step two is handing the two-way ones to whoever is closest.
e.g. Label every proposal one-way or two-way. On the two-way ones cut two layers of approval and cap it at forty-eight hours. Speed itself grows a culture willing to try.

### The parts · Customer obsession is the vaccine because customers are never satisfied
He ranks this first, and the reason is mechanical: customers are divinely discontent even when they say they are happy. Obsession with competitors goes mediocre as the competitors do; obsession with process calcifies. Only discontent is an engine that never stops.
e.g. Change the quarterly goal from beat the competitor to remove an annoyance the customer has stopped complaining about. The first has a finish line; the second does not, and only goals without one keep you young.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the company has grown, everything is orderly, and it feels slower.
Ask first: of the last three significant decisions, which were one-way and which two-way? For the two-way ones, how long did they take and through how many layers?
Where it goes wrong: applying high velocity to the irreversible ones, or turning customer obsession into support scripts while the actual obsession stays on the dashboard.

### Lines to keep
Day 2 is stasis, followed by irrelevance, then decline, then death.
Most decisions belong at seventy per cent of the information you wish you had.
Customers are divinely discontent, even when they report being happy.

## Jeff Bezos · Bet on what will not change
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/bezos/what-wont-change/
Source: Public interviews (re:Invent 2012 among others); the 1997 shareholder letter
Tags: Deep read, Jeff Bezos, The question almost nobody asks

Everyone asks him what the next ten years will change. He says the more useful question is the one he almost never gets.

### Q: What actually happened?
He is asked constantly what will change in the next ten years. He says he is almost never asked what is not going to change — and that the second question matters more, because you can build a strategy around what is stable. His own answer is unglamorous: in ten years customers will still want lower prices, faster delivery, more selection. Nobody will ever say, I love Amazon, I just wish the prices were higher and the delivery slower. Every dollar put into those is still paying interest a decade on.

### The parts · Change is news; constancy is foundation
A strategy that chases change is rebuilt every two years. Investment in a need that does not move compounds for twenty. The sorting question is easy to run: list what you are currently funding and ask whether customers will still want it in ten years. Two piles. The resources belong on the certain one.
e.g. Channels, formats and algorithms change annually. Cheaper, faster, less hassle never do. Re-sort the budget on that test and most companies find they have bet the wrong way.

### The parts · A need that does not change has no ceiling
Faster can always be faster; cheaper can always be cheaper. Improvements aimed at those never reach a day when they are done, so the moat can keep deepening indefinitely. An advantage built on a trend has a shelf life by construction: when the trend passes, the accumulation resets to zero.
e.g. Three days to next day to same day — each layer built on the last. Growth from riding a hot format starts over when the format does.

### The parts · Long term does not mean slow, it means willing to look bad
The 1997 letter says it outright: decisions are made on long-term market leadership, not short-term profit or Wall Street's reaction. Betting on what does not change means years of putting profit back into logistics, with ugly statements and steady ridicule. The ticket price is sitting through that stretch.
e.g. Declaring long-term thinking while reviewing teams quarterly on short-term profit asks people to run a marathon on a sprinter's breathing. Until the review cycle changes, the strategy is wall decoration.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the strategy meeting is all new trends and new tactics.
Ask first: what three things will our customers certainly still want in ten years, and what share of current spending is aimed at those three?
Where it goes wrong: using constancy as an excuse to ignore trends — embracing external trends is one of his own four. What does not change is the need; how you meet it has to change constantly.

### Lines to keep
You can build a strategy around the things that are stable over time.
No customer will ever ask for higher prices and slower delivery.
We make decisions on long-term market leadership, not short-term reactions.

## The Bhagavad Gita · A right to the action, never to the fruit
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/bhagavad-gita/right-to-the-act/
Source: Bhagavad Gita 2.47
Tags: Deep read, The Bhagavad Gita, Chapter two, verse forty-seven

Two thousand years of quotation have made it sound like detachment. In place it is a boundary line drawn under pressure.

### Q: What actually happened?
The verse everyone knows is 2.47: your right is to action alone, never to its fruits; let not the fruit be your motive, nor let attachment to inaction take hold. Gandhi called the book his spiritual dictionary. What the poster version loses is where the sentence is spoken. Not in a study, and not to a calm man. On a battlefield, to someone who has already dropped his bow and is about to pay for whatever he does next.

### The parts · Draw the line: the act is yours, the yield is not
This is a division of property, not a consolation. Whether you do it, how, and how much today sit on your side. Whether the market takes it, the committee approves it, the other person replies, all sit on the far side. Most effort goes into rearranging the far side.
e.g. Put the thing in two columns, mine and not mine. Work only the left one.

### The parts · Not asking for the harvest is not refusing to look at it
Results still get read, because they are information about where the work was wrong. The difference is what you do afterwards. Using them to adjust the next action is the point. Using them to decide whether to continue hands the wheel to something you do not steer.
e.g. Read the numbers for one purpose only: which part of tomorrow's action changes.

### The parts · What the line saves you is the arithmetic of worth
People who are forever computing whether a thing is worth it spend most of their strength computing, and the finer the calculation the less they move. Once the boundary is drawn that strength goes back into the work, not because the outcome stopped mattering but because it was never calculable.
e.g. When you catch yourself pricing the whole venture again, go back to the one concrete thing due today.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have pushed on something for a long time with nothing coming back.
Ask first: which parts of this are actually yours? When you last read the result, were you adjusting the work or deciding whether to keep going?
Where it goes wrong: hearing it as the outcome does not matter — it says do not let the outcome decide today; the work itself still has to improve.

### Lines to keep
Your right is to action alone, never to its fruits.
Let not the fruit of action be your motive.
The finer the calculation, the less anyone moves.

## The Bhagavad Gita · Standing still in front of the line
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/bhagavad-gita/frozen-on-the-field/
Source: Bhagavad Gita, chapter 1 into chapter 2: Arjuna lays down his bow
Tags: Deep read, The Bhagavad Gita, He saw it clearly and that is why he stopped

The book opens with a man who cannot move, and spends eighteen chapters on him. That structure is the argument.

### Q: What actually happened?
Arjuna is the finest archer alive and the poem starts with him putting the bow down. He is not incompetent and he is not afraid of dying. He has looked across the field and seen his own teachers and cousins standing in the ranks opposite, and his limbs give way. Krishna does not tell him to stop thinking about it, and does not hurry him: he argues it through with him, for eighteen chapters. It is a book about a man who will not move.

### The parts · Being stuck is usually seeing the whole cost at once
Nothing is wrong with his ability. What is wrong is that every consequence is laid out in front of him at the same moment. Load the entire road into one view and each single step becomes unbearable. That is not weakness of will, it is too much arriving together.
e.g. Narrow it. Price today's step only, and stop costing out the whole road at the same time.

### The parts · He needed the argument finished, not encouragement
You can do it is useless to someone frozen, because confidence is not what has jammed. What has jammed are the specific things he cannot get past. The method of the book is to take each one out and talk it through until he is willing. That is slower than pushing.
e.g. Find the person who will argue it to the end with you, not the one who cheers.

### The parts · He fights afterwards, and it is no lighter
Eighteen chapters do not make the cost disappear or the act easy. All they do is let him think it through to the bottom and then walk over there himself. Understanding is not a substitute for doing, and it does not come with relief attached.
e.g. Stop waiting for the answer that makes it feel lighter. Being able to move is the answer.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have understood it and costed it and you still cannot take a step.
Ask first: have you loaded the whole road into one view? What does today's step alone actually cost? Who would argue this to the end with you?
Where it goes wrong: expecting clarity to make it easy — he still had to fight, and the cost was unchanged; and someone arguing it with you is not someone deciding for you.

### Lines to keep
My limbs give way and my mouth is parched.
You can do it is useless to a man who is frozen.
Thinking it through buys movement, not relief.

## The Bhagavad Gita · Do it without gripping it
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/bhagavad-gita/act-without-clinging/
Source: Bhagavad Gita, on action without desire for the fruit
Tags: Deep read, The Bhagavad Gita, Not the same as not caring

Action without desire gets read as coldness. What it actually separates are two things that usually travel together.

### Q: What actually happened?
The teaching on action without desire for the fruit is regularly mistaken for indifference. It is a separation of two things: the force you put into the work, and the hand that will not let go of the outcome. The first is meant to be total, the second is meant to open. And it comes with a test that is uncomfortably easy to run. Ask whether the whole effort is held up by the expectation of a return, because if it is, the day the return is ruled out is the day the work stops.

### The parts · The test: is it the work holding you up, or the payoff
Suppose the return is definitely gone. Do you still do it? If the answer is no, then what you have been doing all along is the payoff, and this work is only the road to it. When the road closes, the person disperses. That is not shameful, but it should be known.
e.g. Imagine the reward removed for certain, then ask whether you still do it. The answer is the fact.

### The parts · Letting go means today does not depend on the news
Someone gripping the outcome runs on incoming signals: good word and there is energy, silence and the day collapses. Opening the hand is not ceasing to care. It is taking back from those signals the decision about how much gets done today.
e.g. Set today's quantity in advance and keep to it whether or not anything good arrives.

### The parts · Both halves or neither
Full force with no release is staking yourself on the result, and one disappointment ends it. Release with no force is idleness wearing the language of equanimity. The book asks for them together: everything in the hands, nothing gripped in the head.
e.g. Work out which half is missing: staked too hard, or let go too early.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you want to give it everything and the outcome is dragging you around daily.
Ask first: if the return were certainly gone, would you still do this? Did you set today's amount, or did the news?
Where it goes wrong: hearing it as care less — caring is normal, it just should not decide the day's quantity; and equanimity without effort is idleness with better vocabulary.

### Lines to keep
Remove the reward for certain. Would you still do it?
Gripping the outcome puts every day in someone else's hands.
Everything in the hands, nothing gripped in the head.

========================================================================
## Otto von Bismarck · Iron and blood
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/bismarck/iron-and-blood/
Source: Speech to the budget committee of the Prussian house, 30 September 1862
Tags: Deep read, Otto von Bismarck, Naming the currency a question settles in

One of the most quoted speeches in Europe was delivered in a small room. What he was arguing about there was money.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1862 the chamber had refused to fund the army reforms and the constitutional crisis was stuck. A week into the job, Bismarck spoke to the budget committee. Prussia's borders are not favourable to a healthy state life. The great questions of the day are not settled by speeches and majority resolutions, that was the great mistake of 1848 and 1849, but by iron and blood. The room was appalled and the king feared the scaffold. It was the truth about a budget: the chamber could refuse the money, it could not refuse the geography.

### The parts · Ask what currency this question settles in
Every class of problem has a currency it is actually settled in: votes, cash, capacity, or force. Stockpiling the wrong one buys nothing. The Frankfurt parliament sat for a year in 1848, drafted an admirable constitution, and at the end of it nothing had happened.
e.g. In a market that settles through distributors, spending everything on brand buys noise and no shelf. Work out who pays whom for what before deciding what to hoard.

### The parts · He had priced saying it out loud
The sentence is ugly and he knew it would be held against him. He said it because vagueness in that committee extended the deadlock, and what he needed was everyone negotiating against the real constraint. Naming it moves a room from what ought to be to what is, and the speaker pays for it.
e.g. Saying in the meeting that the real blocker is nobody wanting to cross that department earns instant dislike, and the discussion only becomes useful from there.

### The parts · Iron and blood is a list of means, not a creed
Later readers took four words for a militarist confession. His own use of war was miserly: three short conflicts, each with a limited aim, each stopped on time. He was describing how this class of question gets settled. People who mistake a description of means for a faith are the ones who cannot stop.
e.g. This market competes on price is a reading, not a call for permanent price war. The reading tells you to hold reserves; when to fire and where to halt is a separate decision.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a thing everyone has met about repeatedly, and it has not moved once.
Ask first: what does this question actually settle in, and is that what you have been accumulating?
Where it goes wrong: making bluntness a personal style and producing embarrassment everywhere; or promoting a judgement about means into a belief you can no longer stop acting on.

### Lines to keep
The great questions of the day are not settled by speeches and majority resolutions.
Prussia's borders are not favourable to a healthy state life.
That was the great mistake of 1848 and 1849.

## Otto von Bismarck · The art of the possible
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/bismarck/art-of-the-possible/
Source: Interview of 1867; the peace with Austria, 1866
Tags: Deep read, Otto von Bismarck, Three wins, then the brake

After three quick victories he spent twenty years preventing the next war. Stopping was the part that took more from him than winning.

### Q: What actually happened?
Politics is the art of the possible, the attainable, the art of the next best. He said it to a journalist in 1867, and his conduct after Koniggratz in 1866 is the footnote. Austria was beaten and the king and the generals wanted Vienna. Bismarck held out against all of them for a lenient peace, no territory taken from Austria, no march on the capital, threatening to resign over it. His reason was not mercy. Austria might have to be an ally the following year, and a humiliated one could not be.

### The parts · The best is the enemy, the next best is the art
Entering Vienna was the maximum result available that summer, and would have been the start of twenty years of hatred. Letting Austria leave with its dignity kept the option open. The art of the possible means trading the peak of this round for the expectation across all the rounds after it.
e.g. Pushing a counterpart below his floor is optimal today and leaves him waiting for the chance to reverse it. Agreements with an inch left in them get honoured.

### The parts · The brake goes on when your own side is euphoric
After the victory it was not the enemy demanding the advance, it was the king, the generals and the newspapers. The strongest push to overreach always comes from internal momentum after a win. Plenty of people can start the machine. Very few can stand on it at full speed.
e.g. Three quarters above plan and the board and the team both want double the spend. Whoever proposes restraint is arguing with the mood of the whole company, not with the market.

### The parts · Declaring yourself satisfied is itself a move
Calling Germany a satiated state was not a description of his feelings. It was a signal to every capital that Germany had stopped being a variable and no coalition was needed against it. Stating your own limits buys you neighbours who do not have to prepare for your having none.
e.g. Telling a partner plainly that you will not enter their category buys you the absence of a pre-emptive strike. Undefined ambition makes every neighbour plan against you.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a run of wins, and everybody around you is pressing to push the advantage.
Ask first: what does the maximum result this round leave behind for every round after it? Answer for the counterparty as well as for yourself.
Where it goes wrong: turning the next best into permanent compromise and stopping when you should take the whole thing; or announcing you are satisfied and then expanding anyway, which voids the signal for good.

### Lines to keep
Politics is the art of the possible, the attainable, the next best.
We are a satiated state.
An honest broker who really wants to put the business through.

========================================================================
## BJ Fogg · Small Enough for Your Worst Day
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/bj-fogg/tiny-habits/
Source: BJ Fogg, Tiny Habits, 2019
Tags: Deep read, BJ Fogg, Do not bet on motivation

On the day you decide, anything is possible. The problem is the day with nothing in the tank. What to do then.

### Q: What actually happened?
Fogg's formula says a behaviour happens when motivation, ability and a prompt arrive at the same moment. Most people work only on motivation, and motivation moves like tide, not on your schedule; a habit resting on it will fall over. His own method was a rule: two push-ups after every trip to the bathroom. Two is so few that no state of mind prevents it, so he has never failed, and having done two he often does more. Months later he was doing dozens a day without once leaning on willpower. His principle: shrink the behaviour until you could do it on your worst day.

### The parts · Set the standard by your worst day
Plans are made when motivation is high and carried out on the days when it is lowest. So the standard has to be set for the bad day. If it holds then, the rest of the days manage it easily and usually overshoot.
e.g. Buying the annual membership and the kit on the day you decide is borrowing against a high. What settles it is the empty day.

### The parts · Starting is where the resistance is
The shrinking is not for the yield of that small amount. It is to get past the doorway. Once you have begun, most of the time you carry on. The resistance concentrates at zero to one, not at one to ten.
e.g. Change run three kilometres into put on the shoes and go out. Almost nobody puts the shoes on and stays in; plenty never touch them when the target is three kilometres.

### The parts · Continuity beats volume
Being too small to fail protects the state of this is still going. Break it twice and it turns from in progress into something you once meant to do, and restarting costs far more than keeping it alive.
e.g. Missed today, so tomorrow is compulsory, even the smallest version. You are protecting the identity, not the quantity.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a habit you keep building and keep abandoning.
Ask first: could I hit this standard on my worst day? If not, shrink it again, and keep shrinking until it looks absurd.
Where it goes wrong: staying at the smallest version forever while expecting a large result. The tiny version is the entrance, not the destination.

### Lines to keep
Behavior happens when motivation, ability and a prompt come together.
Shrink the behaviour until you could do it on your worst day.
Most people fail by working on motivation, which naturally rises and falls.

## BJ Fogg · Anchor It, Then Celebrate
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/bj-fogg/anchor-and-celebrate/
Source: BJ Fogg, Tiny Habits, 2019
Tags: Deep read, BJ Fogg, Prompt and emotion

Forgetting to do it and doing it without it sticking are two different faults. How each one is fixed.

### Q: What actually happened?
Fogg's anchor method hangs the new behaviour off something that happens every day without fail: after I brush my teeth, after I pour the coffee. The anchor solves the prompt, so memory and alarms are no longer required. The second move is less intuitive. The instant you finish, give yourself a clear positive signal: a fist, or saying nice out loud. He refuses to let this step be skipped, because what makes the brain keep a habit is the emotion at completion, not the number of repetitions. It sounds silly. It is what fixes the habit in place.

### The parts · An anchor has to be one specific action
In the morning is not an anchor. Putting the cup down after pouring coffee is. The more specific the anchor, the more reliable the trigger; a vague window of time is no prompt at all and leaves you relying on memory again.
e.g. Write every morning usually fails. After I pour the coffee I write three sentences does not, because it has a moment attached.

### The parts · Celebrating is not rewarding
A reward is a benefit handed over afterwards, a meal out when it is done. A celebration is the emotional signal at the moment of completion. Fogg wants the second, because only something simultaneous with the behaviour builds the association. A reward is too far away to do it.
e.g. After the two push-ups, say I did it, and mean it. Saving it for a big meal at the weekend helps almost nothing.

### The parts · Diagnose the three separately
When it does not happen, first work out which part broke: you forgot, which is the prompt; it was too hard, which is ability; or you did not want to, which is motivation. The three have completely different repairs, and mixing them leaves you with I should be more disciplined.
e.g. Always forgetting the tablets is a prompt problem: get a pill box that lives in one place. Finding it a nuisance is ability: sort a week at a time.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the new habit keeps breaking.
Ask first: what daily certainty is it hanging off? Do I give myself a signal at the moment I finish? And when it fails, was it prompt, ability or motivation?
Where it goes wrong: turning the celebration into a ritual of self-praise, which moves your attention off the thing and onto the feeling.

### Lines to keep
What makes the brain keep a habit is the emotion at completion.
Hang the new behaviour after something that happens every day.
You change best by feeling good, not by feeling bad.

## Murray Bowen · In the relationship and still yourself
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/bowen/differentiation/
Source: Bowen family systems theory
Tags: Deep read, Murray Bowen, Fusion and cut-off are the same failure

With family it is either being swept along or getting out. Whether there is a third road.

### Q: What actually happened?
Bowen's central term is differentiation of self. Differentiation is staying in emotional contact with people and still being yourself. Low differentiation takes two forms that look opposite and share a root: one goes along, so that when somebody at home is unhappy you concede, and the other stops going home at all. He calls the first fusion and the second emotional cut-off, and neither of them is being yourself inside a relationship. He also watched anxiety move through a family faster than reason: one person tightens, the whole house tightens, and nobody can say why.

### The parts · Cut-off is not a solution, it is being governed from further away
Refusing contact looks like taking control back, and the other person still sets your position: you have to keep spending distance in order to hold yourself together. Real differentiation means you can go back, and your position does not collapse once you are in the room.
e.g. Pressed about marriage over the new year: miserable all evening is fusion, never going home again is cut-off. The third road is going as usual, not arguing and not changing your mind.

### The parts · Deal with your own anxiety first
If anxiety travels through the system, a parent managing their own share does more than any technique aimed at the child. This is Bowen's most usable conclusion and his hardest, because the first move in it is admitting that the anxiety is yours.
e.g. Your worry about his future arrives whether or not you say a word about it. Handle your part and his state often changes on its own.

### The parts · It runs down the generations, and it can be raised
Your level is largely set in the family you grew up in, and it gets handed on. It can also be lifted deliberately, and the practice happens in the relationship most likely to sweep you off: I know you are unhappy, I understand, and my view has not changed.
e.g. Every time you meet a relative's feeling without going cold and without surrendering, the capacity grows a little, and the next generation starts higher up.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: contact with your family and you are carried off by the feeling in the room.
Ask first: is this fusion, where I go miserable and concede, or cut-off, where I stop turning up? Is there a third road — stay in the room, position unchanged?
Where it goes wrong: reading differentiation as a licence for coldness. Not being swept off is not the same as not caring.

### Lines to keep
Differentiation is staying connected to people and still being yourself.
Anxiety travels the family system and lands on the most vulnerable member.
Cut-off looks independent. The other person still sets your position.

## Murray Bowen · Pulling in a third person
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/bowen/triangles/
Source: Bowen on triangles
Tags: Deep read, Murray Bowen, The tension gets fixed in place

A problem between two people always seems to end up being three people's problem. What that costs.

### Q: What actually happened?
Bowen states it as a rule of the system: when the tension between two people runs too high, a third is automatically drawn in. Complaining about a partner to a friend, parents pulling a child into their own quarrel, colleagues who go around rather than through — the relief is real, and the price is that the original pair no longer has to settle anything, because the pressure now has somewhere to go. He called it triangling, and thought it the most stable structure in a family: once formed, a triangle can run for decades with the third person held in the middle.

### The parts · Relief and permanence are one movement
Bringing in a third party works precisely because it bleeds off pressure, and once the pressure is off the original two lose the motive to fix anything. That is why the relationships people complain about longest are so often the ones that never change.
e.g. Every week you tell a friend what he did. You feel better each time, and a year on you have never said any of it to him.

### The parts · The child is the one most often pulled in
Where the tension between parents is high, a child is the easiest third point: through attention, through a tug of war, or by developing a problem that takes the pressure off. It is why Bowen treated a child's symptoms as belonging to the system rather than to the child.
e.g. The parents start fighting as soon as the child improves. That usually means the problem had been standing in front of the marriage.

### The parts · The way out is a direct conversation, not a side
When you are being triangled, taking sides is the least useful thing available. What works is declining the role: not judging, not carrying messages, handing the problem back to the two who own it. It sounds cold and it is the only route by which they solve it.
e.g. Both parents complain to you about each other. I am not going to sit in the middle, the two of you have to talk, does more than persuading either one.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: two people have been stuck for years and there is always a third person in the middle.
Ask first: is that third person bleeding off their pressure? What part am I playing in it?
Where it goes wrong: reading do not triangulate as never ask anyone for support. The difference is whether you are looking for support or standing in for the conversation that should be happening.

### Lines to keep
Too much tension between two people automatically pulls in a third.
The triangle is the basic building block of an emotional system.
Bringing in a third relieves the pressure and removes the motive.
