## John Boyd · The OODA loop
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/boyd/ooda/
Source: Boyd's briefing, Patterns of Conflict
Tags: Deep read, John Boyd, Fast means turning, not moving

He was a fighter instructor who could win from any position in forty seconds. What 'fast' meant in the loop he built.

### Q: What actually happened?
Boyd compressed all conflict into one loop: observe, orient, decide, act. The claim isn't that each step should be quick, but that you should operate inside the opponent's loop: you finish two cycles while he finishes one, so what he observes is the world your last move made — every reaction fights a version of you that no longer exists. Facing an ambiguous, fast-changing environment, his loop slows until he collapses from the inside. In Korea the outmatched F-86 posted a lopsided kill ratio; Boyd's explanation was hydraulic controls — it switched between manoeuvres faster.

### The parts · The bottleneck is almost always orient
Observe, decide and act can all be sped up with tools. The slow one is orient: fitting new information into your existing frame. The more successful the old frame, the less new information gets in — organisations do see the change, they just file it under the old map.
e.g. The data showed the new channel growing on Monday and it wasn't called a trend until the quarterly review. Those six weeks were orient, not observation.

### The parts · Getting inside means producing rapid change
You don't wait to get faster; you make him slower. Keep the rhythm and direction of your moves unpredictable so his last read expires before he can act on it. He spends more time understanding you and less executing his own plan. That is how initiative changes hands.
e.g. A predictable opponent is the easiest kind: his launches and promotions are on a calendar. Come off the calendar and every response he makes is late.

### The parts · Turning fast requires low internal friction
Boyd's prescription for organisations wasn't acceleration, it was less friction: shared intent, mutual trust, authority pushed down. Every approval layer is delay in the loop; every ounce of suspicion is paid for in confirmations. Trust isn't a soft metric. It is the loop speed.
e.g. Two equally able teams: one acts and reports, one asks first. The gap isn't the people, it's the delegation.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you and your competitor are both accelerating, and you're buying tools for every step.
Ask first: which step is our loop stuck on? Usually the one where we saw it and didn't change the frame.
Where it goes wrong: turning fast into thrashing, motion with no direction; or internally, adding speed without removing friction, which just makes the mess arrive sooner.

### Lines to keep
Observe, orient, decide, act.
Operate inside his loop, and give him an ambiguous, fast-changing world.
Machines don't fight and terrain doesn't fight. People do.

========================================================================
## John Boyd · To be somebody, or to do something
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/boyd/to-be-or-to-do/
Source: The 'fork in the road' talk, recorded in Coram's biography
Tags: Deep read, John Boyd, The fork in the road

He made colonel and never rose again. The speech he gave every young officer who wanted to follow him.

### Q: What actually happened?
Boyd made enemies across the Pentagon: the lightweight fighter he pushed cut into too many budgets. Whenever a young officer wanted to join him he gave the same talk. You will come to a fork. One road: go along, accommodate the system, get promoted, collect the medals, and be somebody. The other: do what should be done, and get things done. Take the second and you won't rise fast, but you won't have to betray yourself. He stopped at colonel. The F-16 and American manoeuvre-warfare doctrine are full of his work.

### The parts · The two roads pay in different currencies
To be pays in position — title, grade, circle — issued by the system and revocable by it. To do pays in results: what you finished stays in the world and nobody can confiscate it. The fork is really asking which currency you intend to accumulate.
e.g. One decade: one person banked three promotions, the other three systems still running. Layoff day shows the difference in liquidity.

### The parts · Accept the price of the second road up front
Boyd didn't dress it up: no promotion, being frozen out, the cold bench — he said all of it. The honesty is in putting the bill first. People who take 'to do' and then complain about missing 'to be' rewards want both and end up with neither.
e.g. Most of the pain comes from scoring yourself on the other road's scoreboard.

### The parts · The system takes the work and withholds the credit
His designs were adopted, his theory written into doctrine, and the credit and the stars went elsewhere. That's the standard ending on this road: the results are absorbed, the person isn't crowned. Knowing that in advance moves your satisfaction to 'the thing is in use' — the only stable pay here.
e.g. Your proposal lands, packaged as your boss's win. The disgust is real. So is the proposal, running.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a chance to move up conflicts with something that should get done.
Ask first: which currency am I accumulating? Having taken this road, am I willing to use this road's scoreboard?
Where it goes wrong: using 'to do' as consolation while nothing actually gets done; or despising 'to be' entirely, forgetting that some things can only be done from a position.

### Lines to keep
One road: promotion and medals. The other: doing what should be done.
You won't rise fast, but you won't have to betray yourself.
People, ideas, hardware — in that order.

========================================================================
## Brené Brown · Guilt is workable, shame is not
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/brene-brown/guilt-not-shame/
Source: Daring Greatly; the 2010 and 2012 TED talks
Tags: Deep read, Brené Brown, Look at what the sentence in your head is pointing at

One mistake, two sentences a few words apart. What separates them, and why the consequences run in opposite directions.

### Q: What actually happened?
Twenty years on shame and thousands of interviews compress into one distinction. Shame is I am bad. Guilt is I did something bad. On the TED stage she put the pair side by side: guilt says I am sorry, I made a mistake; shame says I am sorry, I am a mistake. A few words apart, and one of them points at a behaviour while the other points at a person. A sentence about a behaviour has an action after it. A sentence about a person has nothing after it except hiding. So her conclusion is not stop being hard on yourself.

### The parts · The test is where the subject of the sentence lands
You do not have to analyse the feeling first. Listen to the sentence. Is the subject this thing, or me as a person? I misjudged how long the review would take and I am unreliable describe one late delivery, but the first names a changeable act and the second names a fixed identity.
e.g. The proposal went in late. I underestimated the review rounds leads to a better estimate. I am a procrastinator leads to not taking work on.

### The parts · Shame does not produce action, it produces hiding
This is the counter-intuitive half, because plenty of people believe shaming makes others improve. Her interviews point the other way: shame produces concealment, denial and blame pushed outward, since owning the fault means owning being bad. Guilt produces apology and repair, because it asks only for an act.
e.g. A team asked in public who did it does not make fewer errors next quarter. It files fewer reports.

### The parts · Rewriting is not letting yourself off, it restores the verb
Turning I am useless into I got that step wrong is not finding an excuse. It is putting an action back into the sentence. The test is hard-edged: after the rewrite, can you say what you do next? If you cannot, you are still on the shame side of the line.
e.g. I am bad at talking to people yields nothing. I labelled him before I described what I saw — that one can be changed tomorrow.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something went wrong and the bad feeling will not stop circling.
Ask first: is the subject of that sentence this thing, or me? If it is me, rewrite it down to one act, then check whether you can name a next step.
Where it goes wrong: using the distinction to file away responsibility you actually owe as just a behaviour; or telling somebody else not to feel shame — it is not argued away, it is heard.

### Lines to keep
Shame is I am bad. Guilt is I did something bad.
Guilt: I'm sorry, I made a mistake. Shame: I'm sorry, I am a mistake.
Shame is not fuel for good behaviour. It is the brake.

========================================================================
## Brené Brown · The three things shame needs
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/brene-brown/secrecy-silence-judgment/
Source: Shame resilience theory; I Thought It Was Just Me
Tags: Deep read, Brené Brown, Secrecy, silence and judgment, and how each comes apart

Shame is not a weather system but a mechanism with conditions. Which three it needs, and how you take each one away.

### Q: What actually happened?
Her formulation: shame needs three things to grow exponentially in our lives: secrecy, silence, and judgment. The use of it is that it converts a total, weatherlike feeling into a list you can go down item by item. All of shame's force comes from one unspoken line — it is only me — and that line stops being true the moment one other person has heard it and has not graded you for it. So the remedy is not perspective. It is telling one person who will not use it to define you. She is emphatic about the choosing.

### The parts · Secrecy and silence are one thing from two sides
Secrecy is nobody can know. Silence is they know and we do not speak of it. Both maintain the sealed conditions. Breaking them takes no publicity at all — one person is the whole requirement, because what fails is not a headcount but the sentence it is only me.
e.g. No announcement is needed. One person who has heard the whole thing from beginning to end changes what it weighs.

### The parts · Choosing the listener matters more than opening your mouth
This part decides the outcome. A qualified listener meets one standard: afterwards they do not use the thing to define you. They are allowed opinions; the opinions are not allowed to land on what kind of person you are. Choosing wrong feeds it, so waiting beats settling.
e.g. Anyone who will retell it elsewhere as material, anyone who labels people by habit, anyone who needs you to stay a particular way — none of them qualify.

### The parts · Common humanity is the ingredient people skip
The core of shame is that I am the exception. So the reply that works is rarely reassurance, it is me too. That is not a technique. It removes the premise directly, and it lands faster than any amount of encouragement.
e.g. After somebody finally says the hardest thing, it is fine does less work than I have done something like that too.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: there is one thing you have never told anybody, and it surfaces regularly.
Ask first: can I name a person who would hear this and not use it to define me? If no name comes, find the person before you force the telling.
Where it goes wrong: reading say it out loud as announce it publicly, which widens the source of judgment from one person to a crowd; or telling somebody who grades you and concluding that talking does not help.

### Lines to keep
Shame needs three things to grow exponentially in our lives: secrecy, silence, and judgment.
All of its force comes from one line: it is only me.
Telling the wrong person is worse than telling nobody.

========================================================================
## Bruce Lee · Be like water
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/bruce-lee/be-water/
Source: The Pierre Berton interview, 1971 (on film)
Tags: Deep read, Bruce Lee, Shape follows the container

The line is on film, so it is not something admirers put in his mouth later. What it describes is an operation.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1971, on Pierre Berton's programme, he said it: empty your mind, be formless, shapeless, like water. Put water into a cup and it becomes the cup; into a bottle and it becomes the bottle; into a teapot and it becomes the teapot. Water can flow, or it can crash. Be water, my friend. It is not improvised poetry. It is the summary of his whole system: he came out of Wing Chun and then dismantled the school, because any fixed form is a way of announcing your next move to the person in front of you.

### The parts · A fixed form is an announcement
A set sequence can be studied, predicted and prepared for. Water has no preferred shape, so there is no pattern to study. Staying formless is not an absence of capability; it is a refusal to let capability harden into something someone else can rehearse against.
e.g. A company whose promotions always land at month end and whose launches always follow the same beats can be answered by a plan written a month in advance.

### The parts · Fit the container; do not flatter it
Water in a cup takes the shape of the cup and is still water — it can leave whenever it likes. Shape follows container means total softness of form over something that does not move at all. People who learn only the first half stop knowing what they are after three containers.
e.g. How you talk to different customers is form. What you will quote and what you will ship is the water. The first should change constantly; the second goes into every cup unchanged.

### The parts · Softness and force are one property
He adds the second half deliberately: water can flow, or it can crash. People treat yielding and power as two options. Water shows they are the same thing — precisely because it does not fight the container, all of its energy is still available for the stone it intends to wear through.
e.g. The person who declines to fight over process, seating and tone arrives at the one thing that matters with everything still in hand.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the method you are proud of is being made irrelevant by a change around you.
Ask first: which part of me is form, and should follow the container? Which part is water, and goes into every cup unchanged?
Where it goes wrong: making formlessness into having no centre, so that three containers later there is nothing left; or spending the softness on the stone you were supposed to break.

### Lines to keep
Empty your mind. Be formless, shapeless, like water.
Water can flow, or it can crash. Be water, my friend.
Put water into a cup and it becomes the cup.

========================================================================
## Bruce Lee · One kick, ten thousand times
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/bruce-lee/one-kick/
Source: Tao of Jeet Kune Do and the training notes (ed. John Little)
Tags: Deep read, Bruce Lee, Which repetition, and in which direction

A man famous for speed and variety left behind a sentence about repetition. The two are not in tension.

### Q: What actually happened?
In his notes: I fear not the man who has practised ten thousand kicks once, but the man who has practised one kick ten thousand times. The person who wrote that kept a daily training list dull enough to be unreadable — the same side kick into the heavy bag hundreds of times, lead straight punches counted in sets, running, stretching, grip work, day after day. On screen he is endlessly various. In the log he is a very small number of movements repeated an astronomical number of times. The variety is the surface the opponent sees.

### The parts · Ten thousand kinds is knowing; ten thousand times is having it in the body
Someone who knows ten thousand techniques holds each one at the level of having to remember it. One movement practised ten thousand times goes into the spine and fires at a speed consciousness cannot join. The window in a real exchange only has room for the second kind.
e.g. The person who has read a hundred negotiation tactics is unchanged at the table. The one who drilled a three-second pause into reflex uses it in every round.

### The parts · Repeat past the point where it deforms
The first thousand are competence. Something else happens in the remaining nine thousand: the movement starts fitting your body and grows a personal version that is in no textbook. His own art came out of exactly that — Wing Chun movements ground by repetition into his. A borrowed technique only becomes yours through the count.
e.g. Writing a hundred reports to a template is execution. The day around the three hundredth when you delete the template is when you have a method.

### The parts · Choosing which kick is a decision made earlier
The line hides an earlier judgement: which movement deserves ten thousand? He chose the side kick and the lead straight, because they travel the shortest distance and apply the most widely. Drill the wrong one and the repetition only cuts the error deeper. Repetition is an amplifier; check what is being amplified.
e.g. Ten thousand hours into a skill a tool will absorb in five years turns diligence itself into the loss. Choosing the kick takes more judgement than starting.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the list of things you are learning keeps growing and the list you can actually use keeps shrinking.
Ask first: if I could keep only one movement to practise ten thousand times, which, and why that one?
Where it goes wrong: using the busyness of breadth to avoid the tedium of depth; or starting the count before choosing, and drilling an error into reflex.

### Lines to keep
I fear the man who has practised one kick ten thousand times.
Absorb what is useful, discard what is not, add what is uniquely your own.
Simplicity is the mark of true sophistication.

## Warren Buffett · The circle of competence
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/buffett/circle-of-competence/
Source: Berkshire letters, 1996
Tags: Deep read, Warren Buffett, The edge matters more than the size

Everyone hears it as a licence to stay small. The working part is the sentence after it, and it is about the edge.

### Q: What actually happened?
The formulation in the 1996 letter is that investors need only be able to evaluate selected businesses, and — the part that gets dropped — that the size of the circle is not very important; knowing its boundaries is vital. He stayed out of technology for most of forty years and said so in public, repeatedly, while it was making other people rich. That is not an admission of limitation. It is the discipline itself, performed where everyone could see it.

### The parts · The boundary is a claim you can check
Inside the circle you can say how the thing makes money in a sentence, and say what would have to happen for it to stop. If either sentence comes out vague, you are outside, whatever your job title says.
e.g. He had used the product for years and still could not say who paid, or for what. That is outside, regardless of how familiar it felt.

### The parts · Familiarity is not competence
The most common way the boundary moves without anyone deciding is that something becomes familiar — in the news, in conversation, in the portfolio of someone you respect — and familiarity gets read as understanding.
e.g. Everyone at the table owned it, so it stopped feeling like a decision and started feeling like a default.

### The parts · Staying out has to be sayable out loud
A boundary you hold privately erodes, because there is no cost to crossing it quietly. Said in public it becomes something you would have to explain reversing, and that friction is the point.
e.g. Writing 'we don't do this, and here is why' in the team doc is what stopped it being reopened every quarter by whoever had just read an article.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: about to commit money, time or reputation to something you sort of understand.
Ask first: can you say in one sentence how it makes money, and one sentence for what would stop it? If not, you are outside the edge.
Where it goes wrong: using it as a reason never to learn anything new — the circle is meant to grow, deliberately and slowly, not to be defended forever.

### Lines to keep
The size of the circle is not very important. Knowing its boundaries is vital.
Familiarity gets read as understanding, and nobody notices the swap.
A boundary you never say out loud is one you will cross quietly.

## Warren Buffett · You find out at low tide
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/buffett/swimming-naked/
Source: Berkshire letters, 1992 and 2001
Tags: Deep read, Warren Buffett, Risk shows up late, on purpose

In a rising market every stroke looks good. The question is how to see the risk while it is still invisible.

### Q: What actually happened?
He used the picture repeatedly: only when the tide goes out do you discover who has been swimming naked. It points at a structural feature of risk. Leverage, mismatch and luck do not just stay hidden during a boom — they amplify returns, so the naked swimmer is the fastest one in the water. Which is why his own disciplines are all counter-cyclical, and why Berkshire has carried an amount of cash that looks like underperformance for years at a time.

### The parts · Boom-time returns have risk premium mixed in
Whoever is beating the market may be doing it with skill, or by carrying more leverage and buying less insurance. On the statement the two are indistinguishable. So read a result by asking what is left of it once the borrowing and the exposure are taken out.
e.g. The fund's three great years were one leverage decision made in the first of them, and nobody separated the two.

### The parts · Put the trunks on while the tide is in
Looking for protection at low tide means paying peak prices for the things that are scarcest in a crisis — cash, insurance, credit — if you can get them at all. Every protection has to be bought while it is not needed, which is exactly what makes it hard.
e.g. The credit line arranged in the good quarter cost almost nothing and was the reason the bad one was survivable.

### The parts · Put the tide going out into the model
You cannot know when it turns, but every decision can be run through the test: funding stops, the largest customer leaves, rates double — does this still stand? What does not stand is fragile however much it is currently earning.
e.g. Half of revenue came through one channel, and the plan for that channel closing was a sentence nobody had written.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: things are going well and the returns look like skill.
Ask first: run it through one low tide — funding stops, the big customer leaves, rates double. What is left standing?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as a reason to hold cash forever — the point is buying protection early, not declining to swim.

### Lines to keep
Only when the tide goes out do you discover who has been swimming naked.
Every protection has to be bought while it is not needed.
What cannot survive the test is fragile, however much it is earning now.

## John Cacioppo · Loneliness is a kind of hunger
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/cacioppo/loneliness-is-a-signal/
Source: Cacioppo & Patrick, Loneliness, 2008
Tags: Deep read, John Cacioppo, A signal, not a personality

What loneliness actually is. Why thirty years of research put it in the same category as hunger and thirst.

### Q: What actually happened?
Cacioppo spent thirty years on loneliness, and the first thing he did was tighten the definition: loneliness is not being alone. It's the gap between the connection you want and the connection you have. Which is why a crowded table can be lonely and living alone need not be. Tighten the definition and the category changes too — he filed it with hunger, thirst and pain. All of them are the body flagging something you need to survive.

### The parts · Call it a defect and you hide it, which closes the only exit
Read loneliness as a flaw in your character and the first instinct is to say nothing — which seals the one way out. As a signal it carries no shame: it doesn't say something is wrong with you, it says something needs doing.
e.g. 'I'm just not a people person.' The moment that sentence is out, every available move is switched off.

### The parts · Alone and lonely are different, so most advice aims wrong
With the definition tightened, a lot of standard advice stops working. Move to a bigger city, go to more things — all of it is the opposite of solitude, and none of it closes the gap. The test is subjective: does anyone here know you.
e.g. Dinner plans every night and emptier each time — the thing being added isn't on the ledger.

### The parts · It has physical consequences, not just unpleasant ones
Chronically lonely people show higher blood pressure, worse inflammatory markers, lighter sleep and faster cognitive decline. Cacioppo pressed this point to move the subject out of the 'being precious' box. The body is settling the bill.
e.g. Across multiple studies the effect of long-term loneliness on mortality lands in the same range as long-term smoking.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you feel lonely, and feel embarrassed to say so.
Ask first: am I missing people being present, or people knowing me? The two answers lead to completely different moves — the first is helped by crowds, the second is not.
Where it goes wrong: hearing it as an order to widen your circle immediately, which only adds volume; or turning it back on yourself for not being outgoing enough. The signal doesn't check your personality first — extroverts get it too.

### Lines to keep
Hungry, you go find food. This is the same kind of reminder.
People near you, and people who know you, are not the same count.
It doesn't say something is wrong with you. It says something needs doing.

## John Cacioppo · Loneliness makes you misread faces
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/cacioppo/hypervigilance/
Source: Cacioppo's experimental work on social-threat vigilance
Tags: Deep read, John Cacioppo, The more watchful, the more alone

Why loneliness feeds itself. The loop Cacioppo found, and where you can cut it.

### Q: What actually happened?
Cacioppo's least intuitive finding: lonely people are unusually alert to social threat. Shown neutral faces in the lab, the lonelier the subject, the more likely they were to read unfriendliness into them; they also reacted faster to negative social words. His explanation was evolutionary — an individual cut off from the group has to be watchful to survive. Today that same self-protection turns on you: you read coolness as hostility, so you pull back; the other person feels the distance, and pulls back too.

### The parts · The problem isn't their attitude, it's the reading
'Things have been busy' lands as a fact for one person and as a brush-off for another. Same words in, different conclusion out, and from there completely different moves. The layer doing the work is in the middle.
e.g. No instant reply, so he doesn't want to talk to you. Most of the time he's in a meeting.

### The parts · The loop runs without anyone's help
Watchfulness makes you withdraw; withdrawing thins the relationship; the thin relationship confirms that you're not wanted. Nobody has to have rejected you for any of this to keep turning — which is why more contact alone doesn't break it.
e.g. The more you fear a no, the less you ask; the less you ask, the fewer invitations; the harder the conclusion gets.

### The parts · You break it by testing, not by pep talk
What works isn't telling yourself people do like you. It's treating the reading as a guess that could be wrong and going to check. The vigilance only loosens after the guess has been proved wrong a few times.
e.g. You're sure she's avoiding you. Ask her to something. Most of the time the answer isn't the one you rehearsed.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you feel people around you don't much want you there, but can't point to anything specific.
Ask first: did I observe this or infer it? Write it as a sentence that could be proved wrong, then find one chance to test it.
Where it goes wrong: using this to dismiss every real slight. Some people genuinely aren't friendly. This is about a bias in reading, not a reason to doubt everything you feel.

### Lines to keep
Loneliness will read an ordinary face as unfriendly.
Nobody has to have rejected you for this to keep running.
Whether people like you is something you can test, not guess.

========================================================================
## John Cacioppo · More socialising doesn't fix it
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/cacioppo/not-more-socializing/
Source: Masi, Chen, Hawkley & Cacioppo, meta-analysis of loneliness interventions, 2011
Tags: Deep read, John Cacioppo, The meta-analysis ranks it third

The most common advice for loneliness performs worst. What came first in the data.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 2011 Cacioppo and colleagues pooled the loneliness interventions into four kinds: more chances to socialise, more social support, better social skills, and correcting how social situations get read. The first three are everyone's instinct, and none of them did much. The fourth came first — going after automatic conclusions like 'they must find me boring' and 'if I reach out I'll be a nuisance.' The reason is the same as the last piece: the stuck layer is the reading.

### The parts · When opportunity isn't scarce, adding opportunity does nothing
A university campus, a big city, a company offsite — the objective chances to socialise are plentiful, and lonely people are lonely in all of them. When the bottleneck isn't opportunity, more of it just delivers 'none of these people are mine' more often.
e.g. Ten events and you still went home alone. That usually isn't a shortage of events.

### The parts · Skills rank third, because most people aren't short of them
Filing loneliness under 'bad at talking to people' is the other wrong turn. Skills training came third in the data, because most lonely people are fine everywhere else — they can do it, they just answer on the other person's behalf at the critical moment.
e.g. Easy company all day at work, and the message saying 'lunch this weekend?' never gets sent.

### The parts · What changes is the sentence that appears on its own
The move is small: catch the automatic conclusion, write it down, ask what it rests on. 'He didn't reply' is a fact. 'He doesn't want to talk to me' is a conclusion. You added the step in between. Separate them, then look for another reading.
e.g. Rewrite 'I'm annoying him' as 'he might be busy', and send one more message tomorrow.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you did what everyone said, went to the things, met people, and you're still lonely.
Ask first: the last time I didn't ask someone, was it for lack of a chance, or because I answered for them first? If it's the second, adding events is a road to nowhere.
Where it goes wrong: dropping social occasions altogether — opportunity isn't the most effective factor but it is still necessary; and this is not 'it's all in your head.' Some relationships genuinely aren't worth keeping.

### Lines to keep
For loneliness, changing the reading beats changing the opportunity.
Most lonely people can talk. They answer for the other person first.
The step between the fact and the conclusion is one you added.

========================================================================
## Julius Caesar · The die is cast
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/caesar/the-rubicon/
Source: Suetonius, The Deified Julius 31-32; Plutarch, Life of Caesar
Tags: Deep read, Julius Caesar, The step that has no way back

Taking an army across that small river meant civil war. This one is about what he was calculating while he stood there.

### Q: What actually happened?
January 49 BC. The senate had ordered Caesar to disband his army and return to Rome to stand trial. The Rubicon was the legal boundary between his province and Italy, and to cross it under arms was treason. Suetonius records that he halted at the bank and hesitated a long while, telling those with him that they could still turn back, but that once over the little bridge everything would have to be settled by arms. Then he said the die is cast and crossed. The order matters: the long pause and the arithmetic came before the famous sentence.

### The parts · An irreversible decision has earned a deliberate pause
Reversible decisions should be fast, since a mistake can be walked back. Irreversible ones should be slow, because they delete the option of walking back. The hesitation at the bank was not weakness, it was correct pricing. Most people do it the other way round.
e.g. Switching a tool can be undone in a fortnight, so do not hold three meetings about it. An exclusive contract, a public side taken, a relationship burned: those are worth a night at the bank.

### The parts · Half the war was already won before the crossing
This was not a gambler's throw. Ten years in Gaul had made his legions the best in Rome, Pompey's strength was scattered in Spain, and the city had no troops to hold it. He took Italy almost without blood. The romance of the line hides the arithmetic under it.
e.g. Before going all in publicly, confirm your own core capability, the gap in theirs, and the position you can hold in the first month. The declaration is for outside; the sums are for you.

### The parts · Once thrown, stop looking back at the bank
After the crossing he was famous for speed, holding all Italy within sixty days. The second half of an irreversible decision has its own discipline: spend nothing more on what if I had not crossed. The hesitation budget was used up at the river.
e.g. Deciding to change direction and then reopening whether to change direction every week is fighting two wars at once. Review it in December; until then, only the next step.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: one step in front of you, and past it there is no way back.
Ask first: is this really irreversible, and if it is, have you given the pause enough time and finished the arithmetic?
Where it goes wrong: treating small decisions as Rubicons and living in permanent high drama; or crossing and leaving half your attention on the other bank.

### Lines to keep
We can still turn back; beyond that bridge, arms decide everything.
The die is cast.
I would rather be first in a village than second in Rome.

## Julius Caesar · Mercy as a weapon
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/caesar/clementia/
Source: Cicero, Letters to Atticus 9.7C, quoting Caesar's own letter
Tags: Deep read, Julius Caesar, A new way of winning

In the civil war he killed no prisoners and confiscated no property. He set out his motive plainly in a letter.

### Q: What actually happened?
Early in the civil war Caesar took Corfinium, capturing Pompeian troops and senators, and then did what nobody in a Roman civil war had done: released them all and returned their property. The letter he wrote to his staff survives because Cicero kept it, and the motive is not hidden. Let us try whether by this means we can win all men back and make the victory lasting. Sulla won by cruelty and could not hold it. Let mercy and generosity be our new way of winning. The effect was immediate: mobilising against him got much harder.

### The parts · Mercy changes what it costs them to mobilise
How hard the other side fights depends on what they expect defeat to mean. When defeat means death, everyone fights to the end. When defeat means going home, resistance stops being worth buying. This was not a moral choice; it attacked their recruiting directly.
e.g. Treat the team of the company you just bought well and the next negotiation gets easier immediately, because every future target is watching how you handled the last one.

### The parts · He wrote the method down
The phrase new way of winning shows this was policy and not temperament. He deliberately set it against Sulla's terror and made mercy his brand. One act of clemency is a gesture; clemency that becomes a reliable expectation is a weapon, because only expectation changes behaviour.
e.g. Letting one departing employee off quietly is forgotten by everyone. Writing the rule down and honouring it for three years is why almost nobody breaks your non-compete.

### The parts · The bill for this method arrives later
Brutus and Cassius, among the men who killed him, were Pompeians he had pardoned and promoted. Mercy wins wars, but the pardoned often remember the humiliation rather than the kindness: they owe a life, and the debt makes the creditor hard to look at.
e.g. Keep a beaten rival and give them real responsibility, and understand that they come in every day facing the evidence that they lost to you. That post needs designing, not gratitude.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have won, and how the losing side is handled is in your hands.
Ask first: will this handling make the next opponent fight harder, or make them talk?
Where it goes wrong: making mercy a one-off gesture that never becomes an expectation; assuming the pardoned are now on your side.

### Lines to keep
Let mercy and generosity be our new way of winning.
Let us see whether this way we can win all men back.
Sulla won by cruelty and could not keep what he won.

## Tending the Roots of Wisdom · Leave a step on the narrow path
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/caigentan/leave-a-step/
Source: Tending the Roots of Wisdom: where the path is narrow, leave a step
Tags: Deep read, Tending the Roots of Wisdom, What you give up is your own way back

You are tight with everyone and tired either way. This asks why the book files giving way under making your own life lighter.

### Q: What actually happened?
One entry reads: where the path is narrow, leave a step for others to pass; where the flavour is rich, take three parts off and let others taste it. This is a method of great ease in going through the world. The last clause carries the weight. He does not call it a virtue. He calls it a method of ease, which means a way of making your own days lighter. Hong Yingming wrote in the Wanli years of the Ming, three hundred-odd entries on living among people.

### The parts · Two people wedged on a narrow path, nobody passes
Giving a step is not surrendering the path, it is keeping the path usable. Whoever has to be first at everything wins each occasion and loses the next one, because the man opposite braces on sight from then on and everything easy turns into work.
e.g. Give half a step on the next narrow path, then watch whether that path is easier to walk six months later.

### The parts · A method of ease names the motive
He does not say this is noble, he says it makes you comfortable. Enduring for somebody else's sake keeps a ledger and eventually presents the bill. Giving way so that you need not stay braced is finished the moment it is done. Same action, and only one of them lasts.
e.g. Before giving way, ask which one this is: for him, or so that you can stop holding yourself tight.

### The parts · Three parts, not all of it
The instruction is three parts off, not hand it over. Whoever gives everything away lives on the other person's conscience, which is no steadier than having to be first. A step and three parts are measured amounts, and seven parts stay with you.
e.g. Put a number on it when you give way: how much this time, and what is still mine afterwards.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: everything with people has gone tight, and you are either taking every inch or giving every inch.
Ask first: is this path actually too narrow for two? Is this step for him or for me? Three parts, or all of it?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as give way in all things — he said three parts, and whoever retreats to the end is living on somebody else's conscience; and calculating each concession puts the tightness straight back.

### Lines to keep
Where the path is narrow, leave a step for others to pass.
He calls this a method of ease, not a virtue.
Whoever gives all of it away lives on another man's conscience.

## Tending the Roots of Wisdom · Keep the skill out of sight
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/caigentan/hide-the-edge/
Source: Tending the Roots of Wisdom: hide skill in clumsiness, be bright by seeming dim
Tags: Deep read, Tending the Roots of Wisdom, Not all of what you have has to be on display

Afraid of being found out, and unable to stop proving yourself. This asks what the book offers as somewhere to stand.

### Q: What actually happened?
The entry runs: hide skill in clumsiness, be bright by seeming dim, keep what is clean inside what is muddy, bend in order to stretch. The reason given is not modesty. In his own words these are the three burrows a man hides in, a place to survive in among other people. Which sets the purpose: the point of keeping something out of sight is being able to stay, not looking humble.

### The parts · Show all of it and you are standing in the open
Once the whole of your capacity has been displayed, other people's expectations settle at that height, and every occasion afterwards has to reach the line, with anything under it counted as a failure. Holding some back is not deceit. It is leaving room for a bad day.
e.g. Do not put your best single performance on show as the normal one. Keep something in reserve for ordinary days.

### The parts · The fear of being found out comes from overdisplay
Being afraid of exposure means more has been put out than is actually held. What wants treating is not the fear but the gap. Either fill in what you have or take back some of what you showed. Both are easier than holding up a front that must never be tested.
e.g. When you are afraid of being caught out, measure the gap between what you showed and what you hold, then go and close it.

### The parts · Hiding skill is not playing dumb
He is describing a choice of occasions, not a permanent retreat. Bring it out when it is wanted and put it away afterwards. Someone who has to prove himself in every room spends the year on contests that decide nothing, and the real work goes slack.
e.g. Ask one question first: is this room worth the effort? If not, let it go past.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: braced in front of people, afraid they will see you are not that good, and proving yourself anyway.
Ask first: how far apart are what I showed and what I hold? Is this room worth the effort? Have I left myself room for a bad day?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as never show anything — he said choose the occasion, and not drawing when it is time is the other error; and manufactured clumsiness is heavier to carry than plain skill.

### Lines to keep
Hide skill in clumsiness; be bright by seeming dim.
Three burrows to hide in, not a display of modesty.
Fear of exposure means you showed more than you hold.

## Tending the Roots of Wisdom · Do not measure them by yourself
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/caigentan/dont-measure-by-yourself/
Source: Tending the Roots of Wisdom: do not use your own strength to show up another's weakness
Tags: Deep read, Tending the Roots of Wisdom, Where the sourness at good news comes from

Someone close does well and something in you goes cold. This asks where the book puts the root of it.

### Q: What actually happened?
Two clauses stand together: do not use your own strength to throw another's weakness into relief, and do not let your own clumsiness turn into resentment of another's skill. Side by side they describe one thing with two faces, hurrying to look strong and being unable to bear other people doing well. The verb in the first clause is the sharp part. Nothing unkind has to be said. You place yourself where you stand, and the other person becomes the short one.

### The parts · Throwing into relief is placement, not insult
You can show up somebody's weakness without one hard word: keep steering the conversation back onto the ground you are best on, and he shrinks by himself. People who do this rarely notice doing it. People it is done to do not forget a single instance.
e.g. Notice whether you keep bending the conversation back to your own strong subject, and then stop.

### The parts · Envy comes from your gap, not from his gift
He reverses the causation. It is not that he is so good and therefore you ache; it is that this square of yours is empty and therefore his doing well stings. Seeing that puts the effort somewhere useful, because filling your own square is cheaper than watching his.
e.g. When it stings, ask which square he is good in and whether yours is empty. If it is, go and fill it.

### The parts · After you speak, did he shrink or did the work move
This is a test you can run on the spot. The same piece of feedback can push the work forward or can simply leave the other person looking incapable, and privately you know which one you did. If it is often the second, the thing missing is not tact.
e.g. Take one second before speaking: after this sentence, has the work moved, or has he got smaller?

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: someone near you pulled it off, you congratulated them, and something inside went flat.
Ask first: which square is he good in, and is mine empty? How many things I said this month left someone looking smaller?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as envy is forbidden — he did not forbid it, he said look at where it comes from; and these two clauses are addressed to yourself, not for accusing other people of pettiness.

### Lines to keep
Hurrying to look strong and resenting another's success share one root.
Not that he is too good, but that this square of yours is empty.
After you speak: did the work move, or did he shrink?

## Cal Newport · Attention Residue
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/cal-newport/attention-residue/
Source: Deep Work, chapter two
Tags: Deep read, Cal Newport, The cost is not those few minutes

What one quick look actually costs. How the account should be worked out.

### Q: What actually happened?
Newport gives a counter-example: a manager who required the team to be reachable at all times. They looked extremely productive, messages answered instantly, meetings back to back, and after a year they had produced nothing that required sustained thought. The mechanism he names is attention residue: after you switch tasks, part of your attention is still hooked on the last one and needs time to move across. So the real cost of the interruption is not the five minutes, it is the poor half hour that follows, and that part is nearly invisible, because when you return to the work you feel focused.

### The parts · The loss happens where you cannot see it
The feeling of concentration and the quality of the thinking are not the same thing. After a switch you register immediately that you are back, while the drop in output only shows up afterwards. That is why the price of one quick look is systematically underestimated.
e.g. Answer a message midway through a proposal and the next twenty minutes of writing usually need rewriting when you read it the next day.

### The parts · Fragments do not add up to a block
Four fifteens are not an hour, because each one pays the switching cost again and deep thinking needs a climb. It explains why someone whose diary is cut up by meetings cannot produce work requiring continuity even when the total hours are there.
e.g. The forty minutes between two meetings is hard to think in. Most people can only spend it on small chores.

### The parts · Always available is a default, not a requirement
Most demands for an instant reply have never actually been tested. Newport suggests treating response time as a negotiable parameter: state your rhythm plainly, and in most settings the other side is entirely fine with it.
e.g. Put I do not read messages before noon and reply in one batch in the afternoon in your signature. Far fewer people object than you expect.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the day was full and nothing that needed thinking moved.
Ask first: was there a stretch of more than ninety minutes today with no interruption? If not, who cut it up?
Where it goes wrong: using it as a reason to refuse to collaborate. Deep work is for the tasks that need depth, which is not all of them.

### Lines to keep
Attention residue keeps you off full speed long after you switch.
Deep work is becoming rare exactly as it becomes valuable.
Four fifteen-minute pieces do not make an hour.

## Cal Newport · Book the Block
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/cal-newport/schedule-the-depth/
Source: Deep Work, part three
Tags: Deep read, Cal Newport, The gap will not appear on its own

The thing you will do when you have time never starts. How to take the time instead.

### Q: What actually happened?
Newport's central operational advice is to schedule deep work the way you schedule a meeting: in the diary, announced to other people, entered when the time comes, rather than waited for. The reason is blunt. A gap never appears by itself, and shallow work expands like a gas to fill whatever space is available. He also argues for capping shallow work and handling it in batches, so what remains can join up into blocks. None of it relies on willpower: holding attention by self-control in a place where anyone can interrupt you is a design failure.

### The parts · Taking the time works better than managing the will
Self-control is consumable; a diary is not. Fix the deep block the way a meeting is fixed and you no longer have to make the decision about whether to concentrate today. Making that decision is itself what wears people out.
e.g. Marking two hours each morning as unbookable is more reliable than asking yourself every morning when you will write.

### The parts · Cap the shallow work; do not try to abolish it
Mail, coordination and meetings are necessary and they build no new capability. Newport does not propose removing them. He proposes a ceiling and a fixed slot: the total is unchanged, and the block survives.
e.g. Handle mail at ten in the morning and four in the afternoon rather than whenever it lands.

### The parts · Boredom is trained
If every gap gets filled with a phone, the brain grows used to a constant supply of novelty, and anything demanding a long sit afterwards becomes unusually painful. So part of training attention is letting yourself be bored.
e.g. Two minutes waiting for the lift with the phone in your pocket. Small moments like that decide whether you can sit an hour.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the important and non-urgent thing never gets in.
Ask first: does it have a slot in my diary? If not, what exactly is the gap I am waiting for going to arrive from?
Where it goes wrong: filling the diary with deep blocks and executing none of them. Hold one, do it, then add.

### Lines to keep
A gap never appears by itself. You have to schedule it.
Fill every gap with stimulation and you lose the ability to concentrate.
You have a finite amount of willpower that becomes depleted as you use it.

## Cao Cao · Ability only, character not examined
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/cao-cao/talent-only/
Source: The Order Seeking the Worthy, 210
Tags: Deep read, Cao Cao, One test, and it is a hard one

He announced in public that he would look at ability and not at conduct. Under what conditions that extreme rule holds.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 210 he issued the Order Seeking the Worthy. He opens with a counter-example: if only men of blameless conduct could be employed, how did Duke Huan of Qi ever become hegemon? Guan Zhong had once shot an arrow at him. Then he takes it all the way — the realm is not yet settled, this is precisely the hour of urgent need, so bring me the men of low birth and poor reputation who can govern and command: put forward ability alone, and I will use it. In the moral climate of the time this was scandalous.

### The parts · Few criteria, or you never choose quickly
What a long list of requirements actually does is strain out everyone with an edge and leave the people who are adequate at everything and outstanding at nothing. Cutting to one criterion admits that in fast expansion, one person who can carry the load beats three with no weaknesses.
e.g. The job posting listed eight requirements and everyone hired scored a pass on all eight. The one capability actually wanted got squeezed out by the other seven.

### The parts · The rule comes with an expiry date
He wrote the precondition into the order himself: the realm is not yet settled, this is the hour of urgent need. Disorder wants ability; settled times want order. He ran this rule during expansion while backing it with severe military law — not examining character assumes something else governs behaviour.
e.g. Hiring someone brilliant and hard to work with is fine early on, provided the boundaries are explicit and correction is fast. Loosening the bar with no backstop is gambling with the organisation.

### The parts · Say it with no room left to retreat
The wording of the order is deliberately extreme. He was not after precision; he was breaking the habit of choosing men by reputation. A moderate phrasing gets absorbed by the existing filter and changes nothing. Overturning a deep default takes an oversized signal.
e.g. To end promotion by seniority, saying we also value ability does nothing. Promote the most junior person on the team and everyone understands by lunchtime.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are hiring or promoting and the list of criteria runs long.
Ask first: which single one of these does this seat genuinely require? Can the rest stop being filters?
Where it goes wrong: loosening the conduct bar without setting behavioural boundaries; trying to overturn a hardened default with careful, moderate language.

### Lines to keep
If only blameless men could serve, how did Duke Huan rule?
Put forward ability alone, and I will use it.
The realm is not yet settled. This is the urgent hour.

## Cao Cao · Grow the grain yourself
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/cao-cao/military-farming/
Source: The Order Establishing Agricultural Colonies, 196; Records of the Three Kingdoms
Tags: Deep read, Cao Cao, Fix your own supply first

The same collapse, and every warlord was seizing food. What he did instead was the thing nobody else had patience for.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 196 the central plain was in chaos and the armies fed themselves by plunder. Yuan Shao's men in Hebei lived on mulberries; Yuan Shu's troops on the Huai lived on water snails; when the grain ran out the army dispersed. On Zao Zhi's advice, Cao Cao settled farmers on garrison land around Xu and took a million bushels that first year. His stated reason was one sentence: the method of settling a state lies in a strong army and sufficient food. He then put agricultural officers in every province, and the granaries filled.

### The parts · Plunder is fast and it does not last
Seizing grain feeds you today; sowing it means waiting a season. Every force living off plunder met the same end — the grain ran out and the army dispersed. Whether an outfit is earning or burning down a stock comes to one test: is the supply produced or drawn down?
e.g. Growth on continuous funding and subsidy, and growth on gross margin, can look identical for a while. Close the funding window and the first one disperses that month.

### The parts · Your supply line has to grow on your own ground
The point of the farming colonies was not agriculture. It was moving army grain from asking others to producing it. Any lifeline that depends on outside supply is a switch in someone else's hand. Internalising it is expensive, and it is the only solution there is.
e.g. If every customer arrives through one platform's traffic, no amount of skill at buying that traffic puts the lifeline in your hands. Owned channels are slower, and they are the granary.

### The parts · Planting while everyone else grabs takes nerve
The first year of a farming colony produces nothing while rivals expand on what they seize. The difficulty is not technical; it is holding steady through the year in which you are visibly behind. Every long-cycle advantage has a stretch like that in it.
e.g. While a rival buys share with heavy spending, you work on retention. Two quarters of ugly numbers, and whether you survive them decides who is standing in year three.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: to catch up, you are considering the fastest available way to get resources.
Ask first: did this supply line grow on my own ground, or can someone else close it at will?
Where it goes wrong: counting drawdown as growth; letting short-term numbers turn you around in the year you were supposed to endure.

### Lines to keep
Settling a state lies in a strong army and sufficient food.
When the grain ran out, the army simply dispersed.
A supply line someone else can switch off is not yours.

## Cao Cao · Burning the letters at Guandu
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/cao-cao/burning-the-letters/
Source: Records of the Three Kingdoms, with Pei Songzhi's citation of the Spring and Autumn of Wei
Tags: Deep read, Cao Cao, Some accounts must not be settled

A stack of evidence in hand, enough to name everyone who hedged against you. Why he burned it in front of everybody.

### Q: What actually happened?
After the victory at Guandu his men found a bundle of letters in Yuan Shao's camp: secret correspondence from his own officials at Xu and his own commanders, written before the battle, arranging somewhere to land if he lost. His staff proposed checking every name and arresting them all. He did not look. He ordered the letters burned in the open, and said: when Shao was strong, even I could not be sure of surviving — how much less everyone else. The letters went, the matter ended, and not one man was pursued.

### The parts · Establishing the facts costs you half your people
With the evidence in hand, pursuing it is the natural next move. But those names are the same people who just won the battle. Following it through is unanswerable in logic and dismantles your own organisation in fact. Some accounts can be settled and must not be.
e.g. Investigate one incident to the bottom and assign blame to everyone involved, and nobody reports the second one. What you learn is worth far less than the channel you close.

### The parts · Supply the reason on their behalf
His line was not I am magnanimous. It was that at the time even he was unsure he would live. He attributed the wavering to the situation rather than to character, which let every one of them keep their face. That sentence turned a pardon into a shared account.
e.g. Someone wavered during the bad stretch. Saying nobody could read it back then works far better than saying I forgive you, which is still keeping score.

### The parts · It is over only once it is destroyed
The decisive act is not declining to pursue; it is destroying the evidence publicly. Keeping it unused means everyone knows the list is still with you, and that state drains people more than an investigation would. For a thing to be over, the proof has to physically stop existing.
e.g. You said it was finished, and the records from that time are still in your folder. Everyone can feel that file sitting there, and trust does not come back.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something is over, and you are holding the evidence of who did what.
Ask first: what does establishing it get me? Do I still need the people I would lose?
Where it goes wrong: treating accountability as a process that has to be completed; saying it is finished while keeping the file.

### Lines to keep
When Shao was strong, even I could not be sure.
Some accounts can be settled and must not be.
Kept but unused, the list drains more than the investigation would.

## Carl Rogers · Unconditional positive regard
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/carl-rogers/unconditional-regard/
Source: On Becoming a Person; the 1957 paper on the necessary and sufficient conditions
Tags: Deep read, Carl Rogers, Accept the person, judge the act

Unconditional sounds like having no standards. What exactly is the thing that carries no conditions.

### Q: What actually happened?
Rogers named three conditions on the therapist's side: congruence, unconditional positive regard, empathic understanding. The second is the one that gets argued about, because unconditional sounds like permission. His boundary is exact: what carries no conditions is acceptance of the person, not approval of everything he does. Judgement goes on as usual; it is simply not paid for with the relationship. His reason is empirical — where saying the wrong thing costs you the person, people hand you the version you can bear. The curious paradox is that when I accept myself just as I am, then I can change.

### The parts · Accept the person, judge the behaviour
The two have to be said separately, or acceptance is heard as permission and judgement is heard as rejection of the person. The workable version fixes the order: confirm that the relationship holds, then deal with what happened. Reversed, the second half is not heard at all.
e.g. A child admits he broke something. Take the telling first — you came and said it — then work out the damage. The other order buys silence next time.

### The parts · Conditional regard trains performance
I am pleased with you when you do well transmits one thing: being worth loving has terms. People learn very fast to meet the terms rather than solve the problem, and meeting them includes hiding and dressing up. Teams work identically: praise only good news and only good news arrives.
e.g. A manager who smiles only at a clean number gets people optimising the report instead of the business.

### The parts · Performed acceptance does more harm than none
Congruence stands first in his list precisely to stop this. Acted patience is detected, and it carries an extra message: you do not rate the truth from me. So when you cannot manage it, saying where you actually are beats holding up a container you do not have.
e.g. Irritated inside and using empathic phrasing anyway — they will hear it. I am in a bad state, let us talk later, is more reliable.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you want a particular person to tell you the truth.
Ask first: what does he lose by telling it? Have I been using the relationship itself as the stake?
Where it goes wrong: turning unconditional acceptance into no limits and no hard subjects. The judgement still happens; it just is not charged to the relationship.

### Lines to keep
When I accept myself just as I am, then I can change.
It does not help to act as though I were something I am not.
Accept the person. The behaviour still gets judged.

## Carl Rogers · Say it back until they nod
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/carl-rogers/reflective-listening/
Source: Rogers's recorded cases; Counseling and Psychotherapy (1942)
Tags: Deep read, Carl Rogers, Empathy is a move, not a sentence

I understand how you feel does nothing at all. What the act of empathy actually consists of.

### Q: What actually happened?
Rogers did something his colleagues found close to indecent: he recorded whole sessions, transcribed them word for word and published them. Before that, what happened in the room existed only in the therapist's account, and he held that what is not published cannot be checked. His 1942 book prints a complete case. Those transcripts became the start of empirical research on therapy, and produced a result nobody had wanted: how much a client changed had little to do with the therapist's school and a great deal to do with whether he had actually understood.

### The parts · Saying it back does more than make them feel understood
The larger effect is that many people first hear what they are saying while you are saying it back. A tangle of feeling returns as a sentence, and the shape of the problem shows. It is why being listened to helps at all, and why rushing in with advice cuts the process off.
e.g. When a friend unloads, start with so what you mean is. After he has corrected you twice, the thing has often become clear to him.

### The parts · Getting it wrong is useful too
A restatement does not have to be accurate to work. When it is wrong the other person corrects it — no, what bothers me is this other thing — and the correction is exactly the information you were after. Saying only I understand, for fear of being wrong, moves nothing.
e.g. It sounds like the deadline is the worry. If that misses, he will usually tell you it is the acceptance criteria.

### The parts · Advice waits until it is asked for
Rogers refused the role of instructor, not out of modesty but for effect: unrequested advice moves a person from solving their own problem to handling your opinion. So the order is understand first, and answer when they ask what to do.
e.g. Start offering solutions while he is still describing what happened and he will stop and argue with your plan instead of thinking about his own.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: somebody is telling you their trouble and you already have the advice ready.
Ask first: can I put his meaning back in my own words until he says yes, that is it? Has he actually asked me what to do?
Where it goes wrong: running the restatement as a script, or reflecting for ever and never saying anything of your own.

### Lines to keep
If I can listen to what he tells me, I can help him.
Real communication happens when we listen with understanding.
Change tracks whether the listener understood, not which method he used.

## Chris Voss · Say their feeling out loud
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/chris-voss/labeling/
Source: Never Split the Difference, on labelling
Tags: Deep read, Chris Voss, Name it before you negotiate it

The other side has gone quiet and will not take a call. What Voss says to say first, and why it is not a concession.

### Q: What actually happened?
Voss spent hours outside a door in a Harlem apartment building where armed fugitives were holed up. They would not pick up the phone and they were asking for nothing. He made no offer. In a deliberately slow, low voice he said through the door: It looks like you don't want to come out. It seems like you worry that if you open the door, we'll come in with guns blazing. A long silence, then a voice. He calls the move labelling: not judging the feeling, only naming it accurately.

### The parts · A label is an observation, not a verdict
It seems like the price is a problem, and I think you are just balking at the cost, look similar and land nothing alike. The first can be denied, which means it can be corrected. The second files a finding, and the person on the other end can only defend.
e.g. When a client goes silent, it sounds like something here is worrying you gives them a specific opening. How do you feel about it gives them none.

### The parts · Feelings first, terms second
The working assumption is that nobody takes in terms while their state is still unacknowledged. So the opening move is not a number, it is making the other person feel you know what is in their head. Skip it and every later concession buys nothing.
e.g. Talking terms to someone who is still angry is talking to a shut door. Name where they are and the door can open.

### The parts · A wrong label still works
Most people avoid labelling because they might guess wrong. Voss argues the reverse: a wrong label gets corrected, and the correction is the information you came for. The value is not in guessing right, it is in ending the silence.
e.g. Say it sounds like the timeline worries you and you may hear that the timeline is fine and the acceptance criteria are not. Now you have the real problem.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: someone has gone quiet, is dodging you, or is plainly upset and not saying so.
Ask first: what is the loudest sentence in their head right now, and can you say it back starting with it seems like?
Where it goes wrong: repeating labels as a formula until it becomes performed empathy, or naming the feeling and rushing straight into terms before it has settled.

### Lines to keep
It looks like you don't want to come out.
Labeling is a way of validating someone's emotion by acknowledging it.
Get it wrong and they correct you. That is information too.

## Chris Voss · You want that's right, not yes
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/chris-voss/thats-right/
Source: Never Split the Difference, on that's right
Tags: Deep read, Chris Voss, Two kinds of agreement, nothing alike

They nodded and nothing moved afterwards. This is about telling which of the two agreements you actually walked out with.

### Q: What actually happened?
Voss calls yes the cheapest word in the language: people say it to be polite, to be left alone, to end a conversation. What he wants is two other words. That's right means the other side believes you have understood them completely, and the route there is to summarise their position back until they say it. He pairs this with a counter-intuitive move, going after no. Ask whether they have given up on the project and they start explaining why they have not, because refusing feels safe.

### The parts · Cheap agreement gets reversed at execution
Nodding in the room and doing nothing afterwards means the yes was social lubricant. The test is simple: did they restate the plan in their own words? An agreement nobody can restate is not an agreement, it is the end of an uncomfortable meeting.
e.g. When someone says fine, fine, no problem, ask what the first step looks like. No answer means they were closing the conversation.

### The parts · Summarise until they say it back
The method is to lay out their position, their worries and what they want, in full, until they confirm it. Those two words mark the moment they feel understood, and people only weigh your proposal after that. Everything argued before it is wasted.
e.g. Before offering someone a change of role, list their concerns one at a time. Wait for that's right, then talk about the arrangement.

### The parts · No is safer than yes
Chasing a yes puts the other side on guard, because every yes moves them nearer a commitment. Letting them say no relaxes them, and relaxed people tell the truth. So build the question in a form that can be refused.
e.g. Swap can you agree to this for is this completely off the table. To deny it, they begin telling you which parts are not.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: they have agreed, and you cannot tell whether that was agreement or an exit.
Ask first: have they put it back in their own words, and did you actually hear that's right?
Where it goes wrong: summarising on and on to manufacture the phrase, which turns into a script; or using the no question as a goad rather than an opening.

### Lines to keep
That's right is better than yes.
Negotiation is not an act of battle; it's a process of discovery.
No is the start of the negotiation, not the end of it.

## Chu Shijian · Up the mountain at seventy-four
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/chu-shijian/orchard-at-74/
Source: Public reporting on his life; the orange planting in the Ailao mountains from 2002
Tags: Deep read, Chu Shijian, Beginning one thing from zero

Is it too late to begin at this age? What he decided in the year he turned seventy-four, and the arithmetic behind it.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 2002 he was seventy-four and it was all gone: the position, the name, most of the savings, and his health with them. He and his wife went up into the Ailao mountains, leased four hundred acres of bare hillside and planted sugar oranges. Everyone assumed this was an old man filling his days. He had done arithmetic instead: an orange tree fruits in four or five years, and at seventy-four that put the first crop at seventy-nine — an age most people reach. His first year up there he lived in a work shed.

### The parts · Too late is a feeling. Run it as subtraction
He never told himself he was still young. He counted: how many years until the tree fruits, how many years he probably had left, whether the first number fits inside the second. It cleared, so he went. Too late is almost always a feeling, and feelings cannot count years.
e.g. When it feels too late, write down how many years the thing needs and how many you probably have. Put the two numbers beside each other and look at them.

### The parts · With nothing left, there is nothing to compare against
There was no office to return to and no earlier life to measure the hillside against, because neither existed any more. People who keep a route back tend to work the new thing with one eye on the door. His was cut, so the work got all of him.
e.g. The one still holding a just in case way back gives the new thing half his attention. The one with no way back moves at full speed.

### The parts · The work shed was real, not a posture
At seventy-four he lived in a shed on the mountain, not to demonstrate humility but because that was the accommodation. Beginning again means the conditions begin again too: the pay, the standing, the bed. Accepting that is harder than accepting the age, and it is what settles the age.
e.g. What makes starting over hard is rarely the birthday. It is agreeing that the terms start over as well.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you want to begin something at an age where everyone around you, and some part of you, says it is too late.
Ask first: how many years until this shows a result, and how many years do I probably have? And am I still holding a route back to the old thing?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as no age is too late to start. He counted first and went only because the numbers cleared. Nor should the work shed be romanticised — it was what there was, not what he chose.

### Lines to keep
Too late is usually a feeling, and feelings cannot count years.
A man with no route back works with his whole attention.
The hard part of beginning again is accepting that the terms restart.

## Chu Shijian · Oranges take five years
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/chu-shijian/oranges-take-five-years/
Source: Public reporting on the orange plantation, 2002 to 2012
Tags: Deep read, Chu Shijian, He had done the sums before planting

Everything is invested and nothing is visible for years. What he did with that stretch, and why it was not waiting.

### Q: What actually happened?
A sugar orange tree takes four or five years to bear, and then several more years of adjustment before the fruit is good enough to sell. He was on the hillside every day of it, and not idle. In those years he built the irrigation, had the soil of every plot tested, brought in agricultural researchers to set the fertiliser mix, and cut the planting density from more than a hundred trees per plot to eighty, because crowded trees give sour fruit. The first crop, around 2006, tasted wrong. He kept adjusting. It sold properly in 2012, when he was eighty-four.

### The parts · The years with no result are the years for the foundations
While the trees carried nothing he built irrigation, tested soil and fixed the fertiliser mix. Those are precisely the jobs there is no time for once there is a crop. When nothing is coming out, the right work is the work that becomes impossible the moment something does.
e.g. Spend the stretch before results arrive on the underlying things you will never get back to once you are busy.

### The parts · Cut the wait into one thing a day
Five years is a size the mind cannot hold. What he did each day was specific: which plot to walk today, which mix to adjust today. Waiting is one enormous word; divided into a thousand days with a job in each, it stops being waiting at all.
e.g. Do not swallow it takes five years whole. Ask what the one piece of it is that can be done before tonight.

### The parts · A poor first crop is still a crop
The 2006 fruit was not good and he took it as information rather than a verdict: now he knew which part was wrong, so he could adjust. People who feel they have no results often count a poor result as none. A result can be tuned. Nothing is what cannot be tuned.
e.g. The first version being bad is your first data point, not the judgment on the project.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have put yourself into something that takes years to show anything, and you are in the middle of the stretch with no return.
Ask first: what am I building now that I will never have time to build later? Have I cut the wait into one job a day? When the first version came out badly, did I read it as information or as a verdict?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as long enough waiting wins. He worked every day of those five years. And building foundations is not a licence to delay — the foundations have to be the ones this thing actually needs.

### Lines to keep
When nothing is coming out, do the work success will crowd out.
Waiting divided into a thousand days with a job in each is not waiting.
A result can be tuned. Nothing is what cannot be tuned.
