## Ray Dalio · Weigh the opinion, do not count it
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/dalio/believability/
Source: Principles, the work principles
Tags: Deep read, Ray Dalio, Neither a vote nor a verdict

He rejects the boss deciding and he rejects one person one vote. What replaces them is a weighting, and it needs a record to run on.

### Q: What actually happened?
Two familiar ways to decide badly: autocracy, where the boss rules and information cannot get in, and democracy, where one vote each lets ten amateurs outweigh one expert. Bridgewater runs a third. Everyone gets to speak, and opinions are weighted by the speaker's track record in that particular field. Someone who has called currencies right three times carries more weight on currencies. The foundation is the taping and the public scoring, because without a record a track record cannot be checked. The aim is that the best idea wins whoever it comes from.

### The parts · Equal airtime, unequal weight
Letting everyone speak and letting every opinion count the same are different policies. The first lets information in. The second lets ten hunches outvote one informed judgement. Splitting them is the whole design: speaking is universal, weight is earned inside a field.
e.g. An intern should be able to challenge the technical call, and the two objections should not weigh the same. On what young users like, the weighting may invert.

### The parts · Weight hangs on records, or it hangs on rank
With no record of who judged what and how it turned out, believability quietly becomes a synonym for seniority. That is why the transparency is not a cultural gesture. It is the data layer the weighting runs on, and without it the system reverts to hierarchy.
e.g. Start logging big calls in three columns: prediction, reasoning, outcome. Six months on, the loudest voice and the most accurate one are rarely the same person.

### The parts · Weight resets at the edge of the field
Believability is domain-bound. An investing record does not confer weight on a hiring decision, and technical authority does not confer weight on pricing. The usual failure is halo spill, where the person who is excellent at one thing carries the most weight in every meeting.
e.g. A founder's word on the product is backed by a record. On legal exposure and pay bands, his instinct should queue with everyone else's.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: an important disagreement just got settled by whoever outranked the room.
Ask first: in this specific field, whose track record can actually be looked up? Are we weighing evidence or status?
Where it goes wrong: using believability to freeze the old guard in place so newcomers never build a first record, or invoking the weighting with no log to compute it from.

### Lines to keep
An idea meritocracy is a system in which the best ideas win out.
Everyone speaks. Not everyone's vote weighs the same.
Believability is earned in one field at a time.

========================================================================
## Peter Drucker · The purpose is to create a customer
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/drucker/create-a-customer/
Source: The Practice of Management, 1954
Tags: Deep read, Peter Drucker, Defining the business from the outside in

Ask why a business exists and most people answer profit. Why he called that answer not merely wrong but harmful.

### Q: What actually happened?
The sharpest passage in The Practice of Management: there is only one valid definition of business purpose, to create a customer. Profit is not the purpose. It is the test of validity, the risk premium on the future, a result rather than a cause. Treating it as the purpose turns everyone inward, deciding from the statements. His questions run the other way, because what the customer buys is never a product but the satisfaction of a want. Hence the set every business has to answer again periodically. What is our business? Who is the customer? What does he buy?

### The parts · Profit is the thermometer, not the heart
Profit measures how efficiently you create value for a customer, the way a temperature reports health. Pushing on the thermometer makes nobody healthy. Cut research, squeeze service, raise the price, and the reading improves for a while at the cost of the machine producing it.
e.g. A company that meets its profit target by trimming costs four quarters running finds in the fifth that there is nothing left to trim, and that half its customers left during the year.

### The parts · What the customer buys is nearly always wrong first time
The Cadillac customer, he wrote, buys not transportation but status. He used it to show where the first instinct stops, which is at the product. Push one layer down to what does he solve with this, and the boundary, the rivals and the openings are all redrawn.
e.g. A cafe thinks it sells coffee until it notices the afternoon customer is buying a seat that is neither the office nor home. The rival becomes co-working and the opening becomes power sockets.

### The parts · Create a customer, with the weight on create
Markets are made by businessmen, he said, not by God or nature. Until a want has been satisfied the customer often does not know he has it. Listening is therefore the floor. Identifying what he cannot yet say and turning it into effective demand is the whole ambition here.
e.g. No survey ever asked for overnight delivery. Once somebody built it, it became the pass mark for the trade. Questionnaires collect known wants.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the whole company is organised around a profit number.
Ask first: who is our customer, what is he actually buying, and when were those two answers last updated?
Where it goes wrong: using profit is only a result to excuse years of not making any. A thermometer reading that stays wrong for years means the heart really is in trouble.

### Lines to keep
There is only one valid definition of business purpose: to create a customer.
Profit is not the explanation of business decisions but the test of them.
What is our business? Who is the customer? What does he buy?

========================================================================
## Peter Drucker · Doing efficiently what should not be done
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/drucker/right-things-first/
Source: His 1963 Harvard Business Review article; The Effective Executive
Tags: Deep read, Peter Drucker, Effectiveness comes before efficiency

He pulled apart two words that get used interchangeably. Why a gain in efficiency can conceal an error of direction.

### Q: What actually happened?
In the 1963 article he wrote the warning he is quoted for most: there is surely nothing quite so useless as doing with great efficiency what should not be done at all. Two words come apart. Efficiency is doing things right; effectiveness is doing the right things. One asks how, the other asks whether. With the direction wrong, efficiency is an amplifier, and speed only widens the gap. The Effective Executive is one long argument about choosing: concentrate on the few things that matter, and abandon, systematically, what yesterday's success left behind.

### The parts · Improving efficiency keeps the wrong thing alive
Something that should not be done is easy to cut while it is slow and expensive, because everyone can see it. The moment somebody optimises it into something fast and cheap, it acquires a reason to survive: it runs so well, why kill it. The optimisation becomes its armour.
e.g. A weekly report nobody reads gets automated, and after that nobody proposes killing it. Its cost has fallen below the price of holding one meeting about it.

### The parts · Whether comes before how
Most review agendas open on the details of the proposal, and should this exist at all gets skipped in silence, because it was approved once. The repair is a question in front of every routine: if we were starting today, would we begin this? A no voids the rest of the agenda.
e.g. He called it systematic abandonment. Walk the list of activities once a year asking whether you would enter this today. Most organisations never ask, and carry yesterday on their backs.

### The parts · Busyness is the best disguise an effectiveness problem has
A person doing the wrong thing idly is found out quickly. A person doing the wrong thing at high speed reads to everybody, himself included, as valuable. So diagnose a team by the overlap between what it produces and what the customer needs, not by its efficiency numbers.
e.g. A department at full capacity all year, over target every quarter, finds at the year end that nothing it delivered appears in any customer's reason for buying.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are optimising a process and it is going well.
Ask first: if we were starting from zero today, would we do this at all? If not, what is this optimisation keeping alive?
Where it goes wrong: using the effectiveness point to dismiss all efficiency work. Once the direction is right, efficiency is the entire game. And asking the question daily rather than yearly means nothing ever accumulates.

### Lines to keep
Nothing is so useless as doing efficiently what should not be done.
Efficiency is doing things right; effectiveness is doing the right things.
If we were not in this already, would we go into it now?

========================================================================
## Du Fu · Ten Years in Chang'an
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/du-fu/ten-years-in-changan/
Source: Du Fu, Twenty-two Rhymes Presented to Assistant Director Wei Ji, c. 748
Tags: Deep read, Du Fu, At dawn the rich man's gate, at dusk his horses' dust

What ten years of not getting there actually looks like, and what Du Fu did with the record of it.

### Q: What actually happened?
He arrived in Chang'an at thirty-five to find a post and stayed ten years. He sat the examination, submitted rhapsodies, sent poems to anyone who might help, and got nothing worth having. In a poem to his patron Wei Ji he set down the days as they were: at dawn I knock at the gates of the rich, at dusk I follow the dust of their fat horses; leftover wine, cold scraps, and everywhere a hidden bitterness. Not self-mockery. Bookkeeping. At forty-four he was given charge of an armoury, and the rebellion broke out.

### The parts · A decade with no result still needs a record
The easy way to handle ten years that produced nothing is to never mention them. He wrote down each stretch instead: whose door, what was left in the cup, how it felt. Written down, the decade exists. What later readers actually read is the failing.
e.g. Keep a record of the years that are not working, or they go blank on your own books too.

### The parts · Cold scraps, written straight
He did not write that he was holding to an ideal. He wrote leftover wine and cold meat and a bitterness he kept to himself. A record that flatters nothing survives; the dignified version stops convincing even the person who wrote it.
e.g. Do not write that you are persevering. Write whose door you knocked on today and what it felt like.

### The parts · Not arriving is not the same as not growing
Across those ten years the poems kept changing, from the confidence of a young man to something much heavier. The career went nowhere while the writing moved the whole time, and he did not think of the writing as the main thing.
e.g. Next to the thing that has not worked, look for the thing you have been doing all along that has.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have put years into one thing, always just short, with no date in sight.
Ask first: have I written these years down as they actually were, and is there something beside the failing thing that has been growing?
Where it goes wrong: reading this as ten years of grit will pay off. His career never came good; the other thing did. This is about keeping the record and looking sideways, not about enduring.

### Lines to keep
Ten years came to nothing, and he kept the books year by year.
A record you have flattered stops convincing you a few years later.
Beside the thing that never worked, something else was growing.

========================================================================
## Du Fu · I Came In and Heard Wailing
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/du-fu/the-child-who-starved/
Source: Du Fu, Five Hundred Words on the Road from the Capital to Fengxian, 755
Tags: Deep read, Du Fu, He wrote the thing he least wanted to write

Something happened that you are ashamed of. Whether to say it. Why Du Fu put his son's death into a poem.

### Q: What actually happened?
In the winter of 755 he travelled from the capital back to his family at Fengxian. At the door: I came in and heard wailing; my youngest son had starved to death. He held office. His child had starved. The next two lines are shorter still: shamed to be a father, no food, and so the boy died young. No detour, no explanation, four lines. The poem runs five hundred words and goes on to the suffering of the empire, but it begins with the one thing at home he least wanted to write.

### The parts · Put the worst of it first
The poem is about a country's hunger, and it opens with his own household. Going around your own case to describe other people's is visible to everyone as evasion. Set out the humiliating thing first and the rest of what you say can stand.
e.g. To explain a bad stretch, start with the part you least want to mention. Then people believe the rest.

### The parts · Shamed, and no because after it
War, poverty, a career pursued far from home: all true, and he names none of them. One word, shame, and the responsibility sits with him. Owning it cleanly is what lets a thing finish; a defence keeps it open.
e.g. I did not do it is enough. Everything that comes after because can be left off.

### The parts · Written down, it stops being a hole
He carried this for the rest of his life, but he gave it a place: a formal poem, with lines before it and lines after. Pain that has never been written has no edges. Pain that has been written has somewhere to sit.
e.g. Put the thing you cannot get past into a piece of writing with a beginning and an end.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you did the thing you are most ashamed of, or failed at what mattered most, and have told nobody.
Ask first: if I had to account for this stretch, what is the part I least want to mention, and can I say I did not do it with no because after it?
Where it goes wrong: reading this as a duty to confess in public. He wrote a poem, for the readers a poem has. The point is facing it yourself and not dodging when you speak.

### Lines to keep
Say the thing you least want to say, and the rest is believed.
Owning it cleanly is what lets a thing finish.
Pain never written has no edges; written, it has somewhere to sit.

========================================================================
## Du Fu · Forty-eight, a Hut in Chengdu
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/du-fu/the-thatched-hut/
Source: Du Fu leaves office, 759; Song of My Thatched Hut Wrecked by the Autumn Wind, 761; Thinking of Li Bai at the Sky's End, 759
Tags: Deep read, Du Fu, Build a roof, not a position

Is it too late to begin again in middle age. What Du Fu did first after he walked away, and what he wrote.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 759 he resigned his small post at Huazhou and took the family southwest through Qinzhou and Tonggu, nearly starving on the road. They reached Chengdu in 760, and with help from friends he put up a thatched hut by the Huanhua stream. Forty-eight years old, a family, one roof. The next autumn the wind tore it off and he wrote a poem about that. The best of his poetry belongs to the ten years after this. Writing to Li Bai that year he said something that reads like his own case: good writing hates a life that goes well.

### The parts · Starting again means a roof, not a rank
The first thing he did in Chengdu was build somewhere to live, not look for another post. People rebuilding in middle age reach first for the title, the standing, the old level. He took a place where a day could be lived. The desk comes after the roof.
e.g. The first step in starting over is the smallest setup a life runs on, not the return of your old standing.

### The parts · Good writing hates a life that goes well
The line is an observation, not consolation: his own best work came out of his hardest decade. Not that suffering improves you. That in those years he had nothing else to put his strength into, so all of it went into one thing.
e.g. When everything else is gone, the one thing left gets all of your strength. That is why it turns out well.

### The parts · Forty-eight was not late, it was out of options
By the life expectancy of his time he was already old at Chengdu. Precisely because the official road had closed for good, poetry became the only road. The verdict too late is usually produced by an option you are still holding in reserve.
e.g. When it feels too late, check whether you are still keeping a way back and measuring the new road against it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: middle of your life, the road you were on has closed, and starting again looks too late.
Ask first: am I after a roof or after my old position, and am I still holding a way back to measure the new road against?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as a case for wiping the slate in middle age. He was forced to it, not choosing it, and nearly starved on the way. This is about the order you rebuild in and where too late comes from.

### Lines to keep
Rebuild the smallest setup a life runs on, not your old standing.
When everything is gone, the one thing left takes all your strength.
Too late usually means a way back is still in reserve.

========================================================================
## Duan Yongping · Do the right thing, then do the thing right
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/duan-yongping/right-things-done-right/
Source: Collected public interviews and written answers
Tags: Deep read, Duan Yongping, The two halves have an order

He has repeated one sentence for decades. Why its halves cannot be swapped, and what the stop-doing list is for.

### Q: What actually happened?
He compresses running a business into one line: do the right thing, and do the thing right. The order is the part he insists on. The first matters far more, because doing a thing right is a question of skill and can be learned slowly, while doing the right thing is a question of choice, and once that is wrong, effort makes it worse. The discipline that goes with it: the moment you find it is wrong, stop and change, and whatever that costs is the smallest cost available. To find the right things he keeps a stop-doing list.

### The parts · An error of sign cannot be rescued by magnitude
The order is arithmetic. Direction is the sign and execution is the magnitude. With the sign negative, stronger execution only drives the number further down. So review whether a thing should be done before reviewing whether it can be done well.
e.g. A team polishing the wrong product to a superb finish has built a motorway to the wrong destination. The better the road, the larger the loss.

### The parts · Count the whole bill on stopping now
Money already spent, face, promises made in public: all of it makes stopping look enormously expensive. His arithmetic stretches the timeline instead. Today's cost is fixed and known; the cost of dragging on compounds and is unknown. That is why any cost today is the smallest one.
e.g. Every quarter a wrong direction survives pulls in another cohort, another budget round and a few more public promises. The cut in three months is twice as thick.

### The parts · A stop-doing list is more reliable than a to-do list
What you should do is full of uncertainty. What you should not do can be derived from your principles and stays stable for years. The list also saves judgement: when something on it arrives there is nothing to argue and no meeting to call.
e.g. Write down your three no matter how profitable, never rules. Half your future opportunity reviews will end in ten seconds, and the hours saved cover looking properly at the other half.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something you are deep into, and you half suspect the direction is wrong.
Ask first: if I were starting from zero today, would I still do this? If not, which costs less — stopping today, or stopping in three months?
Where it goes wrong: turning do the right thing into a slogan and never writing down how you judge right from wrong. Or using stop at once as a licence for three-minute enthusiasms, in which case nothing ever gets deep.

### Lines to keep
Do the right thing, and then do the thing right.
Find it is wrong, stop at once; any cost is the smallest.
What you should not do is stable. What you should do is not.

========================================================================
## Duan Yongping · Dare to be last
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/duan-yongping/dare-to-be-last/
Source: Collected public interviews and written answers
Tags: Deep read, Duan Yongping, Come first from behind

Everybody races to launch first; he says openly that he aims to be last. Under what conditions late is an advantage.

### Q: What actually happened?
His product philosophy runs against the fashion: dare to be last, then come first from behind. The reasoning is plain. When a category first appears nobody knows whether the demand is real, which approach works, or where the holes are, and the pioneers answer those questions with their own money. Enter once the answers are visible and build it better. From study machines to DVD players to phones, his companies originated almost nothing and outlasted most of the originators. He states the condition too: late does not mean slow. From the day you enter, quality has to be right immediately.

### The parts · Pioneers pay the tuition; the market remembers the graduate
Early mortality in a new category is enormous. The cost of educating users, the cost of trial and error, the cost of an immature supply chain are all paid by whoever went first. The follower skips the entire tuition bill and competes on demand that has already been proved.
e.g. Music players, smartphones, electric cars: in each category the eventual winner was not the inventor. First is a word that appears mostly on headstones.

### The parts · The price of arriving late is having the better thing
Dare to be last carries a brutal precondition. On the day you enter, your version has to be visibly better than what is already standing, or late is merely late. The whole burden shifts from thinking of it early to building it well, and none of that work can be skipped.
e.g. Waiting until the track is clear and then shipping something merely adequate is not coming first from behind. It is handing the pioneer a validation report.

### The parts · The waiting years are preparation, not idling
What you do while you are behind decides what you are on the day you enter: watch every hole the pioneers fall into, get the supply chain and the team ready, work out exactly where your version will differ. A company that only watches arrives empty-handed when the moment ripens.
e.g. While others burn money teaching the market, build what they have no time for: quality control, a service network, cash. On entry day those are the ammunition.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a new category has caught fire and you cannot decide whether to move now or wait.
Ask first: how far has the demand actually been proved? If I wait, what specifically am I building during the wait? On the day I enter, in what one respect will I be better than whoever is already there?
Where it goes wrong: using dare to be last as cover for watching forever. He waited for clarity, not for the thing to be over. And some windows open once only, which calls for a different game entirely.

### Lines to keep
Dare to be last, then come first from behind.
The contest is not who thought of it first, but who builds it best.
Late does not mean slow. Entry day has to be finished.

========================================================================
## Carol Dweck · Praise the process, not the talent
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/dweck/praise-the-process/
Source: Mindset; the praise experiments
Tags: Deep read, Carol Dweck, Praising cleverness makes people avoid challenge

One sentence of praise changes what a child picks next. This piece is about where the change happens.

### Q: What actually happened?
After a set of problems she gave students one of two kinds of praise: one group heard 'you're so clever', the other 'you worked hard'. Offered a choice of the next set, the ones praised for cleverness took the easier one more often, the ones praised for effort took the harder one. Her reading: praise for talent makes people avoid challenge; praise for process makes them accept it. Talent praise turns results into proof of talent, so every later challenge becomes a threat to the self. The watershed is the moment of failure — information in one mindset, verdict in the other.

### The parts · Praise the specific move, not the label
'You're clever' is a label, and labels need protecting. 'You went back through every wrong answer' is a move, and moves can be repeated. The test is simple: can they do this praise again next time?
e.g. They did well: ask how they prepared. Don't say they've got a good brain. The first is repeatable, the second can only be defended.

### The parts · The moment of failure decides the direction
In good weather the two mindsets look identical. The watershed is the instant something fails: one reads it as 'I can't', the other as 'that approach can't'. The difference isn't the intensity of the feeling. It's whether they go looking for the cause.
e.g. A rejected proposal: the person who asks 'which part doesn't hold' fixes it. The one who decides they're not suited never proposes again.

### The parts · The word 'yet'
Replacing 'failed' with 'not yet passed' turns a result into a point in time. The small change works because it moves attention from what level I am to where I've got to.
e.g. Change 'I can't write' to 'I can't write yet'. One word decides whether the next sentence looks for a method or an excuse.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: giving feedback to a child or a report.
Ask first: is this praising talent or a specific move? Could they do it again next time?
Where it goes wrong: turning process praise into a mechanical formula and never mentioning a genuinely good result — that reads as being fobbed off.

### Lines to keep
Praise for talent makes people avoid challenge. Praise for process doesn't.
In a growth mindset failure is information. In a fixed one it's a verdict.
Use 'not yet' instead of 'can't'.

========================================================================
## Carol Dweck · The effect is much smaller than the popular story
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/dweck/effect-size/
Source: Large-scale replications in recent years; corrections to the original claims
Tags: Deep read, Carol Dweck, The boundary worth drawing

The concept got told as a master key. This piece is about how big it actually is.

### Q: What actually happened?
This layer has to be said plainly: large-scale replications in recent years find the effect of mindset interventions far smaller than the original book conveyed, close to zero in some populations, with the clearer benefits concentrated among disadvantaged students. That doesn't overturn the concept. It overturns the reading that a change of attitude changes everything. It's a real but mild factor, not the switch that decides outcomes. Treating it as a master key means ignoring resources, teaching, foundations and rest — all heavier variables — and putting the whole responsibility on the person's attitude.

### The parts · Mild and real, not a switch
The effect exists and its magnitude is far below the popular story. The correct use is as one improvable factor among many, not the main explanation for success or failure.
e.g. A child struggling: look at teaching, foundations and sleep before attributing it to the wrong attitude.

### The parts · Blaming attitude is the easiest and least fair move
'You just don't believe in yourself enough' converts a systemic difficulty into a defect of character. It is particularly unfair to people short of resources — what they lack is usually not belief.
e.g. Telling an unsupported student to have a growth mindset says the difficulty is something they imagined.

### The parts · Knowing the boundary is what makes it usable
Once you admit the effect is mild the concept becomes more usable: it's worth the cost of one sentence — change how you praise, add the word 'yet' — and not worth a training programme and slogans on the wall.
e.g. Changing your own wording is cheap. Spending heavily on mindset training and expecting results will disappoint.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: someone is explaining a result as a problem of attitude.
Ask first: have the heavier variables — method, resources, foundations, rest — been checked? If not, attitude is the laziest and least accurate attribution available.
Where it goes wrong: dropping it entirely because the effect is mild. Changing how you praise costs almost nothing and is still worth doing.

### Lines to keep
Replications find the effect far smaller than the book conveyed.
The clearer benefits are concentrated among disadvantaged students.
Treat it as a master key and you'll ignore the heavier variables.

========================================================================
## Albert Einstein · Changing the question
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/einstein/formulating-the-problem/
Source: The Evolution of Physics (with Leopold Infeld)
Tags: Deep read, Albert Einstein, The answer's ceiling is set by the question

The line comes from a book he wrote, not from a quotation card. What matters is how he used it himself.

### Q: What actually happened?
In The Evolution of Physics, written with Leopold Infeld, he put it plainly: the formulation of a problem is often more essential than its solution, which may be merely a matter of mathematical or experimental skill. Raising new questions and looking at old problems from a new angle takes imagination, and marks real advance. He is his own example. At sixteen he asked what he would see if he chased a beam of light at the speed of light. The question had no legitimate place in the physics of the time. A decade later it had grown into special relativity.

### The parts · The ceiling of an answer is set by the question
Inside a badly framed question, the most perfect answer is only an elegant error. Lorentz and Poincaré were not worse mathematicians; they were circling how the ether explains the experiment. He asked whether time is the same for every observer. Same facts, different question, and the field moves.
e.g. How do we lower support costs optimises towards cheaper support. Why does anyone have to call support may optimise support away.

### The parts · A good question usually sounds naive first
Chasing a beam of light sounds like a child's daydream, and a trained specialist does not ask it — their training is precisely what makes only the field's legitimate questions occur to them. So the ability to change the question often runs inversely to seniority.
e.g. The new starter asks why this step needs sign-off and everyone smiles. Three months later the step is gone, and that question is why.

### The parts · Push the old question to its wall before you change it
He did not walk around the old problem; he drove it to a contradiction first. What the thought experiment exposed was the conflict between Maxwell's equations and Newtonian space and time. Changing the question is not a licence to escape a hard one — without the wall it is just changing the subject.
e.g. Before saying we should reframe this, show the specific case where the current framing has to fail. No case, no reframe.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the team has been solving one problem for a long time, the solutions keep getting more elaborate and the returns keep shrinking.
Ask first: the question we are answering — who set it, and under what assumptions?
Where it goes wrong: using reframe it as a phrase for avoiding difficulty; or getting senior enough that only the field's legitimate questions still occur to you.

### Lines to keep
Formulating a problem is often more essential than solving it.
New questions and new angles on old problems require imagination.
What would I see if I chased a beam of light?

## Albert Einstein · The patent office years
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/einstein/patent-office/
Source: Bern, 1905; the 1929 Saturday Evening Post interview
Tags: Deep read, Albert Einstein, What the margin buys you

In 1905 he published four papers that changed physics. His job title was technical examiner, third class.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1905, at twenty-six, after being turned down repeatedly for academic posts, he was a third-class examiner at the patent office in Bern. That year he published on the photoelectric effect, Brownian motion, special relativity, and the equivalence of mass and energy. He was flat about his own gifts — no special talent, only passionately curious. To a reporter in 1929 he said the more famous thing: imagination is more important than knowledge; knowledge is limited, imagination encircles the world. The patent work took him a few hours. The rest of the day had no supervisor to please and no school to belong to.

### The parts · The margin costs you resources and pays you in owing nobody
A young person inside the academy builds increments on a supervisor's paradigm, because posts, publications and funding all hang from that chain. An outsider had no sunk cost in the ether and could drop it without betraying anyone. Position decides which ideas you can afford.
e.g. The most radical products in an industry often come from outside it — not because outsiders are cleverer, but because they owe nobody in it, so turning the table over carries no social cost.

### The parts · Examining patents was accidental training
His day job was judging whether assorted inventions actually worked — a great many of them electromagnetic devices and schemes for synchronising signals, which is the engineering version of the relativity problem. An unrelated way of earning a living gave him dozens of daily reps at does this mechanism hold up.
e.g. A post that looks like a detour is often laying the foundation for something else. Instinct for users built on a support desk, a nose for holes built in audit.

### The parts · Curiosity only counts with the other word attached
The weight of his self-description is not on curious, it is on passionately. Physics after hours was not a hobby but a second shift kept without fail. A marginal position supplies freedom and supplies nothing else; what turned the freedom into four papers was intensity nobody was supervising.
e.g. People whose side project becomes something share one trait, and it is not better ideas. Free evenings are common; the intensity is rare.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are outside the important room and you read that as a disadvantage.
Ask first: who does this position let me owe nothing to? Which ideas can I afford that insiders cannot?
Where it goes wrong: treating the margin as a guarantee of output — taking the freedom without the second shift; or learning the room's taboos in advance in order to be let in.

### Lines to keep
Imagination is more important than knowledge.
I have no special talent. I am only passionately curious.
Knowledge is limited. Imagination encircles the world.

## Epictetus · Sort it before you feel anything
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/epictetus/dichotomy/
Source: Enchiridion 1 and 8
Tags: Deep read, Epictetus, The handbook opens with a filing rule, not with advice

The one Stoic line everybody knows, put back where it starts: as the first operation, before the appraisal and before the feeling.

### Q: What actually happened?
He was born a slave and he was lame; the tradition says his master broke the leg. He wrote nothing — the Handbook is a student's notes. Its first line is a filing rule: some things are in our control and others not. Things in our control are opinion, pursuit, desire, aversion, in a word whatever are our own actions; things not in our control are body, property, reputation, command. Chapter eight turns the rule into a daily instruction. Demand not that events should happen as you wish, but wish them to happen as they do happen, and you will go on well.

### The parts · The sorting comes before the feeling
The value of the rule is its position in the sequence. It runs first — before the appraisal, before the reaction, before the misery. A bad thing arrives: ask which half it belongs to. What is yours gets the rest of your hours, and what is not gets none of them.
e.g. The platform rejected the release. Their rules are not yours; the quality of the appeal is. Two hours of fury, or two hours on the appeal.

### The parts · Most suffering is a filing error
Treating what is not yours as yours produces futility and resentment. Treating what is yours as not yours produces excuses and helplessness. The two errors run in opposite directions and have one cause: nobody did the sorting before the feeling started.
e.g. Losing sleep over the economy while writing off your own pricing as what the market does. The same person usually makes both errors in the same week.

### The parts · He put the body outside the line
This is the radical step, and the one the productivity version quietly drops: health and the body itself are filed under not yours. His leg is the evidence. The violence belonged to his master; the view he took of the leg belonged to him. The harder the line, the cleaner the ground left.
e.g. Illness, redundancy, betrayal — the events themselves sit outside. That is not resignation. The inside half becomes wholly yours only once the line exists.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something bad has happened and you keep going over it.
Ask first: which part of this is mine? Which side of the line have my hours actually been going to?
Where it goes wrong: using none of it is mine to drop the part that is; or making the line an excuse for helping nobody.

### Lines to keep
Some things are in our control and others not.
Things in our control are opinion, pursuit, desire, aversion.
Wish them to happen as they do happen, and you will go on well.

========================================================================
## Epictetus · Not the thing, the view you took of it
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/epictetus/judgments-not-things/
Source: Enchiridion 5 and 20
Tags: Deep read, Epictetus, Between the event and the pain there is a step you added

Handbook five is two sentences long. The question worth asking is why it reaches for the death of Socrates as its example.

### Q: What actually happened?
Men are disturbed, not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things. His example is death. Death is nothing terrible, or it would have seemed so to Socrates; what is terrible is the notion that death is terrible. So when we are hindered or disturbed, let us never attribute it to others, but to ourselves. Chapter twenty names the mechanism: what affronts you is not the man who gives the abuse but the view you take of it. So endeavour not to be hurried away with the appearance.

### The parts · There is a step between the event and the feeling
One event lands completely differently on two people, which means the feeling is not produced by the event. Something gets added in between: your reading of it. That step normally runs automatically and invisibly. Making it visible is what gives you somewhere to intervene.
e.g. One curt email. The first reader finds hostility in it, the second finds a man in a hurry. Same email, different manufacture.

### The parts · Gaining time and respite is the whole technique
The operational half of chapter twenty is its last clause: delay the response. Because the interpreting step is automatic, the only thing that catches it is a gap. A few seconds is enough for the automatic reading to be seen, and once seen it can be swapped.
e.g. Answer the message that enraged you twenty minutes later. What you would have said is almost never what you say.

### The parts · Blaming your own opinion is taking control, not taking blame
Blame yourself reads as self-attack, and it runs the other way. While the source of the pain sits inside another person, you can only wait for that person to change. Move it into your own reading and you have, for the first time, somewhere to put your hands.
e.g. He disrespected me, so I am hurt — the handle is his. I read that line as disrespect — the handle is back, and not one fact has moved.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: one sentence, or one incident, is still running hours later.
Ask first: is the pain coming from the thing, or from the reading I gave it? Try a second reading — do the facts still hold?
Where it goes wrong: using it to deny real harm and let the person who did it off; or turning blame your own opinion into one more way of attacking yourself.

### Lines to keep
It is not he who gives abuse or blows, who affronts.
Let us never attribute it to others, but to ourselves.
Gain time and respite, and you will more easily command yourself.

========================================================================
## Anders Ericsson · Practising what you can already do is rest
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/ericsson/deliberate-practice/
Source: The Berlin violin study, 1993; Peak
Tags: Deep read, Anders Ericsson, Stay at the edge of what you cannot do

Two people practise three hours each. One improves and one does not. This page is about what the hours contained.

### Q: What actually happened?
Ericsson and his colleagues sorted the violin students at the Berlin academy of music by how good they were, and the top group had indeed accumulated more hours. The interesting difference was inside the hours. The average students played through pieces they could already play, enjoying the fluency. The best ones spent their time on the few bars they could not play, stopping and repeating and stopping again. Purposeful practice happens outside the comfort zone, and it needs feedback that arrives while you can still use it. Fluency feels like progress. It is the sensation of not improving.

### The parts · Comfortable practice is a performance for yourself
Fluency is a signal of competence already reached, not of competence being built. The test is blunt: how much of the hour did you spend failing and going back? If none of it, you were not practising, you were rehearsing.
e.g. An hour of playing pieces you know is an hour of listening to yourself. The three bars you always fumble are the practice.

### The parts · Blind repetition makes the wrong version stick
If you cannot tell which attempt was wrong, repeating it only makes the wrong version more automatic. This is why thirty years of driving does not produce a better driver: nobody has ever told him which turn was bad. Feedback ranks above hours.
e.g. Writing more does not make you write better. Someone has to say which paragraph they stopped reading, or you leave it a week and become that someone.

### The parts · Experts run on mental representations
Ericsson's term for what a specialist actually owns is a mental representation: a detailed internal model of the domain. A chess player sees a position, not pieces. Models get built by failing against real problems, and cannot be read into place.
e.g. Watching a hundred games buys impressions. Playing ten and going back through each one afterwards builds the model.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have practised for months and cannot see the difference.
Ask first: how much of the last hour went on something you could not do, and who told you which part was wrong?
Where it goes wrong: hearing it has to hurt as grind until you break — his subjects practised in short intense blocks and slept more than anybody.

### Lines to keep
If you never push yourself beyond your comfort zone, you will never improve.
Repetition without feedback engraves the error instead of removing it.
The best students spent their hours on the bars they could not play.

## Anders Ericsson · Ten thousand hours is a misreading
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/ericsson/not-ten-thousand-hours/
Source: Ericsson's own corrections to the ten-thousand-hour rule; Peak
Tags: Deep read, Anders Ericsson, He spent years saying so

The number travelled much further than the research it came from. This page is about what it got wrong.

### Q: What actually happened?
The rule comes from Outliers, not from Ericsson, and he spent the rest of his life correcting it. Ten thousand was an average for the best group at age twenty, and half of that group had not reached it. Thresholds differ enormously between fields. Worse, the number quietly replaced the finding. What the research showed is that the manner of practice decides the level; hours are only correlated with it. A demanding result became a comfortable permit: put the time in and you qualify. That is precisely the half he was arguing against.

### The parts · Ten years of experience, or one year ten times
Time served is not skill. Most roles stop generating new difficulty after the first year or two, and the years after that are repetition wearing a longer title. The honest question about anybody's growth is when they were last out of their depth.
e.g. Ask a candidate what they could not do a year ago and can do now. It carries more information than the number of years on the CV.

### The parts · The threshold is different in every field
Deliberate practice is strongest where the rules hold still and the feedback comes back fast: instruments, chess, surgery. Where results arrive late and luck is loud, hours explain much less. One number cannot cross those boundaries.
e.g. Applying put the hours in to investing is the expensive version of the mistake. The feedback is slow and mostly noise, so repetition alone builds nothing.

### The parts · Change the method before you add the hours
The practical damage of the rule is that it sends people to spend more rather than to practise differently. When you are stuck, the variable with room left in it is the structure of the session, not its length.
e.g. Three years of flashcards and no progress will not be fixed by a fourth. Using the language badly in front of someone who corrects you will.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have put a long stretch into something and the results are flat.
Ask first: when were you last genuinely stuck? How fast does this field answer you back? Is the fix more hours or a different session?
Where it goes wrong: using the misreading as permission to stop accumulating — he wanted high-quality hours over years, not fewer of them.

### Lines to keep
There is nothing special or magical about ten thousand hours.
The manner of practice decides the level. Hours are only correlated.
Growth shows up as when you were last out of your depth.

## Excellent Sheep · Good at hurdles, bad at choosing a road
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/excellent-sheep/hurdles/
Source: Excellent Sheep
Tags: Deep read, Excellent Sheep, Two completely different abilities

Why people who succeeded at every stage go blank the moment the standards stop. What they never practised.

### Q: What actually happened?
Deresiewicz taught at Yale for ten years and sat on admissions. What he saw was young people extraordinarily good at clearing set hurdles — grades, competitions, internships, the CV — and unable to say what they wanted. They were superb at clearing hurdles and could not tell you where they were going. His typical scene: an outstanding student who has no idea why she chose the subject, only that she had to be best at it. He insists this isn't a personal failing. Someone optimised since childhood to meet every standard has never once practised deciding what matters.

### The parts · The two abilities don't substitute
'Be the best at this' and 'decide what's worth doing' are different skills. The first is drilled constantly inside any evaluation system. The second can only be trained where there is no correct answer — so the smoother the run, the likelier the second is blank.
e.g. The drop from star student to lost graduate usually isn't about ability. It's the first time nobody set the standard.

### The parts · Never having failed makes failure unimaginable
The price of an unbroken run is no experience of failing, so failure gets imagined as catastrophic. The result is avoiding anything you might not be good at, and a range that narrows year by year.
e.g. Not switching to the thing you actually want because 'I've built up experience here.' The real reason is being a beginner again.

### The parts · The target is the system, not the students
The book reads easily as blaming young people for lacking independence. The author's subject is the filtering machinery that trains them this way — every step rational, and the sum a life with no direction.
e.g. Fine for self-examination, useless as a lecture. Who set the hurdles and who benefits is the real question.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you know exactly what counts as doing well, and can't answer what you want.
Ask first: is this choice what I want, or is it simply the next hurdle? When did I last do something with no standard attached?
Where it goes wrong: using it to write off effort and achievement. The problem isn't being excellent. It's only being excellent.

### Lines to keep
Superb at clearing hurdles, and unable to say where they were going.
Never allowed to fail, you imagine failure as unsurvivable.
Every step rational, and the sum is a life with no direction.

## Excellent Sheep · Give yourself time with no scoreboard
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/excellent-sheep/no-scoreboard/
Source: Excellent Sheep
Tags: Deep read, Excellent Sheep, Any standard becomes a thing to optimise

How to find out what you actually want. The condition that has to be true first.

### Q: What actually happened?
Deresiewicz's prescription isn't a new major or a new job. It's a stretch of time with no evaluation attached — doing one thing that isn't scored, for long enough. The reasoning is direct: only when nobody is grading you do you find out what you actually want. Where a standard exists, people optimise it automatically, and the optimising drowns out the signal about whether you want to do this at all. The problem isn't that you can't think it through. It's that no environment lets the question surface.

### The parts · A score existing means you'll chase it
This isn't weak will, it's the default. Wherever there's a comparable metric, attention slides to it. So answering 'what do I want' requires temporarily leaving the places that have metrics.
e.g. A hobby starts taking commissions and counting followers, and quickly becomes a second job. Not corruption — a score.

### The parts · It only works if it's long enough
A few days tests novelty. The signal that counts is whether you still want to continue after the novelty has gone and it's got a bit boring. He's describing months, not a couple of weekends.
e.g. Six months on something nobody is watching produces better judgement than any careers course.

### The parts · Separate 'I want this' from 'this is the next hurdle'
This is the usable daily test. Facing an opportunity, ask whether what draws you is the content itself or the fact that it's the obvious next step on the current track. The second disguises itself very well as the first.
e.g. A promotion on the table: separate wanting the work from not wanting to look like you've stalled.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you're making a choice about direction.
Ask first: is it the content that draws me, or is it simply the next hurdle? Have I done anything unscored lately?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as a reason to quit and wander. He's describing carving out an unscored space, not demolishing the structure.

### Lines to keep
Only when nobody is grading you do you find out what you want.
Wherever a comparable metric exists, attention slides to it.
Still willing after the novelty is gone — that's the signal.

## Fan Li · In a drought, stock boats
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/fan-li/stock-the-opposite/
Source: Records of the Grand Historian, Biographies of the Money-Makers
Tags: Deep read, Fan Li, Buy it when nobody wants it

When is a thing cheapest? At the moment everybody agrees it is useless.

### Q: What actually happened?
Among the strategies Fan Li's teacher gave the state of Yue is one very simple rule: in drought, stock boats; in flood, stock carts; and so be ready for the shortage. In a drought nobody wants a boat and the price is lowest; after drought comes flood, and then a boat is dearest. He generalised it into a law of price: examine surplus and shortage and you know dear from cheap. What is dear to the extreme turns down; what is cheap to the extreme turns up. So sell the dear as if it were dung, and take the cheap as if it were pearls.

### The parts · Buy when the demand has gone
Price is set by present demand; value by future demand. The entire difficulty of this rule is that at the moment of buying, every visible piece of evidence says the thing is worthless. A decision with no evidence behind it is exactly what the method requires.
e.g. Hiring during layoffs, signing long deals at the coldest point, starting a project nobody works on — each done without any external confirmation.

### The parts · The cycle is the premise. Not everything comes back
Drought and flood alternate, which is what makes stocking boats correct. If a decline is structural and won't return, buying cheap is catching a falling knife. Before using the rule you have to judge: is this a cycle or an ending?
e.g. Capacity at the bottom of a cycle is worth buying. Capacity replaced by a technology isn't, at any price. Today the two price curves look identical.

### The parts · Money has to keep moving
There's a line of his that gets skipped: money should flow like water. What you stockpile is goods, not capital. Locking your funds in one place to wait for an appreciation is no different from burying them in the ground.
e.g. Everything pressed into one appreciating asset means that even when the call is right, you lost every option in between.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something is cheap right now and everyone says it has no future.
Ask first: is it cheap because the cycle is at a low, or because it has genuinely been replaced?
Where it goes wrong: bottom-fishing a structural decline as though it were a cyclical low; or being right and still locking every last resource inside it.

### Lines to keep
In drought, stock boats. In flood, stock carts.
Sell the dear like dung. Take the cheap like pearls.
Money should keep moving, like water.

========================================================================
## Fan Li · Long neck, beak like a bird
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/fan-li/leave-at-the-top/
Source: Records of the Grand Historian, House of Goujian; Biographies of the Money-Makers
Tags: Deep read, Fan Li, Read the ending off the person

He left the moment Yue destroyed Wu, at the highest point. What he was reading when he decided.

### Q: What actually happened?
With Wu destroyed, Fan Li left at once and took a boat onto the lakes. He wrote to Wen Zhong, who stayed, and his reasoning was not about the situation but about the man: the king of Yue has a long neck and a beak like a bird's; you can share hardship with him, you cannot share ease. Wen Zhong stayed, and was later ordered to kill himself. Fan Li changed his name, went into trade in Qi, made a vast fortune, was offered the chancellorship, returned the seal, gave the fortune away, started again at Tao, and made and dispersed a fortune three times.

### The parts · Reading the person beats reading the situation
Situations change; a person's construction doesn't. Fan Li's judgement wasn't 'this is dangerous now' but 'here is what this man becomes when things go well' — a judgement that already held before Wu fell. It was just not yet needed.
e.g. How a partner behaves when money is short tells you nothing about how he behaves when it's divided. Watch how he treats people below him while he's winning.

### The parts · Sharing hardship and sharing ease are different capacities
The precision is in separating two relationships. People who carried something together can't necessarily divide something together. The first is held by a common enemy; the second demands restraint in dividing gains — far rarer, and only visible after the win.
e.g. Teams that were fiercely united while building often break at the first real payout. The people didn't change. The test did.

### The parts · Letting go is harder than accumulating
He built a great fortune three times and gave it away three times. This wasn't a performance of generosity — returning the chancellor's seal in Qi, starting again at Tao, each time he abandoned a position already in hand. Many can accumulate. Almost nobody puts down what they already hold.
e.g. Handing over the business you built to start an uncertain line is far harder than minding the mature one, even though everyone knows it will decline.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something big has just succeeded and you're weighing what position comes next.
Ask first: the people who did this with me — what are they like at the dividing stage? Have I seen it?
Where it goes wrong: reading only whether the situation is favourable and never the construction of the people; or treating letting go as a posture while actually releasing nothing.

### Lines to keep
You can share hardship with him. You cannot share ease.
Three times he made a fortune, and three times gave it away.
The construction of a person doesn't change. The situation does.

========================================================================
## Feng Dao · Only the emperor can save them
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/feng-dao/only-you-can-save/
Source: The Comprehensive Mirror, Annals of the Later Jin
Tags: Deep read, Feng Dao, If you cannot change it, change the sentence

The Khitan have destroyed the dynasty and the plain expects a massacre. What can a man with no army do in that room?

### Q: What actually happened?
The Later Jin fell, the Khitan ruler Yelu Deguang entered Kaifeng, and the population faced plunder and slaughter. Feng Dao went to see him. Yelu Deguang asked: the common people of the empire, how can they be saved? Feng Dao answered: at this moment the Buddha could come again and not save them; only the emperor can save them. The Comprehensive Mirror records that the people of the plain escaped destruction because of that one sentence. It contains no argument at all. It re-describes a decision as something only he is large enough to make.

### The parts · When persuasion is impossible, change what the act is
Preaching mercy to a man who has just conquered you asks him to concede that he is in the wrong. Feng Dao argued nothing. He moved stopping the killing from you must back down to only you are able to. Same action, and one of them is a display of power.
e.g. Asking a dominant partner to soften terms on grounds of fairness does nothing. Describing the same concession as something only an operator of their size can afford runs at a different rate.

### The parts · With no chips left, wording is the variable
He had no troops, no territory and nothing to trade. In an asymmetry that complete, the phrasing is the only thing still under his control. This is not a belief in clever talk. It is a reminder that even at zero leverage there remains one place where work can be done.
e.g. With no bargaining power, the one lever left is re-describing the options in front of the other side. It shifts nothing about strength and can still shift which option they take.

### The parts · What he preserved was people, not his name
Going to meet the conqueror at all was enough to earn him centuries of contempt, and it duly did. He chose an outcome that can be counted, the number of people not killed, and gave up an abstract one that belonged to himself.
e.g. Compromising upwards to protect your team usually looks spineless from outside the team. Whether to do it depends on which of the two you are treating as the real result.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the other side holds everything and you have nothing to trade.
Ask first: can the thing you want them to do be re-described as something only they are in a position to afford?
Where it goes wrong: arguing principle when you hold no cards; or treating wording as generally powerful, when it is the last resort available only after the substantive options are gone.

### Lines to keep
The Buddha could come again and not save them. Only the emperor can.
The people of the plain were spared because of one sentence.
Keep the square inch of the heart free of evil and stand among tigers.

## Feng Dao · The old man of everlasting joy
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/feng-dao/the-long-happy-old-man/
Source: An Account of the Old Man of Everlasting Joy; the New History of the Five Dynasties; The Comprehensive Mirror
Tags: Deep read, Feng Dao, A thousand years of argument

He served four dynasties and ten emperors and named himself after contentment. The question is where his accusers and his defenders each stand.

### Q: What actually happened?
In his seventies he wrote An Account of the Old Man of Everlasting Joy, listing every office he had held, in a calm tone, saying that thinking over beginnings and ends he understood the way of heaven better. Ouyang Xiu called him a man without shame. Sima Guang called him the worst of treacherous ministers. Wang Anshi thought him a man at the level of a buddha, and Su Shi said he could bend himself to keep people safe. A thousand years, and both sides cite the same facts.

### The parts · The quarrel is about the object of loyalty
Ouyang Xiu's standard is loyalty to one house. Feng Dao's is loyalty to the people under the administration. The identical conduct is shameless serial betrayal under the first and steady adaptation under the second. The argument runs a thousand years because it was never about the facts.
e.g. Whether a colleague joining a competitor is betrayal or ordinary movement depends on whether you think people owe the company or the craft. Both views are internally consistent.

### The parts · In a broken order, continuity is the scarce thing
Fifty-three years produced five dynasties and fourteen emperors, an average reign shorter than a decade. At that frequency, a man who preserved the administration, the tax registers and the un-sacked cities through every handover was supplying something rare. His critics wrote from inside a restored order.
e.g. Three chief executives in four years, and the person who stayed through all of them and kept payroll running gets called both unprincipled and indispensable.

### The parts · And he prevented nothing
The defence has a limit. He saved many people and altered not one succession, and left no institution behind. His method was minimising loss inside a settled frame, and the ceiling of that method is that it produces nothing new. On this point Ouyang Xiu was right.
e.g. Someone who always optimises within the existing constraints can make every single year come out tolerably, and look back after ten to find no constraint has moved.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: somebody's choices leave you unable to say whether that was slipperiness or good sense.
Ask first: what is the thing he is loyal to, and judged against that thing, has his behaviour been consistent?
Where it goes wrong: judging choices made inside a collapse by the standards of the order that came afterwards; and equally, concluding that optimising inside the given frame costs nothing.

### Lines to keep
Thinking over beginnings and ends, I understand the way of heaven better.
Ouyang Xiu called him shameless. Sima Guang called him the worst of traitors.
Five dynasties, eight surnames, watched the way an innkeeper watches guests.

## Richard Feynman · The first person not to fool is you
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/feynman/dont-fool-yourself/
Source: Caltech commencement address, 1974; Appendix F to the Challenger report, 1986
Tags: Deep read, Richard Feynman, And you are the easiest one

He put this ahead of every method in science. This page is about why the first line of defence points inward.

### Q: What actually happened?
At the 1974 Caltech commencement he gave the graduates one rule and called it the first principle: you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool. Twelve years later he sat on the Challenger commission, asked for a glass of ice water at a televised hearing, clamped a piece of the O-ring rubber, dropped it in for a few seconds and took it out. It did not spring back. NASA had hundreds of pages arguing the launch was sound. His appendix said reality must take precedence over public relations.

### The parts · The bias sits wherever your interest sits
Fooling yourself takes no dishonesty, only a stake. Wherever you would prefer a conclusion, your efficiency at finding supporting evidence rises sharply. So the check is not how honest you feel. It is whether the answer pays you.
e.g. Positive evidence is unusually easy to find about the project you sponsored. That is the moment to hand it to somebody whose bonus does not depend on it.

### The parts · Write the disconfirming column first
The order changes the content. Write down what would show you are wrong before you write the support, and both columns come out more honest. Reverse it and you have already chosen a side by the time the second column starts.
e.g. Put the falsifying evidence in the first column of the review template. Same person, same week, same facts, different conclusion.

### The parts · When the report and the world disagree, change the report
Challenger was not a shortage of engineering. It was an organisation that preferred a document. This holds anywhere there is a reporting line: if the reflex when numbers look bad is to adjust the wording, the problem has simply been forwarded.
e.g. The metric missed. Ask whether you are revising the conclusion or the phrasing. Revised phrasing clears this review and is still there at the next one.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: assessing something you have a stake in.
Ask first: does this conclusion pay me? If it does, how hard have I actually looked for the evidence against it?
Where it goes wrong: turning it into never concluding anything, or aiming the principle exclusively at other people.

### Lines to keep
The first principle is that you must not fool yourself.
And you are the easiest person to fool.
Reality must take precedence over public relations, for Nature cannot be fooled.

========================================================================
## Richard Feynman · If you cannot teach it, you have not got it
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/feynman/teach-to-understand/
Source: His teaching at Caltech, as recorded by David Goodstein
Tags: Deep read, Richard Feynman, Jargon is where the hole hides

The internet sells this as a study hack in four steps. This page is about the harder claim sitting underneath it.

### Q: What actually happened?
David Goodstein once asked him to explain why spin one-half particles obey Fermi-Dirac statistics. Feynman sized up his listener and said he would prepare a freshman lecture on it. He came back a few days later. I couldn't reduce it to the freshman level, he said, and that means we don't really understand it. The sentence everyone quotes about explaining things simply is not in his writing. What is documented is this, and the line found on his blackboard when he died: what I cannot create, I do not understand.

### The parts · Ban the jargon and the hole shows at once
A technical term is a compression, and compression only works if both sides can unpack it. Forbid the term and you have to unpack it yourself. Wherever you cannot, you were storing a label rather than an understanding.
e.g. Explain your job to someone at home. Every point where you fall back on the trade word is a point you have not thought through.

### The parts · Deriving it once beats memorising it ten times
A remembered conclusion works on the question it came from. A derivation works on the whole class of questions, because on the way through you collide with why it could not have been otherwise. Those collisions are the structure of understanding.
e.g. Rather than memorising when the formula applies, work out once where it comes from. After that the conditions are obvious and need no memorising.

### The parts · Teaching is the test, not the favour
The usual reading is that explaining helps the listener. His use runs the other way: he explained in order to find out whether he knew. Which means the more ignorant the audience, the better the instrument.
e.g. A colleague silently repairs the steps you skipped. Somebody outside the field stops dead at the first vague sentence, which is the reading you wanted.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you think you understand something and are not certain.
Ask first: without one term of art, can you take an outsider to the point of nodding? Which sentences do you stall on?
Where it goes wrong: confusing simple with shallow — what gets simplified is the telling, never the content.

### Lines to keep
I couldn't reduce it to the freshman level.
That means we don't really understand it.
What I cannot create, I do not understand.

## Finite and Infinite Games · Two kinds of games
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/finite-and-infinite-games/two-kinds/
Source: Finite and Infinite Games, section one
Tags: Deep read, Finite and Infinite Games, Work out which one you are in

The first sentence of the book is the whole conclusion. What the two categories save you from getting wrong.

### Q: What actually happened?
Carse opens with the entire thesis: there are at least two kinds of games, and a finite game is played for the purpose of winning, an infinite game for the purpose of continuing the play. A finite game has a start, a finish and a winner — a match, an election, a lawsuit. An infinite game has no end, its rules can change, and the only object is to keep it going — a culture, a marriage, a craft, a company that means to last. Confusing them produces two symmetrical mistakes.

### The parts · First ask whether there is a final whistle
Sorting comes before anything else. Does this have a defined end and a winner? A negotiation, a tender, a quarter are finite and deserve everything you have. A client relationship, a team, your own reputation are not scored that way at all.
e.g. Squeezing a supplier dry wins the meeting. If you want them for another ten years, you have just booked a loss in the other game.

### The parts · Finite tactics inside an infinite game spend the game
Beating people inside something unending consumes the players: suppliers crushed, staff drained, peers turned into enemies. Win every round and eventually nobody sits down with you, and in an infinite game no opponent means no game.
e.g. Every supplier negotiated down to no margin. Three years on, the only firms still willing to bid are the worst ones.

### The parts · Dragging out a finite game is the other way to lose
Treating something built to end as endless costs just as much: a lawsuit past its stopping point, a project that should close, a partnership renewed forever under the heading of giving it more time. Accepting the whistle is what frees your hands.
e.g. The doomed project stayed funded because of what had already gone into it. What it was holding was not budget, it was people.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are fighting something very hard, or you have been dragging something out for a long time.
Ask first: does this have a final whistle, or is it meant to keep going? Does the way I am playing match its type?
Where it goes wrong: using the infinite game as cover for not competing, or fitting a whistle to everything and settling accounts in every direction.

### Lines to keep
There are at least two kinds of games.
A finite game is played for the purpose of winning.
Every round you win ends. The game itself does not have to.

## Finite and Infinite Games · Playing with the boundaries
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/finite-and-infinite-games/playing-with-boundaries/
Source: Finite and Infinite Games
Tags: Deep read, Finite and Infinite Games, Rules are props, not walls

The two kinds of player treat rules in opposite ways. What separates changing the rules from simply cheating.

### Q: What actually happened?
Carse sets the two players against each other. The rules of a finite game are fixed before play and may not change, because their whole job is to let the game produce a winner. The rules of an infinite game must change during play, and the only test of a change is whether more people can keep playing. Finite players treat rules as walls and strain inside them; infinite players treat them as props. Whoever must win is the one the rules will trap. Finite players train to be powerful; infinite players stay flexible.

### The parts · The right to change a rule comes from wanting play to continue
Changing rules and cheating look identical from outside. The difference is who benefits: change it so you win this round and it is cheating; change it so the play can continue and it is the infinite player's job. Ask whether the change widened the field or narrowed it.
e.g. A platform reworks its revenue share. Done for this quarter's margin it is killing the game; done to keep small creators alive it is extending the game. The action can look the same.

### The parts · The sign the rules own you is that you only win by them
The longer you win inside one set of rules, the more your ability grows into the shape of those rules. Rankings, reviews and algorithms change, and years of accumulation reset. The defence is a standing question: if these rules were replaced tomorrow, what would I still have?
e.g. Skills tuned entirely to one platform's algorithm go to zero the week it updates. What travels is craft, reputation, and the people who follow you.

### The parts · Power is for what you have seen, flexibility for what you have not
Training to be strong prepares you for matches already played. Staying flexible admits that the match that matters has not happened yet. The two need different reserves: one is doing a single thing perfectly, the other is keeping the slack that efficiency would have sold.
e.g. An organisation optimised for today's business, every person fully loaded and no slack anywhere, is unbeatable until the rules change.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the rules you work inside are turning against you.
Ask first: am I trying to win the next round under these rules, or should I be in the room where they get written? Would my change let more people play, or only me?
Where it goes wrong: using the rules should change as a sore loser's excuse, or staying the perfect student of a system until you are shaped like it.

### Lines to keep
The rules of an infinite game must change in the course of play.
Whoever must play, cannot play.
To be prepared for surprise is to be educated.

## Viktor Frankl · The last freedom
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/frankl/the-last-freedom/
Source: Man's Search for Meaning
Tags: Deep read, Viktor Frankl, Where the sentence was collected matters as much as the sentence

Written from a study it would be a maxim. The question worth asking is where the evidence for it was gathered.

### Q: What actually happened?
He was a psychiatrist in Vienna. In 1942 the whole family was deported; his parents, his brother and his pregnant wife all died in the camps. The central claim comes out of what he watched there: everything can be taken from a man but one thing, the last of the human freedoms, to choose one's attitude in any given set of circumstances. The evidence is specific. We who lived in concentration camps can remember the men who walked through the huts comforting others, giving away their last piece of bread. There were few of them. Few is enough.

### The parts · It is an observation report, not a slogan
The same paragraph on a calendar is uplift. As a field note out of a camp it is data. He is reporting the result of a lower-bound experiment: with external conditions pressed to the floor of human experience, the capacity to choose an attitude was still there. In a minority, but there.
e.g. You can choose your attitude sounds hollow in a good year. Its use is on the day you believe you have no options left. That day it is the one that remains.

### The parts · Two battlefields, and only one of them was lost
The prisoners handing over bread could not change their situation. What they changed was who they were inside it. Those are separate fields: on the first they lost everything, and the second stayed entirely theirs. Telling the two apart is what gives a hopeless position somewhere to start.
e.g. The redundancy list is fixed. How you spend the last two weeks, how you hand over, how you say goodbye is yours — and it is the part people remember.

### The parts · He made himself one of the subjects
In the camp he kept picturing himself after the war at a lectern, lecturing on the psychology of the camps, converting the suffering he was inside into material for work not yet done. Not self-deception: assigning the present pain a use. Pain with a use and pain without are different weights.
e.g. Give yourself the job of telling this stretch to somebody later. The notes start, the vantage point lifts, and none of it waits for the situation to improve.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the position has closed in until it feels like there is nothing left to choose.
Ask first: outside the part already lost, what kind of person do I want to be in this? That item cannot be confiscated.
Where it goes wrong: using attitude is free to wave away real harm and excuse whatever caused it; or quoting it only when things are going well.

### Lines to keep
Everything can be taken from a man but one thing.
To choose one's attitude in any given set of circumstances.
They could not change the situation. They changed who they were in it.
