## Viktor Frankl · Happiness cannot be pursued
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/frankl/happiness-ensues/
Source: Man's Search for Meaning
Tags: Deep read, Viktor Frankl, Some targets disappear the moment you aim at them

The people who make happiness the goal are the ones who miss it. The mechanism he gives, and the route around it.

### Q: What actually happened?
He puts it plainly. Success, like happiness, cannot be pursued; it must ensue. One must have a reason to be happy, and the reason does not live inside happiness. His instruction to his students is the same one: do not aim at success, because the more you aim at it and make it a target, the more you are going to miss it. In the clinic he kept meeting the reverse case — the harder someone forces sleep the longer they lie awake, and the closer they monitor their own happiness the more anxious they get.

### The parts · Some states are readings, not activities
Happiness, relaxation, confidence, being liked. What they have in common is that they are gauges on a process rather than the process. Chasing the gauge is breathing on the thermometer to warm the room. His clinical name for it is hyper-reflection: monitoring the state is what wrecks it.
e.g. Monitor your nerves while speaking and they double. Put the whole of your attention on what you are actually saying and they leave on their own.

### The parts · The route around it is the reason
If happiness needs a reason, then the reason is the thing to work on: something worth going into, one particular person you are answerable to. Get that in place and the state settles itself as a side effect. His whole therapy is built on the turn — treat the reason, not the symptom.
e.g. Flat for months, cheer yourself up is a dead end. Take on one thing that is of use to one named person, then read the gauge two weeks later.

### The parts · The same holds for organisations
A team that manages morale, happiness and belonging as targets in their own right collects performed readings. Those are by-products of having done something that mattered, and a by-product cannot be manufactured directly. It only arrives through the actual product.
e.g. Instead of a wellbeing initiative, kill one process everybody hates, or win one fight everybody was in. The readings move by themselves.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are working directly at a state — calm, confident, happy — and it recedes as you push.
Ask first: which process is this state the reading of, and can I move the effort onto that process instead?
Where it goes wrong: reading do not pursue it as giving up, so the reason never gets looked for either; or setting a happiness target for a team and collecting performances.

### Lines to keep
Success, like happiness, cannot be pursued; it must ensue.
The unintended side-effect of one's personal dedication to a cause greater than oneself.
Chasing the reading is breathing on the thermometer to warm the room.

## Benjamin Franklin · One virtue a week
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/franklin/one-virtue-a-week/
Source: The Autobiography, Part Two
Tags: Deep read, Benjamin Franklin, Even character has to be put on a schedule

He drew up thirteen virtues, then did the thing nobody resolving to improve ever does. The design of the little book.

### Q: What actually happened?
In his twenties he listed thirteen virtues, temperance through humility. The list is not the interesting part; the execution design is. I judged it would be well not to distract my attention by attempting the whole at once, but to fix it on one of them at a time. One virtue a week, the other twelve merely recorded and not demanded. A little book, a page per virtue, ruled into columns, examined every evening, a black spot for each fault. Thirteen weeks a course, four courses a year. He admits his scheme of Order gave him the most trouble.

### The parts · Working on thirteen is working on none
Attention is the only scarce resource in the system. Run everything at once and each item gets a thirteenth of it, nowhere near the strength required for anything to become a habit. Serial is not the slow way round. It is the only way anything accumulates.
e.g. Eight resolutions in January are all gone by February. One thing held for four weeks before the next is added leaves you three real habits by December.

### The parts · Record the faults, not the wins
What goes into the book is failure: a mark for every breach. That makes the evening check objective and cheap. You never have to appraise how well the day went, only answer whether it happened. Countable failures drive change harder than a vague sense of progress.
e.g. A tick or a cross against did I cut anybody off today beats rating your own communication out of ten. The first leaves no room for interpretation.

### The parts · The spots never came out and the system still ran
He kept at it for life and the Order column always had marks on it. A man buying an axe wanted the whole face bright, turned the grindstone a while, and decided he liked a speckled axe best. Franklin admits he is that axe. A system needing perfection is abandoned at the first breach.
e.g. The person who stops the whole programme after missing twice loses to the person who goes once a week and never resets the counter.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the list of things you want to change runs to several items.
Ask first: which single one is this week's? Can the rest be recorded only, and not required of you yet?
Where it goes wrong: opening on all fronts and abandoning all of them in three weeks; or declaring the system a failure at the first black spot.

### Lines to keep
Not to distract my attention by attempting the whole at once.
My scheme of Order gave me the most trouble.
I think I like a speckled axe best.

## Benjamin Franklin · Give up the word certainly
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/franklin/never-say-certainly/
Source: The Autobiography, Parts One and Two
Tags: Deep read, Benjamin Franklin, He changed the sentence, not the opinion

Somebody told him to his face that he was insufferable. What he changed was not what he thought but how he phrased it.

### Q: What actually happened?
The young Franklin loved to argue and won everywhere. A Quaker friend told him kindly that he was generally thought proud, overbearing and rather insolent, and gave him instances. He took it, and the remedy is unusually specific. I made it a rule to forbear all direct contradiction to the sentiment of others, and all positive assertion of my own. He banned the words: certainly, undoubtedly. In their place — I conceive, I apprehend, I imagine a thing to be so, or it so appears to me at present. He kept it fifty years.

### The parts · Changing the phrasing is doable; changing the character is not
Become humble is character engineering with no delivery date. Ban two words and substitute three phrases is a rule you can keep this afternoon. He did not wait to feel different — he started at the outermost operable layer. The sentences changed, the exchanges followed, and the character came last.
e.g. To stop steamrollering meetings, a hard rule beats an intention: say I may be missing something before every position you take.

### The parts · An assertion forces a defence; a conjecture leaves a way in
It is certainly this turns the conversation into a win and a loss: the other person concedes or fights, and most fight. I conceive it to be this lets them add, correct, half-agree. They need not admit error in order to come closer to you, and lowering that cost is half of persuasion.
e.g. There is a problem with this plan gets a defence. There is a piece I have not worked out gets an explanation. Same information, opposite circuit.

### The parts · Winning the argument and getting it done are different aims
What he wanted when young was refutation, and refuted people do not help you afterwards. Very few of those who go quiet have been persuaded; most have merely stopped speaking. Change the aim from leaving them nothing to say to leaving them willing to work, and the vocabulary follows.
e.g. You demolish the objectors, the proposal passes, and those people put nothing into delivery. Every argument won is paid for with interest later.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are about to state a judgement you are completely sure of.
Ask first: am I trying to win this sentence, or to have this person put work in afterwards?
Where it goes wrong: using I conceive as sarcastic politeness while the content still flattens people; or refusing to take any position at all because assertion is banned.

### Lines to keep
I made it a rule to forbear all direct contradiction.
I conceive, I apprehend, or I imagine a thing to be so.
No one has ever heard a dogmatical expression escape me.

## Fukuzawa Yukichi · The signs in Yokohama
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/fukuzawa/signs-in-yokohama/
Source: Fukuzawa Yukichi, The Autobiography of Fukuzawa Yukichi, 1899, on his 1859 visit to Yokohama
Tags: Deep read, Fukuzawa Yukichi, Years of study, and not one word legible

Years of hard study turn out to be the wrong thing. What he did the day after he found out.

### Q: What actually happened?
He was in his early twenties in Osaka, studying Dutch, which was then Japan's only window on the West, and he was very good at it. In 1859 he walked into the newly opened port of Yokohama and could not read a single sign on the street. They were all in English. He wrote later that it landed like a blow to the head: years of work, useless in this harbour. He did not go back to his Dutch. The next day he began hunting for English textbooks and started again from nothing.

### The parts · Useless is information, not a verdict
He did not write those years off, and he did not defend them by studying harder. He read the signs as a report on the wind: what has changed is the direction, not your capacity. Once the direction is clear, where the effort should go is obvious.
e.g. When what you trained for stops matching the work, ask what it tells you about direction before you mourn the years.

### The parts · Switch the same week, not next year
He began the day after he got home. Years of sunk cost make the instinct to give the old thing a little longer almost irresistible, and every day of waiting adds another chip to the track you are leaving. He simply started the new one at once.
e.g. Begin the new thing on the day you see the direction change, even ten minutes a day. Do not let the sunk cost keep growing.

### The parts · The old study was not wasted; refusing to switch is
He said afterwards that what he had built learning Dutch carried straight over: how to take a sentence apart, how to hold vocabulary, how to find someone to practise on. The content of a craft expires. The method you built while learning it does not.
e.g. What expires is the material, not your way of learning. The second is portable. Carry it across and replace the first.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you spent years on a body of skill that does not fit where you now work.
Ask first: what direction is this telling me, and have I started the new thing, or am I waiting for the old one to be useful again? What did I build while learning it that transfers directly?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as throw away everything you learned. His Dutch is exactly why his English came fast. Change the content, keep the method.

### Lines to keep
What is useless tells you the direction, not your capacity.
Every day of waiting adds another chip to the old track.
The content expires. Your way of learning does not.

## Fukuzawa Yukichi · Practical learning
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/fukuzawa/practical-learning/
Source: Fukuzawa Yukichi, An Encouragement of Learning, first part, 1872
Tags: Deep read, Fukuzawa Yukichi, Learn what you will use tomorrow first

What to study, and whether to keep studying. What he put ahead of the Confucian classics, and the reason he gave.

### Q: What actually happened?
An Encouragement of Learning opens by asking what learning even is. Not the memorising of difficult old texts, he answers, but practical learning: letter writing, bookkeeping, the abacus, reading a map, some physics and economics, the things you need every single day. He put those ahead of the Confucian classics, and his reason was blunt. A person has to be able to feed himself and finish what is in front of him before anything else is worth discussing. The pamphlets sold over three million copies, mostly to young people who did not know what to study.

### The parts · Sort by how often you will use it
His ordering rule has one term in it: frequency of use. Daily first, once a year later, someday last. He is not saying the later ones do not matter. He is saying a beginner has limited hours and should get fluent in the daily ones first.
e.g. When you cannot decide what to practise, write down the three things you will need at work tomorrow morning and practise those.

### The parts · Feeding yourself is the first gate
Independence is the word he keeps returning to. Someone who does not live off other people can afford to have his own judgement. So what you learn early should serve that one thing: earn, deliver, ask nobody. Past that gate, nothing you study is frightening.
e.g. Learn what lets you stand up first. Learn what lets you go far after you are standing.

### The parts · Keep reading only if it lands in your hands
He is not against books. He is against reading something you cannot use and calling that study. Whether to continue is not settled by the level of the qualification but by whether the reading arrives as something you can now do.
e.g. Before signing up for more study, answer one question. When this ends, what can I do that I could not do before?

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you cannot tell what to practise, or whether to go back for another qualification.
Ask first: what three things will I need tomorrow morning, and am I fluent in them? Of what I am studying now, which part lands in my hands?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as only ever study useful things. He read all his life. This is the ordering for a beginner, not the ordering for a lifetime.

### Lines to keep
Learn what you need tomorrow first. Once a year can wait.
Learn what lets you stand, then what lets you travel.
If reading leaves nothing in your hands, it was not study.

## Fukuzawa Yukichi · Heaven creates no man above another
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/fukuzawa/no-one-above/
Source: Fukuzawa Yukichi, An Encouragement of Learning, opening lines, 1872
Tags: Deep read, Fukuzawa Yukichi, The gap is in study, not in birth

You suspect you were born with less. Why the book opens on that sentence, and what its second half actually claims.

### Q: What actually happened?
The first line of An Encouragement of Learning: Heaven does not create one man above or below another man. Nobody arrives ranked. But he goes straight to the harder question. Then why is the real world so unequal? His answer is not consolation. He puts the cause somewhere a person can reach: the difference comes down to whether you studied. Not fate, not birth. In 1872 Japan this was incendiary, since the hereditary status system had only just been abolished and most people still believed in ranks. The gap was made after birth, which is why it can be closed.

### The parts · Move the cause somewhere you can reach
The worst thing about I was born with less is not that it might be false. It is that it parks the cause where nothing can be done. He moves it to whether you studied. That may not be the whole truth, but it moves, and a movable cause gives you work.
e.g. When you feel outmatched, move the cause from I am simply like this to which part have I not trained. Only the second has a next step.

### The parts · He is better usually means he is earlier
Most of the difference he saw came from the order in which people met things, not from what they were born with. Someone looks steady because they practised something three years before you did. Translate stronger into earlier and most of the anxiety goes.
e.g. When someone is a step ahead of you on everything, first ask whether they met all of it a few years before you did.

### The parts · Born with less is the cheapest explanation, so watch it
The moment that explanation is accepted, nothing further is required of you, because it was settled at birth. He objects to it not only because it is wrong but because it is so convenient. The more effortless an explanation, the more it deserves suspicion.
e.g. An explanation that leaves you with nothing to do is usually not the true one. It is the comfortable one.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: everyone around you seems steadier and faster, and you suspect you were simply born with less.
Ask first: the things I lose on, were they born knowing them or did they meet them three years before me? Is my cause parked somewhere I can reach?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as effort closes any gap. He says the gap was made after birth, not that every such gap can be closed. And it is a line to say to yourself, not one to use on someone doing worse than you.

### Lines to keep
Heaven does not create one man above or below another man.
The gap was made after birth, so it can be closed.
Translate stronger into earlier and most of the anxiety goes.
An explanation that asks nothing of you is comfortable, not true.

## Gandhi · The salt march
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/gandhi/salt-march/
Source: The salt march, 1930
Tags: Deep read, Gandhi, Pick a target nobody has to explain

How do you take on an empire, and where? This is why the smallest item on the list was the right place to start.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1930 Congress was arguing about how to run non-cooperation. Tariffs, land tax, self-rule: all of it large and complicated. Gandhi picked salt. British law monopolised its manufacture and taxed it, and every Indian ate it every day. On 12 March he left the ashram with 78 followers and walked 24 days and 240 miles to the sea at Dandi, where he bent down and lifted a lump of natural salt. With this, I am shaking the foundations of the British Empire. Tens of thousands were arrested for making their own.

### The parts · Shrink the issue until it needs no explaining
Tariffs and self-rule take a speech to explain. Salt takes none, because every tongue already knows it. The ceiling on mobilisation is set not by how important an issue is but by the lowest effort needed to understand it. Choosing the issue is choosing how many can join.
e.g. To move an organisation, lead with expenses taking three weeks to land rather than with optimising the finance process. Everybody has felt the first one.

### The parts · Pick the target that traps the other side
The salt tax raised very little, but arresting people for picking up salt looked appalling. Tens of thousands of ordinary arrests turned each act of enforcement into publicity for the movement. A good target makes repression costly and permission fatal.
e.g. Open with a small and obviously fair demand. Refusing it looks brutal, granting it sets a precedent. No dignified option left is the sign you chose right.

### The parts · The 24 days of walking were part of the work
He could have taken a car to the coast and picked up salt the same afternoon. Walking made every village on the route a venue, gave the papers 24 days of running coverage, and let attention gather. Slowness here was not a cost, it was amplification.
e.g. A run-up before a launch is not delay. It gives each layer of the audience time to be drawn in. What detonates in a day is forgotten in a day.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you want to start something, and there is a pile of possible entry points.
Ask first: which one needs no explaining, has hurt everybody already, and leaves the other side looking bad however they respond?
Where it goes wrong: choosing the most important issue even though it takes a speech to make clear; or compressing the process and cutting out the time people need to join.

### Lines to keep
With this, I am shaking the foundations of the British Empire.
Nonviolence is the weapon of the strong.
My life is my message.

## Gandhi · The means are the seed
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/gandhi/means-are-seeds/
Source: Hind Swaraj, 1909
Tags: Deep read, Gandhi, However you win is what you get

If the cause is right, can the method be rough? He closed the question in 1909 with a single image.

### Q: What actually happened?
In Hind Swaraj a reader asks Gandhi what is wrong with violence if it gets the British out. His answer is a comparison: the means may be likened to a seed, the end to a tree, and the connection between means and end is as inviolable as the one between seed and tree. Sow a poisonous seed and no rose comes up. He follows it through. An India taken by force will be governed by people who are good at force, and that, he says, is English rule without the Englishman.

### The parts · How you won gets written into what you won
The method does not retire on the day it succeeds. It becomes the organising material of whatever comes next. Whatever capability won the fight is the capability the winners admire, and reward and promotion follow it from then on.
e.g. A team that got there on faked numbers makes faked numbers the internal currency. Next round the same weapon comes out, only pointed inward.

### The parts · Just this once has no once
Adopting a method is a one-way door. Once it has worked it is in the toolbox, and things in the toolbox come out by themselves at the next difficult moment. Only this time is, in practice, a long-stay visa issued to the method.
e.g. Break the contract floor once to keep a large customer, and every later negotiation starts from the new floor. The exception happens once; the precedent is permanent.

### The parts · The test of the end is applied to the means
Stated ends cannot be checked, because everybody claims to want justice. The means are the only observable part of a purpose. A movement that promises freedom and cannot tolerate dissent inside itself has already shown you what it will build.
e.g. Assessing a partner, ignore the vision and watch how they treat suppliers and people who have left. Your future is being rehearsed on somebody else.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a method that would get you there quickly is available, and it is not clean.
Ask first: if this becomes one of our standard weapons from now on, do you accept that?
Where it goes wrong: using the rightness of the end to sterilise the means; or turning fastidiousness about method into a permanent reason never to act.

### Lines to keep
The means may be likened to a seed, the end to a tree.
As is the means, so is the end.
We want English rule without the Englishman.

## John Gottman · The four horsemen
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/gottman/four-horsemen/
Source: The Gottman marriage lab; The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work
Tags: Deep read, John Gottman, Four signals that predict a breakup

He watches fifteen minutes of one argument. This piece is about what he is actually watching.

### Q: What actually happened?
Gottman recorded thousands of couples talking, coded expression, tone and heart rate frame by frame, then tracked who divorced years later. What predicted a breakup wasn't how fiercely they fought but whether four signals appeared, which he called the four horsemen: criticism (attacking the person, not the act), contempt (sarcasm, eye-rolling), defensiveness (returning the blame) and stonewalling (shutting the other out). The single strongest predictor of divorce is contempt — and the research found it affects the recipient's immune function.

### The parts · Criticism and complaint are different things
A complaint targets behaviour: you didn't do the washing up and I'm exhausted. Criticism targets character: you're just lazy. The first can be solved; the second can only be defended. Many people think they're raising an issue while every sentence defines the other person, and so the same problem runs ten years.
e.g. Swap 'you never deal with the kids' for 'I did all three pickups this week'. Same event, and the second can be caught.

### The parts · Contempt is a slow poison, not venting
Eye-rolling, mockery, mimicking their tone — all of it says I am above you. It differs from anger: anger is about the event, contempt says the person is unworthy. It's the strongest single predictor in his data because it destroys the foundation, not one conversation.
e.g. 'What would you know' and 'fine, you're always right' need correcting on the spot. That isn't arguing, it's demolition.

### The parts · Defensiveness returns the ball, it doesn't clarify
'I've been busy, and so have you' looks like explaining and is a counter-attack. Its function is to refuse any share of responsibility, and once both sides are defending, the conversation becomes mutual evidence and never reaches a solution.
e.g. When the pickups come up, take the part you can admit — 'you did do all three' — before explaining your side.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the same thing gets fought about and every round escalates.
Ask first: was that last sentence about the event or about the person? Any sarcasm or eye-rolling? Am I explaining or returning the ball?
Where it goes wrong: using the four horsemen to charge the other person — 'that's contempt' is itself an attack. It's a checklist for yourself, not a verdict.

### Lines to keep
The strongest single predictor of divorce is contempt.
Criticism targets the person. A complaint targets the act.
The more often the four appear, the likelier the breakup.

========================================================================
## John Gottman · Repair attempts
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/gottman/repair-attempts/
Source: The Gottman marriage lab
Tags: Deep read, John Gottman, Whether you fight matters less than whether you stop

Healthy relationships argue fiercely too. So where do they differ from the ones that break.

### Q: What actually happened?
One of Gottman's counterintuitive findings: happy couples aren't the ones who don't fight, they're the ones who repair while fighting. He called the move of reaching for the brake mid-escalation a repair attempt — a joke, an offered way out, a 'wait, we've gone off topic'. In stable relationships repair attempts succeed more often, and not because the technique is better: because the other person is willing to take it. That willingness depends on the balance built up beforehand. He put a number on it — in stable relationships positive interactions run about five to one against negative.

### The parts · Repair succeeds or fails on the ordinary days
The same joke defuses things in a relationship with a healthy balance and reads as not taking it seriously in one that's overdrawn. So what decides whether a conflict can be stopped is the unremarkable responses, presence and small concessions of the past weeks. Technique in the moment mostly fails.
e.g. 'Let's not fight' after three months of silence rarely works. What would have worked is what wasn't done in those three months.

### The parts · Taking the offered way out is harder than offering it
Offering it risks being refused; taking it means giving up winning this round. Most relationships stick on the second: they heard it, and 'why should I be the one to let it go' stops them. Insisting on winning wins the round and loses the relationship.
e.g. 'Have we gone a bit far?' — answering 'yeah, a bit' is worth more than another round of evidence.

### The parts · Five to one is a balance, not a formula
The ratio gets misused as licence to say one cruel thing per five kind ones. Gottman means the everyday texture of the relationship should be mostly positive, not that praise offsets attacks. An attack costs far more than praise pays — that's why the ratio is lopsided.
e.g. Use it as a check: over the past week, was the texture between us warm or cold? Not 'have I complimented them five times'.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: mid-argument, both waiting for the other to give way first.
Ask first: did they offer a way out that I didn't take? Is our balance healthy enough to cover this overdraft?
Where it goes wrong: making repair something the same person always does. That isn't repair, it's one-sided depletion.

### Lines to keep
Happy couples aren't the ones who don't fight. They repair.
In stable relationships, positives run about five to one.
Whether a repair works depends on the account built beforehand.

========================================================================
## Benjamin Graham · Mr. Market
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/graham/mr-market/
Source: The Intelligent Investor, chapter 8
Tags: Deep read, Benjamin Graham, A quote is a service, not a verdict

He turns the entire market into one manic-depressive business partner. What that story actually unlocks is smaller and stranger than it looks.

### Q: What actually happened?
Chapter eight asks you to imagine a partner in a private business. His name is Mr. Market and he turns up every single day with a price, ready to buy your share or sell you his. His moods are extreme: elated, he names an absurd figure; depressed, he sells everything cheap. The part that matters comes next. He does not mind being ignored, and he is back tomorrow with a new quotation. Which makes him useful in proportion to how unstable he is, provided you use his prices rather than catch his mood.

### The parts · A quote is an option, not a grade
Most people read the tape as a live score on their own judgement, so a fall means they were wrong. The parable separates the two. A price is one man's mood today, and you have three responses: buy from him, sell to him, or ignore him. The third is where the initiative lives.
e.g. Down twenty per cent, ask what changed: the business, or the quotation? If the business is intact, that was a mood, and moods come back tomorrow.

### The parts · Volatility is the service you are not charged for
An emotional partner is not the risk; he is the only source of your return. Without his depressions nothing is ever cheap, and without his manias nothing is ever dear. Complaining about swings is complaining that your one supplier keeps turning up for work.
e.g. In the same fund, the holder who treats a drawdown as a disaster sells at the low to the holder who treats it as a delivery window.

### The parts · Do not let him do your valuation
The discipline sits in the fine print. Using his prices requires a valuation of your own, or you cannot tell a bargain from a trap and contrarianism decays into reflex. Whether he is servant or master depends on whether you brought your own ruler.
e.g. It has fallen this far, it must be oversold is not a valuation. It is measuring today's quotation against yesterday's quotation.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the price is swinging hard and your pulse is following the chart.
Ask first: what is my own valuation, and against it, is today's quote an opportunity, a trap, or noise?
Where it goes wrong: turning ignore him into never looking, so a real deterioration goes unnoticed; or going contrary with no valuation of your own, which is only reflex.

### Lines to keep
One of your partners, named Mr. Market, is very obliging indeed.
He is back again tomorrow with a new quotation.
Price fluctuations have only one significant meaning for the true investor.

========================================================================
## Benjamin Graham · The margin of safety
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/graham/margin-of-safety/
Source: The Intelligent Investor, chapter 20
Tags: Deep read, Benjamin Graham, The room you leave for being wrong

He said the whole secret of sound investment fits in three words. The question is what those three words are actually buying.

### Q: What actually happened?
The last chapter of the book is the answer, and its title is the phrase. Distill the secret of sound investment into three words, he writes, and the motto is margin of safety. Pay fifty cents for a dollar of value, and the gap is not an expected profit. It is room for bad luck and for your own arithmetic being wrong. His definition of investing is colder still: thorough analysis, safety of principal, an adequate return, and anything short of that is speculation. Note the order.

### The parts · What you are buying is surviving your own error
The margin does not make a correct judgement pay more. It makes a wrong one affordable. Its price is set by self-doubt: the valuation could be thirty per cent out, the industry could turn, something unmodelled could arrive. Size the discount to how much you distrust your own estimate.
e.g. Schedule buffer is not for slow workers. It is for the requirement being misunderstood. A plan that has never slipped has usually spent its margin early.

### The parts · A good asset with no margin is still dangerous
Graham is explicit that the counter-example is not a bad company. It is a good company bought at the wrong price. Quality and safety are two independent variables, and the largest losses tend to start with the sentence that something this good does not need a discount.
e.g. The outstanding candidate names an outsized number; the celebrated project asks for unconditional commitment. Both are good, and both trades assume no mistakes.

### The parts · The margin comes from the price, not from your confidence
Conviction cannot serve as a buffer. The more certain a judgement feels, the easier it is to conclude the discount is unnecessary, which is exactly when it should be widest. So the rule has to be mechanical: below this discount, no action, however sure you are.
e.g. Write down a position cap and a required discount and let them stand. They exist for the handful of occasions when you are most convinced.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: an opportunity you feel certain about, and the cushion looks like money left on the table.
Ask first: if my estimate is thirty per cent out, does this price still protect the principal?
Where it goes wrong: using the margin as a reason to haggle forever and never own anything fairly priced, or trading the discount away for a feeling of certainty.

### Lines to keep
Distill the secret of sound investment into three words: margin of safety.
An investment operation promises safety of principal and an adequate return.
The margin of safety renders an accurate estimate of the future unnecessary.

========================================================================
## Mark Granovetter · The strength of weak ties
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/granovetter/weak-ties/
Source: Granovetter, The Strength of Weak Ties, AJS, 1973
Tags: Deep read, Mark Granovetter, Opportunity arrives from people you rarely see

Who to ask when you're looking for work. Your instinct gives the wrong answer; here's what the data gave.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1973 Granovetter surveyed 282 people about how they found their jobs. Among those who got there through a personal contact, 56% said they saw that person only occasionally, and 28% said rarely — the people who mattered were the ones they barely knew. That runs against instinct: your closest friends want to help you most. But the reason isn't willingness, it's information. Your circles overlap almost completely with your closest friends'; someone you rarely see is standing in a different network.

### The parts · What matters isn't willingness, it's whether the news is new
Close friends are more willing to help and hold almost the same information you do — same people, same news. A weak tie is not more generous. He is standing somewhere else, holding the part you can't reach from where you are.
e.g. You already knew about the opening in the team chat. The genuinely new thing comes from the person you see once a year.

### The parts · So maintain breadth, not depth
This changes where the effort goes: rather than pouring all of it into a few people, keep more weak ties in the 'still knows who you are' state. The cost is tiny — an occasional message, a hello with no request attached — and that's enough to keep the line usable.
e.g. Contacting old colleagues only once you want to move is usually too late. That line has to be kept while you don't need it.

### The parts · When you move, weak ties are what breaks first
Change city or leave an industry and what disappears isn't the close friends — those survive — it's the wide band of people you saw occasionally. That's exactly the layer that supplies new opportunities, so the drought after a move isn't imagined. It's structural.
e.g. Six months in a new city and nothing comes to you. You didn't get worse. That layer hasn't been built yet.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you're looking for something — a job, a partner, customers — and circling the same few people.
Ask first: of everyone I've contacted in six months, how many do I see only a few times a year? If almost none, one whole source of opportunity is switched off.
Where it goes wrong: reading it as collect contacts — a weak tie only works if the person still knows who you are and what you do; and don't neglect close friends for this. That's a different loss.

### Lines to keep
Of people who found work through a contact, 56% saw them only occasionally.
Your closest friends want to help most. The useful news sits further out.
When you move, the layer that breaks first is the one that brought opportunities.

========================================================================
## Mark Granovetter · No strong tie is a bridge
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/granovetter/no-strong-tie-is-a-bridge/
Source: Granovetter 1973, on bridges
Tags: Deep read, Mark Granovetter, The people closest to you know what you know

It sounds like a turn of phrase. It's a structural result, and here is what it rests on.

### Q: What actually happened?
Granovetter states it flatly: no strong tie is a bridge. The reason isn't sentiment, it's geometry. If you're close to A and close to B, then A and B probably know each other — close people introduce each other, and the circle closes. Once it's closed, the three of you know largely the same things, and none of you is a route to anywhere outside. Only rarely-used ties can be bridges, because only they have non-overlapping networks at each end.

### The parts · Closure is what strong ties inevitably produce
This isn't a question of social strategy, it's geometry: closeness means frequent contact, and frequent contact makes your friends meet each other. Closure itself is good — it's where support and trust come from — but it also means information circulates rather than arrives.
e.g. A tight team is superbly informed internally and the slowest in the building to notice what's changing outside.

### The parts · To test whether a tie is a bridge, look at the overlap
The test is simple: if this person knows most of the people you know, he isn't a bridge; if you share very few mutual contacts, he probably is. A bridge's value has nothing to do with how close you are and everything to do with the overlap at each end.
e.g. The person you share two mutual friends with is likelier to bring you something new than the one you share thirty with.

### The parts · A group's health shows in how many bridges it has
Applied to a team: an organisation made entirely of strong ties is warm inside and slowest to react to anything outside. What needs protecting is the few people who don't quite fit in and spend time elsewhere. They are the bridges, and bridges are what cohesion squeezes out first.
e.g. The one who's always off with another department is usually the door news comes through.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you want yourself or your team to hear sooner what's happening outside.
Ask first: how many lines do I have into circles that don't overlap with mine? Name them. If you can't name one, build a bridge before deepening what you already have.
Where it goes wrong: using this to dismiss close ties — they supply support and trust, a different job entirely; or setting out to 'network outward', which makes the tie a task, and those don't hold.

### Lines to keep
No strong tie is a bridge.
Close to A and close to B? A and B probably know each other.
Bridges are what a group squeezes out first when it wants cohesion.

========================================================================
## Andy Grove · The revolving door test
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/grove/revolving-door/
Source: Only the Paranoid Survive
Tags: Deep read, Andy Grove, Become your own successor

Intel was built on memory chips and nearly died of them. What was said in one office in 1985.

### Q: What actually happened?
By 1985 Japanese makers had driven memory prices through the floor, Intel had lost money for several quarters, and the argument over whether to hold the business had run for a year. Grove asked Moore: if we got kicked out and the board brought in a new chief executive, what do you think he would do? Moore answered without hesitating: he would get us out of memories. Grove looked at him and said, why shouldn't you and I walk out the door, come back, and do it ourselves? Intel amputated and went all in on microprocessors.

### The parts · A successor's view is the same machine with the feelings removed
A new chief executive sees exactly the data you see. One thing differs: no sunk cost, no credit from the old days, no this is what we were founded on. The test borrows his eyes, and the answer usually turns out to have been there already, held under by feeling.
e.g. Stuck on cutting a line you raised yourself, ask what a parachuted successor does in his first week. If he cuts it, the only open question is who swings the axe.

### The parts · Walk out and walk back in. Both steps count
The precision of the image is that it has two halves. Walking out sheds the old identity; walking back in executes under the new one. The first alone is avoidance, seeing clearly and not moving. The second alone is butchery, cutting without having changed your mind.
e.g. Announcing a new direction while still measuring everyone on the old business is walking back in with your head left outside. The change happened in the memo.

### The parts · Doing it yourself is how you keep the people who do it
The half of his sentence that gets dropped is by ourselves. Wait for a board to bring somebody in to do the identical thing and the company bleeds two more years first. Do it yourself and the pain is the same, but the memory is we turned, not we were rescued.
e.g. The same cut announced by the founder who takes the blame leaves a different organisation than one made by an incoming team. The first team will turn with you again.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a business you have feelings about is bleeding steadily and you cannot bring yourself to act.
Ask first: what would my successor do with it in his first month? Does that answer contain any information I do not have — and if it does not, the only thing stopping me is feeling.
Where it goes wrong: using the test as a switch for turning off responsibility, cutting and then disowning the cut. Or playing successor with everything, until the patience some things need gets cut too.

### Lines to keep
If we got kicked out, what would a new chief executive do?
Why shouldn't you and I walk out the door and do it ourselves?
The first thing to overcome is your own emotional attachment.

## Andy Grove · Inflection points and the people who warn you
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/grove/inflection-and-cassandras/
Source: Only the Paranoid Survive
Tags: Deep read, Andy Grove, The channel bad news travels down

When the tenfold change arrives the top floor is almost always last to hear. His prescription for that structural lag.

### Q: What actually happened?
Grove calls a change that rewrites the foundations of an industry a strategic inflection point: one factor moves by a factor of ten and the old map is void. Its cruellest property is that it comes with no alarm bell, and by the time the data is clear the best window has shut. His remedy is a kind of person, the helpful Cassandras: the middle managers and front-line staff who feel it first. He asks management not to be cleverer but to let bad news travel faster than good, and to stay close to the frightened messenger.

### The parts · The turn is late in the data and on time in the feel
Early in a tenfold change the statements still look healthy, because existing customers carry you a year or two on inertia. The first signals are qualitative: the questions customers ask, where the hiring market moves, how deals are now lost. By the time those reach a report they are an obituary.
e.g. Revenue is still climbing, and new customers start putting you on the same comparison sheet as a rival you look down on. That is page one.

### The parts · How the Cassandras are treated decides whether the alarm exists
Somebody always felt it earlier. The question is what happened to them when they said so. If the last person to bring bad news was quietly frozen out, the warning system shut down that day. Not nobody saw it: everybody who saw it learned to be silent.
e.g. In a review, ask who noticed first, whether they spoke, and what happened to them afterwards. The third answer decides whether anyone speaks next time.

### The parts · Put money behind the unease at the edge, not just an ear
Hearing the Cassandra is only step one. His practice was to fund the unease: real budget for hedging experiments, so a judgement at the edge gets a chance to grow into data. Open-mindedness that funds nothing ends where deafness ends, because the turn will not wait.
e.g. When the front line keeps saying a new category is taking customers, stop arguing about whether it is true. Give a small team a budget and three months. You are buying information, not a business.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a signal from the edge is making you uneasy, and the numbers are still calm.
Ask first: who stands closest to this signal? What happened to them the last time they brought bad news? Could a small sum let the signal turn itself into evidence?
Where it goes wrong: turning paranoia into a general alarm where every noise mobilises everybody. Or protecting the messengers beautifully and then never acting on what they said.

### Lines to keep
A strategic inflection point rarely comes with an alarm bell.
Let bad news travel faster than good news.
Snow melts first at the periphery.

========================================================================
## Guan Zhong · Full granaries come before manners
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/guan-zhong/granaries-first/
Source: Guanzi, Shepherding the People
Tags: Deep read, Guan Zhong, Look at the accounts before the values

Why does saying it again never land. He inverted the order: check the storehouse first, discuss propriety second.

### Q: What actually happened?
Shepherding the People is the first chapter of the Guanzi, and it opens not on morality but on storage. Whoever holds land and shepherds people attends to the four seasons and guards the granaries. A state with wealth draws people from far away; land brought under cultivation keeps them where they are. Only then comes the famous line: when the granaries are full the people know propriety; when food and clothing suffice they know honour and shame. The order was counter-intuitive then. Teaching first was the mainstream. He put it second — not because instruction is wrong, but because below a certain floor it does not work.

### The parts · Conditions are the premise of behaviour, not an excuse
The same person under different resource conditions makes entirely different choices. So when behaviour disappoints, examine the conditions before the attitude — leave the conditions alone and replacing the person produces the same result.
e.g. A salesperson overpromises to hit quota. Check first whether the quota is only reachable by overpromising. Leave the number and the next hire does the same thing.

### The parts · The order cannot be reversed
Talking about values and then about pay, versus getting the pay right and then talking about values, produces very different outcomes. The first sounds like vision substituting for wages; only the second is actually setting a standard. His sequence is storehouse first, and propriety follows.
e.g. A team paid below market holds a culture workshop and leaves faster. The identical workshop after the pay correction is a completely different event.

### The parts · The four bonds are a result, and a guardrail
He names propriety, right, integrity and shame as the four bonds of the state, and says that when they fail the state perishes. But he places them after the granaries: they are upper structure needing material support, not a precondition you can demand from nothing.
e.g. Under maximum survival pressure the first norms to fail are the ones that need slack: documentation, reviews, helping each other. The people did not change. The slack went.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you restate the standard over and over and the behaviour does not move.
Ask first: under the present conditions, does the person who does this correctly end up worse off?
Where it goes wrong: treating a conditions problem as an attitude problem; raising the volume on values while the material floor is still missing.

### Lines to keep
Full granaries, and the people know propriety.
Propriety, right, integrity, shame: the four bonds of a state.
Wealth draws people from far away; cultivated land keeps them.

## Guan Zhong · Government succeeds by following what people want
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/guan-zhong/follow-the-people/
Source: Guanzi, Shepherding the People
Tags: Deep read, Guan Zhong, Dig the channel where the wanting goes

A policy that will not go through is rarely an execution problem. The single measure he used to test one.

### Q: What actually happened?
Government flourishes by following the hearts of the people, and fails by going against them — he reduces policy success to one test. Then he makes it very concrete: people hate toil, so give them ease; people hate poverty and low standing, so make them prosperous and honoured; people hate danger, so keep them secure; people hate being cut off, so let them raise families. All four begin by naming what people do not want, and design from there. He does not try to reform desire. He digs it a channel.

### The parts · List what they do not want first
Designing a measure, people habitually start from the benefit it brings. His sequence starts from what the other side finds hateful, then makes sure the measure does not touch it. Avoiding the aversion decides acceptance more than offering the benefit does.
e.g. Rolling out a new system, rather than advertising its power, confirm it adds no forms, no extra login, and makes nobody's work newly visible to inspection.

### The parts · Against the grain, enforcement has no ceiling
A rule that violates a widespread preference is never opposed openly; it is quietly worked around. The workarounds get more sophisticated, supervision costs rise to chase them, and the chase never closes. That is not an execution problem. It is a design problem.
e.g. Ban personal matters during working hours and the actual result is that everyone learns to look busy. The rule was not defeated. It just stopped doing anything.

### The parts · Following is not indulging
Following the hearts of the people means setting the path along the direction of the wanting, not removing the constraint. He was simultaneously a severe legislator, with tight household registers, military organisation and market regulation. The direction is followed; the route is governed.
e.g. Accept that everyone wants to leave earlier, so compress meetings and cut approvals — without relaxing what has to be delivered. Go with the direction, keep the bar.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a rule you consider entirely reasonable is meeting resistance everywhere it lands.
Ask first: what does this rule ask people to give up, and what did they already hate most?
Where it goes wrong: blaming the workarounds on weak execution; using go with human nature as a reason to drop the standard.

### Lines to keep
Government flourishes by following the people, and fails by opposing them.
A rule against the grain is not opposed. It is bypassed.
Follow the direction of the wanting. Govern the route.

========================================================================
## Guan Zhong · Buying deer to break Chu
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/guan-zhong/buying-deer/
Source: Guanzi, Light and Heavy, section Wu
Tags: Deep read, Guan Zhong, Fight with prices

How do you actually make a rival yield without a single soldier. One economic campaign, run end to end, long ago.

### Q: What actually happened?
Duke Huan of Qi wanted Chu subdued. Guan Zhong's method was not an army: he had Qi buy live deer from Chu in quantity at prices driven far above what farming returned. The people of Chu put down their tools and went into the hills after deer. Money piled up in Chu and the fields went to weeds. Qi had spent those years stockpiling grain. At the right moment Qi closed the border and stopped buying. Chu held money and deer and could buy no grain: four in ten of the people of Chu came over to Qi. Not one battle; the production structure changed instead.

### The parts · Change their incentives, not their intentions
Persuading an organisation to change its behaviour is extremely hard; changing the prices it faces is easy. He never asked anyone in Chu to abandon farming. He only made deer more profitable, and every household in Chu completed the rest themselves.
e.g. To make a team value documentation, ten meetings do less than making a document an unavoidable step in the release process. Behaviour follows constraints, not exhortation.

### The parts · The more they earn, the worse their position
Chu's books at the time looked superb: exports booming, reserves piling up, household income rising. The danger was inside the prosperity — it rested on demand that one rival decided unilaterally. To judge a business, ask whether its buyer could vanish overnight.
e.g. Nine tenths of revenue coming from one platform's subsidy or one large customer. The growth curve looks wonderful and the switch for it sits in someone else's office.

### The parts · The stockpiling is where it was won
Bidding the price of deer up is only the first half. What decided the outcome was the grain Qi quietly accumulated in those same years. Every economic manoeuvre needs a matching preparation on your own side, or it is just money given away.
e.g. When a rival takes share on price, matching the discount is answering the move. Locking the supply chain and signing the key people is preparing for the turn.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: head-on competition costs more every quarter and you are considering raising the stake.
Ask first: among their key resources, is there one whose price I can change? And what should I be storing on my side?
Where it goes wrong: doing the bidding half without the storing half; handing nine tenths of your revenue to a switch somebody else owns.

### Lines to keep
Four in ten of the people of Chu came over.
Where profit lies, no mountain is too high to climb.
The buying was visible. The storing was not.

## Guiguzi · Open and close
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/guiguzi/open-and-close/
Source: Guiguzi, Opening and Closing
Tags: Deep read, Guiguzi, Decide which one this is before you speak

The most important decision in a conversation gets made before it starts. This asks which of the two decisions this one is.

### Q: What actually happened?
The first chapter puts two words above everything else: opening and closing are the way of heaven and earth. To open is to let out; to close is to draw back. The principle underneath is plain — the mouth is the door of the heart, and when the door opens what is inside goes out, when it shuts the intent stays in. So before an exchange you settle one thing: how much of me does this person see, and how much stays. Neither is better. Only the wrong one for the occasion is.

### The parts · Settle open or closed before you settle words
Most people prepare content — what am I going to say. His order puts a layer in front of that. Is this one an opening or a closing? Get that wrong and the more elegantly you speak the more damage you do.
e.g. An investor asks what the biggest risk is. Opened, you take it apart and give your answer to it. Closed, you reply briefly without evading.

### The parts · You open so that he opens
Opening is not only expression, it is extraction. Show part of your own footing and he has a reason to show his. So it goes in order: open something small and survivable, watch whether he follows, and only then decide how much further to go.
e.g. Name one real reservation of your own and the other side usually names theirs. Ask what their reservations are, cold, and you get politeness.

### The parts · Closing is chosen silence, not absence
Closing is an active withdrawal. You may close so that he has to come and take it, or close in order to end the thing. Without that distinction, closing decays into awkwardness, and awkwardness reads as something to prod.
e.g. Naming your price and adding nothing is closing to draw him in. Going vague when he presses for detail looks similar and means the opposite.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: an important conversation, and you are working on what to say in it.
Ask first: how much do I want him to see this time, and what does not have to be given at this stage?
Where it goes wrong: treating open and closed as a personality trait rather than a choice; or, when it is time to close, going vague instead of simply not saying it.

### Lines to keep
Opening and closing are the way of heaven and earth.
The mouth is the door of the heart.
To open is to speak; to close is to keep silent.

## Guiguzi · Listening in reverse
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/guiguzi/listen-in-reverse/
Source: Guiguzi, Reacting
Tags: Deep read, Guiguzi, To make him talk, stop talking

How do you get a person who does not want to talk to talk? The answer is four reversals, and one precondition under them.

### Q: What actually happened?
The Reacting chapter runs a set of paired instructions: to hear him speak, be silent; to have him open out, draw in; to stand high, stand low; to take, first give. Behind the pairs is a harder demand. Knowing begins with yourself, and you know yourself before you know others — because every judgement you make about another person has to pass through your own instrument, and an instrument nobody has calibrated adds error to everything it measures.

### The parts · Silence is the strongest question
People find a silence uncomfortable and move to fill it. So ask, and then add nothing: no softening, no restating, no second question. It routinely returns more than three further questions would have. That is what the first reversal means.
e.g. Say the price and stop. He often supplies there may be some room on that himself. Whoever hurries on never hears the sentence.

### The parts · Give first, or there is nothing to take
To take, first give is a sequence rather than a posture. Information, concessions and goodwill all obey it: until something has been put down, the other side has no reason to start an exchange. What you put down should be real and bounded.
e.g. Want to know their timeline? Say yours. Most people match it, and it is information you cannot get by asking for it.

### The parts · Calibrate your own instrument first
Know yourself and then you know others is the precondition for everything else here. Your reading of a person is mixed with your own taste, the mood you are in, and what you already think about people like him. Uncalibrated, more information only loads a crooked scale.
e.g. If slow talkers always strike you as unreliable, that is not skill at reading people, it is a fixed offset. Knowing it is there is what lets you subtract it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you need the real position out of someone who is not saying much.
Ask first: what am I putting down first, and can I hold my tongue after the question?
Where it goes wrong: replacing the pause with a run of follow-up questions; or mistaking your own preferences for experience in reading people.

### Lines to keep
To hear him speak, be silent. To take, first give.
Knowing begins with yourself; know yourself, then you know others.
Ask, and then add nothing. The silence does the work.

## Guiguzi · Sounding out what he wants
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/guiguzi/sound-out/
Source: Guiguzi, Weighing and Sounding
Tags: Deep read, Guiguzi, Measure at the peaks, not in the middle

What a person says day to day and what he actually wants are rarely the same. This asks when the reading comes out true.

### Q: What actually happened?
The Weighing chapter is almost coldly specific about timing. Go to him at the height of joy and press on what he wants, and having wanted it he cannot hide it; go to him at the height of fear and press on what he dreads, and having dreaded it he cannot hide it. The Sounding chapter supplies the matching technique: rub gently along the line of what he wants, test and probe, and the inside answers. Not an interrogation. A light touch, and then watching.

### The parts · What people say at rest is edited
In a level state a person says what he believes he ought to say. To reach the real preference you have to watch when there is no attention left over for editing: very pleased, very frightened, very tired. Not manipulation. Choosing the observation window.
e.g. What someone says offhand about the next step at the celebration dinner beats anything in the formal meeting. So does what he said the night it broke.

### The parts · Touch lightly, then watch the reaction
Sounding means to rub, not to press. Put out a small hypothesis that can be denied at no cost, then watch the direction and the speed of what comes back. The reaction is the answer; the content of the reply matters much less.
e.g. If we moved this two weeks later, would that be hard? Whether he starts calculating or first asks why tells you two completely different things.

### The parts · Use it to understand, not to work someone
The method plainly invites manipulation, and he says himself that the sage works in the dark. The larger value is in reversing it: knowing when other people are unguarded tells you when you are, and big decisions do not belong at either peak.
e.g. Long contracts signed the week the funding landed have a high rate of regret. The useful response is a cooling-off rule you apply to yourself.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: trying to work out what the other side actually cares about.
Ask first: the information I am holding — what state was he in when he gave it to me?
Where it goes wrong: pointing it only outward and never at yourself; or turning the light touch into an interrogation, which spends the relationship in one go.

### Lines to keep
Approach him at the height of joy and his wants show.
Rub gently at what he wants, and the inside answers.
The sage works in the dark; the fool works in the light.

## Guns, Germs, and Steel · Yali's question
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/guns-germs-steel/yalis-question/
Source: Guns, Germs, and Steel, Prologue
Tags: Deep read, Guns, Germs, and Steel, Move the cause off the people

The whole book is an answer to one question asked to his face. Why the answer moved from people to place.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1972 Diamond was walking on a beach in New Guinea when a local politician named Yali asked him: why is it that you white people developed so much cargo and brought it to New Guinea, but we black people had little cargo of our own? Diamond knew Yali's people were in no way less clever than Europeans. The fashionable answers were race and culture. His was environment: which plants and animals could be domesticated, the shape of the continents, the history of germs. Different starting conditions, compounded for millennia, come out as cargo.

### The parts · Rule out they are just not capable first
It is the laziest attribution available and it terminates the inquiry. Diamond disproves it before he earns the right to look for real variables: inside their own environment New Guineans show no deficit at all. Take the people out and what is left is the part you can change.
e.g. A regional market that will not grow gets explained by no spending power there, and the day is over. Find one local competitor doing well and the answer is void.

### The parts · The gap is compound interest on the starting conditions
Eurasia had fifty-six species of large-seeded wild grass and thirteen domesticable large mammals; the Americas had one and Australia none. That head start ran through food surplus, population, specialisation, technology and immunity for thousands of years.
e.g. Two companies look nothing alike after ten years. Trace it back and the first year holds one small difference — one landed a seed customer — and the rest is compounding.

### The parts · Environment does not cancel present responsibility
He explains where a long-run gap came from, not that individuals and this generation have nothing left to do. Turning environment into fate is the same early clock-out as blaming race. The use of it is to name the structural handicap, then work the parts of the structure that move.
e.g. Admitting you started late with less is honest. Making it the explanation of every result is fleeing. Late entrants need the route that does not reward being first.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a group or a team has lagged for years and the popular explanation is that they are not good enough.
Ask first: how do these same people perform under different conditions, and which of their starting conditions were actually worse?
Where it goes wrong: using environment to excuse everything happening now, or ignoring a real structural gap and demanding equal output anyway.

### Lines to keep
Why is it that you white people developed so much cargo?
History followed different courses for different peoples because of differences among peoples' environments.
They are just not capable is the answer that ends every inquiry.

========================================================================
## Guns, Germs, and Steel · The axis of a continent
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/guns-germs-steel/axis-of-continents/
Source: Guns, Germs, and Steel, chapter ten
Tags: Deep read, Guns, Germs, and Steel, What a starting line looks like

Eurasia lies sideways; the Americas and Africa stand upright. Why a fact from school geography is worth a chapter.

### Q: What actually happened?
Diamond's prettiest argument needs only a map. Eurasia's main axis runs east to west, while the main axis of the Americas and of Africa runs north to south. East-west means one latitude — comparable daylight, rains, temperature — so a crop domesticated once travels thousands of miles sideways: wheat went from the Fertile Crescent to Ireland and to India. North-south means crossing latitudes, and maize moving north out of Mexico had to be re-adapted to a different day length, which cost it centuries. Nobody tried harder. The shape of the map was paying a dividend.

### The parts · Neighbours that are alike pay a dividend on spreading
The real content of an east-west axis is that adjacent units are built the same way, so one solution copies cheaply. Before expanding, ask it directly: is the next market at the same latitude — habits, channels, regulation — or across one?
e.g. Shanghai to Hangzhou is east-west and the product ships almost unchanged. Shanghai to the Gulf is north-south: payments, content and compliance all get rebuilt.

### The parts · What blocks the spread is usually the middle stretch
Maize was held up by the isthmus and the deserts of Central America. Source and destination matched well enough; the ground in between did not. In any chain diffusion the bottleneck sits in the transfer zone, which resembles neither end.
e.g. Head-office method never reaches the front line because the middle layer has neither the head office's context nor the front line's situations, and it dies there.

### The parts · The dividend comes from structure, so go and choose the structure
You cannot change an axis, but you can choose which one you stand on. The same effort inside a structure where a solution replicates sideways, against one where every step must be re-adapted, is an order of magnitude apart after ten years.
e.g. Two businesses, identical margins. One rebuilds supply in every city; for the other one piece of work serves the whole network. That axis is the valuation gap.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are choosing the direction of your next expansion.
Ask first: is the candidate at the same latitude as the ground you already hold, or across one? What does the stretch in between look like?
Where it goes wrong: budgeting a north-south campaign at east-west prices, or only ever picking lookalike markets and never building the ability to cross.

### Lines to keep
Eurasia's main axis runs east-west; the Americas' and Africa's run north-south.
Places at the same latitude share day length and seasonal variation.
The axis decided how fast crops, herds, writing and wheels could travel.

========================================================================
## Guo Jia · Ten defeats, ten victories
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/guo-jia/ten-victories/
Source: Records of the Three Kingdoms, Book of Wei, Biography of Guo Jia, with Pei Songzhi citing the Fuzi
Tags: Deep read, Guo Jia, Morale broken into checkable items

Facing an opponent stronger on every axis, how do you make a team believe? He said nothing encouraging at all.

### Q: What actually happened?
Before Guandu, Yuan Shao had more men and more grain, and Cao Cao's side was broadly pessimistic. Guo Jia did not give a speech. He made a list. Shao has ten defeats, you have ten victories, and then set them out one at a time. Shao is thick with ceremony, you follow what is natural. Shao is outwardly generous and inwardly suspicious, employing men while doubting them; you use a man without doubt and fit him to the work. Shao plans much and decides little. Ten items later, the judgement was no longer a feeling.

### The parts · Break the whole judgement into items checkable one by one
We can take them is a single impression nobody can argue with. Supporters and objectors each produce examples and neither moves. Split it into ten and each item can be granted or refuted on its own; anyone who disagrees has to say which one fails.
e.g. We are stronger than them produces nothing. Cost structure, delivery time, decision speed and channel depth, compared line by line, produce something you can act on in an afternoon.

### The parts · Name where they are strong, or nobody believes the rest
The ten items do not dodge Yuan Shao's advantages: more troops, more territory, greater standing, all true. Because none of that is avoided, the differences that remain carry weight. A comparison listing only your own strengths reads as a pep talk.
e.g. If the competitive review finds nothing good about the rival, the team discounts the whole thing. Write the three ways they genuinely beat you first.

### The parts · Each difference has to land on something you can do
Not one of the ten is we want it more. Judgement means using a man without doubting him; strategy means acting once the plan is set. Each names an organisational behaviour that can be kept or wrecked. One vague item spoils the whole table.
e.g. We have more passion is a blank cell. Three approval layers against seven is something you can hold on to and can also lose.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: up against an opponent obviously stronger, and the team has stopped believing.
Ask first: can our advantage be split into ten items that each stand or fall on their own?
Where it goes wrong: encouragement standing in for the count; a comparison that lists only your strengths and skips where they are genuinely better.

### Lines to keep
Shao has ten defeats and you have ten victories.
He employs men and doubts them; you use a man without doubt.
Encouragement is not a comparison. Ten items you can check is.

## Guo Jia · Leave the baggage, march light
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/guo-jia/leave-the-baggage/
Source: Records of the Three Kingdoms, Book of Wei, Biography of Guo Jia
Tags: Deep read, Guo Jia, Speed is what is left after subtraction

Everyone said a thousand-mile raid was too risky. He said the risk was not the distance but what you were carrying.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 207 Cao Cao wanted to march north against the Wuhuan, and his generals objected: with the army beyond the frontier, Liu Biao might send Liu Bei against the capital. Guo Jia judged that Liu Biao would only talk and would never trust Liu Bei with troops, and pressed for the campaign. At Yi county he raised something more urgent still. Speed is the essence of war; a thousand-mile raid with heavy baggage cannot seize the advantage. Leave it behind and march light day and night. Cao Cao did, went out by Lulong Pass, and broke the Wuhuan at White Wolf Mountain.

### The parts · Speed is not running faster, it is carrying less
The pace of a long march is set by its slowest part, and the slowest part is always the baggage. The only way to be quick is to decide what not to bring. That is subtraction, and preparation is almost always addition.
e.g. Three months went into analytics, an admin console, permissions and every screen size, for a test meant to be quick. Which of those would still have answered the question?

### The parts · Accept the price of travelling light before you go
Leaving the baggage means no supply and no line of retreat if it goes badly. Marching light is not free; it trades margin for error against speed. So the decision rests on one prior judgement: does this have to be fast, or can it be slow?
e.g. Dropping monitoring and the rollback plan to hit a date is allowed, as long as you know what you sold. Whoever thinks light costs nothing panics the first time.

### The parts · Answer the fear everybody already has
He did not skirt the worry about the capital; he ruled on it first, and only then proposed the raid. Meeting the largest objection head on is what makes the rest of a plan movable at all.
e.g. Pitching something aggressive, put the thing the team is most afraid of on the first page: why it will not happen, and what you do if it does.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something has to be fast and you are still finishing the preparation.
Ask first: which of these could be skipped and still give you the answer, and do you accept the cost of skipping them?
Where it goes wrong: treating light as free; walking around the risk the team is most worried about instead of ruling on it.

### Lines to keep
Speed is the essence of war.
Leave the baggage, march light, and come at them unlooked for.
Liu Biao is a talker, and knows he cannot control Liu Bei.

## Guo Jia · The last plan: Liaodong
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/guo-jia/waiting-out-liaodong/
Source: Records of the Three Kingdoms, Book of Wei, Biography of Guo Jia and Annals of Emperor Wu
Tags: Deep read, Guo Jia, Do not press, and they turn on each other

The remnants fled onto somebody else's ground. Do you chase? The plan he left behind runs against the instinct.

### Q: What actually happened?
Beaten, Yuan Shang and Yuan Xi fled to Gongsun Kang in Liaodong. The generals urged pursuit and the taking of Liaodong in one stroke. Cao Cao said there was no need: Kang would send him their heads. He withdrew. Shortly afterwards Kang killed both brothers and sent the heads on. Asked why, Cao Cao said, he has always feared Shang; press him and they combine, ease off and they plot against each other. The judgement had been left to him by Guo Jia before he died.

### The parts · Outside pressure welds enemies together
Two parties watching each other will drop the watching the moment a larger threat appears outside. So when a crack already runs through the other side, the last thing to hand them is a common enemy.
e.g. Two rivals were poaching each other's staff. You started a price war and within a month they were supplying each other.

### The parts · Withdrawing puts the conflict back where it was
Leading the army home was not giving up. It handed the principal conflict back to the other side's interior. The move looks like doing nothing and is in fact very specific: removing the reason they have to stay united.
e.g. Two departments deadlocked, and the more you intervened the more they aligned their story against you. Step out and the original clash of interests reappears.

### The parts · The judgement rests on the relationship, not on strength
He has always feared Shang. The whole basis of the plan is an old wariness that existed long before you arrived. Without that ledger between them, withdrawing is simply letting a tiger back into the hills.
e.g. Counting on competitors to fight each other assumes an unsettled account already exists. Where none does, stepping back just lets them both grow.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the opponent has broken up and you are weighing whether to finish the pursuit.
Ask first: is there already a conflict inside them, and does my pressure make it larger or smaller?
Where it goes wrong: reading withdrawal as surrender; counting on infighting where no crack exists.

### Lines to keep
Press him and they combine; ease off and they plot against each other.
Do not pursue. Kang will behead them and send them to you.
A common enemy is the cheapest gift you can give two rivals.
