## Guo Ziyi · The gates were never shut
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/guo-ziyi/open-gates/
Source: Old Book of Tang, Life of Guo Ziyi; The Comprehensive Mirror
Tags: Deep read, Guo Ziyi, Be visible whenever anyone looks

The usual way to survive outranking your emperor is to shrink. He did the opposite, and could explain the arithmetic.

### Q: What actually happened?
He had put down the An Lushan rebellion and retaken the capital twice, and the eunuchs at court denounced him for years. His answer was not seclusion. His mansion in the Qinren ward took up a quarter of the ward, three thousand household members lived in it, and the gates were left open to anyone who wanted to walk in. A son asked him to shut them. Five hundred of my horses eat state fodder, he said; if I build a wall and someone accuses me, who is left to say what I was doing?

### The parts · Visible beats quiet
Keeping a low profile only reduces how often you are noticed. It leaves every unobserved hour available to whoever wants to describe it. An open house removes the guessing itself: if anyone can see what you are doing, an accusation has nothing left to fill in.
e.g. Holding the budget, publish the decision log where anyone can read it. That kills speculation; being careful in meetings only reduces the supply of material.

### The parts · Slander lands on what cannot be checked
His reasoning was exact. Once a wall stands between you and everyone else, whether a charge sticks depends on other people's mouths rather than on the facts. So make sure any charge can be held against the record on the spot.
e.g. Accused of favouring a supplier, if the scoring sheet and the people in the room are still there, it ends that afternoon. With only a conclusion, it never ends.

### The parts · It costs, and it never stops costing
Open gates mean giving up privacy and comfort, for decades. The moment you start closing them, every year of openness before that becomes the contrast that convicts you. This is not a clever move; it is a condition you have to keep paying for.
e.g. After promising transparency, the hard part is the week you would rather not publish. One exception, and openness stops being armour and becomes the new suspicion.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: your position or your resources have started people talking.
Ask first: if someone accuses me tomorrow, what can I put on the table that same afternoon?
Where it goes wrong: treating a low profile as defence; going transparent halfway, then closing the door on the inconvenient week.

### Lines to keep
His merit covered the empire and his ruler did not suspect him.
The man who hides is the one who has to be checked.
If I wall myself in, who is left to say what I was doing?

## Guo Ziyi · He rode out without armour
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/guo-ziyi/riding-out-alone/
Source: Old Book of Tang, Life of Guo Ziyi
Tags: Deep read, Guo Ziyi, Trading a battle for who you are

Hundreds of thousands of troops on the border, ten thousand men on his side. This is about why he took his helmet off.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 766 Pugu Huai'en told the Uighurs and the Tibetans that Guo Ziyi was dead, and brought a joint army of several hundred thousand up to Jingyang. Guo Ziyi had a little over ten thousand men. He judged that the Uighurs had fought alongside him for years, respected him, and had been lied to. So he brought no troops: he took off his helmet, unbuckled his armour, threw down his lance and rode forward with a few dozen horsemen. Their chiefs looked at each other and said, it is him, and dismounted to bow.

### The parts · First work out why they came
An army at your gate that was tricked into coming is a different problem from one that came prepared. The first thing he established was that their reason for marching was the report that he was dead. Overturn the false premise and the march has no cause.
e.g. A team is fighting your proposal. Find out whether they object to the proposal or to a rumour about it. The second only needs correcting.

### The parts · Taking the armour off was the only available proof
To prove that he was alive and that he was the man, talking was useless, an envoy was useless, and arriving with soldiers would have confirmed the hostility instead. Walking over stripped puts your life up as the evidence. Trust cannot be declared, only staked.
e.g. To show you have no private interest, give up in public something you were entitled to take. That does more than a hundred statements.

### The parts · The move spends a deposit you cannot make quickly
The conditions are severe: years of fighting beside these men, faces they knew, respect they actually held. Without that accumulation the same gesture is suicide. Nerve at the decisive moment is a withdrawal against decades of credit.
e.g. Steadying a partner in a crisis with one sentence rests on every earlier promise you kept. Without those, the same sentence carries nothing.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something is bearing down on you and you cannot meet it head on.
Ask first: is one of the things they believe simply untrue, and what would it take to disprove it?
Where it goes wrong: treating the risk itself as the method and forgetting the credit it draws on; expecting a gesture to work when the other side is not mistaken.

### Lines to keep
He took off his helmet, unbuckled his armour, and rode forward.
Huai'en lied to us. He told us the Duke was dead.
Trust cannot be declared. It can only be staked.

## Han Feizi · Don't build a system that needs good people
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/han-feizi/not-counting-on-goodness/
Source: Han Feizi, Eminent Learning; The Five Vermin
Tags: Deep read, Han Feizi, Make the right move the cheap one

A system that only runs when people are conscientious hasn't started working yet. How to design rules that don't need it.

### Q: What actually happened?
Han Feizi puts it coldly: I do not count on people being good to me; I make it so they cannot do wrong. He offers an arithmetic. Wait for arrow shafts that straighten themselves and in a hundred generations you get no arrows; wait for wood that rounds itself and in a thousand you get no wheels. Yet everyone has arrows and wheels, because someone invented the jig that straightens them. His conclusion: government cannot wait for sages. It builds tools.

### The parts · Conscientiousness is scarce and can't be the foundation
Depending on people to be conscientious stakes the system's stability on its least controllable variable. His alternative is the jig — the tool that straightens timber. Rules don't exist to improve people. They exist so that ordinary people produce acceptable results.
e.g. 'Everyone please follow the style guide' won't converge in ten years. A linter converges it in a day. Not conscience — tooling.

### The parts · Make the right road the least effortful one
The practical version of 'make it so they cannot do wrong' is to build the non-compliant road so it costs more than the compliant one. If going round the process is faster than going through it, no amount of exhortation matters. People are choosing the cheaper path.
e.g. Expenses take five steps and three signatures, and paying yourself back later takes one. Somebody will pay themselves back later.

### The parts · Don't design for the rare case
The commonest misuse is constraining everyone to stop one or two. Han Feizi is describing universal tools, not patches aimed at individuals. The cost of a rule is borne by everybody and the benefit accrues against a few. That ledger rarely balances.
e.g. One faked claim, so now every claim needs three photos. The faker adapts; several hundred people lose two hours a month.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the same class of problem keeps recurring and you've raised it many times.
Ask first: is the right road currently more effort than the wrong one?
Where it goes wrong: substituting announcements for tools; making everyone pay a cost in order to block a handful.

### Lines to keep
I do not count on people being good. I make wrong impossible.
Wait for arrows that straighten themselves and you get no arrows.
Rules don't make people better. They make ordinary work acceptable.

## Han Feizi · The two handles
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/han-feizi/two-handles/
Source: Han Feizi, The Two Handles
Tags: Deep read, Han Feizi, Reward and punishment can't be lent out

What power actually consists of. It turns out to be two things, and neither can be handed to anyone.

### Q: What actually happened?
Han Feizi states it like a definition: the ruler controls his ministers by two handles, and the two handles are punishment and favour. Killing is punishment; reward is favour. His example is the state of Qi, where the minister Tian Chang obtained ranks and stipends from the ruler to distribute to the officials, and lent grain by a large measure while collecting by a small one, putting the people in his debt. The ruler ended up hollow. His verdict: Tian Chang wasn't too strong. The ruler gave away the handle of favour.

### The parts · Power's substance is reward and consequence
Titles, grades and reporting lines are the form. What actually decides who listens to whom is who can grant good outcomes and who can bring bad ones. Everything else can be delegated; hand over these two and the seat is empty. The name remains and nobody is looking at you.
e.g. You're nominally in charge, and raises, promotions and ratings are decided elsewhere. The team aligns to the other person. That's structure, not loyalty.

### The parts · Lending them out is easy; taking them back is not
Once one person exercises reward and punishment for long enough, the organisation re-forms around them. Taking it back is no longer a question of authority — you face a network of dependence, and everyone who benefited will instinctively defend them.
e.g. One senior person has allocated resources for years. Moving them means moving everyone they lifted.

### The parts · Deliver both yourself
Letting someone else announce the good news and carrying the bad yourself sounds considerate. It gives away the favour and keeps the punishment. Han Feizi advises the opposite: both must come from you, or people only remember whoever handed them the good thing.
e.g. HR announces the raise and the manager delivers the criticism. Gratitude goes to the company, resentment to the manager.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you're nominally responsible for something and can't move it.
Ask first: on this, who currently decides the good outcomes and the bad ones?
Where it goes wrong: delegating reward and punishment as though they were admin; letting others announce good news while you absorb the bad.

### Lines to keep
The ruler controls by two handles: punishment and favour.
A tiger masters a dog by claws. Lend them out and it reverses.
Everything else can be delegated. These two empty the seat.

## Han Feizi · Match the deed to the word
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/han-feizi/form-and-name/
Source: Han Feizi, The Way of the Ruler; The Two Handles
Tags: Deep read, Han Feizi, What was said, what was done

The hard part of review isn't setting standards. It's what you do when the standard and the facts disagree.

### Q: What actually happened?
Han Feizi's method is matching form to name: the official states what he will accomplish (the name), and you check it against what was actually produced (the form). His extreme example: Marquis Zhao of Han fell asleep drunk, and the keeper of the hat, seeing him cold, covered him with a robe. On waking the marquis punished both the keeper of the robes and the keeper of the hat — one for neglect, one for overstepping. Overstepping is the worse harm, because it dissolves the boundary. The principle being established: your own words are the measure.

### The parts · The standard comes out of his mouth
Let the name define itself and the task define itself. Not a target imposed from above but a commitment stated by the person carrying it. At review there is then no arguing about whether the standard was reasonable — he set it. The only question left is whether it was met.
e.g. Rather than assigning a number, have them write what they will deliver this quarter and how it will be judged. Review only that page.

### The parts · Overshooting counts too
Form exceeding name is also pursued. Doing more looks good, and it means the judgement at commitment time was wrong, and it usually consumed someone else's resources. A system that punishes only shortfalls trains everyone to commit as low as possible.
e.g. Everyone sets targets at what they can certainly hit and exceeds them yearly. That organisation no longer knows its own capacity.

### The parts · Reconcile against the page agreed beforehand
If the ruler is chosen at review time, the whole thing becomes retroactive approval. Matching requires the name first and the form after, with no change in between. Change it once and the system reverts to personal favour.
e.g. Swap the criteria at quarter end, however reasonably, and nobody writes a serious commitment next quarter.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: it's review time and the two of you disagree on whether it counts as done.
Ask first: before this started, what standard did he write down himself?
Where it goes wrong: chasing only shortfalls and never overshoots, which pushes everyone to commit low; deciding which ruler to use only after the fact.

### Lines to keep
Let the name define itself, and the task define itself.
Deed fits the task and task fits the words: reward. Otherwise: punish.
Change the ruler at review and nobody writes a real commitment again.

========================================================================
## Han Xin · With the river at their backs
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/han-xin/back-to-the-river/
Source: Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of the Marquis of Huaiyin
Tags: Deep read, Han Xin, Take the retreat away first

Drawing up with a river behind you is the classic blunder, and he won anyway. Two preconditions get left out of the telling.

### Q: What actually happened?
At Jingxing, Han Xin had tens of thousands of raw recruits against two hundred thousand Zhao. He sent two thousand light horse with red banners to hide behind the Zhao camp, then drew his main body up with the river at its back. The Zhao laughed at a man with no retreat. His troops feigned a rout, the Zhao poured out after them, and the two thousand rode in and changed every flag to red. Asked afterwards, he said: throw them onto dead ground and they will live. Then the part that matters: these were men levied off the market, and on live ground they would have run.

### The parts · Dead ground is for a particular kind of troops
He gave the precondition himself: these were men driven in off the market, not a seasoned force that could be manoeuvred. Cutting the retreat is a remedy for that kind of army, not a general method. Used on trained troops it simply wastes them.
e.g. A hard deadline on a team that has just formed and barely knows itself can force cooperation. The same move on a mature team only wrecks a rhythm that was better.

### The parts · The visible half is never the whole thing
What everyone remembers is the line drawn up against the river. What decided it was two thousand horse and a camp full of swapped flags. The theatrical part, the part with an audience, is usually cover; the move that settles the outcome happens quietly elsewhere.
e.g. Behind a rival's loud launch there is usually something unannounced happening at the same time: locking a supplier, signing an exclusive, hiring your people.

### The parts · If you cut the retreat, cut it properly
With the river at your back means the way out is actually gone, not apparently gone. If the ranks know there are boats on the river, the device stops working at once. A half-burned bridge only makes people fight while timing their withdrawal.
e.g. Announcing that the company pivots if this fails, while keeping every person and every pound on the old line, tells everyone the retreat is intact and starves the new direction.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you want a hard deadline or a burned bridge to force your team to perform.
Ask first: is this the kind of team that needs to be forced, and what is the other half of my arrangement?
Where it goes wrong: treating dead ground as a cure-all and using it on people who could already fight; a retreat that is cut in name while everybody can see it is still there.

### Lines to keep
Throw them onto dead ground and they will live.
These are men levied off the market; give them ground and they run.
Cut the retreat halfway and they fight while timing the withdrawal.

## Han Xin · Neither revolt nor retire
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/han-xin/neither-nor/
Source: Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of the Marquis of Huaiyin
Tags: Deep read, Han Xin, The middle is the dangerous place

He held the chance to split the empire three ways and the chance to walk away whole. Taking neither is what killed him.

### Q: What actually happened?
With Qi pacified and a large army under him, Kuai Tong urged Han Xin to set up on his own, saying the balance of the empire hung on him alone: he whose valour overawes his lord stands in danger, and he whose merit covers the world goes unrewarded. Han Xin wavered, said the king of Han had treated him generously and he could not bring himself to betray him, and after a second appeal still did not decide. His command was taken, he was moved from king of Qi to king of Chu, demoted to marquis of Huaiyin, held in the capital, and finally killed for revolt.

### The parts · Refusing both roads is choosing the worst one
Setting up alone and standing down each have a price, and each price can be worked out. Whoever stops in the middle believes he has lost nothing and is in fact carrying both risks: still holding force that frightens people, with no plan for using it to protect himself.
e.g. Neither really taking the thing on nor clearly handing it over, on the grounds of let us see. Three months later there is no result and the old position is gone too.

### The parts · Holding power you do not intend to use is the danger
People assess your threat by your capability, not your intention. His refusal to betray was sincere, but sincerity is invisible from outside; what is visible is the army. Valour that overawes the lord names exactly this: the danger comes from the strength existing at all.
e.g. Whoever is the only person who can maintain the one critical system is treated as a risk however loyal they are. The fix is not protesting loyalty; it is making it a two-person system.

### The parts · Hearing a sentence and using it are different things
When the hares are dead the hounds are cooked. He had heard that from Kuai Tong long before the end and quoted it only on the way to execution. What lay between was not understanding but action. Most failures live in that gap.
e.g. Everyone knows to build the second business while the first is strongest. Almost no company actually moves resources across at that point.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you hold something that makes people wary, and you feel the relationship is fine.
Ask first: if they judged me only on capability and never on attitude, what would they conclude?
Where it goes wrong: stopping in the middle under the name of waiting and seeing; treating having understood a principle as having dealt with it.

### Lines to keep
He whose valour overawes his lord stands in danger.
The hares dead, the hounds are cooked; the birds gone, the bow stored.
Refusing both roads is a way of choosing the worst one.

## Harvard Study of Adult Development · Your relationships at 50 predict your body at 80
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/harvard-study/relationships-predict-health/
Source: Harvard Study of Adult Development, 1938–present; Robert Waldinger
Tags: Deep read, Harvard Study of Adult Development, More accurate than cholesterol

What actually decides how healthy you are late in life. What eighty years of tracking put in first place.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1938 Harvard began following 268 sophomores, later adding 456 boys from Boston's poorest neighbourhoods. Every two years they asked how life was going; every five they ran medical exams. It is still running. Robert Waldinger, the fourth director, says the sturdiest finding in all of it is this: how satisfied you are with your close relationships at fifty predicts your health at eighty better than your cholesterol does. Not income. Not fame. Not class.

### The parts · It runs through the body
This one gets read as a greeting card, but it lands on hard measures: people in chronically strained relationships report more chronic pain in later life and show earlier memory decline. The researchers keep repeating that this isn't about mood. The body settles the bill.
e.g. The cohort who were professionally successful and personally isolated have visibly lower health curves in old age.

### The parts · A relationship that survives isn't the same as one that protects
There's an unwelcome line in the data: a long, high-conflict, mutually draining marriage does more damage to health than separating. What protects you is the quality inside it, not whether it's still standing. 'Staying for the kids' does not balance on this ledger.
e.g. Twenty years of holding it together, and both people's medical results are paying for it.

### The parts · The window to change it is later than most people assume
Most people decide after midlife that the circle is set. In this study the clearest improvements came from people who started in their fifties and sixties — reconnecting with estranged family, turning acquaintances into regular company. Fifty is not too late for eighty.
e.g. Getting back in touch with old classmates at sixty lifted both mood and medical results across the decade that followed.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you're trading health for career, or filing relationships under 'later'.
Ask first: in the last month, how many times did I see someone for no practical reason? If you can't count one, it isn't a 'later' problem.
Where it goes wrong: reading it as needing lots of friends — the data is about quality, not headcount; or using it to force yourself to keep a draining relationship, which is precisely the most damaging category in the data.

### Lines to keep
Your body at eighty is decided by your relationships at fifty.
A marriage held together for the children bills both bodies.
'My circle is already set' is usually a conclusion you reached alone.

## Harvard Study of Adult Development · Relationships need training, like a body
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/harvard-study/social-fitness/
Source: Robert Waldinger's term, social fitness
Tags: Deep read, Harvard Study of Adult Development, Untrained, they decline

Everyone knows a body declines without training. So do relationships. What social fitness actually asks you to do.

### Q: What actually happened?
Waldinger attached a phrase to the study's conclusion: social fitness. Relationships behave like muscle — you don't finish them, and untrained they decline. Very few people in the study fell out with anyone. They moved once, changed jobs once, got busy for a few years, and by the time they looked up the numbers were still in the phone and the people were gone. The action he gives is small: pick one person and get in touch this week, not to arrange anything, just to say how things are.

### The parts · It isn't whether you have them, it's whether it moved recently
Most people judge that they 'have friends' from their contact list and their memory. What does the work is the live part — the people you have actually exchanged something with in the last six months. Counted that way, the number is usually far smaller than assumed.
e.g. Two thousand contacts, fewer than ten spoken to in six months. That second number is the real size.

### The parts · Small moves beat plans
'We should get together more' almost never happens, because it names no day and no person. What works is the smallest step: one message to one person about nothing in particular. The bar is low enough to survive a busy month, and going quiet is what relationships can't survive.
e.g. One person a week is fifty a year. Waiting until things calm down is usually zero.

### The parts · Which gap to fill depends on which one is empty
The study separates relationships by what they do: someone to fall back on, someone to enjoy things with, someone to say the true thing to, someone whose judgement you want. They don't substitute. Find the empty slot first, then decide who.
e.g. A crowd to drink with and nobody to call at 2am isn't a shortage of socialising.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you don't think of yourself as unpopular, but when you actually need someone you don't know who to call.
Ask first: who have I contacted in the last six months for no practical reason? Write the names. If you can't reach five, start there.
Where it goes wrong: turning it into a task with a streak — a relationship that becomes a metric is harder to keep; and it doesn't mean reviving everyone. You're training a few lines, not the whole address book.

### Lines to keep
Nobody sets out to lose a friend. They get busy and it goes quiet.
'We should get together' fails because it names no day and no person.
People to drink with and one person to call at 2am are different things.

## Harvard Study of Adult Development · Who can you call at 2am
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/harvard-study/someone-to-count-on/
Source: A measure used throughout the study
Tags: Deep read, Harvard Study of Adult Development, The count doesn't matter, the catch does

The shortest way to measure your relationships. Why this question is so hard to fool.

### Q: What actually happened?
The study has long used one very short question to measure relationships: if you were sick or frightened at two in the morning, who could you call. It beats 'how many friends do you have' because it asks three things at once — whether the person exists, whether you believe they'd pick up, and whether you could bring yourself to dial. Miss any one and the answer is blank. Plenty of socially busy people have no name here; plenty of quiet ones name two or three immediately.

### The parts · Three tests in one question, so it can't be gamed
Someone to call tests supply. Believing they'd answer tests quality. Being able to dial tests you. Other people supply the first two; only you can clear the third — and a lot of people stall there, carrying it alone rather than making the call.
e.g. You can think of the name, and then: 'it's too late to bother them.' That's the third test.

### The parts · No name doesn't mean no one
This answer is found by trying, not by thinking. A relationship you've never asked anything of is one whose strength you don't know. And asking the first time is usually easier than imagined — most people feel trusted rather than imposed upon.
e.g. After the first real ask, the relationship usually gets closer, not more distant.

### The parts · Turn it around: whose name are you
The question works in reverse. Does anyone think of you at two in the morning? Being someone's fallback runs both ways, and being permanently filed as 'lovely, but I wouldn't trouble them' is a shallow relationship. Letting people impose on you is its own kind of reliability.
e.g. Nobody ever asking you for help may not mean you're well-liked. It may mean nobody expects you to say yes.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you want to know how solid your relationships actually are, and have no way to measure it.
Ask first: who could I call at 2am? Write the names down. If none come, don't panic — ask the follow-up: is it that there's no one, or that I couldn't make the call?
Where it goes wrong: using it to rank the people around you or tally what you owe; and a blank answer is not a verdict. It measures where you are now, not who you are.

### Lines to keep
If something happened at 2am, who could you call.
No name may not mean no one. It may mean you never asked.
Letting people impose on you is its own kind of reliability.

## Friedrich Hayek · Knowledge is dispersed
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/hayek/knowledge-is-dispersed/
Source: The Use of Knowledge in Society (1945)
Tags: Deep read, Friedrich Hayek, Nobody can hold the whole picture

A paper of a dozen pages, later voted one of the century's most important in economics. What assumption it destroyed.

### Q: What actually happened?
The 1945 paper attacks an assumption everybody was making: collect the data centrally and the centre can compute the best allocation. His refutation takes the ground out from under it. The knowledge we must make use of never exists in concentrated or integrated form, only as dispersed, incomplete and often contradictory bits held by separate individuals. The kind that matters most is knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place, which cannot be reported upward without going stale. Prices solve that: when tin is short, users need no reason, only the new number.

### The parts · Local knowledge goes false on the way up
What the front line holds is immediate, specific and attached to a situation. Each level of aggregation strips out the time and the detail, so what arrives at the top is a stale average. An organisation that waits for reports steers today with yesterday's blur.
e.g. Sales knew the real reason that account left on Wednesday. By the time it reads as satisfaction down two per cent in the monthly, the available move is a different one.

### The parts · Move the decision to where the knowledge already is
His conclusion follows: since that knowledge cannot travel, send the authority to it and let whoever stands in the situation decide inside a mandate. The centre's job is not to decide for them but to supply signals — price, cost, priority — that carry the wider picture.
e.g. Rather than have a shop queue for promotion approval, give it a margin floor and live costs. The manager knows it is raining and the shop opposite is clearing stock.

### The parts · Inside the organisation you also need something priced
The beauty of a price is compression: it explains nothing and transmits weight. Most internal coordination fails because what gets passed around is reasons and stories with no shared measure of importance. Put a number on a scarce resource and the scramble turns into arithmetic.
e.g. Compute, design and legal are demanded infinitely while they are free. Give them an internal transfer price and every team cuts its own optional requests.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are designing a mechanism where all the information is gathered centrally and then decided on centrally.
Ask first: how much of the knowledge this depends on is local knowledge that expires the moment it is reported?
Where it goes wrong: turning delegation into abandonment with no signal to align on, or setting internal prices and then letting people go around them by relationship.

### Lines to keep
The knowledge we must make use of never exists in concentrated or integrated form.
The price system is a mechanism for communicating information.
A telegraph system: it carries the weight and not the reason.

## Friedrich Hayek · The fatal conceit
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/hayek/fatal-conceit/
Source: The Fatal Conceit (1988)
Tags: Deep read, Friedrich Hayek, The curious task of economics

He defined his own discipline's task as pouring cold water, not forecasting. Why the cleverest people need that water most.

### Q: What actually happened?
The title of his last book is the diagnosis: the fatal conceit, the idea that man can shape the world around him according to his wishes. His definition of the discipline became the famous line. The curious task of economics is to demonstrate how little men really know about what they imagine they can design. Markets, language, law and morals all work, and none of them was designed; they grew through countless trials. The designer's fatal position is that he has to pretend to hold knowledge scattered across millions of heads.

### The parts · A grown order has load-bearing walls you cannot see
Each clause in a set of old rules may be holding up a problem you never meet. They were filtered by elimination rather than argued into place. The rebuilder's risk is not a shortage of ideas; it is being unable to tell which wall is carrying weight.
e.g. The new manager cuts an obviously redundant old process. Three months later it turns out to have been the only gate against one class of accident, and whoever built it left years ago.

### The parts · The cleverer you are, the further you push design
Conceit scales with intelligence: the better you are at running a system through in your head, the easier it is to forget the variables the real one contains. His cold water is aimed at clever people. Design is legitimate over the patch where you genuinely hold the relevant knowledge.
e.g. The most meticulous five-year plan dies worst, because its own rigour left no room for the world outside it. A rough map with quarterly corrections survives.

### The parts · The alternative is to make trial and error run
Accepting that knowledge cannot be centralised is not an argument for doing nothing. It swaps designing the best solution for designing an environment that sorts solutions: parallel attempts allowed, failure made cheap, winners left free to spread. You design the track, not the result.
e.g. Instead of one head-office store layout for the country, let a hundred shops adjust and rank them on sales per square metre. What grows in six months nobody could have drawn.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have both the ability and the authority to redesign an entire system.
Ask first: which clauses of the old one can I not explain the original purpose of? Where is the edge of what I actually know?
Where it goes wrong: using orders grow, they are not made to block every reform including the rotten walls, or hiding behind trial and error where the arithmetic was available all along.

### Lines to keep
The curious task of economics is to demonstrate how little men really know.
How little they know about what they imagine they can design.
The extended order our civilisation rests on was designed by nobody.

========================================================================
## Arlie Hochschild · The second shift
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/hochschild/second-shift/
Source: The Second Shift, 1989; time-use surveys of the 1960s–70s
Tags: Deep read, Arlie Hochschild, The shift that starts when work ends

Housework and care have never appeared on a timesheet. Who ends up paying when nobody counts them.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1989 Hochschild gave the thing a name: the second shift. Women with jobs came home to another one — cooking, cleaning, children, ageing parents, all unpaid and absent from every statistic. Adding paid and unpaid hours from the time-use surveys of the period, she found women worked about 15 hours a week more than men, which over a year is an extra month of 24-hour days. The power of the concept isn't the accusation. It made invisible labour countable.

### The parts · Work that misses the timesheet is paid for by whoever does it
Any work that isn't measured gets treated as something done in passing. It doesn't disappear for going unrecorded; it becomes one person's invisible load, and that person often has no language to complain in, because on paper nothing happened.
e.g. 'You don't work, you're at home' stings because it prices a ten-hour day at zero.

### The parts · List it before you divide it
Most negotiations about chores fail not because nobody will share but because the two people are looking at different lists. Write every task down with the hours it takes each week and the argument moves from 'you don't appreciate me' to a table you can work on.
e.g. Log two weeks: who did what, how long. The gap is usually between what's remembered and what happened.

### The parts · Care time can't be compressed, only moved or dropped
You can stay up late and write a document faster. You cannot feed a child faster or sit with a sick parent faster. Care work is close to rigid in duration, so 'efficiency' barely applies. It can only be taken over by someone else, or not done — and then someone else pays.
e.g. Families hoping better organisation will free up time usually free up sleep.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the work at home lands on you, and saying so has changed nothing.
Ask first: are the two of us looking at the same list? If not, spend two weeks writing it all down before discussing who does what.
Where it goes wrong: using the concept as a moral charge, which turns the conversation into a tally of old debts; or the reverse — 'it's hard on everyone' erases the list all over again.

### Lines to keep
About 15 hours more a week. A year of that is an extra month.
The first shift is at work, the second at home. Only one pays.
Labour nobody books gets billed to one person anyway.

## Arlie Hochschild · Emotional labour
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/hochschild/emotional-labor/
Source: The Managed Heart, 1983; fieldwork with flight attendants, waiters and debt collectors
Tags: Deep read, Arlie Hochschild, That smile isn't hers

Some jobs ask you not only to do the work but to feel the right thing. What that requirement costs.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1983, after fieldwork with flight attendants, waiters and debt collectors, Hochschild named emotional labour: work that requires you to display a prescribed feeling — warmth for the attendant, hardness for the collector. Her central observation was alienation. That smile is not 'her' smile, and over time the worker becomes estranged not only from the expression but from what she actually feels, unable to tell which happiness is her own. She placed it beside physical labour: required feeling is workload, only nobody clocks it.

### The parts · Surface acting and deep acting cost differently
Surface acting is putting the face on while knowing you're putting it on. Deep acting is persuading yourself you really feel it. The first exhausts through tension; the second exhausts because afterwards you can't find yourself again. Both have a bill. They arrive at different times.
e.g. A day on the support line and no words left by evening — that's surface. Years in and feeling hollow is the other bill.

### The parts · Only once you count it as work can you schedule recovery
As long as feelings are treated as your own private business, no rest can ever be arranged for them. Admit that it's workload and you start scheduling recovery the way you would after physical work, instead of expecting the feeling to bounce back on its own.
e.g. Twenty minutes of not speaking to anyone after a run of clients is maintenance, not slacking.

### The parts · The cost rises with the distance from what you feel
The further the required feeling sits from the real one, the more expensive it is. Being asked for warmth while you're grieving costs far more than being asked for calm while you're calm. The most damaging roles aren't the busiest — they're the ones that most often require the opposite of what you feel.
e.g. Straight off an abusive complaint call and into the next one in the same bright voice. That second is the most expensive.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you got little done today and can't face saying a word this evening.
Ask first: how much of today was spent holding a required feeling? Was any of that counted as part of my workload?
Where it goes wrong: using it as licence to drop basic courtesy and professionalism; or the reverse — using 'it's the job' to push yourself into deep acting until you can't tell what's real. That's precisely the cost she documented.

### Lines to keep
That smile is not 'her' smile.
In time you're estranged not just from the face but from what you feel.
Required feeling is workload. Nobody clocks it.

## The Last Hot-Metal Edition · A craft that ended in one night
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/hot-metal/one-night/
Source: The documentary Farewell, Etaoin Shrdlu, 1978; the night the New York Times changed over
Tags: Deep read, The Last Hot-Metal Edition, 1 July 1978

What it looks like when an entire trade disappears at once. What happened to the compositors the morning after.

### Q: What actually happened?
On 1 July 1978 the New York Times set its last edition in hot metal. The same day, photocomposition took over. A documentary filmed that night: the machines still roaring, the compositors locking up the final page, then the power off. The trade took years to learn, and the Linotype keyboard has nothing in common with a typewriter. What came out of those years was a body of skill that worked in exactly one place. The next morning there was no position for it in the building.

### The parts · Not a slow decline, a single switch
Inside an industry, replacement is rarely gradual. Once the equipment is installed and the workflow cuts over, the old roles stop as a block rather than thinning year by year. People counting on a few years of cushion usually do not get one.
e.g. It is not that orders shrink each year. It is that from one month on, the whole line is run a different way.

### The parts · The more specific the skill, the harder it travels
The Linotype layout means something only on a Linotype. Years of muscle memory in those keys are worth nothing anywhere else. The closer a skill sits to one particular machine, the more precisely it retires on the day that machine does.
e.g. If all you can run is one system, the day that system is switched off, what you know goes to zero.

### The parts · Check what your skill is attached to
Within the same job, knowing how a page reads and how a headline should break is not attached to the Linotype. Finger speed on that keyboard is welded to it. The question is how far a given skill sits from one specific piece of equipment.
e.g. Knowing a piece of software and knowing how the work should be done retire on completely different dates.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a new way of working is spreading in your trade, and most of what you are good at was trained around the old equipment.
Ask first: of the things I do best, which still hold outside this particular toolset, and which go to zero the moment it changes?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as depth is pointless. This trade fed families for generations. The point is to also hold one skill that is not bolted to the equipment, not to stop going deep.

### Lines to keep
Inside an industry, replacement is rarely gradual.
A skill welded to one machine retires when the machine does.
The question is how far the skill sits from the tool.

## The Last Hot-Metal Edition · The most valuable part went first
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/hot-metal/speed-was-the-craft/
Source: The move from hot metal to photocomposition in 1970s newspapers; Farewell, Etaoin Shrdlu
Tags: Deep read, The Last Hot-Metal Edition, The thing they were fastest at

Why the most skilled are often replaced first. The conditions under which mastery turns into a liability.

### Q: What actually happened?
The compositors everyone respected were the fast ones. Lines set per minute was the trade's public scoreboard. Photocomposition arrived and the whole board was void, because the machine set faster than any of them and never tired. What followed was counterintuitive. The most skilled took the hardest hit, since their entire worth was staked on the one thing being replaced. The ones who had never been fastest, but who understood something besides speed, were the ones who could move.

### The parts · The scoreboard was set by the trade, not by you
The thing you compete to be first at was usually chosen for you long before you arrived. When that board is voided, the people near the top lose most, because they have put every chip on a position that can be lifted away whole.
e.g. Fastest, most accurate, most practised. Those are precisely the measures a tool catches up with first.

### The parts · Mastery blocks the view of other directions
Getting very fast at one thing pays clearly, so people keep putting the hours there. When it stops counting, nothing else has been started. This is not unwillingness to learn. Every single year, continuing to sharpen the main thing was the best available move.
e.g. For years the smart choice was another hour on your strongest skill, right up until it stopped being worth anything.

### The parts · Keep one thing that is not on the board
Skills off the scoreboard pay slowly and attract no attention at the time. Because they attract no attention, they are also not in the first wave of what gets matched. They cannot replace the main skill. They decide whether you are standing when it is voided.
e.g. The fastest hands could not move. The one who understood how a page reads still had somewhere to go.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you rank high on your trade's public scoreboard, and tools are closing in on the events it measures.
Ask first: which measures does my trade actually compete on? Which of them is a tool already better at than me? Beyond that board, what else do I have?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as do not get very good. Being the best was never the mistake. The mistake is staking your whole worth on a board that can be lifted away whole.

### Lines to keep
The most skilled took the hardest hit.
Every year, sharpening the main thing was the best available move.
What is off the scoreboard is not in the first wave.

## The Last Hot-Metal Edition · Who made it across
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/hot-metal/who-got-across/
Source: Changes in newspaper composing-room jobs through the 1970s and 1980s
Tags: Deep read, The Last Hot-Metal Edition, Not the fastest hands

Why some people came through the same shock. What the ones who stayed were actually holding, rather than luck.

### Q: What actually happened?
Photocomposition, and computer setting after it, did not leave newspapers without people. It changed which people. The job moved from setting metal fast and clean to knowing why this page is laid out this way. Someone who understood type sizes, which line must not break, what an editor's one-sentence change pulls along with it, could do the work on any tool. Someone whose whole skill lived in hand speed had very little to show once the new equipment arrived.

### The parts · Say why, and changing tools costs you nothing
In any job, how it is done belongs to the tool and why it is done that way belongs to judgement. The first expires with the equipment; the second travels with the person. Most people train only the first, because it shows results the same day.
e.g. Operating the software and knowing why it is set up that way are two skills with very different retirement dates.

### The parts · Get the tacit part into words first
The most valuable thing in an old hand is often the part they cannot state: they see instantly that something is wrong and cannot say why. Tools match the half that can be stated. The unstated half needs stating even more urgently, or it cannot be handed on at all.
e.g. That looks wrong has to break down into three specific reasons before it is portable.

### The parts · The ones who crossed had started half a step early
Learning on the day the new equipment is installed is a different starting line from having played with it for a year. Half a step is not much. Touching the new thing while the old work still pays is far cheaper than after it stops.
e.g. Trying the new tool while the old job still feeds you costs less than learning it from scratch unemployed.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the tools in your trade are turning over and you want to know which group you are in.
Ask first: which part of this work can I explain the reasons for? For the part I cannot, how many specific reasons can I write down this month?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as experience keeps you safe. The people who were replaced had plenty of experience. The line runs between experience that lives in the hands and experience that lives in the judgement.

### Lines to keep
How it is done is the tool. Why is judgement.
Tools match the half of a craft that can be stated.
Touch the new tool while the old work still pays.

## Hu Xueyan · The board that faces inward
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/hu-xueyan/no-cheating/
Source: The No Cheating board at Hu Qing Yu Tang, 1878
Tags: Deep read, Hu Xueyan, Put the rule where the cheating is possible

Adulterating medicine is easy and almost never detected. What is worth studying is where he chose to hang the rule about it.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1878 he wrote two characters for his pharmacy, Hu Qing Yu Tang: No Cheating. Underneath ran a note. No trade can afford the word cheat, and medicine, which holds lives, least of all; he would not take a fat profit with an inferior drug, and he asked the managers to hold this as their own. The board was not hung at the front for customers. It faces inward, where only the staff and the managers pass it every day. A second board, One True Price, faced the shop floor.

### The parts · Put the rule on the side where cheating is possible
A customer cannot tell good herbs from bad, so no external check exists. Hanging the board inward concedes that the only available constraint is internal, and that an internal constraint needs a physical reminder people walk past daily. A rule posted where outsiders read it is mostly advertising.
e.g. Promising customers you never use cheap inputs matters less than the spec sheet taped above the benches where the only people who could substitute actually stand.

### The parts · Where nothing can be verified, honesty is an asset choice
In a trade the buyer cannot audit, adulteration pays immediately and invisibly. Giving up that informational advantage converts a certain current profit into something long-dated and unseeable. His bank failed and he was ruined; the pharmacy is still trading.
e.g. Holding the standard where the client could never check always shows on the books as money wasted. It pays back years later, as people not needing to check you.

### The parts · Two boards, two audiences
One True Price faces out; No Cheating faces in. He treated them as separate jobs. Outward you owe a clear promise; inward you owe an enforceable discipline. A promise without the discipline eventually breaks, and a discipline nobody announces builds no expectation at all.
e.g. Telling customers the price is fixed needs a matching internal rule that nobody may discount, ever. Without the second, the first lasts about a quarter.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: there is a step the customer could never audit, and the cost pressure is real.
Ask first: where is this rule currently posted, and who reads it there?
Where it goes wrong: turning the promise into marketing with no matching internal rule, or assuming that what cannot be detected does not exist.

### Lines to keep
No trade can afford the word cheat; medicine, which holds lives, least of all.
I will not take a fat profit with an inferior drug.
One true price, and no second price.

## Hu Xueyan · The silk corner
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/hu-xueyan/the-silk-corner/
Source: The raw silk campaign of 1882 to 1883
Tags: Deep read, Hu Xueyan, What it costs to bet everything once

The richest merchant in the empire lost everything inside two years. The interesting question is which step was the mistake.

### Q: What actually happened?
From 1882 he used his bank and his silk business to hoard raw silk, meaning to control supply and force the foreign houses to his price. The first year worked; they had to pay. Then Europe turned. Silk prices fell, the Italian crop came in large, and the foreign buyers simply bought elsewhere. His money was locked in silk for a season, while the deposits funding it could be withdrawn in a day. With Zuo Zongtang dead he had no protection at court, a rumour started, and the branches were run on at once.

### The parts · Cornering a good whose supply you do not own
A corner only works if you control the supply and the buyer has nowhere else to go. Raw silk failed both tests, because China was not the only source and Italy was having a good year. Before squeezing anyone, establish whether they have a second seller.
e.g. Locking up capacity to lift a price requires knowing whether the other side can find a second supplier within three months. If they can, you have bought inventory.

### The parts · Long bets on short money
Silk needed a year or more to come back. Deposits could leave in an afternoon. An asset that outlasts its funding looks completely normal in calm weather and fails on the first tremor. What finished him was not the wrong view; it was the mismatch.
e.g. Funding a three-year build with money that can be recalled on notice means any ordinary wobble removes you, even when the direction was right all along.

### The parts · A borrowed advantage expires with the lender
Cheap funding, government deposits and official convenience all rested on one patron. That kind of advantage looks like capability while it lasts and reveals itself as a lease when it ends. Sorting your moat means separating what you grew from what you rent.
e.g. The exclusive channel you hold because of one executive expires the day he leaves. Counting it as durable advantage is keeping a false set of books.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are convinced something will rise and you want to concentrate everything into it.
Ask first: can the other side buy elsewhere, and what is the earliest my funding can be taken away?
Where it goes wrong: counting a borrowed relationship as your own moat, or holding a long position on money that is short.

### Lines to keep
A corner needs the supply, not only the money.
Across five thousand years of trade, the first man is Fan Li.
Never wear arrogance; never be without a backbone.

## Jensen Huang · Zero-billion-dollar markets
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/huang/zero-billion-markets/
Source: Public talks and interviews over the years
Tags: Deep read, Jensen Huang, Entering before the market exists

He has his own name for how the company chooses. How to stay alive inside a market that does not exist yet.

### Q: What actually happened?
He describes the choice in one phrase: we go after zero-billion-dollar markets. Not billion-dollar markets. Markets whose present size is zero, where nobody is competing because nobody is yet buying. CUDA is the case. From 2006 the graphics chip was rebuilt for scientific computing and handed free to researchers everywhere, and the spending looked terrible on the statements for close to a decade, until deep learning arrived and everyone discovered the AI world was standing on his foundations. His explanation: if the market already exists, you are playing a game somebody else wrote the rules for.

### The parts · A zero market buys the seat where the rules get written
Enter a mature market and the product, the channels and the standards belong to somebody else; you are scoring on their board. Enter at zero and the toolchain, the developer habits and the interfaces are yours to write. What you buy is not a head start. It is the referee's chair.
e.g. Early in a category the valuable move is not selling units. It is making your interface the default, so later arrivals build on your ground however good they are.

### The parts · Getting through it takes two lines of blood supply
A zero market pays nothing for ten years, so what keeps the company alive? Two tracks. Gaming cards as the mature business feeding cash, CUDA as the zero track burning it. Without the first the second is suicide; without the second the first is merely a good business.
e.g. Feed one dark line off the cash cow and exempt it from revenue targets for five years. Most companies fail this on the quarterly question, not on the money.

### The parts · Which zero to pick is read off physics, not off research
A zero market has no users to survey, because the demand is not there to ask about. His basis was harder: the growth curve of demand for computation, the physical advantage of running things in parallel. The only dependable map here is where the technology curve points.
e.g. Surveys cannot ask about the unseen. Watch where the underlying cost curve is falling and what crossing a threshold would unlock. That crossing is the market's birthday.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a direction with no market today, and every projection tells you to drop it.
Ask first: if it does come true, who writes the rules? Do I have a line of supply that lasts until then? Am I betting on an opinion or on a physical curve?
Where it goes wrong: treating everything nobody is doing as a zero-billion gold mine. Most markets that are zero stay zero permanently.

### Lines to keep
We go after zero-billion-dollar markets.
There are no competitors there, because there are no customers yet.
If the market already exists, you are playing somebody else's game.

## Jensen Huang · Retreating with dignity
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/huang/strategic-retreat/
Source: Commencement address at National Taiwan University, 2023
Tags: Deep read, Jensen Huang, The second story in the Taipei address

One of the three stories he told the graduates is about giving up. Why he says retreat is hardest for the ablest.

### Q: What actually happened?
At the 2023 Taipei commencement he told the story of leaving mobile chips. Nvidia had entered mobile processors early, then saw giants ringing the category and the margin being squeezed out, and knew that dropping it meant dropping the biggest growth story it had. They dropped it, and moved the chips toward robotics and AI. Then he named the psychology out loud: retreat does not come easily to brilliant, successful people like you; but strategic retreat, sacrifice, deciding what to give up, is core to success. Hence the second half of the famous line: run, don't walk.

### The parts · The abler you are, the dearer admitting defeat costs
A clever person's record holds no failures, and that is precisely the burden. Retreat is not a business adjustment for him, it is a threat to identity: the story I never give up is what stops him doing the right thing. Watch for star teams defending ground that should be given up.
e.g. The failing project hardest to kill is the one handed to the best team. Not because it deserves rescuing, but because nobody wants a loss on that record.

### The parts · Retreat on the structure, not on this quarter's fighting
Mobile chips were still growing when they left. What they read was not the quarter but the structure: giants subsidising the modem, a visible ceiling on margin, their own comparative advantage sitting elsewhere. Retreat timed off the fighting always comes too late to bring the troops out whole.
e.g. It is still growing, so let us look again is reading the fighting. Growing does not change who upstream takes the margin is reading the structure.

### The parts · A retreat has to become a redeployment the same day
The period that took them out of mobile put the engineers onto the robotics platform. The value of a retreat is not the loss it stops but the freed strength having somewhere to go immediately. Withdrawal without redeployment is bleeding; withdrawal into a new formation is manoeuvre.
e.g. The announcement that cuts a line has to name the new position and who goes there. Retreat first and think later cuts the team's belief in the next attack too.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a business that is still growing, has no structural way out, and is the team's pride.
Ask first: is what stops us a structural judgement, or the story that we never give up? For the people and money coming out, have we named where they go?
Where it goes wrong: reading strategic retreat as a pass to withdraw whenever things get hard. Or retreating without redeploying, so the freed resources sit in the account going mouldy.

### Lines to keep
Retreat does not come easily to brilliant, successful people.
Strategic retreat, sacrifice, deciding what to give up, is core to success.
Run, don't walk.

## Huineng · There was never a thing there
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/huineng/originally-not-a-thing/
Source: Platform Sutra, chapter one
Tags: Deep read, Huineng, Subtraction is harder than addition

Two verses. Everyone admired one; the other went to an illiterate kitchen worker. What separates them.

### Q: What actually happened?
The fifth patriarch asked his students for a verse to decide his successor. Shenxiu, the head monk and everyone's expected heir, wrote on the corridor wall at night: the body is a bodhi tree, the mind a bright mirror's stand; polish it constantly, let no dust settle. It is an entirely correct account of practice — wipe daily, keep the dust off. Huineng, illiterate and pounding rice out the back, had his written beside it: there was never a tree, nor any stand; there was never a thing there, so where would dust settle? He doesn't dispute the polishing. He asks where the mirror came from.

### The parts · Shenxiu's verse isn't wrong. It's heavy
'Polish it constantly' is executable, checkable and almost impossible to get wrong. The trouble is it can never be finished: as long as you assume a mirror that gets dirty, wiping has no end. A great deal of effort is stuck in that correct, infinite loop.
e.g. Managing anxiety with more lists, more reviews, more reminders. The stack grows and the anxiety doesn't move — each addition is one more thing to maintain.

### The parts · Ask who installed the premise
Huineng's move pushes the question back a layer: don't optimise the solution, audit the setup. 'There was never a thing there' means the object you keep wiping may be one you erected yourself. Remove the premise and the whole discipline goes with its anxiety.
e.g. 'Everyone has to be satisfied with me' makes every conversation exhausting. Ask who set it. Usually you did, and it can be unset.

### The parts · Subtraction is hard because it has no progress bar
Adding a method gives you something to do immediately. Removing a premise gives you nothing to do at all. The second pays far better and shows no progress along the way, so most people keep wiping.
e.g. Cutting half the meetings beats adding a collaboration tool. The first produces nothing to report, so almost nobody does it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something you're managing carefully has never once got lighter.
Ask first: does this need constant managing because it's inherently like that, or because I set a premise?
Where it goes wrong: reading subtraction as giving up; optimising only at the level of solutions and never inspecting the setup.

### Lines to keep
There was never a thing there, so where would dust settle?
Not the wind moving, not the flag moving. Your mind is moving.
The object you keep wiping may be one you put there.

## Huineng · The practice is here, not elsewhere
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/huineng/in-the-world/
Source: Platform Sutra, chapters two and three
Tags: Deep read, Huineng, There is no better place to start

People wait for a quiet enough setting to begin. Why Huineng said that setting doesn't exist.

### Q: What actually happened?
Asked whether a layperson could practise at home, Huineng was flat about it: the teaching is in the world, and awakening is not apart from the world; to seek it outside the world is to hunt for a rabbit's horns — the thing simply isn't there. He pulled the whole practice back into daily life: if the mind is level, what need of precepts; if conduct is straight, what need of meditation. He lived it too — after receiving the transmission he spent fifteen years among a band of hunters, taking the days as they came.

### The parts · There is no better place to begin
Waiting for a quieter environment, an emptier calendar, a riper moment is itself a form of avoidance. To seek it outside the world is to hunt a rabbit's horns — the fully-prepared place doesn't exist, because the conditions never all arrive.
e.g. 'I'll start exercising when this project ends.' There is another project after it. People who start, start while busy.

### The parts · The ordinary thing in front of you is the training ground
Huineng breaks practice down into specific actions inside specific relationships: how you treat your parents, how you treat those above and below, what you do when treated unfairly. None of it needs separate time. It already occupies all of your time; it just wasn't counted as practice.
e.g. The hardest call of the day and the message you least want to answer are that day's entire curriculum.

### The parts · Complete form isn't the same as the thing done right
'What need of precepts, what need of meditation' doesn't abolish either. It warns that form serves substance. When someone's forms are immaculate, that is often exactly when the substance has gone wrong — the form became the substitute.
e.g. The team with the most beautiful process documentation is sometimes the worst at executing. The document felt like the work.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you're waiting for a better moment to begin something that matters.
Ask first: if that moment never arrives, what is the smallest step available today?
Where it goes wrong: turning preparation into procrastination; substituting completeness of form for completion of substance.

### Lines to keep
The teaching is in the world. Awakening is not apart from it.
To seek it outside the world is to hunt for a rabbit's horns.
If the mind is level, what need of precepts.

## Huo Qubing · Never mind the old manuals
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/huo-qubing/no-old-manuals/
Source: Records of the Grand Historian, Wei Qing and Huo Qubing
Tags: Deep read, Huo Qubing, Read the ground, not the book

The emperor offered to teach him the classics of war and he declined. The question is whether that was arrogance or judgement.

### Q: What actually happened?
Emperor Wu wanted to teach him Sun Tzu and Wu Qi. Huo Qubing answered that what matters is how the plan for this campaign is drawn, and there is no need to study the old military texts. The line has been read as a boy's arrogance for two thousand years. His campaigns say otherwise. At seventeen he took eight hundred riders hundreds of li beyond the main army; at nineteen he ran two long flanking marches through the Hexi corridor; at twenty-one he reached Mount Langjuxu. Han doctrine was infantry and cavalry together, advancing along a grain road. His war was all cavalry, long range, and had no rear.

### The parts · A manual encodes the last generation's constraints
Sun Tzu and Wu Qi were written when the mass of an army was infantry and chariots and the grain road set the marching radius. Huo Qubing had decades of imperial horse-breeding behind him. The tools had changed, so the best answer had changed, and the book holds the old one.
e.g. The growth playbook everyone copies was built when attention was cheap. Copy it faithfully now and you fail faithfully.

### The parts · Refusing the template is not refusing to think
The weight of his answer falls on the word plan. He did not fight on instinct; he drew a fresh scheme for every campaign. What he threw out was the general template, not the work. People collapse the two, and only the second is actually arrogance.
e.g. We ignore the competition and go our own way is a judgement when a worked-out model sits behind it, and laziness when nothing does.

### The parts · The method came with the man attached
No rear, high intensity, raids run back to back: this asks for a body and a tolerance of risk almost nobody has, and it forbids caution. Which is why it never transferred. Hand the same tactics to an older and steadier general and they do not execute.
e.g. The punishing pace a founder can carry usually stops working once the team doubles and the original people have gone.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a ready-made methodology is sitting there and something about it feels wrong.
Ask first: are the conditions that made this method work still in place today? Name them one by one and check.
Where it goes wrong: treating not copying as not needing a plan; and pushing a method welded to one particular person as though it were general.

### Lines to keep
What matters is the plan for this campaign, not the old texts.
A manual is the best answer to a problem you no longer have.
Refusing the template is not the same as refusing to think.

========================================================================
## Huo Qubing · Feed off the enemy
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/huo-qubing/feeding-off-the-enemy/
Source: Records of the Grand Historian, Wei Qing and Huo Qubing
Tags: Deep read, Huo Qubing, A supply line is also a leash

The hard limit on any long march is grain. This one is about how he took the limit away altogether.

### Q: What actually happened?
The Records compress his method into one line: he took his food from the enemy, and so marched extraordinarily far without his grain ever running out. Han expeditions were governed by the grain road, and the marching radius was set by the distance from the rear. He swapped the constraint out: no baggage train, resupply from the Xiongnu camps he broke on the way. That is what made a raid of two thousand li possible. The same chapter records the other half of him. Sent out with dozens of carts of palace food, he came home throwing away fine grain and meat while his own soldiers went hungry.

### The parts · A supply line is a lifeline and a tether
A grain road gives you a radius, and a radius gives the other side a number he can compute. Giving it up costs you safety and buys something else: he can no longer predict you. He deploys against your supply capacity, and you appear where his arithmetic says you cannot be.
e.g. A branch that clears every move with head office moves at head office tempo, which a rival can read straight off a calendar.

### The parts · Living off the land means winning every time
The hidden premise is that every encounter must be won, won quickly, and won with enough taken. Lose once, or win slowly, and the column starves within days. So it is not the easy option. It moves the risk out of logistics and into fighting strength.
e.g. Funding expansion from the cash each new market throws off works only while every market turns positive fast. One that does not breaks the whole chain.

### The parts · The same chapter records what he was bad at
Raised at court, high-born, careless of his men: he did not know what the ranks were going through, and threw good food away rather than share it. Extreme tactical skill and neglect of the people carrying it sat inside one man, and the historian let both stand.
e.g. The manager with the best numbers on the floor can also have the worst attrition. Read only one of those facts and you will staff the next team wrong.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: an expansion is about to stretch the supply line and you are working out how far it will reach.
Ask first: if this had to live off what it takes, could I guarantee a fast win every single time?
Where it goes wrong: assuming that carrying no grain has only upsides; and letting one person's results settle the question of how he runs a team.

### Lines to keep
He took his food from the enemy and never ran short.
A supply line gives you a radius. A radius can be computed.
This is not the safe option. The risk has only moved.

========================================================================
## The I Ching · The hidden dragon does not act
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/i-ching/hidden-dragon/
Source: Book of Changes, Qian hexagram, bottom line; Commentary on the Words
Tags: Deep read, The I Ching, Newly in place, do not move yet

Just arrived, just promoted, just moved. This one asks why the first line of the first hexagram says do not act.

### Q: What actually happened?
The six lines of Qian read from the bottom up as one dragon moving from hidden to flying to overreaching. The bottom line has four words: the hidden dragon does not act. The dragon is under water. Not for lack of power, since a dragon is a dragon. The position is still lowest, and force used from there is all your own, with all of the risk on you. One step up is the dragon appearing in the field. A step above that, the noble man is busy all day and wary at night. Capacity and the right moment are two different times.

### The parts · Being able and being due are two different times
The first line and the fifth are both the dragon. What differs is not power but position. Rushing to prove yourself in a new place spends your own force and carries all the risk; from the second or third line the same act is far easier.
e.g. New to a team, change nothing in the first month. Not because it should not be changed, but because that is when changing it costs the most.

### The parts · Not acting is accumulating, not waiting
The hidden dragon is not lying down. The third line is explicit: busy all day, wary into the evening. The time under water goes on reading the ground and gathering what you will need. What is waited for is a change of position, not a change of mood.
e.g. Before you are in a position to decide anything, find out everything worth finding out. That is the work of the hidden stretch.

### The parts · Every line has its own move, and skipping costs
The six lines give six different pieces of advice because the positions differ. Acting from the first line as though you stood at the fifth is using force that is not yours to use. Knowing which line you are on matters more than knowing all six.
e.g. Ask which line am I on before deciding whose advice to follow, including your own from the last job.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: newly in a position or a new place, wanting to produce something fast to prove yourself.
Ask first: which line am I on here, and if it is the bottom one, have I gathered what that line is for?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as hide and do nothing. The bottom line withholds action, not effort, and the third line is busy all day; it is also not a reason to stay under water forever, because the dragon is meant to rise.

### Lines to keep
The hidden dragon does not act.
Being able and being due are two different times.
Ask which line you are on before choosing how to act.

## The I Ching · The overreaching dragon repents
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/i-ching/arrogant-dragon/
Source: Book of Changes, Qian hexagram, top line; Commentary on the Words
Tags: Deep read, The I Ching, The line above the peak

What the risk is when everything has gone your way for a long time, and why the top line is not the best one.

### Q: What actually happened?
Counting up Qian, the fifth line is the dragon flying in the heavens, which looks like the summit. There is one line above it. The top line reads: the overreaching dragon repents. The Commentary on the Words glosses that word: to know advancing and not retreating, to know preserving and not perishing, to know gaining and not losing. Three knowings against three not-knowings. A whole ascent spent learning advance, preservation and gain, and never once practising the other half. At the highest point the missing half is what brings you down.

### The parts · There is a line above the summit, and it repents
Most people take the fifth line for the end; the hexagram is not finished. Keep pushing in the same direction after the dragon is flying and you arrive at the top line. The problem with a peak is not the height, it is adding after you have reached it.
e.g. Most of those who double down straight after their best year are on their way to the top line.

### The parts · What is missing is not the skill of advancing
To know advancing and not retreating. A run of good fortune trains half a person. Advance, preserve and gain become fluent; retreat, perish and lose are never rehearsed. What the summit calls for is precisely the unrehearsed half, which is why people fall.
e.g. Someone who has only ever added is clumsy the first time subtraction is the right move.

### The parts · Repentance is not ruin, it is a warning
The line says repents, not disaster. The overreaching dragon does not necessarily die of the fall, but will certainly regret not having stopped at the fifth. It is written for someone still in the air: the position one step above yours is that one.
e.g. Reading this line while everything is still going well is worth more than reading it after the fall.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a long run has gone your way and you are standing higher than you ever have, thinking about adding.
Ask first: am I at the fifth line or already at the top one, and have I ever practised retreat and loss, or only advance and gain?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as quit while ahead. The flying dragon at the fifth line is good and the hexagram wants the ascent; this says only that one more line exists above the peak.

### Lines to keep
The overreaching dragon repents.
To know advancing and not retreating, gaining and not losing.
Above the summit there is one more line, and it repents.
