## The I Ching · After Peace comes Standstill
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/i-ching/peace-and-stagnation/
Source: Book of Changes, hexagrams Tai and Pi and their order; Great Commentary
Tags: Deep read, The I Ching, Run it to the limit and it turns

What to prepare when everything is going well, and what to hope for when it is jammed. Why the two sit side by side.

### Q: What actually happened?
Among the sixty-four, the eleventh is Tai, free passage, and the twelfth is Pi, blockage. They are placed next to each other, and the top line of Tai already reads: the wall falls back into the moat. The last position of the smooth run is itself the beginning of the turn. It works the other way too, since the top of Pi reads standstill first, then joy. The Great Commentary states the rule. At the limit it changes; changed, it passes through; passing through, it lasts. Not a fated cycle: every state carries its own end inside it.

### The parts · The turn is written into the top line of Peace
The wall falling back into the moat is not in Pi; it is in Tai. The reversal does not begin when the bad days start, it begins at the last position of the good ones. The moment most worth preparing is the one that looks least like it needs preparing.
e.g. The year the business is best is the year to work out how it ends. Waiting until it has ended means you are already in Pi.

### The parts · At the limit it changes, so being jammed is the condition
People try to change things while they still just about work, and cannot, because the limit has not been reached. Fully jammed, change becomes possible, because the old way has run out and nobody is defending it any more.
e.g. Stop forcing the change while it still half works. Push at the moment it genuinely seizes and the resistance is at its lowest.

### The parts · Adjacent means neither one lasts
Tai does not stay Tai and Pi does not stay Pi. The same sentence is a warning to whoever is up and a comfort to whoever is down. What matters is reading which hexagram you are in rather than treating the present as permanent.
e.g. Now is not the normal state. It is one line of one hexagram. Ask yourself which.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: either everything is going well and you expect it to continue, or you are jammed and expect never to get out.
Ask first: if this is Tai, which line am I on and how far off is the wall falling back into the moat? If this is Pi, am I treating the jam as the entry ticket for change or only as bad luck?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as fatalism, that it will turn anyway so nothing matters. The Great Commentary says at the limit it changes, and changing is something a person does.

### Lines to keep
The wall falls back into the moat.
At the limit it changes; changed it passes through, and so lasts.
Now is not the normal state. It is one line of one hexagram.

## Ivan Illich · The two watersheds
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/illich/two-watersheds/
Source: Tools for Conviviality (1973); Medical Nemesis (1975)
Tags: Deep read, Ivan Illich, A tool that starts eating its own purpose

Everyone says tools are neutral and it depends how you use them. What is worth reading is why he says they are not.

### Q: What actually happened?
Every tool, he argued, crosses two watersheds. Before the first it solves a real problem: antibiotics keep alive people who would have died. Between the two it is steadily useful. Past the second it begins producing the thing it was built to remove. He gave the medical version a name, iatrogenesis — illness produced by the treatment. The claim is not that doctors are bad, but that a system at scale acquires an appetite: it needs patients, so more of an ordinary life gets redefined as a condition requiring care. Schooling runs the same way — the more education is institutionalised, the more learning means being taught.

### The parts · The question is not whether it works
Between the watersheds a tool is a benefactor; past the second it is a creditor. So does it work has no useful answer — it does, and has since the first watershed. The question is when what you pay to keep it began to exceed what it gives you.
e.g. The group chat saved ten emails the week it started. At two hundred people you spend an hour a day reading it and anything real still arrives privately.

### The parts · The signal is that it starts producing the opposite
Not inefficiency — the reverse of the original purpose. Medicine producing illness, transport producing distance, school producing a sense of ignorance. That signal is far more sensitive than any efficiency number, because efficiency often keeps climbing after the crossing.
e.g. After the project tool went in, the time reporting got beautiful and people began splitting tasks to make the board look right. What the tool wants is replacing the work.

### The parts · He wants a ceiling on tools, not a bonfire
Illich is not against technology. He is against technology without an upper bound. A convivial tool is one an ordinary person can master, repair and decline. The test is whether it lets you leave: the higher the exit cost, the less it is your tool and the more you are its.
e.g. A system you can export everything from and a system you renegotiate with once you are locked in can have identical features. The difference is whether you can still walk.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a tool that genuinely saved effort at first, and you can no longer say whether it helps you or occupies you.
Ask first: how many hours a week go into keeping it? Has it started producing the opposite of what it was for? What would leaving cost?
Where it goes wrong: reading past the watershed as a reason to burn everything. Before the first watershed the tool is a real benefactor; he wants a ceiling, not a zero.

### Lines to keep
Past the second watershed a tool produces what it was meant to remove.
Illness produced by the treatment itself I call iatrogenesis.
A convivial tool is one you can master, repair, and do without.

## Ivan Illich · Count what the tool costs you
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/illich/effective-speed/
Source: Energy and Equity (1974)
Tags: Deep read, Ivan Illich, Time saved and time spent belong on one ledger

An arithmetic problem about cars, and the reason it applies without modification to the tools on your machine.

### Q: What actually happened?
He did the sum. A typical American man spends more than sixteen hundred hours a year on his car — driving, sitting in traffic, taking it to be repaired, and **working to pay for it**: purchase, petrol, insurance, loan. Those sixteen hundred hours buy him about seven and a half thousand miles. Divide, and it comes to under five miles an hour — roughly walking pace. The point is not that cars are useless. It is that we count the hours spent travelling and never the hours spent earning the thing. Savings go on one ledger and costs on another, which is how every tool saves time.

### The parts · Put both ledgers on one page and the answer often flips
Every tool advertises the time it saves. The real cost also includes learning it, maintaining it, firefighting when it fails, working to pay for it, and getting back into the work after it has interrupted you. Those land on different days, which is why nobody adds them up.
e.g. Convert the monthly fee into your own hours, then add the weekly maintenance. A surprising number of tools stop making sense at that step.

### The parts · Fragmented time costs more than occupied time
A five-minute interruption does not cost five minutes. In his arithmetic the working-to-pay-for-it hours are the visible cost; the larger hidden cost of a modern tool is that it cuts the day into pieces, and anything requiring real thought can only be done in a whole one. Fragments do not add up to it.
e.g. Six fifteen-minute meetings occupy ninety minutes and take the day, because no remaining stretch is long enough to get in.

### The parts · Measure first, then decide; do not pick a side first
The value of the method is that it is arithmetic rather than attitude. He did not say stop driving; he published a division anyone can run again. Run it on a specific tool and the answer is sometimes worth it and sometimes I have been working for this thing. Both beat a position.
e.g. Run it on the three tools you lean on hardest: total hours in, divided by what it actually finished for you. The worst score is the one to renegotiate.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have installed a stack of things that save time and your days are fuller than before.
Ask first: adding the hours to learn it, maintain it, pay for it and recover from its interruptions — how much did it actually save?
Where it goes wrong: using the sum to dismiss tools in general. He calculated a specific number, not a stance; whatever comes out ahead deserves to be used harder.

### Lines to keep
Count the hours worked to pay for it: five miles an hour.
Savings on one ledger, costs on another: that is how tools save time.
Work that needs thought happens in whole hours, never in fragments.

## Kazuo Inamori · The way of thinking is a multiplier
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/inamori/the-multiplier/
Source: Ikikata, his book on how to live
Tags: Deep read, Kazuo Inamori, And it can be negative

He reduced a life to a single multiplication. Why only one of the three factors carries a sign.

### Q: What actually happened?
The formula: the result of life and work equals way of thinking times enthusiasm times ability. He explains the notation. Ability and enthusiasm run from zero to a hundred; the way of thinking runs from minus a hundred to plus a hundred, the only factor with a sign. So ordinary ability with enormous enthusiasm can outproduce an able but arrogant and idle talent, while a man whose thinking is negative does more damage the abler and the keener he is. He called his own gifts ordinary, and offered this as the arithmetic available to everybody.

### The parts · The factor with a sign needs examining on its own
Assessment forms are usually all positive scales: ability out of ten, drive out of ten. The formula points at a structural gap. One dimension is not how much but plus or minus: who takes the credit, what he does with rules, how he treats the weak when things go well.
e.g. A top performer who grabs credit and pushes blame downward computes to a large negative. His ability is amplifying his direction, and most places keep him until the day it detonates.

### The parts · An ordinary person's odds sit in the two positive factors
Ability improves slowly and has a ceiling. Enthusiasm and the way of thinking can change today. Kyocera began with neither technology nor money behind it, and those two are what he bet on: effort and direction at full marks, and let multiplication overturn the natural gifts.
e.g. The least gifted person on a team, at full marks for direction and effort, routinely passes the most dazzling recruit within two years.

### The parts · Multiplication means any single factor can veto
In an additive system a weakness is covered by a strength. Not in a product: any factor near zero pulls the total near zero, and any factor turned negative turns the total negative. So the formula is also a running order. Repair the one risking a minus sign first.
e.g. Reviewing somebody's stall, do not reach for skills training first. Check whether enthusiasm has fallen near zero. At a multiplier of zero, no course multiplies out.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are assessing a person, or working out why you yourself have stalled.
Ask first: what is each of the three factors worth here? Is any of them near zero, or carrying a minus sign?
Where it goes wrong: swinging the way of thinking as a moral club to judge people with. Or repairing only the direction and never the ability — positive numbers still have to be large enough to multiply into something.

### Lines to keep
Result of life and work equals thinking times enthusiasm times ability.
The way of thinking runs from minus a hundred to plus a hundred.
Ordinary ability burning with enthusiasm beats able talent that is idle.

## Kazuo Inamori · Pure motive, no self-interest
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/inamori/pure-motive/
Source: His own account of founding DDI; his talks on the Japan Airlines rescue
Tags: Deep read, Kazuo Inamori, Six months of asking before he started

Before entering telecoms he interrogated himself for half a year. What that self-examination was actually guarding against.

### Q: What actually happened?
Japanese telecoms opened in 1984 and Inamori wanted to take on the giant NTT with the strength of Kyocera. He did not move. Every night before sleep he put two questions to himself: is my motive pure, is there any self-interest in it? Is this really about lowering the country's phone bills, or about being told that Inamori is remarkable? He asked for six months, and only once he was sure of a motive wholly good, with no private interest left in it did he found DDI. Twenty-six years later he took the bankrupt Japan Airlines through the same gate.

### The parts · The motive check guards against deforming later
A venture with private interest mixed into it shows no problem at the start, because self-interest and the common good often travel the same road. The fork comes in the hard moments. What was done for glory gets dropped when the glory goes; what was done for vanity bends.
e.g. A project taken on to prove yourself jams on the day you must ask a rival for help. Bowing serves the business and insults the proof.

### The parts · Six months, because self-interest wears a disguise
Ask once whether you have a private motive and the answer is always no; self-interest's first skill is finding a public-spirited account of itself. He asked for half a year to see what was still standing after each wave of feeling had gone out.
e.g. Set a cooling period before a large decision and put the same question into it repeatedly. Week one's answer was written by excitement. Week six's was written by you.

### The parts · A pure motive is a mobilisation order, not a talisman
A leader with nothing to gain borrows strength nobody else can: staff worked for a salaryless man of seventy-eight because what is he in it for had no answer, and the airline was profitable within the year. But he never said motive replaces management.
e.g. A founder who takes no pay and gives away shares earns real trust. If the numbers are still wrong, that trust only makes everyone pull harder into the iceberg.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a large opportunity has you excited and you are about to move on it today.
Ask first: take being praised and proving myself entirely out of the returns — would I still do it? How many times have I asked, and across how long?
Where it goes wrong: using a pure motive as a substitute for competence. Or running endless self-examination until every action dies of it — six months was his ceiling, not his routine.

### Lines to keep
Is my motive pure? Is there any self-interest in it?
A motive wholly good, with no private interest left in it.
If the motive is good, the thing tends to go well.

## Influence · Reciprocity
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/influence/reciprocity/
Source: Influence, chapter 2
Tags: Deep read, Influence, The sense of owing is the lever

Of the six principles he puts this one first. Why the side that gives first is the side holding the initiative.

### Q: What actually happened?
Cialdini states the rule plainly: we should try to repay, in kind, what another person has provided us. How deep does it go? In 1985 Ethiopia, in the middle of poverty, civil war and famine, sent five thousand dollars to earthquake victims in Mexico, because Mexico had sent aid when Ethiopia was invaded in 1935. The debt had held for fifty years. The other face of the rule is that it can be switched on. A flower, a can of Coke, a free sample, and the return regularly outruns the gift.

### The parts · Being in debt does not require your consent
The strongest feature of reciprocity is that the favour can arrive uninvited and the obligation still forms. You did not ask for the small gift, and having taken it you find refusing the request hard. The initiative sits with whoever gives first.
e.g. A supplier insists on doing a free first draft. By the time you assess the others, the fact that they did it for nothing is already voting.

### The parts · The return is usually out of proportion
The rule asks for repayment and says nothing about matching value, and people overpay to be rid of the feeling quickly. In Regan's experiment an unasked-for Coke produced raffle ticket purchases worth several times its price. The small favour is the cheapest lever here.
e.g. Solving a colleague's ten-minute problem buys more long-term cooperation than one large formal favour. Small enough to be awkward to ignore, light enough to settle.

### The parts · The defence is to reclassify, not to refuse
Cialdini's counter is not to turn gifts down, which costs too much socially. It is to relabel: if the favour is a sales device then it is not a favour, and the rule stops applying. Favours are owed to favours, and tactics are owed nothing.
e.g. Take the sample, sit through the free seminar, then ask one question at decision time. With the gift removed, does this proposal still pass?

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have taken something small from someone and are about to weigh their proposal.
Ask first: if that favour had never happened, what would you score this proposal?
Where it goes wrong: using reciprocity as bare purchase, which spends itself in one go; or keeping every kindness at the door so as never to owe anyone anything.

### Lines to keep
We should try to repay, in kind, what another person has provided us.
There is no duty more indispensable than that of returning a kindness.
An uninvited favour still creates the debt.

## Influence · Social proof
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/influence/social-proof/
Source: Influence, chapter 4
Tags: Deep read, Influence, When unsure, we watch each other

Everyone hates canned laughter and everyone laughs more with it. This is about the conditions that make the principle strongest.

### Q: What actually happened?
Cialdini's definition: we determine what is correct by finding out what other people think is correct. Networks keep the laugh track although audiences say they dislike it, because experiment after experiment shows it works. But the principle is not constant, and he names two amplifiers. The first is uncertainty — when we are unsure of ourselves and the situation is ambiguous, we are readiest to accept the actions of others as correct. The second is similarity: people read mainly from people like themselves.

### The parts · In an unclear situation, people read each other
When the facts are plain, people look at facts. When they are not, people look at each other. The danger is that everyone is doing it at once, so a group with no information quotes itself into an apparent consensus. Newer and murkier makes the loop stronger.
e.g. Industry consensus on a new technology forms in weeks. Chase it down and every view traces back to the same two articles and to each other.

### The parts · Similarity picks the reference group
People do not follow everyone, they follow people like themselves. So a case study persuades in proportion to how closely its subject resembles the listener, not to how impressive it is. A giant's success story is weaker than a peer's.
e.g. To move an internal change, use an ordinary team down the corridor rather than a famous company. One invites they did it, so can we.

### The parts · In a crowd, responsibility is divided by the crowd
The bystander effect runs on two layers: everyone reads everyone else's stillness as evidence that nothing is wrong, and everyone assumes somebody else will act. Cialdini's advice to a person in trouble is therefore very specific. Single one person out of the crowd.
e.g. You, sir, in the blue jacket, call an ambulance. The group email nobody answers gets a reply the day it names a person.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you cannot make the call, and you notice you are checking what everyone else does.
Ask first: did these people reach their views independently, or are they also reading each other?
Where it goes wrong: seeing through the principle and then opposing every consensus on principle; or, when you need somebody to act, still addressing the room instead of a name.

### Lines to keep
We determine what is correct by finding out what other people think is correct.
When uncertainty reigns, we accept the actions of others as correct.
You, sir, in the blue jacket, I need help. Call an ambulance.

## The Innovator's Dilemma · Beaten by good management
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/innovators-dilemma/good-management-fails/
Source: The Innovator's Dilemma, introduction and chapter one
Tags: Deep read, The Innovator's Dilemma, The textbook moves that put you out

Every generation of disk-drive leaders was killed by the next. Why the autopsy keeps reading: cause of death, good management.

### Q: What actually happened?
Christensen spent years on disk drives because the industry turned over fast enough to watch: leader after leader wiped out by the following generation. His finding was blunt. Good management was the most powerful reason they failed to stay atop their industries. These firms listened to their best customers, invested aggressively in what those customers asked for, and put capital behind the highest returns. Sustaining technologies improve the mainstream measure and incumbents almost always win them. Disruptive ones start out worse on that measure, thinner on margin, wanted by nobody important, and are therefore declined by a rational process until they grow up from the edge.

### The parts · Listening to your customers hides the change of track
Your best customers want more of what they already have, because they are locked into the same value network you are. The first users of a disruptive product are people you have never served, so polling your existing customers is polling the wrong panel entirely.
e.g. Ask heavy users whether they want a lighter, simpler version and they will say no. Heavy users are precisely the people your current complexity selected for.

### The parts · The financial model vetoes disruption automatically
Disruptive products carry lower margins, smaller markets and uncertain demand, so on any return-on-investment sheet they finish last. The more rigorous the allocation process, the faster it kills them. That is not short-sightedness; it is a process correctly running the wrong comparison.
e.g. A new line competing for budget against a mature one, reviewed on the same return table, loses every time. Give it its own table or watch it die in the meeting.

### The parts · Overshoot is the signal light
Christensen names an observable warning. Once mainstream performance runs past what most customers can use, the basis of competition migrates, from performance toward convenience, price and size. Disruption enters exactly there, as good enough but cheap and simple. The day people call your product too complicated is the day to look at the edge.
e.g. Nobody uses the flagship spec sheet to its limits, and buyers start saying good enough. That is not a marketing problem. It is a reading of where competition has moved.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a visibly smaller, cruder substitute has appeared at the edge of your market.
Ask first: on which new measure is it better than us, and could our mainstream customers even answer that question?
Where it goes wrong: turning vigilance into chasing every new toy; or vetoing every signal from the edge with the line that no customer is asking for it.

### Lines to keep
Good management was the most powerful reason they failed to stay atop their industries.
Precisely because these firms listened to their customers, they lost their positions of leadership.
Disruptive technologies bring to a market a very different value proposition.

========================================================================
## The Innovator's Dilemma · Small markets cannot save big companies
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/innovators-dilemma/small-markets/
Source: The Innovator's Dilemma, chapters five and six
Tags: Deep read, The Innovator's Dilemma, A mismatch of growth needs

Big firms do not fail to see the new market; they decline it. Why the refusal is arithmetic, and the remedy he proposes.

### Q: What actually happened?
Christensen's second principle is cruel in its plainness: small markets don't solve the growth needs of large companies. A four-billion-dollar firm holding twenty per cent growth has to find eight hundred million in new revenue a year, and a market worth forty million today rounds to nothing. To a forty-million company the same market is a doubling. By the time it is large enough to be worth entering, the first movers hold positions nobody can shift. His remedy for the incumbent is one line: give the job to an organisation small enough to get excited about small orders.

### The parts · The same opportunity is two things under two denominators
An opportunity's pull is not its absolute size but its ratio to the body weighing it. On a large organisation's scales the small one always loses, which is not about eyesight but about the denominator. Asking the main process to incubate it is asking an elephant to sit on an egg.
e.g. Inside a billion-dollar division a ten-million line cannot get approved to start. Inside a ten-person team the same line is everyone's livelihood.

### The parts · Waiting until it is clear means waiting until the walls are up
Enter when the market is big sounds prudent, but the rules, channels and customer relationships of a new market are written by whoever is already there. Latecomers do not arrive at open ground, they arrive at somebody's home field. Markets that do not exist cannot be analysed, only joined.
e.g. By the time the large firm enters the proven category, supply chain, mindshare and ecosystem all belong to the first mover. Ten times the money buys a third of the share.

### The parts · Independent means independent down to budget and scorecard
The keyword in the remedy is independence: its own cost structure, its own definition of profitable, independent enough that it never competes for a line on the parent's budget sheet. An innovation unit hanging off the parent's process has merely postponed the veto.
e.g. If the new business presents quarterly beside the mature one and is ranked on the same returns, its death date is the parent's first bad quarter.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a new direction looks too small for the company to take seriously.
Ask first: to a team of what size would this be everything, and can we build that team?
Where it goes wrong: independence turned into abandonment, with no resources and no route back to the parent; or strategic patience that lets the main process starve it slowly.

### Lines to keep
Small markets don't solve the growth needs of large companies.
Markets that don't exist can't be analyzed.
Match the size of the organization to the size of the market.

========================================================================
## Steve Jobs · Focus is what you say no to
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/jobs/focus-is-saying-no/
Source: WWDC 1997 Q&A (on film); the 1997–98 product-line cuts
Tags: Deep read, Steve Jobs, The things you cut are the good ones

Everyone says they are focused. What makes his definition worth reading is that it points the opposite way from the instinct.

### Q: What actually happened?
Apple in 1997 had dozens of overlapping product lines and was close to insolvent. He drew a two-by-two on a whiteboard — consumer and pro, desktop and portable — one machine per square, everything else cancelled, including the Newton, which had years of work in it. At WWDC that year he said the part people leave out: people think focus means saying yes to the thing you have got to focus on; it means saying no to the hundred other good ideas that there are. And then the harder sentence — that he was as proud of the things they had not done as of the things they had.

### The parts · The test comes from good ideas, not bad ones
A bad idea does not require focus to refuse; it dies on its own. What dilutes a company is the hundred directions that are genuinely decent — each with a champion, a deck and a reason. The whole difficulty of focus is that every cut lands on something that was right.
e.g. The real work in a roadmap review is not killing the weak proposals. It is keeping one of five that all hold up. Keeping two is not a decision.

### The parts · The number of squares is the discipline
The grid works because it is a physical constraint. There are four squares; for something new to enter, something has to leave. Without a container that hard, focus always loses to one more will not hurt — addition needs no argument, only subtraction does.
e.g. Put the current work in a table with a fixed number of rows on the wall. Any new proposal answers one question first: which row does it replace?

### The parts · Give credit for what was not done
Organisations reward shipping, so everyone starts things and nobody stops them. As proud of what we have not done is a medal for subtraction — markets not entered, features not added. Those decisions are invisible, and unless they carry the same standing as a launch, no is something people say and never do.
e.g. Add a page to the annual review: what we turned down this year and what it saved. The day someone is willing to own that page is the day no becomes politically possible.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the list of directions keeps growing and each one makes sense on its own.
Ask first: if only one could stay, which? And who will publicly own saying no to the rest?
Where it goes wrong: turning no into contempt for anything new. He killed the Newton and shipped the iPod two years later — the squares are there to be emptied, not sealed.

### Lines to keep
Focus means saying no to the hundred other good ideas that there are.
As proud of what we have not done as of what we did.
Simple is harder than complex. You must get your thinking clean.

========================================================================
## Steve Jobs · The dots only connect backwards
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/jobs/connecting-the-dots/
Source: Stanford commencement address, 2005 (full text and film)
Tags: Deep read, Steve Jobs, Collect first, connect later

A dropout sat in on a class with no use whatsoever. The famous line about it is usually run in the wrong direction.

### Q: What actually happened?
The first of the three Stanford stories is about dropping out: with no required courses left to take, he sat in on the calligraphy class that fascinated him — serifs, the space between letter pairs — with no prospect of any of it being useful. Ten years later, designing the Mac, all of it came back, and the Mac became the first computer with beautiful type. His summary: you cannot connect the dots looking forward; you can only connect them looking backwards. So you have to trust that they will somehow connect later — because looking forward there is no evidence at all.

### The parts · Connecting is hindsight, not a forecast
The common misuse runs the line forwards: that you can work out in advance which dots will join up. He is saying the reverse. In the moment he walked into that classroom there was no argument for it. The causality only exists afterwards; beforehand it was a bad use of a term.
e.g. Anyone who asks what this will do for my career only ever studies things whose answer is already known — and everyone has those dots, so everyone draws the same line.

### The parts · Pick dots by obsession, not by usefulness
If forward reasoning cannot justify the choice, the choice needs a different signal, and his was curiosity to the point of absorption. That is not romance, it is odds: you go deeper into what grips you, and only a dot that goes deep is worth connecting to anything. Shallow dots join to nothing.
e.g. Rather than spending evenings on a strategically chosen skill, take the thing you actually cannot leave alone as far as being able to teach it. Depth is the entry fee.

### The parts · Trusting they connect is what lets you commit now
The function of trust here is not comfort, it is solving a problem in the present: without it nobody puts real time into work with an unclear return, so they collect only safe dots. What the trust buys is the nerve to commit; the bill does not come due for a decade.
e.g. Taking the sidelined project, or a craft with no market yet — the question at the moment of choosing is not where does this lead, it is would I bet three years on it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something has hold of you and you cannot see any use in it.
Ask first: am I judging it by what it leads to, or by how deep I am likely to go?
Where it goes wrong: using the line to excuse a series of three-week enthusiasms. What fails to connect is not the unfashionable dot, it is the shallow one.

### Lines to keep
You cannot connect the dots looking forward, only looking backwards.
You have to trust that the dots will somehow connect in your future.
Stay hungry. Stay foolish.

## John Ratey · Exercise is for the brain
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/john-ratey/exercise-for-the-brain/
Source: Spark; the Naperville school programme
Tags: Deep read, John Ratey, You can feel the return the same day

Filing exercise under the gym leaves the cheapest medicine unused. What it's actually changing.

### Q: What actually happened?
A high school in Naperville, outside Chicago, ran an experiment: move PE to first period, and stop measuring who runs fastest — students only had to hold their own high heart-rate zone. That cohort went on to score far above their peers in international maths and science assessments. Ratey uses it to show the link isn't mystical: exercise prompts the brain to release proteins that support neuron growth and connection, which he calls fertiliser for the brain. Exercise doesn't only shape the body. It shapes the brain.

### The parts · Change the motive from your shape to today's state
Aim at your body and the return arrives months later, carried entirely by willpower. Aim at attention and mood and you can feel the return within hours. The second is real, and easier to sustain, because the feedback is fast.
e.g. Attention gone by mid-afternoon: twenty minutes of brisk walking usually beats another coffee, and borrows nothing.

### The parts · Intensity matters more than duration
Naperville had each student hold their own high heart-rate zone rather than race each other. That's good news for ordinary people: you don't need long sessions, you need the heart rate to actually have gone up. Fifteen real minutes beats an hour of strolling.
e.g. With no time, do fifteen minutes that leaves you out of breath rather than an hour of turning up at the gym.

### The parts · Put the hard thing after the exercise
If the window after exercise is when new connections form most readily, then schedule accordingly: the hardest learning or thinking goes after. Moving PE to first period was exactly this logic.
e.g. Before attacking a difficult document, move for twenty minutes. It saves time overall.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: your head won't turn over and you're forcing it.
Ask first: when did I last actually raise my heart rate? Is twenty minutes of moving a better trade than another hour of grinding?
Where it goes wrong: treating exercise as a cure-all and using it to replace the sleep you need and the problem you should be handling.

### Lines to keep
Exercise doesn't only shape the body. It shapes the brain.
The growth factors physical activity releases are fertiliser for the brain.
Schedule the hardest learning for after the exercise.

## John Ratey · When anxious, move before you think
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/john-ratey/move-before-you-think/
Source: Spark, the chapters on anxiety and stress
Tags: Deep read, John Ratey, Start with the physiology

The more you think, the worse it gets, and knowing that doesn't stop it. Why this is the moment to go outside.

### Q: What actually happened?
Ratey points out how physical anxiety is: the body has already gone on standby and the hormones are circulating, and talking yourself down at the cognitive level barely reaches it. Exercise works because it acts on that system directly — burning off the standby hormones and giving the brain the signal that you already ran and the danger has passed. That explains a common experience: after a walk the thing is less frightening, and nothing about it has changed. So his advice is blunt: when the feeling is jammed, handle the physiology first, the thinking second.

### The parts · Bring the arousal down before you reason
Reasoning at high arousal is extremely inefficient, with yourself or with anyone else. The order should be: get the body down — walk, breathe, leave the room — then return to the content. It's also why reasoning mid-argument doesn't work.
e.g. Chest tight and the same thought circling: go outside for twenty minutes. Come back to the same thing and it weighs differently.

### The parts · Rumination has to be interrupted, not resolved
The twentieth pass over the same thought produces no new information, only a deeper groove. You don't get out of that loop by continuing to think. It needs an external action to break it, and exercise is the most reliable — it occupies attention and burns the hormones at once.
e.g. Catching yourself chewing the same sentence again is the signal to interrupt, not the signal to keep going.

### The parts · Don't let it replace the problem
Exercise lowers the intensity of anxiety. It doesn't resolve what caused it. What you buy is a state in which you can think properly, not an escape. The thing is still there when you get back — you can just see it more clearly.
e.g. Running daily to hold down a fear about a decision. However far you run, the decision is still waiting.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something has gone round your head many times and each pass makes it worse.
Ask first: am I thinking or ruminating? Move for twenty minutes, then come back to the same thing.
Where it goes wrong: using exercise to avoid, so that once you've moved you never deal with the thing at all.

### Lines to keep
Anxiety is heavily physical. Talking yourself down barely reaches it.
Exercise gives the brain the signal that the danger has passed.
The twentieth pass over a thought produces no new information.

========================================================================
## Carl Jung · You can't run the afternoon on the morning's programme
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/jung/afternoon-of-life/
Source: Jung, The Stages of Life, 1930–31
Tags: Deep read, Carl Jung, Not wrong. Expired

Something feels wrong around forty. Is it a fault? Jung said it's the hour.

### Q: What actually happened?
Jung compared a life to a day. In the morning the task points outward — a career, a family, a place in the world — and the standards come from outside and genuinely work. His observation was that many people stall in midlife not because their capacity declined but because they are still running the afternoon on the morning's programme. His line is severe: what was great in the morning will be little at evening. Not that the programme was wrong. It expired.

### The parts · Stalling is usually the hour, not a malfunction
Someone in their late thirties doing well and suddenly unable to summon anything looks first for a defect: tiredness, wrong industry. Jung offers another reading — the morning's task is largely done, the afternoon's hasn't been picked up, and the gap between them is the feeling.
e.g. Having everything you were meant to want and feeling emptier is harder to explain to anyone than having nothing.

### The parts · The morning's fix fails twice as hard in the afternoon
Stuck in the morning, the answer is push harder and ask for more. Use that again in the afternoon and it only packs the empty place fuller. Plenty of people add in midlife — bigger house, higher title — and find the feeling entirely unchanged.
e.g. The promotion made it emptier, which says the thing being added was never on the ledger.

### The parts · The afternoon's task points inward, not outward
Jung says the direction reverses: from acquiring to sorting, from proving outward to picking back up the parts of yourself that never got used. The judge changes too — the morning is scored by others, the afternoon only by you.
e.g. Picking up the thing you put down at twenty, mostly not in order to achieve anything with it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you're in your thirties or forties, doing reasonably well, and increasingly unable to summon anything, without being able to say what's wrong.
Ask first: is the effort I'm making still answering the morning's question? If that one is largely answered, adding more won't work.
Where it goes wrong: using it as a reason to abandon a career — Jung is describing a shift of weight, not walking off; and don't read every bout of tiredness as a turn in your life. Sometimes you're tired.

### Lines to keep
What was great in the morning will be little at evening.
Adding more in the afternoon only packs the empty place fuller.
The direction reverses: from proving outward to picking yourself back up.

========================================================================
## Carl Jung · What you push down comes back
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/jung/the-shadow/
Source: Jung on the shadow and projection
Tags: Deep read, Carl Jung, It jumps out of other people

The kind of person you can't stand — why they can enrage you instantly. Jung said part of you is in there.

### Q: What actually happened?
Jung called the part of yourself you deny and push down the shadow. To become an acceptable person, everyone suppresses something: ambition, laziness, temper, wanting to be seen. Those things don't disappear. They move somewhere you can't see, and then jump out of other people. So the kind of person you least tolerate usually carries the very thing you won't own. The harder it was pushed down, the faster you're enraged.

### The parts · Disproportionate dislike is a signal
Not liking someone is ordinary. But if the reaction is out of proportion — the mention of them irritates you, you have to comment even when it doesn't concern you — it is probably not only about them. Ordinary dislike doesn't consume this much.
e.g. People who loathe attention-seekers are usually the ones who most want to be seen.

### The parts · Suppressed things don't vanish, they reroute
Jung's framing is conservation-like: what isn't acknowledged finds another exit. It can become fault-finding in others, a sudden loss of control, or a physical complaint. Acknowledging it is the least-effort option available.
e.g. The person who never gets angry, when they finally do, frightens everyone including themselves.

### The parts · Owning it isn't acting on it
Admitting you'd also like to slack off, be praised, have the ambition, is not the same as slacking or grabbing. Jung means putting it back into consciousness where it can be managed — what's hidden can't be, what's on the table can.
e.g. People who can say 'I want that position too' are less likely to do something ugly to get it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: there's a type of person you can't think about without anger, and you know your reaction is too big.
Ask first: which exact quality am I reacting to? Write it down, then ask whether I have it and never let it out.
Where it goes wrong: using it to excuse every dislike — some people should be disliked; and owning something isn't permission to do it. You own it in order to manage it.

### Lines to keep
When the dislike is out of proportion, it isn't only about them.
What you push down doesn't vanish. It changes exit.
You own it in order to manage it, not to act on it.

========================================================================
## Carl Jung · Wear the mask long enough and it grows in
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/jung/the-persona/
Source: Jung on the persona
Tags: Deep read, Carl Jung, Necessary, but it has to come off

What happens after years inside a role. Jung says the mask isn't the problem — here's where the problem is.

### Q: What actually happened?
Jung used the word mask for what a person puts on outside: the post, the identity, the version of you others expect. The mask is necessary; without it you can't deal with the world. The danger lies elsewhere — wear it long enough and you take it for yourself. Then every judgement starts from the role, and when the role is removed — retirement, redundancy, children leaving — whoever is left finds they don't know who to be.

### The parts · A mask isn't dishonesty. It's a necessary interface
The voice you use at work, the way you are with clients — masks, and they should exist. Jung isn't asking anyone to take theirs off. He's asking that you can tell them apart: which part the role requires and which part is yours. Telling them apart is what keeps it removable.
e.g. Still using your meeting voice at home means this layer isn't coming off easily any more.

### The parts · The moment the role is taken is the moment you find out
Retirement, redundancy, children leaving are the same event: the mask removed from outside. How badly you panic then measures how much of what you built grew only on the role. The more complete the panic, the less the separating was ever done.
e.g. The hardest part of the first six months of retirement is usually not the empty days. It's not knowing who you now count as.

### The parts · Keep one area the role can't reach
In practice: hold on to something unrelated to your identity — an interest, a set of people who don't know your job title. Its usefulness isn't in how important it is but in not moving when the role does. It's what you're standing on when the role goes.
e.g. A group of friends who know your name and not your title is worth more than anything else here.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you've been in one role for years and find that with it off, you don't know who you are.
Ask first: if this identity vanished tomorrow, what would be left? If you can write three things, it hasn't grown in yet.
Where it goes wrong: using it to dismiss professional identity — the mask is a necessity, not a burden; and 'being your real self' doesn't mean never adjusting for the room. That removes the interface too.

### Lines to keep
The mask is necessary. The trouble is taking it for yourself.
What's left when the identity goes can't be seen in advance.
Keep one thing the role can't reach. That's what you stand on.

========================================================================
## Garry Kasparov · After losing to it, he changed the rules
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/kasparov/advanced-chess/
Source: The six-game rematch, New York, May 1997; the first Advanced Chess event, León, 1998
Tags: Deep read, Garry Kasparov, Let people bring machines to the board

When a machine wins at your craft, what's left of it. Why Kasparov invited the computer onto his own board.

### Q: What actually happened?
He beat Deep Blue in Philadelphia in 1996. In the New York rematch of May 1997 it beat him 3.5–2.5, the first time a world champion lost a formal match to a machine. A year later he staged an event in León under new rules: each side brought a computer to the board and could consult it at any time. He called it Advanced Chess. The reasoning was plain — calculation was already lost, so stop competing on who calculates faster.

### The parts · First identify what's no longer worth competing on
The day machines won on depth of calculation, the 'who sees furthest' track closed. Training on a closed track has no exit however hard you train. The first step isn't redoubling effort; it's striking the lost item off your own list of what you're worth.
e.g. Speed of looking things up, of arithmetic, of making a sentence read properly — none of these are things to compete on now.

### The parts · Change the rules, not the effort
He didn't train harder and he didn't switch fields. He changed what the contest permits. When a tool matches an ability, the valuable position moves to how the tool gets used — and somebody has to define that position before it exists.
e.g. Not 'I'll write faster than it' but 'I decide what this piece is and which parts are whose'.

### The parts · Inviting the tool in holds better than keeping it out
A contest that bans tools survives only on enforcement, and collapses the moment enforcement slips. A contest that permits them is measuring something else — something that doesn't expire as tools improve, because it improves alongside them.
e.g. You can ban calculators in an exam. You can't hold that line at work, and the sneaks end up ahead.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a core skill in your field has been matched by a tool, and you're still training on the old track.
Ask first: which item in my field is now clearly lost to the tool? Strike it out — what's left that it can't replace?
Where it goes wrong: hearing 'if you can't win, don't train' — he didn't stop playing chess, he stopped competing on calculation; and changing the rules isn't open to everyone. First you have to know the old game well enough to see them.

### Lines to keep
Calculation was already lost, so stop competing on calculation.
The first step isn't more effort. It's striking out what's lost.
A contest that bans tools survives only while enforcement holds.

========================================================================
## Garry Kasparov · The winner wasn't the best human or the best machine
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/kasparov/process-beats-both/
Source: The 2005 PAL/CSS freestyle tournament; Kasparov, Deep Thinking, 2017
Tags: Deep read, Garry Kasparov, It was the pair with the best process

What human plus tool is actually good at. Why two amateurs won a tournament where everyone could use a computer.

### Q: What actually happened?
A freestyle online tournament in 2005 admitted grandmasters and supercomputers, with humans and machines free to team up. The winners were two American amateurs, Steven Cramton and Zackary Stephen, running three ordinary PCs. Their method was to ask all three and apply their own judgement only where the three disagreed. Kasparov later compressed it: a weak human plus a machine plus a good process beats a strong human plus a machine plus a poor one.

### The parts · The value moves from answering well to asking well
Where all three machines return the same answer, adding a person adds nothing. The human value concentrates entirely in the few moves where they disagree — finding the disagreement and judging which side to believe. That is a different job from playing chess.
e.g. Two tools give different conclusions and you can say why you trust one. That's your work.

### The parts · Process makes up for ability; ability can't make up for process
The amateurs won on a stable checking routine. The grandmasters lost by treating the machine as a reference and calling it themselves at the end. The first doesn't depend on how you feel that day; the second does. That is how weaker players beat stronger ones.
e.g. Same tool: one person asks three times and cross-checks, the other asks once and ships it.

### The parts · Don't keep only one tool
With one machine there is no disagreement to look at — you either believe all of it or none of it. Three aren't valuable because the compute adds up. They're valuable because the places they disagree mark exactly where the problem is genuinely hard.
e.g. Ask two different tools the same question. Where the answers fight is where you should be thinking.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you already use the tools, and what you get out looks like what everyone else gets out of the same ones.
Ask first: do I have a fixed way of checking? Do I ever put the same question to a second tool?
Where it goes wrong: hearing it as 'just open more tools' — they won on the checking routine, not the count; and don't skip the fundamentals because amateurs won. Recognising a real disagreement takes knowing the subject.

### Lines to keep
Where all three agree, adding a person adds nothing.
The human value sits in the few moves where they disagree.
Process makes up for ability. Ability can't make up for process.

## Garry Kasparov · He spent years arguing the match didn't count
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/kasparov/excuses-cost-years/
Source: His 1997 post-match statement and rematch demand; Deep Thinking, 2017
Tags: Deep read, Garry Kasparov, Conceding is cheaper than appealing

What the first year after being replaced usually looks like. What he did, and what he said twenty years later.

### Q: What actually happened?
After the loss he told the press that IBM had used human intervention mid-match, and demanded a rematch. IBM refused, and dismantled Deep Blue — leaving him without even an opponent to play again. He told that version for years. By the time he wrote Deep Thinking in 2017 he had withdrawn it himself: Deep Blue won, and that is all. The 1997 explanations were what he couldn't accept at the time.

### The parts · Appealing and moving on can't run in parallel
The effort to prove that match didn't count and the effort to work out what to train next come out of the same person in the same stretch of time. The first buys no new skill even when it wins.
e.g. Six months proving the tool was used wrong is six months not spent learning to use it right.

### The parts · The other side isn't waiting for your post-mortem
IBM dismantled the machine, which shows the pattern: whatever replaced you doesn't need your agreement and won't hold a rematch open for you. Hoping to end this by getting the other side to concede is usually a wait with no end.
e.g. A role is cut and it's cut. Nobody comes back to debate whether cutting it was right.

### The parts · Conceding isn't surrendering
The same year he accepted the loss he was staging a tournament under new rules. Accepting a result and giving up the craft are two different things — accepting it first is what freed his hands to change the track. Nobody swallowing their pride changes anything.
e.g. 'The machine is faster at this than me' and 'my field is done with me' are not the same sentence.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a tool or a new method has beaten you, and most of your energy is going into explaining that it's unfair or that it isn't actually good.
Ask first: how many times this month have I said it's unfair? In the same month, what new thing did I practise?
Where it goes wrong: hearing it as 'no feelings allowed' — it took him twenty years. The point is not to let the appeal become the only thing you're doing, not to demand you accept it today.

### Lines to keep
Whatever replaced you does not need your agreement.
Proving it didn't count and deciding what to train next cost the same hours.
Accepting the result and giving up the craft are different things.

## Kevin Kelly · A thousand true fans
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/kevin-kelly/thousand-true-fans/
Source: 1,000 True Fans, 2008, kk.org/thetechnium
Tags: Deep read, Kevin Kelly, Not famous, but deep enough

Creators assume fame has to come first. This asks whether that assumption is necessary at all, and what replaces it.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 2008 Kelly worked out an arithmetic problem for independent creators: a creator needs to acquire only 1,000 True Fans to make a living. One thousand customers at a hundred dollars is a hundred thousand, which is enough for one person. His definition of a true fan is hard: someone who will buy anything you produce, who will drive 200 miles to see you sing, who buys the hardback and the paperback and the audio version of the same book. The value of the sum is not the number. It is that fame has been taken off the list of requirements.

### The parts · A thousand can be counted one at a time; a million cannot
This is the solid part of the sum. A thousand people, three a day, takes a year, and that is a schedule you can execute. A million is not something effort assembles, it is a lottery ticket. The two ask for completely different working days.
e.g. Did one more person who will actually come back arrive today? You can ask that every evening. Did I go viral today? You cannot.

### The parts · A hundred dollars a year is a question about what you make
Run the number backwards and it turns into a design brief: what do you have to produce in a year that someone who genuinely likes you will spend a hundred dollars on? It pushes you off make more content and onto make one thing worth buying, which is different work.
e.g. A year of free updates is worth less than one thing they will pay for: a course, a printed book, an evening in a room with you.

### The parts · Kelly says this can become a second full-time job
He never sold it as the easy road. Maintaining a thousand direct relationships, answering mail, shipping orders, running events, is slow and absorbing work, and done properly it is another full-time job. Reading it as a shortcut around fame is a misreading.
e.g. The worst stretch is a few hundred fans: not yet a living, and already two hours of replies every day.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you make things, and you are waiting for one of them to break out.
Ask first: how many people would actually pay me today, and how many of them can I name? Can I make one hundred-dollar thing this year?
Where it goes wrong: treating a thousand as a follower count to farm, so the fans exist and nothing is for sale; or believing this road is lighter than fame, when Kelly says it may be a second job.

### Lines to keep
A creator needs to acquire only 1,000 True Fans to make a living.
A True Fan is defined as a fan that will buy anything you produce.
They will drive 200 miles to see you sing.

## Kevin Kelly · Nobody in the middle
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/kevin-kelly/direct-relationship/
Source: The second condition in 1,000 True Fans, rechecked against the platform era
Tags: Deep read, Kevin Kelly, The money has to reach you directly

The sum carries a second condition almost everyone skips. This is what happens to the arithmetic once you skip it.

### Q: What actually happened?
Kelly set two conditions and most people remember only the first. The second is this: you must have a direct relationship with your fans; they must pay you directly. Put a platform in the middle and everything changes. It takes a cut, it holds the list, it decides who gets to see you. His 2008 reference points were blogs and MySpace. The present is tighter: a service like Spotify will hand you chart positions and never hand you an address. This is not a footnote to the essay. It is the switch that decides whether the sum works.

### The parts · Whoever holds the list holds your living
There is one test. If this platform throttles or bans you tomorrow, can you still reach those thousand people? If you cannot, you never had a thousand fans. You were renting somebody else's traffic and calling it an audience.
e.g. A mailing list, a group chat, your own site: anything you could walk out with counts. A follower number does not.

### The parts · The cut takes more than money, it takes the feedback
With a platform in between you cannot see who bought, why they bought, or when they stopped. What you lose is not only the percentage, it is the information that would let you improve. The expensive part of a direct relationship is the feedback, not the cash.
e.g. One reply explaining why somebody unsubscribed is worth more than a retention curve on a dashboard.

### The parts · Fix the exit before you chase the growth
Order matters here. Settle how do I take these people with me before you spend a year growing on somebody else's surface. Done the other way round, the day your follower count looks best tends to be the day your leverage is lowest.
e.g. Put one route to reach you directly into every piece you publish. It only gets more expensive the longer you wait.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have readers or customers on a platform, and the platform holds every contact detail.
Ask first: if I were throttled tomorrow, how many of them could I still reach by myself?
Where it goes wrong: making the experience awkward in order to own the list, herding people off the platform; or assuming the list lets you drop the platform, when one is the door and the other is the insurance.

### Lines to keep
You must have a direct relationship with your fans; they must pay you directly.
The platform gives you chart positions. It never gives you an address.
Fans you cannot reach without permission were never really yours.

========================================================================
## Arthur Kleinman · The Disease and the Illness
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/kleinman/disease-and-illness/
Source: Arthur Kleinman, The Illness Narratives, 1988
Tags: Deep read, Arthur Kleinman, Two different things

The doctor says it is manageable and your life has caved in. Why Kleinman insists these are two separate things.

### Q: What actually happened?
Kleinman is a Harvard medical anthropologist and a practising psychiatrist, and his career turns on splitting one word into two. Disease is what the clinician creates: the numbers on the chart, the lesion in the organ. Illness is the lived experience of symptoms and suffering: the pain, the fear, the things you can no longer do, the person you have become at home. Modern medicine spends almost all of its effort on the first, and what people are actually undergoing is the second. The two sides are not discussing the same object, which is why they so often fail to meet.

### The parts · Normal results is not the same sentence as you are fine
A chart can declare a lesion gone. It cannot declare gone what the months did to a life. Plenty of people feel worse once treatment ends, because medicine has completed its task and the other half has nobody assigned to it. It was never on the form.
e.g. Every test comes back clean and you still cannot leave the house alone. That is not weakness, it is the unattended half.

### The parts · What the patient says about it is evidence
Kleinman treats the account a person gives of their own sickness as a serious source: what they call it, what they think caused it, which part frightens them most. None of that is a medical fact, and all of it decides whether they take the drug and come back.
e.g. A man convinced the illness came from something that happened years ago will act on that conviction, whatever the notes say.

### The parts · Split the words and the work becomes visible
While the two are fused there is only one available move, which is to treat. Split them and there are two tracks: one belongs to the clinician, the other to you and the people at home. How the day is arranged, what to explain, what to set down.
e.g. The doctor sets the protocol. Whether you still go up the hill at weekends is yours to settle.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you or someone at home has a diagnosis you will carry for years, the doctor was clear, and you are more frightened than before.
Ask first: is the thing the doctor described the same thing that is hard every day? Write the two columns out separately.
Where it goes wrong: using this to belittle medicine or skip the treatment. Kleinman is a physician and is adding the missing half, not replacing the other one; and telling the story is not itself a cure.

### Lines to keep
Illness is the lived experience of symptoms and suffering.
Disease is what the clinician creates out of that experience.
What frightens him most tells you more than what he has.

========================================================================
## Arthur Kleinman · The Eight Questions
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/kleinman/eight-questions/
Source: Kleinman, Eisenberg and Good, Culture, Illness, and Care, Annals of Internal Medicine, 1978
Tags: Deep read, Arthur Kleinman, The last one asks what you are afraid of

What to ask, and what to be asked, in a consultation. Why Kleinman's list has these eight questions on it.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1978 Kleinman and two colleagues published a short set of questions for clinicians, since known as the explanatory model interview. What do you call this problem. What do you think caused it. Why did it start when it did. What does it do to you, and how. How severe is it, and how long will it last. What treatment should you have. What trouble has it caused you. And last: what do you fear most about it. Seven of them ask how the person understands the thing. The eighth asks what frightens them, which is usually what is actually in the way.

### The parts · They ask about the person, not the pathology
Not one of the eight asks about symptoms, because the clinician can find those without help. They ask after the explanation the person is carrying around: cause, timing, consequence. That explanation can be wrong and it still governs every decision they make afterwards.
e.g. Someone who believes the tablets are damaging his liver will not take them for three months, whatever he is told.

### The parts · The fear and the clinical priority rarely match
What the clinician is watching and what the patient is dreading are usually different objects. The clinician has the numbers. The patient may be afraid of never lifting a grandchild, of becoming a burden, of losing the job. Unasked, every reassurance lands beside the point.
e.g. The doctor keeps repeating that it is controllable. What he is afraid of is what the office will think.

### The parts · The list works on yourself and on your family
It is not reserved for clinicians. Run it before you take someone to an appointment and you know what to ask on their behalf. Run it on yourself and the fear and the judgement come apart. The written answers are usually shorter than the dread was.
e.g. Ask a parent what frightens them most before the appointment. It is worth more than asking where it hurts.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are taking a family member to an appointment, or carrying a long problem you cannot describe.
Ask first: how many of the eight can I answer? The last one above all. Write down exactly what frightens you.
Where it goes wrong: using it to challenge a doctor for not asking. The structure of a clinic makes it hard for them. And do not turn it into an interrogation. It is an opening, not a form.

### Lines to keep
What do you fear most about this illness?
Seven questions ask for understanding. The eighth asks for the fear.
Fear is usually the thing actually standing in a person's way.

========================================================================
## Arthur Kleinman · When Curing Fails, Care Does Not
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/kleinman/caring-when-curing-fails/
Source: Arthur Kleinman, The Soul of Care, 2019
Tags: Deep read, Arthur Kleinman, Ten years looking after his wife taught him this

Some illnesses cannot be cured. What is left to do. The answer Kleinman reached after ten years of caring for his wife.

### Q: What actually happened?
Joan Kleinman was diagnosed with early-onset Alzheimer's in her fifties. For the next ten years her husband looked after her, until she died. He was the field's leading authority on caregiving and says he was not remotely ready: he had taught it his whole life and only learned what it costs when it was his own. He wrote the decade down, and the book rests on one distinction. Cure has a point at which it fails. Care does not. Medicine arrives at a place where it can do nothing, and being there is still available on the last day.

### The parts · Cure and care are two different goals
Cure asks whether this can be made to go away, and the answer is sometimes no. Once it is no, anyone working to that goal has nothing left to do. Care asks whether today can be made a little easier, which has an answer every single day, and the answer stays in your hands.
e.g. After nothing more can be done there is still a whole day to get through, and how it goes is decidable.

### The parts · Most of care is presence, not technique
What he returns to is not nursing skill. It is being there: recognising which version of the person turned up today, absorbing whatever comes up without warning, staying a while longer in the hours they are still themselves. No training required, only time, which is the scarcest thing.
e.g. Half an hour sitting beside someone without speaking often does more than another trip to the hospital.

### The parts · The carer is being used up, and that is a separate line
The least forgiving pages in the book are about his own collapse: exhaustion, guilt, resentment surfacing where he did not want it. He insists this is structural rather than moral. The cost of long care has to be seen and shared, or two people go down instead of one.
e.g. Two years of carrying it alone and the carer falls ill first. In long-term care that is the norm, not the accident.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: someone at home has an illness that will not be cured, or you carry a problem that is not going to leave.
Ask first: set cure aside for a moment. What one small thing would make today easier? Do that one.
Where it goes wrong: letting care stand in for treatment that should happen; or reading it as an order to carry it alone. A large part of his book is about what happens when you cannot.

### Lines to keep
Treatment can be handed over. Being there cannot.
When medicine hands it back, what you can do is not zero.
Carry it alone and two people usually go down, not one.

========================================================================
## Maria Konnikova · The con artist does not build trust
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/konnikova/not-manufacturing-trust/
Source: The Confidence Game, 2016
Tags: Deep read, Maria Konnikova, He uses the need you already have

The first question after being taken in is how could I be so stupid. That question is itself the wrong one.

### Q: What actually happened?
Konnikova worked through a large number of cons and arrived somewhere counter-intuitive: the con artist does not manufacture trust, he finds a need you already have and uses it. The opening stage, what the trade calls the put-up, answers three questions about the mark. Who is this person, what do they want, and how does that want get me what I want. So the hinge is not intelligence, it is whatever you happened to be short of at the time. Which is why the educated and the worldly are on the list too.

### The parts · Ask which want it answered
When an offer moves you, hold off on whether it is true and ask why it lands now. The answer usually points at whatever you were most short of. This order matters, because checking gets steered by wanting and you go looking for what supports it.
e.g. People desperate to recover a loss are the ones who meet guaranteed high yield. That is not coincidence, it is selection.

### The parts · Being taken in is about circumstance, not intelligence
Filing it under I was stupid does two kinds of damage. It is inaccurate, and it makes the story too shaming to tell, so the same con keeps working on the next person. Filing it under what was I short of produces something you can actually change.
e.g. The line victims say most often is that they are not normally like this. It is usually true.

### The parts · Rules beat vigilance
Vigilance fails in the presence of wanting, because wanting is the thing eroding it. What works is a rule set in advance: above this amount, sleep on it; a second person has to look at it; there has to be an independent source. Made cool, applied hot.
e.g. Anything over this figure waits a day before I sign it. That single rule has saved more people than any talent for reading faces.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: somebody has made you an offer that is hard to refuse, and something about it is off in a way you cannot name.
Ask first: which of the things you are currently short of does it answer? If that is obvious, that is the warning.
Where it goes wrong: turning it into trusting nobody, which is its own disability; or using it to blame someone already conned, when the whole argument is that this is not about intelligence.

### Lines to keep
The con artist does not build trust. He uses the need you already have.
Who is this person, what do they want, and how do I use it.
What gets used is the wanting, not your judgement.

## Maria Konnikova · A transition is the dangerous window
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/konnikova/transition-is-the-window/
Source: The Confidence Game, on when a mark is vulnerable
Tags: Deep read, Maria Konnikova, When the old method stops fitting

One person's judgement is roughly constant across a life, yet the losses cluster in a few stretches. This is about which ones.

### Q: What actually happened?
Her answer is the transition. Cons land most easily in periods of upheaval, when something new is happening and the old way of reading the world no longer covers it. A move to an unfamiliar city, a divorce, a death, redundancy, retirement, a sum of money arriving. What these share is not fragility, it is the absence of a usable template, which is why any explanation that hangs together sounds unusually credible. The practical value is direct: it turns not being conned from a personality into a calendar.

### The parts · The risk is a missing template, not low spirits
The real problem in a transition is that old experience does not map onto the new situation. You have never rented in this city, never handled an estate, never held this much money. What is missing is a reference, and a reference is exactly what the con supplies.
e.g. Newly arrived somewhere, you have no idea what a normal price looks like. That gap is the window.

### The parts · Put the dangerous months in the diary
This is the operational part. For the first months after a move, a new job, a death or a large payment, add a procedure in advance: anything above a set amount goes past somebody who is not inside the situation with you.
e.g. Every large decision in these three months gets run past this person. Agreed beforehand, it is far more reliable than judging it in the moment.

### The parts · The same window rebuilds, so do not only defend
In the same stretch that old templates stop working, new habits and relationships form most easily. So a transition should not be spent entirely on defence. Split it: put procedure around judgement, and do more, not less, of the meeting people.
e.g. Newly moved, be careful about contracts and transfers. Do not be careful about getting to know anyone.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have just been through a large change, a new city, a new job, a divorce, a death, or money arriving.
Ask first: which decisions in the next three months have no precedent for you? Put a step in front of those and find somebody outside the situation to look.
Where it goes wrong: spending the whole transition on defence and avoiding the relationships you should be building. It asks for procedure around judgement, not a wall around your life.

### Lines to keep
Cons land hardest when something new is happening in your life.
The danger is not that you are weak. You have no template.
It turns not being conned from a personality into a calendar.
