## Kristin Neff · Self-compassion is not self-esteem
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/kristin-neff/not-self-esteem/
Source: Self-Compassion; the Self-Compassion Scale and its reviews
Tags: Deep read, Kristin Neff, One of them needs a comparison and the other does not

Self-esteem is the word this generation grew up inside. The question is why it goes missing exactly when it is needed.

### Q: What actually happened?
Self-esteem runs on an algorithm: I am better than others. It draws its power from comparison, so it is at full strength when things go well and is first to leave when you fail. The moment you need it most is the moment it is not there. What she puts in its place does not compare: self-compassion asks not am I good enough, but what do I need now that this hurts. Across studies it does better on most measures — lower depression and anxiety, more motivation to correct mistakes — without the fragility of having to keep winning.

### The parts · Comparison is the fuel, so it fails in the trough
As long as better than others sits inside the definition, supply depends on continuing to win. One failure and the supply is cut, which is precisely the moment support was required. Self-compassion does not depend on rank, so it is still present in the trough.
e.g. Somebody from your own year overtakes you. Self-esteem says I am finished. Self-compassion says this hurts, that is normal, what is the next move.

### The parts · It does not lower the bar, it raises the will to fix things
The standing objection is that being kind to yourself makes you slack. The data point the other way: moving attention off am I a failure and onto what do I do about this makes people readier to admit errors and quicker to start repairing. Shame makes people hide.
e.g. An evening spent insulting yourself over a bad result means not opening the paper next day. Change the sentence and you can go through the wrong answers that night.

### The parts · The usable test is whether you would say it to a friend
This is the most operable thing in her work. Take the sentence you are saying to yourself and say it, word for word, to a friend in the identical position. If it will not come out of your mouth, the sentence is faulty. It is a calibration, not an exercise in leniency.
e.g. You are too stupid to be doing this — you would not say it to a friend, so it does not get said to you either.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you made a mess of something, the abuse in your head is getting louder and you are getting less able to move.
Ask first: could I say this sentence, unchanged, to a friend in the same position? If it will not come out, it is not the truth, it is an attack.
Where it goes wrong: taking it as permission to stop reviewing what happened — it asks you to move attention from who I am back to what to do; or using it to chase feeling good, which is self-esteem again.

### Lines to keep
The question is not am I good enough. It is what do I need.
Self-esteem needs you to be better, so it leaves when you fail.
Say it to a friend in the same position. Would it come out?

========================================================================
## Kristin Neff · Three parts, all present at once
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/kristin-neff/three-parts/
Source: Neff's three components: self-kindness, common humanity, mindfulness
Tags: Deep read, Kristin Neff, Take one away and it turns into something else

Self-compassion gets summarised as be nicer to yourself. It is three components, and they have to hold at the same time.

### Q: What actually happened?
She breaks it into three: self-kindness, common humanity and mindfulness. The point is that all three have to be present at once, because removing one turns it into a different thing. Kindness without common humanity is self-pity: why is it always me. Common humanity granted while you go on berating yourself is gritted teeth. Watching the pain clearly and refusing to be kind is detachment. So these are not three suggestions, they are three parts; a machine missing one is not running slightly worse, it is not that machine.

### The parts · Common humanity is the part that gets skipped
The most damaging thing inside pain is rarely the pain. It is the sense that it is only me. Acknowledging that many people have been through this is not consolation, it removes the premise. Skip it and the kindness left over degrades into self-pity.
e.g. Everybody's first year is like this does far more work than you are doing great.

### The parts · Mindfulness is neither amplifying nor denying
Both directions are out: sinking in and replaying it, and insisting it is fine. What is asked for is seeing how big the thing actually is, with nothing added and nothing taken off. Without that step the other two have nowhere to land.
e.g. This is painful, and the size of it is painful rather than ruinous — weigh it before you do anything else.

### The parts · Remove one and it changes name, so check them one at a time
The model earns its keep as a diagnostic rather than as encouragement. When it hurts, go down the three, and usually only one is missing; supplying that one is enough. Most people are missing common humanity, a smaller number are missing mindfulness.
e.g. Clear-eyed about it, aware that others go through it, and still refusing to be civil to yourself — the missing part is the first one.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you know you should go easier on yourself, and every attempt feels fake or slides into self-pity.
Ask first: which of the three is missing — the kindness, the sense that others have been here, or a clear reading of how big this actually is?
Where it goes wrong: treating the three as three consoling phrases to recite; or using common humanity to dismiss your own situation — everyone goes through it turned into so stop complaining has gone backwards.

### Lines to keep
Self-kindness, common humanity, mindfulness — all three at the same time.
Kindness without common humanity is self-pity.
A machine missing a part is not that machine running worse.

## La Rochefoucauld · Nobody complains about their judgement
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/la-rochefoucauld/memory-vs-judgment/
Source: Maxims, numbers 89, 31 and 149
Tags: Deep read, La Rochefoucauld, The shape of the blind spot

One sentence draws the border of self-knowledge. This is why the first admission is easy and the second nearly impossible.

### Q: What actually happened?
La Rochefoucauld was a defeated nobleman of the Fronde who spent his later years turning what he had seen at court and in the field into a few hundred maxims. Number 89: everyone complains of his memory, no one complains of his judgment. Admitting a poor memory costs nothing, since it is a hardware fault. Admitting poor judgement concedes that the ground under every past decision was unsound, and nobody can carry that. Number 31 travels with it: if we had no faults, we would not enjoy noticing them in others.

### The parts · People only admit faults that leave the base intact
Memory, stamina, a weak second language: these cost nothing to concede, because none of them disturbs the belief that you are a person who sees clearly. The real blind spots sit in the class nobody will own. A volunteered fault can usually be crossed off the list.
e.g. Asked for a weakness in an interview, the candidate who says they are too much of a perfectionist has told you nothing. Listen to how they explain their last failure.

### The parts · Failures of judgement get rewritten by memory
After a bad call, memory quietly adds a layer of narrative: the information was thin, someone misled us, the luck was strange. A few rewrites later, no misjudgement has ever occurred. The only defence is writing the call and the reasons down at the time.
e.g. Before a major decision, write one page: what you expect to happen and why. Read it six months later. Most people are startled the first time.

### The parts · Finding fault in others is a painkiller
Number 31 names the payoff in eager correction. Attention on somebody else's defects gives temporary relief from noticing your own. So the moment your urge to criticise runs hottest deserves suspicion: it tracks your position, not their error rate.
e.g. In the weeks your own project is stuck, every proposal that crosses your desk looks full of holes.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are reviewing what happened, and the conclusion has landed on external factors again.
Ask first: in this account, what percentage is your own judgement? And in the one before it?
Where it goes wrong: letting self-suspicion paralyse every decision; or using the maxim only as an instrument for reading other people.

### Lines to keep
Everyone complains of his memory, no one complains of his judgment.
If we had no faults, we would not enjoy noticing them in others.
The refusal of praise is only the wish to be praised twice.

## La Rochefoucauld · Hypocrisy is a tribute
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/la-rochefoucauld/vice-pays-tribute/
Source: Maxims, number 218
Tags: Deep read, La Rochefoucauld, The disguise tells you the exchange rate

He wrote hypocrisy up as an act of homage. Inside the sneer there is a working method for reading a place.

### Q: What actually happened?
Number 218: hypocrisy is the homage vice pays to virtue. Vice has to dress as virtue in order to circulate, and that fact alone proves virtue is the hard currency there, since nobody disguises themselves as something worthless. The whole book runs this operation. Our virtues, he writes, are most frequently but vices disguised. Neither the sun nor death can be looked at steadily. He is not arguing that people are wholly bad. He is taking the wrapping off so the structure of the exchange underneath becomes visible.

### The parts · What people fake tells you what the place pays for
Whatever people imitate is the currency of that environment. Where everyone performs long hours for the boss, hours are money. Where everyone competes to sound profound in meetings, talk outranks delivery. The direction of the pretence reads truer than the values on the wall.
e.g. To learn what a company actually rewards, skip the culture handbook and watch what a new hire has learned to perform by month three.

### The parts · The existence of the disguise is worth more than exposing it
If vice has to dress as virtue to pass, then the norm requiring the dress has real value, because it constrains the surface of behaviour. A place where nobody bothers to pretend has stopped treating virtue as currency, and that is the deeper rot.
e.g. Somebody gives to charity for the reputation. Unmasking them gains nothing. The rule that reputation follows good deeds is the part worth defending.

### The parts · Run the same operation on yourself
The hardest thing about the book is that it exempts nobody, the author included. Taking apart one of your own moral positions to see the interest underneath is not self-abasement. It lets you predict where you will wobble when the interest moves.
e.g. A principle you hold has always happened to pay you. Work out now what will be left of it on the day it starts costing you.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have noticed that someone's good deed has an interest sitting behind it.
Ask first: what does the shape they chose to fake tell you about what this place rewards, and what will you do with that?
Where it goes wrong: making a career of unmasking, so that every decent act becomes suspect; or running the operation only on other people and never on yourself.

### Lines to keep
Hypocrisy is the homage vice pays to virtue.
Our virtues are most frequently but vices disguised.
Neither the sun nor death can be looked at steadily.

## Lee Kuan Yew · Does it work
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/lee-kuan-yew/does-it-work/
Source: Collected interviews, including Lee Kuan Yew: The Grand Master's Insights on China, the United States and the World
Tags: Deep read, Lee Kuan Yew, Theory comes after the result

Theorists on both the left and the right attacked Singapore. This is about the single question he used to dismiss all of them.

### Q: What actually happened?
He told interviewers the same thing for forty years: he was not an ideologue, he was not enamoured of any theory, and reality and common sense were what guided him. One test decided everything. Does it work? Let's try it and if it does work, fine, let's continue it. If it doesn't work, toss it out, try another one. So the policy mix fits no spectrum: state-built housing next to unrestricted trade, harsh criminal law next to a sovereign fund. Inviting in multinationals was read across the developing world as selling out. He did not argue. He waited for the numbers.

### The parts · The theory is the map, the result is the ground
A theory earns its keep before you set out, by choosing a starting point. Once real feedback exists it outranks the theory: when map and ground disagree, the map is wrong. Most arguments are absurd because the ground is already visible and both sides are still comparing maps.
e.g. Two camps are trading citations about whether the channel works. The team next door has been running it three months and the data is sitting there.

### The parts · Working has to be defined in advance
The pragmatism has a premise people skip: what counts as working was fixed beforehand — employment, housing, savings rates, hard numbers nobody can dress up. Without that, pragmatism decays into finding a story for whatever happened.
e.g. Before starting, write down which three numbers you will look at in three months and what counts as good. Skip that and any result can be called a success.

### The parts · Working costs you a decade of being wrong in public
Bringing in multinationals made him a traitor to the developing world's intellectuals in the 1960s; dependency theory said that road ended in vassalage. He carried the name for ten years until the results arrived. Anyone unwilling to pay that tax stays on the theoretically correct road.
e.g. Pick the route your industry despises and every meeting for two years is one where you are being corrected. Quit before the data lands and you took the abuse for nothing.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: two theories are deadlocked in the meeting.
Ask first: can this be run small enough to produce real feedback, and can you write down today what would count as working?
Where it goes wrong: using pragmatism as putty to explain any outcome afterwards; deciding that as long as it works, no line is off limits.

### Lines to keep
Let's try it and if it does work, fine, let's continue it.
If it doesn't work, toss it out, try another one.
When the map and the ground disagree, the map is wrong.

## Lee Kuan Yew · I would get up from my sickbed
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/lee-kuan-yew/from-my-sickbed/
Source: National Day Rally speech, 1988
Tags: Deep read, Lee Kuan Yew, Welding yourself to the outcome

A sentence spoken on the edge of handing over, and it frightened people. This is about what such a binding buys and what it poisons.

### Q: What actually happened?
At the 1988 National Day Rally he was sixty-five and about to hand over. He told the country the line everyone has quoted since: even from my sick bed, even if you are going to lower me into the grave and I feel something is going wrong, I will get up. It was not rhetoric running away with him. It described his relation to the place exactly: he had built it piece by piece, from the day of the weeping press conference that followed expulsion from Malaysia. He then stayed in cabinet for more than twenty years.

### The parts · The binding buys a promise nobody else can make
The line is credible because it cannot be withdrawn. He welded the rest of his life to the outcome and left no exit marked leave if it goes badly. A hired executive cannot structurally offer this: their rational stopping point is the edge of the promise.
e.g. A founder saying if this fails I do nothing else and an executive saying I am fully committed are heard by investors as two different kinds of information.

### The parts · The same sentence is the successor's ceiling
A predecessor who announces he will rise from his sickbed means every decision the next person makes is being examined by those eyes. That is the poison: the course is protected, and the room the next generation needs in order to be wrong and grow is gone.
e.g. The founder retires without leaving. Nothing drifts off course, and five years later not one senior person has made a decision that was really their own.

### The parts · Bind yourself to the result, not to the seat
What he bound himself to was something going wrong — the country's outcome, not his own office. That distinction decides what the binding is. A predecessor watching results is insurance; a predecessor missing the chair is a shackle. The test is how he reacts to being outdone.
e.g. If the previous holder appears only when the numbers turn bad, that is insurance. If he appears when everything is fine, he never handed anything over.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are handing over something you built from nothing.
Ask first: am I binding myself to its result or to my position, and how much room to be wrong does my presence leave the next person?
Where it goes wrong: using I could come back at any time as a management tool, so the successor never grows up; or cutting clean and staying silent while it capsizes.

### Lines to keep
I feel something is going wrong, I will get up.
Bind yourself to the result, not to the seat.
The insurance watches the results. The shackle misses the chair.

## Li Bi · Take Fanyang first
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/li-bi/strike-the-base/
Source: The Comprehensive Mirror, Tang chronicles
Tags: Deep read, Li Bi, The base camp or the capital

In the middle of the An Lushan rebellion the emperor wanted his capitals back. This is about why Li Bi called that the worst move.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 757 Emperor Suzong asked how to end the rebellion. Li Bi's plan: let Guo Ziyi and Li Guangbi pin the rebels down, running them back and forth between Guanzhong and Hebei until they were exhausted, then drive straight at Fanyang, An Lushan's home and base, where the families and the baggage were. Suzong wanted the two capitals first. He got them, the rebel core withdrew to Hebei, and the war ran six more years. Your Majesty wanted the capitals quickly, so the rebels grew strong again and we grew weak again.

### The parts · The conspicuous target is rarely the decisive one
The two capitals were the symbol, the legitimacy, the place everyone was watching. Fanyang was the supply, the families, the way home. Taking the first lets you announce a victory; taking the second ends the war. The return curves are not the same shape.
e.g. Landing a marquee client makes the news. Fixing the renewal flow that has been leaking for a year does not, and decides whether you are here in three years.

### The parts · Leave the base and they have somewhere to rebuild
Driving an opponent off and removing him are different outcomes. While the base stands, whatever you pushed back goes home, refills, reorganises and returns. So the quality of a victory is measured by whether the other side can still recover.
e.g. You priced them out of one city and their supply chain and their team are intact. In three months they come back with a different approach.

### The parts · Announcing early has a price, and it is payable
Suzong was not stupid. A newly enthroned emperor needed something he could proclaim, and that need was real. The price was six years. Every decision made in order to have something to report should be costed that way first.
e.g. Shipping half a product so the year-end number exists is a loan. The repayment is the rework and the reputation over the two years after.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: there is a conspicuous target and a decisive one, and resources for only one.
Ask first: after you take the conspicuous one, can the other side still recover?
Where it goes wrong: treating a repulse as a solution; choosing the fast result because something has to be announced, and never costing the long half.

### Lines to keep
Strike Fanyang, destroy the nest, and the root is gone for good.
You wanted the capitals quickly, so they grew strong and we grew weak.
Driving them off and removing them are two different outcomes.

## Li Bi · He would not take the office
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/li-bi/no-office/
Source: Old Book of Tang, Life of Li Bi; The Comprehensive Mirror
Tags: Deep read, Li Bi, What refusing a post buys you

He entered the centre of government four times and went back to the mountains four times. This is about what refusing rank bought him.

### Q: What actually happened?
Li Bi served four emperors — Xuanzong, Suzong, Daizong, Dezong. Each time he was fetched at the worst hour; each time he left once the thing was done. Suzong tried to give him office and he answered, I take no grain and have no household; what office could I hold? The emperor slept on a facing couch and rode beside him, and he still called himself a guest and wore a Taoist's robes. He remonstrated constantly — against killing Prince Jianning, against suspecting loyal commanders, against deposing the heir. Some of it was taken. He finally accepted the chancellorship in his sixties.

### The parts · With no seat, your words are not discounted
Once you hold a post, everything you say is heard as serving that post. Speaking as a guest, Li Bi gave the listener no motive to subtract. That is the structural reason he could keep saying the least welcome things for forty years.
e.g. The outside consultant names the same problem the staff named last year, and this time it is heard. The difference is not the content but the attribution.

### The parts · The ability to leave is the strongest chip
He could go back to the mountain at any moment, and he actually did. Advice from someone who can walk out weighs differently from advice from someone whose living depends on staying. What gets called backbone is usually an exit being available.
e.g. People with other options say true things. If you want candour on a team, making sure nobody is ruined for saying the wrong thing matters more than any policy.

### The parts · The price is that you never hold the execution
No office means someone else carries out your plan. Fanyang refused is the ceiling of that arrangement: he could propose and could not decide. Taking the chancellorship at last is the admission that advice alone stops working at some point.
e.g. Advise and never deliver and your hit rate can stay high while nothing you touched changes direction. Sooner or later you have to take the execution.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have something to say and you are afraid it will be heard as angling for yourself.
Ask first: from where I am standing, how will people attribute this? Is there a footing that cannot be discounted?
Where it goes wrong: dressing up not being accountable as purity; staying an adviser forever and never taking the execution.

### Lines to keep
I take no grain and have no household. What office could I hold?
He declined firmly, and asked to follow as a guest.
What gets called backbone is usually an exit being available.

## Li Ka-shing · Ninety per cent of the time, thinking about failure
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/li-ka-shing/ninety-percent-failure/
Source: Li Ka-shing, interviews, around 2006
Tags: Deep read, Li Ka-shing, Think about losing before winning

The richest man in Hong Kong describes his own split of attention, and it is not what you'd expect.

### Q: What actually happened?
In interviews Li Ka-shing has been blunt about it: ninety per cent of my time I spend considering failure. His image is a mechanical watch — one gear slightly faulty and the whole watch stops, and a company is the same. From his plastic-flowers days the habit was set: before a project starts, work through the ways it can fail. When success comes it needs very little thinking about. Beside it runs his rule on cash: a company can go bankrupt while profitable. Through decades of expansion his gearing stayed low.

### The parts · Rehearsing failure is insurance on the decision
Ninety per cent on failure isn't pessimism, it's a division of labour: failure modes are finite, listable and preventable. Having gone through each and set a gate, you can spend the remaining tenth committing hard. Optimism without that step stakes the company on luck.
e.g. The most valuable page in a project review isn't the market size. It's the list of ways this dies. Fewer than five means nobody has thought yet.

### The parts · Find the gear that stops the whole watch
The watch image is precise about 'one gear'. What sinks a company is often not the main business but some unremarkable connector — a guarantee given, a maturity mismatch, one key person. So rank risks by whether they stop the watch, not by how big the business is.
e.g. Healthy companies die of a guarantee made for someone else, or a licence that wasn't renewed.

### The parts · Cash flow is the floor under every failure case
Every rehearsed way of dying converges on the same place: is there enough in the account to get through. So his answer isn't don't take risks. It's make sure no single failure can cut the cash. Low debt isn't caution. It buys more chances to be wrong.
e.g. Ask of an aggressive plan: can its worst outcome reach the cash artery? If not, be aggressive. If so, slow down even the safe version.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a project looks strong and the team is uniformly optimistic.
Ask first: has the list of ways it dies been written? Which gear stops the watch? Does the worst case touch cash?
Where it goes wrong: turning rehearsing failure into only rehearsing failure and never moving; or covering business risks and missing the small gears — guarantees, mismatches.

### Lines to keep
Ninety per cent of my time, I spend considering failure.
One gear with the slightest fault and the watch stops.
A company can go bankrupt while it is profitable.

## Li Ka-shing · Knowing where to stop
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/li-ka-shing/knowing-when-to-stop/
Source: The scroll in his office, widely reported; Cheung Kong's operating principle
Tags: Deep read, Li Ka-shing, The two characters on his office wall

A businessman famous for expansion looks up at a scroll telling him to stop. Stopping and not daring aren't the same.

### Q: What actually happened?
Li Ka-shing's office carries a scroll with two characters usually read as 'know where to stop', from a classical line: know where to stop and then you can be settled. Alongside it is the principle he repeats: never forget stability while growing, never forget growth while stable. In practice that meant selling down in overheated property, and walking away when a bid passed his line — moves others read as missing the market. He hung that scroll during Cheung Kong's most aggressive expansion. The faster you accelerate, the more you need a brake pad in permanent view.

### The parts · Write the stop before you sit down at the table
In practice this means writing the exit condition before every entry: above this price we don't chase, past this amount we don't add, at this date we don't renew. Written while unemotional, it needs no heroism to execute. Recalculating 'is it worth it' in the room is calculating your pride.
e.g. Write your maximum before the auction and give it to a colleague. Every extra pound buys the feeling of not losing, not the asset.

### The parts · What stops is the exposure, not the ambition
This gets misread as contentment with a little. His record says the opposite — decades from plastics to property to ports to telecoms, the ambition never paused. What was capped was the exposure of any single bet. Aggressive on direction, limited per bet: the second is what keeps the first alive.
e.g. Long-term ambition about the field, a hard ceiling on each round. Companies that cross several cycles usually run that combination.

### The parts · Hang the brake pad where you see it daily
Framing those two characters on the office wall is mechanism design. This is the string that goes first when things are going well, so the reminder has to be physically present — hit once a day when you look up. A principle that lives only in the annual speech is gone by the expansion season.
e.g. Print the per-project ceiling and the gearing red line in the header of the decision-meeting template.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the market is hot, the team is confident, and you're considering adding more.
Ask first: has the exit condition for this one been written? When — before entering, or just now?
Where it goes wrong: using 'know where to stop' as cover for never acting; or writing the line and then stepping over it because this time is special.

### Lines to keep
Know where to stop, and then you can be settled.
Never forget stability while growing; never forget growth while stable.
What gets capped is the exposure, not the ambition.

## Li Shimin · Listen to all sides
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/li-shimin/hearing-all-sides/
Source: Essentials of Government of the Zhenguan Era, The Way of the Ruler
Tags: Deep read, Li Shimin, One source is not listening

The emperor asked what makes a ruler clear-sighted. The answer he got describes an information structure, not a virtue.

### Q: What actually happened?
Taizong asked Wei Zheng what separates a clear-sighted ruler from a benighted one. Listening to all sides makes you clear; trusting one source leaves you in the dark. Then the examples: Yao and Shun opened the four gates, so no one could screen them off; the Second Emperor of Qin trusted Zhao Gao alone and did not know the realm had risen until it was over; Yang of Sui trusted Yu Shiji, and provinces were in revolt while the news never reached him. The conclusion is practical: when a ruler hears widely, the great ministers cannot block, and what is below reaches the top.

### The parts · Screening you off requires no lying
Zhao Gao and Yu Shiji need not have lied in every sentence; they only had to control which reports went up. When all information passes one person, that person decides the world you see without inventing anything. The root is the number of channels, not anyone's loyalty.
e.g. If one team assembles and presents all the business data, it need not falsify a figure. Choosing which metrics reach the dashboard has already shaped your judgement.

### The parts · The channels have to be strangers to each other
The value of hearing all sides comes from independence between the sources. Three accounts drawn from the same meeting and the same document are one thing heard three times. Real breadth requires people with no shared boss and no shared interest.
e.g. Ask three directors the same question and get one answer. That may mean the facts are clear, or that they met yesterday. Ask a fourth who was not there.

### The parts · Measure how fast bad news arrives
Yang of Sui's problem was not an absence of bad news; it was that bad news could not get to him. The most direct gauge of an organisation's information health is one number: from the moment a clear problem occurs to the moment you hear, how long, and through how many people?
e.g. A live incident took six hours and four layers to reach you. The thing that actually needs fixing is not that bug.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: everything you know about this arrived through a single reporting line.
Ask first: who else knows about this and has no stake in that line?
Where it goes wrong: taking hearing all sides to mean asking more people from the same circle; counting good news and never timing how long bad news takes.

### Lines to keep
Listening to all sides makes you clear; one source, dark.
Hear widely and the great ministers cannot block what comes up.
Three accounts from one meeting are one thing heard three times.

## Li Shimin · Water carries the boat
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/li-shimin/boat-and-water/
Source: Essentials of Government of the Zhenguan Era, On Governance; Instructions to the Crown Prince
Tags: Deep read, Li Shimin, What holds you up can turn you over

The line has been recited for over a thousand years. Under Taizong it was a piece of daily working discipline.

### Q: What actually happened?
Taizong told his attendants that the way of a ruler must begin with keeping the people whole; injuring the people to serve yourself is like cutting flesh off your thigh to fill your stomach — the belly fills and the body dies. To the crown prince he repeated one figure again and again: the ruler is the boat, the common people are the water; water carries the boat and water can capsize it. The image comes from Xunzi; in these years it was used as a check to run before every call on the people's labour. It was there to be applied, not admired.

### The parts · The thing holding you up is the thing that overturns you
What makes the figure sharp is the identity: it is not one force supporting you and a different force opposing you. The force carrying you is the one that can turn you over. So stability does not come from suppressing it; it comes from never taking it to the tipping point.
e.g. Your core users are both the revenue and the public voice. The same people are the moat when handled well and the loudest critics the next morning when not.

### The parts · Cutting the thigh happens gradually
The belly fills and the body dies describes a slow process: each extraction from below relieves the immediate difficulty at once, while the cost is spread across a future nobody is looking at. That is why it is almost always the best move this period, and exactly why it is dangerous.
e.g. Stuff the channel with inventory at each quarter end and every quarter looks good. Three years on the channel is loss-making and gone, and each single decision was reasonable.

### The parts · Keep one person whose job is to disagree
Wei Zheng remonstrated on more than two hundred matters and repeatedly left the emperor nowhere to go, and stayed. With bronze as a mirror you straighten your dress; with a man as a mirror you see your gains and losses. In practice: institutionalise the objector and do not move him for objecting badly.
e.g. Name someone to argue the opposite case at a major decision meeting, and make explicit that doing it will not affect their review. Without that role, meetings only confirm.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: to hit the target in front of you, you need to take a bit more from one side.
Ask first: is that side also the one holding me up? How much margin is left after this time?
Where it goes wrong: reading the people's support as a mood to be soothed; having nobody near you whose job is to disagree and who is not punished for it.

### Lines to keep
Water carries the boat, and water can capsize it.
The belly fills and the body dies.
With a man as a mirror, you see your losses.

## Li Shimin · The argument at the start of Zhenguan
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/li-shimin/the-first-debate/
Source: Essentials of Government of the Zhenguan Era, On Governance
Tags: Deep read, Li Shimin, He took the slower road

You inherit a wreck. Harsh law, or lenient rule? He picked the option everyone told him there was no time for.

### Q: What actually happened?
Early in the Zhenguan years the country was exhausted. Taizong asked what to do. Wei Zheng argued for government by benevolence and right. Feng Deyi rebutted him forcefully: after the Three Dynasties human character grew thin, which is why Qin used law and Han mixed in force — they wanted to transform people and could not. He called Wei Zheng a bookish man whose advice would wreck the state. Taizong went with Wei Zheng. Some years later: traders camped in the open, there were no more bandits, the jails stood empty, and doors were left unbarred. Taizong told his court: this is what Wei Zheng urged on me.

### The parts · The realistic-sounding option is usually the faster one
Feng Deyi's evidence was all historical experience and sounded far more solid than Wei Zheng's case. But his real advantage was not being right; it was showing results sooner. Harsh law works within the year, transformation takes several. The side called realistic usually has the short cycle.
e.g. Strict targets lift the numbers this month; building capability takes a year. The first always argues better in the room, because its evidence arrives early.

### The parts · To beat a prejudice, take its premise to the end
Wei Zheng's counter was hard: if human character really declines one generation after another, by now everyone would be a ghoul, and there would be nothing left to transform. He did not out-read his opponent in history. He showed the premise produces an absurdity.
e.g. Against new hires are not as solid as the old ones, skip the counter-examples. Ask instead why, on that logic, the company still runs after twenty years.

### The parts · Choosing slow means carrying the years in the middle
The result showed up several years later, and through those years there was nothing to display while Feng Deyi's route could be proposed again at any moment. The difficulty of a long-cycle choice is not the moment of deciding. It is not turning at each subsequent challenge.
e.g. Commit two years to rebuilding the platform and by month three someone asks why you did not just add people. Whether you hold through those asks decides it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: two options, one that shows results quickly and one that is more fundamental but has to be waited for.
Ask first: is the reason it is called realistic that it is more correct, or that it is faster?
Where it goes wrong: mistaking a short cycle for realism; picking the long option and turning at the first challenge.

### Lines to keep
Traders camped in the open, and the jails stood empty.
The side called realistic is often only the faster one.
If character always declined, there would be nothing left to teach.

## Liu Bang · The three men he was not the equal of
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/liu-bang/three-i-cannot/
Source: Records of the Grand Historian, Annals of Emperor Gaozu
Tags: Deep read, Liu Bang, Saying out loud who is better than you

At the victory banquet he asked why he had won, then answered himself. The answer is not modesty. It is an exercise of power.

### Q: What actually happened?
At a banquet in the southern palace at Luoyang he asked his officers why the empire had come to him and not to Xiang Yu. Someone said he was generous where Xiang Yu was grudging. He said they knew only half of it. In the tent, planning what settles a victory a thousand miles away, I am not the equal of Zhang Liang. For the state, the people, the supply lines, not the equal of Xiao He. For an army of a million, not the equal of Han Xin. These three are exceptional men, and I could use them. Xiang Yu had one Fan Zeng and could not.

### The parts · Naming who is better puts a price on a seat
Saying in public that a man beats you at one thing does two jobs at once. It fixes the value of his seat, and it makes plain who did the fixing. Handing out valuations is not handing over power; the man who prices the others is standing above them.
e.g. Naming, in front of everyone, the one thing a colleague does better than you settles his standing faster than any bonus, and settles yours at the same time.

### The parts · He defined his own skill as the using
His account of himself was not that he was good at everything. It was that he could use these men. That one move takes a leader off the track where he competes with his own staff, and on that track the ceiling is whoever is the weakest person he can bear to keep.
e.g. If hiring somebody stronger than you produces unease rather than relief, the height of the team is already decided, and it is your height.

### The parts · One Fan Zeng, and he could not use him
Xiang Yu's problem was never a shortage of talent. It was talent he would not let decide anything. Recognising ability is common and cheap. Actually letting the recognised person make the call is rare, and it is the rare half that determines the outcome.
e.g. You brought in the specialist and then rewrote every recommendation to match your own reading. Present or absent, that specialist changes nothing.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: somebody on your team is plainly better than you at something, and it sits badly.
Ask first: can you say out loud, in front of everyone, exactly what he is better at? If the sentence will not come, that is the thing to look at.
Where it goes wrong: treating the admission as weakness and avoiding it; or making it and then still making every call yourself, which is Xiang Yu's version.

### Lines to keep
In the tent, settling a victory a thousand miles off, Zhang Liang beats me.
These three are exceptional men. I could use them. That is all.
Xiang Yu had one Fan Zeng and could not use him.

## Liu Bang · Three clauses, and the rest repealed
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/liu-bang/three-articles/
Source: Records of the Grand Historian, Annals of Emperor Gaozu
Tags: Deep read, Liu Bang, A rule nobody can recite is not a rule

He reached the capital first and held the entire legal code of an empire. He replaced it with three sentences.

### Q: What actually happened?
First into the passes, he took Xianyang, called together the elders and the powerful men of every county, and said they had suffered under the harsh laws of Qin long enough. Then the announcement: a covenant of three clauses only, that a killer dies, and that wounding a man or robbing him answers for itself. Every other Qin law was repealed. He sent his own men out with the Qin officials to explain it in the villages. They brought oxen and wine to feed the army; he refused, saying the granaries were full and he did not wish to put anyone to expense.

### The parts · Three, because three can be remembered
A rule works in proportion to the share of people who can recall it. Qin law was complete and unmemorable, so to an ordinary man it was a minefield he crossed daily. Three clauses can be recited, and recitation is the precondition of both obedience and trust.
e.g. A fifty-page handbook nobody finishes binds less than three lines on the wall that every person in the building can repeat from memory.

### The parts · Subtract first, add later
Taking over a mess, the instinct is to write more rules. He did the opposite, cut down to three, and established the minimum order that had to hold. Everything else waited. Trust is the thing you build first; complexity is what you earn the right to add.
e.g. Inheriting a process nobody follows, delete four fifths of it, keep the two steps that must happen, and get that much running before designing anything new.

### The parts · Refusing the oxen is the second half of the same move
Announcing a rule is speech. Turning down the food is the act. The granaries are full, I do not wish to put you to expense — declining at the one moment he could have taken anything he liked did more for the covenant than any amount of explaining.
e.g. Having announced the freeze, cut your own travel first. Everyone is watching to see whether the first exception turns out to be you.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have just taken over something disorderly and you want rules in place quickly.
Ask first: can the team say your rules back to you without opening a document? If not, you have written a document, not a rule.
Where it goes wrong: answering disorder by adding rules; or announcing the rule and then making your own first act the first exception to it.

### Lines to keep
The elders have suffered long enough under the harsh laws of Qin.
Three clauses only: a killer dies, wounding and robbery answer for themselves.
The granaries are full. I do not wish to put you to expense.

## Liu Bang · Turning the sentence around
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/liu-bang/changing-mid-sentence/
Source: Records of the Grand Historian: Biography of the Marquis of Huaiyin, and the Annals of Emperor Gaozu
Tags: Deep read, Liu Bang, A foot under the table, and a new answer

Half the sentence is out of your mouth before you see it is wrong. What he did next looks bad, and was right every time.

### Q: What actually happened?
Han Xin, having taken Qi, sent a letter asking to be made acting king of it. Liu Bang, penned in at the time and waiting daily to be relieved, read it and swore at the messenger. Zhang Liang and Chen Ping trod on his foot under the table. He understood, kept swearing without a pause, and turned the whole sentence around: a real man who settles the feudal lords becomes a real king, so what is this acting? Zhang Liang was sent with the seal to install Han Xin properly.

### The parts · Turning round beats being right the first time
His first reaction was wrong, and already spoken. What he had was not accuracy but the ability to change track the instant a signal arrived, and to fold the first half of the sentence into the new direction. People differ in judgement. They differ far more in turning speed.
e.g. You state a view, a colleague adds a fact you did not have. Say that changes it, in the room, and watch how much more people bring you next quarter.

### The parts · Keep a channel open for the foot
None of this works unless somebody nearby dares to tread on your foot while you are shouting, and unless you know what the pressure means. That channel is not a gift of character. It is built by years of letting yourself be interrupted and not punishing it.
e.g. If nobody will cut across you when you are wrong, every error you make gets carried out in full, at full speed, by people who could see it.

### The parts · Face is the cheapest chip on the table
Reversing looks bad, and reversing from a curse to a coronation looks worse. He never hesitated at these moments, because he treated his own dignity as a cost he could pay at any time. Xiang Yu priced it high, at Hong Gate and again at the river.
e.g. Letting the team run three more months rather than admit the call was wrong saves one bad afternoon and spends a quarter.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: mid-sentence, and you have just realised the judgement behind it is wrong.
Ask first: which costs more, finishing this sentence or turning it round now? Price both before you decide which one hurts.
Where it goes wrong: treating the reversal as a loss of face and pushing through; or having nobody around you who is allowed to stop you mid-flow.

### Lines to keep
A man who settles the lords becomes a real king. Why acting?
Zhang Liang and Chen Ping trod on his foot, then spoke into his ear.
The king of Han understood, and went on swearing.

## Jesse Livermore · Sitting tight
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/livermore/sitting-tight/
Source: Reminiscences of a Stock Operator, chapter 5
Tags: Deep read, Jesse Livermore, Being right was never the hard part

A speculator famous for speed put the credit somewhere unexpected. The chapter explains why sitting is harder than being right.

### Q: What actually happened?
His own summary is not what anyone expects from him. It never was his thinking that made the big money, he says; it was his sitting. He had watched the alternative all his life: men who saw the move coming and made nothing from it, shaken out by every pullback or cashing a small gain early. Men who can both be right and sit tight are uncommon, he concludes, and that is the whole difficulty. The hard part is not the analysis. It is that every day of sitting is a day of refusing to act.

### The parts · The money lives in the back half of the hold
A large move does not pay out evenly. The early stretch is the choppiest and the most testing; the compounding happens later. Getting off partway takes the uncomfortable section and hands over the valuable one, which is how people are right about direction and collect almost nothing.
e.g. Eight months into the direction you chose, nothing has moved, so you switch. It works in month fourteen and your successor collects the degree you paid for.

### The parts · Not moving is an action that needs defending
Sitting is not the easy option; it is continuous resistance. The news, the swings and every friend's better idea all argue for a change. So it needs fortification: write the original thesis and the conditions that would falsify it, and permit movement only when one of those trips.
e.g. Set a hard rule for the long position: look once a quarter, and only against the three reasons you wrote at the start. Red or green is not a reason.

### The parts · Sitting only protects a judgement that is right
The sentence says right and sitting tight, and the two conditions are joined by an and. Using it to keep a broken position alive is the expensive misreading. Patience and stubbornness look identical from outside; the only test is whether the written thesis still stands.
e.g. Two of the three reasons you bought have already failed and you are still holding on. That is not sitting tight. That is refusing to be wrong.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the direction looks right and the wobbles are making your hands itch.
Ask first: has the thesis I wrote at the start actually broken? If not, is this urge coming from evidence or from discomfort?
Where it goes wrong: applying it to a position already falsified, or never writing a falsifier at all, so holding on becomes not looking.

### Lines to keep
It never was my thinking that made the big money for me.
It always was my sitting. Got that? My sitting tight!
Men who can both be right and sit tight are uncommon.

## Jesse Livermore · Hope and fear, the wrong way round
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/livermore/hope-and-fear-inverted/
Source: Reminiscences of a Stock Operator, chapter 10
Tags: Deep read, Jesse Livermore, The instinct points in the wrong direction

Four fortunes and several bankruptcies, distilled into one rule about two emotions pointing the wrong way.

### Q: What actually happened?
He traced his losses to a single inversion. When the position goes against a man he hopes, waiting for it to come back, and the loss grows. When it goes his way he becomes afraid of losing the profit, so he takes it early. His rule swaps them outright. Instead of hoping he must fear; instead of fearing he must hope. Fear the small loss becoming a large one and cut. Hope the small gain becomes a large one and hold. And he adds why it never stops working: speculation is as old as the hills, because people are not new.

### The parts · The instinct runs exactly backwards
Hoping over a loss and fearing over a gain is not a character flaw; it is the factory setting for humans facing gains and losses. Losses make people gamble and gains make people lock in. So the inversion cannot be run on reminders. It has to be run by mechanism.
e.g. Automate the exit on the downside and use a trailing stop instead of a manual sale on the upside. In the moment you will always side with the instinct.

### The parts · Cut fast, because a loss accrues interest
Hope applied to a loss compounds. Every extra day adds sunk cost, makes the admission harder, and raises the stake required to get back to level. That is where the fear belongs: not fear of this loss, but of the version that starts dictating every later decision.
e.g. Every month you extend the project that is missing its numbers, killing it gets harder: more spent, more promised, nobody willing to say it. The first cut is cheapest.

### The parts · The rule does not excuse you from the work
Cutting losses and running winners assumes you can say what counts as going against you. Without a thesis set in advance, the inversion degrades into buying strength and selling weakness. His own ruin came in the stretches when he broke his rules, and a rule cannot save the man who suspends it.
e.g. Cut it when it drops, applied by someone with no entry thesis, means being stopped out by every ordinary fluctuation. Discipline cannot stand in for judgement.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: one position is losing and you want to wait, another is winning and you want to bank it.
Ask first: which emotion is speaking in each case, and does the rule say to swap them?
Where it goes wrong: running it as blind momentum chasing, or knowing the rule and granting yourself exceptions, which is exactly how he went broke.

### Lines to keep
Instead of hoping he must fear; instead of fearing he must hope.
He must fear that his loss may develop into a much bigger loss.
There is nothing new in Wall Street. Speculation is as old as the hills.

## Peter Lynch · The tenbagger at the mall
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/lynch/tenbagger-at-the-mall/
Source: One Up on Wall Street
Tags: Deep read, Peter Lynch, Noticing is only the first step

Invest in what you know is his most quoted line and his most misused. The half that gets dropped is the work.

### Q: What actually happened?
He ran Magellan for thirteen years at twenty-nine per cent a year, and his signature find came from a supermarket. His wife liked a pair of tights called L'eggs, so he looked into the maker, Hanes, and the stock became one of his best. Investing without research, he warns in the same book, is like playing stud poker and never looking at the cards. The find is a lead, not a decision. And the amateur's real edge, he argues, is seeing the change in your own work and life six months to a year before Wall Street.

### The parts · What you see on the floor is a leading indicator
An analyst reads the quarterly. You see what feeds it: which brand keeps going out of stock, which store has a queue, which supplier everyone in your trade is quietly switching to. Those run about two quarters ahead, provided you log them as leads instead of retelling them as anecdotes.
e.g. Purchasing notices a small supplier's lead times suddenly full; sales notices a client's budget line has been renamed. Industry reports write that up half a year later.

### The parts · Between liking a product and buying a company sits a questionnaire
A good product answers the demand side only. His checklist is on the supply side: how much of the revenue comes from this, how heavy the debt is, how many years of growth remain, whether the success can be repeated. Most I use it so I understand it losses skip that page.
e.g. A heavy user buys shares in a favourite app without checking that its cost of acquiring a customer already exceeds what a customer spends.

### The parts · Knowing it well has its own blind spot
Investing inside your own industry gives a real information advantage and a real emotional debt. You will overrate the importance of your own link in the chain and underrate whatever is replacing it from outside. Use the knowledge to check facts, not to reach conclusions.
e.g. Nobody understands the value of the channel better than the people who run it, and nobody is slower to admit it is being bypassed.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something in ordinary life looks like an opportunity and you want to act on it.
Ask first: have I finished the checklist, meaning how it earns, whether that repeats, and what it owes?
Where it goes wrong: reading invest in what you know as invest in what you like; or the reverse, sitting on a real front-line advantage and deferring to reports.

### Lines to keep
Investing without research is like playing stud poker and never looking at the cards.
Never invest in any idea you can't illustrate with a crayon.
The person that turns over the most rocks wins the game.

## Peter Lynch · The organ is the stomach
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/lynch/stomach-not-brain/
Source: One Up on Wall Street
Tags: Deep read, Peter Lynch, Holding is harder than choosing

His fund compounded at twenty-nine per cent for thirteen years, and most of the people in it did worse. The gap has an anatomy.

### Q: What actually happened?
Magellan rose more than twenty-fold in his thirteen years, and Fidelity's own figures showed the average holder captured far less, with many losing money. They bought after the run and redeemed on every fall. The key organ for investing, he says, is the stomach, not the brain. His measure of normal is bracing: his big holdings could fall thirty per cent in an ordinary year, and if you cannot sit through a decline of fifty per cent, he writes, you should not own stocks at all.

### The parts · Drawdowns are the toll, not the accident
The path of a good asset includes regular sharp falls. That is the terrain, not a malfunction. Treat every drop as an incident and you will get out at each of them and watch the thing leave without you. The question before boarding is what will hold you through the fall.
e.g. Commit to a three-year direction and write in advance that it will be widely written off at least twice. On the day, reading that beats improvising conviction.

### The parts · Dodging the dip costs more than the dip
Stepping out to avoid a fall requires being right twice, on the exit and on the re-entry. Miss either and you permanently forfeit a stretch of the return, and long-run returns are concentrated in a handful of days. Sitting it out sounds prudent and is the most expensive habit available.
e.g. Let us wait for the uncertainty to pass works the same way inside a company. Uncertainty never passes, and the waiting costs the whole building phase.

### The parts · Stomach capacity is designed, not inherited
How much you can hold through is set by position size and by a written plan. A stake big enough to cost you sleep will break any conviction on a bad night. Decide in advance what happens at each level, so panic executes a document instead of a feeling.
e.g. Before committing heavily to one direction, cap it at what you could lose entirely and review it once a quarter. Rules stand guard so the stomach does not have to.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the number is falling, or the outlook has turned, and you want to step aside and watch.
Ask first: has the underlying thing changed, or only the price and my mood? What did the plan say to do here?
Where it goes wrong: turning holding on into refusing to admit a real deterioration, or taking a position so large that no stomach could carry it.

### Lines to keep
The key organ for investing is the stomach, not the brain.
More money is lost preparing for corrections than in the corrections themselves.
If you cannot stomach a fifty per cent decline, do not buy stocks.

## Machiavelli · Start from what is done
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/machiavelli/as-it-is/
Source: The Prince, chapter 15
Tags: Deep read, Machiavelli, How men live, not how they ought to live

He has been abused for five hundred years over one sentence. This asks what that sentence actually claims.

### Q: What actually happened?
Chapter 15 opens by separating him from everyone before him. Many have imagined republics and principalities that were never seen or known to exist; but how one lives is so far distant from how one ought to live that a man who neglects what is done for what ought to be done learns his own ruin rather than his preservation. That is not a recommendation to do harm. It is a statement of subject matter. He intends to write about how politics runs, not about how it should run.

### The parts · Design on ought, and it leaks on day one
Any arrangement resting on people being expected to behave has been built on an untested assumption. The realist order is the reverse: watch what people do when nothing is constraining them, and design for that. Concede first, handle second.
e.g. An allowance everyone is trusted not to abuse will be used to the last unit. Assume that, then decide what the number should be.

### The parts · Describing is not endorsing
He has been misread for five centuries because people took the description for the proposal. The distinction still costs money. Explaining why a mechanism works and recommending it are separate acts, and refusing to study the ugly ones leaves you unable to name what hit you.
e.g. Working out why a competitor's grey tactic pays is not advice to copy it. Refuse the analysis and the same move lands on you again.

### The parts · Necessary harm still has to be costed
He does not abolish morality, he turns it into an account that has to be settled. What does the thing you may have to do cost, can you carry that, is there a substitute? We don't do that sort of thing is cheap to say and useless on the day.
e.g. Redundancies are hard to do decently. Settle the severance, the sequence and what it says to the people staying before the week it happens, not during it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: writing a rule, and quietly assuming people will co-operate with it.
Ask first: if everyone used this to maximise their own position, what would it turn into?
Where it goes wrong: writing ought into the assumptions; or refusing to understand a method because the method is not respectable.

### Lines to keep
How one lives is so far distant from how one ought to live.
A man who professes goodness in everything will come to ruin.
The prince must know how to use both the beast and the man.

========================================================================
## Machiavelli · Feared, and not hated
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/machiavelli/feared-not-hated/
Source: The Prince, chapter 17
Tags: Deep read, Machiavelli, Deterrence has an edge, and he names it

Loved or feared is the question everybody knows. The answer has a second half, and the second half matters more.

### Q: What actually happened?
Best to be both, he says, but the two are hard to hold together, and if one of them has to be given up, it is far safer to be feared than loved. The reason is structural: love runs on the other person's willingness, fear on means you hold yourself. Then comes the clause that rarely travels with the quotation. The prince must avoid being hated, and the way to avoid it is specific — keep off their property and their women, because men forget the death of a father sooner than the loss of a patrimony.

### The parts · Love is theirs to withdraw, fear is yours to hold
Compliance built on goodwill ends the moment the other person changes his mind, and you cannot stop him changing it. This is not an argument for coldness. It is an argument against resting your stability on a variable you do not control.
e.g. A team held together by one person's charisma loosens fast after a bad call. Rules stated and then honoured do not depend on anybody's mood that morning.

### The parts · Hatred is the line you cannot cross
Fear and hatred are one step apart, and the step is whether you touched what the person treats as his own foundation. Penalties inside the rules produce fear. Reaching for dignity, property or family jumps straight to hatred, and hatred will pay any price to hit back.
e.g. Cutting a bonus or moving someone sideways is inside the rules. Humiliating him in front of the room, or withholding pay already agreed, is over the line.

### The parts · Deterrence has to be predictable
Fear that works is built on consistent follow-through, not on unpredictability. Someone nobody can read produces dread and paralysis rather than order, because when consequences cannot be forecast the safest move available to everybody is to do nothing.
e.g. The same mistake waved through once and punished hard the next time teaches people to read your face, not the standard.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: setting a precedent on something, and swinging between severe and lenient.
Ask first: what does this actually touch — something inside the rules, or something he treats as his own foundation?
Where it goes wrong: mistaking unpredictability for deterrence; or building order on being liked, which lasts exactly as long as the liking does.

### Lines to keep
It is far safer to be feared than loved, if you cannot be both.
Inspire fear in a way that avoids hatred, even without love.
Men forget the death of a father sooner than the loss of a patrimony.

========================================================================
## Machiavelli · Fortune and the half left to you
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/machiavelli/fortune-and-virtu/
Source: The Prince, chapter 25
Tags: Deep read, Machiavelli, Half is luck; the other half has a deadline

How much is fate and how much is mine? He gives a ratio, and then says exactly when the half that is yours can be spent.

### Q: What actually happened?
Chapter 25 puts a number on it: fortune is the arbiter of one half of our actions, but she leaves the other half, or nearly so, to be governed by us. Then the image everyone remembers. Fortune is a violent river that carries everything before it when it floods; yet in quiet weather men can raise dykes and embankments, so that when the water rises again it runs off in a channel. His conclusion is not resignation. It is that the half you govern has to be finished before the flood.

### The parts · The window for preparing is the calm
Dykes cannot be built during the flood. Inside a crisis the room for choice is tiny, and nearly every move that helps had to be completed while nothing was happening. What an organisation survives is decided by what it spent when spending looked unnecessary.
e.g. Cash buffer, a second supplier, a backup for the one person who knows the system. All look like waste until the day they are the only things working.

### The parts · The cautious man loses when the times turn
His counter-intuitive point: a method succeeds because it happens to suit the moment. When the moment changes and the method does not, it fails. People almost never change their nature, so the caution that made a man is what finishes him when boldness is wanted.
e.g. Whoever took the market by pushing hard in the expansion keeps pushing in the contraction. Whoever survived the contraction by holding back misses the next expansion.

### The parts · Concede the half that is not yours
Charge the whole result to yourself and you will be arrogant in good years and shattered in bad ones. Granting half to fortune concentrates attention on the half that moves, including the uncomfortable version of the question, asked after a win rather than after a loss.
e.g. A quarter beats plan. Ask what the number would have been if the whole market had been flat. A team that cannot answer will run luck as method.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: everything is going well, and you are weighing whether to spend on something that has not happened.
Ask first: if it did happen, would there still be time to do this preparation then?
Where it goes wrong: booking the whole of a good year to your own account; or running the method that worked in the last phase into a phase that has already changed.

### Lines to keep
Fortune is the arbiter of half our actions; she leaves us the rest.
In quiet weather men can raise their dykes and embankments.
The cautious man, when it is time to act boldly, is ruined.

========================================================================
## Nelson Mandela · Turning the trial into a platform
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/mandela/rivonia/
Source: Statement from the dock, Rivonia Trial, 1964
Tags: Deep read, Nelson Mandela, Setting your own terms inside their venue

Facing a possible death sentence, his lawyers urged a plea. This is why he read a statement from the dock instead.

### Q: What actually happened?
The Rivonia charges carried the death penalty. Mandela made a decision that was terrible law: he would not give evidence and would not be cross-examined, but would read a statement from the dock, trading the chance of acquittal for hours nobody could interrupt. The closing passage became the most famous courtroom speech of the century. It is an ideal which I hope to live for and to achieve. But if needs be, it is an ideal for which I am prepared to die. He got life, not death. The world outside had heard those hours.

### The parts · Work out which arena decides it
Inside the rules of the court he could not win, because the evidence was there. But the trial was also running in a second arena, the watching world. He gave up the one he could not win and put everything into the one he could. Before judging the odds, work out who is judging.
e.g. An internal review certain to fail can be lost by the process, or used to lay the whole problem out for the senior people sitting in. One meeting, two arenas.

### The parts · Giving up the defence bought wholeness
Under cross-examination his case would have arrived in fragments shaped by the prosecution's questions. Refusing bought one unbroken account. Breaking you into pieces is the main way an opponent controls what you can say, and dropping the exchange is sometimes how you keep the structure.
e.g. Answer a public dispute point by point and your position exists only in their edit. One complete statement, with no line-by-line reply, keeps the story yours.

### The parts · Prepared to die was calculated
The line was not rhetoric. The prosecution was asking for death, so saying it in court was a public surrender of the posture of trying to survive. That visible cost is what made the statement unanswerable. Credibility is bought with exposure.
e.g. A stated position weighs what you risk for it. Anonymous fury weighs less than one mild sentence with your name on it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have been pulled into a contest whose rules guarantee you lose.
Ask first: is there a second arena here, and who is judging in that one?
Where it goes wrong: spending every chip in the arena you cannot win; or using the other arena as an excuse to never answer the case in front of you.

### Lines to keep
It is an ideal for which I am prepared to die.
I have fought against white domination, and I have fought against black domination.
Courage was not the absence of fear, but the triumph over it.

## Nelson Mandela · Wearing the other side's jersey
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/mandela/springbok-jersey/
Source: The 1995 Rugby World Cup; Laureus Awards speech, 2000
Tags: Deep read, Nelson Mandela, Requisition the enemy's symbol

Black spectators had spent years cheering the opposition. This is what he accomplished on the day he put the shirt on.

### Q: What actually happened?
The Springboks were a white team and an emblem of apartheid, and black South Africans had long supported whoever they played. At the 1995 World Cup final Mandela walked onto the pitch in the green and gold jersey, wearing the captain's number 6. A crowd of sixty thousand, mostly white, was briefly stunned, then chanted his name. South Africa won and he handed the trophy to the white captain. Five years later he gave the method away: sport has the power to change the world, the power to inspire, the power to unite people in a way that little else does.

### The parts · Destroying a symbol makes enemies, taking it over makes belonging
A new order normally abolishes the old symbols, renames the team, redesigns the badge. That confirms to the other side that they are losers being settled with. He reversed it: keep what they treasure exactly as it is and wear it himself. The emblem unchanged, the meaning replaced.
e.g. Taking over an acquired team, scrapping their product name asserts ownership. Keeping it and championing it yourself takes the people.

### The parts · Reconciliation has to be spoken in their language
A hundred speeches about forgiveness would have done less for that community than wearing the jersey once. Speeches were his language and rugby was theirs. A message sent in the receiver's own language needs no translation, and goodwill that needs translating arrives discounted.
e.g. To make peace with an engineering team, do not send a company-wide note. Turn up and take part properly in one of their technical reviews.

### The parts · The resistance he had to hold off was his own side
The hardest opposition did not come from white South Africans. Most of his own party wanted the Springboks abolished, and he pushed this through over them. The first obstacle to reconciliation is never the enemy's hostility, it is your own side's appetite for a reckoning.
e.g. Pushing a partnership with an old rival, the hardest people to convince are those on your team the rival has hurt. Skip that and the handshake is a photograph.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have won, their symbols and habits are still standing, and your people want a reckoning.
Ask first: what does this symbol mean to them, and what would it say if you were the one using it?
Where it goes wrong: making the gesture and changing nothing, so the emblem is worn while the policy still settles scores; or keeping everything on principle, including what should go.

### Lines to keep
Sport has the power to change the world.
It has the power to unite people in a way that little else does.
It has the power to create hope where once there was only despair.
