## Mao Zedong · On Contradiction
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/mao/on-contradiction/
Source: On Contradiction (1937)
Tags: Deep read, Mao Zedong, Untie one knot at a time

Everything is urgent and all of it is yours. The question is not effort but which knot to pull first.

### Q: What actually happened?
Written at Yan'an in 1937, the essay turns a tangle into a diagram. At any stage many contradictions exist at once, but only one of them is principal, and its existence and development determine the rest. Find it and the other problems change shape on their own. Miss it and effort gets spread evenly across ten urgent things, which looks like working on everything and lands on nothing. Every later application repeats the same opening question: what is the principal contradiction of this stage?

### The parts · The principal one is not the loudest one
The principal contradiction is not the most urgent item and not the hardest. It is the one whose solution changes the shape of the others. Until you have found it, more action ties the knot tighter.
e.g. Weak product, few users, no channel and a loud competitor all shout at once. Supply was the switch, and everything else moved once it did.

### The parts · Finding it is half; cutting the rest is the other half
Better to sever one finger than to wound ten. Naming the priority is the easy half. The other half is genuinely putting the rest down, which means not doing them this stage, not doing them later. Spreading effort is usually reluctance, not blindness.
e.g. Plenty of people can name their priority. The ones whose list keeps growing and whose main thing still does not ship have not cut anything.

### The parts · When the stage turns, the knot moves
The principal contradiction is not fixed. Solve this one and the next stage surfaces a different one. The common death is holding on to yesterday's priority until the situation has changed the question and you are still answering the old one.
e.g. The team that won the first market kept optimising acquisition for two more years, while the actual question had quietly become whether anyone stayed.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: several things are all sounding at once and none of them feels droppable.
Ask first: which single one, solved, would loosen most of the others?
Where it goes wrong: the list keeps growing and the one thing that would move the rest still does not ship; the quarter turned and the method did not.

### Lines to keep
Among the many contradictions, one is principal and determines the rest.
Grasp the principal contradiction and every problem is readily solved.
Better to sever one finger than to wound all ten.

========================================================================
## Mao Zedong · On Practice
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/mao/on-practice/
Source: On Practice (1937)
Tags: Deep read, Mao Zedong, Knowing arrives through doing

You understood the idea and nothing changed. This one asks where knowledge comes from, and answers: from carrying something out.

### Q: What actually happened?
Written at Yan'an the same year as On Contradiction. Two failures were common in the ranks: one man memorised manuals and treated conclusions drawn on somebody else's battlefield as his own knowledge; another charged on instinct alone. The essay refuses both. Real knowledge comes out of doing, then has to be checked against what happened, then done again. If you want to know the taste of a pear, you must change the pear by eating it yourself. Memorising without that loop is what he called book worship.

### The parts · Knowledge comes out of doing
Following an argument is not the same as being able to run it. A judgement that has never been struck back at by events is a sentence nobody has paid for yet. What survives hardens after you have taken something out into the world.
e.g. Many people can describe the product well. Few have closed the first paying customer. The first group is still outside the knowledge; the second is inside it.

### The parts · Doing once is not the loop
One pass is not enough. Do without looking back and all you keep is fatigue. Look without going again and all you keep is an impression. Knowledge is a circle: act, review, act again, and the review has to be able to change the next act.
e.g. A team running the same playbook for three quarters with flat numbers, adding hours rather than reading them, has stopped at the doing.

### The parts · A book hands you the result, not the circuit
What somebody wrote down is the product of a loop they finished. You get the conclusion; the trials, corrections and second attempts are not on the page. So reading can shorten your route and cannot walk it for you.
e.g. Twenty books of method and still no plan anyone can execute is normal. That is twenty circuits other people walked, and none of them yours.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a shelf of method and not one live situation of your own.
Ask first: which already-finished thing has this sentence been through?
Where it goes wrong: you can explain more and more and deliver less and less; somebody else's review gets filed as your own experience.

### Lines to keep
If you want to know the taste of a pear, eat it.
Practice is the criterion of truth.
What is merely perceived cannot at once be understood.

========================================================================
## Mao Zedong · On Protracted War
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/mao/on-protracted-war/
Source: On Protracted War (1938)
Tags: Deep read, Mao Zedong, Trading time for strength

The weaker side that fights at the stronger side's tempo loses. This one is about changing the shape of the war itself.

### Q: What actually happened?
After Xuzhou and Nanjing in 1938, two errors were loud: that China was finished, and that victory would be quick. The lecture puts fought and unfought battles on one diagram, strategic defensive, strategic stalemate, strategic counter-offensive. It is not a forecast of dates; it is a rule about what may not be done. Do not trade your main force for the news value of one city. Do not seek a decisive battle before the fist has formed.

### The parts · Survive first, then talk about winning
The weaker side's first objective is not to destroy the other but to remain impossible to destroy. While the main force exists, time exists. Gamble it away and time goes to zero the same afternoon.
e.g. Nine months of cash left: cutting three lines to keep one alive beats starving four at once. A win reported for every position held is helping the other side get its decisive battle.

### The parts · Stalemate is not a pause, it is a change of rules
The middle stretch looks most like no progress. It is the war moving off the quick decision the stronger side is good at and onto the attrition you can survive. Whoever cannot bear the stalemate will reach for a decisive battle early.
e.g. While the rival burned funding on discounts and city launches, the side that refused the speed contest and ground on retention let them hold points they could not hold.

### The parts · The counter-offensive waits for the fist
Going over to the attack is not a change of mood. It is scattered strength gathered into something that can be moved as one. Attacking before that is a donation; staying in stalemate after it wastes time on a stage that has already ended.
e.g. Going to full war before word of mouth has joined into a network is graduating early. The slogan changed; the supply lines did not.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are the weaker side and they want it settled this week.
Ask first: is this engagement buying time or spending it?
Where it goes wrong: trading the main force for visible small wins to prove you are not stalling; a calendar full of battles and no week that grew the fist.

### Lines to keep
Both the defeatists and those who promise a quick win are wrong.
Weapons matter in war, but the decisive factor is people.
Is this fight buying time, or spending it?

========================================================================
## Mao Zedong · Problems of Strategy
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/mao/strategy-of-the-revolution/
Source: Problems of Strategy in China's Revolutionary War (1936)
Tags: Deep read, Mao Zedong, Fight the war your weapons allow

Someone else's victory does not transfer. This one asks what a method has to look like given your ground, your people and your weapons.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1936 the Red Army was still in the northwest, and two imported methods were in fashion: Soviet field manuals, and the memory of the Northern Expedition. He put both down and asked a prior question. What is the character of war on this particular ground? Against a stronger and larger opponent, the method cannot be the stronger side's method. The essay turns opposition to book worship into a battlefield rule and writes concentrate a superior force and destroy the enemy one by one as an operating order.

### The parts · Against book worship
Opposing book worship is not opposing study. It is refusing to skip the look at your own ground. How the Soviets fought and how the Northern Expedition fought are other people's answers; imported as doctrine, the first engagement is lost on terrain.
e.g. A forty-person company running the org chart of a forty-thousand-person one, or a workshop copying a software release cadence: both are doctrine without ground.

### The parts · Concentrate a superior force
Concentrate and destroy them one at a time: three against one, finish, then move to the next. Spread out, it looks as though fighting is happening everywhere and nothing is punched through. On Contradiction says what to put down; this says how to place what is left.
e.g. Five features shipped the same quarter and not one of them gives a customer a reason to stay. Punch one through first, then start the second.

### The parts · Your battlefield is not theirs
Where you are weaker and smaller, the method built for parity does not apply. Fighting with the weapons you have is not consolation; it is nailing the method to your actual strength instead of to the strength you are reading about.
e.g. A six-person team borrowing a public company's campaign calendar runs out of money and people by week three. Ask what these six can punch through, then pick that.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are holding a method that won for somebody else, on ground unlike yours.
Ask first: how many of the conditions that method depends on do we actually have?
Where it goes wrong: still running their org chart and their campaign calendar; five lines open and not one of them punched through.

### Lines to keep
No investigation, no right to speak.
Concentrate a superior force and destroy the enemy one by one.
Someone else's victory arrives without the ground it was won on.

========================================================================
## Mao Zedong · Methods of Work
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/mao/methods-of-work/
Source: Methods of Work of Party Committees (1949)
Tags: Deep read, Mao Zedong, Put it on the table

The call was right and everyone still went their own way. This one is about getting a group to actually move on one judgement.

### Q: What actually happened?
March 1949. The organisation was about to change from fighting to administering, and what he wrote down was twelve rules of craft rather than a line of argument: how to run a meeting, how to question the people below you, how to push ten things along at once without noise, how to turn I think into I have counted. The earlier essays settle the judgement; this one starts after it. One person seeing clearly and a group moving accordingly are two different problems.

### The parts · Put the problem on the table
A disagreement that is not aired does not go away; it moves into the corridor afterwards and ferments. Tabling it is not about arguing. It lets whoever objects finish the reason out loud, because a reason left unfinished comes back in some other form.
e.g. Unanimous in the room, full of reservations in private messages afterwards. That agreement is the expensive kind: everyone executes their own unspoken version of it.

### The parts · Learn to play the piano
All ten fingers move, but they do not come down together. Push only one thing and the rest rot; press ten evenly and what comes out is noise. The craft is in sequence: which is the melody this stretch, what accompanies it, who takes over next.
e.g. One word shouted all quarter while the other lines are left to rot, or twelve goals every one of them marked highest priority. Neither is playing.

### The parts · Have the numbers in your head
Any quality shows up as a definite quantity. Feedback is good is an impression, not a situation. Retention is thirty-eight per cent this month against forty-one last month is a situation. Without quantity, the discussion is won by whoever is loudest.
e.g. Ask a manager what the biggest problem is and most can answer. Ask how many times a week it happens and half the answers disappear.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the direction is settled and the group is still each running its own reading of it.
Ask first: has the disagreement been finished out loud, in front of everyone?
Where it goes wrong: nobody objects in the room and reservations are everywhere afterwards; twelve goals all marked top priority; two hours of discussion without a single number on the table.

### Lines to keep
Put problems on the table; a meeting that hides them settles nothing.
Ten fingers all move, but pressed down together they make no tune.
Any quality shows up as a quantity; without quantity there is none.

========================================================================
## Marcus Aurelius · What stands in the way becomes the way
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/marcus-aurelius/obstacle-is-the-way/
Source: Meditations, Book 5
Tags: Deep read, Marcus Aurelius, The line, and the mechanism under it

The most quoted line in the book, and the only one many English readers ever meet. Here is what surrounds it.

### Q: What actually happened?
He wrote it as emperor, in a reign with almost no quiet year in it: plague, war on the Danube frontier, a trusted general in revolt. The note reads: the impediment to action advances action; what stands in the way becomes the way. The mechanism is in the lines around it. The mind turns whatever blocks it to its own purpose, the way a fire takes what is thrown on it and makes flame out of it. The obstacle is not removed. It is burned.

### The parts · What is blocked is the route, not the destination
Almost always the thing in the way has closed one particular path you had imagined. Separate the path from the goal and most obstacles change from this cannot be done into take another road. People who cannot separate them read a route failure as a goal failure.
e.g. If the goal was customers through that channel, the channel closing ends it. If the goal was customers, it moved you out of something already getting expensive.

### The parts · The fire image is about capacity
A small fire is smothered by a large log; a big one turns the log into more of itself. So the same setback lands differently on different people, and the difference is not in the setback but in how much was already burning. What you absorb depends on what you stocked.
e.g. One public criticism costs one person three months and another an afternoon of rewriting. The gap was built earlier.

### The parts · The conversion has to name an action
Turn adversity into fuel is a slogan until it produces a next step. His use is concrete. This thing has blocked one route, so ask what it exposed, what it freed up, and whose real attitude it just showed. All three questions have specific answers.
e.g. Losing the biggest account exposed a hole in renewals, freed the delivery team it monopolised, and showed who in the building actually cared.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something you planned has been shut down by something outside you.
Ask first: is it the goal that has been blocked, or only the route you chose for it?
Where it goes wrong: reading a route failure as a goal failure; or saying this is an opportunity and then producing no next step.

### Lines to keep
The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way.
A fire makes flame and brightness out of everything thrown into it.
The obstacle is not removed. It is burned.

========================================================================
## Marcus Aurelius · The view from above
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/marcus-aurelius/view-from-above/
Source: Meditations, Books 6, 9 and 12
Tags: Deep read, Marcus Aurelius, Pull the scale back

A year from now most of this will be gone from memory. The exercise is how to borrow that later view now.

### Q: What actually happened?
He runs the same drill over and over: pull the eye back until the thing in front of him is small. Asia and Europe are corners of the universe, he writes, and the whole ocean a drop. He reminds himself that the men with the loudest names are long gone, and so are the people who remembered them. This is not nihilism, it is calibration. He was the emperor. Everything on his desk was described to him as gravely important, and he needed a ruler that could tell him which ones really were.

### The parts · Urgency is mostly proximity
A thing looks enormous largely because it is close. Stretch the timescale to a year or five and nearly everything currently costing you sleep shrinks to its right size. The two or three that do not shrink are the ones worth the whole week.
e.g. Re-sort this week's list by will anyone remember this in a year. Two of your top three usually move.

### The parts · Pulling back is not opting out
The point of the wide view is to allocate attention, not to cancel action. He kept governing and went to the front in person. The exercise hands out weights, not excuses, and using it to prove that nothing matters is using it backwards.
e.g. In the long run none of it matters is escape. This gets thirty minutes, not three hours, is allocation.

### The parts · Use the same ruler on people
He turns it on whoever has just offended him: in a few decades that person is gone and so are you. It does not delete the offence. It lowers the volume of the response, and the response is usually where the actual damage comes from.
e.g. Being contradicted in a meeting costs far less than firing back does. Widen the frame and you will wait.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: one thing has taken over and you cannot work on anything else.
Ask first: will this still be on my list a year from now?
Where it goes wrong: using the long view to argue that nothing needs doing; or widening the frame for events and never for the person who offended you.

### Lines to keep
Asia and Europe are corners of the universe; the ocean, a drop.
Not the thing disturbs you, but your judgement about it.
Everything you are looking at is already changing.

========================================================================
## Marcus Aurelius · The morning rehearsal
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/marcus-aurelius/morning-preparation/
Source: Meditations, Book 2
Tags: Deep read, Marcus Aurelius, Go through the people you will meet today

Book Two opens with a preparation, not a reflection. The claim is that offence you expected does about half the damage.

### Q: What actually happened?
The first line of Book Two is a script to be said on waking: today I shall meet with the busybody, the ungrateful, the arrogant, the deceitful, the envious, the unsocial. Then the reasoning. They are like this because they cannot tell good from harm; I can, so they cannot injure me and I will not be angry with them, since we were made to work together, like hands, like feet, like the two rows of teeth. It is a daily rehearsal, not a one-off complaint.

### The parts · Expected offence lands at half strength
Most of the force in anger comes from surprise rather than from the event. Walk through the difficult turns the day may take, and when one arrives you are in of course rather than in how dare they. That gap is where a choice about the response fits.
e.g. Before the negotiation, write the three hardest things they could raise. Then you are answering, not reeling.

### The parts · Rehearse your own move, not their behaviour
You cannot make the other person easier. The whole preparation lands on your side of the table: how I intend to answer, when I do not answer at all, where the line is. Turned into a list of grievances about them, it does the opposite of its job.
e.g. He will dodge the blame again is useless. When he does, I state the facts and do not defend is usable.

### The parts · Assume they do not know, not that they are bad
His attribution is ignorance, not malice. The practical value is that ignorance and conflicting interests are both things you can work on, whereas once you decide the other person is bad the only move left is to fight him.
e.g. If a colleague keeps crossing a line, assume he cannot see it and say where it is. Then judge.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: there is a meeting today that you already expect to go badly.
Ask first: what is he most likely to do, and what exactly do I intend to do at that moment?
Where it goes wrong: writing the rehearsal as a list of complaints about them; or starting from malice, which leaves only one move available.

### Lines to keep
Today I shall meet the busybody, the ungrateful, the arrogant, the deceitful.
They are like this because they cannot tell good from harm.
We were made to work together, like the two rows of teeth.

========================================================================
## Howard Marks · Second-level thinking
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/marks/second-level-thinking/
Source: The Most Important Thing, chapter one
Tags: Deep read, Howard Marks, Pricing in the consensus

Two people can look at the same good company and reach opposite conclusions. Marks says the difference is which level the thinking happens on.

### Q: What actually happened?
The Most Important Thing opens on the contrast. First-level thinking says: it's a good company, let's buy the stock. Second-level thinking says: it's a good company, but everyone thinks it's a great company, so the stock is overpriced — let's sell. The first level handles facts. The second handles what everybody believes about those facts, which is also a fact, and one already sitting inside the price. His conclusion is blunt: you cannot do what everyone else is doing and expect to outperform. Different, and more right. Both, or neither.

### The parts · The consensus is already in the price
If everybody knows the company is good, you have paid full price for that knowledge. So the second-level question is never whether it is good. It is whether it is better or worse than the price already assumes. The object of judgement has moved.
e.g. When the taxi driver is telling you the sector has an enormous future, that future is already inside the hiring, the funding round and the ad auction.

### The parts · Being different is only half of it
Marks says it plainly: different and right wins, different and wrong loses worse. Contrarianism is not a strategy, it is exposure — it magnifies whichever one you are. So the weight falls on a single question: what do I know that the consensus does not?
e.g. You are expanding while the whole industry contracts. Either you have data nobody else has, or you have missed what everybody else saw. Settle which before you sign.

### The parts · The second level is a questionnaire, not a thought
He lists what it takes: what is the range of outcomes, which do I think will happen, what odds am I giving myself, what does the consensus expect, where do I differ, and which of the two is in the price? The first level is one sentence.
e.g. Review proposals in two columns: everyone agrees this will work, and here is where we differ from that. Projects with an empty second column earn the average.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have spotted an opportunity that looks obvious.
Ask first: how many people can see the same obvious thing, and how much of it is already in the price, or in the level of competition?
Where it goes wrong: turning contrarianism into an identity and being different for its own sake; or nesting the second level so deep that you never decide anything.

### Lines to keep
You can't do the same things others do and expect to outperform.
Second-level thinking is deep, complex and convoluted.
Investment success doesn't come from buying good things, but from buying things well.

## Howard Marks · Taking the temperature
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/marks/taking-the-temperature/
Source: The Most Important Thing; Mastering the Market Cycle
Tags: Deep read, Howard Marks, Don't forecast, locate

He refuses to forecast and still bought two generational bottoms. What replaces the forecast is a reading of where we are standing now.

### Q: What actually happened?
Marks gives up on prediction: nobody knows the macro reliably, so he stops trying. Then he changes the question. We may never know where we're going, but we'd better have a good idea where we are. The cycle cannot be forecast; your position on it can be measured. He calls it taking the temperature — is credit loose or tight, are buyers begging their way in or sellers begging their way out, are the sceptics or the believers louder. Two rules sit underneath: nothing runs one way forever, and the mood swings like a pendulum that barely pauses at the midpoint.

### The parts · What forecasting can't answer, location can
Nobody knows what next year does. But where you sit on the arc has readings you can take today: how hard it is to raise money, how thorough diligence has become, how bad news gets absorbed. That will not date the turn. It tells you whether to lean forward or back.
e.g. You cannot call the sector's inflection. You can count whether investors chase founders or founders chase meetings, and that already says whether to store grain.

### The parts · The extremes give the cleanest readings
Mid-arc the thermometer is vague; at the ends it is obvious. Universal fear and universal fearlessness are both easy to recognise. The hard part is acting on the reading, because the action it calls for is the exact opposite of how the moment feels.
e.g. How often this time it's different and it will never come back reach the headlines is itself a reading. Whichever you keep hearing, check your position against it.

### The parts · Being early is the fixed cost of this method
Acting on position means being early almost by construction: you turn cautious past the midpoint and the pendulum runs on for another year. Marks says being too far ahead of your time is indistinguishable from being wrong. That stretch is the ticket price.
e.g. Trimming on the thermometer and then watching everyone else earn for another year is the standard script. Write that year into the plan or you will abandon the plan inside it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you cannot call which way this goes, so you have stopped moving.
Ask first: forget direction — what is the position? What do funding, sentiment and behaviour say about where on the arc we are standing?
Where it goes wrong: turning location back into timing and demanding that you catch the turn; or taking the temperature and then not acting on the reading, which wastes the whole exercise.

### Lines to keep
Trees don't grow to the sky, and few things go to zero.
The mood swings of the securities markets resemble the movement of a pendulum.
Being too far ahead of your time is indistinguishable from being wrong.

========================================================================
## Christina Maslach · Burnout has three parts. Tired is one
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/maslach/three-signs/
Source: Maslach & Jackson, Maslach Burnout Inventory, 1981
Tags: Deep read, Christina Maslach, The other two warn you earlier

Tired and burnt out are not the same thing. The three measures Maslach used to separate them.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1981 Maslach built an inventory that split burnout into three components: emotional exhaustion (drained in a way sleep doesn't repair), depersonalisation (you start handling people as items, and can't summon interest in any of them), and a fall in personal accomplishment (nothing you do feels like it matters). Only the first overlaps with being tired. So somebody can look like they're working normally and still be delivering, while the other two have been running for months.

### The parts · Detachment warns earlier than exhaustion, and gets misread
Rest fixes tired. It does not fix detachment. Detachment looks like having nothing for colleagues, customers or family, and speech going formulaic. Others read it as someone turning cold; the person reads it as their personality changing. It's the second measure lighting up.
e.g. Your own voice on the phone sounds unfamiliar to you, like reading from a script.

### The parts · 'I'm useless' isn't modesty, it's a reading
The third component is accomplishment collapsing: the same work finished, and where there used to be a little satisfaction there is now nothing. It gets treated as an attitude problem. On the inventory it is as measurable as the other two.
e.g. The project landed and you felt nothing, only wanted it over. That is not being low-key.

### The parts · They don't arrive together, so don't wait for the set
For most people detachment comes first, then exhaustion, and accomplishment collapses last. By the time all three are present, recovery takes far longer than it would have when one appeared. One of the three is enough to take seriously.
e.g. 'I can still handle it' usually means using the one that hasn't shown up to deny the one that has.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you suspect you're burnt out and keep telling yourself it's just tiredness.
Ask first: which of the three do I have — drained, nothing left for people, no satisfaction on finishing? Only the first is tiredness. Either of the other two is a different thing.
Where it goes wrong: using it to diagnose yourself and stopping there — it's for locating the problem, not labelling yourself; and don't use it to judge whether someone else is slacking.

### Lines to keep
Sleep fixes tired. It does not fix detachment.
Still working normally and still delivering proves nothing about the other two.
'I can still handle it' denies what's here using what isn't.

========================================================================
## Christina Maslach · Fix the job, not the person
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/maslach/fix-the-job/
Source: Maslach & Leiter, The Truth About Burnout, 1997
Tags: Deep read, Christina Maslach, Teaching people to relax repairs the wrong thing

What to do about burnout. The mainstream answer may have the whole thing backwards, and she says why.

### Q: What actually happened?
The moment burnout was named, the market's fix became teaching people to relax: mindfulness, time management, resilience training. Maslach has argued against that direction for decades. Her claim is blunt: burnout is a problem of the work environment, not of individual resilience. Spending the effort on remaking the individual asks the person absorbing the damage to repair the thing causing it — and carries a second message along with it: if you can't take this, you aren't strong enough.

### The parts · Putting the responsibility in the wrong place makes it worse
Tell someone the problem is their attitude and they add a layer of self-blame, then stay in the same environment. The two together are much harder to climb out of than the exhaustion was on its own.
e.g. The company runs a mindfulness course and doesn't touch the rota. Everyone comes back to the same schedule.

### The parts · Personal fixes aren't useless, they're second
Maslach never said sleep and exercise don't work. She said the order matters: see what in the working conditions can change, then talk about personal regulation. Reverse the order and personal regulation stops being support and starts being cover.
e.g. Cut the two hours of daily meetings first. Then discuss how to unwind. Not the other way round.

### The parts · For an individual, this means check the environment first
You may not be able to change the company, but you can do the accounting: is it too much work, or no say, or work that runs against what you care about? Each diagnosis points at a completely different move — what to negotiate, what to leave, what to refuse.
e.g. You think you need a holiday; the audit says what's crushing you is needing sign-off for everything.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you're close to done, and everyone advises you to adjust your mindset and rest more.
Ask first: if I took a month off, would I come back to the same arrangement? If yes, the problem isn't your mindset.
Where it goes wrong: using it to deny everything an individual can do — she gives an order, not an exemption; and don't let it replace medical help. Burnout and depression aren't the same thing, and if you can't tell, see a doctor.

### Lines to keep
Asking the person absorbing the damage to repair its cause is backwards.
A mindfulness course and an unchanged rota send everyone back to the same schedule.
If a month off returns you to the same arrangement, it isn't your mindset.

========================================================================
## Christina Maslach · Six ways to be mismatched
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/maslach/six-mismatches/
Source: Maslach & Leiter's six areas of worklife
Tags: Deep read, Christina Maslach, Workload is only the first

Same hours, and one person breaks while another doesn't. The six places she found the mismatch.

### Q: What actually happened?
Maslach and Leiter split the sources of burnout into six areas — the places where a person and a job fail to match: workload, control, reward, community, fairness and values. Most people watch only the first. In her data the later ones are often more lethal, particularly having no say (control) and doing work that runs against what you believe (values). At identical hours, people matched on all six rarely break; people short two or three break quickly.

### The parts · Little work with no control hurts more than lots with control
Control is the second area and the most underrated. Few tasks, each needing sign-off and liable to be overturned at any moment, costs far more than a heavy load you get to arrange yourself. This matches what the stress research found independently.
e.g. Three things a day, each waiting on three people to nod, is more tiring than ten you decide yourself.

### The parts · A values mismatch is the slowest and the deepest
The sixth area is doing work that runs against what you care about. It doesn't strike the same day; it hollows out the meaning gradually — the longer you do it the emptier it gets, and the less you can say why. Fix the other five and this one still takes you down.
e.g. Having to say things you don't believe every day. No salary fills that particular hole.

### The parts · Score them separately or you can't tell what to move
'Work is exhausting' implies no action at all. Score the six one by one and the answer usually gets specific: what you need to fight for is decision rights, or what you need to raise is fairness, or what you need is different work.
e.g. You think you need less volume; the audit says what's missing is any say in it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you can't say what is draining you, only that you can't keep this up.
Ask first: workload, control, reward, community, fairness, values — which of the six am I clearly mismatched on? One sentence each.
Where it goes wrong: using it to prove quitting is the only option — several of the six are negotiable; and don't fail all six and then do nothing. Move the worst one.

### Lines to keep
Little work needing sign-off costs more than lots you decide yourself.
A values mismatch doesn't strike today. It hollows the meaning out slowly.
'Work is exhausting' implies no action at all.

========================================================================
## Konosuke Matsushita · The tap-water philosophy
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/matsushita/tap-water/
Source: Address at the Matsushita founding anniversary, 1932
Tags: Deep read, Konosuke Matsushita, Setting the mission at the price

He watched a stranger drink from somebody's outdoor tap and go unscolded. The company mission he wrote out of that scene.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1932 Matsushita named the year the first year of knowing the mission. At the founding anniversary he described the scene: a passer-by turns a roadside tap, drinks, and nobody scolds him, because tap water is so plentiful and so cheap that it is nearly free, though it plainly has value. Then the mission: the mission of a manufacturer is to make goods as inexhaustible and as cheap as tap water, and by that route to drive poverty out of the world. It is not a charitable declaration. It is a product strategy with scale, process and distribution all ordered behind one number.

### The parts · Write the mission as something you can measure
Most missions are adjectives, excellent or leading or people-first, and an adjective can neither be checked nor give an order. This one is a quantity: price against reach. Every quarter you can answer whether you got closer to tap water, so the mission becomes a production schedule rather than wall decoration.
e.g. Let more people use it is a slogan. Cut the price of this feature to a tenth within three years is an order that reorganises the supply chain.

### The parts · Cheap is a capability, not a concession
Making cheapness the mission forces the hard crafts: yield, scale, turnover, distribution efficiency. Every cent of price cut has to be paid for by a real improvement in the cost structure. Cheapness bought by giving up margin is bleeding; cheapness bought by capability is a moat. Short term the statements look alike.
e.g. Two firms sell at the same low price. Look at what each spent on tooling and research in the year it cut, and the difference shows up.

### The parts · Below a threshold the market changes order of magnitude
Under a certain price a product changes species: from something worth considering into something used without thinking, and the market widens from those who can afford it to everyone. The tap-water philosophy is a bet on that phase change, on the far larger market underneath the threshold.
e.g. Printing, computing and phone calls all did this. Cut the price by an order of magnitude and both the uses and the users changed kind.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are drafting a mission for the product or the company and the page is all adjectives.
Ask first: can this be rewritten as a quantity, a price, a reach or an elapsed time, that we can check every quarter?
Where it goes wrong: making cheapness the end in itself and paying for it out of margin; or using tap water to dismiss every premium position, when luxury has a case of its own.

### Lines to keep
The mission of a manufacturer is to overcome poverty and bring society wealth.
Make goods as inexhaustible and as cheap as tap water.
Nobody scolds the passer-by who drinks from a roadside tap.

========================================================================
## Konosuke Matsushita · When it rains, open your umbrella
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/matsushita/umbrella-in-rain/
Source: Matsushita's management writings and question sessions
Tags: Deep read, Konosuke Matsushita, Management by the obvious

Asked for the secret of management, he answered in six words. Why the almost dismissive answer is the hardest one to follow.

### Q: What actually happened?
Somebody asked Matsushita the secret of management. His answer: when it rains, open your umbrella. There is no trick to it. Do the obvious things in the obvious way, without exception: pay your suppliers, collect what you are owed, close the books daily, fix the product until it is good. Listeners were often disappointed, and he insisted that was all of it. In the slump of 1929, warehouse full and everyone urging layoffs, his move was just as plain: not one employee dismissed, production halved, the whole workforce out selling stock. Months later the inventory was gone.

### The parts · Hunting for a secret is avoidance of the basics
People who ask for the secret usually want a way round the things everybody knows and nobody does daily: collection, inventory, quality, keeping your word. Six words close that road off. What looks like mastery is the obvious, executed without exceptions.
e.g. A stalled company shops for methodologies while its delivery slippage and collection cycle have not improved in three years. The rain never stopped and the umbrella never opened.

### The parts · The hard part is opening it while standing in the rain
The counter-examples happen daily: knowing you should chase the invoice and not chasing it because the client matters, keeping a line alive for pride, producing while the inventory towers. Between the simplicity of the principle and the difficulty of the act sit luck, face and habit. Six words treat those three.
e.g. Receivables ninety days past due with no collection process started, because the relationship is important. That is standing in the rain arguing the umbrella is ugly.

### The parts · The umbrella of 1929 covered what would not move
Handling a crisis is entirely about choosing what varies and what does not. He varied output and job content, and did not vary employment itself. Putting people in the fixed column is what let a whole workforce switch to selling without hedging. Management by the obvious includes judging what is obviously untouchable.
e.g. Write the list of what will not move in a downturn, the core team, the quality floor, the promises made. Everything else is negotiable, and the clearer the list, the faster you turn.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are shopping around for the clever move that breaks the deadlock.
Ask first: are the obvious things, collection, delivery, quality, keeping our word, being done here without exceptions?
Where it goes wrong: using there is no secret to dismiss all method and all innovation; or reading open your umbrella as drifting with the weather until you cannot tell which way you are facing.

### Lines to keep
When it rains, open your umbrella.
Do the obvious things in the obvious way, without exception.
Not one employee dismissed. Production halved. Everyone out selling the stock.

========================================================================
## Mencius · The people come first
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/mencius/people-first/
Source: Mencius, Jin Xin II and Li Lou I
Tags: Deep read, Mencius, Where the ground under power actually is

Read for two thousand years as ancient humanism. It reads better as a technical claim about where a government's power comes from.

### Q: What actually happened?
The people are the most important; the altars of grain and land come next; the ruler counts least. He ranked all three, and put the ruler at the bottom. This is not a plea for kindness, it is his judgement about what keeps a regime standing. Elsewhere he is blunter. There is a way to gain the empire: gain the people. There is a way to gain the people: gain their hearts. So benevolent government, in Mencius, is not the ruler's private virtue. It is the condition of his continuing to be the ruler.

### The parts · Consent is a thing that gets withdrawn
The heart of the people is not affection, it is consent. People rarely revolt at the moment they turn; they stop cooperating first. The tax gets harder to collect, the levy comes up short, the order goes down and nobody carries it out with care. The power is already hollow while the name is intact.
e.g. Nobody objects in the meeting, nothing moves afterwards, the reports start being padded, and the people leaving give a reason that is not the reason.

### The parts · The order cannot be inverted
Put the institution, or the man at the top, in front of the people who carry the cost, and you get one specific family of bad decisions: the ones that protect a reputation or an earlier judgement by charging somebody else for it. Authority holds. The ground under it goes.
e.g. Rather than admit the last decision was wrong, the team spends another month filling the hole. The authority survives; half the people worth keeping do not.

### The parts · Tax, service and punishment are three measurable lines
He never leaves benevolence at the level of a concept. The items are specific: do not take men away in the farming season, keep the taxes light, keep the punishments few. All three are countable, and all three are set by the person in charge, alone.
e.g. Judge any new policy with two questions. What did it give the people doing the work, and what did it take? Run the ratio over a year, not a week.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a decision that is easy to justify upwards and hard on the people who have to carry it.
Ask first: will the side paying for this still cooperate with the next thing you ask? That, not the objection, is the reading you want.
Where it goes wrong: reading silence as agreement; or defending a judgement you have already made by having other people keep paying for it.

### Lines to keep
The people come first, the altars of the state next, the ruler last.
Gather for them what they want; do not impose what they hate.
Treat them as your hands and feet and they treat you as their heart.

========================================================================
## Mencius · Two different ways of being obeyed
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/mencius/force-vs-virtue/
Source: Mencius, Gongsun Chou I
Tags: Deep read, Mencius, Compliance and conviction look identical

Two people are doing what you asked, and the two cases have nothing in common. This is how to tell which one you have.

### Q: What actually happened?
He sets them side by side. Those subdued by force do not submit in their hearts; they submit because their strength is not enough. Those won over by virtue are pleased in the heart and submit in earnest. Then the mechanical detail: obedience bought by force has to be paid for continuously, and the moment the balance of strength shifts it disappears. Which is why he adds that a man using force under a borrowed name becomes a hegemon, and a hegemon needs a large state, while one who acts from virtue becomes a king, and a king need not be large.

### The parts · The measurement is taken while you are away
In your presence the two kinds of obedience are indistinguishable, which is why watching harder tells you nothing. The difference only appears in your absence, so the test is simple: over the stretch when nobody was checking, did the standard hold or drop?
e.g. Take the two weeks of leave and look at what shipped while you were gone. It is a better instrument than any engagement survey.

### The parts · Force costs the same every day, then more
Their strength is not enough names the property that matters: force has to keep being applied. Supervision, scoring and checking never get cheaper with time, and they get dearer as people learn to handle them. Conviction costs most at the start and then tends towards nothing.
e.g. The clock-in system works for a month. By month three there are workarounds, and somebody is being paid to design defences against them.

### The parts · A king need not be large
Force needs mass behind it, so the smaller party always loses that contest. Conviction does not. This is the route Mencius leaves open to the weaker side: you cannot become stronger than them this year, but you can become more worth following than them this year.
e.g. A small firm cannot beat the salary. It can offer real say in decisions, a visible path, and promises that get kept. None of that costs money. All of it has to be honoured.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the team looks disciplined and you cannot tell whether it is real or propped up.
Ask first: over the last stretch when you were not watching, how far did the standard fall? Measure it before you add anything.
Where it goes wrong: answering a delivery problem with more supervision, which prices upward for ever; or taking the absence of complaints as evidence of agreement.

### Lines to keep
Those subdued by force submit for lack of strength, not in their hearts.
The hegemon needs a large state. The true king does not.
Heaven's timing yields to ground; ground yields to people in accord.

========================================================================
## Mencius · The flood-like breath
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/mencius/flood-like-qi/
Source: Mencius, Gongsun Chou I
Tags: Deep read, Mencius, It accumulates, and it cannot be hurried

Asked what the flood-like breath was, he said it is hard to put into words. Here is where it comes from, and how it leaks away.

### Q: What actually happened?
He calls it vast and unbending, and then says where it comes from: it is produced by an accumulation of right acts, and is not seized by one righteous act from outside. Then the counter-example. A man of Song, impatient at how slowly his rice was coming on, went through the field pulling every shoot up a little, and came home saying he was worn out from helping the rice to grow. His son ran out to look. The whole crop had withered. The breath cannot be hurried.

### The parts · Accumulated, never acquired
Steadiness comes out of the record of things you have actually got right, one at a time. That is why it cannot be rushed and cannot be borrowed. Confidence somebody else hands you does not survive contact with the first real pressure; the sort you banked yourself does.
e.g. The first contract you closed alone, the first outage you carried on your own. Ten talks about composure replace neither of them.

### The parts · One thing done against yourself and it leaks
Do a thing your own heart cannot approve, he says, and the breath starves. The mechanism is practical rather than mystical: next time you have to hold a line, you know about the exception, and so does everyone who watched you make it.
e.g. You waved through one soft number to make a date. The next time you ask the team to hold the standard, the sentence comes out a shade quieter.

### The parts · Do not pull the shoots
The opposite failure is impatience: pressure, slogans and short-term targets used to force a state of mind into existence. The shoots do look taller. His instruction is to always have the work in hand, never to forget it, and never to help it along.
e.g. To get a new hire up to speed you hand him a project well past his reach. It looks like an opportunity and ends as a person somebody else has to repair.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: under pressure you find there is nothing solid underneath you, and you want to fix that quickly.
Ask first: in the last six months, how many things did you carry from beginning to end yourself? That number is the account balance.
Where it goes wrong: substituting encouragement and slogans for real completed work; or accelerating somebody by putting him somewhere far beyond his reach.

### Lines to keep
It is produced by accumulated rightness, not seized by one act from outside.
Do a thing your heart cannot approve, and the breath starves.
Keep the work in hand. Do not forget it. Do not help it grow.

## Montaigne · To philosophise is to learn to die
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/montaigne/learning-to-die/
Source: Essays I.20; II.6, Of practice
Tags: Deep read, Montaigne, After he was thrown from the horse

He tells you to think about death daily, which sounds morbid. Then he reports having very nearly done it.

### Q: What actually happened?
One essay is titled That to philosophise is to learn to die, and its method runs against instinct: do not look away, think about it daily, until it stops being strange. This is not theory. In his thirties a rider knocked him off his horse from behind; he was unconscious a long time and the people around him thought he was dead. Coming back, he wrote the whole passage down. It had been light, like falling asleep, nothing like the horror he had spent decades imagining.

### The parts · Mostly you fear the imagining, not the thing
He came close enough to find the moment itself quiet. Decades of dread had been aimed at a version his own head had built. The experience cannot be lent to anyone, but the sorting can: separate fear of the event from fear of your picture of it.
e.g. The dread that arrives at two in the morning is usually a film, not the event.

### The parts · Avoided it stays terrible, looked at it flattens
His method is to make death ordinary: mention it, think of it, keep it as an acquaintance. Only the unfamiliar is frightening; once familiar it is merely a fact. Refuse to look and the fear stays permanently new, which is exactly what keeps it strong.
e.g. Say the thing you fear out loud, write it down, and look at it once a day.

### The parts · Learning to die is learning to weigh
He says whoever has taught people to die has taught them to live. Once the heaviest item has genuinely been handled, the arguments and the wounded pride of an ordinary week change weight. This is not detachment, it is pricing: using the heaviest thing to value the rest.
e.g. Weigh the thing keeping you awake against I am going to die anyway, and see what is left of it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you lie awake thinking about dying and have never said so to anyone.
Ask first: is it the event I fear, or my version of it? Have I ever thought it through in daylight, from beginning to end?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as think it through and the fear goes — he was still afraid in old age, only no longer run by it; and the daily thinking is for familiarity, not for sinking into it.

### Lines to keep
The thing I fear most is fear.
He who has learned how to die has unlearned how to serve.
Let us deprive death of its strangeness. Let us frequent it.

========================================================================
## Montaigne · What do I know?
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/montaigne/what-do-i-know/
Source: Essays II.12; the medal he had struck in 1576
Tags: Deep read, Montaigne, Put your own weaknesses on the table first

He wrote down his cowardice, his bad memory, his dithering. Not as confession. As a position that cannot be attacked.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1576 he had a medal struck for himself carrying three words: What do I know? The Essays are that question worked out at length. He writes that his memory is poor, that he dislikes pain, that he hesitates and contradicts himself from one page to the next, and he softens none of it. I do not portray being, he says, I portray passing. Four hundred years on it is still read, partly because the author's faults are placed at the front, where nobody else can pick them up and use them.

### The parts · A card you play yourself cannot be played against you
What people afraid of exposure actually fear is somebody else naming the weakness first. He inverts it and names it himself, more fully than anyone else could be bothered to. Once a thing is face up on the table it has stopped being in anybody's hand.
e.g. Saying this part is not my area, up front, costs far less than being caught out on it later.

### The parts · What do I know is a stance, not a modesty formula
He is not performing ignorance. He has made I might be wrong his permanent standing position. From there, being corrected requires no defence, because no claim to being right was ever made. Defending is the expensive part, and he simply removed the bill.
e.g. Open with I may have this wrong, and the correction costs you nothing to absorb.

### The parts · Inconsistency is not a flaw, it is a person
He says he portrays passing, not being. Most people panic when someone says that is not what you told me last time. He does not, because he announced from the start that he changes. Admit that you move and nobody can pin you to a fixed position.
e.g. Told you never used to think this, yes, I changed is shorter than any explanation you could give.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are in a seat that feels hollow, and you expect to be found out.
Ask first: of the three faults you most fear being exposed, has one ever come out of your own mouth? Do you have a ready this is not my area?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as confess everything and drop all guard — every fault he set down was thought about first; and what do I know is not a licence to judge nothing, he judges constantly, just never as final truth.

### Lines to keep
What do I know?
I do not portray being. I portray passing.
A card you turn over yourself cannot be played against you.

## Montaigne · At thirty-eight he moved into the tower
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/montaigne/the-tower/
Source: The 1571 inscription on his study wall; Essays III.13, Of experience
Tags: Deep read, Montaigne, He fenced off a piece for himself

The famous retirement was not a retirement. What he actually did is smaller, repeatable, and the reason the book exists.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1571, aged thirty-eight, he resigned his post as a magistrate in Bordeaux, went home to the family estate, and turned the third floor of a tower into a library, with an inscription on the wall saying he was weary of public duties and meant to give what remained to himself. The Essays were written in that room over the next twenty years. He also served two terms as mayor of Bordeaux in the middle of it. When kidney stones arrived he wrote the pain down there, page by page.

### The parts · Not withdrawal, a fenced-off piece
He did not become a hermit; he was mayor twice afterwards. What he did was nail down one space and one stretch of time as his and leave everything else running. Full retreat is flight, no retreat is being eaten. The position that holds is between them.
e.g. One hour and one room a day that nobody else can reach, everything else unchanged. Far easier than a new life.

### The parts · Mark it, and say it out loud to yourself
He had the decision carved into the wall. That is not decoration, it is turning a vague intention into a visible fact he walked past every morning. A decision that has been written down outlives one that was only thought about.
e.g. This stretch is mine, put where you will see it, works better than the same sentence held in your head.

### The parts · The pain got written in that room too
When the stones came he did not stop. The illness became material rather than an interruption. Having a place of your own means bad things also have somewhere to be put, which is precisely the moment most people give the place up.
e.g. When your health goes, that reserved hour is the right container for it. Do not cancel it first.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the calendar is full, none of it is yours, and clearing all of it looks impossible.
Ask first: can I fence off one place and one fixed stretch of time as mine and leave the rest alone? Have I written it down anywhere?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as quit and go and live in the country — he was mayor twice after moving into the tower; and the room is not a hiding place, he worked in it for twenty years.

### Lines to keep
Full retreat is flight. No retreat is being eaten.
A decision written down outlives one that was only thought.
Somewhere of your own is where bad news can be put.

## Maria Montessori · Change the environment before the behaviour
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/montessori/prepared-environment/
Source: The Casa dei Bambini, Rome, 1907
Tags: Deep read, Maria Montessori, Out of reach is what looks like defiance

Children considered unmanageable changed when the room changed. What was it that actually changed?

### Q: What actually happened?
In a poor district of Rome, Montessori did something then considered absurd: child-sized furniture, tools a child could work alone, children choosing their own activity, adults stepping in only when needed. Three- to six-year-olds thought unmanageable began repeating an activity for tens of minutes and tidying up afterwards. She called the state normalisation, and drew the foundation of the whole method: a child's work isn't taught into them; it happens in a prepared environment.

### The parts · Check whether the environment matches
A cup out of reach, a tool only an adult can operate — these manufacture dependence and frustration. Change the environment so the child can finish alone and the behaviour problem often disappears. It holds for adults too: plenty of self-discipline problems are environment problems.
e.g. The child keeps knocking the cup over. A small jug they can grip beats saying 'careful' a hundred times.

### The parts · Concentration grows, it isn't demanded
She saw children concentrate for a long time on self-chosen work and lose focus quickly on assigned tasks. So the route to concentration is offering attractive choices and not interrupting — and the most common interruption is an adult's well-meant attention.
e.g. The child is absorbed in the blocks. Don't praise and don't correct. Praise interrupts, and moves the motive from the work to your reaction.

### The parts · The adult steps back into observer
This method asks more of the adult than the child: hold back from directing, from doing it for them, from prompting early. Montessori required teachers to learn observation first — see where the child is stuck and what they need, rather than pushing a plan along.
e.g. When the tower won't stand, don't reach in. Watch for thirty seconds. Most of the time they try another way.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: your child repeatedly can't do something and saying it again hasn't helped.
Ask first: at their height, with their grip, with these tools — is it actually possible? Which single thing in the environment could change?
Where it goes wrong: turning 'change the environment' into removing all difficulty, which leaves nothing to practise on.

### Lines to keep
A child's work isn't taught in. It happens in a prepared room.
Education is not what the teacher said. It's what the child did.
What the adult most needs to learn is to observe and wait.

## Maria Montessori · Help me to do it myself
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/montessori/help-me-do-it-myself/
Source: The Secret of Childhood
Tags: Deep read, Maria Montessori, Doing it for them saves your time

Doing it for them takes two minutes. What those two minutes bought, and what they cost.

### Q: What actually happened?
Montessori compressed the whole method into a child's request: help me to do it myself. That draws the boundary of help — the goal is that they can finish alone, not that the task finishes sooner. What an adult saves by taking over is their own time; what is spent is that one chance to learn. She also described sensitive periods: stages when a child absorbs a particular capacity with almost no effort. Hit the window and it is nearly free. Miss it and the same thing costs several times as much.

### The parts · Lower the difficulty to just within reach
The right intervention is neither taking over nor leaving them to it. It's adjusting the difficulty: break the task to a step they can do now and leave that step to them. It's the same thing deliberate practice calls the edge of the comfort zone, happening at three.
e.g. They spill the water every time. Give them a small container to practise the feel, rather than pouring it yourself from now on.

### The parts · Sensitive periods: wrong timing doubles the work
At two, a child is intensely sensitive to order, and habits of putting things away form easily. Try to establish the same rule at seven and the difficulty is completely different. Reading which period they're in beats working from an age chart.
e.g. Suddenly everything must go back in its exact place. That's not stubbornness. It's the window.

### The parts · Slow is a cost and an investment
Letting a child do it will be slower and messier. Accepting that cost requires a longer time horizon: the ten extra minutes today buys years of not having to be involved. When the arithmetic doesn't get done, adults take over indefinitely.
e.g. Dressing them yourself on a rushed morning is fine. If every morning is rushed, the arithmetic never happened.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: they're slow and doing it badly and you can't stop yourself taking over.
Ask first: am I taking over so they learn, or so this ends sooner? Could I just drop the difficulty one notch?
Where it goes wrong: turning 'let them do it' into no help at all. Repeated failure makes a child give up outright.

### Lines to keep
Help me to do it myself.
Every unnecessary help is an obstacle to development.
Ten extra minutes today buys years of not being involved.

## Charlie Munger · Invert, always invert
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/munger/invert/
Source: Harvard Law commencement, 1986
Tags: Deep read, Charlie Munger, Study the ways it dies first

He was asked how to have a good life and answered the other question instead. The swap is the whole method.

### Q: What actually happened?
Invited to address a graduating class, he announced he would explain how to guarantee a miserable life, and then worked through it: be unreliable, learn only from your own experience, go down when you take your first reverse, be consumed by envy and resentment. If you knew where you were going to die, he liked to say, you would simply never go there. The talk is the method demonstrated on itself, and it is more usable than any list of virtues he could have read out instead.

### The parts · One list is short and the other isn't
There are countless ways a thing can go well and a small number of ways it reliably goes wrong. The inverted question is simply a smaller problem, and a smaller problem is one you can actually finish.
e.g. Nobody in the room could say what would make the product work. Everyone could name the three things that would kill it, and two were already true.

### The parts · Failure modes are checkable; success stories aren't
You can go and look at whether the runway is short, whether one customer is half the revenue, whether the one person who understands the system is leaving. 'Is this a great idea' has no such test.
e.g. The post-mortem was written before the launch, and two of its causes were fixed in the week it was written.

### The parts · It does not tell you what to do
Avoiding every failure mode leaves you alive, not successful. Inversion clears the ground; something still has to be built on it. Used alone it produces people who are very good at not losing and have not won anything.
e.g. Three years of avoiding every avoidable mistake, and nothing shipped that anyone remembers.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: about to commit to a plan you believe in.
Ask first: spend twenty minutes writing only the ways this fails, then check how many are already true today.
Where it goes wrong: stopping there — a list of avoided deaths is not a direction, and people who only invert end up very safe and very still.

### Lines to keep
Invert, always invert.
If you knew where you were going to die, you would never go there.
Inversion clears the ground. It does not build anything on it.

## Charlie Munger · One hammer is not enough
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/munger/latticework/
Source: USC Business School, 1994
Tags: Deep read, Charlie Munger, The danger is the skill, not the ignorance

What he warned about was not ignorance. It was being very well trained in exactly one thing.

### Q: What actually happened?
At USC in 1994 he laid out the method of his life: you have to carry a number of models in your head and hang experience on that latticework. He put the count at eighty or ninety, drawn from mathematics, psychology, physics, biology and engineering. The warning attached to it is the line everyone knows: to a man with only a hammer, every problem looks like a nail — and the man with the hammer is not the ignorant one, he is the well-trained one.

### The parts · The deeper the training, the better hidden the distortion
The hammer problem is not incompetence. It is that your discipline arrives with a viewfinder: the finance person sees a cost problem, the growth person a funnel problem. Each account is coherent, because any problem does have that face — and the coherence is what stops the search.
e.g. Churn was diagnosed as a pricing problem for three quarters by the only people who were asked, who all came from pricing.

### The parts · Problems do not arrive by department
A pricing decision is economics and psychology and, because the competitor reacts, something close to biology. The latticework means laying several models over the same situation and seeing which one explains the most, rather than which one you already own.
e.g. The retention question turned out to be a queueing problem, and nobody in the room had ever been handed that model.

### The parts · Load the models before you need them
A model you go and look up during the decision arrives too late to shape it. The models have to be in the head and automatic. There is no shortcut: take the two or three hardest ideas from each field and keep them.
e.g. He read about critical mass years before the network product, which is why the question came up in week one instead of year two.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: diagnosing a problem inside your own speciality.
Ask first: how would someone from a completely different field describe this? If you cannot produce a second account, you have one model, not a diagnosis.
Where it goes wrong: collecting models as trivia — the test is whether one of them changed a decision.

### Lines to keep
To a man with only a hammer, every problem looks like a nail.
The hammer man is not the ignorant one. He is the trained one.
A model you look up during the decision arrives too late to shape it.

## Haruki Murakami · Stop while it is still running
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/murakami/stop-while-it-flows/
Source: Haruki Murakami, What I Talk About When I Talk About Running, 2007
Tags: Deep read, Haruki Murakami, So tomorrow has somewhere to start

Not being able to write is the normal case. What to do on the day it is flowing, and why he stops there.

### Q: What actually happened?
Writing a novel, he holds himself to one rule: ten pages a day, four hundred characters a page, no more and no less. On a bad day he fills the ten anyway. On a good day, when the sentences are coming and he wants to keep going, he still stops there. This is not a performance of discipline, he says. It is for tomorrow. Say everything today and tomorrow you face a blank page. Leave a piece unfinished and you can pick it up. Running works the same way: however good the legs feel, he finishes the day's distance and goes home.

### The parts · Stop where something is left to pick up
The hard part of writing is not writing, it is starting again. End the day at a point where you already know the next sentence and tomorrow's cost of entry is close to zero. Finish a section cleanly instead and tomorrow begins with hunting for the door.
e.g. Stop in the middle of a sentence. Tomorrow you sit down and simply keep typing.

### The parts · A ceiling matters as much as a floor
Most people set only a floor: at least this much every day. The ceiling exists to stop the good day from borrowing. What you overspend when it is flowing is usually repaid out of the next three days. The real enemy of output is not laziness but swing.
e.g. Twenty thousand words over a weekend, then a fortnight of touching nothing. The books balance, or come out worse.

### The parts · A fixed amount deletes the daily question
Whether to work today and how much, decided fresh every morning, spends part of the day's energy on the deciding. Fix the amount and the question disappears, and everything left goes into the work. That is also why it is steadier than waiting for inspiration.
e.g. Do not ask whether you feel like writing today. Ask whether today's ten pages are done.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are in something long, writing, a product, a craft, and progress rises and falls with your mood.
Ask first: do I have a daily amount that does not consult my state? Is it low enough that my worst day still finishes it?
Where it goes wrong: treating it as a demand for finished output every day. What he fixed was input, not results. And do not defend the ceiling to the point of absurdity. The rule exists so that tomorrow still works, not for its own sake.

### Lines to keep
Stop while it is still flowing, so tomorrow connects.
The hard part was never starting. It is restarting tomorrow.
What a good day overspends, the next few days repay.

## Haruki Murakami · Two things besides talent
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/murakami/focus-and-endurance/
Source: What I Talk About When I Talk About Running, on talent, focus and endurance
Tags: Deep read, Haruki Murakami, Focus and endurance can be trained

Whether a person without talent should bother. He names two other requirements, and says both can be trained.

### Q: What actually happened?
Asked what a novelist most needs, he answers talent first, then points out that talent is not something you can manage. You have what you have. The energy in the passage goes to the other two. Focus, and after focus, endurance. Focus is putting your limited powers entirely on one thing for a stretch of hours. Endurance is doing that every day for half a year, a year. Unlike talent, he says, these can be acquired and sharpened through training, in the same way muscle is.

### The parts · Put down the part you cannot control
How much talent you were given is settled, and worrying about it produces no action. Two of the three are available to work on, so the hours belong there. This is not consolation. It is moving attention from where there is no leverage to where there is some.
e.g. I have no talent may even be correct, and it still cannot tell you what to do today.

### The parts · Focus is worth more than hours
Three hours entirely undivided beat eight broken ones. He gives the early morning to writing, no calls and no visitors, because once concentration breaks, getting back to the same depth costs time again. The quality sits in the depth, not in the total.
e.g. Eight hours cut into six pieces produce less than three whole ones.

### The parts · Endurance is bought by lowering the daily difficulty
Things people sustain for years are usually not very hard on any given day. Setting the daily amount where your worst day can still finish it trades the ceiling of one day for the total of one year. Willpower alone does not survive the first bad stretch.
e.g. Four thousand words a day for ten years is far more than twenty thousand a day for two months.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you want to do something for a long time and keep circling the question of whether you are cut out for it.
Ask first: how many unbroken stretches did I give this in the past week? If none, fix that before talent gets a turn.
Where it goes wrong: using it to deny that talent exists. He puts talent first and only says it is not yours to manage. And endurance is not gritting your teeth. Anything held together by force is not held for long.

### Lines to keep
Unlike talent, focus and endurance can be acquired through training.
Talent is not yours to manage. The other two are.
Set the daily amount where your worst day still finishes it.
Endurance that is forced does not survive the first bad stretch.

## Haruki Murakami · Nobody asked you to do this
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/murakami/no-one-asked-you-to/
Source: What I Talk About When I Talk About Running, on placings and other people's verdicts
Tags: Deep read, Haruki Murakami, So the reason has to be your own

How to hold a long effort nobody required of you. The reason he found for himself, and where he keeps it.

### Q: What actually happened?
He has run for over thirty years, finished more than thirty marathons and one hundred-kilometre ultra. Nobody asked him to run, and there is no placing worth chasing. So what keeps him going? The only opponent you have to beat is yourself, the way you used to be. A little further than yesterday, a slightly steadier stride, and that is enough. Writing runs on the same fuel. His own country's literary establishment kept him at arm's length for years, and it never became a reason to stop, because he had not been writing for them in the first place.

### The parts · Nobody asked, so the reason has to come from you
A job has reviews and school has exams, and in both the reason is supplied from outside. Something you chose has none of that, and the moment you make the outside response your reason, the views, the likes, other people's verdicts, that reason can be withdrawn at any time.
e.g. Three posts, nobody reads them, and you stop. The reason for writing was in other people's hands from the start.

### The parts · Yesterday's version of you never runs out
Comparing yourself to others makes winning slack and losing bitter, and there is always somebody better. Yesterday's version is present every day and sets a bar you can actually reach. It does not get the blood up. It also does not stop.
e.g. Half a page more than last time. Only you know it, and only you need to.

### The parts · Silence is not a reason to stop, attention not a reason to continue
Nobody reading does not mean you should stop, and people reading does not mean you should go on. Both are signals from outside. The question worth asking is whether not doing this would hurt. That answer holds still while the response moves.
e.g. People who go quiet after a spell of attention were usually running on the response the whole time.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have been doing something nobody asked for, long enough to start wondering whether to keep going.
Ask first: the last time I wanted to quit, was it because the work was bad or because nobody saw it? If the second, separate the two before deciding anything.
Where it goes wrong: using it to justify working with your eyes shut. Not being governed by feedback is not the same as not reading it. And comparing yourself to yesterday should keep you moving, not become one more review to pass.

### Lines to keep
The only opponent you have to beat is yourself.
If nobody asked you to do it, the reason must be yours.
No readers is not a reason to stop; readers are not either.
