## Miyamoto Musashi · No favourite weapon
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/musashi/no-favorite-weapon/
Source: The Book of Five Rings, Earth Scroll; the Dokkodo
Tags: Deep read, Miyamoto Musashi, Do not fall in love with a tool

A swordsman who never lost a bout wrote down a rule against loving your sword. This is about why he bothered.

### Q: What actually happened?
In the Earth Scroll he sets down a rule of his own: you should not have a favourite weapon. Leaning too hard on one is the same error as not knowing how to use it. A long blade has long-blade weaknesses and a short one has short-blade weaknesses, and neither deserves attachment. He is his own evidence. At Ganryujima his opponent Sasaki Kojiro carried a famous long sword; Musashi came ashore with a wooden one cut from a boat oar. Late in life, in the Dokkodo, he wrote twenty-one vows for himself. One of them: in all things whatsoever, rely on nothing.

### The parts · Affection for a tool ends by defining you
Favour one weapon and your method quietly grows around it, until the tool is choosing which fights you can take rather than the other way round. Dropping the attachment is not a claim that the tool is bad. It is a refusal to let one object mark your edge.
e.g. The engineer who knows one framework, the team that only knows paid acquisition. First it reads as expertise; three years on it is the only shape of work they can take.

### The parts · Long loses one way, short loses another
He never says which blade is better. He says each has a bout it must lose. Tools carry no absolute rank, only a fit with the situation, so what you train is not one weapon taken to its limit but the reading of which one this round needs.
e.g. Heavy process protects a large programme and shackles a team of three. Flat structure runs the other way. Any outfit with a creed will keep it in the wrong place.

### The parts · The oar won by being off the scale
Kojiro's long sword was a named blade and the centre of everything he did. The wooden one Musashi carved was longer still and belonged to no school anyone could read. Beating a man on the parameter he is proudest of turns years of his training into a liability.
e.g. If their strength is response time, open where their response process does not reach. The stronger the strength, the slower the turn.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have a tool or a method you handle better than anything else and never think of changing.
Ask first: what does the bout this thing has to lose look like, and am I standing in it right now?
Where it goes wrong: reading rely on nothing as being half good at everything; and switching tools for novelty rather than because the situation changed.

### Lines to keep
Do not have a favourite weapon.
Over-familiarity with one weapon is as much a fault as not knowing it.
In all things whatsoever, rely on nothing.

## Miyamoto Musashi · Perception strong, sight weak
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/musashi/two-ways-of-seeing/
Source: The Book of Five Rings, Water Scroll
Tags: Deep read, Miyamoto Musashi, Two ways of looking

He split looking into two words. This is about why watching the other man's blade means you have already lost.

### Q: What actually happened?
The Water Scroll gives the gaze of the strategist, and Musashi splits looking in two. Perception is strong; sight is weak. Perception takes in the whole and the intention behind it, and should be strong. Sight tracks the particular movement, and should be weak. See distant things as if close, he says, and close things as if distant. Lock onto the sword and the sword leads your eyes and then your feet. What is worth watching is the man entire, his balance and his breathing and what he means to do. The blade is the last joint of that. The gaze, he adds, must be the same off the field.

### The parts · Watch the last joint and it drags you
The sword is the final link in a chain of movement. By the time you see it move the thing is decided, and with your eyes fixed there your tempo belongs to him. Watch balance and intention and you are seeing what comes before the sword, which is early enough to matter.
e.g. Answering each competitor launch keeps you a beat late. Their hiring and where their money goes is the weight shifting before the launch.

### The parts · Close things far, far things close
What is right in front of you is magnified out of proportion; look at it from a distance and the proportion returns. What is far off blurs into a concept and gets discounted; look at it close and it becomes detail. Two corrections in opposite directions, and only together are they a calibrated view.
e.g. This week's crisis shrinks when set against the year. A trend three years out becomes real when you ask which part of the business it hits first.

### The parts · Train the gaze until it is the default
He adds a line: this holds in ordinary life too. In the bout there is no time to change how you are looking, so what you use is whatever has already become habit. The man who remembers mid-fight to take in the whole is still watching the blade.
e.g. The quality of your judgement in a crisis is set by which gaze you use reading a weekly report. Watch only the last number and that is all a crisis will show you.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are tracking every movement of one rival or one metric.
Ask first: am I watching the blade or the man holding it? What is the link immediately before this movement?
Where it goes wrong: using take in the whole as licence to skip the detail; and switching gaze only for big occasions while the everyday one stays fixed on the last joint.

### Lines to keep
Perception is strong; sight is weak.
See distant things as if close, and close things as if distant.
The same gaze serves single combat and large-scale strategy.

========================================================================
## Elon Musk · Boil it down to what is physically true
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/musk/first-principles/
Source: TED interview, 2013
Tags: Deep read, Elon Musk, Analogy quotes the going rate; physics gives the floor

The phrase is everywhere now. What is worth having is his own definition, and the arithmetic he did on a battery.

### Q: What actually happened?
In the 2013 TED interview he set it out plainly: reason from first principles rather than by analogy. Analogy is everyone does it this way, so we will too. First principles is boiling a thing down to its most fundamental truths and reasoning up. His example was batteries. Everyone said a pack costs six hundred dollars a kilowatt-hour and always will. From first principles: what is a battery made of? Cobalt, nickel, aluminium, carbon, polymers, a steel can. Buy those on the metal exchange and it comes to eighty. The other five hundred is the price of how they are currently assembled — and assembly can be reinvented.

### The parts · Analogy gives you the market rate, physics gives the floor
It has always cost this and the industry standard both quote the price of other people's methods, not the cost of the thing. Separate the two: where is the floor set by materials and physical law, and who collects the gap between that floor and today's price?
e.g. Margins in this kind of service are just thin — take it apart: what does delivery actually cost, and how many hands take a cut in between? The gap is the opportunity list.

### The parts · Keep going until you hit something that cannot be reduced
Most attempts stop halfway and treat a supplier quote or an industry convention as bedrock. Those are still somebody's decisions. The test is whether you can still ask why. If you can, you are not at the bottom. The bottom feels like a physical law or a published market price.
e.g. Servers are expensive is not bedrock. The market price of silicon, electricity and bandwidth is. Stopping at the invoice is haggling; going to the floor is rebuilding.

### The parts · It is expensive, so spend it where the leverage is
He has said himself that analogy is usually the cheaper move, and he is right: reasoning up the whole chain costs an enormous amount of attention. The correct use is selective — the one or two assumptions that decide whether the thing lives. Doing it everywhere means reinventing the wheel everywhere.
e.g. Apply it to the cost structure that decides the business and buy stationery by analogy. Teams that cannot tell the difference exhaust on wheels the attention the rocket needed.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: everyone is telling you that some cost or method simply is what it is.
Ask first: what irreducible facts is it made of, and who is collecting the difference between their sum and today's price?
Where it goes wrong: using the phrase as a way of dismissing all experience, or spending it on things too small to be worth rebuilding.

### Lines to keep
We reason from first principles rather than by analogy.
Boil things down to the most fundamental truths and reason up from there.
Those materials, bought on the metal exchange, come to about eighty a kilowatt-hour.

## Elon Musk · Part price over material price
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/musk/idiot-index/
Source: Isaacson's biography, on the SpaceX costing method
Tags: Deep read, Elon Musk, A number that tells you where to start

He gives every component a humiliating score. What it does is turn a way of thinking into something you can run on a spreadsheet.

### Q: What actually happened?
Isaacson records a hard metric inside SpaceX: the idiot index — the finished price of a part divided by the cost of its raw material. An aluminium part holding a few hundred dollars of metal, bought for tens of thousands, scores in the dozens. A score that absurd says what you are paying for is process and inertia, not physics. The rule follows: a high index is either explained or made in house. Many Falcon parts ended up built on site, at a fraction of the industry price. What makes the index good is that it turns a judgement call into a list you can sort.

### The parts · The index turns judgement into a scanner
First principles depends on someone deciding to think. The index makes the candidates queue up on their own: run the ratio across every purchased line, sort descending, and the rebuild priority list writes itself. The best form a method can take is decaying from an insight into a division anyone can do.
e.g. Divide each outsourced fee by what doing it in house would cost in people and tools. The few at the top of that list are the ones to bring back.

### The parts · A high score is a toll booth left by history
A part selling at fifty times its metal usually has no villain behind it: years of safety margin, layers of certification, small batches, a sole supplier. Every layer had a reason once; stacked up they are a row of toll booths. You do not negotiate those away, you route around them.
e.g. Half of an incumbent supplier's quote is paying for a process set twenty years ago. What will not come down under pressure often goes to zero on a different route.

### The parts · Where the score is low, leave it alone
The tool carries its own limit. A part scoring near one is already priced against physics; making it yourself will not be cheaper, only slower. So it guards against more than overpaying — it guards against the compulsion to build everything. Vertical integration belongs where the index is high, not everywhere.
e.g. Bringing a part scoring thirty in house saves money. Bringing one scoring one point two in house trades somebody else's scale for your own tuition.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: costs will not come down and you cannot see where to cut.
Ask first: divide every line by its underlying material or compute cost. Who scores highest?
Where it goes wrong: bringing everything in house on sight of a high score without doing your own scale and yield arithmetic, or using the index as a stick to squeeze suppliers.

### Lines to keep
The idiot index: a part's finished cost over its material cost.
A ratio that high means you are paying for process and inertia, not physics.
High index: either explain it, or make it ourselves.

========================================================================
## Napoleon · More men where it is decided
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/napoleon/decisive-point/
Source: Maxims of War
Tags: Deep read, Napoleon, Being outnumbered overall is fine

He usually fought with fewer men and was usually the stronger side at the moment of contact. This is how.

### Q: What actually happened?
One of his maxims holds the whole method: the art of war consists in always having more force than the enemy at the point attacked or defended, even when the army as a whole is weaker. The Italian campaign of 1796 is the textbook case. He had a little over thirty thousand men against nearly seventy thousand Austrians and Piedmontese, but they came in separate columns, and he used his interior position to move between them and meet each part with everything he had. On the ledger he was the weaker side. At every place they actually met, he was the stronger one.

### The parts · A shortfall in total can be traded away by movement
Resource comparisons are a summary table; outcomes happen at particular points of contact. The smaller side can still be larger at each point, and the price is moving faster than the other side and giving up the idea of holding everything at once.
e.g. A small team cannot compete across a market and can outspend a large company inside one account. At that point you are the big company.

### The parts · Their dispersal is something you can cause
The allied columns were not only careless. His line of march threatened several objectives at once and forced them to garrison each. Making the other side afraid to leave anything uncovered is the same act as making him too weak everywhere. Splitting him and massing yourself are one movement.
e.g. Put visible probes into three directions and their defensive budget divides three ways. You mean to attack one; they have to hold all of it.

### The parts · The method runs on a time difference
Beating two forces in turn requires that finishing the first and turning on the second is faster than the two joining. Slow the movement down with longer supply or more layers of approval and the interior position inverts into encirclement. That is how it later failed in his own hands.
e.g. Any strategy living off a timing gap loses a beat for every layer the organisation adds. The old lightning method, run through a long chain, walks into the trap.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: your total resources are plainly smaller than theirs.
Ask first: at which few points is this actually decided, and can I be the larger side at one of them?
Where it goes wrong: turning concentration into one throw you cannot survive losing; and running a timing-gap method after the organisation has slowed down.

### Lines to keep
Have more force at the point attacked, even when weaker overall.
Splitting him and massing yourself are the same movement.
In war, the moral is to the physical as three to one.

========================================================================
## Napoleon · One step from the sublime
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/napoleon/sublime-to-ridiculous/
Source: De Pradt, on words spoken at Warsaw in December 1812
Tags: Deep read, Napoleon, A success with no exit condition

The witticism has an origin that is not witty at all. This is about the road he was on when he said it.

### Q: What actually happened?
In December 1812 he left what remained of his army in the Russian snow and went back to Paris by sleigh. Passing through Warsaw he said it to the ambassador de Pradt, more than once: from the sublime to the ridiculous there is only one step. Six months earlier he had crossed the Niemen with over six hundred thousand men, and fewer than a tenth came back. He lost no major battle on that campaign. He entered Moscow. He lost the war for having no plan at all for winning while the other side refuses to concede. Moscow was empty, the Tsar would not negotiate, winter arrived.

### The parts · You can win every battle and lose the war
His script assumed that holding Moscow was victory, but the definition of victory sat with the other side. They declined, and the occupation became merely a long way in. Any victory condition that requires your opponent's cooperation is not a condition you control.
e.g. Winning the price war and taking the share assumes they withdraw. If a parent company keeps funding them, every round you win deepens your own drain.

### The parts · Write the way home before you leave
A supply line two thousand li long for six hundred thousand men only works inside a quick-victory script. He set no automatic stop for a war still running in October. Every large bet needs an exit that does not depend on judgement, because by then judgement is the thing most heavily committed.
e.g. Before entering a market, write down the date and the number at which you withdraw. Write it while clear, because later one more push will feel obvious.

### The parts · There is no buffer between sublime and ridiculous
The exact word is step. Collapse was not gradual. Authority built on continuous victory cannot structurally survive one large defeat: the loyalty of the client states, the mood of the army and the politics of Paris were all premised on his being unbeatable.
e.g. A person or a team sold on never missing falls hardest the first time they publicly miss. Keeping a visible record of failures is what makes a fall survivable.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: an operation far bigger than anything you have run, and the early stretch has gone well.
Ask first: does my victory condition need them to cooperate, and is my stop a fixed date or a we will see?
Where it goes wrong: reading never having lost as cannot lose; and using the good start to add investment until the resources for the way home are committed too.

### Lines to keep
From the sublime to the ridiculous there is only one step.
A victory condition that needs their agreement is not yours.
Write the exit while you are still clear-headed.

========================================================================
## Naval Ravikant · Assets that earn while you sleep
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/naval/assets-while-you-sleep/
Source: How to Get Rich (Without Getting Lucky), the tweetstorm
Tags: Deep read, Naval Ravikant, Wealth is not money

The first line cuts one word into three. What matters is where each of the three leads.

### Q: What actually happened?
The storm opens: seek wealth, not money or status. Each is defined. Wealth is assets that earn while you sleep — businesses, code, content, equity. Money is how we transfer wealth. Status is your place in the social hierarchy. What matters is the kind of game each is. Creating wealth is positive sum: everyone can get richer. Status is zero sum — for you to rise somebody falls, which is why people attacking wealth creators are usually playing status. And there is one road to the first: ownership. You will not get rich renting out your time, because time does not copy.

### The parts · Work out which game you are actually playing
A great deal of hard work leads to status rather than wealth: titles, visibility, rankings. Those prizes produce no cash flow and require you to keep showing up to hold them. One test: stop for three months. Is it still producing? If yes it is an asset.
e.g. Two people work equally hard for a year. One accumulates a title and photographs with useful people; the other accumulates a tool with subscription revenue. The difference shows itself the first time either takes a holiday.

### The parts · Selling time has a ceiling because time will not copy
Work priced by the hour earns rate times hours. Both factors are hard-capped, and the whole thing goes to zero while you sleep. The way out is not raising the rate, it is changing the formula — detaching output from duration. Things made once and sold many times: code, content, courses, systems, equity.
e.g. A top consultant and an ordinary one differ by rate. A consultant and someone who turned the method into software differ by formula. The first is optimisation, the second is a different race.

### The parts · Recognising a status attack saves you the reply
Anyone who does something visible attracts a portion of criticism whose purpose is not correction but position — pushing you down in a zero-sum game. Separating the two kinds matters practically: the first deserves a careful answer, and answering the second is scoring a point in somebody else's game.
e.g. Feedback after a launch splits in two. Specific problems go on the fix list. Insinuations about your motives and your standing are best left where they are.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: busy, doing reasonably well, and it all stops the moment you do.
Ask first: of what I built this past year, what keeps producing when I am not there? What proportion?
Where it goes wrong: using not playing status games to excuse being bad at people — reputation and relationships are themselves assets. What is worth avoiding is ranking for its own sake.

### Lines to keep
Seek wealth, not money or status.
Wealth is assets that earn while you sleep.
You will not get rich renting out your time. You need equity.

========================================================================
## Naval Ravikant · Productise yourself
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/naval/productize-yourself/
Source: The How to Get Rich tweetstorm; The Almanack of Naval Ravikant
Tags: Deep read, Naval Ravikant, Specific knowledge times leverage

He compresses the whole method into two words. What each of the two refers to, and why the new leverage is different in kind.

### Q: What actually happened?
The formula collapses into a phrase: productise yourself. Yourself means specific knowledge — the kind you cannot be trained for, growing out of your temperament, obsessions and history; it feels like play to you and looks like work to others. Productise means putting leverage on it. Labour and capital are the old kinds and both need somebody's permission. The new kind replicates at zero marginal cost: code and media, which need permission from nobody. What you wrote keeps working while you sleep.

### The parts · Specific knowledge is not on any syllabus
Any skill taught in a standard way is supplied in unlimited quantity and priced accordingly. Specific knowledge comes from the part that cannot be standardised: your combination of oddities, the crossings between fields, an obsession out of proportion to its subject. The detection method is his own line — play to you, labour to others.
e.g. Someone technical who can also make complicated things funny; someone clinical who is compulsive about spreadsheets. Each piece is ordinary. The combination has no second supplier.

### The parts · Permissionless means you can start today
The bottleneck in the old leverage is persuasion: nothing moves until you have hired someone or raised something. Code and media delete that step. Writing, recording, publishing — live today, at the cost of time rather than consent. The opportunity of this generation is essentially that the entry price of leverage fell to zero.
e.g. The same insight can wait for funding and a team, or go out as a public series of posts that grows an audience. The second needs nobody's approval, and frequently produces the first.

### The parts · Productising means taking yourself out of delivery
Where the two words end up: packaging your judgement, taste and method into something that delivers without you present. The test is replication — each additional user should cost you an amount of time approaching zero. Until then what you own is a good job. After it, an asset.
e.g. Five years of consulting turned into a book, a course, a self-serve tool. The same knowledge moves from sold by the occasion to permanently on sale.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: capable, and your income is welded to your hours.
Ask first: what do I do that is play to me and labour to others? Can it be packaged as code or as content and published without anyone's permission?
Where it goes wrong: reading productise as everyone should sell a course — without specific knowledge, leverage only amplifies the average. And do not use polishing the knowledge to postpone publishing forever; leverage only counts what shipped.

### Lines to keep
Productise yourself.
Specific knowledge feels like play to you but looks like work to others.
Code and media are permissionless leverage.

## Nietzsche · What does not kill me, conditions included
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/nietzsche/what-does-not-kill/
Source: Twilight of the Idols, Maxims and Arrows 8 and 12
Tags: Deep read, Nietzsche, It is a maxim, not a law of nature

Probably the most quoted sentence he wrote, and the most misused. The question is what has to be true for it to hold.

### Q: What actually happened?
Maxims and Arrows, number eight, opens with a clause the poster cuts off. Out of life's school of war: what does not kill me makes me stronger. School of war. It is not a general blessing on suffering — the man writing it spent years in violent headaches and vomiting, with his eyesight close to gone, describing how he handled his own. Four maxims later in the same book: if we have our own why of life, we shall get along with almost any how. Read together the two complete each other. Surviving is only the input.

### The parts · By default suffering leaves you weaker
The maxim does not describe an automatic process. The same blow usually leaves wear and a flinch behind it. Turning it into strength takes a deliberate operation: going back over it, giving it a place, taking out the thing you can use next time. Skip the operation and the sentence is a placebo.
e.g. Two people, one failed project. One writes it up and changes the process; the other says it made him stronger. Six months on, only one of them is.

### The parts · Without a why, the pain has nowhere to go
The second maxim supplies the condition. Someone with a direction can book a blow as a cost on the way there. Someone without one can only book it as loss. The same quantity, entered in two different ledgers, is not the same thing at all.
e.g. Overtime for a goal you chose and overtime for nothing cost the same hours. One accumulates progress, the other accumulates grievance.

### The parts · It is a first-person sentence only
Used on your own history it is a way of processing. Said to somebody who is still bleeding, it asks them to translate their disaster into your inspirational story before you will listen. He wrote a school motto, not a condolence card.
e.g. Tell a friend made redundant last week that what does not kill him makes him stronger, and all he learns is that you were not going to listen.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a bad stretch is behind you and you want it to have counted for something.
Ask first: what is the operation that turns it into material, and is my why still in place?
Where it goes wrong: treating the line as a law that applies itself, so the work never happens; or handing it to somebody else to close their pain down.

### Lines to keep
Out of life's school of war: what does not kill me makes me stronger.
Without a why, the blow goes into the ledger as pure loss.
Suffering does not compound by itself. Someone has to do the work.

## Nietzsche · Fighting monsters, and the bill for it
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/nietzsche/gazing-into-abyss/
Source: Beyond Good and Evil, aphorism 146
Tags: Deep read, Nietzsche, The method you borrow grows into the person who borrows it

Two sentences, and between them a complete occupational hazard notice. The question is how the change actually happens.

### Q: What actually happened?
Aphorism 146 of Beyond Good and Evil. He who fights with monsters should look to it that he himself does not become a monster. And when you gaze long into an abyss the abyss also gazes into you. This is not horror-story decoration. The first sentence is about the contagion of method: to beat the thing you take up its methods, and methods grow into the people who use them. The second is the price of attention. Study something long enough and it is shaping you back while you believe you are only observing it.

### The parts · The method grows into the user
Against an opponent who will do anything, what works is usually the same thing. The first time is an exception, the second is fluency, the third is your style. Adoption is close to irreversible: once a method has worked, it arrives first at the next difficulty.
e.g. You smeared them back once and won that round. Two years on it is a standing option in the communications plan.

### The parts · Whatever you watch for long enough calibrates you
People who study fraud all day begin to assume everybody is running one. People who analyse failures all day stop being able to place a bet. Attention is a loop: choosing what to look at for years is choosing what gets to set your defaults.
e.g. Put someone on the competitor full time for six months and he becomes the most competitor-like person in the building. That is why the post gets rotated.

### The parts · The defence is a line drawn early
He gives the warning and no remedy, but the warning locates one. Before it starts, write down which things you will not do even to win. The line has to be drawn while you are not yet cornered, because the person doing the drawing at the wall is no longer you.
e.g. Alongside the list of tactics keep a page of what this company does not do, and require a higher approval to change that page than to approve a tactic.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: locked into a long fight with somebody who does not keep to rules.
Ask first: which of his methods have I picked up this year, and which one is now my first move?
Where it goes wrong: using he started it to retire your own limits; or turning the warning into never engaging at all, including where you should.

### Lines to keep
When you gaze long into an abyss the abyss also gazes into you.
The method you borrowed to win once is now your first move.
Draw the line before you are cornered. At the wall it is too late.

## Nonviolent Communication · Observation first, never evaluation
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/nonviolent-communication/observation-not-evaluation/
Source: Nonviolent Communication, chapter 3
Tags: Deep read, Nonviolent Communication, The first sentence settles it

Most arguments are lost in the first second of speaking. This is about the exact word that loses them.

### Q: What actually happened?
Rosenberg lays his foundation on a line from Krishnamurti: observing without evaluating is the highest form of human intelligence. He then separates two sentences that look alike. You were late three times this week is an observation, and there is nothing in it to argue with. You are always late is an evaluation, and it has to be argued with. The difference sits in words like always and never, which promote a piece of behaviour into a verdict on a person. Once the defence is up, nothing else gets in.

### The parts · Take the frequency words out and the sentence comes alive
Always, never, constantly and again are the markers of evaluation. Strip them and what remains is usually a checkable fact. Facts can be discussed and verdicts can only be resisted, and that is the whole divide between two outcomes of the same conversation.
e.g. You never deal with the children becomes three of this week's school runs were mine. The first starts an argument, the second starts an explanation.

### The parts · Adjectives that rate people are evaluations too
You are lazy and he is unprofessional look like descriptions and are labels. The checkable form describes behaviour and effect: the document he sent was missing three figures. A label turns a person into its defender; a description leaves them room to change.
e.g. In a performance conversation, you have an attitude problem can only be denied. Four emails in two weeks went unanswered for over two days can be discussed.

### The parts · Observing is not softening
The common misreading is that observation means being tactful, so the point never actually gets made. Rosenberg is asking for more precision, not less edge. A fact can be very hard as long as it is a fact, and vague kindness fails exactly as a sharp verdict does.
e.g. Things have been a bit off lately says nothing. Three deliveries slipped this month is accurate, carries no judgement, and lands harder.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are about to raise a problem with someone and you have been rehearsing it for days.
Ask first: does your sentence contain always, never or constantly? Swap them for a count or a specific action, and see whether you can still say it.
Where it goes wrong: turning observation only into conflict avoidance so the point is never made; or stacking exact facts into a trial of somebody's character.

### Lines to keep
Observing without evaluating is the highest form of human intelligence.
When we combine observation with evaluation, others are apt to hear criticism.
Always and never turn one action into a verdict on a person.

## Nonviolent Communication · Underneath the blame is a need
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/nonviolent-communication/needs-behind-blame/
Source: Nonviolent Communication, chapters 5 and 6
Tags: Deep read, Nonviolent Communication, Hearing the half that was not said

Somebody is shouting at you. Underneath the words they are asking for something. This is how to get that half out.

### Q: What actually happened?
His central claim is that every criticism, attack and judgement is a tragic expression of an unmet need. Speaking at the Deheisha refugee camp, he was called a murderer to his face, because American-made tear gas canisters had been used there. He did not defend himself. He asked whether the man was furious, and needed his family's safety to be understood. The man stopped, then talked for an hour, and by the end of the evening had invited Rosenberg home for a Ramadan meal. Nothing was conceded and nothing was argued. The need under the shouting was simply said out loud.

### The parts · The words are an accusation, underneath is a gap
All you care about is work reads as a judgement. Underneath it is a need to matter to you. Answer the words and you are in a debate about whether that is true. Answer the need and the direction changes. One sentence, two layers, two destinations.
e.g. When a colleague says your department never cooperates, do not start listing evidence. Ask whether they are stuck waiting on something.

### The parts · Keep feelings apart from judgements
I feel that you do not respect me is not a feeling, it is a judgement in a feeling's clothing, and the subject has slid over to the other person. I am upset is a feeling: the subject is you, and nobody can deny it. Where the subject sits decides everything.
e.g. Swap I feel brushed off for I am anxious about this. The first assigns a motive, the second reports a state.

### The parts · A request must be concrete enough to refuse
Could you make a bit more effort is not a request, because nobody knows what would count as doing it. Send me one line before the meeting is. A vague request fails, and after it fails both sides believe more firmly that saying things changes nothing.
e.g. Replace be more involved at home with you do the Wednesday school run. The first is a complaint, the second is something that can be agreed.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: somebody is blaming you and your first instinct is to answer the charge.
Ask first: what is the thing underneath this sentence that they want? What happens if you say that out loud before anything else?
Where it goes wrong: using translate the need as a way of never accepting criticism. Some accusations mean exactly what they say, and the thing really was done badly.

### Lines to keep
All criticism is a tragic expression of an unmet need.
What others do may be the stimulus of our feelings, but not the cause.
Everything we do is in service of our needs.

========================================================================
## Taiichi Ohno · Ask why five times
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/ohno/five-whys/
Source: Taiichi Ohno, Toyota Production System, 1978
Tags: Deep read, Taiichi Ohno, Replacing the fuse, or fitting the strainer

The same fault keeps coming back and the review was written. What his five whys found on one stopped machine.

### Q: What actually happened?
There is an example in the book. A machine stopped. Why did it stop? An overload blew the fuse. Why the overload? The bearing was not sufficiently lubricated. Why not? The lubrication pump was not pumping enough. Why not? The pump shaft was worn and rattling. Why was it worn? No strainer had been fitted, so metal scrap got in. Only the fifth answer reaches the thing to repair: fit a strainer. Ask once and you replace the fuse, and it blows again next week. He called this the basic discipline of the Toyota floor.

### The parts · The first cause is almost never the cause
A blown fuse is a fact, not a cause. It is the first link in the chain to show itself, and most reviews stop there because it is the easiest to see and the cheapest to change. Change it, and next time it is the same link again.
e.g. He was careless this time is a fuse. Keep going: why was he careless, and what made being careful impossible in that spot?

### The parts · Five is not a ritual. It is the length of the chain
Fuse to strainer is exactly five steps, and each step is the answer to the why before it. Skip a level and you stop halfway, repairing something that will fail again. The number is not mystical. It is roughly how long these chains run.
e.g. In a review, take every because and ask why that, in turn, until nobody in the room can answer.

### The parts · The bottom layer is usually small and cheap
A strainer costs less than a pump, less than a bearing, far less than the stoppage. Chasing a fault to its root usually ends at the smallest available action, and that is the reason to keep asking: not to be thorough, but to reach the cheap point.
e.g. A genuine root cause maps to a tiny change. If your fix is large, you have probably not reached the bottom yet.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: one kind of problem keeps recurring, you deal with it every time, you write the review, and it recurs.
Ask first: last time, did I change the fuse or fit the strainer? Counting down from the incident, how many layers did I actually reach? Was the change at that layer small?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as dig deep into everything. Five whys is for problems that repeat, and a one-off does not need it. And never let why turn into whose fault — he was tracing a chain, not a person.

### Lines to keep
Repeat why five times and the real cause shows itself.
The first cause is only the first link to appear.
A genuine root cause usually maps to a very small change.

========================================================================
## Taiichi Ohno · Anyone may pull the cord
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/ohno/pull-the-cord/
Source: Taiichi Ohno, Toyota Production System; Sakichi Toyoda's self-stopping loom
Tags: Deep read, Taiichi Ohno, The problem surfaces where it happens

What you hand out comes back wrong every time. Why Toyota let any worker on the line halt the entire line.

### Q: What actually happened?
Toyota began as a loom maker. Sakichi Toyoda's loom had one design feature: when a thread broke the machine stopped itself, instead of weaving out a whole bolt of ruined cloth. Ohno moved the idea onto the car line. A cord hangs above every station, and anyone who sees a problem can pull it and stop the whole line. Management feared the lost output. He held. The result is that a fault surfaces in the second it occurs and is handled there, rather than accumulating into a pile of scrap found at the month-end count.

### The parts · The earlier a defect stops, the cheaper it is
An error caught at the first station costs a minute. The same error found at the last one costs the whole unit. Work that comes back to you wrong every time is telling you there was no point along the way where anyone could halt it.
e.g. If there is no checkpoint between handing the work out and getting it back, what comes back will be wrong.

### The parts · Give the power to stop to the people furthest down
Whoever sees the problem first is on the line, not in the office. If only a manager may stop, the problem has to travel upward and wait for permission, and by then it has flowed past. Give the stop to whoever can see, and it stops where it started.
e.g. Letting the person doing the work say wait, this is not right is worth ten times any inspection you run afterwards.

### The parts · Fear of stopping the line manufactures defects
The instinct of management is to keep running, because output matters. But what keeps running is defective output, and more of it is worse. His ordering is the reverse of the instinct: stopping is what produces, and refusing to stop is what really cuts production.
e.g. Get it out now and fix it later mostly produces rework, and rework costs far more than the pause would have.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: what you hand out comes back looking nothing like what you asked for, and you send it back every time.
Ask first: between handing this out and receiving it, how many points are there where somebody could call a halt? When the person doing the work sees something wrong, may they stop, and do they dare?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as everything must be escalated. The cord is pulled on an abnormality, not on the normal flow. And it is not a licence to watch people harder — the power moves down, not up.

### Lines to keep
A thread breaks, the loom stops, and nothing ruined is woven.
Give the power to stop to whoever can see the problem.
Stopping is what produces. Refusing to stop is what cuts output.

========================================================================
## Taiichi Ohno · Inventory is there to hide problems
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/ohno/inventory-hides-problems/
Source: Taiichi Ohno, Toyota Production System, 1978
Tags: Deep read, Taiichi Ohno, Lower the water and the rocks appear

Everything obvious has been cut and the cost will not move. Why he treated stock as a cover rather than a cushion.

### Q: What actually happened?
He had a picture for it. Inventory is water and problems are rocks on the riverbed. With the water high the boat runs smoothly, because every rock is submerged: an unreliable machine, a supplier who misses dates, a handover nobody has sorted out, all of it carried by the stock. Lower the water and the rocks come up one at a time; hit one, repair it, and the channel is genuinely open. Toyota cut stock not to save warehouse rent but to leave problems nowhere to hide.

### The parts · Wherever there is slack, something is being covered
An extra week in the schedule, extra material, an extra pair of hands: every piece of slack is underwriting some problem. A problem that is underwritten never gets repaired, so the slack turns into a permanent cost. Hunt the slack first. There is a rock beneath it.
e.g. Whichever stage always keeps a margin has, underneath that margin, a problem nobody has fixed.

### The parts · You lower the water to hit rocks, not to save water
His purpose in cutting stock was never the storage bill. It was forcing problems into the open. Lower the water and leave the exposed rocks unrepaired and the boat is holed, which is why the imitators failed: they copied the cutting and skipped the repairing.
e.g. After you cut a margin, something will go wrong. That is the rock surfacing. Repair it instead of putting the margin back.

### The parts · A little at a time, one rock per pass
He did not drain the river. Lower the level slightly, one rock appears, repair it, lower it again. Take it all out at once and ten rocks arrive together and none of them get fixed. Cost comes down in layers, never in a single cut.
e.g. Cut a margin a little, wait until this layer of problems has been repaired, and only then cut the next slice.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: every obvious cost has been cut, and cutting further would damage the people or the goods, so you cannot see where to go next.
Ask first: which stages always keep a margin? If I removed the margin at one of them, what problem would surface? Am I prepared to repair that one?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as all margin is waste. What he cut was stock being used to hide problems, not genuine safety margin. And never cut it all at once — that is holing the boat, not clearing the channel.

### Lines to keep
Inventory is water, problems are rocks, and high water runs smooth.
Every margin is underwriting a problem, and underwritten problems go unrepaired.
Cut the margin and something breaks. That is the rock you wanted.

========================================================================
## The Old Regime and the Revolution · The moment reform begins
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/old-regime/most-dangerous-moment/
Source: The Old Regime and the Revolution, Book Three
Tags: Deep read, The Old Regime and the Revolution, Loosening the grip is what detonates

The twenty years before the Revolution were the old order's most prosperous. The law Tocqueville drew out of that paradox.

### Q: What actually happened?
The archives told Tocqueville the opposite of what instinct says. The Revolution did not arrive in the poorest years or in the most oppressed provinces — the reign of Louis XVI was the most prosperous period of the old monarchy, and the rising came where the burden was felt least. His explanation became a law. The most dangerous moment for a bad government is when it begins to reform. The mechanism sits in one sentence: people bear an evil patiently while it seems beyond redress, and the moment someone proposes removing it, it turns unbearable.

### The parts · Discontent is set by expectation, not by conditions
Hold conditions still and raise expectations and discontent rises — and reform is the strongest generator of expectation there is, because it is an official admission that the old state was not right. So complaints go up first, not down. That is the mechanism working, not the reform failing.
e.g. Satisfaction scores drop in the quarter after the pay review is announced, because everyone has started measuring today against what it ought to be.

### The parts · Half reformed is the most dangerous setting
The old constraints are loose and the new arrangement has not landed. In that middle state the old reason for patience, that it could not be helped, has been dismantled, and the new satisfaction is still in transit. Louis XVI was stuck there. Never park at the halfway point.
e.g. You announce that authority will be devolved, and six months later not one approval has been removed. The resentment now beats anything silence would have cost.

### The parts · Each abuse removed magnifies the ones left
Every abuse that goes makes the remaining ones easier to notice. Solve one problem and the rest become less tolerable by contrast. That is not greed; you updated the frame of reference yourself. So sequence improvements, starting with those that do not light up a bigger hole.
e.g. Expenses go from three weeks to three days, and the stingy travel allowance is instantly the grievance of the month. Nobody had mentioned it before.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are about to launch a reform people have wanted for a long time.
Ask first: how will I manage the expectation curve after the announcement, and will I sit too long in the gap where the old is loose and the new has not arrived?
Where it goes wrong: changing nothing because you fear lighting expectations, or reading the rise in complaints as ingratitude and braking halfway, which is the most dangerous step of all.

### Lines to keep
The most dangerous moment for a bad government is when it begins to reform.
A grievance becomes intolerable once the possibility of removing it crosses men's minds.
Every abuse removed seems to reveal the ones that remain.

========================================================================
## The Old Regime and the Revolution · The centralisation that survived
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/old-regime/centralization-survived/
Source: The Old Regime and the Revolution, Book Two
Tags: Deep read, The Old Regime and the Revolution, Overturn everything, inherit the core

The Revolution claimed a clean break with the past. The unbroken line Tocqueville dug out of the provincial archives.

### Q: What actually happened?
In the provincial archives Tocqueville found that the central administration everyone credited to the Revolution or to Napoleon was in fact an institution of the old regime, and the only part of it left standing afterwards. For a century and more the monarchy had used its intendants to hollow out the nobility and pull every matter to Paris; by 1789 local self-government was already a shell. So the Revolution destroyed the crown, the nobles and the church as appearances, and took the centralising machine over intact, then ran it harder.

### The parts · What gets replaced is the appearance; what stays is the structure
Signs, slogans and the names of the people in charge are the easy part. The pipes power actually runs through are the hard part, because whoever takes over discovers on day one how useful they are. Judge a change by approvals, budget authority and information flow.
e.g. A large reorganisation renames every department and rotates the executives. Three months later the same few people still sign the budget, and the change happened only in slides.

### The parts · Revolutionaries fall in love with the tools of the people they overthrew
A centralising machine is irresistible to anyone governing: ready-made, efficient, point and shoot. So those who overthrow it almost always inherit and reinforce it. If you want a bad structure to die, dismantle it during the handover, before the new owner grows attached.
e.g. The incoming head denounces one-man rule, then finds that centralised decisions are fast. Six months on it is one-man rule with a different mouth.

### The parts · The stronger the sense of rupture, the harder to look for the continuity
Tocqueville's method is worth stealing. Everyone was saying 1789 divided two worlds; he read deeds, tax rolls and the correspondence of intendants, and found the line nobody could see. For any earth-shattering change, ask what passed through it untouched.
e.g. Each time an industry declares a change of paradigm, check the channel structure and who takes the margin. The new throne usually stands on the old foundation.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a thorough change has just finished and everything looks new.
Ask first: have the pipes that money, approvals and information actually run through changed at all? What came through unaltered?
Where it goes wrong: reading a new surface as a new structure, or using nothing ever really changes to deny progress that is real.

### Lines to keep
Centralisation is an institution of the old regime, not a creation of the Revolution.
They built the new order out of the debris of the old.
Of all the institutions the Revolution destroyed, this one alone survived.

## On War · The continuation of policy
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/on-war/continuation-of-politics/
Source: On War, Book One, Chapter One
Tags: Deep read, On War, You fight in order to settle

The most famous line in the book gets read as a cynical observation. It is in fact a restraining clause.

### Q: What actually happened?
Clausewitz defines war on two levels. First its nature: an act of force to compel the enemy to do our will, and force left to its own logic escalates without limit. Then the rein: war is merely the continuation of policy by other means. The second statement exists to bind the first. War is not a thing standing on its own. It is begun by a political purpose and serves one. The political object is the goal, war is the means, and the means can never be considered apart from the goal. He spent his life warning soldiers that the longer a war runs, the easier this is to forget.

### The parts · A means left alone starts eating the end
War has an internal logic, win this one and then the next, and once running it powers itself until the fighting is the point. Every strong instrument behaves this way: price wars, litigation, public campaigns. They demand continuation once started, so the rein goes on at the beginning or not at all.
e.g. A price war opened to force them to the table becomes, by the third month, a matter of not losing face. Nobody remembers the table.

### The parts · Audit every step against the purpose
The working version of the means never being separable from the goal: each move has to answer whether it brings the political outcome nearer. Taking a city that makes the negotiation harder is a military success and a net loss. The test is the purpose, not the spoils.
e.g. You won the case and wrecked your standing in the industry. You took the share and taught them your whole method. Re-audit each move against the original aim.

### The parts · When the aim changes, resize the means
The political object determines the effort and the scale it warrants, so limited aims call for a limited war. Aims shifting mid-course is ordinary. The danger is the scale of the means not being reset with them, a small aim carrying a large war, or the reverse.
e.g. A project meant only to test a market rolls on under its own momentum until the scale no longer matches the word test. Resize it, or admit the aim changed.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a contest has been running a long time and each round is fiercer than the last.
Ask first: what was this opened for, and is the next step still bringing that outcome nearer?
Where it goes wrong: letting the means take over the end and fighting for its own sake; or using everything serves the big goal to license any escalation, which turns the rein into a whip.

### Lines to keep
War is merely the continuation of policy by other means.
The political object is the goal, war is the means.
War is an act of force to compel the enemy to do our will.

========================================================================
## On War · Friction
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/on-war/friction/
Source: On War, Book One, Chapter Seven
Tags: Deep read, On War, Even the simplest thing is difficult

He borrowed a word from physics for the study of war. This is where friction comes from and why it can only be budgeted for.

### Q: What actually happened?
In the seventh chapter he coins it: everything in war is very simple, but the simplest thing is difficult. The difficulties accumulate and produce a friction that nobody who has not seen war can imagine. His picture of it is concrete. The machine is made of individuals, each of whom keeps his own friction: an order passes through hundreds of people who get tired, frightened, or misunderstand it, and on top of that come weather, ground and false reports. Friction makes what looks easy hard. It is, he says, the one concept that distinguishes real war from war on paper.

### The parts · Friction comes from a plan having to pass through people
A plan is a frictionless abstraction; execution is warm-blooded transmission, and each person it crosses adds a layer of fatigue, misreading, self-interest and delay. So the complexity of a plan is not counted in logical steps but in how many people it must pass through.
e.g. A three-step process spanning five teams is harder than a ten-step one closed inside a single group. Count handoffs before you count steps.

### The parts · Friction cannot be removed, only allowed for
He does not teach you to eliminate it, because it cannot be eliminated. He teaches conversion. The good commander prices friction into the plan and leaves slack at every link. Scheduling to the theoretical limit is not efficiency; it is never having been in the field.
e.g. A timeline summed from each stage's best case declares that one head cold gives the whole line a fever. Old hands plan at eighty per cent and call the rest friction.

### The parts · What resists friction is habit, not willpower
The only lubricant, he says, is the habit of war: drill and combat grinding a force until difficulty is the default. Willpower in the moment does not hold against systematic friction. Only rehearsing the common failures into muscle keeps friction from eating your decisions.
e.g. The teams that hold up are not the ones with high morale. They are the ones that have rehearsed a rollback, run a degraded mode and sat through a night shift.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a plan that is simple on paper, and you are about to schedule it along the ideal path.
Ask first: how many people does it have to pass through, and where exactly did I leave slack?
Where it goes wrong: treating friction as an excuse and refusing every claim of it; or using it to excuse all delay while never drilling the habit that absorbs it.

### Lines to keep
Everything in war is very simple, but the simplest thing is difficult.
Friction is what distinguishes real war from war on paper.
Three quarters of the factors in war lie in a fog.

========================================================================
## Paul Graham · Do things that do not scale
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/paul-graham/dont-scale/
Source: Do Things That Don't Scale, 2013
Tags: Deep read, Paul Graham, The early work is meant to be handmade

Founders think about scale constantly. He argues for the opposite direction — and is specific about what the handmade phase actually buys.

### Q: What actually happened?
The essay opens against the instinct: startups do not take off by themselves; the founders make them take off. The common mistake is chasing something scalable on day one, when the early period calls for recruiting users by hand. Airbnb had stalled, so the founders flew to New York week after week, knocked on hosts' doors and photographed their apartments themselves. Completely unscalable — and it found the switch that moved conversion. The output of that phase is not the handful of users; it is an unusually concentrated understanding of them, plus people so over-served they will tell others.

### The parts · Doing it by hand is the highest-bandwidth research there is
Surveys and dashboards show the shadow a behaviour casts; being in the room shows the behaviour. In people's living rooms it turned out photograph quality was the bottleneck — an insight the analytics could only ever have shown as low conversion. The expensive thing early on is not slow growth, it is understanding wrongly.
e.g. Have the founders deliver the first hundred customers personally. Every one is a piece of research arriving with its full context. Time saved by delegating it comes back doubled on the wrong roadmap.

### The parts · Over-serving is how you manufacture the first advocates
If early users get service indistinguishable from a large company's, they have no reason to speak about you. The handmade phase gives what no scaled operation could — a founder replying in minutes, the product bent around one person. That unreasonable care is the raw material of word of mouth.
e.g. Answering the first cohort at any cost brings customers later that are cheaper than any advertising, because the story they tell cannot be bought.

### The parts · Unscalable is a stage, not a creed
The essay gets quoted in halves. The correct loop is: do it by hand, extract the one move that was actually doing the work, then build that move into the product or the process. Airbnb turned professional photography into a platform feature. Handwork without extraction is diligence covering for an absence of leverage.
e.g. After three months of founders closing deals personally, the deliverable is a list of the three actions that decide a sale — then those get standardised. Not a fourth month of closing deals.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the product just launched and you are torn between building growth machinery and serving users by hand.
Ask first: is our understanding of why people buy or leave at dashboard level or living-room level?
Where it goes wrong: keeping it handmade past the point of scale, so founders are still carrying the business on their backs; or doing it by hand for a long time and never extracting the repeatable move.

### Lines to keep
Startups do not take off by themselves. The founders make them take off.
In the early days you have to recruit users manually.
They went door to door photographing the hosts' apartments themselves.

========================================================================
## Paul Graham · Default alive or default dead
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/paul-graham/default-alive/
Source: Default Alive or Default Dead?, 2015
Tags: Deep read, Paul Graham, Run this number before anything else

He asks founders one question first, and most of them cannot answer it. Why it comes before every other conversation.

### Q: What actually happened?
The first thing he asks a startup is are you default alive or default dead? The definition is hard-edged: assuming expenses stay constant and growth continues as it has been, do you reach profitability on the money you have left? If yes, default alive. If no, default dead. What surprised him is how many founders do not know which they are. It comes first because it sets the character of every other conversation: a default alive company can talk about ambition; a default dead one has a single agenda item, getting out of that state — and is usually still discussing hiring, assuming the next round will arrive.

### The parts · You have to run it yourself, because nothing raises an alarm
A default dead company looks entirely normal from inside: the product ships, the team grows, there is money in the account. Death is scheduled months out on a calendar nobody turns to. The question brings that date forward to today — three numbers, ten minutes.
e.g. Put the current answer and the death date on this trajectory as page one of the monthly meeting. The existence of that page reorders everything after it.

### The parts · Counting on the next round outsources your survival to a mood
He names the standard consolation: investor appetite swings with the market and your death date does not. The right move when default dead is not to fundraise harder but to move the two variables under your control — expenses and growth — until you are back on the living side.
e.g. A survival plan with raise a B round written into it has handed the switch to somebody else's fund cycle. Cut to within reach of break-even first; the negotiation even smells different.

### The parts · The usual cause is hiring too early
His first-named cause of default dead is over-hiring — using growth needs people to raise the burn ahead of growth that then does not arrive. The remedy is counter-intuitive: early growth comes far more from founders making the product better than from headcount. People should be added when growth is dragging you into adding them.
e.g. Build the team and wait for the business bets a fixed cost on a forecast. Let the pain of growth force each new hire instead, and the company stays on the living side.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: things are running normally and you cannot say where the cash-flow threshold is.
Ask first: flat expenses, current growth — profitable before the money runs out? If the answer is no, today's agenda should be replaced entirely.
Where it goes wrong: using default alive as an excuse not to grow — safe and stationary. The question protects the floor; the ceiling still takes ambition.

### Lines to keep
Are you default alive or default dead?
With expenses flat and growth as it is, do you reach profitability in time?
What surprises me is how many founders do not know the answer.

## Esther Perel · Security and desire want opposite things
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/perel/security-and-desire/
Source: Esther Perel, Mating in Captivity, 2006
Tags: Deep read, Esther Perel, Which is why the better it gets, the flatter

The steadier life gets, the less you feel, and most people assume they changed. Perel says the structure did it.

### Q: What actually happened?
Perel has done couples therapy for over thirty years, and the sentence she hears most is: everything is fine, we just don't feel anything. Her explanation blames nobody. Intimacy wants closeness, familiarity and predictability; desire wants distance, the unknown, the thing not yet fully held. Both are real needs and they point in opposite directions. So the more settled a relationship, the more easily the second gets squeezed out — not love going wrong, but one thing perfected until it crowds out the other.

### The parts · It isn't love fading. Two needs are crowding each other
Read as love fading, the only available moves are blaming yourself or blaming them. Read as two needs crowding, the move is clear: not repairing the love, but making room again for the one that got squeezed out.
e.g. Ten years together, everything fine, nothing there. Not one word of that sentence says the love went wrong.

### The parts · Familiar to the point of no unknown leaves nothing to miss
Desire needs a little opacity. When their schedule, thoughts and reactions are all inside your predictions, missing them has nowhere to land. So the problem often isn't too little communication — it's everything being accounted for.
e.g. Both schedules known to the hour is often the first bit of air a long relationship loses.

### The parts · Room comes from separateness, not more closeness
The instinct is more time together, more talking. Perel's prescription often runs the other way: each go and do something the other isn't part of, become two people again, then come back. Distance isn't the enemy of love. It's the fuel of desire.
e.g. A few days apart and then meeting: that touch of strangeness is useful, not a warning sign.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: no fights, no crisis, and no feeling, and you can't say what's wrong.
Ask first: when did we last each do something separately and come back with something to say? If you can't recall, start there.
Where it goes wrong: using it to justify neglect — making room isn't withdrawing; and it doesn't mean falling in love again from scratch. This is about clearing space, not applying more force.

### Lines to keep
Intimacy wants closeness. Desire wants distance. Both are real.
'Everything's fine, we feel nothing' says nothing about love failing.
When everything is accounted for, missing them has nowhere to land.

========================================================================
## Esther Perel · Feeling nothing isn't the same as something being wrong
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/perel/not-a-problem-to-solve/
Source: Perel's distinction in couples work
Tags: Deep read, Esther Perel, First tell a wound from an emptiness

'We can't go on like this' can sit on top of two completely different things. Tell them apart before you act.

### Q: What actually happened?
Perel warns about a common misdiagnosis: treating flatness as if it were rupture. Rupture has a wound — contempt, betrayal, sustained attack — and that needs mending. Flatness has no wound; it is simply empty, and emptiness needs filling, not mending. The two moves point in opposite directions: mending a wound means stopping first, apologising first, making it safe first; filling an emptiness means going outward and adding something new. Get it wrong and it worsens — apologising when you should be adding, booking trips when you should be apologising.

### The parts · Check for a wound before choosing a move
The test is concrete: in the last three months, has there been contempt, dragging up old grievances, belittling in front of others? If yes, that's the wound and it comes first. If none of it, this is emptiness, and the treatment is entirely different.
e.g. Never fighting and growing quieter, versus every argument reopening old accounts. Two different illnesses.

### The parts · For emptiness, more communication makes it worse
Repeatedly sitting down to discuss the relationship when it's empty talks away the last of the ease. What it needs is experiencing something new together, not analysing why there's no feeling — the analysis itself turns the relationship into a task.
e.g. The weekly scheduled 'let's talk about us' often turns life into a status report.

### The parts · Only after telling them apart is 'should we leave' answerable
People decide about leaving while the two states are mixed together, so the answer keeps swinging. See first whether it's a wound or an emptiness, then ask — the answers under those two premises were never meant to match.
e.g. Asking whether to break up over and over usually means the previous step hasn't been done.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you don't fight and you aren't close, and you're weighing mending against leaving.
Ask first: in the last three months, any contempt, old grievances, belittling in front of others? Yes — that's a wound, handle it first. No — it's emptiness, and wound treatment is the wrong tool.
Where it goes wrong: using 'it's just flat' to cover a real wound; and equally, reading ordinary dullness as proof the relationship has broken.

### Lines to keep
A wound is mended, an emptiness is filled. Opposite directions.
Talking it through while empty talks away the last of the ease.
Ask whether to leave before telling them apart and the answer swings.

========================================================================
## Esther Perel · It isn't how often. It's not being there
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/perel/quality-not-frequency/
Source: Perel on presence in long relationships
Tags: Deep read, Esther Perel, Present in the room, absent in attention

You live in the same place. So why does it feel like long distance? What she says to count instead.

### Q: What actually happened?
Most people count time: how many evenings a week, how many meals together. Perel says that's the wrong ledger — what decides the quality isn't how long you're together but how many moments both people were actually there. Two people on the same sofa on separate phones have spent a whole evening together and zero minutes present. She asks clients something very concrete: when did you last look at each other and talk with no screen interrupting?

### The parts · Count 'together' and 'present' separately
They're different ledgers: together is duration, present is attention. The first stacks up easily; the second can be zero for a whole week. What makes someone feel loved is the second, and it has almost nothing to do with the first.
e.g. A whole weekend together, and afterwards you can't say what they were thinking about for either day.

### The parts · Presence can be practised, and it's cheap
It doesn't need large blocks of time: fifteen minutes a day, person facing person, phones face down, is enough to change how it feels. The difficulty isn't the duration, it's not glancing away — one break and that stretch is over.
e.g. Fifteen minutes before sleep with no phone does more than an expensive holiday.

### The parts · Long enough absent and it reads as not caring
They don't know what your head is busy with. All they can read is where your attention goes, and from that, where they rank. So sustained distraction doesn't communicate 'I'm busy'. It communicates 'you're not important'.
e.g. Listening while answering messages: they remember none of what you said, only that you were looking elsewhere.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you're together every day and drifting further apart.
Ask first: when did I last look at them and talk without touching my phone? If you can't name the day, start there before discussing the relationship.
Where it goes wrong: turning it into a new metric to hold over them; and it doesn't mean being present every waking moment. Fifteen real minutes a day, not permanent standby.

### Lines to keep
Together counts duration. Present counts attention.
Same sofa, separate phones: zero minutes present.
Sustained distraction says 'you're not important', not 'I'm busy'.

========================================================================
## Karl Popper · Can it be shown wrong
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/popper/falsifiability/
Source: Conjectures and Refutations
Tags: Deep read, Karl Popper, A theory that explains everything explains nothing

Astrology explains events and so does physics. This page is about the line Popper drew between them.

### Q: What actually happened?
As a teenager in Vienna he was reading Einstein alongside the theories then in fashion, whose followers could account for any case at all and treated that as proof of strength. General relativity did the opposite. It predicted that starlight passing the sun would bend by a specific amount, and a different measurement would have finished it. The 1919 eclipse matched. A theory which is not refutable by any conceivable event is non-scientific, he concluded, and irrefutability is a vice rather than a virtue. The difference was never explanatory power.

### The parts · Ask what would refute it, not what supports it
Facing any claim, the useful question is not what evidence there is but what observation would make you drop it. If nothing would, the claim carries no testable content, and being internally consistent does not make up for that.
e.g. Market sentiment drove the rise. And the fall? Also sentiment. It covers every outcome, which is exactly why it tells you nothing.

### The parts · The refuting condition has to be written down first
People are extremely good at reading any result as support. The only reliable antidote is to nail the criterion in place before the result arrives. Setting the standard afterwards leaves you a position that cannot lose, which is the same as one that cannot inform.
e.g. Before launch, write down that if this number has not moved in two weeks the assumption was wrong. In advance, so there is nothing left to renegotiate.

### The parts · Being refuted is not the same as being discarded
The common misreading is that a falsified theory goes in the bin. His demand is that a theory be exposed to serious attempts to break it, and good ones usually come out stronger. What matters is whether you genuinely tried.
e.g. Every quarter, go hunting for the strongest case against your central judgement. If you look hard and find nothing, that is when it is worth trusting.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: somebody has handed you a claim that sounds thoroughly reasonable.
Ask first: under what circumstances would this be false, and can they answer that at all?
Where it goes wrong: using the criterion to dismiss every field that cannot be measured, or as a debating move that leaves nobody able to conclude anything.

### Lines to keep
A theory which is not refutable by any conceivable event is non-scientific.
Irrefutability is not a virtue of a theory but a vice.
Say in advance what would make you admit you were wrong.
