## Karl Popper · Go looking for the counter-example
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/popper/seek-refutation/
Source: The Logic of Scientific Discovery
Tags: Deep read, Karl Popper, One black swan beats a hundred white ones

No number of white swans settles the question. This page is about what you should be collecting instead.

### Q: What actually happened?
The swan is his illustration of the problem of induction. However many white swans you observe, none of it establishes that all swans are white, and a single black one settles it. Evidence is wildly asymmetric. A confirming instance carries almost no information; a refuting one is decisive. People run the other way by default, gathering supportive cases and feeling steadier at the hundredth than at the first. So his method: propose boldly, then attack your own proposal as hard as you can.

### The parts · Go and ask the people who left
Where you take the sample decides the answer. Ask current users whether they like it and the reply is close to guaranteed. The information lives with the ones who stopped. This is the most practical thing that falls out of Popper.
e.g. To test whether customers love the feature, do not survey the ones still using it. Interview three who cancelled.

### The parts · Bold conjectures, severe attempts to refute
He is not asking for cautious hypotheses. He wants large ones, paired with serious efforts to destroy them. The two halves go together: conjecture without refutation is daydreaming, refutation without conjecture is timidity.
e.g. Put forward the aggressive plan, and name the three observations that would show the route is closed. Then go and look for them.

### The parts · Confirmation bias is the factory setting
Hunting for support is pleasant and fast, because the motive sits on that side. Good intentions do not correct it. Only procedure does: make finding the counter-example a step on the checklist rather than something you remember to do.
e.g. Add a permanent field to the review template for the strongest argument against, and require the proposer to fill it in himself.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the more you check, the more certain you get.
Ask first: in the last hour, were you collecting support or hunting a counter-example? What is the strongest evidence against, and did you look for it?
Where it goes wrong: making refutation a way of never deciding — the point is a judgement you can rely on, not a paralysed one.

### Lines to keep
No number of white swans establishes that all swans are white.
One black swan is enough to settle it.
It is easy to obtain confirmations for nearly every theory, if we look.

========================================================================
## Pu Songling · Forty years of sitting the exam
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/pu-songling/forty-years-of-failing/
Source: Chronology of Pu Songling; his preface to Strange Tales
Tags: Deep read, Pu Songling, Never passing, and never a turning point

There's a kind of failure with no decisive battle in it. How you get through that kind of life.

### Q: What actually happened?
At nineteen Pu Songling sat the entry examinations and came first at county, prefecture and circuit level. He was locally famous. Then he sat the provincial examination for the rest of his life, from his twenties into his sixties, and never once passed, supporting his family as a live-in tutor. At seventy-one he was granted a minor honorary status by seniority. No single year in all of it was decisive — not one big defeat and a restart, but once every three years, each time just short, until he was old.

### The parts · Failure with no turning point is the hardest kind
Lose a battle and you can review it and change direction. Forty years of being just short offers no single event worth reviewing and no signal about whether to stop. Most advice about handling failure assumes there is a turning point to point at. Here there isn't one.
e.g. Six years of sitting the same qualifying exam, a few marks short every time. That isn't one failed venture.

### The parts · He didn't stop, and he didn't make it everything
Worth noticing: he neither gave up the exam nor staked the whole of his life on it. The tutoring continued, the family was kept, the stories were collected. Running them in parallel means that when the thing that never worked fails again, something else in your hands is working.
e.g. While the main thing refuses to happen, the important part is not letting it become the only thing you do.

### The parts · You may keep more than one ruler
The examination was a ruler handed to him from outside, clear and unambiguous — which is exactly what makes it easy to let it become the only one. He had a second: how many stories this year. The second doesn't make the first easier. It stops there being one reading.
e.g. If a whole year yields only 'failed again', that isn't a year in which nothing happened.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something you've worked at for years hasn't happened, and you can't say when it would.
Ask first: this year, apart from the thing that didn't happen, what did move? If you can't name one, fill that gap before deciding whether to continue.
Where it goes wrong: using him to argue that persistence pays — he never passed; or the reverse, that he should have quit. He didn't quit. He just didn't let it be the only thing.

### Lines to keep
No year was decisive. Just short every time, until he was old.
A lost battle can be reviewed. Being just short cannot.
Don't let the thing that never works become the only thing you do.

========================================================================
## Pu Songling · The main thing failed. The side thing didn't
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/pu-songling/the-side-thing/
Source: His preface to Strange Tales, and its posthumous publication
Tags: Deep read, Pu Songling, And he never knew

What he spent his life trying to do never happened. What he did on the side did. Can that be arranged?

### Q: What actually happened?
Pu Songling's real work, as he saw it, was the examination. Strange Tales from a Chinese Studio was a diversion — forty years of writing, circulated in manuscript among friends, and he did not live to see it printed. Of the people who remember him today, essentially none do so for his examination essays. The thing ranked first didn't happen and the thing ranked last did — and he died not knowing it.

### The parts · You don't get to set the ranking
Where a thing sits in your own ordering and what it eventually grows into are unrelated. The first is decided by today's standards; the second takes decades to show. So 'which is the main thing' is a question that, asked at the time, usually gets the wrong answer.
e.g. The thing you push hardest often yields nothing, and the thing done casually is what people remember.

### The parts · But don't therefore do both casually
Strange Tales wasn't written carelessly — forty years, nearly five hundred pieces, revised repeatedly. It was last in his ranking, not last in his investment. A side thing can only grow into something if it gets real investment; it just doesn't get the status.
e.g. The moment 'it's only a side project' reaches the investment, it really does become only a side project.

### The parts · Don't wait until you approve of it to take it seriously
He never considered it his achievement. If you have to wait until you can admit 'this is my real work' before putting the hours in, a great many things simply never grow. The steadier practice is to work seriously and leave the ranking undecided.
e.g. Do it properly for five years and then look back at which one worked, rather than choosing now.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: your day job is flat and the thing you do in the evenings keeps growing, and you don't know whether to swap them.
Ask first: how much have I actually put into the side thing over three years? Talk about swapping after the investment is there, not before.
Where it goes wrong: using him to justify doing several things half-heartedly — he did two things for forty years; or rushing to promote the side thing. Rankings are only accurate looking back.

### Lines to keep
The thing ranked first failed. The thing ranked last didn't.
It was last in his ranking, not last in his investment.
Wait until you approve of it and many things never grow at all.

## Pu Songling · Collecting stories by the road
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/pu-songling/collecting-at-the-roadside/
Source: The tea-stall account, told by later writers rather than by him
Tags: Deep read, Pu Songling, Using the hours nobody wants

Forty years of a tutor's scattered hours. What he did with them, and how the material accumulated.

### Q: What actually happened?
There is a persistent account that Pu Songling set out tea by the roadside and asked passers-by for strange stories, waiving the price of a bowl for each one, then wrote them up at home. It comes from later writers, not from him, and may not be literal. But it matches a checkable fact: he spent forty years as a live-in tutor in gentry households, with a great deal of scattered time around the teaching, and the nearly five hundred pieces accumulated across exactly those years. He didn't quit the job to write. He wrote on the job.

### The parts · Accumulation needs somewhere fixed for things to land
Scattered hours turn into something not because there are many of them but because there is one fixed place that catches them. A thing overheard, a sentence that occurs to you — all into the same notebook. Without that catch, the same forty years simply disperse.
e.g. Every loose idea into one file beats the same ideas spread across ten places.

### The parts · The material is local. You don't go far for it
His sources were the ordinary talk of villagers in the county he tutored in, not the fruit of travels through famous mountains. What's genuinely scarce isn't remarkable experience. It's the eye that treats what's around you as material — most people have as much of it and aren't collecting.
e.g. The complaints, gossip and small events you hear daily. A year separates the person who writes them down from the one who doesn't.

### The parts · Not quitting is what let it run so long
The tutoring fed him and gave him forty uninterrupted years. Had he staked everything on writing, he probably couldn't have lasted. What kills a side project isn't too little investment. It's gambling your living alongside it and being forced to stop.
e.g. Keeping the job is what let the thing reach its tenth year.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you want to do something long-term, you have only scraps of time, and you can't afford to quit.
Ask first: do I have one fixed place that catches whatever comes up? Build that before asking whether there's enough time.
Where it goes wrong: using him to argue against focus — he collected one kind of thing for forty years; or treating 'don't quit' as a reason to delay. What matters is that the catch gets used daily.

### Lines to keep
He didn't quit the job to write. He wrote on the job.
Scattered hours add up because something catches them, not because there are many.
What kills a side project is gambling your living alongside it.

## Rat Park · Swap the cage for a park
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/rat-park/rat-park/
Source: Bruce Alexander et al., the Rat Park experiments, 1978–81
Tags: Deep read, Rat Park, Same rat, different situation

The most famous addiction experiment gave a conclusion against intuition. What happens when you change the cage.

### Q: What actually happened?
The standard 1970s addiction experiment went like this: put one rat alone in an empty cage with two bottles, one water and one laced with morphine. The rat drinks the morphine until it dies. The conclusion looks solid — touch it once and you're finished. Bruce Alexander in Canada asked a different question: what if the cage weren't empty? He built a much larger enclosure with companions, wheels, tunnels and places to hide. Same two bottles, and the rats in the park were far less interested in the morphine.

### The parts · The variable isn't only the bottle. It's the cage
The original design treated the cage as background and the drug as the only variable. Once Alexander made the cage a variable too, the conclusion moved: same rat, same bottle, different situation, very different behaviour. The drug's effect isn't denied. It just isn't the only term.
e.g. The same game, played by a child with nothing on all summer and by a child with things to do, is not the same game.

### The parts · The empty cage is manufacturing the demand
The park rats weren't restrained; they didn't much want it. Alexander later used the word dislocation: pull an individual out of the relationships and position they belong in and they will look for anything that fills the gap. The gap is what's being filled.
e.g. The stretch after moving to a strange city with no friends is when anything becomes easy to get hooked on.

### The parts · This has a boundary, and it has to be stated
Rat Park's replications were not uniformly successful and its interpretation is still argued over. The safe reading is that situation is the chronically underrated term, not the only one. Explaining everything with it delays people who need medical care.
e.g. 'Just change your environment' is true for some people and dangerous advice for others.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you want to stop something — the phone, drinking, whatever — and the few attempts you made all ran on holding out.
Ask first: when do I usually do it? Log the last ten times — hour, place, whether you had anything else on. Look at what the gap is.
Where it goes wrong: using it to deny the physiological side of addiction, or to talk someone out of getting treatment. It adds the situation term. It doesn't replace medicine.

### Lines to keep
Same rat, same bottle. Different cage, different behaviour.
They weren't holding out. They didn't much want it.
What's being filled is the gap. The substance was just to hand.

========================================================================
## Rat Park · Back home, most of them simply stopped
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/rat-park/vietnam-veterans/
Source: Lee N. Robins et al., follow-up study of returning Vietnam servicemen, 1974
Tags: Deep read, Rat Park, The hardest natural experiment there is

Is there harder evidence than rats? What the numbers on returning soldiers actually showed.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1971 the US government discovered an awkward problem: a substantial proportion of American servicemen in Vietnam were addicted to heroin. Everyone braced for a disaster — these men would carry it home into the cities. Robins's team followed them and found the opposite. The overwhelming majority simply stopped once home, with only a small fraction relapsing within a year. Same people, same drug, different place. It is one of the very few natural experiments in addiction research with a sample this size.

### The parts · Its strength is that nobody designed it
Laboratory findings always carry the worry that they were engineered. This one wasn't — nobody sent hundreds of thousands of people to a war and brought them back in order to prove a point. Not being designed is exactly what makes it more persuasive than any experiment.
e.g. The same person, at war and back at home, responds completely differently to the same substance.

### The parts · What changed wasn't the place. It was the whole situation
Coming home swapped out an entire set of conditions: no longer possibly dying at any moment, family instead of fellow soldiers, a job and a schedule, and the substance much harder to get. So changing environment isn't moving house. It's withdrawing the conditions holding it up.
e.g. Only the address changed and the hours, the circle and the pressure are identical. That isn't a change of environment.

### The parts · The fraction who relapsed says something else
Some did continue after returning. That fraction is the reminder: situation explains the bulk, not all of it. Who lands in it has more to do with what home was like and what else was going on than with the drug.
e.g. If the home you return to was already an empty cage, the change of place never actually happened.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you're trying to help yourself or a family member stop something, and you've been fighting the substance head-on.
Ask first: what conditions hold this up — hours, place, people, the gap it fills? Removing one at a time beats holding out.
Where it goes wrong: assuming a new city fixes it — what this cohort changed was an entire situation; and don't conclude that willpower doesn't matter. It says willpower shouldn't be the only term.

### Lines to keep
Same people, same substance. Home again, and they stopped.
The weight of this data is that nobody designed it.
Changing environment isn't moving house. It's removing the props.

## Rat Park · Take the cage apart before the willpower
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/rat-park/change-the-cage/
Source: The applied reading of Rat Park and Robins 1974
Tags: Deep read, Rat Park, And where this stops being true

Once you know the situation matters, what exactly do you move? How to take the cage apart one bar at a time.

### Q: What actually happened?
Put the last two pieces together and you get a method that runs against common sense: to stop something, don't fight the thing itself first. Look at what keeps it alive. A habit that lasts usually has a whole set of props — a fixed hour, a fixed place, nothing else to hand, people doing it with you. Withdraw those one at a time and the thing gets harder by itself, whereas fighting it head-on withdraws only your willpower, which is the first thing to run out.

### The parts · Keep the log before you move anything
Log ten in a row: the hour, the place, whether anything else was in your hands, who was there. Most people finish the log and find the trigger isn't craving, it's one recurring empty slot. Finding the slot is worth more than studying how to resist.
e.g. Eight of ten were in bed before sleep. What needs changing is that half hour.

### The parts · Whatever replaces it has to actually work
Removing something leaves a gap, and a gap gets filled back the same way. What worked in Rat Park wasn't the absence of morphine, it was companions, wheels, somewhere to go. So the second step is putting something you genuinely like into that slot, not leaving it bare.
e.g. Replacing the phone with staring at the ceiling rarely holds. Replacing it with something your hands are doing does.

### The parts · When the cage can't be moved, this doesn't apply
The method assumes the cage is movable. Some situations aren't — you can't leave the job, move the family, replace the person. Forcing 'change your environment' there only adds a layer of failure. That's when to find professional help rather than keep pushing on the situation.
e.g. Blaming yourself for not changing an environment you genuinely cannot change is effort in the wrong place.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you want to stop something, you've tried, each attempt ran on holding out, and each broke in the same place.
Ask first: for the last ten times — what hour, what place, what state? Find the common factor and move that, not the thing itself.
Where it goes wrong: turning it into a universal explanation that replaces medical help; and don't assume removal is the end. The vacated slot needs filling or it fills itself back.

### Lines to keep
Take apart the props holding it up, not the thing itself.
The trigger is often not craving. It's one recurring empty slot.
The slot you vacate will be filled back the same way.

========================================================================
## Records of the Grand Historian · No empty praise, nothing concealed
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/records-of-the-grand-historian/no-praise-no-hiding/
Source: Ban Gu's assessment in the History of the Han; the biographies
Tags: Deep read, Records of the Grand Historian, The credit and the damage in one paragraph

Six characters from a later historian, and still the standard for the form. What makes doing it so hard.

### Q: What actually happened?
Ban Gu's verdict on the Records: the writing is straight, the facts checked, no empty praise and no concealment of evil, and so it may be called a true record. The weight of that shows only in the entries. He wrote Li Guang as the general beneath whom a path wore itself smooth, and also as the man who put eight hundred men who had surrendered to death, and who cut his own throat after losing the way and missing the rendezvous. He wrote Huo Qubing's indifference to his soldiers. He wrote his own emperor hunting immortality.

### The parts · Concealing nothing is hardest about your own side
Recording the faults of people you dislike is easy. Recording the faults of people you admire is very hard, because it amounts to admitting your own judgement was not pure. He plainly sympathised with Li Guang and set the problems down anyway.
e.g. Reviewing a project you pushed for, the part most easily skipped is how badly the reasons you gave at the time have aged.

### The parts · No empty praise is a protection for the reader
Write someone as flawless and the reader takes nothing usable away, because flawless people do not exist and there is no way to tell which part to copy. Set out where a person was strong and how exactly they wrecked things, and the record becomes usable.
e.g. An internal case study with only the good parts teaches nothing. Put the holes and the near-miss back in and it turns into an asset.

### The parts · The standard has to bind the most powerful subject too
He wrote Emperor Wu while serving under Emperor Wu, including the cost of the sacrifices, the magicians and the campaigns. The credibility of any recording system is decided by whether it still applies to the one person you cannot afford to offend.
e.g. Every incident review drives to root cause, except where a senior executive's decision is involved and it becomes external factors. After that, no review is worth reading.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have to write something up, and a person or a decision you backed is inside it.
Ask first: is there a line in this record I would rather not put down?
Where it goes wrong: reading objectivity as severity towards enemies, and making one exception for the person you cannot afford to offend.

### Lines to keep
No empty praise, no concealment of evil: therefore, a true record.
Peach and plum trees do not speak, yet a path forms beneath them.
Objectivity that stops at your own side is only selection.

## Records of the Grand Historian · I find myself in much perplexity
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/records-of-the-grand-historian/i-am-confused/
Source: Records of the Grand Historian, Biography of Bo Yi
Tags: Deep read, Records of the Grand Historian, Write down what you could not work out

He admits in the first of the biographies that he cannot work it out. Why those words outrank any conclusion.

### Q: What actually happened?
In the Biography of Bo Yi he lays out a problem he cannot solve. The saying goes that Heaven's way has no favourites and always sides with the good man. Yet Bo Yi and Shu Qi, who kept themselves clean, starved to death; Yan Hui, who loved learning, died young; Robber Zhi killed innocent men daily, gathered thousands and ranged over the empire, and died of old age. So he writes: I find myself in much perplexity. Is this so-called Way of Heaven right, or is it wrong? He supplies no answer.

### The parts · Admitting there is no answer beats supplying a false one
Forcing an unexplained thing into an existing explanation is the cheapest move available and the most damaging, because everyone after you will assume the matter is settled and stop asking. Writing down that you do not understand hands the question on intact.
e.g. A post-mortem concluding that the main cause was poor execution does far more harm than one saying the cause is not yet understood. The first closes the file; the second leaves a door.

### The parts · A perplexity has to be specific enough to be checked
His is not abstract doubt. It is three concrete cases held against each other: Bo Yi, Yan Hui, Robber Zhi. Being specific is what lets later people carry the question forward. A vague sense that life is unfair is not a question, only a sigh.
e.g. Why do users not renew is a sigh. These three churned accounts behaved in their final month exactly like the ones who stayed is something you can chase.

### The parts · He put it first
Seventy biographies, and the one with no answer opens the sequence. The placement is itself a statement: what follows deals with a world where even basic cause and effect is uncertain. Declare what you do not know first and the rest can be trusted.
e.g. An analysis that opens with which data are missing and which conclusions are guesses is the one whose judgements people dare to act on.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a review or an analysis contains a stretch you have not actually worked out.
Ask first: am I about to give it a presentable explanation, or mark it and leave it for whoever comes next?
Where it goes wrong: closing the inquiry with an all-purpose cause, or writing the perplexity as a sigh instead of as a comparison somebody could check.

### Lines to keep
I find myself in much perplexity.
Is this so-called Way of Heaven right, or is it wrong?
Robber Zhi killed the innocent daily and died of old age.

## Ren Zhengfei · Huawei's winter
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/ren-zhengfei/huaweis-winter/
Source: Ren Zhengfei, Huawei's Winter, 2001, published
Tags: Deep read, Ren Zhengfei, Talking bankruptcy in a record year

In the company's best year he circulated an essay about failing. The parts that turn a mood into a mechanism.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 2001, revenue just past twenty billion yuan and profits high, Ren published Huawei's Winter. It opens with a question: what do we do on the day sales fall, or the company goes under? Then the admission: for ten years I have thought about failure every day, blind to success, with no sense of honour or pride, only a sense of crisis. Then the verdict, that the day of failure will certainly come and everyone should be ready to meet it. He insisted this was an assignment rather than a mood. Winter passes and spring arrives, but the coat is sewn beforehand.

### The parts · Make the sense of crisis in a good year; a bad one makes only panic
Raise the alarm while results are falling and people scatter. Raise it in the best year and there is slack to convert worry into coats: contingency plans, cash, spare capability. The timing of the essay is the method. The drill happens while nothing is burning.
e.g. Stress tests, cutting redundant process and stockpiling cash look ugly in a record year. Done in a falling quarter, every cut lands on morale instead.

### The parts · Thinking about failure daily is a way of aiming attention
Blind to success is not modesty theatre, it is allocation. Good news arrives by itself and bad signals have to be hunted. Wherever a leader's scarce attention rests, the organisation grows an information system to match: watch success and you grow pipes that carry congratulations.
e.g. Change the first item of the weekly meeting from this week's wins to the thing that came closest to going wrong. Three months later the reporting has changed shape.

### The parts · Hand how do we survive to every single person
The essay keeps saying every one of us. A sense of crisis owned only by the founder is just the founder's insomnia. Translate it into a question anyone can answer: if a cheaper method replaced your job tomorrow, what keeps you here? That is what institutionalising it means.
e.g. Ask every team to write one page a year on what would remove this group's reason to exist. Teams that can write it usually do not die.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the company is at its best and nobody wants to hear bad news.
Ask first: are our winter coats, cash, contingency, a second capability, being made in this good year, or after it gets cold?
Where it goes wrong: turning the sense of crisis into permanent high-pressure fear until everyone is numb. He said prepare for winter, not live in it.

### Lines to keep
For ten years I have thought about failure every day, not success.
The day of failure will certainly come. Be ready to meet it.
Winter always passes and spring comes. Use the winter to prepare.

========================================================================
## Ren Zhengfei · Let those who hear the gunfire call for artillery
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/ren-zhengfei/sound-of-gunfire/
Source: Ren Zhengfei's 2009 speech to the sales and service organisation, published
Tags: Deep read, Ren Zhengfei, Turning authority toward the front

Headquarters that will not release authority leaves the front line unable to fight. The organisational inversion behind the slogan.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 2009 Ren named the big-company disease inside Huawei: right now the front line fights and the rear directs. Authority sat with the headquarters furthest from the customer, and by the time resources were approved the opening had closed. His direction was to move the command post to where the guns can be heard: let the people who hear the gunfire call in the artillery, the front line drawing resources itself, headquarters converting from a control centre into a service and support centre. He added the counterweight in the same breath. Calling for artillery costs money, and the caller carries it.

### The parts · Command belongs where the information is
The front line learns first that a customer has cooled or a rival has moved, but the resources are decided by a headquarters that knows the battlefield through reports. Five retellings sit between the decision and the fact, each adding distortion and delay. Move authority to the information, rather than making information climb to authority.
e.g. An urgent customer request queues upward for scheduling, and by the time it is approved the customer has signed elsewhere. Give the account manager a spending limit and the game changes.

### The parts · The call for artillery has to carry a price
Devolve authority without accounting and the front treats firepower as free, which is exactly why headquarters will not devolve it. His design pairs them: resources drawn are booked against the unit's own results, wins share more, waste is carried locally. Authority, responsibility and reward descend together.
e.g. Give the front its own budget, then put gross margin and resource use into its bonus formula. The call is free and the invoice is theirs.

### The parts · Headquarters is now measured on response time
The other half of the inversion happens at the rear. If headquarters becomes a service rather than an approver, the scorecard has to move too, from how many non-compliant requests we stopped to how fast we answered the front. Leave the scorecard alone and service stays a word.
e.g. Add average response time on front-line requests to the back-office scorecard and publish the ranking. Only then does service centre become a job rather than a slogan.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the front line says resources never come through and headquarters says the front asks for anything it likes.
Ask first: who holds the information this decision needs, how many layers separate it from the authority, and did the cost accounting go down with the power?
Where it goes wrong: devolving authority without the ledger, so the front sets off fireworks; or using the front line is calling to override every professional check, when compliance and risk are gunfire too.

### Lines to keep
Let the people who hear the gunfire call in the artillery.
Right now the front line fights and the rear directs.
Headquarters must become a service and support centre, not a control centre.

========================================================================
## Sapiens · Cooperation runs on fiction
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sapiens/fictions-that-cooperate/
Source: Sapiens, chapters 2 and 10
Tags: Deep read, Sapiens, A company is a story too

Chimpanzees top out at a few dozen collaborators. Sapiens run to millions. Harari says the difference is something nobody can touch.

### Q: What actually happened?
Harari's claim is flat and strange: any large-scale human cooperation is rooted in myths that exist only in our collective imagination. States, money, laws, human rights, limited companies — none can be touched, and each works the moment enough people believe at once. His example is Peugeot. The plant could burn, every employee could leave, every shareholder could sell, and Peugeot would still exist, because it was never the building or the people. Money he calls the most universal and most efficient system of mutual trust ever devised: two men who hate each other will still take each other's cash.

### The parts · The organisation is the story people still believe
Assets can be sold, staff replaced, offices moved. While the story of who we are and what we are for still holds, the organisation exists. When the story goes, the assets and the people are all still there and the thing has already dissolved.
e.g. One public gap between what a founder says and what he does costs more than a bad quarter. A bad quarter damages assets; that damages the story.

### The parts · Rewriting the story beats rewriting the process
Harari's point about Sapiens is that we can revise a fiction fast and change behaviour with it — France went from divine right to popular sovereignty inside a year. Change the process without changing the story and people will read the new process through the old one.
e.g. Going from sales-led to product-led is not an org chart. It became real the day a large contract was turned down in public to protect the roadmap.

### The parts · Trusting the note is cheaper than trusting the person
What makes money the strongest of the fictions is that it converts trust in a person into trust in a system. Cooperation stops requiring that either side like or understand the other. It requires only that both accept the same token.
e.g. Two departments that cannot stand each other do not need an away day. They need one unit of account both sides accept — hours, credits, an internal transfer price.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you need people who do not know each other, and may not like each other, to cooperate.
Ask first: what is the story or the token they all believe in, and is it still credible this week?
Where it goes wrong: treating the story as a lie you can improvise — one exposure zeroes it — or repairing the rules and then wondering why nothing moved.

### Lines to keep
Any large-scale human cooperation is rooted in common myths.
Money is the most universal and most efficient system of mutual trust ever devised.
Peugeot is a figment of our collective imagination.

========================================================================
## Sapiens · Wheat domesticated us
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sapiens/wheat-domesticated-us/
Source: Sapiens, chapter 5
Tags: Deep read, Sapiens, The luxury trap

The agricultural revolution multiplied people and made the average life worse. This is how a species can win while every member of it loses.

### Q: What actually happened?
Harari turns the standard account inside out: we did not domesticate wheat, it domesticated us. Sapiens bent over weeding, hauling water, spreading manure; the diet narrowed, the hours lengthened, disease arrived. Counted in copies of DNA, wheat became the most successful plant on earth. Counted in how a life went, the farmer did worse than the forager. He calls the agricultural revolution history's biggest fraud. The mechanism is the luxury trap: luxuries tend to become necessities and to spawn new obligations. Each step made the day easier and the sum was one-way, because by then the population was too large for the old life to feed.

### The parts · A total can rise while every unit inside it falls
The species wins and the individual loses is a structure that shows up everywhere: headcount, revenue, users, gross domestic product. Aggregate measures and individual conditions are not two views of one thing. They can move apart, and they can move in opposite directions.
e.g. In the two years revenue doubled, hours per head, attrition and sick leave all rose together. The annual report and the medical notes describe the same period.

### The parts · The luxury trap is a one-way door
Every new convenience arrives as an option. Once it is in use, life reorganises around it, and then it is a requirement carrying maintenance of its own. The test is simple: if this broke for a week, could I go back to how things were?
e.g. A vendor taken on to try it out, a platform adopted for now. Two years later the whole workflow has grown into it and there is nothing to unplug it from.

### The parts · The exit closed when the scale changed
Why not go back to foraging? Because farming had already raised the population past what foraging could feed. Every step of expansion raises the minimum output needed just to stand still, and that floor is the real lock — harder to undo than any contract.
e.g. A team tripled on the cash flow of a new line cannot drop that line later even when it turns marginal. The opportunity became the mortgage.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: an upgrade is on the table and every step of it makes today easier.
Ask first: once this is in, how much does my minimum running cost rise, and could I go back if it broke for a week?
Where it goes wrong: refusing every tool in the name of avoiding traps, or watching the aggregate number and ignoring what is happening to the people inside it.

### Lines to keep
We did not domesticate wheat. It domesticated us.
Luxuries tend to become necessities and to spawn new obligations.
The Agricultural Revolution: more people kept alive under worse conditions.

========================================================================
## Robert Sapolsky · Built for escape, left switched on
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sapolsky/stress-mismatch/
Source: Why Zebras Don't Get Ulcers
Tags: Deep read, Robert Sapolsky, The problem is that it won't turn off

People and zebras run the same stress system. Why only one of them gets sick from it.

### Q: What actually happened?
The title is the whole argument. Zebras don't get ulcers because their stress response runs for a few minutes. A lion charges: heart rate up, glucose released, immune function paused — and the moment they've escaped, it shuts off. Ours is identical, and we run it against mortgages, managers and an unanswered email. So Sapolsky's verdict is that what makes people ill isn't the stress, it's the response staying on. Its price is suspended repair, digestion and long-term building. Fine briefly. Left on, it diverts the maintenance budget indefinitely.

### The parts · It isn't intensity, it's duration
A week-long sprint doesn't damage anyone. Two years of being permanently on call does. To assess your own state, the question isn't how tired you've been lately. It's when the system was last genuinely switched off.
e.g. One project straight into the next for two years. The body never entered repair mode, which is more dangerous than any single hard week.

### The parts · The cost is charged somewhere you can't see
What gets paused under stress is immunity, digestion and tissue repair, and those debts don't show up the same day. So people misjudge how well they're coping. By the time symptoms appear the account has usually been running a long while.
e.g. Rarely ill through a punishing stretch and flattened the moment the holiday starts. Relaxing didn't weaken you.

### The parts · The specifically human problem is imagination
A zebra starts the response on seeing an actual lion. A person can start the entire thing by thinking about something that might happen. That's the core mechanism of chronic human stress, and why working on the thoughts themselves is a real intervention.
e.g. Rehearsing the worst version of a conversation that hasn't happened produces much the same physiology as having it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: tense for a long time, unable to point at what's wrong.
Ask first: when did this system last actually switch off? Has there been any stretch where I wasn't on call?
Where it goes wrong: hearing it as 'stress is all in your head' — real pressure has real physiological consequences. This is about duration, not whether it's genuine.

### Lines to keep
Zebras don't get ulcers because the response runs for minutes.
What makes people ill is the response that won't switch off.
A person can start the whole thing by imagining it.

## Robert Sapolsky · Uncertainty hurts more than intensity
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sapolsky/predictability/
Source: Thirty years of baboon field research; stress physiology experiments
Tags: Deep read, Robert Sapolsky, Predictability and control

Same pressure, and one person breaks while another doesn't. What the actual variable turns out to be.

### Q: What actually happened?
Sapolsky spent thirty years watching wild baboons in East Africa. Low-ranking animals ran chronically high stress hormones and worse health across the board. But rank wasn't the key thing: at the same low rank, individuals who could anticipate when they'd be harassed, and who had social allies, had markedly better markers. The lab agrees. At the same pressure, predictability and a sense of control cut the damage sharply. That moves the intervention from reducing stress to adding certainty and autonomy — usually far cheaper.

### The parts · Definite bad news beats being left hanging
People and animals adapt to a certain bad. They don't adapt to uncertainty. Which is why delaying an announcement often does more harm than the announcement — for the whole delay, everyone is on call.
e.g. A restructuring where the plan never lands costs more than the plan itself. A firm date saves half of it.

### The parts · Control is a cheap buffer
At identical workload, people who decide their own order and pace show a markedly lower stress response. Adding autonomy doesn't require removing any tasks and cuts the wear substantially.
e.g. Swap 'these five, in this order, today' for 'these five today, you choose the order'. Same load, different experience.

### The parts · Social support is a physiological variable
Baboons with allies, and people with stable relationships, show better markers under equal pressure. This isn't reassurance, it's a measurable difference. Isolation is itself a health risk.
e.g. Keeping one or two colleagues you can be honest with through a brutal project beats an extra hour of sleep.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: under heavy pressure that isn't going to decrease.
Ask first: is there any way to make what's coming more predictable — a fixed date, a definite answer? Can I take back some say over the order and pace?
Where it goes wrong: turning 'control helps' into needing to control everything, which is a new load of its own.

### Lines to keep
Same pressure. With predictability and control, far less damage.
Low-ranking baboons ran high hormones. The ones with allies didn't.
People adapt to a certain bad. They don't adapt to hanging.

========================================================================
## Virginia Satir · The iceberg: layers under the act
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/satir/iceberg/
Source: The Satir model
Tags: Deep read, Virginia Satir, The fight is happening on the surface

The same argument for ten years and no movement. The reason is that it is being had on the wrong layer.

### Q: What actually happened?
Satir splits a person into the behaviour above the waterline and, below it, feelings, perceptions, expectations, yearnings and the self. Conflict happens almost entirely on the surface and is settled underneath: his anger is behaviour, under it sits disappointment, and under that sits I want to be treated as though I matter. Argue about who is right at the surface and it never ends, because the sentence at the surface was never the point. The problem is not the problem; coping is the problem is her own summary of the whole method.

### The parts · Look for the expectation under the words
A partner complains that you come home late. On the face of it this is scheduling; underneath it is usually where do I rank in this house. Answer the face of it and you are in an argument about calendars. Answer the expectation and the conversation turns.
e.g. All you care about is work does not want the reply that is not true. It wants: have you been feeling left behind lately?

### The parts · Under the feeling there is a reading
Many people think naming the feeling is the end of the work, but feelings are produced by readings. The same late arrival, read as he does not care about me and read as he is flat out today, makes two different feelings. What often needs changing is the reading.
e.g. A remark that ruined your whole day: ask what you took it to mean, and whether a second reading also fits the same facts.

### The parts · The yearning layer is common ground
The further down you go the more alike people are: to be loved, accepted, of some worth. Two people locked in opposition at the surface usually want the same thing three layers down. Seeing that layer takes the hostility out of a room faster than any argument.
e.g. Parents pushing marriage and a child refusing look like enemies. Below: I want your life to go well, and I want to be treated as an adult.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the same argument keeps coming back and reasoning does not touch it.
Ask first: what feeling sits under that sentence, and what expectation sits under the feeling? Which layer am I answering?
Where it goes wrong: using the iceberg to analyse the other person. What you really want is attention is a verdict, not understanding.

### Lines to keep
The problem is not the problem; coping is the problem.
The conflict is on the surface. The solution is underneath.
Further down we are alike: loved, accepted, worth something.

## Virginia Satir · Four stances under pressure
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/satir/coping-stances/
Source: Satir on communication stances
Tags: Deep read, Virginia Satir, Placate, blame, compute, distract

In a fight people turn into somebody else. This is the list of who they turn into.

### Q: What actually happened?
Under pressure, Satir found, people fall back into placating, blaming, being super-reasonable or distracting. Placating gives up the self, blaming gives up the other, super-reasonable gives up both and keeps the logic, distracting gives up the subject. All four are automatic and all four avoid what is actually happening. She proposed a fifth, congruence, holding self, other and situation at once, and insisted it is trained rather than inherited. She would also stand a family up as a sculpture: who is near whom, who has their back turned. Set it up, she said, and everyone sees it at once.

### The parts · The stances set each other off
Blaming usually pulls placating or super-reasonable out of the other person; distracting pulls harder blame. So escalation is not a question of who went too far, it is two stances locking together. Reading the pair is more use than establishing who started.
e.g. The more carefully you set out the logic, the louder he gets: that is super-reasonable meeting blame, and neither of you is in the room.

### The parts · Placating has the best-hidden bill
Placating costs least in the moment, which is why it so often passes for maturity. What it does is take your own needs out of the account, and the account gets settled somewhere else: in a sudden detonation, or in years of quiet distance.
e.g. Fine, whatever you want, for years, and then one small thing sets off the whole backlog, and the other person genuinely cannot see where it came from.

### The parts · Congruence is not saying whatever you feel
Congruence holds three things together: what I feel, where the other person is, and what this occasion is. Drop any one and it is not congruence. Only yourself is venting, only the other is placating, only the occasion is being super-reasonable.
e.g. Contradicted by a junior colleague in public, the congruent move is neither crushing it there nor pretending it did not happen, but saying your piece to him afterwards.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the conflict starts and both of you turn into somebody else.
Ask first: which stance did I fall back into? Which one is he in? Are the two of them setting each other off?
Where it goes wrong: using the four as labels for people. You are just a blamer is itself blaming.

### Lines to keep
Under pressure people placate, blame, go super-reasonable, or distract.
Congruence holds three things: myself, the other person, the situation.
A family's real structure cannot be said. Stand it up and everyone sees.

========================================================================
## Scarcity · The bandwidth tax
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/scarcity/bandwidth-tax/
Source: Mullainathan and Shafir, Scarcity (2013); the Indian sugarcane study
Tags: Deep read, Scarcity, Every shortage takes the same mind

People short of money get called short-sighted. This piece asks whether that is a character trait or a description of the situation.

### Q: What actually happened?
They tested Indian sugarcane farmers twice: the same men before the harvest, when money was tight, and after it, when the money had arrived. The same person scored differently on the same cognitive tests. They call it the bandwidth tax — scarcity captures the mind, and what it captures is not available for anything else. So being short-sighted may be a consequence of having no money rather than the cause of it. The size of that effect has been contested since. This piece takes the direction and leaves the number alone.

### The parts · One bandwidth, and both shortages draw on it
This is the model's most useful move: it folds two apparently unrelated troubles into one. Doing the month's arithmetic and racing a deadline draw on the same attention, which is why the two arriving together are so much worse than either alone. Not weak will. Bandwidth pulled from both ends.
e.g. Working out how far short this month is while finishing a proposal, and doing both badly. That is not laziness.

### The parts · The test is whether he does it when things are loose
Swapping a character explanation for a situational one needs something you can check. The sugarcane study is strong precisely because it compares one group of men at two moments, instead of comparing poor people with rich ones.
e.g. A mistake that stops happening after the harvest does not belong on that man's personality.

### The parts · The conclusion is for institutions, not for self-blame
The real use of this model is in design: take away things a stretched person has to remember, forms to fill in, decisions to make. That beats telling him to think more clearly. Turned on yourself it is a reminder, not an amnesty.
e.g. Setting the repayment to leave the account automatically beats reminding yourself every month not to forget it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: money or time is tight, and you keep making decisions that look stupid a week later.
Ask first: would I make these mistakes when things were loose? If not, stop trying to fix your character and start removing things that occupy the bandwidth.
Where it goes wrong: using it as an amnesty for every lapse; or turning it outward to label somebody else. It explains a situation, it does not classify a person.

### Lines to keep
Scarcity captures the mind.
Being short of money and short of time draw on one bandwidth.
This model is built for designing systems, not for blaming yourself.

## Scarcity · Tunnelling
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/scarcity/tunneling/
Source: Scarcity: the twin concepts of tunneling and slack
Tags: Deep read, Scarcity, The urgent crowds out the important

The busier you get, the less the important things get done. This piece argues that is a mechanism rather than bad planning.

### Q: What actually happened?
Scarcity narrows attention, and the narrowing has a name: tunneling. The most urgent thing is lit brilliantly, and everything outside the tunnel — the check-up, the insurance, the repayment plan, the call you owe somebody — goes dark. It is not purely a loss; focus inside the tunnel genuinely rescues the emergency. The cost simply lands outside it, and lands late. Their companion idea is slack: with slack, one small accident stays one small accident. Without it, the same accident capsizes you.

### The parts · The efficiency inside the tunnel is real, and so is the bill
People genuinely work faster and sharper near a deadline. That speed is borrowed: it is drawn from attention that belonged outside the tunnel, and the loan comes due in weeks or in years. Run it as a normal operating mode and every quarter goes on clearing the last one.
e.g. The output a deadline forces out of you usually costs a stretch with no check-ups, no replies and no long-term decisions taken at all.

### The parts · Slack is not waste, it is room to be wrong
Filling the calendar and the account to the last unit looks like maximum efficiency. It is actually setting your tolerance for error to zero. With room, one surprise stays one surprise. Without it the same surprise chains: borrowing, penalties, the real work missed.
e.g. An emergency fund you are not allowed to touch is not there for the return. It is there so that one accident does not turn into five.

### The parts · You fix a tunnel with structure, not with reminders
Reminders fail inside the tunnel, because you did not forget — at that moment you could not see it. What works is moving the important thing somewhere that needs no attention: the automatic payment, the appointment already booked, the schedule somebody else watches for you.
e.g. A check-up already booked and already paid for is more reliable than intending to arrange one when things calm down.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: everything lately is firefighting, and nothing important but unurgent has moved at all.
Ask first: which of the things being squeezed out becomes the next fire if it waits? Move that one into a form that does not need you to remember it.
Where it goes wrong: using tunnelling as a reason not to plan; or building so much slack that you stop putting out the fire actually in front of you.

### Lines to keep
The urgent is lit up; everything outside the tunnel goes dark.
Slack is not waste. It is room to be wrong.
The same mistake costs the poorer side far more.

========================================================================
## Thomas Schelling · The advantage of tied hands
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/schelling/binding-yourself/
Source: The Strategy of Conflict, chapter 2
Tags: Deep read, Thomas Schelling, Trade options away for credibility

Game theory says more options are better. This is about the case where Schelling proved the opposite.

### Q: What actually happened?
The Strategy of Conflict sets up a proposition against instinct: the power to constrain an adversary may depend on the power to bind oneself. In bargaining, tying yourself to a position and burning the way back can win. The mechanism is credibility. You say you will never concede, and what the other side reads is not your tone but whether you still can. Anyone holding a concession in reserve has his threats discounted. His extreme case is the game of chicken: the driver who pulls the steering wheel off and throws it out of the window, in full view, wins.

### The parts · Credibility comes from cannot, not from will not
I do not want to concede is a preference and can change at any moment. I cannot concede is a fact the other side has to plan around. A strong commitment therefore converts preference into structure: a public statement, a clause, an agent with no authority to vary. Each welds will not into cannot.
e.g. This is my final price convinces nobody. The price is locked by head office sends them to the other terms. The second is strong because it made you weak.

### The parts · Whoever binds first sets the problem
While both sides can still move, bargaining is a two-way pull. The moment one side locks itself irreversibly, the whole remaining room to adjust belongs to the other, who either crashes or goes around. The order of commitment is therefore a weapon in its own right.
e.g. A company announcing a shipping date in public has handed the question of who adapts to whom to its entire supply chain. After that, everyone else bends.

### The parts · Bind the wrong hand and it stays bound
The cost is written into the principle: credibility comes from irreversibility, so a mistake cannot be walked back. Two checks before using it. Is this position worth all of your flexibility, and might they prefer to crash? Make self-binding a daily posture and you will end up welded to something small.
e.g. A public never discount flag looks strong until the market turns, share drains away and there is no way down. The bargaining edge is repaid with interest.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you need them to believe you will not move.
Ask first: can I turn will not into a cannot they can verify, and is this position worth burning my flexibility for?
Where it goes wrong: binding yourself weekly until the word irreversible means nothing; or tying your hands and quietly untying them, which is found out once and ends every commitment you make afterwards.

### Lines to keep
The power to constrain an adversary may depend on the power to bind oneself.
In bargaining, weakness is often strength.
A threat works when they believe you have no choice left.

## Thomas Schelling · The Schelling point
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/schelling/focal-points/
Source: The Strategy of Conflict, chapter 3
Tags: Deep read, Thomas Schelling, Meeting without being able to talk

Two people are lost in New York and cannot call each other. This is about why most of them pick the same spot.

### Q: What actually happened?
Schelling ran a famous informal experiment. You have to meet someone in New York. Neither of you was told where or when, and you cannot communicate. Where do you go, and at what hour? The answers clustered hard: the information booth at Grand Central, at noon. Nothing makes that place better on any logical test. It wins on prominence, because everybody guesses that everybody else will guess it. Schelling called such places focal points: when people cannot communicate, they converge on the place each expects the other to expect. The force is not in being reasonable. It is in everyone knowing that everyone knows.

### The parts · Coordination runs on shared prominence, not optimality
When several parties must line up without enough communication, the winner is not the best option but the most visible and the most easily guessed at by everyone else: round numbers, precedent, last time's place, first on the list. Designing a default means looking for the point everyone would blindly point to.
e.g. A team across time zones can never compute the slot that suits everyone. Ten on Monday morning is not optimal, and everyone can guess it, so it holds.

### The parts · Focal points are the hidden floor of a negotiation
Where does haggling actually land? Often on a focal point: split it down the middle, a round price, last year's terms. Once you move off the focal point every particular number needs a reason, and reasons are a new battlefield. Controlling a negotiation is sometimes just placing that point in advance.
e.g. The gap between asking a hundred and asking ninety-seven is not three. A hundred needs no explanation; ninety-seven invites why not ninety-five.

### The parts · A convention is valuable because it is focal
Plenty of conventions are not defensible on their merits, and they are still the point everyone knows everyone knows. Abolish one without supplying a new focal point and what you get is not an improvement, it is dispersal. Have the replacement ready and equally prominent.
e.g. Cancel the weekly report with nothing to replace it and information does not move to a better channel. It scatters into private messages.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: several parties have to line up and the cost of talking it all through is too high.
Ask first: what is the natural focal point here, and can the answer I want be placed at it?
Where it goes wrong: insisting on an optimum nobody would ever guess; or abusing focal points to dress an unfair split as the way it has always been done.

### Lines to keep
When people cannot communicate, they converge on what each expects the other to expect.
A focal point wins on prominence, not on merit.
Meeting in New York? Most said the information booth at noon.

========================================================================
## Seneca · Time is the one cost you cannot earn back
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/seneca/on-shortness-of-life/
Source: On the Shortness of Life
Tags: Deep read, Seneca, Price things in hours before you price them in money

The same man haggles over a small bill and gives away a whole evening without a thought. Where the arithmetic goes wrong.

### Q: What actually happened?
The essay has one argument. It is not that we have a short time to live, but that we waste a lot of it. He is savage about the busy — men occupied with everybody's affairs but their own, who find at the end that they spent the whole of life getting ready to live. And he points at an asymmetry: people guard money down to the last coin and hand out their time to anyone who asks. Money lost can be earned again. His conclusion is not gloomy: life is long enough, if you know how to use it.

### The parts · Convert the cost from money into hours
The question to ask of a commitment is not what it costs but how many of your hours it takes, and where those hours would otherwise have gone. Run the conversion and a mass of apparently free consumption shows up: the free meeting, the small favour, the thing you had to attend.
e.g. Price a three-hour dinner at your own hourly rate and write the number on paper. Most people decline on the spot.

### The parts · The most expensive waste is living on someone else's agenda
His busy men are not idle. They are the most industrious people in the book, and their time is full of other people's business, every item of it with a good reason. That is exactly the danger: no single item looks refusable, and the sum of them is a life.
e.g. Every entry in the calendar can justify itself and not one of them was your idea. What needs cutting is not an entry, it is the default of saying yes.

### The parts · You do not have to be ready in order to begin
His sharpest observation is that people postpone living: after the promotion, once the children are grown, in retirement. The future is the least reliable asset there is. A life spent in preparation is not a short life, it is one that never started.
e.g. Once this project is over, I will — if you have been saying that for three years, what it needs is not a better moment but one small step today.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the week is full, every item is defensible, and you cannot name one thing in it you chose.
Ask first: how many hours does this take, where would those hours have gone, and who is writing my calendar?
Where it goes wrong: running the ledger on the people closest to you; or using my time is precious as cover for work you owe.

### Lines to keep
Life, if you know how to use it, is long.
You live as if you were destined to live for ever.
Price it in hours first. The money question hides the real cost.

## Seneca · Anger has a gate, and it is the second step
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/seneca/on-anger/
Source: On Anger
Tags: Deep read, Seneca, You cannot stop the impression. You can withhold the assent

Anger looks like a single explosion. It is three movements, and exactly one of them is available to you.

### Q: What actually happened?
He takes anger apart into three movements. An impression arrives on its own: that was an insult. Then you assent to it: yes, an insult it was. Only then comes the decision to hit back. The first is reflex and cannot be stopped; by the third you are already moving. The middle one is the only place reason can get in. So the training is not to bottle the heat, it is to withhold the stamp: refuse to sign and the chain comes apart. Certain of the wise men, he notes, have claimed that anger is temporary madness. His own prescription is duller. The greatest remedy for anger is delay.

### The parts · Only the assent is catchable
The racing heart and the blood in the face are physiology. They cannot be suppressed and do not need to be. The choice arrives a second later: do I certify this as malice aimed at me? A great many insults are clumsiness, exhaustion, or somebody with no attention to spare.
e.g. Contradicted in a meeting, hold off on he is picking a fight. Spend three seconds on what his week looks like. The verdict usually changes.

### The parts · Delay is the plainest technique and the best one
His advice is to push the response out — to tomorrow, or to the far side of a walk. Not because time solves anything, but because the assent passes most easily at the peak. Once the tide goes out, the same event weighs less on its own.
e.g. Write the furious email and leave it in drafts overnight. Most of them get rewritten heavily. A good number never get sent.

### The parts · Not being angry is not the same as not acting
The method gets read as swallowing it. What he wants is the handling separated from the heat: hold people to account, draw the line, end the arrangement — but do it with the judgement you have when calm. What anger settles usually needs clearing up afterwards.
e.g. If they really did cross a line, say so and cut it off. Just pick the hour when you can put the sentences together properly.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: somebody got to you and you are composing the reply.
Ask first: am I still receiving the impression, or have I already signed the judgement? What is actually lost by answering tomorrow?
Where it goes wrong: letting delay turn into never dealing with it at all; or using I am working on myself to suppress a boundary that ought to be stated out loud.

### Lines to keep
The greatest remedy for anger is delay.
Certain of the wise men have claimed that anger is temporary madness.
Only the middle step is yours. Refuse the assent and it stops.

========================================================================
## Shang Yang · Moving the pole
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/shang-yang/moving-the-pole/
Source: Records of the Grand Historian, Life of Lord Shang
Tags: Deep read, Shang Yang, Prove you mean it before you ask

The new code was already drafted and he went and moved a piece of timber first. This is about what the timber solved.

### Q: What actually happened?
The laws were written and not yet published, and he was afraid the people would not believe them. He had a pole thirty feet long set up at the south gate of the capital and offered ten pieces of gold to anyone who would carry it to the north gate. Nobody moved; they thought it strange. He raised it to fifty. One man carried it across and was handed fifty on the spot — to make clear that there was no deception. Then the laws were published. The act had nothing to do with their content.

### The parts · A rule takes effect only once it is believed
A rule nobody expects to be enforced does not exist. So the first spending on a new system should not go on explaining the content; it should go on one small, certain thing you can deliver immediately. Prove delivery first, argue content second.
e.g. Rather than announce that promotions now follow the new standard, run the new standard once and pay out, however small the case. After that people listen.

### The parts · The reward has to be unreasonable
At ten nobody moved; at fifty someone tried. He was not economising, he was manufacturing a signal impossible to ignore. The stranger the price, the further it travels and the longer it is remembered. On this particular job, proportionate is ineffective.
e.g. Reward the first person who reports a hole in the process so publicly that everyone is startled. For six months afterwards candour rises. The money bought that, not the report.

### The parts · Credit has to be paid in advance
He delivered before he had a single achievement to point at. The order cannot be reversed: you cannot say that once the reforms work people will naturally trust them. A system's credit must exist before it starts asking anyone to pay, or the first demand is met at a discount.
e.g. Ask the team for a quarter of overtime and promise to make it up afterwards. With no record of having made anything up before, the promise is discounted on day one.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are introducing a rule and you doubt anyone will take it seriously.
Ask first: before I ask anyone for anything, which visible thing have I already delivered?
Where it goes wrong: repeating the announcement instead of delivering once; keeping the cost of the first proof so low that the signal is invisible.

### Lines to keep
They thought it strange and nobody dared move it.
He paid the fifty on the spot, to show there was no deception.
Doubtful action wins no name; doubtful work wins no result.

## Shang Yang · The law does not bend for rank
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/shang-yang/law-above-rank/
Source: The Book of Lord Shang, Rewards and Punishments; Records of the Grand Historian
Tags: Deep read, Shang Yang, The first exception is the end of it

A year into the new code the crown prince broke it. This is about how that one hour set the strength of the system for a decade.

### Q: What actually happened?
A year in, thousands of Qin subjects came to the capital to say the new laws were unworkable. Just then the crown prince broke one. When the law is not carried out, it is because those above break it, Shang Yang said. The heir could not be punished, so his tutor Prince Qian was, and his other tutor Gongsun Jia was branded. The next day the people of Qin obeyed. Ten years on, nothing dropped on the road was picked up and there were no bandits in the hills.

### The parts · The first exception is the end of it
A system's strength is not set by its text but by what happens to the first person important enough to test it. Let one through and everyone immediately learns that the real rule is who you are. After that, restating it changes nothing.
e.g. The first person to file late is a senior one and nothing follows. Next month everyone is late, and none of them feel wrong. They learned from the handling, not the text.

### The parts · If you cannot touch him, touch the man beside him
He did not go at the heir directly; he took the tutors. That is a workable compromise: the fact that the law acts is preserved, and a head-on collision nobody could survive is avoided. If you cannot enforce it fully, enforce it where everyone can see.
e.g. The owner's relative breaks a rule and cannot easily be touched. Handle the direct manager's failure to supervise, in public. The signal still lands and nobody can call it waived.

### The parts · A real system eventually catches its author
Shang Yang was finally trapped and killed by the code he wrote. That is not irony, it is the proof. A set of rules that binds everyone except the designer is still personal rule wearing a different word. A real one will one day stop you.
e.g. Run your own approval process when it is your turn, even at a cost of three days. Those three days buy the process its standing with everyone else.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the first person to break the new rule is the one you can least afford to touch.
Ask first: if this one goes, who takes it seriously next time?
Where it goes wrong: treating the hardest case as a special case; binding those below and not those above, then wondering why nothing sticks.

### Lines to keep
When the law is not carried out, those above have broken it.
One punishment means no grades of punishment, from ministers to commoners.
The first exception is where the rule ends.

## Shi Tiesheng · Once Born, No Longer Open to Debate
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/shi-tiesheng/not-a-question-to-debate/
Source: Shi Tiesheng, The Temple of Earth and I, 1991
Tags: Deep read, Shi Tiesheng, The Temple of Earth and I

Whether to keep asking why this happened to you. Which questions Shi Tiesheng closed during fifteen years in a park.

### Q: What actually happened?
His legs stopped working at twenty-one. For fifteen years after that he wheeled himself almost daily into the old Temple of Earth park near his home and sat there. He says he was working on three things: whether to die, why to live, and why write. The first one he settled took years: once a person has been born, that is no longer a question open to debate. Nobody chooses to arrive, so it is not yours to rule on. With that off the list, the other two finally had somewhere to sit.

### The parts · Some questions are closed, not answered
Why me has no answer and needs none, because it is only a fact. It took him years to concede that: this one is not solved, it is crossed off the list. Once it is crossed off, the strength goes to questions that have answers.
e.g. Stop asking why me and ask what now, given that it is me.

### The parts · Sit down first, rally later
He did not go looking for a way forward. He sat in one place for years. The sitting is not passivity; it is time given to letting the worst layer of feeling finish. People who rally early have not finished, and they collapse a second time later on.
e.g. Just after it happens, having one place you go to matters more than planning the next step.

### The parts · The park was not scenery, it was somewhere he went back to
What he stresses is the daily part: the same place, fifteen years of it. A person who has come apart needs one coordinate that does not move. It solves nothing at all. It is there every day, and that turns out to be enough.
e.g. One place you go every day, or one person you see every day, holds people better than any argument.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something happened that cannot be undone, illness or disability or loss, and your head is full of why me.
Ask first: how long have I been asking it, and is it a question to cross off rather than solve? Do I have one place I go back to every day?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as accept your fate. He did not accept anything and fought his body for decades. Only this one question is not worth fighting; the strength belongs to the others.

### Lines to keep
Why me is not solved. It is crossed off the list.
Rally too early and the feeling comes back for a second collapse.
It solves nothing and it is there every day. That is enough.

## Shi Tiesheng · Being Ill Is the Job; Writing Is the Sideline
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/shi-tiesheng/job-is-being-ill/
Source: Shi Tiesheng, Scattered Notes in the Gaps of Illness, 2002
Tags: Deep read, Shi Tiesheng, Put the illness in first position

How to lay out a day around a long illness. What Shi Tiesheng meant by calling illness his profession, and how to use it.

### Q: What actually happened?
From 1998 he had kidney failure: dialysis three times a week, four hours at a time, and a day afterwards with nothing left in him. The book he wrote in those years was written in the gaps between sessions, and the title says so. In it he puts the arrangement plainly: being ill is my profession; writing is what I do on the side. Not a joke about himself. A working order. Once the order is admitted, there is no need to be angry every evening about how little got written, and the few usable hours all get used.

### The parts · Illness goes first so the rest of the time can work
Anyone who refuses to admit the illness is the main job spends each day competing with it for time, loses, and then spends what is left in resentment. He reversed it. Give the illness every hour it demands first; what remains is genuinely yours, with no minute lost to anger.
e.g. Fix treatment and rest into the calendar first. What is left is my time. Do not do the arithmetic the other way round.

### The parts · A book can be written in the gaps
Two or three hours between sessions will not hold a novel, so he wrote fragments instead, one piece at a time. The form followed the time available rather than waiting for a clear stretch. Clear stretches were not coming back, and waiting for them is giving up.
e.g. If all you have is broken time, do work that comes in pieces. Do not hold out for a whole day.

### The parts · On the side does not mean carelessly
He calls the writing a sideline, and that book took four years. On the side describes the ranking, not the standard: behind the illness, and every paragraph written properly. Admitting that your strength is limited and doing sloppy work are two different things.
e.g. If you have strength for one small thing, do that one thing properly. Less is not licence for worse.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have a condition you will carry for years, or you have been flattened a long time, and every day hurts because you cannot do what you used to.
Ask first: if the illness is the main job and goes first, how many hours are actually left? What is the smallest thing those hours can hold?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as permission to stop. He was on dialysis for twelve years and produced several books. This is about admitting the order and using the gaps, not surrendering them.

### Lines to keep
Give the illness its hours first; what is left is yours.
The clear stretches are not coming back. Waiting is giving up.
Limited strength and sloppy work are two different things.
