## Shi Tiesheng · Death Is a Festival That Will Certainly Arrive
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/shi-tiesheng/death-is-not-urgent/
Source: Shi Tiesheng, The Temple of Earth and I, 1991
Tags: Deep read, Shi Tiesheng, Nothing to hurry toward

For people who lie awake until dawn thinking about dying. Why Shi Tiesheng called death a festival, and what that did for him.

### Q: What actually happened?
After several years in the park working on whether to die, the conclusion he arrived at is very calm: death is not a thing to hurry toward; death is a festival that is certain to arrive. Since it is coming anyway, there is no need to go and meet it. Once he had seen that through, he said, what is left is the question of how to live. The problem of dying had not been solved. It had been put back where it belongs: certain, therefore not to be thought about, and every day of being alive turns out to be his.

### The parts · Certain is what makes it possible to put down
Most people who fear death are afraid of the uncertainty: when, and how. He fixed it as something settled that requires no management. It is coming; do not rush it. Once settled, the item comes off the daily list.
e.g. Saying out loud that it is certainly coming is lighter than turning over what if it comes.

### The parts · Thinking it through once is not thinking about it always
He did not avoid the subject. He went at it seriously and followed it to the end. Having gone to the end, there is no need to return. The version that surfaces at three in the morning is the one that was never followed through.
e.g. The thought that keeps returning at night is usually the one you would not follow to the end in daylight.

### The parts · Put death back and living has room
His conclusion is that what remains is the question of how to live. Two questions were competing for the same attention, and the one about dying produced no result while occupying the space. Put it back and the other one has a surface to lie on.
e.g. How to live cannot be worked on until whether to die has been cleared off the table.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you lie awake thinking about dying and cannot say so to anyone in the daytime.
Ask first: have I ever sat down in daylight, clear-headed, and followed this all the way through? Can I say out loud that it is certainly coming?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as being above life and death. He was not above anything and fought illness for thirty-eight years. This is about putting death back where it belongs, not about ceasing to mind.

### Lines to keep
It is certainly coming, so there is no need to hurry.
The thought that returns at night was never followed through by day.
How to live waits until whether to die leaves the table.

## Sima Qian · Why he did not kill himself
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sima-qian/letter-to-ren-an/
Source: Letter to Ren An, c. 93 BC
Tags: Deep read, Sima Qian, The letter to Ren An

The convention was clear and he broke it. Years later he wrote one man a letter explaining exactly why.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 99 BC a general named Li Ling surrendered to the Xiongnu. Sima Qian, the court historian, spoke a few words in his defence, and the emperor had him imprisoned and then castrated. For a man of his rank the honourable course was to kill himself, and he did not take it. Years later, writing to Ren An, he gave the reason plainly: what he could not bear was to die with the work unexpressed and leave nothing behind. He had moved the question of staying alive off his honour and onto an unfinished thing.

### The parts · Swap the question about face for a question about work
The first question has no answer and sinks the longer it is held. The second has one, and the answer points at something to do. That substitution is the whole move in the letter: not that the shame was resolved, but that it was taken off the switch controlling whether he lived.
e.g. After a public disgrace, do not ask whether you deserve to be here. Ask what you still owe.

### The parts · The hardest sentence went to one person
The letter is addressed to Ren An, not to the world. For roughly twenty years nobody knew what he thought, and he explained himself to no one else. A thing you cannot say does not have to be said to everyone. Said properly once, it stops being held in.
e.g. You do not need an audience. One person, the whole story, start to finish, is enough.

### The parts · He did not wait to stop hurting
The letter is explicit that the shame never left: every time he thinks of it, he writes, the sweat soaks through his robe. He finished the history carrying that, not after curing it. Waiting until it no longer hurts usually means never starting.
e.g. Shame does not leave the room first. The move is to work while it is still standing there.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you did something you find shameful, or you were humiliated in public, and you cannot imagine facing anyone.
Ask first: is there one thing unfinished that only you can finish? Have you told the whole of it to one person, start to finish?
Where it goes wrong: hearing it as endurance is a virtue — he endured because the book was not done, not for its own sake; and shame is not something you think your way out of, he never did.

### Lines to keep
Every time I think of this shame, the sweat soaks my robe.
A death may be heavier than Mount Tai or lighter than a feather.
He knew what was expected. The book was not finished.

## Sima Qian · Those books were all written at the worst time
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sima-qian/written-in-adversity/
Source: The roll call in the Letter to Ren An; the postface to the Records
Tags: Deep read, Sima Qian, King Wen was in captivity when he expanded the Changes

One paragraph of the letter is almost entirely a list of names. What the names have in common is not talent.

### Q: What actually happened?
The passage runs almost as a roll call: King Wen was in captivity when he expanded the Book of Changes; Confucius was in distress when he made the Spring and Autumn Annals; Qu Yuan was banished and wrote the Li Sao; Zuo Qiuming lost his sight and there is the Guoyu; Sun Bin lost his feet and set out his military methods. Seven or eight of them in one breath. He calls this writing pressed out by frustration, not spare capacity in good times. Then he puts his own name at the end of the list.

### The parts · Find yourself a row of precedents first
While someone believes nobody has ever had it this bad, no argument gets through. His first move is not reasoning but assembling a line of people whose situation resembled his and who went on to make something. The list itself is the remedy.
e.g. If you believe you are the only one this unlucky, go and find three who had it worse and finished something.

### The parts · What was taken away is often why they could sit down
King Wen had time because he was locked up. Sun Bin could concentrate because he could no longer campaign. Nothing good is being claimed about suffering. The things stripped away, the dinners, the promotions, the standing, were what had been occupying the hours.
e.g. The hours that open up after you are sidelined are the ones you could never free before.

### The parts · Frustration is fuel, not mood
What he means is not venting. It is taking the sense of injustice and burning it inside one long piece of work. The same charge aimed at people becomes resentment; aimed at a task it becomes output. Same fuel, different direction, entirely different result.
e.g. Two people equally aggrieved: one complains daily, one writes daily. Five years later they are not comparable.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are being squeezed out, sidelined, or laid low, and the whole stretch feels wasted.
Ask first: what has been taken away, and what has that freed up? Can you name three people whose position was worse and who finished something?
Where it goes wrong: turning it into suffering is good for you — most of the men on his list never saw their work read; the claim is that the worst time is workable, not that it is best.

### Lines to keep
King Wen was in captivity when he expanded the Book of Changes.
Not spare capacity in good times. Pressed out in bad ones.
When you feel singular, a list beats an argument.

## Sima Qian · Staying alive takes one unfinished thing
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sima-qian/one-thing-to-finish/
Source: The postface to the Records of the Grand Historian; the Letter to Ren An
Tags: Deep read, Sima Qian, To complete the words of one school

The task he set himself was absurdly large. That size is doing work, and so is the fact that he did not choose it.

### Q: What actually happened?
His father, dying, handed him the history, and he knelt and wept and agreed. In the letter he states the scale without flinching: to examine the boundary between heaven and man, to penetrate the changes of past and present, to complete the words of one school. Not to record a few events. To set in order everything from the Yellow Emperor to his own day. After the mutilation this is what held him up, and he says so directly: with the book finished, ten thousand deaths would bring no regret.

### The parts · Big enough to be worth it, small enough to touch today
The words of one school is the far end. The daily end is copying a passage, checking a date, drafting one life. Worth dying for at one end, advanceable by a line at the other. With only the far end people spin; with only the near end they run out.
e.g. One aim far enough off to be worth it, one action you can finish tonight. Neither works alone.

### The parts · Handed to you beats thought up by you
This was not a meaning he constructed for himself. It was a charge from a dying father. An obligation received from another person still stands on the days you do not want to be alive, because it does not depend on your current state. Self-made meaning moves with the mood.
e.g. When you cannot think of a reason to hold on, ask who has left something in your hands.

### The parts · Only I can finish it is the load-bearing condition
The archives were in his keeping, his father's notes were in his keeping, the chronological frame was in his head. Nobody else could have produced that book. The irreplaceability is not vanity, it is fact, and it is what makes if I die this ends actually true.
e.g. Find the thing nobody picks up if you put it down. It holds more weight than any job.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are at the bottom, you know you should hold on, and you cannot name a reason.
Ask first: is there anything someone else placed in your hands that nobody would pick up if you stopped? What is the smallest step on it today?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as you must find a grand purpose — his was inherited and built over decades, not invented under pressure; a purpose invented to fill the gap will not survive the first bad day.

### Lines to keep
To complete the words of one school.
Worth dying for at one end, a line at the other.
An obligation from someone else holds on days you cannot.

## Sima Yi · A thousand li in eight days
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sima-yi/eight-days/
Source: Book of Jin, Annals of Emperor Xuan
Tags: Deep read, Sima Yi, Their schedule is built on your procedure

Your opponent has your arrival time worked out precisely. What he got wrong is not the distance but whether you keep to the rules.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 227 Meng Da was plotting at Xincheng to leave Wei and go back to Shu. He had done the arithmetic in a letter to Zhuge Liang. Wancheng is eight hundred li from Luoyang and twelve hundred from me; when Sima Yi hears, he must first memorialise the throne and wait for a reply, and that is a month, and by then my walls will be finished. Sima Yi did not memorialise. He marched at once and was under the walls in eight days. Meng Da's next letter is stunned: I raised my standard eight days ago and the army is already here. Sixteen days later the city fell.

### The parts · Their timetable is a list of your openings
Every item in Meng Da's arithmetic was right. The single error was assuming the other man would complete the procedure. Any plan resting on he must finish this before he can do that is writing your opponent's choreography for him, and he is free to decline to dance.
e.g. They have always shipped at quarter end, so every defence is scheduled for quarter end. The real threat arrives when they do not need that process.

### The parts · Acting before reporting has a price
Marching without a memorial exceeded his authority and he would answer for it afterwards. His justification was arithmetic: spending a month of supply against a year of preparation only makes sense if it is fast. The value of speed has to cover the cost of breaking the rule, or it is recklessness.
e.g. Skipping the review to catch a window requires a sum afterwards showing the window was worth nothing otherwise. Without the sum it is only rule-breaking.

### The parts · Timing matters more than strength
His reading before marching was that Meng Da had no credit with anyone, that this was the moment of mutual suspicion, and that he should be forced to a decision before things settled. The target was not a weakness but a window of confusion that would not stay open.
e.g. The two months after a rival's leadership change, while they are still aligning inside, is the cheapest window to take accounts. Later the same move costs triple.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are moving at the ordinary tempo and it feels like there is still time.
Ask first: does any part of their plan rest on my going through every step in order?
Where it goes wrong: calling rule-breaking decisiveness without being able to price the speed; and watching their strength while ignoring the weeks when they are internally at their most confused.

### Lines to keep
He did not report. He was under the walls in eight days.
A month of supply against a year of it. Only speed justifies it.
Their timetable is a list of the openings they left you.

## Sima Yi · Waiting for the moment that will not repeat
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sima-yi/waiting/
Source: Records of the Three Kingdoms with Pei Songzhi's commentary; Book of Jin, Annals of Emperor Xuan
Tags: Deep read, Sima Yi, Wait until they stop watching

How far do you have to take feigned weakness before it works? This is about the moment the porridge went down his chest.

### Q: What actually happened?
With Cao Shuang in power, Sima Yi pleaded illness and stayed out of affairs for ten years. Cao Shuang was still uneasy and sent Li Sheng to look in on him. Sima Yi had two maids hold him up, pointed at his mouth to say he was thirsty, and could not hold the cup when the porridge came: it ran out and soaked his chest. Li Sheng said he was leaving for Jingzhou; Sima Yi kept hearing Bingzhou and repeating the mistake. Li Sheng reported back that the man was a breathing corpse. At the new year the Cao brothers left Luoyang, and he shut the gates that day.

### The parts · Feign weakness until the watching stops
Half-hearted quietness achieves nothing, because they keep an eye on you anyway. To get the surveillance genuinely withdrawn, the display has to reach the point where watching any further looks like a waste. Porridge down the front of a robe exists to cross exactly that line.
e.g. To move a competitor's attention off you, a vague public posture will not do it. There has to be nothing on you worth following up.

### The parts · What you wait for is a structural gap
He was not waiting on a mood but on one specific condition: the Cao brothers out of Luoyang on the same day, the centre of power and the centre of force both gone at once. Windows like that are recognised, not made. The point of the patience is to still be there when one appears.
e.g. Turning points in an industry are usually triggered from outside and not on your schedule. What you control is being at the table that day, holding cards.

### The parts · When it comes, finish it in one move
Ten years of nothing, and when he moved there was no probe and no phasing: the gates that day, the armoury, the guard. A window like this does not offer a second chance, and doing half of it hands you to an opponent who is now wide awake.
e.g. A reorganisation long in preparation should be announced, handed over and explained inside one week. Split it into three passes and the second meets resistance.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have judged that this is not the moment to move, and doing nothing is unbearable.
Ask first: what exact condition am I waiting for, and could I finish the whole thing the day it appears?
Where it goes wrong: feigning weakness halfway, so they keep watching; and wanting a small trial run at the very moment the window opens.

### Lines to keep
It ran out of the cup and soaked his chest.
A breathing corpse, they reported. Past worrying about.
The patience exists to keep you alive until the window opens.

## Jim Simons · Slaves to the model
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/simons/slave-to-the-model/
Source: Simons in public interviews, on how Medallion is run
Tags: Deep read, Jim Simons, Discipline handed to the system

The best-returning fund on record forbids its brilliant people from improvising. This piece asks who that rule is actually protecting against.

### Q: What actually happened?
Medallion has compounded at better than thirty-nine per cent a year after fees for decades, and Simons described the method in one rule. If you're going to trade using models, you just slavishly use the models; you do whatever the hell it says, no matter how smart or dumb you think it is. The reason is mechanical. Allow one override and you can never again say whether a loss belonged to the model or to the person, so the system stops improving. And the urge to override peaks exactly when the model most needs leaving alone.

### The parts · One override and attribution is dead
Improvement depends on clean attribution: was this loss the model or the execution? The moment a person intervenes the two are inseparable, every loss can be blamed on the other party, and nothing gets changed. The rule's real job is protecting traceability.
e.g. Operations tweaked the agreed campaign parameters three times. At the quarterly review nobody could say whether the strategy or the tweaking produced the result, so the quarter taught nothing.

### The parts · Write the rule when calm, run it when frightened
The urge to intervene scales with how extreme things get, and extreme is precisely when the system most needs to be trusted. So the authority has to be fixed in advance: what lets a person touch it — a code error, corrupted data — and what never does.
e.g. Put the three conditions that permit manual intervention on the wall in writing. On the day it crashes, check the list. Fear is not on the list.

### The parts · People move out of execution and into improvement
This division of labour is not an insult to judgement, it is a promotion for it. Instead of a thousand decisions taken while emotional, you make one change to the model that alters a thousand decisions. The leverage sits in the system, not in the seat.
e.g. Reviewing a hundred tickets a day by hand consumes judgement. Spending a week turning that review into a written rule copies it instead.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the system's answer conflicts with your instinct right now, and you want to override it just this once.
Ask first: am I changing this decision or the model? Can the reason I would override be written as a rule that applies every time from now on?
Where it goes wrong: turning follow the model into never servicing the model, so a bad rule runs forever; or applying the discipline to everyone except yourself.

### Lines to keep
Slavishly use the model, however smart or dumb it looks today.
Override it once and you never learn what actually failed.
We do not overrule the model. We improve the model.

## Jim Simons · Beauty, and the best people
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/simons/simons-principles/
Source: Simons, Mathematics, Common Sense and Good Luck, MIT 2010
Tags: Deep read, Jim Simons, He published his own principles

A man who made his fortune out of algorithms summed up a career in five principles. Not one of them is about mathematics.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 2010 Simons went back to MIT and compressed a career into a short list. Work with the smartest people you can find, ideally smarter than you are. Be guided by beauty — he said it applies not only to theorems but to a company that runs well or a problem solved elegantly, and that following it rarely goes wrong. Don't give up easily: the paper he wrote with Chern took years. And the last one he refused to dress up. Hope for good luck. The room laughed. He said he meant it.

### The parts · Hiring above yourself is a rule, not a pose
The first teams he built after leaving academia were mathematicians, astronomers and speech-recognition scientists, none of whom knew finance. He was betting on raw problem-solving power, not domain experience. The rule has a hard test: if you are always the sharpest person present, you are not following it.
e.g. Ask of every hire whether there is a part of the job they are visibly better at than you. A year of hires with nobody intimidating in it means the bar has slipped.

### The parts · Beauty is compressed experience
Be guided by beauty sounds mystical and works as a fast classifier. After years in a field, a solution that is spare and well-jointed registers as beautiful, and one patched on top of patches registers as wrong, before the argument is finished. The signal is not proof. It says where to dig.
e.g. Two architectures both work. One feels right to the old engineer, the other feels off and he cannot say why. Dig into the second one first.

### The parts · Putting luck on the list is honest and also strategic
Admitting how much was luck stops you filing a random success under personal genius. The outward consequence is that if luck matters you should enlarge the surface you expose to it: more attempts, more years still in the game, more time near well-informed people.
e.g. Give every success post-mortem a column for tailwinds you did not control. Teams that can fill it in do not despair the first time the wind turns.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are writing down your own method and the list is all technique.
Ask first: do people, taste and luck appear anywhere on it? When did I last work beside somebody clearly better than me?
Where it goes wrong: using beauty to veto anything unfamiliar; or using luck matters as cover for not having done the work.

### Lines to keep
Be guided by beauty.
Work with the smartest people you can find, ideally smarter than you.
Don't give up easily, and hope for some good luck.

## Socrates · Not supposing that you know
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/socrates/knowing-not-knowing/
Source: Plato, Apology
Tags: Deep read, Socrates, The whole margin is that thin

The poster says he knew that he knew nothing. This page is about the narrower and far more useful thing he said.

### Q: What actually happened?
A friend asked the oracle at Delphi whether anybody was wiser than Socrates, and was told nobody was. Socrates did not believe it, so he went out to test it: politicians, poets, craftsmen, one after another, questioning each. The result came back the same every time. They supposed they knew things they did not. I do not think I know what I do not know, he says, and that thin margin is the whole of his advantage. He kept questioning until Athens executed him for it.

### The parts · His response to good news was to go and test it
He was handed a judgement flattering to himself and his first move was to look for a counter-example rather than to accept it. The habit is independent of content: the more agreeable a conclusion, the earlier you should go looking for what would break it.
e.g. When the research comes back entirely positive, go and find three people who left. Confirming cases are unlimited; one counter-example saves half a year.

### The parts · Competence in one place leaks into confidence everywhere
He found the craftsmen genuinely expert, and precisely because of it convinced they were wise about the greatest matters too. Somebody whose judgement has been repeatedly validated in one domain is the least able to say I do not know in another.
e.g. A founder whose technical calls are excellent rules on pricing, contracts and hiring with identical confidence. The record in the first is the risk in the rest.

### The parts · Examination is a procedure, not a posture
His examining had a fixed shape: make the other person define the term they are using, then test that definition against concrete cases. Modesty can be performed. A procedure produces something every time, either a definition that holds or a gap that opens.
e.g. Are we confident about this is an attitude. Which three assumptions is it resting on, and which is weakest, is examination, and it always yields an answer.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: about to give a confident verdict outside the field you are good at.
Ask first: is the confidence coming from this question, or from your record somewhere else?
Where it goes wrong: wearing modesty as a manner with no procedure attached, or examining only the conclusions you dislike.

### Lines to keep
I do not think I know what I do not know.
The unexamined life is not worth living.
Good at their craft, they supposed themselves wise about everything.

## Socrates · The midwife's trade
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/socrates/midwifery/
Source: Plato, Theaetetus
Tags: Deep read, Socrates, No answers, only delivery

His mother delivered babies and he said he had inherited the trade. This page is about why he withheld answers.

### Q: What actually happened?
In the Theaetetus he explains his own method outright. My art of midwifery is in general like theirs, except that my patients are men, and my concern is with the soul in travail rather than the body. The god compels him to act as midwife and never allows him to bring forth. The young men who come to him seem to know nothing at first and later produce a great deal, all of it found in themselves. He keeps the other half of the craft too: telling a real child from a wind-egg, and disposing of the false one.

### The parts · A given answer has no roots
Tell somebody the conclusion and they hold a sentence they can repeat. Bring them to it by questions and they hold a route they walked. The first gets dropped at the first counter-example. The second gets defended, because it is theirs.
e.g. Point out the flaw and he fixes that one line. Ask three questions until he sees the flaw and he fixes the two others like it.

### The parts · Delivery is slower and harder than handing it over
The answer takes ten seconds; questioning somebody into producing it can take an hour. The slowness buys a filter. Only what is already forming in them can be delivered, and if nothing comes, telling them would not have helped either.
e.g. What you have explained four times and they still cannot do is rarely explained badly. There is nothing yet for it to attach to. Let them hit the wall once, then explain.

### The parts · The false one has to be removed on the spot
The second half of the craft is judgement. What gets produced is not automatically true, so he tests his interlocutor's own conclusions against counter-examples and throws out what fails. Delivery without inspection manufactures confident error.
e.g. Make whoever proposed the idea answer the three hardest questions immediately. Drop what cannot stand, before it acquires the protection of being the group's.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you can see the answer and are about to say it.
Ask first: has he anything for this answer to attach to, and could three questions get him there himself?
Where it goes wrong: turning questions into a guessing game with the answer already locked, or delivering without ever inspecting what came out.

### Lines to keep
My art of midwifery is in general like theirs.
They have never learned anything from me.
An answer counts only when it came out of the other person.

========================================================================
## George Soros · Reflexivity
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/soros/reflexivity/
Source: The Alchemy of Finance
Tags: Deep read, George Soros, Perception rewrites the thing

Textbooks say prices reflect fundamentals. This piece asks why Soros says the arrow runs both ways, and how that loop manufactures a bubble.

### Q: What actually happened?
The Alchemy of Finance turns on a two-way arrow. Market prices always distort the underlying fundamentals — and the distorted price then changes the fundamentals it was supposed to be reflecting. The mechanism is concrete. The share price rises, so the company raises money at a better valuation, acquires more cheaply, hires more easily, and the results genuinely improve, which confirms the rise. The participants' bias has entered reality through the price. Markets are not forecasting the future so much as helping to make the one they forecast.

### The parts · First check whether the loop is connected
Reflexivity is not everywhere. Whether price can rewrite the fundamentals depends on the pipe: funding, hiring, customer confidence. Where the pipe is wide — finance, property, platforms — trends make themselves true. Where it is narrow, a price move does not improve the product.
e.g. A startup's valuation is part of its product quality: a high mark hires stronger people and the product really does get better. Reading only today's product reads half the loop.

### The parts · A self-feeding error can outlast you
If perception can manufacture reality for a while, then the market is wrong is not by itself a reason to trade against it. Mispricing feeds itself through the loop and can stay funded longer than your margin lasts. Soros often rode the thing and watched for the leak.
e.g. Shorting or leaving the moment a sector looks overheated usually dies halfway up. Overheating brings real funding and real growth. Wait until the price starts hurting the business.

### The parts · The turn comes when the loop bites back
Self-reinforcement always has a limit: high prices start crushing buyers, high valuations start forcing fraud, expansion starts burning through the cash. The point where positive feedback becomes negative is the trend's expiry date. Watch the sign of the effect, not the level of the price.
e.g. The sector is still rising, but new customers are worse and collection is slower. Price up, loop already turned around and biting. That is the exit signal.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have decided something is overvalued and you want to trade against it.
Ask first: does this price have a pipe into the fundamentals? Is the loop still feeding itself, or has it started biting back?
Where it goes wrong: using reflexivity as an excuse to buy any bubble; or going short while the loop is still thick, and being right about direction while dying on timing.

### Lines to keep
Market prices always distort the underlying fundamentals.
Markets can influence the events that they anticipate.
The cognitive and participating functions interfere with each other.

## George Soros · Knowing when you're wrong
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/soros/knowing-when-wrong/
Source: Soros interviews; The Alchemy of Finance
Tags: Deep read, George Soros, Not right or wrong, but how much

A man famous for enormous bets credits his survival to admitting mistakes. This piece asks why those two things are not in conflict.

### Q: What actually happened?
His summary of himself is unexpectedly humble. I'm only rich because I know when I'm wrong. I basically have survived by recognizing my mistakes. Beside it sits the line traders keep on their desks: what matters is not whether you are right or wrong, but how much you make when you are right and how much you lose when you are wrong. Together they are a system. The judgement may be wrong often, and his frequently was, as long as wrong is recognised fast and cut small, and right is backed heavily.

### The parts · Hit rate and payoff are two different accounts
Most people optimise the hit rate, wanting every call to come good, which leaves them too timid to size up and too invested to admit an error. This system optimises payoff. The precondition is moving your self-worth off being right and onto the shape of the wins and losses.
e.g. Nine of ten attempts fail, each failure costs two weeks, and the tenth becomes the business. That year beats five projects none of which was allowed to fail.

### The parts · Admitting error needs a mechanism, not a mood
He said a backache told him a position was wrong. Underneath the mysticism is a real point: recognition cannot depend on your reasoning at the time, because a trapped judgement is the least trustworthy thing you own. Write the signs down in advance and act on them without debate.
e.g. When you take the position, write the falsifying condition and the exit beside it, and give a colleague the job of enforcing it. Wait a bit longer is what the rule exists for.

### The parts · Small when wrong is what makes big when right possible
The nerve behind an enormous position does not come from courage. It comes from being certain you can get out fast. Loose stops force small bets, so the rare good opportunity arrives and you cannot fill it. Small losses are the infrastructure of large wins.
e.g. The teams that commit everything to a high-conviction bet are the ones who built the if it misses for three months we stop rule first.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the world has gone against a call of yours and you cannot decide whether to hold.
Ask first: has the falsifying condition you wrote at the start actually been met? Is the case for waiting made of new evidence, or of pride?
Where it goes wrong: turning fast admission into no patience at all and bailing at the first jolt; or quoting right or wrong does not matter to excuse betting without doing the work.

### Lines to keep
I'm only rich because I know when I'm wrong.
There is no shame in being wrong, only in failing to correct our mistakes.
I basically have survived by recognizing my mistakes.

## The Sovereign Individual · The logic of violence
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sovereign-individual/logic-of-violence/
Source: The Sovereign Individual, chapters 1 to 3
Tags: Deep read, The Sovereign Individual, Institutions follow costs

This book explains a thousand years of institutions without ideas and without great men. One variable does the whole job.

### Q: What actually happened?
Davidson and Rees-Mogg build a frame as cold as physics: what shapes history most is the cost of using force and the cost of defending against it. Armour and stone made defence expensive and effective, so power broke into pieces and Europe went feudal. Gunpowder made castles pointless, returns to scale went up, and power gathered into nation-states the size that could pay for artillery. Run the same logic forward and you get their prediction: information technology is changing the payoff to violence. When the most valuable thing a person owns moves at the speed of light, there is less and less for force to seize.

### The parts · Read the cost structure before you read the creed
The reigning ideas of an age are often the manual written afterwards for that age's arrangement of force. Feudal loyalty and national patriotism each supplied a story for whatever protection was cheapest at the time. Treat ideas as the driver and you are permanently one step behind.
e.g. You must own the fleet is a manual for a particular cost of logistics. When the cost changes the creed gets replaced, and its defenders think they are defending values.

### The parts · How seizable an asset is decides who it obeys
Land can be taken and a factory cannot be moved, so wealth in the agrarian and industrial ages had to pay tax to whoever held the guns. Knowledge, code and relationships can be neither seized nor held, which hands their owner a bargaining position for the first time.
e.g. Two people worth the same on paper: one tied to a local licence and a building, one to portable skill and a public body of work. Ask what survives confiscation.

### The parts · When returns to scale flip, the right size flips too
In the gunpowder era force paid better the more of it you had, so states grew. In the information era the cost of defence collapses — encryption, distribution — and a small unit can hold its own ground. Any industry deserves the same question about whether size still pays.
e.g. When distribution was the moat, scale was the moat. Once distribution cost nothing, three people reached the same market. Building at the old size raises an army for the last war.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are trying to call where an industry or an institution is heading.
Ask first: can the most valuable asset here be taken by force, and which way is the cost of taking it moving?
Where it goes wrong: treating force as the only variable — beliefs and loyalties do bend costs back — or reading it as proof that every rule is about to fail. Cost structures turn slowly, and the early mover dies on the way.

### Lines to keep
What shapes history most is the cost of using and resisting violence.
Gunpowder ended the armoured knight. Information technology ends something else.
When wealth travels at the speed of light, force cannot reach it.

## The Sovereign Individual · From citizen to customer
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sovereign-individual/citizen-to-customer/
Source: The Sovereign Individual, chapters 7 to 10
Tags: Deep read, The Sovereign Individual, Jurisdictions start competing

Written in 1997, the book predicts governments will have to compete. This is the chain that gets them there, and who pays.

### Q: What actually happened?
Written in 1997, the chapter reads like a memoir. Digital cash will appear, outside the reach of any government's printing press. Work will come loose from place, so the most productive people can create wealth anywhere. Then the chain closes: once both the money and the people can move, leaving stops being a threat and becomes a Tuesday. Governments then have to bid for residents the way a company bids for customers, with tax rates, courts and services as the quotation. The citizen is turning into a customer. The cold part of the argument is who is left: those who cannot move and depend on what redistribution pays.

### The parts · The right to leave is the hardest card at the table
The mechanism under the whole book is exit beating voice. When the cost of walking away is low enough, you no longer have to persuade anyone to improve; the possibility of leaving does the arguing. So the first move in a personal strategy is making income and assets portable.
e.g. Two equally good people: one whose ability is only worth something inside this company, one with a portfolio anybody can check. The second never has to raise his voice.

### The parts · Run due diligence on a jurisdiction like a supplier
If the citizen is a customer, then where you live, where you incorporate and where you pay tax are three separable contracts, each with a price and a service level. Most people take the place they were born as the default on all three and have never once compared.
e.g. A company weighs five legal systems before it registers. The same person picks a city out of habit, though it is the largest hidden expense of his life.

### The parts · The predictions came true unevenly
Digital cash and remote work arrived. What the authors underrated was the staying power of the nation-state: identity, welfare and safety are needs nobody can pack in a suitcase, and they hold most people in place. Take the direction of this book and discount its timetable.
e.g. Allocate along the trend — portable skills, more than one option on jurisdiction — and act at the pace of the actual world. No burnt bridges, no bet on a date.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are laying out a decade of your work or your life.
Ask first: what fraction of my income and assets travels with me, and have I ever compared the contract I hold with the place I live?
Where it goes wrong: reading sovereign individual as permission to leave every community — exit is leverage, not a way to live — or buying the timetable whole and mortgaging the present to a world twenty years out.

### Lines to keep
Digital cash will appear, beyond the reach of any government's printing press.
The information age divides people into those who can move and those who cannot.
Governments will bid for taxpayers the way companies bid for customers.

## Strategies of the Warring States · Burning the bonds
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/strategies-of-the-warring-states/burning-the-debts/
Source: Strategies of the Warring States, Qi IV
Tags: Deep read, Strategies of the Warring States, Buying what the ledger cannot hold

The man sent to collect the debts burned the contracts instead. This is about how that apparently pure loss was finally settled.

### Q: What actually happened?
Lord Mengchang sent Feng Xuan to Xue to collect debts, and asked before he left what he should buy with the proceeds. Whatever the house is short of, he was told. At Xue, Feng Xuan called the people together, checked the bonds against them, then announced a pardon in his lord's name and burned every contract. The people cheered. Asked what he had bought, he said righteousness, since the house lacked nothing else. Lord Mengchang was displeased. A year later, out of office and back at Xue, he was met a hundred li out by the whole population. Today, he said, I see what you bought for me.

### The parts · Some assets are not on the books
A debt is a measurable asset and goodwill is not. What Feng Xuan performed was a conversion: a receivable most of which was never coming back, exchanged for something carried at zero and useful in exactly one kind of moment. Whether the trade was right depends on whether you counted that moment.
e.g. Over-compensating your earliest users is pure loss in the accounts. When a public crisis lands they are the people speaking for you, and no budget line buys that.

### The parts · You do not choose when it pays out
He was displeased on the spot and understood a year later. Spending of this kind shares a shape: the cost is now and certain, the return is later and uncertain, and the trigger is usually bad news about you. Which is exactly why it is the first line cut.
e.g. A customer team looks most redundant while growth is easy and proves itself the quarter renewals slip. The cuts happen in the first phase.

### The parts · Feng Xuan did not ask permission
He acted and reported afterwards, which from another angle is exceeding his authority. He could do it because the brief he was given was extremely wide: buy whatever the house is short of. Wide authority and unforeseen action are one thing, not two.
e.g. Say use your judgement and you have accepted a choice you would not have made. Taking back control of the detail takes that possibility back with it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a spend that shows no return anywhere in the accounts.
Ask first: what is it actually buying, under what conditions does it pay out, and are those conditions likely?
Where it goes wrong: writing off everything unmeasurable as waste; and handing out wide authority while still expecting every step to match what you would have done.

### Lines to keep
I bought you righteousness. Your house lacked nothing else.
Today I see what you bought for me.
The cost is now and certain. The payout waits for bad news.

## Strategies of the Warring States · Zou Ji at the mirror
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/strategies-of-the-warring-states/three-mirrors/
Source: Strategies of the Warring States, Qi I
Tags: Deep read, Strategies of the Warring States, Three people praise you, three motives

Wife, concubine and guest all said he was the handsomer man. This is about the three different things he heard in one answer.

### Q: What actually happened?
Zou Ji asked his wife whether he or Xu Gong of the northern city was the better looking. Far handsomer, she said. His concubine said Xu Gong was not his equal. The next day a guest said the same. Then Xu Gong came in person, and Zou Ji judged himself the lesser man. Lying awake he worked it out: my wife praises me because she favours me, my concubine because she fears me, my guest because he wants something. He told the king of Qi, then applied it to a kingdom of people who favour, fear or want. Seen this way, your majesty is very thoroughly screened.

### The parts · One compliment, three different sources
Partiality, fear, want: three motives producing wording that is word for word identical, so the sentence itself cannot tell them apart. The only way to sort them is the structure of the relationship. What someone stands to gain from you decides what he says to you.
e.g. Your report says the plan is good, your supplier says the plan is good, your investor says the plan is good. Three reliabilities, one identical sentence.

### The parts · The higher you sit, the fuller the set
Zou Ji's inference is the hard part. He had three people and the king had a kingdom. Every step up adds another cohort with a reason to praise you and removes people willing to say the hard thing. The screening grows with the position, with nobody deceiving anybody.
e.g. The more senior you get, the more positive the feedback, and the change has nothing to do with your standard. Reading it as progress is the usual mistake.

### The parts · He calibrated against Xu Gong
He worked it out because Xu Gong actually turned up and gave him a reference point uncontaminated by any relationship. Without that external ruler, three people agreeing is the whole body of evidence. Breaking the screen is not a matter of reminding yourself to be humble. It is going and finding the comparison.
e.g. Do not ask the team whether the product is good. Look at a rival's real numbers, and at what users say when you are not in the room.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: your plan has come back with unanimous approval.
Ask first: for each person who praised it, what do they stand to gain or lose from me?
Where it goes wrong: treating unanimity as proof of quality; and never going to find one reference point that owes you nothing.

### Lines to keep
My wife favours me, my concubine fears me, my guest wants something.
Seen this way, the king is very thoroughly screened.
Three people agreeing is not evidence. It is a relationship map.

## Su Shi · No wind, no rain, no sun
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/su-shi/no-wind-no-rain/
Source: Dingfengbo, 1082
Tags: Deep read, Su Shi, Switching off the scoring

Everyone else on the road was miserable. He was not. What exactly did he switch off in that moment?

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1082 Su Shi — a Song poet two years into exile, recently released from a prison that nearly killed him — was caught in rain on a country road. The servant with the rain gear had gone ahead. Everyone was wretched; he wasn't. When it stopped he wrote a short poem. It ends by looking back at the road he had just walked: there had been no wind, no rain, and no sun either.

### The parts · Wretched is a verdict, not a fact
Same rain, same road. The difference isn't who got wet. It's who filed the afternoon under 'this is going badly.' Misery needs a scoring system to exist. Switch that off and what's left is water hitting you.
e.g. Same demotion: one person is flattened for three months, another starts something new that week. The facts match. One of them kept looking through the frame.

### The parts · Why not walk slowly
The rain gear is gone. Walking faster gets you marginally less wet and costs you the walk. His line isn't bravado; it's arithmetic: don't spend more of yourself accelerating through the part you can't change.
e.g. It's decided and the result is in. Do the post-mortem once. The replaying changes nothing — it's just running in the rain.

### The parts · The last line is the hard one
'No wind, no rain, no sun' doesn't claim it never rained. It says that from far enough along the road, neither the storm nor the sun is an event. That view is only true afterwards — which is why it's worth borrowing early.
e.g. Stuck on a criticism from one meeting: what share of my memory will this hold in three years? The answer is almost always none.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something bad is settled and you keep replaying it.
Ask first: is the pain the thing itself, or the frame I keep putting around it?
Where it goes wrong: reading this as permission not to deal with the problem, or using 'this too shall pass' to skip the thing you should do today.

### Lines to keep
Don't listen to the rain in the leaves. Walk on, and hum.
Looking back at that bleak road — no wind, no rain, no sun.
A bamboo stick and straw sandals beat a horse. Who's afraid?

## Su Shi · Huangzhou, Huizhou, Danzhou
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/su-shi/three-exiles/
Source: Written on My Own Portrait; History of Song
Tags: Deep read, Su Shi, Doing real work where you were sent to rot

Asked at the end of his life to name what he'd accomplished, he named three places he'd been banished to. Why those?

### Q: What actually happened?
A year before he died, Su Shi saw a portrait of himself in a temple and wrote a few lines under it. He had been a Hanlin academician and a minister of rites. He listed none of that. Asked what I accomplished: Huangzhou, Huizhou, Danzhou — his three places of exile, each further from the capital than the last, the third on a tropical island then considered the edge of the world.

### The parts · Treat the exile as a term in office
Sent somewhere with no resources and no future, most people wait it out. He treated each posting as a term: what does this place most lack, and what can I leave behind. Rank sets your authority, not whether you work.
e.g. Moved to a dead-end team you can wait two years for an opening — or ask what the worst thing in this team is and whether you can fix it. One of those leaves you holding something.

### The parts · Leave things somebody can point at
A lake dredged and a causeway built. A society to stop infant drowning. A public clinic. A school on an island that had never produced a scholar. Abstract achievements evaporate when the scoring changes; objects stay.
e.g. Three years in a job — how many things can someone point at and say he did that? If the answer is none, the three years are hard for anyone to credit.

### The parts · He set the measure himself
By the official ledger his career was the titles. By listing three places of banishment he announced that the ruler measuring his life was in his own hand. That isn't consolation. It's taking the scorekeeping back.
e.g. A CV of titles held, or a CV of three things finished — two different accounts of who you think you are.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you've been put somewhere with no resources and no prospects.
Ask first: what does this place most lack right now, and what could I leave behind that someone could point at?
Where it goes wrong: treating endurance as a strategy; scoring yourself in titles instead of finished things.

### Lines to keep
Asked what I accomplished: Huangzhou, Huizhou, Danzhou.
While I am here, the water will not take this city.
A heart like burnt-out wood, a body like an unmoored boat.

## Su Shi · I see no bad people
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/su-shi/no-bad-people/
Source: His brother Su Zhe's epitaph for him
Tags: Deep read, Su Shi, Treating a person as a person

A man whose enemies nearly had him executed said he could see no bad people anywhere. This is not naivety.

### Q: What actually happened?
Su Shi was jailed over lines from his own poems and came close to execution. For twenty years afterwards, as two factions traded power, he was demoted again and again — the last time to a tropical island. He opposed the reformers' new laws, then opposed the conservatives when they scrapped every one of them. Neither side could keep him. Late in life he told his brother: I could sit with the Jade Emperor or with a beggar. I see no bad people.

### The parts · Refusing to sort people into sides
Faction logic labels the person first and lets the label decide every interaction after. He judged each measure on its merits and was exiled by both sides for it. Not neutrality — a refusal to use the frame.
e.g. Sort colleagues into 'with me' and 'against me' and you have just guaranteed you will never again receive useful information from the second column.

### The parts · 'Bad person' is an expensive verdict
Once you decide someone is bad, your available moves collapse to guarding and fighting, and both burn enormous amounts of you. Seeing a person with their own situation and interests is what lets you work the actual disagreement.
e.g. Decide he's out to get you and every email needs a paper trail. A year of that costs more than the disagreement ever did.

### The parts · This is not the same as having no judgement
He knew exactly who was working against him, and knew his own mouth was the danger. 'No bad people' describes how he treated people, not how he assessed them. Confuse the two and you become either a pushover or a cynic.
e.g. You can judge that someone can't be trusted with something big and still work with him properly and credit his work. Assessment and conduct are separate.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: there's history with someone, and now every contact is defensive.
Ask first: if I treat him as a person with his own situation, can this specific disagreement be discussed?
Where it goes wrong: mistaking generosity for having no judgement; letting your assessment of someone dictate how you treat them.

### Lines to keep
I could sit with the Jade Emperor or with a beggar.
I see no bad people.
Like a fly in the food: you spit it out before you rest.

## Su Shi · Clear the ground first
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/su-shi/east-slope/
Source: Letters from Huangzhou; Eight Poems of East Slope
Tags: Deep read, Su Shi, The first thing he did when the salary stopped

Exiled to Huangzhou, his salary essentially gone. The first thing he did was not write poetry.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1080 Su Shi arrived in Huangzhou holding an empty title, barred from official business, with almost no income and twenty-odd people to feed. What he did first was unglamorous: he petitioned for an abandoned military plot east of town — fifty acres of scrub hillside, which he and his family broke themselves — and planted wheat and rice, dug a well, built a house. 'East Slope' is not a poetic sobriquet. It's the name of the field. The poems came after the ground did.

### The parts · Solve eating before you solve meaning
When income stops, the easiest thing to do is work out what this means about you. His order was the reverse: get this month and next year fed, and put the rest later. Not a refusal to think — thinking done hungry doesn't count anyway.
e.g. Newly out of work, the job is to do the arithmetic and find the next inflow, not to re-found your identity.

### The parts · He also kept a ledger
Arriving in Huangzhou he split what money was left into thirty portions and hung them from a beam, taking one a day and saving the remainder in a tube for guests. The point isn't the amount. It's that 'how long can I last' became a number he could see.
e.g. Savings divided by monthly spend. Write the number of months down and keep it somewhere visible — a fear with a number attached is half the size.

### The parts · What you make gives you a place to stand
The field produced more than grain: it produced a name. He stopped being a demoted official and became the layman of East Slope. When the old position is taken, finishing one concrete thing grows a new one faster than waiting to be recognised again.
e.g. One small complete thing finished while unemployed puts you back on your feet faster than a hundred applications.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the income has stopped, or is about to, and you're circling what it means about you.
Ask first: where does this month's and next month's money come from? Write the numbers down, then count the months.
Where it goes wrong: reading this as never think long-term — he wrote his best work on that field; and 'farming' means any concrete thing that produces income now, not manual labour.

### Lines to keep
Meaning arrived at while hungry mostly doesn't count.
When the old place is taken, finish one small thing.
A fear with a number attached is half the size.

## Su Shi · The mud had to go somewhere
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/su-shi/silt-into-a-causeway/
Source: Hangzhou, 1090
Tags: Deep read, Su Shi, Turning the by-product into the thing

Dredging a lake leaves you holding the mud. What he did with it is still there a thousand years later.

### Q: What actually happened?
By 1090 West Lake at Hangzhou was half weed and silt, and Su Shi, posted there as prefect, put twenty thousand men on clearing it. That solved one problem and created another: the spoil had to go somewhere, and carting it out of the city would have cost more than the dredging. He laid it across the water instead, as a causeway with six bridges. A walk that had taken most of a day around the shore became a short crossing. It still carries his name.

### The parts · The waste is only waste until you name a use
Nobody asked him to build a causeway; the job was to clear the lake. The mud became a road because he was willing to ask what else it could be, at the moment everyone else was asking where to dump it.
e.g. The meeting notes nobody reads are the onboarding doc nobody has written.

### The parts · Solve it where the work already is
He did not start a second project. The men, the boats and the spoil were already on the water — the causeway cost the difference between carting mud away and setting it down in a line.
e.g. The cheapest test is the one that rides along with a release you were shipping anyway.

### The parts · The real job came first
The causeway is what people remember, but the case he argued was for the lake: without it the farms lost their water, the canal silted, the brewing tax fell. The road was what the work left over, not the reason for it.
e.g. Keep the tool you built on the way, but don't stop the job to build tools.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Next time a job leaves you with something to get rid of — a half-finished draft, a dataset built for one question, a team freed up by a cancellation — spend ten minutes on what it could be before you spend an hour on where it goes.

### Lines to keep
The spoil from the dredging is the causeway.
Everyone was asking where to dump it. He asked what it could be.
The road was what the work left over, not the reason for it.

========================================================================
## Su Shi · I dare not write
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/su-shi/no-more-writing/
Source: Letters after the Crow Terrace poetry case
Tags: Deep read, Su Shi, Stopping the defence is a decision

After his own words were used to build a case against him, did he keep writing? The question is which kind he stopped.

### Q: What actually happened?
In the Crow Terrace case, Su Shi's poems were read line by line as evidence of slander against the throne. He spent over a hundred days in prison and nearly lost his life. Afterwards, in letter after letter to friends, the same sentence: I dare not write. It wasn't fear — he wrote his most famous work in those same years. What he stopped was a different thing: defending himself, arguing who was right. He kept the two clearly apart.

### The parts · You pay for the defence yourself
Arguing over who was right spends your hours and the other person's patience, and winning returns neither. Worse, it has no end: every reply earns another, unless somebody stops. Stopping isn't conceding. It's capping the cost.
e.g. Answering every objection in the comments until 2am, and waking up to three more.

### The parts · It's an action you can tell you took
'Let it go' can't be executed — there's no way to know you've done it. 'I don't write that kind of thing anymore' can: next time your fingers move, you know what you're doing. A mood can't be kept. An action can.
e.g. Write it and don't send it. Leave it 24 hours. Most of the time you no longer want to.

### The parts · Know which kind stops and which continues
He stopped the defending, not the writing. The distinction matters: putting down the pen entirely is self-punishment and takes the real work with it. Only one kind should stop — the kind whose purpose is to make someone admit you were right.
e.g. Correct the record once. The second time is usually no longer about the record.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you're being misread or blamed, you keep explaining, and it keeps getting worse.
Ask first: is the next thing I write meant to make the facts clear, or to get someone to say I was right? If it's the second, that's the sentence to stop at.
Where it goes wrong: hearing this as say nothing — clarify a fact once; and don't stop the real work along with it. He stopped the defence, not the writing.

### Lines to keep
He stopped defending himself. He did not stop writing.
Every reply earns another, unless somebody stops.
'Let it go' can't be done. 'I don't write those' can.

========================================================================
## Su Yu · Daring to say it plainly
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/su-yu/daring-to-state/
Source: Telegrams to the Central Military Commission, 22 January and 18 April 1948
Tags: Deep read, Su Yu, How to overturn an order from above

The strategy settled above him sent his force south across the river. This is how a subordinate turned a standing order around.

### Q: What actually happened?
Early in 1948 the plan from above was for Su Yu to take a hundred thousand men across the Yangtze and operate in the south. Working it through, he reached the opposite conclusion: keeping the main force in the central plains for large battles of annihilation would change more than dividing it for the crossing. On 22 January he sent a long telegram, daring to state it plainly, with his whole reasoning. The reply restated the crossing. He kept the crossing preparations running at full speed and kept recalculating, and on 18 April sent a second telegram. He was called in, and the recommendation was taken.

### The parts · Dissent lands when the execution is already ready
Through both rounds of argument the training, the boats and the officer assignments for the crossing never stopped. That posture separates dissent from unwillingness: I can go on your plan at any hour, and I am asking you to look at my figures once more.
e.g. The strongest way to oppose a settled direction is to have its preparation genuinely finished before you open your mouth. Otherwise the objection sounds like reluctance.

### The parts · Refused once, come back with a finer account
The April telegram did not repeat January's position; it changed the arithmetic. How many enemy divisions a crossing would pull away, how many could be destroyed by staying, and the gap between the two. Against a settled judgement, position and feeling are worth nothing. The lever is the sum they have not done.
e.g. If a rejected proposal comes back two months later as the same deck, do not bring it. What was refused was the old version, not you.

### The parts · Sign the risk over to yourself
Adoption came with a requirement: a stated result inside a set number of months, and he took it. Changing an order means the person above carried a risk for you, and signing a measurable result back into your own name is what closes the loop, and why the next dissent still gets heard.
e.g. Having talked the company into a new route, put the hard number for that route on your own name. A recommendation nobody will sign for is worth half as much.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are convinced the direction already settled above you has a better alternative.
Ask first: is my preparation for their plan actually finished, where is my account finer than last time, and will I sign for the result?
Where it goes wrong: repeating the same position louder while the arithmetic stays the same; and leaving the risk with the person who approved your idea.

### Lines to keep
I venture to state my view plainly. Correct me if it is wrong.
Concentrate in the central plains and fight large battles there.
Half of a dissent's credibility is your record of executing.

## Su Yu · Turning a small plan into a large one
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/su-yu/enlarging-huaihai/
Source: Telegrams to the Central Military Commission, 24 September and 8 November 1948
Tags: Deep read, Su Yu, Enlarging when the opening appears

The name of the campaign came from his telegram. This is about how an operation got enlarged into a decisive battle while it was running.

### Q: What actually happened?
On 24 September 1948, with the Jinan operation not yet finished, he sent a telegram recommending that the Huaihai campaign be undertaken. That is where the name comes from, and the first version was limited: destroy the enemy on the Huaiyin and Haizhou line. Once it opened the field changed. The forces at Xuzhou showed signs of a general withdrawal south. On 8 November he telegraphed again, proposing that they not be allowed back across the Yangtze but held around Xuzhou and destroyed there in stages. The small plan had become a decisive battle, and the proposal was approved.

### The parts · Leave an upgrade socket in the plan
The limited version was open by design: take the first step, watch the response, then decide the second. A plan's value is not in predicting the whole route but in standing at each step where a win can be widened and a stall folded up. A plan with a fixed endpoint watches openings go past.
e.g. Alongside the target, add a line for what we do if this runs far ahead of plan. Most teams prepare only for failure.

### The parts · Enlarge on their movement, not on your excitement
The trigger was the sign of a withdrawal. The moment they contract, the window for destroying the main force opens and will not open twice. The legitimate reason for enlarging always comes from a new fact in the situation. The test is whether you can name the new variable.
e.g. Before doubling down on a product that beat forecast, ask what the market or the other side did to widen the window. Adding without a named variable is a mood.

### The parts · An enlargement re-prices the supply immediately
Going from the small plan to the large one shifted the balance to six hundred thousand against eight hundred thousand, and it held because the logistics behind it were scaled at the same time. Every upgrade re-runs the whole resource account, or a winning position is dragged into a losing one.
e.g. Turning a three-month pilot into a national rollout on the pilot's budget, headcount and supply chain does not enlarge the result. It enlarges the exposure.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something is going better than you planned and a much larger opportunity is in view.
Ask first: which new fact made the opening bigger, and have I re-run the resource account for the larger version?
Where it goes wrong: treating every good stretch as a reason to enlarge until the thing is spread too thin; or holding to the original small plan when the opening is genuinely there.

### Lines to keep
Recommending that the Huaihai campaign be undertaken.
Hold the main force around Xuzhou and destroy it in stages.
Name the new fact that widened the window, or do not enlarge.

## Sun Tzu · Win first, then fight
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sun-tzu/win-before-fighting/
Source: Art of War, Form
Tags: Deep read, Sun Tzu, The work happens before the clash

Everyone quotes it as bravado. Read slowly it says the opposite: by the time you are fighting, it is mostly decided.

### Q: What actually happened?
The line is four characters longer in Chinese than in any translation, and it is built as a pair: the victorious army wins first and seeks battle afterwards, the defeated army fights first and looks for the win afterwards. It is not advice about how to fight. It is a claim about when the outcome is set. The book spends its early chapters on measurement — ground, numbers, supply, weather, the character of the commander — because that is where the decision actually happens.

### The parts · Preparation is not the same as planning
A plan is a description of what you intend to do. Preparation is changing the conditions until the intended thing becomes easy. The first can be done at a desk in an afternoon; the second takes months and shows up as very little visible activity.
e.g. The negotiation that went well was decided in the six weeks of getting a second supplier to the point of being usable.

### The parts · If it needs courage, something upstream went wrong
Reaching for nerve is usually the sign that the conditions were not set. Sometimes there is no choice. But treating courage as the plan converts an upstream failure into a personal one, and hides the part that could have been fixed.
e.g. He had to wing the board meeting because the numbers had not been reconciled the week before, and afterwards told himself he was bad under pressure.

### The parts · Not starting is a move
If the conditions are not there, the strongest available action is to not begin yet. This is the hardest part to practise, because waiting looks identical to doing nothing, and only one of them has a reason.
e.g. They held the launch a quarter and shipped into a market that had already heard of them, instead of into silence.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something is coming that you are bracing for.
Ask first: what would have to already be true for this to go well? Write the list, and see how much of it is still available to change.
Where it goes wrong: reading it as never act until certain — the book is about setting conditions, not about waiting; and the conditions include a deadline.

### Lines to keep
The victorious army wins first and seeks battle afterwards.
The defeated army fights first and looks for the win afterwards.
If it takes nerve, look at what was left undone upstream.

========================================================================
## Sun Tzu · Know both, and know which is harder
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sun-tzu/know-both/
Source: Art of War, Attack by Stratagem / Estimates
Tags: Deep read, Sun Tzu, Your own numbers are the flattered ones

Quoted for two thousand years, usually as a case for research. The half everybody skips is the one about yourself.

### Q: What actually happened?
The Estimates chapter is not a maxim, it is a form to fill in: five dimensions and seven comparisons — whose ruler has the way, whose commanders are abler, who has the ground and the season, whose discipline is enforced, whose troops are stronger, whose are better drilled, whose rewards and punishments are clear. Then a coldly practical conclusion: if the count comes out favourable, fight; if it does not, don't. He called it reckoning in the temple — settle it before you decide whether to go at all.

### The parts · Knowing is a filled-in table, not an impression
'I have a rough sense of the competition' is not knowing. The value of a list of comparisons is that it forces out the row you cannot answer, and the row you cannot answer is usually the one that decides it.
e.g. Nobody could say what their support costs per account were. That empty cell was the entire margin difference.

### The parts · Your own side is the harder half
Their information is outside you and can be gone and found. Yours has been through several people who each had a reason to round it kindly. The order in the sentence puts them first; the difficulty runs the other way.
e.g. The competitor's timeline came from their own blog. His own timeline came from a manager reporting to the person who set it.

### The parts · The count has to be allowed to say no
More reckoning wins, less reckoning loses. The point of the exercise is not to find a way to win; it is that it can output 'this one should not be fought'. A process that ends in action whatever it computes is not a decision, it is a ceremony.
e.g. Every quarterly review ended with the same launch date. The review was not deciding anything and everyone knew it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: about to commit to something competitive on the strength of a general sense.
Ask first: which rows can you actually fill in, and which is blank? Go and fill the blank one before anything else.
Where it goes wrong: turning it into endless analysis — the count has a deadline, and 'we cannot know' is itself a row.

### Lines to keep
More reckoning wins. Less reckoning loses.
Theirs is outside and findable. Yours has been through people.
A process that ends in action whatever it computes is a ceremony.

## Sun Tzu · The best fight is the one nobody has
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sun-tzu/win-without-fighting/
Source: Art of War, Attack by Stratagem
Tags: Deep read, Sun Tzu, Winning a hundred times is not the top of the list

A hundred victories sounds like the ceiling. He says it isn't, and the reason is arithmetic rather than modesty.

### Q: What actually happened?
The chapter gives a ranked list that runs against instinct: attack the enemy's plan first, his alliances second, his army third, and his walled cities last. Each step down costs more and returns less. On sieges he is unusually specific — three months to prepare the engines, three more for the ramps, and a commander who loses patience and sends men up the walls like ants, a third of them dead and the city still standing. He calls that the disaster of assault.

### The parts · Winning is also spending
A hundred victories is not the height of skill; subduing the enemy without fighting is. Every win costs people, money, time and trust. The side that won five times can easily be stronger than the side that won a hundred.
e.g. They won the pricing war and came out of it with a team that had shipped nothing new for a year.

### The parts · Plan, then alliances, then force
Attacking the plan means making their approach stop making sense on its own terms. Attacking alliances means removing the support it rests on. Neither requires contact. By the time only fighting is left, the first two were skipped or botched.
e.g. The integration deal with the distributor ended the competitor's route to market without a single price change.

### The parts · The most expensive move is the one you take personally
Assault happens when there is nothing else left, or when someone cannot stand to walk away. He singles out the commander who attacks in anger. Losing a third of your strength to a wall you did not need is a decision made by a mood.
e.g. The lawsuit was about being right. Two years and a quarter of the budget later, it was still about being right.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: locked into a fight you expect to win.
Ask first: what does winning this cost, and what would have to be true for it not to be necessary at all?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as avoid all conflict — the ranking has fighting on it; it is just not at the top.

### Lines to keep
Winning a hundred battles is not the height of skill.
Every win you take spends people, money, time and trust.
A third of your strength on a wall you did not need.

========================================================================
## Sun Tzu · The flank only works if the front holds
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sun-tzu/orthodox-and-surprise/
Source: Art of War, Energy
Tags: Deep read, Sun Tzu, A clever move on its own is a donation

Everyone wants the unexpected move. The chapter is mostly about the unglamorous thing it has to stand on.

### Q: What actually happened?
The Energy chapter asks why the same troops behave like a rolling log one day and a scattered crowd the next. His answer is the pairing: engage with the orthodox, win with the extraordinary. The orthodox is the part that meets them head on and holds; the extraordinary is what comes from the side. He insists the two convert into each other endlessly — which means today's surprise, once used, becomes tomorrow's front.

### The parts · Without the front, the flank hits air
The surprise works because the other side is already gripped and cannot turn. Let the front go slack and the clever move lands on nothing, with your best people stranded out in the open.
e.g. The campaign was inventive and the sales team could not answer the second question, so it produced attention and no orders.

### The parts · A surprise used once becomes the expected thing
Any unexpected move, once used and written up, enters the other side's expectations and becomes part of the front. Planning to live for years off one trick is spending a one-time resource as if it were income.
e.g. The referral loop worked brilliantly, was copied within two quarters, and is now the baseline everyone has.

### The parts · Position, not heroics
The chapter ends not on cleverness but on structure: put the rock at the top of a thousand-foot mountain and the force of it coming down is not the rock's. Seek it in the position, and do not demand it of the people.
e.g. Before asking the team to try harder, someone should ask why the same work takes three approvals.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: pinning your hopes on one inventive move.
Ask first: what is holding the front while that move happens, and is it actually holding?
Where it goes wrong: concluding that only the basics matter — the front alone defends and never wins.

### Lines to keep
Engage with the orthodox, win with the extraordinary.
Used once, the surprise becomes the thing they expect.
Seek it in the position; do not demand it of the people.
