## Sun Tzu · Take the shape of what you meet
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/sun-tzu/form-like-water/
Source: Art of War, Weak Points and Strong
Tags: Deep read, Sun Tzu, Avoiding the strong part is the hard half

'Be like water' became a poster. The chapter is stricter than the poster, and most of it is about what not to do.

### Q: What actually happened?
The chapter is about who is setting the terms: bring the enemy to you; do not be brought to him. Strike what he must defend and he has to come. Decline the engagement and he cannot force it. Then the image everybody knows: water has no constant shape, it avoids the heights and runs to the low ground, and an army has no constant form either — it avoids what is solid and strikes what is hollow.

### The parts · Having no fixed shape is the point
What water resembles is not softness, it is the absence of a preset form. Its shape is decided entirely by what it meets. Which makes 'what is our style of competing' a question with a flaw built into it.
e.g. The playbook that won the first market was applied unchanged to the second, where the constraint was regulatory rather than technical.

### The parts · Avoiding the solid part is discipline, not opportunism
The hard half is the avoiding. The places that look most worth taking, most prestigious, most expected of you are usually exactly where they are thickest. Declining them means absorbing internal pressure, which is harder than spotting the gap.
e.g. Everyone wanted the flagship account. The three unglamorous ones nobody was fighting over paid for the year.

### The parts · Who wrote this week's calendar
Initiative is not moving first. It is that the other side has to answer at your tempo. There is a simple test: look at the week you just had and ask whether you scheduled it, or whether their moves did.
e.g. Four of the five priorities were reactions to a competitor's announcement, and nobody had decided that was the plan.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: reacting to a competitor, or defending the position you are proudest of.
Ask first: where are they actually thin, and what would it cost you internally to walk away from the thick part?
Where it goes wrong: using it to justify having no strategy at all — no fixed shape is not the same as no direction.

### Lines to keep
Bring the enemy to you; do not be brought to him.
Water has no constant shape. That is what it is being praised for.
Did you write this week's calendar, or did their moves?

========================================================================
## Nassim Taleb · The turkey problem
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/taleb/turkey-problem/
Source: The Black Swan, chapter four
Tags: Deep read, Nassim Taleb, The evidence peaks just before the break

What conclusion does a turkey reach if it thinks statistically? This piece asks why the day with the most evidence is the day before the accident.

### Q: What actually happened?
Taleb borrows Russell's turkey to show where induction dies. Consider a turkey that is fed every day. Every feeding strengthens its belief that human beings are looking out for its interests. The data is clean, the sample is large, there is not one counter-example, and its confidence reaches its maximum on the afternoon before Thanksgiving. The point is the asymmetry: what is a Black Swan for the turkey is not one for the butcher. Surprise belongs to whoever held the wrong model. Calm is not proof of safety. It can be the incubation.

### The parts · A clean record does not prove safety
A thousand days without an incident has two readings: the system is genuinely robust, or the risk is accumulating and has not detonated. The two histories look identical. You separate them by looking at structure — hidden leverage, single points of failure, volatility suppressed rather than released.
e.g. Ten years with this supplier and never a missed shipment is the turkey's thousand days. Look at where their capacity sits and who is upstream, not at the record.

### The parts · Ask whether you are the turkey or the butcher
The same event is a different species depending on where you stand, and Thanksgiving is written plainly in the butcher's calendar. So when something surprises you, ask who it did not surprise, and what structure they could see from there that you could not see from here.
e.g. The platform policy change blindsided you and the platform had prepared it for six months. Your Black Swan is their roadmap. Read their hiring and their filings.

### The parts · The dangerous moment is when confidence rises with the data
The turkey's structure is three lines climbing together: evidence accumulating, vigilance falling, exposure growing, all settled at once at the break. So risk discipline has to be hung backwards. The longer the calm runs, the more drills and redundancy, not fewer.
e.g. Three years with no incident, so the drill budget and the backups get cut. From the day of that cut you are on the turkey's nine-hundredth morning.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something has been stable for a long time and somebody is proposing to cut the protection around it.
Ask first: is this calm produced by the structure, or is the risk simply not due yet? And who is this not a surprise to?
Where it goes wrong: reading the turkey as an argument for distrusting all data; or agreeing about Black Swans in conversation while reducing nothing about your actual exposure.

### Lines to keep
Consider a turkey that is fed every day.
A Black Swan for the turkey is not one for the butcher.
Past knowledge is trusted most on the day it is worth least.

========================================================================
## Nassim Taleb · Skin in the game
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/taleb/skin-in-the-game/
Source: Skin in the Game; the doctor heuristic Taleb credits to Gerd Gigerenzer
Tags: Deep read, Nassim Taleb, Read the position, not the opinion

He revived a very old filter. This piece asks why advice from someone who bears none of the consequences should be discounted automatically.

### Q: What actually happened?
Taleb puts it crudely and clearly: don't tell me what you think, tell me what you have in your portfolio. The book argues one thing — a judgement is credible only when the person judging shares the consequences. The doctor heuristic quoted there he credits to the psychologist Gerd Gigerenzer. His historical exhibit is Hammurabi: if a builder builds a house and it collapses and kills the owner, that builder shall be put to death. The builder knows where the flaws are hidden better than any inspector ever will.

### The parts · Asymmetry is where bad advice breeds
When the upside belongs to the adviser and the cost to the listener, advice drifts systematically towards the aggressive and the complicated: being wrong does not hurt, being right gets credit. So the first filter is not the content, it is the structure. What has this person staked?
e.g. Ask the consultant whether half the fee can ride on the outcome of the plan they are recommending. The plans of those who say yes get simple very fast.

### The parts · Ask what they would do, not what you should do
What should I do puts the other person into persuasion mode: thorough, respectable, liability-free. What would you do puts them into survival mode. The same expert often gives two different answers, and only the second one is worth anything to you.
e.g. Asking a surgeon whether to have the operation, and asking whether he would have it done to his own mother, frequently produce different answers.

### The parts · Declare your own position before you speak
The principle is only complete when you turn it inward. Pushing a large recommendation, say what you have staked and what you carry if it fails. A strong opinion with no consequence attached deserves your own discount too. That is signal-to-noise, not virtue.
e.g. Push hard for a direction and ask in the same breath to have your own review tied to it. A team hears the difference immediately.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have been handed advice that sounds thoroughly professional.
Ask first: what has this person staked in the outcome? Does the answer change when you ask instead what they would do themselves?
Where it goes wrong: using skin in the game to dismiss every outside view. Having no position is not the same as having no information. It only means a discount.

### Lines to keep
Don't tell me what you think, tell me what you have in your portfolio.
Those who don't take risks should never be involved in making decisions.
Make the builder sleep in the house he built.

========================================================================
## Tao Te Ching · Whatever peaks, turns
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/tao-te-ching/reversal/
Source: Tao Te Ching 40
Tags: Deep read, Tao Te Ching, The top is where to start worrying

Usually read as comfort for bad times. It is more useful as an instrument, and it is sharpest when things are going well.

### Q: What actually happened?
Four characters: reversal is the movement of the way. The claim is not that things get better, nor that they get worse. It is that anything carried to its extreme starts producing its opposite. Which means the most dangerous moment is not the trough — it is the peak, because that is where nobody is looking for the turn. In the trough the rule is working for you and nothing needs to be done about it.

### The parts · Read it at the top, not at the bottom
In a bad stretch the line reads as reassurance and asks nothing of you. In a good stretch it asks a question you would rather not answer: which of the things carrying us right now is at full stretch, and what happens when it stops.
e.g. The year revenue doubled is the year nobody asked what share of it came through one partner.

### The parts · Extremes, not durations
It says nothing about how long anything lasts. A thing at moderate stretch can run for decades. What turns is what has been pushed as far as it goes — margin at its thinnest, hours at their longest, patience at its end.
e.g. The team was not tired because two years had passed. It was tired because the last four months had run at the rate of a launch week.

### The parts · The move is to give something back early
If the turn is structural, the cheap version is to stop short of the extreme on purpose: take some off the table, keep the slack, decline the last increment. The expensive version is to have it taken from you at the turn.
e.g. He cut his own hours in the good quarter, which cost output, and was the reason he was still there for the bad one.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something is going unusually well and you are being asked to push it further.
Ask first: what is at full stretch right now, and what breaks when it stops?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as fatalism, or as a reason not to grow — it is about not running any single thing to its limit, not about staying small.

### Lines to keep
Reversal is the movement of the way.
The dangerous moment is the peak, because nobody is looking for the turn there.
Stop short of the extreme on purpose, or have it taken at the turn.

========================================================================
## Tao Te Ching · The part you don't do
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/tao-te-ching/wu-wei/
Source: Tao Te Ching 37, 57, 63
Tags: Deep read, Tao Te Ching, A list of moves to leave out

Usually translated as non-action and read as passivity. It is closer to a list of the moves that make things worse.

### Q: What actually happened?
His verdict on governing is cold: the more prohibitions there are, the poorer the people; the more laws are published, the more thieves there are. The alternative he offers is not letting go. It is: I do nothing and they transform themselves, I stay still and they correct themselves, I leave them alone and they prosper. The load-bearing word is themselves. The point is not to stop things happening; it is to stop being the thing that prevents them.

### The parts · Subtracting moves, not making none
In learning you gain daily; in the way you lose daily. Getting good at running something is largely removing the actions that look like management and function as interference. Take out enough and the thing moves on its own.
e.g. Cancelling the weekly status meeting is what finally got the status written down where anyone could read it.

### The parts · There is a mechanism behind more rules, more problems
Every prohibition creates an incentive to route around it, and every correction leaves room for the next deviation. This is not a claim about morality; it is that a control grows the behaviour it was built to stop.
e.g. The expense policy got three pages longer and the number of creatively categorised dinners went up.

### The parts · Act while it is still small
Deal with the difficult while it is easy, the large while it is small. Non-action is not never acting — it is moving the action earlier, when a small one is enough. Wait and you need a large one, and large ones have consequences of their own.
e.g. A ten-minute conversation in March, or a reorganisation in September. It was the same problem.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: about to add a rule, a process or a meeting to fix something.
Ask first: which existing action is producing this problem, and what happens if you remove it instead?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as never intervene — it argues for intervening earlier and smaller, not less.

### Lines to keep
The more laws are published, the more thieves there are.
Every prohibition creates a reason to route around it.
Deal with the difficult while it is easy.

========================================================================
## Tao Te Ching · Go to the low ground
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/tao-te-ching/water/
Source: Tao Te Ching 8, 66
Tags: Deep read, Tao Te Ching, Not competing is a choice of location

Water has been praised for two thousand years. The text credits it with one specific thing, and it is about position.

### Q: What actually happened?
He gives water two lines, and both are needed. It benefits all things without contending — and it settles in the places people find distasteful. The second is what makes the first possible: not contending is not a posture, it is a choice of site. He is blunter later — the reason the rivers and seas are king of the hundred valleys is that they are good at being below them. Things flow to you because you are lower.

### The parts · Not contending means standing where nobody is
The line is usually read as moral advice and is closer to geometry: if the position you are in is one nobody wants, the act of contending does not arise. It is settled at the siting stage, not in the fight.
e.g. Everyone was building the assistant. He built the boring importer that all of them needed and none of them wanted to own.

### The parts · The places people find distasteful
Low competitive density hides in the work that is dirty, slow, or takes years to show a result. Those positions are empty precisely because they look bad and produce nothing reportable for a long time.
e.g. Nobody wanted the migration. The person who took it ended up the only one who understood how the whole thing worked.

### The parts · Height stops the flow
If you want people, information or resources to come to you, you have to be positioned below them. This is most visible with information: the higher the posture, the less of what is actually happening reaches you.
e.g. Nobody brought him bad news for a year, and he took that as evidence there wasn't any.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: choosing what to work on, in a space where everyone is going for the same thing.
Ask first: which necessary job is empty because it looks unrewarding, and what would being there let you see?
Where it goes wrong: mistaking it for accepting bad treatment — the low ground is a position, not a status.

### Lines to keep
It benefits all things without contending, and settles where people find distasteful.
The rivers rule the valleys by being below them.
The higher the posture, the less of what is happening reaches you.

========================================================================
## Tao Te Ching · The empty part is the useful part
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/tao-te-ching/usefulness-of-emptiness/
Source: Tao Te Ching 11
Tags: Deep read, Tao Te Ching, What you left out is doing the work

Which part of a wheel is doing the work? The chapter is short enough to be a definition and it underwrites the whole book.

### Q: What actually happened?
Three parallel examples: thirty spokes share one hub, and because of the nothing at its centre the cart is useful; clay is worked into a vessel, and because of the space inside it holds; doors and windows are cut for a room, and the emptiness is what you live in. One conclusion: what is there provides the advantage, what is not there provides the use. The visible part gets the credit. The gap does the job.

### The parts · Slack is not waste
The schedule with every slot filled, the interface with every field used, the plant run at full capacity — all have removed the room that absorbs surprise. One thing goes off plan and there is nowhere for it to go.
e.g. The team with two unbooked afternoons absorbed the outage. The fully booked one moved every deadline by a week.

### The parts · The empty place belongs to nobody
The hole in the hub is not owned by any spoke, and that is exactly why the wheel turns. Organisations need the same thing: capacity that belongs to no department, available for whatever actually turns up.
e.g. The unassigned engineer was the reason the incident was handled the same day instead of entering a queue.

### The parts · Less is what makes it usable
Function is not improved by addition. Everything added spends someone's understanding and someone's maintenance. The hard judgement is never what else could go in; it is what should be left out.
e.g. Removing four of the seven options doubled the number of people who finished the setup.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a plan, a schedule or a product that is full.
Ask first: where is the room for the thing you did not predict? If there is none, the plan only works if nothing surprises you.
Where it goes wrong: using it to defend doing less — the point is deliberate space, not low effort.

### Lines to keep
What is there provides the advantage. What is not there provides the use.
The hole in the hub belongs to no spoke, which is why it turns.
The hard judgement is what to leave out.

========================================================================
## Tao Yuanming · Eighty Days as Magistrate
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/tao-yuanming/eighty-days/
Source: Book of Song, Biographies of Recluses; Tao Yuanming, The Return, 405
Tags: Deep read, Tao Yuanming, What he resigned was that day, not the office

Whether to turn now or wait for a better moment. Why Tao Yuanming left after eighty days instead of finishing the term.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 405 he took the post of magistrate at Pengze and held it for a little over eighty days. An inspector came down from the commandery; his staff told him to dress properly and go out to receive the man. He said the line that has lasted: I cannot bend my back for five pecks of rice to a petty official of the district. He unfastened the seal that same day. Before leaving he wrote The Return, which turns on distance rather than resolve: I strayed, but not far. He never took office again.

### The parts · I strayed, but not far
What the poem presses is not determination but distance. The road was wrong and he has not gone far enough to be unable to return. The price of turning rises with time; eighty days back is not the same price as eight years back. Waiting for the right moment usually buys a worse one.
e.g. Turning the moment you notice is cheapest. Turning after a full term means you already owe the term.

### The parts · What breaks it is something small
He did not leave over a great matter of principle. He left over having to dress up and go out to greet an inspector. The thing that decides people is usually of this size: unimportant in itself, and it puts what am I doing here in front of your face.
e.g. What makes you want to go is rarely the big thing. It is the small day that suddenly shows you the whole shape.

### The parts · Today is right and yesterday was wrong
He offers no case for the years he spent in office. He says outright that yesterday was wrong. Admitting the old stretch was a mistake is what makes the turn clean; insisting it was defensible drags the old logic along and nothing actually moves.
e.g. Do not rush to justify the past when you turn. Say first that it was not what you wanted.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: things are going acceptably, you know this is not it, and you keep telling yourself to wait for a better moment.
Ask first: how far from far am I? What does the small thing that makes me want to go actually show? Can I call the old stretch simply wrong?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as walk out whenever something annoys you. He resigned a career, not an incident, and he had served and tested it several times before. And he was poor for the rest of his life; the price was real and he paid it.

### Lines to keep
I cannot bend my back for five pecks of rice.
The price of turning rises with time. Eighty days is cheaper.
Do not justify the past. Say it was not what you wanted.

## Tao Yuanming · He Made a Poem of the Day He Begged
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/tao-yuanming/begging-poem/
Source: Tao Yuanming, Begging for Food; Returning to Dwell in Gardens and Fields; Book of Song, Biographies of Recluses
Tags: Deep read, Tao Yuanming, Begging for Food

Going broke on the road you chose. How poor Tao Yuanming actually got, and what he did with that fact.

### Q: What actually happened?
After the resignation he was genuinely poor. At forty-four a fire took the house. One year the grain ran out, he went out to beg, and came home and wrote a poem called Begging for Food: hunger drove me out and I did not know where I was going; I came to this village, knocked at a door, and the words would not come. He set the most humiliating thing down as it was, with no polish and no complaint. In the same years he wrote of his five sons, none fond of books, and ended: if heaven has decreed it, pour another cup.

### The parts · Poverty was the price of the road, so no complaint
He writes himself as neither victim nor saint. He keeps accounts: hungry, went to beg, could not speak. Take the cost of the road you chose as it comes, without pushing it onto anyone or gilding it. Resentment ties you to the road you did not take.
e.g. If money is tight after you chose your own way of living, do not blame the world or perform serenity. You bought this.

### The parts · Written down, the humiliating thing stops being unspeakable
Begging was the most shameful thing that could happen to him, and he made a poem of it that outlasted him. The act of writing converts shame into something that happened. What cannot be said is holding you; once written, you are holding it.
e.g. Write out once, for yourself, the thing you least want anyone to know. It gets lighter as soon as it exists.

### The parts · He was poor and he still did not go back
Twenty-odd years out of office, twenty-odd years poor, and he refused every summons the court sent. The poverty is real and the not going back is real, both at once. That is what shows the turn was priced rather than impulsive.
e.g. A hard life after the turn does not mean the turn was wrong. The test is do I want to go back, not is this hard.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you moved to a road you actually wanted, money is now tight, and you have started doubting the choice.
Ask first: is the pain that life is hard, or that I want to go back? Have I ever written this stretch down exactly as it was?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as contentment in poverty. He was not content. He wrote that the words would not come at the door. The point is owning the price, not complaining and not returning, and not calling poverty good.

### Lines to keep
Take the cost of the road you chose without gilding or blame.
Unsaid, it holds you. Written down, you are holding it.
The test is whether you want to go back, not whether it hurts.

## Tao Yuanming · By Mistake I Fell into the Dusty Net
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/tao-yuanming/knowing-what-you-dont-want/
Source: Tao Yuanming, Returning to Dwell in Gardens and Fields I, c. 406
Tags: Deep read, Tao Yuanming, Know what you do not want first

You cannot say what you want. What Tao Yuanming actually knew when he knew it was time to go.

### Q: What actually happened?
The first of the garden poems opens: from youth I was out of tune with the common world; by nature I loved the hills. By mistake I fell into the dusty net, and thirty years went by. Note the wording: not I always wanted to farm, but I was never suited to that. What he is sure of is the no. No rounds of greeting, no bending for five pecks of rice, not that net. What he wants, the poem says, is to clear ground on the southern moor and keep to his own clumsiness. He started from no and reached somewhere livable.

### The parts · The no is answerable when the yes is not
Most people are stopped dead by what do you actually want, because it demands a positive answer. His route runs the other way: cross off what is definitely not wanted, and with the field narrowed the answer arrives by itself. People generally do know the no.
e.g. If you cannot list what you want, list three things you absolutely will not have. The roads left thin out fast.

### The parts · By mistake, and no self-blame
Thirty years on the wrong road, and the word he uses is fell. Something he dropped into, not I was an idiot. Giving the past a description that carries no verdict is what frees your hands; a person still cursing those thirty years is standing inside them.
e.g. Looking back at a wrong stretch, I fell into it moves you forward better than how could I be so stupid.

### The parts · Keeping to my clumsiness is a small enough target
He set himself no impressive new direction. He set keeping to his own clumsiness: not clever, not manoeuvring, farming and drinking and writing. A target small enough to be certainly reachable is what stops a person failing a second time on the new road.
e.g. Just out of one road, set the next goal small. Take one you can certainly hit, not one that sounds impressive.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you cannot say what you want and you are sure this is not it.
Ask first: what are the three things I definitely will not have? What is left once they are crossed off? Is my next step small enough to be certain?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as settle for anything you do not hate. Keeping to his clumsiness was a considered choice, not a compromise. And the no is not the destination; it narrows the field, and you still have to walk the road.

### Lines to keep
People generally do know what they do not want.
Give the past a description with no verdict in it.
Straight out of one road, make the next target certainly reachable.

## Technological Revolutions · The bubble is in the script
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/technological-revolutions/bubble-in-the-script/
Source: Carlota Perez, Technological Revolutions and Financial Capital
Tags: Deep read, Technological Revolutions, Frenzy is how installation gets funded

Canals, railways, steel, cars and the internet each ran mad in turn. This piece asks why Perez calls the madness part of the process.

### Q: What actually happened?
Perez traces five technological revolutions across two hundred years and finds the same script every time. Each divides into an installation period and a deployment period, with a turning point between them that usually shows up as a crash. Installation is led by financial capital: hot money, valuations detached from reality, fraud breeding in the frenzy. But that over-investment is exactly what lays the new infrastructure at a scale rational capital would never fund. Britain's rail network and America's fibre were both built with bubble money. Then production capital takes over and the golden age begins on the wreckage.

### The parts · Frenzy is the financing mechanism for premature infrastructure
On a rational return calculation nobody lays a national rail network or a continent of fibre in one go, because the demand does not exist yet. The bubble's function is to bypass that calculation. The losses belong to the investors; the infrastructure belongs to everybody.
e.g. The cloud capacity, logistics networks and developer ecosystems the last cash-burning war produced are the ground this generation of founders now buys at cost.

### The parts · One technology, two markets, two playbooks
Installation rewards whoever can tell a story, raise money and grab ground. Deployment rewards whoever takes the cheap infrastructure and runs a real business. The usual way to die is holding the wrong script: prudence during installation misses the window, and burning cash after the turn meets a room with no money in it.
e.g. Companies still raising on lose money for three years to buy scale cannot raise after the crash. Those buying bankrupt rivals cheaply and minding unit economics are on the right side of the turn.

### The parts · The turning point has two readings
To place yourself in the script, Perez's features work as instruments: how far valuations have detached from real revenue, and how dense the fraud scandals have become. When both spike together the turning point is close. Cheap assets everywhere afterwards, with real demand surviving, opens deployment.
e.g. When money raised on narrative in a sector dwarfs the total revenue of the companies that have revenue, and the fraud headlines start clustering, the move is to draft the shopping list.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: your field is either in the middle of a capital frenzy or just out of a crash.
Ask first: installation or deployment? And which of the two scripts is the playbook currently in my hands written for?
Where it goes wrong: using bubbles have a function as a reason to keep buying the top; or writing the technology off after the crash and missing the deployment period its cheap assets open.

### Lines to keep
Every technological revolution has an installation period and a deployment period.
The frenzy builds infrastructure that rational capital would never have funded.
Golden ages begin after the crash, on infrastructure the frenzy paid for.

## Peter Thiel · Competition is for losers
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/thiel/competition-is-for-losers/
Source: Zero to One, chapters three and four
Tags: Deep read, Peter Thiel, Both sides lie, in opposite directions

Business school teaches you to compete. He says competing is the loss. The usable part is how to hear through what both sides say.

### Q: What actually happened?
His verdict is blunt: competition is for losers. In a perfectly competitive market, price falls to cost and the profit is consumed in the fighting. What earns over time is some kind of monopoly — patent, network effect, scale or brand — ten times better with no substitute. The good part is where he takes apart the language. Monopolists pretend to be in fierce competition, defining the market as enormous so their share looks small. Competitors pretend to be unique, slicing the market thin enough to lead it. So when you read a company, start by inverting whatever it says about where its market ends.

### The parts · Profit measures monopoly; it is not a prize for competing
The closer an industry gets to the textbook picture of perfect competition, the more uniformly everybody in it grinds for thin margins. Fierce competition is not health; it is profit being burned collectively. So the first question about a battlefield is not can I win, it is whether winning leaves anything to eat.
e.g. In a subsidised delivery war there are no roles other than loser. Everyone is funding the customer's discount. Choosing that fight means losing even when you win it.

### The parts · How a company draws its market is a mirror
We are nought point one per cent of all restaurant spending and we lead local organic lunch are one move pointed two ways: the first hides profit, the second manufactures it. Redraw the boundary by hand — what would this customer actually choose instead?
e.g. Pull in everything a user genuinely considers alongside it, and a company calling itself the segment leader often turns out to be seventh.

### The parts · The way out of competition is a gap nobody can close
What he prescribes is not monopolistic behaviour but a monopoly-sized gap: be ten times better in a small market, own it completely, then expand in concentric circles — the way Amazon started with books. Deliberately choose small, become overwhelming, then widen. Better to be unanswerable in a narrow market than seventh in a large one.
e.g. A product benchmarked against a whole industry from day one is guaranteed to be average. Pick a use case narrow enough to own outright; expansion then travels with a monopoly's margin and reputation.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: choosing a new battlefield, or listening to a company describe its position.
Ask first: if we win here, is there any profit left? And the market boundary it just described — is it hiding something or inventing something?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as avoid every direct fight. Some positions can only be taken. What he objects to is the profitless kind of attrition, not fighting.

### Lines to keep
Competition is for losers.
Monopolists pretend they are in competition; competitors pretend they are unique.
All happy companies differ: each earns a monopoly solving a unique problem.

========================================================================
## Peter Thiel · The important truth few agree with
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/thiel/the-contrarian-question/
Source: Zero to One, chapters one and eight
Tags: Deep read, Peter Thiel, The question he asks in every interview

He opens with a question that has no model answer. What it is screening for, and what a good answer looks like.

### Q: What actually happened?
Zero to One opens on it: what important truth do very few people agree with you on? A good answer takes the form most people believe X, but the truth is the opposite of X. It is hard because it asks for two scarce things at once — independent judgement, and the nerve to say it out loud, when everyone learned at school that being different is dangerous. It runs into his argument about secrets: there remain many important truths not yet widely known, and every great company is built on one. Most people have stopped believing secrets exist, and so stopped looking.

### The parts · The question screens for where a judgement came from
Someone who cannot answer is not short of opinions; every opinion arrived pre-formed. Whether the answer is right is secondary. What it exposes is whether this person's judgement is produced or forwarded — and a forwarder, however clever, only takes you where the crowd already is.
e.g. Ask a candidate which consensus in their field they think is wrong. If the answer is hollow, every call they make later will be the average of the voices already in the room.

### The parts · Secrets are where nobody wants to look
Secrets are not gone because they were all found, he says, but because four pressures stopped people looking: incrementalism, risk aversion, complacency, and a flat certainty that the world is understood. So the method runs backwards — go to the corners nobody looks at.
e.g. Markets that reports call settled, technical routes a big company abandoned, an old defect users have gone numb to. That is usually the address.

### The parts · A contrarian position needs the discipline of evidence
The dangerous misuse is treating difference as proof. Going against consensus is the entry fee; after it you owe heavier evidence, not lighter. The full answer has three parts: the consensus is X, I think the opposite, and here is what I see that others cannot.
e.g. Everyone is wrong about this has to be followed immediately by because I have seen this data, these users, this cost structure. If it cannot be, demote it to an untested guess and do not bet on it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: testing whether you — or a candidate — has judgement of your own.
Ask first: on what important question do I differ from most people, and what is my evidence? Is it something I have seen, or something I want?
Where it goes wrong: disagreeing for its own sake, or using the question to disqualify anyone holding a consensus view. The consensus is usually right; the secret is the exception.

### Lines to keep
What important truth do very few people agree with you on?
A good answer: most people believe X, but the truth is the opposite.
There are still many important truths that are not yet widely known.

## Thinking, Fast and Slow · What you see is all there is
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/thinking-fast-and-slow/wysiati/
Source: Thinking, Fast and Slow, chapter 7
Tags: Deep read, Thinking, Fast and Slow, Nothing announces the missing information

Kahneman gave the mind's largest defect an acronym. This page is about why ignorance produces no sensation at all.

### Q: What actually happened?
He named it WYSIATI: what you see is all there is. The fast, associative part of the mind builds the most coherent story available out of whatever material is to hand, and never enquires about what is missing. Confidence then reads off the smoothness of that story rather than the amount or quality of evidence behind it, which is why less information often produces more certainty. There is less to contradict. He was careful, too, that System 1 and System 2 are fictitious characters, not departments you can address.

### The parts · Certainty measures coherence, not evidence
The feeling of being sure is a reading of narrative fit, not of proof. Three facts that happen to form a causal chain generate more conviction than ten that conflict. So weigh a judgement by counting what stands behind it, never by its tone.
e.g. Twenty minutes with a candidate and the interviewer just knows. Twenty minutes is exactly little enough to assemble an impression with no contradictions in it.

### The parts · Nothing in you flags the gap
There is no internal alarm for what you have not seen. The story simply closes over the hole. The repair has to come from outside: a fixed list forcing you to name what this decision needs, what you hold, and how the missing pieces would change the answer.
e.g. Add one line to the template: key information not yet obtained. It usually fills with three items, and one of them turns the decision around.

### The parts · Whatever arrives first becomes the foundation
Because the story is assembled from what is present, the earliest information lays the foundations and later evidence can only be fitted around them. The order of reporting is therefore a form of power. Whoever speaks first has framed it for everybody.
e.g. In a serious dispute the side heard first usually wins. Have both put it in writing, submitted at the same time, and opened together.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you feel very sure about a judgement.
Ask first: is the certainty coming from the quantity of evidence or the smoothness of the story? Can you name three things this judgement is missing?
Where it goes wrong: treating never having complete information as a reason never to decide, or running the audit only on other people's confidence.

### Lines to keep
What you see is all there is.
A remarkable aspect of your mental life is that you are rarely stumped.
Naming which system is speaking does not stop it speaking.

## Thinking, Fast and Slow · Losses loom larger
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/thinking-fast-and-slow/loss-aversion/
Source: Thinking, Fast and Slow, chapters 26 to 28
Tags: Deep read, Thinking, Fast and Slow, Losing hurts about twice as much

The same hundred hurts about twice as much going out as coming in. This page is about what that decides for you.

### Q: What actually happened?
The hardest finding in prospect theory is that losses loom larger than gains, by a factor most experiments put between one and a half and two and a half. Kahneman measures it with a coin toss: tails and you lose a hundred, so how much must heads pay before you will play? Most people want about two hundred. A chain of behaviour follows. People take the safe option over gains and gamble to avoid losses, they overvalue whatever they already hold, and every result is counted from a reference point.

### The parts · The double weight is a thumb on the status quo
Any proposal that changes things has its possible losses silently doubled while its possible gains are counted at face value. Two options of identical expected value are not judged equally. To give change a fair hearing, put the cost of standing still on the table.
e.g. The case for replacing the old system counted migration risk and left out what another year of maintenance and forgone work costs. Written as a number, the scales level.

### The parts · People who are behind start gambling
Faced with a certain loss, most people prefer a larger uncertain one for the chance of getting back to even. That is not weak character, it is the standard output of the mechanism, which makes an unrealised loss the most dangerous moment there is.
e.g. Three million down, and another two might save it sounds like resolve. Bring in somebody carrying none of the sunk cost to judge it.

### The parts · Reference points can be set
Gain and loss are always relative to something. A bonus rumoured at thirty and paid at forty is a delight; rumoured at fifty and paid at forty it is an insult. Same money. Whoever controls the comparison controls what the fact feels like.
e.g. Quote high, then give the real price, and the client experiences a saving. Give the real price first and they experience a cost. Identical number.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a proposal to change something feels far too risky.
Ask first: have you counted what staying costs? And are you sitting inside a loss right now?
Where it goes wrong: learning that reference points move and using it only on other people, or citing loss aversion as a reason never to change anything.

### Lines to keep
Losses loom larger than gains.
Facing gains people take the safe option; facing losses they gamble.
A slow procedure catches what a fast individual cannot.

========================================================================
## Thinking in Systems · Structure drives behaviour
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/thinking-in-systems/structure-drives-behavior/
Source: Thinking in Systems, chapters 1 and 4
Tags: Deep read, Thinking in Systems, Stop blaming the parts

The same problem has now survived three different people. This is Meadows on why that is the moment to stop blaming anyone.

### Q: What actually happened?
Meadows builds the whole book on one sentence: system structure is the source of system behavior. She demonstrates it with a car dealer who orders new stock from what he sold last week. Deliveries take three days, he waits a few days before believing a change is real, and the result is a showroom that swings between empty and overflowing. Nothing in the model is a bad decision. Every order is sensible on the day it is placed; the oscillation lives in the delays. Replace the manager and the same graph comes back. Stocks, flows and loops decide what a system does, whatever the parts are made of.

### The parts · A problem that keeps returning is a structural signal
A one-off can be put down to a person or to luck. A problem that recurs and survives a change of personnel cannot: it means a loop in the structure is producing it reliably. Handling the person is swapping a part, and the part goes back into the same machine.
e.g. Three people have left this role inside a year. Before the fourth advert goes out, draw who this job answers to and what it is allowed to decide.

### The parts · Look at the pattern, not at the events
Events are waves on the surface; patterns are the current beneath. Meadows tells you to stretch the time axis and ask what shape this number has made over two years — oscillation, exponential rise, an S-curve, overshoot and collapse. Each shape belongs to a particular arrangement of loops.
e.g. Stock keeps swinging from famine to glut. Auditing orders one by one never ends. Plot two years, recognise the standard oscillation, and go looking for the delay.

### The parts · Structure is not an alibi
No separate villains is easily heard as nobody is accountable. Meadows means the reverse. Precisely because structure produces behaviour, whoever can change the structure carries the most responsibility: whoever sets targets, writes the process and decides what information reaches whom is writing what this system will do.
e.g. Salespeople keep overpromising and no amount of policing stops it. The person most responsible is whoever made signed revenue this quarter the only measure.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the same problem has been handled several times, the people have changed, and it is still here.
Ask first: which loop produces this behaviour, and who has the authority to change that loop?
Where it goes wrong: using structure to excuse everybody; or drawing the diagram and then still intervening only at the level of the parts.

### Lines to keep
System structure is the source of system behavior.
A system's behaviour cannot be known from its elements alone.
A chronic problem is not a bad person. It is a loop.

========================================================================
## Thinking in Systems · Leverage points
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/thinking-in-systems/leverage-points/
Source: Meadows, Leverage Points: Places to Intervene in a System
Tags: Deep read, Thinking in Systems, Right place, wrong direction

She ranked twelve places to intervene in a system, weakest to strongest. This is why almost nobody uses the strong ones.

### Q: What actually happened?
Her famous essay puts the twelve in order. Weakest are the numbers — tax rates, budgets, thresholds — the dials everyone spends the day turning while the system carries on doing what it did. Above them sit feedback loops and flows of information. Higher still are the rules and the goals, and the strongest place of all is the goal of the system and the paradigm underneath it. Then comes the line that stings: people know intuitively where the leverage points are, and push them in the wrong direction. The dials are crowded because they are easy. The paradigm is empty because it is not.

### The parts · Numbers are the busiest and the weakest lever
Moving a target, adding or cutting budget, shifting a threshold: instant to do, instant to see, which is why they absorb nearly all management attention. But while the loop structure holds, the system absorbs the change and a few months later the old behaviour is back.
e.g. Cut the response deadline from twenty-four hours to twelve. Compliance rises for a fortnight, then everyone learns to send a holding reply. The dial moved; the behaviour did not.

### The parts · Information flow is the best value on the list
Putting a piece of information where it was previously absent often beats changing the rules, because being seen changes conduct by itself. Meadows keeps a Dutch housing estate as her example: identical houses, meters in the hall instead of the basement, and a third less electricity used.
e.g. Show each team the live cost of the calls it makes to an internal service. Set no quota at all. Wasteful traffic halves within a quarter.

### The parts · Wrong direction is commoner than wrong place
Her sharpest observation is that people find the point and then push the wrong way. Growth too fast, so the instinct is more control, when the lever is often less fuel in the growth loop. Morale low, so the instinct is more incentive, when the lever is removing a punishing feedback.
e.g. Too many meetings means coordination demand is high. Banning meetings pushes it into private messages and makes it worse. The lever is the coupling that requires coordinating.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you want to shift a stubborn system behaviour and your hand is already on one of the switches.
Ask first: where does this switch sit in the twelve, is there a higher place for the same effort, and am I sure the push goes this way rather than that?
Where it goes wrong: talking about paradigms while every actual action is a parameter; or turning information transparency into surveillance, so being seen becomes being watched.

### Lines to keep
People know intuitively where leverage points are, then push the wrong way.
The weakest leverage points are numbers, constants and parameters.
The paradigm out of which a system arises is the strongest lever.

========================================================================
## Thomas Gordon · The I-message
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/thomas-gordon/i-message/
Source: Parent Effectiveness Training
Tags: Deep read, Thomas Gordon, Say the effect, not the character

The same event, said one way, starts a fight; said another, starts action. Where the structural difference is.

### Q: What actually happened?
Gordon studied under Carl Rogers and turned his teacher's clinical stance into steps ordinary parents could learn. The core tool is the I-message, in three parts: the specific behaviour, its actual effect on me, and how I feel. Use an I-message, not a you-message: say what this does to me, not what kind of person you are. It works because no part of it judges the other person, so there's nothing to defend against, and the effect is a fact they can't argue with. Most people's default is the you-message — you're so careless, you never help — and every one of those defines the person.

### The parts · All three parts, or it doesn't work
Behaviour alone is a statement. Feeling alone is emotion. Only with all three does the other person see why it needs to change. The part most often dropped is the middle one — the actual effect — and that is exactly where the persuasion lives.
e.g. 'Things on the stairs, I can't see them carrying a box and I'll fall, and that worries me.' All three, and it gets moved.

### The parts · The effect has to be real and concrete
If you can't name an actual effect, this may be a preference of yours rather than a problem. That makes the step a filter as well: when you can't fill it in, ask yourself why you're insisting.
e.g. Their room is messy and it affects nobody. No effect to name means it's a difference of taste, not a problem.

### The parts · An I-message isn't a softened accusation
'I feel you're being selfish' wears the word I and is still a you-message. The test is the subject and the content: are you describing your state or what kind of person they are? The first can't be denied; the second guarantees an argument.
e.g. 'I feel fobbed off' still names their motive. 'I'm getting anxious' is your own state.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you need to raise something and you've been holding several sentences in.
Ask first: what is the specific behaviour? What is the actual effect on me? What do I feel? Is there a part I can't fill in?
Where it goes wrong: memorising the three parts as a script and reusing it — people hear the template. What matters is that the content is true, not that the sentence is well-formed.

### Lines to keep
Say what this does to me, not what kind of person you are.
No effect you can name may mean a preference, not a problem.
Most people's default is the you-message, and each one defines them.

========================================================================
## Thomas Gordon · Whose problem is this
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/thomas-gordon/problem-ownership/
Source: Parent Effectiveness Training
Tags: Deep read, Thomas Gordon, Different owner, opposite method

Your child is upset, you explain, and each explanation pushes them further away. What to do in that moment.

### Q: What actually happened?
Gordon's second tool is problem ownership: work out whose problem this is before choosing a method. A child upset about a bad grade owns the problem, and the move is listening. A child wrecking the living room so you can't work — that's yours, and the move is an I-message. Getting it backwards is the common error: parents rush to analyse and advise while the child is hurting, which lays their own anxiety on top. He also noted most parents know only two moves, win or lose, when conflict needn't end with either.

### The parts · When it's theirs, listen and don't lecture
This is counterintuitive, because seeing a child upset makes you want to help. But advice at that moment moves them from solving their own problem to handling your opinion. The right action is to say back what they meant and let them go on.
e.g. 'I'm never going back to school.' Answer 'sounds like something bad happened today' — they'll keep talking.

### The parts · The third method isn't a compromise
Splitting the difference leaves both parties unsatisfied. Gordon wants each side's real need named, then a way that meets both — which often exists and nobody asked.
e.g. They want ten o'clock, you want nine. Nine thirty annoys everyone. Ask, and it turns out they want to finish the game: start before nine.

### The parts · Ownership moves, so keep re-judging
The same situation shifts: a teenager staying up is their problem until it affects the whole household's sleep, and then it's shared. Get the ownership wrong and every subsequent move is wrong, so this is judged repeatedly, not once.
e.g. At first you only listen. Once it starts affecting you, switch to an I-message. Reverse the order and neither works.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: your child or a colleague is upset and you're about to give advice.
Ask first: whose problem is this? Theirs — listen, and only say back what you heard. Mine — use an I-message and name the effect.
Where it goes wrong: using ownership as a way to hand things off. 'That's your problem' pushes the person away by itself.

### Lines to keep
Work out whose problem this is before choosing a method.
Conflict doesn't have to end with somebody winning.
Advice moves them from solving their problem to handling you.

========================================================================
## Lev Vygotsky · The zone of proximal development
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/vygotsky/zpd/
Source: Thought and Language
Tags: Deep read, Lev Vygotsky, Look at the second line

Two people at the same level today may end up far apart. Which measure the difference shows up in.

### Q: What actually happened?
Vygotsky pointed out that ability has two lines: what a person can do alone, and what they can do with help; between them lies the zone of proximal development. His example is two children who stop at the same point solving a problem alone, and then, given a small hint, one goes a long way further and the other doesn't. Identical actual level, completely different zone — and it's the zone that decides what they can learn next. Against the orthodoxy of his day he argued that teaching should run ahead of development, not wait for it.

### The parts · Assess by the response to a hint
Independent performance alone underestimates the difference. What actually predicts is how far someone moves once given a little help — that shows where they can grow next. For managing people and for teaching children this is the same measure.
e.g. Two reports produce about the same today. Give the same pointer: one advances at once, one doesn't. Invest in the first.

### The parts · Pitch it just above where they are
Hard enough to need help, not so hard that help doesn't get it done. Below that is repetition; above it is discouragement. It's the same location that deliberate practice calls the edge of the comfort zone, named differently.
e.g. Teaching equations to a child who has just learned addition is wasted. So is only ever doing addition.

### The parts · First between people, then inside one
He held that higher thinking happens in interaction first and is internalised after — a child is questioned by adults before learning to question themselves. That is why discussing, retelling and teaching someone else beat reading silently.
e.g. Explain the thing you can't grasp to another person. You're borrowing the structure you haven't internalised.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: teaching someone or teaching yourself, and unsure where to set the difficulty.
Ask first: can they do this alone? Can they do it with one hint? The stretch between is what to practise.
Where it goes wrong: reading 'run ahead of development' as the further ahead the better. Too far ahead only discourages.

### Lines to keep
Between what you can do alone and with help lies the zone.
Teaching should run ahead of development.
Higher thinking happens between people before it happens inside one.

========================================================================
## Lev Vygotsky · Scaffolding: give it, then take it away
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/vygotsky/scaffolding/
Source: The teaching application of Vygotsky's school
Tags: Deep read, Lev Vygotsky, Left up, it becomes dependence

How much help is the right amount? The test is whether it comes down.

### Q: What actually happened?
Scaffolding is this school's metaphor for help: you put it up so someone can reach higher, and once they've reached, it comes down. Help that stays becomes dependence and leaves the person at the level where they're being held — which is how many patient teachers and parents end up producing students who can't work alone. So every intervention should carry the question of when it will no longer be needed. Whether a piece of help was good isn't judged by whether the task got done. It's judged by whether less support is needed next time.

### The parts · Help should decrease by design
First time, demonstrate one step and have them do the next. Second time, prompt only the opening. Third time, nothing. The decrease is designed, not spontaneous — unless you actively withdraw, help gets waited for.
e.g. Demonstrate the whole solution every time and the child waits for the demonstration and never starts.

### The parts · The test is less support needed next time
Whether help worked isn't whether this problem came out right; it's how many prompts the next one takes. That test transfers directly to managing people and stops you mistaking doing it for them for teaching.
e.g. They finished under your guidance, and the next similar task needs exactly as much guidance. That wasn't teaching.

### The parts · Taking it down too early is also wrong
Scaffolding fails in two directions: left up it creates dependence; removed too early it discourages and pushes someone back into not trying. The pace is set by their response, not by your patience.
e.g. Struggling, give one more line. Making progress, say nothing. The test is their progress, not your discomfort.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you're teaching someone and unsure how much to give.
Ask first: when does this help come down? Does the next round need less support?
Where it goes wrong: using 'it has to come down' as a reason to stop helping altogether. It comes down once they can reach.

### Lines to keep
Scaffolding goes up in order to come down.
Whether help worked shows in how much they need next time.
Help that stays leaves people at the level where they're held.

========================================================================
## Wang Jian · Six hundred thousand or nothing
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wang-jian/sixty-thousand/
Source: Records of the Grand Historian, Bai Qi and Wang Jian
Tags: Deep read, Wang Jian, Give the real number

Asked how much you need, too much looks incompetent and too little loses. This is why Wang Jian held to a frightening number.

### Q: What actually happened?
The king of Qin asked Li Xin how many men it would take to conquer Chu. Two hundred thousand, said Li Xin. He asked Wang Jian, who said it cannot be done with fewer than six hundred thousand. The king said the general had grown old and timid, that Li Xin was bold and right, and sent Li Xin with two hundred thousand. Wang Jian pleaded illness and went home to Pinyang. Li Xin won at first, was then pursued for three days and three nights, and was broken, with seven commanders killed. The king went to Pinyang in person to apologise. Wang Jian named the same number again.

### The parts · The low bidder is winning the meeting, not the job
Two hundred thousand pleased the king and six hundred thousand displeased him. In the room where resources are handed out, whoever asks for less always has the advantage: he looks capable and he looks thrifty. The bill is deferred to execution, where there is no longer a way back.
e.g. Say three weeks in planning and you are praised on the spot; say eight and your efficiency is questioned. The eight-week estimate is usually the right one.

### The parts · Do not revise after the refusal
Turned down, Wang Jian did not compromise at four hundred thousand. He went home. That step carries the weight: had he revised, he would have proved the six hundred thousand was padding all along. Holding the number and accepting the cost of being passed over is the only thing that gives it force.
e.g. Estimate two people, get cut to one, and say you will try to make it work, and every estimate you give afterwards is discounted automatically.

### The parts · When they come back, do not soften the terms
With the king at his door apologising, his first move was still to decline, and the figure at the end was the same figure. People at their lowest concede most easily, out of gratitude for being wanted again, which is precisely the one moment when the terms can be made real.
e.g. Being called back to rescue a project is when your conditions are easiest to accept. Say nothing out of gratitude and you finish exactly where you started.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have to name a resource figure and you are wavering between the real one and the presentable one.
Ask first: if the smaller number turns out not to be enough, who carries that?
Where it goes wrong: adding I will try to make it work after being cut; and being too grateful to set terms when they come back asking for help.

### Lines to keep
It cannot be done with fewer than six hundred thousand men.
If you must use me, it is still six hundred thousand.
Revise the number after a refusal and you have proved it was padding.

========================================================================
## Wang Jian · Asking for fields and houses
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wang-jian/asking-for-fields/
Source: Records of the Grand Historian, Bai Qi and Wang Jian
Tags: Deep read, Wang Jian, Hand them a hold over you

Holding almost every soldier in the state, how do you let the king sleep? This is about choosing to look greedy.

### Q: What actually happened?
Wang Jian set out with six hundred thousand men, very nearly the whole army of Qin in one pair of hands. Before leaving he asked the king for a large grant of good fields, houses, gardens and ponds. Go on, said the king, laughing, why worry about being poor. At Hangu Pass he sent men back five more times to ask for good land. Someone told him he was asking too much. The king is suspicious and trusts nobody, he said; he has handed me the whole army, and if I do not ask for a great deal, would I not leave him sitting there doubting me?

### The parts · When you could threaten them, show a weakness on purpose
Holding the army and wanting nothing does not read as high-minded to a suspicious king. It reads as a larger design. What Wang Jian supplied was a want that could be understood, quantified, and withdrawn at any time. Greed is a reassuring weakness to have.
e.g. The one person holding a company's only core technology, if visibly indifferent to money and title, unsettles people. Being known to want something is safer.

### The parts · Ask for what they can afford to give
Fields and ponds cost the king almost nothing and could be granted. Had Wang Jian asked for a marquisate, for troops, for standing, the request would itself have become the new threat. The trick lies in the nature of the thing asked for: small, specific, and revocable at will.
e.g. Asking in a negotiation for cash and a defined title is easier to grant, and raises fewer alarms, than asking for vaguer influence over decisions.

### The parts · Five times was deliberate
He did not ask once. He asked five more times on the march. A single request reads as normal. Repeating it until it is nearly embarrassing is what builds a signal that keeps transmitting, through exactly the stretch when the king most needs reassurance.
e.g. Reporting your progress and your difficulties over and over during a critical project looks like fussing. It is continuous dissolving of the other side's uncertainty.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: what you hold, or what you can do, has become large enough to make the people above you uneasy.
Ask first: do they know what I want, and is it something they can comfortably give?
Where it goes wrong: assuming that wanting nothing is the safest posture; and asking, when you do ask, for power or standing, which becomes the new threat.

### Lines to keep
The king is suspicious and trusts nobody.
Would I not leave him sitting there doubting me?
A want they can see is safer than a want they have to guess.

========================================================================
## Wang Xing · Watch the core, not the boundary
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wang-xing/core-not-boundary/
Source: Interview with Caijing, 2017
Tags: Deep read, Wang Xing, The test for expansion

With Meituan fighting on four fronts at once, everyone asked where its boundary was. What he replaced the question with.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 2017 Meituan was fighting at the same time in food delivery, hotels, ride-hailing and groceries, and Caijing asked Wang Xing where the boundary lay. He swapped the question. Nothing really has a simple boundary, so he saw no reason to fence himself in. Too many people watch the boundary instead of the core. The core he had set was one line: the service core is eating, and the platform exists to help people eat better and live better. The test follows from it. A new business is judged by its distance from that core, not by an industry line.

### The parts · Boundaries are drawn by other people; a core grows out of you
Industry boundary is taxonomy, drawn on an observer's map: delivery company, hotel company, transport company. Run the business by the map and every expansion looks like trespass. Run it by the core and the question becomes what else the same users and the same fulfilment can serve.
e.g. A bookshop reasoning by boundary can sell books. Reasoning by core, the hours of the same reading people, coffee and talks and objects are all in range.

### The parts · Distance from the core sets the odds
No boundary does not mean anything goes. Measure each new business against the core: how much user overlap, how much of the fulfilment network is reused, how much of the supply side is entirely new. Near expansion spreads fixed cost. Far expansion is founding a company again.
e.g. Score a new business on three lines: existing users, reused capability, things to be built. When the third line is the longest, do not call it expansion.

### The parts · Having no boundary assumes the core is thickening
The move carries a hidden condition. The core has to keep hardening, or fighting on many fronts only spreads a thin thing thinner. While Meituan fought everywhere, delivery scale and fulfilment efficiency kept pulling away. Let the core stall and no boundary turns into no focus.
e.g. Diversification launched as the main business slows is the dangerous kind: not radiating from a core but jumping off a sinking boat. Ask whether the core thickened this year.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: an opportunity sits outside the usual industry line and the team is arguing about whether to take it.
Ask first: how far is it from our core, how much of the users, the capability and the supply carries over, and is our core thicker this year or thinner?
Where it goes wrong: using no boundary to license aimless diversification; or defining the core so narrowly that genuinely adjacent things are all ruled out.

### Lines to keep
Nothing really has a simple boundary, so I refuse to fence myself in.
Too many people watch the boundary instead of the core.
As long as the core is clear, we know where to go.

========================================================================
## Wang Xing · Avoiding the real thinking
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wang-xing/escape-from-thinking/
Source: Wang Xing's posts on Fanfou
Tags: Deep read, Wang Xing, The illusion of diligence

One line he wrote on a microblog is quoted more than anything else he has said. How busyness became a substitute for thought.

### Q: What actually happened?
The most quoted thing Wang Xing has written is a line from Fanfou: most people will do anything rather than face real thinking. The blade is in anything, which includes overtime, meetings, research and retrospectives, the activities that most resemble thought. Real thinking points at uncomfortable questions. Should this be done at all? Does the premise still hold? What would we choose starting over? A full calendar is a perfect reason not to answer them. Another of his lines works as a footnote: no clinging to what is past, go forward with everything.

### The parts · Busyness is the most respectable form of avoidance
Avoiding by scrolling produces guilt; avoiding by working late produces applause, which makes it far harder to quit. The tell is a mismatch between the activity and the question: the real question is direction and people optimise execution, the real question is whether and people debate how.
e.g. A project whose premise has already shifted enters its most industrious phase: polish, process, detailed weeklies. Everyone is voting with effort not to ask the question.

### The parts · Real thinking leaves something behind
To separate thinking from activities named after thinking, look at the output. Real thinking produces a judgement that could be overturned: a premise written down, a trade-off quantified, a thing explicitly given up. Three hours of meeting that produced nothing capable of being wrong was socialising.
e.g. Search the minutes for one sentence of the form: we believe X, and if Y happens this is void. A meeting without that shape never thought.

### The parts · Put the uncomfortable questions on the calendar
What gets avoided is always the same short list, so the fix can be mechanical. Write them down and force an answer on a schedule: what should we stop, which premise is shakiest, would we start this from zero today? Thinking cannot wait for inspiration, it needs a slot it cannot escape.
e.g. Half a day each quarter, everyone answering three uncomfortable questions, execution banned from the room. That half-day often outearns the quarter's diligence.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you or the team are in an unusually busy, unusually full stretch.
Ask first: which question are we avoiding, and when did we last produce a judgement that could be proved wrong?
Where it goes wrong: using the line to sneer at all execution, when after it is clear diligence is the whole job; or turning real thinking into permanent abstraction with no output at all.

### Lines to keep
Most people will do anything rather than face real thinking.
No clinging to what is past; go forward with everything.
The more confident about the future, the more patient about now.

## Wang Yangming · Knowing and doing are one thing
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wang-yangming/unity-of-knowing-and-doing/
Source: Instructions for Practical Living, part one
Tags: Deep read, Wang Yangming, Not done means not known

'I understand it, I just can't do it.' Wang Yangming argued that the sentence itself is the error.

### Q: What actually happened?
A student objected: plenty of people know they should honour their parents and don't, so knowing and doing must be two things. Wang Yangming's reply closes the road. There has never been anyone who knew and did not act. To know and not act is simply not to know. He adds the test: to say a man knows filial duty, he must already have practised it, not merely be able to use the word. As with pain — to know it is to have hurt.

### The parts · 'I understand but can't do it' is a self-issued exemption
Split knowing from doing and you have carved out a permanently safe position: my understanding is fine, my execution is a little short. 'To know and not act is simply not to know' deletes that position. There is no middle state.
e.g. 'I know I should start earlier, I just procrastinate.' By his test that person hasn't grasped the cost. He has heard about it.

### The parts · Knowing is signed off in the doing
How do you tell whether you actually understand something? Not by whether you can explain it, but by whether you used it in the moment it was needed. Explaining well is one ability. Using it is another, and the first doesn't contain the second.
e.g. You can recite every framework in the negotiation book and still negotiate on old habit. It stopped at the telling.

### The parts · The thought starting is already the act
He puts the start of action extremely early: where a thought arises, the act has already begun. Not when the movement happens — at the instant of the thought. That moves the ground of the work from behaviour back to intention, which means there is no such thing as 'only thinking about it'.
e.g. The first time 'I can fudge this one' occurs to you and you don't cut it off, it has already started.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something you keep telling yourself you should do, and have never done.
Ask first: if I can't say when I last did it, on what grounds do I say I know it?
Where it goes wrong: treating 'I've understood it' as a milestone; or policing only behaviour and leaving the thought completely unguarded.

### Lines to keep
There has never been anyone who knew and did not act.
To know and not act is simply not to know.
Where a thought arises, the act has already begun.

## Wang Yangming · You are polished by events
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wang-yangming/polish-on-things/
Source: Instructions for Practical Living, part three
Tags: Deep read, Wang Yangming, Sitting still trains nothing

Someone said he felt perfectly steady sitting quietly and fell apart the moment anything happened. Why that steadiness doesn't count.

### Q: What actually happened?
A student complained that in quiet meditation things felt clear, and the moment something happened it was different. Wang Yangming's answer: that's because you only cultivate stillness and never do the work of mastering yourself. A person must be polished by events to stand firm. He was his own evidence. After his awakening in exile he didn't return to the cushion; he went on to put down four rebellions in succession, all of it done in the middle of events.

### The parts · Steadiness in a quiet room is fake
With nothing interrupting, everybody is steady. Composure can only be measured while you're being cut off, misread, or pushed against a deadline. A state trained in a silent room scatters the moment something happens because it was never tested.
e.g. The plan made on Sunday is clear and firm. Three urgent messages on Monday and it's gone. The plan was fine. It was never tested.

### The parts · Events are the only training ground
Being polished by events means treating every piece of trouble as the equipment, not as the thing preventing practice. Cultivation and getting things done aren't two activities competing for time. The first can only happen inside the second.
e.g. 'I'll sort myself out once this busy stretch is over', so it never gets sorted. The busyness is the material.

### The parts · Mastering yourself is a specific action
Cultivating stillness without mastering yourself, he said, is a cat watching an empty hole. Mastery isn't a vague resolution to be better. It's holding down one specific impulse at one specific moment: not interrupting when you want to, hearing it out before defending yourself.
e.g. The three seconds after being corrected in public are the only real practice you get all day.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you think clearly when things are calm and lose shape the moment you're in the room.
Ask first: when was I last genuinely thrown? What did I do in that moment?
Where it goes wrong: scheduling self-cultivation as a separate project needing a quiet environment; treating interruptions as what breaks the practice rather than as the practice.

### Lines to keep
A person must be polished by events to stand firm.
Cultivating stillness without self-mastery is a cat watching an empty hole.
Steady in stillness, steady in motion — one is not the other.
