## Wang Yangming · Act on what you already know
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wang-yangming/innate-knowing/
Source: Instructions for Practical Living, part two
Tags: Deep read, Wang Yangming, The answer is in your first reaction

Most of what we call being unable to decide is being unwilling to admit. Why he said the judgement is already there.

### Q: What actually happened?
Late in life Wang Yangming compressed everything into three characters usually rendered as 'extending innate knowing'. The knowing is the judgement every person already has: that bit of innate knowing in you is your own standard. The moment an intention stirs, he said, right is right and wrong is wrong, and it cannot be fooled. Don't cheat it, act on it, and that is the whole of it. So the difficulty was never knowing right from wrong. It is admitting the one you already know.

### The parts · The first reaction has usually already answered
Before you have begun finding reasons, the judgement in that instant is generally accurate. The weighing that follows is mostly not a search for the answer. It's a search for an acceptable substitute for the answer you have.
e.g. You see the figures are wrong and know in one second it goes back. The next half hour of 'no time', 'close enough' isn't analysis. It's negotiation.

### The parts · The hard part is not cheating it
Three things cover the knowing: not wanting the hassle, not wanting to look bad, not wanting to offend. Extending it isn't improving your judgement. It's moving those three screens aside so the judgement that's already there can reach an action.
e.g. You know this call is yours to make and hand it to someone else, because 'it lands better from him'.

### The parts · Sages fill the street
If everyone has it, the gap between people in judgement is smaller than we imagine — the gap is in willingness to act on it. That sounds egalitarian and is actually severe: you can no longer plead that you lack the insight.
e.g. The most reliable person on a team is rarely the cleverest. It's the one who does it knowing it's a hassle.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you've been turning something over for a long time without deciding, and there has been a direction in you the whole while.
Ask first: what was my judgement in the first second? Are these later reasons testing it, or replacing it?
Where it goes wrong: mistaking unwillingness for lack of clarity and gathering more information; using 'I need to think more' to postpone an answer you have.

### Lines to keep
That bit of innate knowing in you is your own standard.
Everyone has a sage inside. Most bury him by not trusting him.
The difficulty was never knowing. It is admitting.

## Wang Yangming · The bandits inside
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wang-yangming/bandits-in-the-heart/
Source: Letter to Yang Shide and Xue Shangqian
Tags: Deep read, Wang Yangming, The hardest battle is the interior one

He never lost a campaign. Why he said all of those were the easy ones.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1518, while suppressing bandits in Jiangxi, Wang Yangming wrote to two students: to break the bandits in the hills is easy; to break the bandits in the heart is hard. He had just put down, with very few troops, an insurgency entrenched for decades — the thing everyone else considered impossible — and he called it easy. Bandits in the hills have a form: position, numbers, supply lines, all discoverable. The ones inside have none. They aren't out there. They are the one doing the judging.

### The parts · Problems with a shape are always the easier ones
A problem you can list is already half solved. What really holds a person is the stuff with no name: resentment, fear of being thought less of, a grudge against one particular person. None of it enters any list, and all of it quietly rewrites every decision.
e.g. The meeting lists resourcing, scheduling, dependencies. The real cause may be a bad exchange between two leads three months ago.

### The parts · The interior bandit disguises itself as reasoning
It never arrives looking like emotion. Resentment says 'there's still an opportunity in this direction'. Fear of embarrassment says 'switching now is too expensive'. So you catch it by auditing arguments, not by inspecting feelings — check whether the reason always points at the same conclusion.
e.g. You oppose the same person's proposals every time, and the reason is different every time. The reasons aren't what's operating.

### The parts · Break your own first, then talk about anyone else's
He wrote that letter while commanding troops and governing a province. He didn't file the interior work under things to do once the fighting stopped; he treated it as the inside of the same job. Campaigning outward and mastering yourself draw on one supply of energy.
e.g. A manager who audits every external account and never his own preferences ends up with an organisation shaped like them, and can't see it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something won't move, and you have the full list of external causes.
Ask first: the reasons are different each time — is the conclusion the same each time?
Where it goes wrong: scheduling the interior work for after the job is finished; admitting only the causes that can be written into a list.

### Lines to keep
Breaking the bandits in the hills is easy. The ones inside aren't.
When this mind does not move, you can move with the moment.
The reasons change and the conclusion doesn't. That tells you something.

========================================================================
## The Wealth of Nations · Not from benevolence
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wealth-of-nations/not-benevolence/
Source: The Wealth of Nations, Book I, chapter 2; Book IV, chapter 2
Tags: Deep read, The Wealth of Nations, Aim at their interest

The most quoted sentence in economics is about dinner. Read closely, what it hands you is a protocol for asking.

### Q: What actually happened?
Book I, chapter 2: it is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker, that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest. Smith then says the operative part out loud. We address ourselves not to their humanity but to their self-love, and never talk to them of our own necessities but of their advantages. It reads as a verdict on human selfishness and it is closer to a protocol. If you want a stranger to act for you dependably, his interest is the only reliable interface. Goodwill exists; its supply is unsteady and it does not scale.

### The parts · Goodwill is scarce; do not build infrastructure on it
Between friends a favour runs on affection. Cooperation at scale cannot: goodwill tires, plays favourites, and moves with mood. Smith's observation is that a system built on the other side's interest is maintained by every participant, while one built on goodwill has to be topped up by you.
e.g. Trading on being liked gets a colleague to help you three times. Attaching the work to his own targets or his own numbers gets it for three years.

### The parts · Word order: say what they get first
Never talk of our own necessities but of their advantages is a sentence structure you can copy without alteration. Most requests open by describing the asker's difficulty, which is an application for charity. Open with what the other side receives and the same request becomes an offer of trade.
e.g. We urgently need your team to schedule this, against once this endpoint ships, three of your open tickets close themselves. Same request. The second one gets answered today.

### The parts · The invisible hand appears once, with conditions attached
The phrase occurs once in the entire book, in a passage about why merchants invest at home. Self-interest serves the public conditionally: Smith's butcher stands in a market with competition, law and customers who return. Under monopoly or fraud or a one-shot deal, the same self-interest points elsewhere.
e.g. Sellers on a marketplace serve you well while reviews bite and prices are easy to compare. Switch those two off and the same sellers wear a different face.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you need steady cooperation from someone under no obligation to give it.
Ask first: what does this person get when it is done, and can that sentence go first?
Where it goes wrong: turning the interest interface into naked purchase; or invoking the hand inside a monopoly or a one-shot deal, where it was never claimed to work.

### Lines to keep
It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker.
We address ourselves not to their humanity but to their self-love.
Led by an invisible hand to promote an end no part of his intention.

========================================================================
## The Wealth of Nations · The pin factory
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wealth-of-nations/pin-factory/
Source: The Wealth of Nations, Book I, chapters 1 to 3; Book V, chapter 1
Tags: Deep read, The Wealth of Nations, What division of labour costs

The book opens in a small workshop. This is how the forty-eight thousand were counted, and what the same author says they cost.

### Q: What actually happened?
The book's first sentence is not about gold. The greatest improvement in the productive powers of labour came from the division of labour, and the evidence is a pin factory. A workman not trained to the business could scarce, with his utmost industry, make one pin in a day. Split pin-making into eighteen operations and ten persons could make among them upwards of forty-eight thousand pins in a day. Three causes: dexterity, time no longer lost changing tasks, and machinery invented by people who do one motion all day. Chapter three adds the ceiling: the division of labour is limited by the extent of the market.

### The parts · The gain comes from three separate places
Dexterity is bought with repetition, switching cost is saved, and machinery is what occurs to somebody who has performed the same motion ten thousand times. The third is the one that gets forgotten: until the work is cut fine enough, there is nothing for automation to take hold of.
e.g. Support as one undivided job can never be automated. Cut into triage, lookup and templated reply, the first two are on a machine by the second month.

### The parts · Market size decides how fine you can cut
The least quoted and most useful chapter says the division of labour is limited by the extent of the market: only enough volume can keep a full-time specialist fed. Widening the market you can reach is therefore not merely selling more. It unlocks finer division, and with it lower cost.
e.g. One city's volume supports a general repairer. National volume supports someone who fixes only one fault. Scale comes before specialisation, not after it.

### The parts · Smith wrote the bill for it himself
Book V carries the warning: a man whose life is spent performing a few simple operations becomes as stupid and ignorant as it is possible for a human creature to become. The efficiency and the damage are in one book by one author. Quoting only chapter one is half the accounting.
e.g. Slice the roles thin enough and the productivity report looks superb. Two years on, nobody in those roles has an overview or a transferable skill.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you want more output by cutting the work into steps.
Ask first: does current volume feed every specialist the split creates, and who pays the human side of the bill?
Where it goes wrong: splitting before the volume is there, so every station sits half idle; or counting only the efficiency and leaving the people on the narrow jobs with no way out.

### Lines to keep
The greatest improvement in the productive powers of labour was the division of labour.
Ten persons could make among them upwards of forty-eight thousand pins.
The division of labour is limited by the extent of the market.

========================================================================
## Why Nations Fail · The two Nogaleses
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/why-nations-fail/two-nogales/
Source: Why Nations Fail, chapter 1
Tags: Deep read, Why Nations Fail, A natural controlled experiment

A fence cuts one city in two and income differs threefold. This is what that single case rules out.

### Q: What actually happened?
The book opens on a city split by a border: Nogales, Arizona and Nogales, Sonora. Same desert, same climate, same ancestors, same food, often the same families. North of the fence household income runs about three times the southern figure, and policing, health and life expectancy separate the same way. Geography, culture and ignorance are eliminated at a stroke, because everything else is held constant. One thing differs, and it is institutions. From here the authors set up the book's division: inclusive institutions give the many property, participation and a return; extractive ones let the few draw value off the many. Nations fail because their institutions are extractive.

### The parts · Go looking for a pair that differs by one variable
The value of Nogales is methodological. Climate, ancestry and culture are identical, so whatever remains has to carry the difference. Before analysing any gap, hunt for a natural pair like this. One of them is worth a hundred pages of general argument.
e.g. Two teams, comparable backgrounds, identical market, output differing threefold. Before discussing talent, find the one structural difference. It is usually in incentives and permission.

### The parts · Under extraction, effort does not change the ending
Nogales, Sonora is not lazier or less able; the same people become highly productive after crossing the fence. What defines an extractive structure is that the increment produced gets intercepted, so a rational person stops producing increments. Collective slackness is a question about who takes the return.
e.g. A team that has gone quiet is rarely a hiring mistake. They have worked out that the extra does not reach them. Change the split before changing the people.

### The parts · Inclusive means predictable, not generous
The heart of an inclusive institution is not how much is handed out but how securely it is kept: property that is not confiscated, rules that do not bend to the person, a way up that is open to most. People invest more in a small certain return than in a large uncertain one.
e.g. A modest commission that is never trimmed outperforms a doubled one whose rules are rewritten every year. Predictability is itself the incentive.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: two groups on similar terms are producing wildly different results.
Ask first: is there a pair here that differs by one variable, and what is that variable?
Where it goes wrong: charging every gap to institutions and refusing to see real differences in skill and execution; or the reverse, replacing people when the problem is structural.

### Lines to keep
The two cities share a climate, a geography and a set of ancestors.
Nations fail because extractive institutions destroy the incentive to save, invest and innovate.
Prosperity rests on inclusive economic and political institutions.

========================================================================
## Why Nations Fail · Why elites block progress
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/why-nations-fail/fear-of-creative-destruction/
Source: Why Nations Fail, chapters 2 and 3
Tags: Deep read, Why Nations Fail, Not stupid, afraid

A tsar refused railways; an emperor refused factories. This is why the people blocking a technology are the ones who understand it.

### Q: What actually happened?
The book collects cases that look like stupidity and are not. Francis I of Austria blocked railways and restricted factories; when a steam line was put to him he said he would have nothing to do with it, lest the revolution come into the country. Russia built almost none before the 1840s. Innovation brings creative destruction, replacing old industries and old power together. Railways move people, factories concentrate them, new money asks for a voice. For an elite living off the existing arrangement the gains go to society and the risk comes home, so blocking is rational. What obstructs progress is usually not ignorance but fear of creative destruction.

### The parts · Work out who loses before you push
When a change will not move, do not begin by assuming the other side cannot follow it. List whose position it devalues. The obstructor's judgement is often sharper than the reformer's, because he can see exactly what he is about to lose. The target is his ledger, not his understanding.
e.g. Middle managers stall the new system not because they cannot use it, but because it removes the information brokerage they stand on. A hundred training sessions will not help.

### The parts · Paying the losers is part of the price of change
Creative destruction has one political solution: give the likely losers a place in the new arrangement. Buy-out, redeployment, equity — the form does not matter. The money looks wasted and is actually the toll. Skip it and the cost returns doubled, as delay and quiet sabotage.
e.g. Closing an old line while giving that team options and first refusal on new roles costs far less than optimising them out, which teaches every watching team to start protecting itself.

### The parts · Watch for the moment you become the obstacle
The mechanism is not selective. Anyone holding a good position inside an existing arrangement sees his own risk first when something new appears. The signal to look for is this: your reason for opposing it changes every time and your conclusion never does. Position is doing the work, not reasoning.
e.g. You have objected to the new tool on security, then on cost, then on timing. Ask which piece of your ground gets smaller the day it goes live.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a plainly useful change is being held up by somebody.
Ask first: whose position does this devalue, and what have I prepared for those people?
Where it goes wrong: filing every objection under vested interest and missing a real risk warning; or buying people off without limit, until the toll sinks the reform.

### Lines to keep
Fear of creative destruction is the main obstacle to inclusive institutions.
Creative destruction redistributes not only income and wealth but political power.
They do not oppose the technology. They oppose what it redistributes.

========================================================================
## Norbert Wiener · He wrote to the union first
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wiener/wrote-to-the-union/
Source: Wiener's 1949 letter to Walter Reuther of the UAW; The Human Use of Human Beings, 1950
Tags: Deep read, Norbert Wiener, Before automation landed

Is there a move to make before a technology reaches you? What the man who built it did first.

### Q: What actually happened?
Cybernetics was published in 1948, and Wiener was the person who put machine control into the world. The next year he did something nobody was doing: he wrote to Walter Reuther, head of the United Auto Workers, saying automation would displace assembly-line workers on a large scale, that he was unwilling for this to happen with no preparation, and that the union should get involved early. In 1950 he turned the same worry into a book.

### The parts · The people who see it coming usually aren't hit yet
The year Wiener wrote, automation wasn't deployed and nobody had lost a job. Precisely because it hadn't landed, there was time to arrange something. Once it lands you only get to react; there is no room left to prepare.
e.g. The stretch while you still have work and haven't been cut is the only window you get to plan in.

### The parts · Find people in the same position before you find answers
He didn't start by writing a survival guide for workers. He went to the people who were already organised. One person carrying this kind of shock has almost no leverage; tens of thousands do. Making contact comes before working it out.
e.g. Finding people in your field already dealing with it beats sitting alone devising a strategy.

### The parts · The people pushing it and the people hit by it aren't two groups
He was both the inventor and the person raising the alarm, and in him those didn't conflict. The tool you use every day — the better you get with it, the sooner you can see which tasks it will take. Those are exactly the ones to prepare for.
e.g. The work you're saving yourself with it is work somebody else still eats from.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: something is spreading through your field, it hasn't reached your income yet, and you plan to wait and see.
Ask first: which task of mine can it already do? Who in my field have I actually talked to about it?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as a call to oppose things early — he went to the union to move the preparation forward, not to block automation; and this isn't personal heroism. His first move was to find people already organised.

### Lines to keep
Once it lands you only get to react. There is no room to plan.
Finding people in the same position comes before working it out.
The work you save with it is work somebody else eats from.

## Norbert Wiener · What a machine can do, and what to give it
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wiener/human-use/
Source: The Human Use of Human Beings, 1950
Tags: Deep read, Norbert Wiener, Two separate questions

Which work belongs to a tool and which doesn't. Why Wiener said capability doesn't settle it.

### Q: What actually happened?
Through The Human Use of Human Beings, Wiener keeps returning to one point: what a machine is capable of and what people are for are two independent questions. Whether a machine can do a task is technical. What is left of the person once you hand it over is a different question, and the answer isn't automatically good. What worried him wasn't machines getting stronger. It was people being arranged to do the machine's kind of work: repetitive, judgement-free, instruction-following.

### The parts · 'It can' does not imply 'it should'
Tool capability and division of labour are separate layers. Hand over everything it can do and what's left is often the scraps it can't do and you learn nothing from. What should go is the repetition, not the judgement.
e.g. Letting it draft is fine. Letting it decide what the piece is arguing hands over the wrong half.

### The parts · The fear is people used as machines
Wiener's worry ran the other way round. He wasn't afraid machines would be like people; he was afraid people would be arranged like machines — executing, not judging, not knowing why. Those roles go first, because they were already designed in a machine's shape.
e.g. A job that works a ticket queue and never asks why is in the first batch automation takes.

### The parts · Keep the part where you decide
Once the repetition is handed over, what has to remain is the stretch that needs a call made. Otherwise you gave away repetition and kept repetition. Judgement doesn't get cheaper as the tools improve. It gets dearer.
e.g. The tool gives you three options. Which one and why is the step you can't also hand over.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you're shifting work onto a tool and can't say which part should go and which shouldn't.
Ask first: am I handing over the repetition or the judgement? After it's gone, does anything left on my desk require a decision?
Where it goes wrong: using it as grounds for distrusting tools and doing everything yourself — he objected to handing over the judgement, not the repetition; and it isn't a list of things machines may not touch. He's describing a division of labour.

### Lines to keep
What a machine can do and what people are for are separate questions.
He feared people being arranged like machines, not machines resembling people.
Hand over the repetition. Not the judgement.

========================================================================
## Norbert Wiener · Control is a loop, not an order
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wiener/feedback-not-command/
Source: Cybernetics, 1948
Tags: Deep read, Norbert Wiener, Seeing the result beats issuing instructions

Why the thing you carefully explained still comes back wrong. How Wiener defined control instead.

### Q: What actually happened?
Cybernetics defines control not as issuing an instruction but as using the actual result to correct the next move — the feedback loop. Wiener's example is reaching for a cup: the eyes keep reporting the gap between hand and cup, and the hand corrects as it travels. Cut that report and the movement immediately goes off, however well it was aimed to begin with. Machines and living things, he said, obey the same thing here.

### The parts · An instruction with no report back isn't control
However clearly you explained it, without a channel carrying the actual result back you hold an intention, not control. Things come back wrong not because people don't listen but because the loop is cut and nobody can tell how far off it has drifted.
e.g. Brief it and wait for delivery, never seeing the thing in between, and what arrives will not be what you pictured.

### The parts · The report has to arrive while it can still be changed
Feedback later than the correctable window is worthless. The value of a loop isn't whether it exists but how often it reports — weekly and daily differ by an order of magnitude in how much drift can still be pulled back.
e.g. Finding out at month end that the month went wrong means the month is already spent.

### The parts · Practising alone runs on the same rule
Stuck on a skill is usually not a shortage of practice. It's the absence of any mechanism reporting the result back: you finish and don't know whether it was good or where it went wrong. More hours won't fix that. A report channel will.
e.g. Months of practice and no progress: first check whether anything tells you which move was wrong.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: what you asked for keeps coming back different, or you've practised something for months with no progress.
Ask first: how often does the actual result come back to me? Inside that interval, how much is still changeable?
Where it goes wrong: reading it as watch more closely — he means shorten the reporting cycle, not raise the intervention rate. They aren't the same, and the second usually crushes the loop itself.

### Lines to keep
Control isn't issuing an order. It's correcting from the result.
It came back wrong because the loop was cut, not because nobody listened.
Feedback later than the correctable window is no feedback.

========================================================================
## Wu Zetian · Promote out of turn, drop just as fast
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wu-zetian/promote-and-drop/
Source: The Comprehensive Mirror, Tang chronicles
Tags: Deep read, Wu Zetian, Fast in, and fast out

Many of the people she raised were later demoted or killed. This is about why a method that looks chaotic actually worked.

### Q: What actually happened?
Sima Guang, who did not approve of her, wrote the most precise account of how she appointed people. She was not sparing with rank, using it to draw in able men everywhere as her own support; even an absurd man, if what he said fitted, was promoted out of turn. Those who could not do the job were dismissed soon after, or executed. Holding the two handles of punishment and reward, she governed from herself, saw clearly and decided well, so the able men of the age competed to be used by her.

### The parts · Bold intake requires cheap removal
The risk in promoting out of turn is picking wrong. She moved that risk onto the exit: fast in, fast out. Most organisations dare not promote boldly, and the real reason is not poor judgement of people; it is that removing someone is expensive, so the gate has to be conservative.
e.g. If probation is a formality and confirmation is automatic, interviews can only get harder. Lower the cost of changing your mind and hiring gets braver by itself.

### The parts · A wide gate is a way of enlarging the sample
Even an absurd man, if what he said fitted. She did not ask for a person to be reliable overall, only to have been right about one thing. That turns selection from judging a person into collecting samples and filtering, with real work replacing prior assessment.
e.g. Instead of three months hunting a flawless candidate, give three people one real job each and look at the results in a month. Sample size beats accuracy of judgement.

### The parts · Both handles have to stay in one hand
Holding the two handles is the pivot the whole thing turns on. Promotion and dismissal were hers alone, with no layer in between to cushion or to plead. Once those two are dispersed, fast in and fast out degrades into in only.
e.g. Promotion needs five meetings and dismissal needs eight. The outcome is fixed: people can enter and cannot leave, and the organisation only swells.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you want to promote someone with an incomplete record and one outstanding side, and you are hesitating.
Ask first: if this is wrong in three months, can I move them out, and what does that cost?
Where it goes wrong: doing the bold intake without the exit, so the team runs away from you; handing both handles to committees, then wondering why nobody ever leaves.

### Lines to keep
She was not sparing with rank, and used it to draw in talent.
Those who could not do the job were dismissed soon after.
Daring to promote out of turn rests on daring to remove.

## Wu Zetian · How did the chancellor lose this man
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/wu-zetian/the-manifesto/
Source: New Book of Tang, Biographies of Men of Letters
Tags: Deep read, Wu Zetian, Recruiting from the pamphlet attacking you

A document tearing you to pieces is put in front of you. This is about what she said at the cruellest line in it.

### Q: What actually happened?
Xu Jingye rose against her, and Luo Binwang wrote the proclamation: an attack running from her private life to her usurpation, in the most vicious terms available. She laughed her way through it. Then she came to the earth on the late emperor's grave is not yet dry, and where have you put the orphan entrusted to you — and stopped laughing, and asked who wrote this. Luo Binwang, they said. How did the chancellor come to lose this man? It was a document abusing her, and what she took from it was the writer.

### The parts · Handle the content and the stance separately
A passage carries two things at once: what it says, and which side the speaker is on. Almost everyone rejects both the moment they feel the hostility. She assessed the quality first and dealt with the position second. That order decides how much you can learn from an opponent.
e.g. A competitor's public teardown of your product usually contains its real weaknesses. Refusing to read it because of the source throws away the most honest review you get.

### The parts · The line that hurts most is the most accurate
Where she stopped was the one sentence in the whole piece she could not answer. An attacker looking to hurt you goes hunting for the truest thing available, so hostile text often carries more information per line than friendly feedback, which is padded with politeness.
e.g. The furious one-star review is usually far more specific than the five-star one. How uncomfortable something is to read often tracks how much it tells you.

### The parts · She sent the blame back to her own system
Her response was not that the man was vile but that the chancellor had failed. The problem was assigned to her own machinery for finding talent. Few people manage this step: facing an able person who has gone to the other side, the first move is to audit yourself.
e.g. When a key person leaves for a competitor, asking why our own assessment never spotted them is more useful than discussing their ingratitude.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: someone is attacking you or your work, in public and hard.
Ask first: setting the stance aside, which sentence in it is hardest to refute?
Where it goes wrong: rejecting the whole thing because of who wrote it; treating talent going to a rival as their failing and never auditing your own machinery.

### Lines to keep
The grave earth is not yet dry; where is the orphan entrusted?
How did the chancellor come to lose this man?
The line you cannot answer is the one worth keeping.

## Xiang Yu · Break the pots, sink the boats
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/xiang-yu/sinking-the-boats/
Source: Records of the Grand Historian, Annals of Xiang Yu
Tags: Deep read, Xiang Yu, Everything on one throw

Julu was the high point of his life. This is about why the thing that won it so completely never changed afterwards.

### Q: What actually happened?
Zhang Han had Zhao besieged and a dozen allied armies were camped nearby, not one of them willing to fight. Xiang Yu killed the commander Song Yi, took the army across the river, and then sank the boats, broke the cooking pots, burned the huts and carried three days of rations, to show the men they would die there and had no thought of return. The Chu army fought nine engagements and won nine. Afterwards he summoned the allied generals, and they came through the gate of his camp on their knees, not one daring to look up. He was twenty-seven.

### The parts · All in works only while nobody else will move
The setting at Julu was a dozen armies waiting and nobody willing to be first. Where everyone is conserving strength, the one side that commits everything collects a return far larger than the input. The identical move on a field where everyone is straining is only expenditure.
e.g. When an industry contracts and everyone waits for someone else to move, one heavy counter-cyclical bet takes several times the usual share. In a boom it only raises the price.

### The parts · The more complete the win, the harder it is to change
Julu convinced him that overwhelming frontal attack answers everything, and a belief confirmed by an enormous success is nearly impossible to revise. Every deadlock afterwards was met the same way, all the way to Gaixia. The most successful experience is usually the least falsifiable one.
e.g. A company founded on one wildly successful method keeps running it after conditions change. Not for failing to see the change: the success was too large to doubt.

### The parts · What you do after winning decides the rest
He won at Julu, and what he then did with the surrendered Qin troops, and later at Xianyang, spent down the position the victory had bought him. A battle is settled once. How you place the defeated and the allies afterwards decides how long the victory keeps.
e.g. How you treat the losing side's team and channels after a commercial win matters more to the next round than the win. Win ugly and everyone lines up opposite you.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you want to put every resource you have into one decisive push.
Ask first: is everyone around me holding back right now, or is everyone already charging?
Where it goes wrong: treating one successful method as permanently correct; and not thinking about how the thing gets settled once you have won.

### Lines to keep
They sank the boats and broke the pots, with three days of rations.
The generals came through the gate of his camp on their knees.
The most successful experience is the hardest one to overturn.

## Xiang Yu · Brocade worn at night
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/xiang-yu/brocade-at-night/
Source: Records of the Grand Historian, Annals of Xiang Yu
Tags: Deep read, Xiang Yu, Deciding in order to be seen

He was urged to make Guanzhong his capital and went home instead. This is about what his reason gave away.

### Q: What actually happened?
After entering Xianyang and burning the Qin palaces, he was advised to stay: Guanzhong has mountains and rivers to defend it, the land is rich, and he could rule from there. Xiang Yu looked at the burnt palaces, thought of home, and said that to be rich and not go home is to wear brocade at night, and who is going to see it. The man who had advised him remarked on the way out that people said the men of Chu were monkeys in caps, and it was true. Xiang Yu had him boiled. He went east to Pengcheng and gave Guanzhong to three surrendered Qin generals.

### The parts · Decisions made to be seen are the expensive ones
The strategic distance between Guanzhong and Pengcheng was obvious, and he was not incapable of seeing it. What made him give up Guanzhong was not an error of judgement but a stronger motive. When the real aim is recognition, the objective conditions get downweighted automatically.
e.g. Choosing the visible direction over the one that grows, with a stack of reasons ready, and the real reason being that former colleagues will see it.

### The parts · Kill the man who says it and nobody says it again
Monkeys in caps was an ugly line and the only true sentence available at the time. Boiling him did more than remove a person: everyone still willing to speak plainly received a definitive demonstration. Information channels rarely close gradually. They close in a single act.
e.g. Deal publicly with one person for objecting and for six months the room contains nothing but agreement. That cost appears on no statement.

### The parts · The distribution ran on the same logic
He gave Guanzhong to three surrendered Qin generals and handed the best territory to old nobility and men of reputation, on a standard of seniority and face rather than control. That distribution served being acknowledged too. He wanted princes honouring him, not a structure that worked.
e.g. Allocate the key posts by seniority and goodwill and everyone is satisfied for a while. A year later the most important seats hold the least suitable people.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: two options, one better on the merits and one that more people will see.
Ask first: if this worked and nobody ever heard about it, would I still choose it?
Where it goes wrong: dressing the wish to be recognised up as a strategic reason; and dealing with the one person who names it out loud.

### Lines to keep
To be rich and not go home is to wear brocade at night.
They said the men of Chu were monkeys in caps, and it was true.
Channels do not close gradually. They close in a single act.

## Xunzi · Where the rules came from
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/xunzi/origin-of-rites/
Source: Xunzi, Discourse on Ritual; Human Nature is Bad
Tags: Deep read, Xunzi, Scarcity wrote them, not virtue

Rules feel like morality handed down. His answer names no morality at all: only wants, shortage, and no line drawn.

### Q: What actually happened?
The Discourse on Ritual opens with a question and answers it in one breath: where do rites come from? People are born with wants; wanting and not getting, they cannot help seeking; seeking without measure or division, they cannot help fighting. Fighting brings disorder, disorder brings poverty. The former kings hated the disorder, so they set out rites to draw the lines — to feed the wants and supply the seeking, so that wants and goods grow up supporting each other. Nowhere in the chain does anyone turn bad.

### The parts · The fight is in the missing line, not in the person
Blaming someone's character is the cheapest diagnosis available and the least useful one. His diagnosis is seeking without measure or division: nobody drew the boundary. Replace the people and the same argument arrives with the new ones.
e.g. Two teams have fought over the same budget for a year. Write down who gets it under which conditions and the fighting stops that week.

### The parts · Rites feed the want; they do not forbid it
Rites exist to feed the wants and supply the seeking. Desire is treated as legitimate and given a channel, not a fence. A rule that only makes the wanted thing harder to reach gets routed around; a rule that makes the honest route the fast one gets used.
e.g. An expenses policy that only makes spending difficult gets bypassed. One that makes compliant spending fast and legible gets followed without anyone being told twice.

### The parts · Deliberate effort, not hypocrisy
Human nature is bad; what is good in people is deliberate effort. The word usually translated as artifice means made, worked, put there on purpose. Cooperative order is not native to anyone. That cancels the expectation of self-motivation and hands the job back to whoever designs the rules.
e.g. Complaining that nobody takes ownership is waiting for something innate. The real question is what behaviour the current incentives are actually manufacturing.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the same conflict keeps coming back and you have already changed the people.
Ask first: is there a written division of this boundary that both sides have read?
Where it goes wrong: treating a boundary problem as a character problem; designing rules that only make things harder instead of making the right route smooth.

### Lines to keep
People are born with wants, and wanting without division ends in fighting.
Rites were made to feed the wants and supply the seeking.
Human nature is bad; what is good in people is deliberate effort.

## Xunzi · Borrow the horse, don't grow legs
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/xunzi/borrow-from-things/
Source: Xunzi, An Exhortation to Learning
Tags: Deep read, Xunzi, Leverage beats effort

Two people of equal ability, and one of them gets much further. He says the difference is not in the person.

### Q: What actually happened?
The chapter on learning stops midway for an oddly practical observation. A man who borrows a horse and carriage has not grown faster feet, yet he reaches a thousand li; a man who borrows a boat and oars cannot swim, yet he crosses rivers. The conclusion: the gentleman is not different by birth; he is good at borrowing from things. The whole chapter is called An Exhortation to Learning and lands almost entirely on tools, surroundings and accumulation. Talent is barely mentioned.

### The parts · Look for the lever before you look for more effort
Native ability improves slowly and tools improve in steps. So the first response to work that will not move should be what can I borrow, not I must try harder. Borrowing a horse does not make the feet quicker; it still covers the thousand li.
e.g. Checking three thousand rows by hand takes two days; a short script takes twenty minutes. The person working until midnight moved his effort before he moved his tools.

### The parts · Your surroundings are the strongest tool you own
Mugwort growing in a hemp field stands straight without being tied. Environment is the most powerful instrument available because it works every hour and costs no willpower. Choosing the setting is far cheaper than disciplining yourself inside a bad one.
e.g. Putting the phone in another room beats reminding yourself not to reach for it. One changes the surroundings; the other spends will you need elsewhere.

### The parts · Accumulation is the cheapest leverage there is
Without piling up small steps you never reach a thousand li. He sets the thoroughbred against the nag: a fine horse cannot clear ten paces in one leap, a poor one pulling for ten days arrives. Talent sets the single output; persistence sets the total.
e.g. Three hundred words a day is a hundred thousand in a year. The person waiting for one inspired weekend usually has nothing at all.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have worked hard at this and it still will not move.
Ask first: what tool, whose experience, or which change of setting could carry part of it for you?
Where it goes wrong: adding hours instead of finding leverage; fighting your surroundings with willpower rather than changing them.

### Lines to keep
The gentleman is not different by birth. He is good at borrowing.
Borrowing a horse, his feet are no quicker, yet he arrives.
A fine horse cannot leap ten paces; a nag walking ten days arrives.

## Xunzi · A group is a set of clear lines
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/xunzi/division-makes-groups/
Source: Xunzi, The Regulations of a King
Tags: Deep read, Xunzi, Headcount without division is a crowd

Slower than an ox and weaker than a tiger, people use both. The one-word answer he gives, and what follows from it.

### Q: What actually happened?
In The Regulations of a King he asks why oxen and horses, stronger and faster than any man, end up in harness. Because people can form groups and they cannot. Then the follow-up: how are people able to form groups? By division. And what makes division hold? A shared sense of what is right. He runs it out as a chain — divide and there is harmony, harmony makes one body, one body has strength, strength overcomes things. The fighting power of any organisation begins at how clearly the work is split.

### The parts · A group is not a number of people
Putting people together does not generate force on its own. Divide and there is harmony; harmony makes one body; only then is there strength. Where the division is unclear, more people means more friction, and the added force is negative.
e.g. A project of ten with nobody named against each piece often ships less than three did. The extra seven spend their days confirming and waiting.

### The parts · The division needs a reason people accept
He says division holds by a shared sense of what is right — meaning the split has to look defensible, not simply reflect who pushed hardest. Without a stated basis, every allocation is challenged again next quarter and the org chart is decoration.
e.g. Split resources by seniority or by results, either can work. What cannot work is a split nobody can say the reason for out loud.

### The parts · Name an owner for the gaps
The hard part of dividing work is never the core duties, it is the border. Everyone competes for the centre and everyone pushes away the edge. So the real task is assigning the things that fall between two people to one of them.
e.g. Who follows a live incident after release? Engineering says testing, testing says operations. That empty square is why response time never comes down.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you added people and the output did not follow.
Ask first: is each new person's boundary written down, and who owns the things that fall between them?
Where it goes wrong: throwing headcount at a coordination problem; dividing the core duties and leaving every gap unassigned.

### Lines to keep
People can form groups and animals cannot. How? By division.
Divide and there is harmony; harmony makes one body; one body has strength.
Everyone competes for the centre and everyone pushes away the edge.

## Xunzi · Heaven runs to its own schedule
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/xunzi/constant-heaven/
Source: Xunzi, Discourse on Heaven
Tags: Deep read, Xunzi, Sort the fixed from the movable

Bad year, bad market, bad luck. He closed this exit two thousand years ago, and not by denying the conditions.

### Q: What actually happened?
The Discourse on Heaven opens hard: heaven's course is constant; it did not persist for the sage king Yao and it did not vanish for the tyrant Jie. Nature does what it does regardless of who is on the throne. Respond to it with order and the result is good fortune; respond with disorder and the result is ruin. Then the famous line: rather than revering heaven and longing for it, why not master its workings and use them? He does not deny that outside conditions have force. He denies that they are an explanation.

### The parts · Constant means predictable, not unstoppable
Having a constant course means having a regularity. The regularity will not listen to you, but precisely because it is stable it can be used. Calling an outside condition an act of God is usually a way of not having studied its pattern.
e.g. Industries have cycles, and that is the constant. Firms that know it bank cash at the top and hire at the bottom; firms that call it weather miss both ends.

### The parts · Same sky, different response
His contrast is blunt: respond with order and it goes well, respond with disorder and it goes badly. Heaven did not move; the response did. A post-mortem that stops at the external condition has surrendered the only half that was ever adjustable.
e.g. Same year, same market: one company closes and another takes share. A shared input cannot account for the difference between them.

### The parts · Master it and use it
Rather than revering heaven and longing for it, master its workings and use them. This is where he parts company with everyone around him: attention moves from petition to command of the mechanism. The posture is startlingly modern and entirely practical.
e.g. Instead of waiting for the rules to settle, work through the part already settled and adjust to it. The waiters watch; the users have the first move.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the results are poor and the handiest explanation is the environment.
Ask first: in that same environment, what did the one who did well do differently?
Where it goes wrong: treating an external condition as an explanation rather than an input; refusing to study a pattern because you cannot change it.

### Lines to keep
Heaven's course did not persist for Yao nor vanish for Jie.
Respond with order and it goes well; with disorder, badly.
Rather than revering heaven, master its workings and use them.

## Zeng Guofan · Solid camp, dull fight
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/zeng-guofan/solid-camp-dull-fight/
Source: Xiang Army siege doctrine
Tags: Deep read, Zeng Guofan, A clumsy method that removes the uncertainty

He fought almost no brilliant battles and finished with the army still standing. This asks why the dullest method is the hardest to break.

### Q: What actually happened?
Wherever the Xiang Army arrived it did not attack. It camped: trench, wall, stockade, and no fighting until the work was finished. Cities were not stormed either. A long trench was cut the whole way round and pulled tighter ring by ring, which turned taking a city from an event full of accidents into a matter of time and supply. Anqing was held under siege for over a year, Tianjing for more than two. The method was mocked as dull. It also had a property nobody else's had: no single mistake could collapse it.

### The parts · Be unbeatable first, then discuss winning
The entire purpose of the solid camp is to take I could be destroyed off the board. Once that is done, what is left is time. This is not conservatism. It converts the outcome from a question of probability into a question of arithmetic.
e.g. Get cash, delivery quality and the people who hold the system to a state where none of them can fail suddenly. Then talk about expansion.

### The parts · Trade the flash of inspiration for a repeatable move
The other side of a dull method is that it copies. Any commander with any unit can follow it and reach a passing grade, while a brilliant stroke depends on that person on that day. An army raised from nothing could be carried by this because it did not need talent.
e.g. A sales process worth eighty that anyone can run beats one closer worth a hundred. The first goes to thirty cities; the second leaves when he does.

### The parts · Slow puts time on your side
A siege is far slower than an assault, but every day of an assault spends you and every day of a siege spends them. Speed cannot be judged off the progress bar alone. The question is who is getting weaker across this stretch.
e.g. Six months on retention before spending on acquisition looks half a year behind. Their users leak and yours do not, and by month seven the gap compounds.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: the other side is nimbler and bolder than you, and you are wondering whether to speed up too.
Ask first: would this method of mine still work if an ordinary person were running it?
Where it goes wrong: resting your hopes on one beautiful battle; or looking fast on the progress bar while spending yourself faster every day than the other side spends itself.

### Lines to keep
Argument from outside the game is useless. Step in and carry it.
Fight without haste: first make it stable, then look for change.
No single mistake could collapse it. That was the whole point.

## Zeng Guofan · Watched when nobody is watching
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/zeng-guofan/self-watch/
Source: Zeng Guofan's diaries and family letters
Tags: Deep read, Zeng Guofan, The stretch of the day with no observer

He set himself twelve daily disciplines and kept the record for thirty years. This asks why changing yourself is the one item available daily.

### Q: What actually happened?
At thirty he resolved to learn to be a sage, and was taught a method: write the diary every day, go through every thought and act in it, and enter the wrong ones and the bad impulses exactly as they were. He recorded a lewd thought on seeing a friend's womenfolk. He recorded the self-disgust after talking too big in company. Then the harder step — he passed the diary round his friends, which turned private self-examination into something with an audience. Watchfulness when alone stands first among the four maxims of his last years.

### The parts · Watchfulness alone installs an absent audience
Anybody keeps the rules while being watched. The test is the stretch when nobody is. His answer was not willpower but record-keeping: write it down and the moment acquires a witness. Where systems cannot reach, a record reaches part of the way.
e.g. Expenses nobody audits, code nobody reviews, a report nobody reads. The standard in those three places describes a person better than any appraisal.

### The parts · The value of a daily discipline is its grain size
I will become more disciplined cannot be executed. His twelve were checkable actions: rise early, sit in stillness, read one book at a time, keep the diary, note what was said over tea, let no month pass forgetting what he could do. Small enough to judge today.
e.g. Read more this year cannot be settled in December. Ten pages a day and three lines written afterwards can be ticked tonight. One is a wish, the other a discipline.

### The parts · Being seen is the cheapest constraint
Circulating the diary cost him almost nothing and did far more than resolve did. This is not performance, it is deliberately importing an outside correction, because a person's estimate of himself always runs high and honesty alone will not bring it down.
e.g. Post this week's commitments where other people read them. Completion rises sharply against the same list kept privately. The difference is not resolve.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you have set the goal many times and it has disappeared by the third week every time.
Ask first: can tonight's version of this be answered with did it or did not do it?
Where it goes wrong: goals made entirely of adjectives; or keeping the whole self-examination inside your own head, where no outside person will ever see it.

### Lines to keep
Watchfulness when alone brings peace of mind.
Steady work that never breaks off beats a burst of courage.
Do not go out to meet the future or cling to the past.

## Zeng Guofan · Take in widely, employ carefully
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/zeng-guofan/recruit-and-test/
Source: Zeng Guofan's practice with his personal staff
Tags: Deep read, Zeng Guofan, Judge people inside real work

A great many provincial governors came out of his staff. This asks how he judged a man before the man had anything to show.

### Q: What actually happened?
His method had two halves. Taking in widely meant a low bar at the door: bring people onto the staff and keep the pool large. Employing carefully moved the bar to the far end — not the record and not the conversation, but a real piece of work handed over, and then watching how he judged under actual pressure, how he reported, and what he did with the part he could not do. Li Hongzhang came up exactly that way, from the staff to independent command. What he looked for all his life was principle without officialdom, order in the head and few big words.

### The parts · Widen the entrance, tighten the exit
Selecting hard at the door assumes you can see through a man in one conversation, and that assumption usually does not hold. Moving the weight of the filter onto the first real task costs less and judges considerably better.
e.g. Rather than take the interview from four rounds to six, design the first project of the probation period as something genuinely hard that shows judgement.

### The parts · Watch how he accounts for it, not how it ended
A thing that came off may have come off by luck. What exposes a person is the process: whether he raises the part he cannot do early or holds it to the end, whether detail questions find him solid or vague, whether a failure comes back as a cause or as an excuse.
e.g. Ask where this is not finished. Whoever answers cleanly can be handed something bigger. Whoever says it is basically all fine usually does not know either.

### The parts · Few big words
Principle without officialdom, order in the head and few big words. He was wary of two kinds: the man whose manner exceeds his content, and the man whose talk exceeds his work. The first drains an organisation and the second manufactures a gap between what was promised and what arrives.
e.g. The more adjectives and the fewer numbers in a report, the further it sits from the actual work. Whoever can say this week's figures offhand is usually doing it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: choosing one of several people to hand something that matters.
Ask first: on the most recent real thing each of them did, how did they account for it?
Where it goes wrong: adding interview rounds instead of giving real work; or taking someone who talks well for someone who thinks clearly.

### Lines to keep
Principle without officialdom, order in the head and few big words.
For great undertakings, finding successors is the first business.
Ability runs high or low according to what a man aims at.

## Zhang Juzheng · The evaluation ledgers
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/zhang-juzheng/kaocheng/
Source: Memorial on auditing documents and assessing each matter, 1573
Tags: Deep read, Zhang Juzheng, Hang every item on a name and a date

Orders go down and nobody carries them out. This is about the ledger he used to fix a failure every dynasty had.

### Q: What actually happened?
In 1573 he described the situation plainly: the memorials were endless and no office held to anything. Once an order left, nobody tracked it, and there was no record of whether it had been done. His fix was crude. Everything due was entered in a register, in three copies, with a deadline, and struck off item by item when it fell due. If the governors delay, the ministries report it; if the ministries conceal, the six offices report it; if the six offices miss it, we report it. Within a few years an order issued in the morning was obeyed by evening ten thousand li away.

### The parts · Issued is not finished; struck off is
Most organisations break in the same place: there is a record that the order went out and no record that it came back. Without the act of striking off, work evaporates between layers naturally, and nobody has to answer for the evaporation.
e.g. The minutes list thirty actions and not one carries an owner and a date. Two weeks later, fewer than five have a status anyone can state.

### The parts · The point of three copies is the third one
One copy stayed with the office, one went to the supervising bureau, one to the cabinet. The same item sits in three places that do not report to each other, so any attempt to soften it shows up in the other two. A single ledger never cures delay.
e.g. If the task lives only on the delivery team's own board, they define progress. The same list held by the requester and by management is what makes the wording match.

### The parts · The audit has to reach the top layer
The decisive clause is that if the supervising offices miss it, the cabinet reports them. Nearly every assessment system stops at the supervisors, which makes the supervisors the one link nobody checks, and the whole chain slackens from there.
e.g. Who checks the checkers? Without that clause the quality team's own late reports are never pursued, and everyone can see it.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: plenty is decided and little lands, and you want more execution.
Ask first: is there a list with an owner and a deadline on every item, struck off one by one when due, and how many people hold that list?
Where it goes wrong: substituting meetings and emphasis for records; leaving the top layer of the assessment system unexamined.

### Lines to keep
The memorials are endless and no office holds to anything.
If the six offices miss it, we report it ourselves.
An order issued in the morning was obeyed by evening.

## Zhang Juzheng · The single whip
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/zhang-juzheng/single-whip/
Source: History of Ming, Treatise on Food and Money
Tags: Deep read, Zhang Juzheng, Merge the accounts into one payment

Why does the same sum shrink the more hands it passes through? This is about merging dozens of levies into one.

### Q: What actually happened?
Mid-Ming taxes and labour service were absurdly tangled: land tax, head service, tribute goods, labour levies, silver levies, dozens of headings, each with its own collection date, its own collector, its own conversion rate. Every stage was an opportunity to take a little more, and what the people paid and what the treasury received were far apart. The single whip totalled a county's taxes and services together, measured by land and counted by head, and all of it was paid in to the government. The state now hired labour for the year instead of levying it. Dozens of payments became one, in silver, on one date.

### The parts · Every stage is a chance to lose something
Complexity is itself a cost. More headings and more hands mean more room for interpretation, and every scrap of interpretive room eventually gets used. Simplification is not valuable because it saves effort; it is valuable because it removes the positions where things are done quietly.
e.g. Twenty expense categories with boundaries a person has to judge. Merge them into three and the disputes and the grey areas both vanish, without anyone becoming more honest.

### The parts · One unit of measurement
Converting to silver is the step people skip past, and it is the pivot of the whole reform. Goods, labour and time are not commensurable, so they cannot be reconciled. Once everything is in one unit, over-collection and under-collection are visible at a glance.
e.g. Each department reports on its own basis — leads, sign-ups, paid accounts. Until there is one basis, no total means anything.

### The parts · Simplifying offends whoever lives on the complexity
Complexity did not arise by itself; it is useful to somebody. The single whip cut into exactly the clerks and gentry who profited from the stages, which is why he was condemned after his death — and why the law survived, because it worked. Predict who will resist, and why.
e.g. Cut one useless approval and the loudest objection comes from whoever runs that approval. This is foreseeable. Have somewhere for them to go before you start.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a process is full of headings and every stage says it is necessary.
Ask first: converted into one unit, how many payments are actually left?
Where it goes wrong: merging without unifying the measure, so the books still do not reconcile; not predicting who lives on the complexity.

### Lines to keep
Total a county's taxes and services, measure by land, count by head.
A year's labour service, hired by the government instead.
Complexity is useful to somebody. That is why it grew.

## Zhang Liang · The old man on the bridge
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/zhang-liang/picking-up-the-shoe/
Source: Records of the Grand Historian, Hereditary House of the Marquis of Liu
Tags: Deep read, Zhang Liang, The test before the test

An old man puts a young man through a series of pointless humiliations. The question worth asking is what was being tested.

### Q: What actually happened?
On the bridge at Xiapi an old man dropped his shoe over the side and told the young Zhang Liang to fetch it. He wanted to hit him, held off because of the man's age, brought it up, then knelt and put it on his foot. The old man walked away laughing and turned back to say the boy can be taught, then set a meeting at dawn five days on. Twice the old man was there first and furious. The third time Zhang Liang went at midnight and waited, and was given a book.

### The parts · What is tested is whether you can take an unreasonable rule
The old man never explains anything. He sets the terms alone and raises them whenever he likes. What Zhang Liang passes is not a test of temper but a harder practical judgement: with the rules unexplained and plainly unfair, going along still pays more than fighting.
e.g. A newcomer meets a pile of customs nobody will justify. Working inside them for three months before objecting buys information that the person objecting in week one never gets.

### The parts · Restraint has a target
He was not a mild man. He had spent the family fortune to hire a strongman to hurl an iron club at the First Emperor's carriage. The same person would not endure an emperor and would endure an old man. Restraint is a verdict on the occasion, not a temperament.
e.g. You can absorb an unreasonable demand about scheduling. You cannot absorb one about the clause the whole contract rests on.

### The parts · The third attempt was the right one
Both earlier times he thought he had come early and was still late. After the second failure he neither gave up nor argued about the standard. He raised his own by a notch and went at midnight. Most people stop at the second failure to ask whether this means anything.
e.g. Twice you did exactly what they asked and it came back. Asking what they actually want is normal. Raising the bar and redoing it is rare, and it returns something else.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: you are being asked to accept a set of rules that nobody explains and that look unfair.
Ask first: what does fighting this instance actually get you, and what does going along with it get you? Answer both in specifics.
Where it goes wrong: turning restraint into a personality and yielding everywhere; or deciding after two failures that the thing was meaningless.

### Lines to keep
The boy can be taught.
He had already fetched the shoe, so he knelt and fitted it on.
Read this and you can be teacher to a king.

## Zhang Liang · Lend me the chopsticks
URL: https://ourword.ai/en/i/zhang-liang/borrowing-chopsticks/
Source: Records of the Grand Historian, Hereditary House of the Marquis of Liu
Tags: Deep read, Zhang Liang, Take the plan apart into conditions

A proposal sounds entirely right. How do you show that it is wrong? This is the method he ran at the table, in one sitting.

### Q: What actually happened?
Chu and Han were deadlocked and Liu Bang was shut up in Xingyang. The adviser Li Yiji proposed re-establishing the heirs of the six old states, who would be grateful, so that the empire would come over. Liu Bang liked it and ordered the seals cut. Zhang Liang came in, was told, and said let me borrow the chopsticks in front of you and lay this out for Your Majesty. Then eight items, each one a question about whether it could be done now. Liu Bang stopped eating and had the seals destroyed.

### The parts · Do not argue the conclusion, audit the premises
Li Yiji's conclusion, that enfeoffment buys allegiance, is nearly impossible to refute head on. Zhang Liang never tried. He broke it into the conditions it requires and asked of each whether it was available today. A plan that collapses at the condition layer stays collapsed.
e.g. We should build our own channel is unanswerable. Who runs it, where does the content come from, what catches the repeat buyer, what does month one cost? Three questions in, it shows itself.

### The parts · Put a physical object where the abstraction was
Borrowing the chopsticks turns a strategy into pieces on a table that people can point at. The value of that move is that it shifts the room from whether this is sound to how this would run. Almost every bad plan is sound. Very few of them run.
e.g. Lay the plan out against a calendar as weeks of work. The weeks it will not fit into are exactly where the hole is.

### The parts · If it is wrong, turn round now
The one who is really tested here is Liu Bang. He had already ordered the seals cut, heard eight objections, and destroyed them the same hour. Finding the flaw in a plan is the easy half. Withdrawing something you personally approved an hour ago is the other one.
e.g. The direction was announced publicly and two weeks later the flaw is visible. Pulling it costs a bad day. Not pulling it costs the quarter.

### Q: How do I use it today?
Where you are: a proposal sounds convincing and you cannot name what is wrong with it.
Ask first: what has to be true for this to work? List the conditions, then go down the list asking which of them you can meet this quarter.
Where it goes wrong: fighting at the level of the conclusion; or finding the flaw and then running the plan anyway to avoid looking changeable.

### Lines to keep
Let me borrow the chopsticks in front of you and lay it out.
Take that man's advice and Your Majesty's cause is finished.
He stopped eating, swore, and ordered the seals destroyed.
